items.label: May 1960
items.sum: Report of Belgrave's fourth successive R.W.A. 10 miles team championship at Hendon, with the club's history in the event, the Inter-Counties walk and the full Belgrave and team results.
items.s: BELS. WIN R.W.A. 'IO' AGAIN Report of Belgrave's fourth successive R.W.A. 10 miles team championship at Hendon, with the club's history in the event, the Inter-Counties walk and the full Belgrave and team results. Held on March 19th from the Met. Police Sports Ground at Hendon, Belgrave won this Championship for the fourth time in succession; and by tremendous margin. Thus was the Club's powerful strength at this distance once again emphasised beyond all doubt; and in starting and finishing three teams- the only club to do so-our strength in depth was also amply demonstrated. The race began at tremendous pace with A.A.A. Champion and R.W.A. Champion at the distance, Ken Matthews(R.Sutton Coldfield W.C.) in the lead and our Stan Vickers closely tucked in behind, with Eric Hall not far away. At a mile, however, Stan suffering from the aftermath of a severe cold was compelled to let Matthews go, and settled down to make sure of second place and lead a Belgrave team to victory once more. Eric was hardly ever out of third place and not very far back. George Williams persued a very even way in excellent style. Ray Middleton, our fourth man also once again demonstrated splendid style and ease of movement; and with a little more strength and experience- which could come very quickly- there is no doubt he will trouble them all. This scoring four of ours seemed to have the Championship well in hand but pressure came from a very gallant Metropolitan W. C. team, who lack effective numbers and yet with four walkers of very high merit, and little support, they manage to annex Championships and generally do well at all distances. So, once again for a long while they were our greatest rivals, but disqualification of one of their walkers put paid to their chances, and the minor placings were wide open and were eventually filled by Sheffield United H and Leicester W.C.. Our quartet pursued their way evenly to the finish to give us an excellent team win with four in eleven scoring positions; and we had very adequate support further back should it have been needed. Among our younger school John Knifton and Bob Barnes did splendidly and here could be a Vickers and Hall of a few years time. We are very grateful to all who did so well in the Club name. This was our sixth win in this Championship, the only other winners being Sheffield United H. who recorded eight successive wins from 1949-1956 inclusive. No other club has as yet been successful, and our initial win in the first Championship at this distance (at Sheffield in 1947) still stands as the best win yet. Our winning team thirteen years ago was 1. H.G. Churcher, 2. J.E. Rutland, 4. D. McMullen, and 6. J.G. Coleman giving us a score of 13 points which still requires a lot of beating ! The Inter-Counties Championship held in conjunction with the R.W.A. Championship this year as usual, saw a stirring struggle for the team championship and Middlesex prevailed by one point from Surrey, which team included three Belgrave men. Stan Vickers (Kent) took the second individual medal, and Eric Hall (Surrey) third. R.W.A. CHAMPIONSHIP RESULT Pos Name Club Time 1 K. Matthews R. Sutton-Coldfield W.C. 70:57 2 S. We were very pleased to see so many supporters out for the National 'Ten' at Colindale. Besides the usual faithful band we saw several of the Club Elders. Another who was introduced to the not so gentle art of walking was George Piddington accompanied by the new Club photographer(!)- a vast improvement on Eddie Lacey, and we hope she can also take photo's as well! items.h: BOY & YOUTHS: YOUNG ATHLETES WEEKEND COACHING COURSE.
items.sum: A.A. Harley's report on the weekend coaching course for 48 young club athletes at Belgrave Hall and Battersea Park, with a full-page group photograph; the photo caption says March 1960 while the report dates the course to 1st and 2nd April.
items.s: BOY & YOUTHS: YOUNG ATHLETES WEEKEND COACHING COURSE. A.A. Harley's report on the weekend coaching course for 48 young club athletes at Belgrave Hall and Battersea Park, with a full-page group photograph; the photo caption says March 1960 while the report dates the course to 1st and 2nd April. A most successful course was held on Saturday and Sunday the 1st and 2nd of April. No less than 48 young Club athletes enjoyed and revelled in the concentrated instruction which was dispensed with good humour and practical example. The Saturday morning session at Belgrave Hall was followed most attentively; and was brought to an end by the showing of an athletic film which was followed in turn by lunch. In the afternoon the scene transferred to Battersea Park Track and it was indeed a grand sight to see so many young athletes, many of such obvious promise, enjoying to the full the active programme which had been arranged Nearly all the lads showed pride in their Club, displaying Belgrave lettering on their training tops, and it certainly was a heartening and impressive sight to see so many worthy young athletes beginning to shape their athletic destinies towards the Championships of the future under the Club Hon. coaches. Some specialist instruction followed with individual tuition and this was again carried out on the Sunday morning. It is obvious that one week-end course of this nature cannot act as a magic wand and convert all who attended into super athletes overnight. It did however, point out a way and a method of attaining a high degree of physical fitness and athletic technique. Each individual must make up his own mind, do his own work, set his own targets, assess his own determination. Our Coaches will always be there to help; our general Club organisation there to provide unrivalled training, competitive and social amenities- so go to it! and let's see your name on our trophies in the future. A great debt of gratitude is due to our President, Charlie Jones, and Tom Carter for the tremendous work they did, in which they were assisted by other Club Honorary Coaches in Frank Simmons (who never spared himself for a second) Mike Lyons, Bill Couzens, and to the specialist demonstrators who gave of their time. It is certain that this Course did a great deal of good- it is equally certain that there must be others. In conclusion may I repeat my request of a few month's ago; that any senior members who feel they can assist the Youth of our Club by coaching, instructing or by just giving the other Coaches a hand, should let me know. It can be most rewarding work. items.label: May 1960
items.h: SPOTLIGHT: BISHOP HARRIERS (ALAN, LEN, ERIC) FOUNDED 1943
items.sum: Spotlight profile of the three Bishop brothers, Alan, Len and Eric, tracing their careers and service to Belgrave on track, country and road since 1943, with photographs of Len and Eric.
items.s: SPOTLIGHT: BISHOP HARRIERS (ALAN, LEN, ERIC) FOUNDED 1943 Spotlight profile of the three Bishop brothers, Alan, Len and Eric, tracing their careers and service to Belgrave on track, country and road since 1943, with photographs of Len and Eric. In June 1943 Syd Jarlett did a great service to the Club by signing on a sturdy Junior—H.A. Bishop. No doubt Alan's physique, which five year's later made him an obvious choice for the honour of helping the Olympic torch on its way to Wembley, recommended him to Syd, though I doubt if the latter realised he was signing on a potential 50-miler and, indirectly, a trio who would be a team in themselves. After a season of sprinting, Alan tried his hand at half-miling and by 1945 had reduced his time for this distance to a promising 2.4, whilst still running some useful sprints and quarters. At the end of the year two more Juniors joined the Club in rapid succession. The family likeness was such that they needed no introduction as Alan's brothers- Eric and Len. We soon learned that the resemblance was more than the superficial one of appearance. All three were endowed with the spirit that was to make them the backbone of our teams on track country and road for so many years. Theirs was—and is—the 'old fashioned' type of club loyalty found in the man who travels miles on a mid-week evening to run in a 'B' team 440 and arrives home having competed in the mile and the 4X110 relay. In his first summer season Eric was placed 3rd in the club Junior half. Len proved himself first over the country, finishing 4th in the Junior 'Savage Shield' race whilst still a youth and taking 5th place in the Surrey Youths Championship. Later that year 'big brother' Alan achieved his first prominent Cross-Country placing when finishing 32nd in the South of the Thames 'Junior'; Len being 9 places in front of him and earning a winning team medal. 1947-8 saw Alan and Len in the R.A.F., the former being able to manage some training, a 4.37 mile(still his fastest time) and a 3rd place in the Club 880 Championship. Len, out in Egypt, was less fortunate and was robbed of an opportunity of improving on his 21st place in the 1946 Southern Junior Cross Country Championships. Eric in the Navy, based at Chatham, was able to give Belgrave his usual support over a wide range of distances, achieving most success over the country with 7th place in the Surrey County, 27th in the Southern and 65th in the National Junior races. He still looks upon his Southern Junior placing as his best performance. For the next few years nearly every Belgrave Cross-Country team for everything from mob matches to National Championships contained at least two 'Bishops'. On the track the three-man-team continued to perform in sprints and middle-distance, Alan and Len achieving best half-mile times of 2.0.0. and 1.59.6. respectively, and Len a 4.21 mile. It was significant that Alan was running more 2 and 3 mile races and that Len was making his mark in Road Relays, repeatedly gaining a place in our 'Brighton' team and in 1955 achieving fastest time of the day on the last leg of the 'National Brighton' and bringing us home in fourth place. That year Alan took to the road in a big way. Few thought his large frame suited to the longer distances but he fooled them all by progressing from 15's via 20's and the Poly Marathon to 12th place in the London Brighton 52 miler in his first year of distance road running! Eric also started road work, contenting himself with 10-20 milers. Len followed suit two years later and since then at least one of the brothers has scored in nearly every one of our placed road teams. Last year the Belgrave team which was placed 2nd in our open 20 was exclusively 'Bishop Harriers', a great club family success. I must content myself with reporting only a few high-lights from these years. Alan has repeatedly beaten 2h 45m for the marathon and has won the Club '20' Championship. Eric, who must warrant the title of 'most injury prone Belgravian' has frequently persisted with training despite considerable pain. He has a Kent 20 mile Championship to his credit but was 'robbed' of a county vest on that occasion too because the selectors were too slow to realise that he had a county qualification. He earned a vest last year, however, and finished 37th in the Inter-County race. He has earned A.A.A. and R.R.C. First Class Certificates. Len has earned vests from both Surrey and Kent and among the many fine performances standing to his credit are:- 3rd Belgrave '20' (1h 52m, Club Championship Record), 5th Isle of Wight Marathon (twice), 6th Poly Marathon, 7th A.A.A. Marathon. He holds the Club marathon record at 2h 30m 39s. The manner in which the performances detailed above have been achieved impresses one even more than the successes themselves. The Bishops have never been angry young men and though always eager to gain a place in club teams, they have never been discouraged or disgruntled at being 'dropped' They have met success with modesty and defeat with equanimity. Their performances on track, country and road only represent a fraction of the Bishop's service to the club. Alan has acted as Track and Distance Running Captain and Eric as Hon. Auditor, Press Secretary and Treasurer's assistant, putting in an enormous amount of work buying prizes and medals and getting them engraved. For three years the 'Belgravian' was a Bishop Bros enterprise. They have had their full share of such difficulties as injury, studies and domestic upheavals but the Club has never been without their support. Brothers such as the Piries and the Kielys may have achieved greater athletic prominence, but no family was ever more devoted to the welfare of their club. Mrs. Bishop too was a source of great encouragement to her sons and was greatly missed when she died just over a year ago. There are some who consider the type of loyalty shown by the Bishops outdated in our modern, individualistic world of athletics, but I am sure that we should be a happier, better club if this spirit were more prevalent. It is unwise to dwell in the past, but who will deny that those times when the Bishops were Juniors and that benevolent dictator Ernie Duffett was 'Mr Running' as far as Belgrave was concerned, were Halcyon days? A little more of the Bishop attitude to our sport and the present era could be just as happy and successful. Few have put more into the Club than the Bishops and, by the same token, few have achieved more satisfaction from it. Let us wish them many, many more years of sevice and satisfaction. C.N.C. items.h: A VICTORY IS TOLLED BY THE BELS. ILFORD ROAD RELAY (10 X 3½ mls)- 19th MARCH
items.sum: Report of Belgrave's surprise win in the Ilford Road Relay (10 x 3½ miles) on 19 March 1960, by 1¼ minutes from T.V.H., with team times; John Davies in the text appears as J.Davis in the times.
items.s: A VICTORY IS TOLLED BY THE BELS. ILFORD ROAD RELAY (10 X 3½ mls)- 19th MARCH Report of Belgrave's surprise win in the Ilford Road Relay (10 x 3½ miles) on 19 March 1960, by 1¼ minutes from T.V.H., with team times; John Davies in the text appears as J.Davis in the times. If anyone at West Bromwich the previous week had forecast Belgrave to win this premier road relay doubts would have been cast on his sanity. Yet win they did ! Not by a small margin in a mediocre time, but by a full 1¼ mins and only 19 secs outside the course record. Before Pat Newell and Charlie Dabbs had been called on to run the last two legs Belgrave were already holding a 20 sec lead over their nearest rivals ! Conditions were cold with a strong breeze when the 38 teams started out on the first leg. Eric Gebbett and Jim Heathfield represented the "A" and "B" teams. Eric held a forward position thro'out and his tenth position was only 19 secs behind the second man. Charlie Walker, once again beginning to show his old form, swept into the lead; only to be passed by Haith of T.V.H. who had moved up from 13th. However, Chas hung on and although 9 secs down at the hand-over he was our second fastest runner of the day the fastest being the man to whom he handed over- Ranjit Bhatia. Ranjit had left his studies at Oxford to run in this event and was on his way back before the race had finished- but not before he had well and truly left his impression on the race itself. Running in his amazingly relaxed style he opened up a formidable lead of 33 secs, and in so doing became the second Belgravian to have ever beaten 18 mins on this course. Highgate, thro' George Brown, had taken over in 2nd place closely followed by V.P.H. and Blackheath. T.V.H. had dropped to 6th, Poly were 10th and Woodford (last year's record holders) 18th! John Davies, moved up from the 'B' team to take Clive Shippen's place, soon had Marlow of Highgate breathing down his neck and at halfway was forced to relinquish the lead. Acute stitch added to his troubles, and despite a strong finish his 19-05 had left us 33 secs in arrears with Mitcham right on our heels. John Moore had not been seen in action for some time and on the next leg it was soon quite clear he was not showing the form of last year. In the last half mile he had to give way to Mitcham which left us third with Highgate 56 secs ahead. However, the halfway stage had been reached and the big clubs still behind us were Blackheath (5th), T.V.H. (7th), Poly (8th) and Woodford (11th). Alan Black soon caught Gillet of Mitcham on stage 6 and running shoulder to shoulder they both passed the leader with a mile to go. In the last half mile the Mitcham lad made his effort and went ahead again by a margin of 14 secs. Brian Hallowell produced an encouraging performance in taking us back into the lead once more and David Jones ran consistently in improving the margin to 20 secs; leaving Newell and Dabbs to do no more than underline our superiority. By savouring the sweet smell of success once again the team's morale was boosted to great heights and all felt the corner had at last been turned. Our 'B' team finished 16th, being second to T.V.H. 'B' (11th). Radford, Thresher and Heck recorded times close up on those of the slower 'A' team men and eight of the 10 runners broke 20 mins. items.h: CLUB 5¾ MILES CHAMPIONSHIP: BHATIA & DABBS SMASH RECORD
items.sum: Report and full result of the Club 5¾ miles championship, won by Ranjit Bhatia in a record 27-56.6 with Charlie Dabbs also inside the old record; the result prints E. Penny's 21st-place time as 30.29, faster than the runners ahead of him.
items.s: CLUB 5¾ MILES CHAMPIONSHIP: BHATIA & DABBS SMASH RECORD Report and full result of the Club 5¾ miles championship, won by Ranjit Bhatia in a record 27-56.6 with Charlie Dabbs also inside the old record; the result prints E. Penny's 21st-place time as 30.29, faster than the runners ahead of him. In the fastest and probably the most exciting Championship for many years Ranjit Bhatia recorded a fantastic 27-56.6 to chop almost half a minute off Pat Newell's existing record. Second man, Charlie Dabbs, ran well enough to win on any other occasion and was 13 seconds inside the old mark. In ideal conditions a field of over 30 faced the starter for this most important race. For not only was there a Championship at stake, with Charlie Dabbs anxious to add this trophy to his 7 and 10 mile cross-country titles but the results would go a long way to deciding the National Relay team two weeks later. The first circuit of the common showed us that Dabbs, Walker and Bhatia were to have a ding-dong battle. Soon after came a bunch of runners in which Shipley (second claim member from Farnham A.C.) Gebbett, Robinson, Thresher and Hallowell were prominent. Going off down Copse Hill the three leaders were still locked together but the field behind had started to string out, although it was noticed that John Moore, Jim Radford and Archie Bedford who had started slowly were working their way through. Up Cambridge Road the pace at the front barely slackened although both Dabbs and Walker were showing signs of wear, but Ranjit Bhatia was running perfectly relaxed and seemed to be hardly breathing. It was therefore no surprise when Ranjit left the others and slowly opened up a gap which he increased steadily over the last lap of the Common and down Lauriston Road. The final time showed that no less than twenty five seconds had been sliced off the record set last year by Pat Newell and that Charlie Dabbs who had whipped away from the other Charlie over the last mile or so had also easily broken the former best time. Charlie Walker who was third put up a personal best. What a pity Pat Newell, who was working, could not have joined in the fray—who knows what might have happened! After the first three came Shipley in the good time of 29.14 and then followed our other stars in quick succession. Ranjit's win also gave him first place in the handicap with second place being taken by Ken Shackleford, a relatively new member, who could with regular training be a useful addition to our teams. Third was Ron Linstead who showed a welcome return to form by finishing sixth in the scratch race in 29.32 after a long absence from our events. If Ron would only stick to his training and race more often there are but few members who could hold him in races of this type and his value in our road relay teams would be inestimable. RESULT. items.label: May 1960
items.h: BELS. GAIN HONOURS IN NATIONAL RELAY
items.sum: Stage-by-stage report of the National London to Brighton road relay, in which Belgrave recovered from Eric Gebbett's fall on the first leg to finish 4th behind Derby, with Ranjit Bhatia's club-record 28.56 and the team's stage times.
items.s: BELS. GAIN HONOURS IN NATIONAL RELAY Stage-by-stage report of the National London to Brighton road relay, in which Belgrave recovered from Eric Gebbett's fall on the first leg to finish 4th behind Derby, with Ranjit Bhatia's club-record 28.56 and the team's stage times. In 1958 and 1959 we finished in eleventh position on both occasions and in the qualifying race for Southern Clubs in October 1959 we could do no better than sixth. This, combined with our poor season on the country produced little for the followers of Belgrave to enthuse about. Nevertheless those more intimately connected with our road running teams had noted that we had won the "Ilford" in fine style and that the performances in our road championships were well above the average. The wise men who write in the newspapers gave us not a mention and when Eric Gebbett awaited the ten o'clock strike of "Big Ben" there were few who would have offered odds on us being amongst the medal winners. Eric had been entrusted with the first leg after his grand showing in similar position in the Ilford, and the selectors felt that they would get the best out of him this way, and so it was proving, for at the top of Cedars Road with only half a mile to go Eric was with the leaders and running strongly. However, lady luck intervened at this point and with only 800 yards to go he was sent sprawling over the road and could do no more than limp gamely home in twelfth place 35 seconds behind the leading team. Was this a bad omen and were we once more to languish in the second half of the race? Brian Hallowell took over on the second stage and appeared to be running smoothly but there was that lack of fire which we have seen from him in earlier runs on the Brighton road and instead of making up some of the lost ground we were dropping even further behind. At Tooting Bec Brian seemed to be really struggling but a belated burst of energy enabled him to make a final determined effort accross Figges Marsh and although dropping one place the situation was not as bad as at first seemed likely. Nevertheless it was a disappointing performance from such a stylish athelete. Pat Newell soon set about the opposition on the third leg to Purley and that quick stride began to eat up the ground in no mean fashion. Manchester A.C., Bolton United and Woodford had to give ground and although Derby out in front and Coventry, through the good auspices of Basil Heatley, were going further away we were brought to within reach of our other dangerous rivals, Blackheath, Walton, T.V.H. and Birchfield. Charlie Walker has probably had a better season than for some years and was in a confident mood and we looked for more gains. Our greatest enigma however was not at his best and when Mick Firth of S.L.H. swept past him without even a challenge we wondered what would happen. Charlie seemed to pull himself together when his namesake from Sheffield caught up and for some time he dogged his rival's footsteps aided and abetted by our more noisy supporters. I dont think Charles had realised how long the hill is from Coulsdon to Hooley and it was a very tired Walker who handed over to John Moore at "The Joliffe" in tenth place, 2-34 behind Derby who were by now established at the front in what was to be a winning lead. John Moore had not been at his best this year probably due to the distractions of the fairer sex or other such interesting pastimes but he certainly made amends for his earlier lapses by taking us up to seventh through Redhill and over the Earlswood Switchback- a good performance which gave him the sixth fastest time of the day on his leg and kept us within striking distance of all but Derby. It was on this leg that tragedy struck T.V.H.; Cameron collapsing with an injury when in 2nd place a mile from the take over. Ken Miller, dogged by injury during the previous few months had come into the team only during the previous few days, when Malcolm Robinson was forced to withdraw. This was Ken's first Brighton but to see him run one would have thought he had been at it for years. The Sheffield man never knew what hit him and by the time we had reached "The Thorns" at Horley we were up to a more respectable sixth position. Ken's performance will I am sure earn him many places in our Brighton teams of the future. David Jones was our runner on Stage 7. Twelve months ago no one would have even considered David as a Brighton prospect but hard work and determined effort have produced a most stylish and relaxed performer who has shown most consistent running throughout the winter. This race was to prove that to David that all his worries about his capabilities are completely unfounded. He ran a beautifully judged race which kept us in sixth position still within easy reach of most of the teams ahead, although now 4½ minutes behind Derby. This performance should give David much confidence for the future and he will without doubt be entrusted with more important stages very soon. The most crucial part of the race was now to begin- those two long six mile legs over which we have fared so badly in the past few years. Charlie Dabbs who had run so well on this stage in October was again on this most important stretch and he set about his task in most determined fashion. Knowing that he was running well, he must have been badly jolted when Martin Hyman passed him at phenomenal speed on the way to a new stage record which took Portsmouth from tenth to fourth. Nevertheless Charles still produced the sixth best time of the day and gained one place in addition to knocking 13 seconds off his October Club Record. Ranjit Bhatia, unfortunately running in his last Brighton, as he returns home in the summer, had been given this other vital stage after his inspired record-breaking run in our own road championship two weeks earlier. I have rarely seen a Belgravian run with such fire and spirit and his time of 28.56 (the third best of the day) sliced half a minute off the Club record besides being faster than such seasoned and star runners as Gordon Pirie and Bruce Tulloh. Although gaining no places it brought us within touching distance of Blackheath who were then in fourth position. Jim Radford was next to run. Unfortunately, Jim in his enthusiasm set off far too fast and after a mile or so was definitely feeling the pinch. He continued to flog himself to the utmost and to some extent recovered over the last part of the stage but Blackheath and the clubs ahead had again widened the gap. I think Jim will have learnt his lesson for future races. Clive Shippen who had also been troubled with injury during the preceding weeks took the Dale Hill stage and with a magnificent effort and more than his share of encouragement from the excited supporters again caught Blackheath to do second fastest time on his leg and to give Alan Black a small lead for the run into Brighton. Alan using his head like a veteran gave us all some misgivings by staying with the Blackheath runner for most of the stage. But with about half a mile to go he left the opposition with grand style to romp home in 4th place, also doing second fastest time of the day. Considering our unfortunate start, we almost achieved the impossible by finishing so well up, but the bitter pill that must be swallowed is the fact that we were 6 mins-21 secs behind Derby, the winners- perhaps I am never satisfied!!! items.label: May 1960
items.h: MITCHAM A.C. BOYS OPEN ROAD RELAY
items.sum: Report of the Mitcham A.C. boys' open road relay, where Belgrave's A team, coached by Tom Carter, finished 3rd and the club was the only one to finish three teams, with results and individual times.
items.s: MITCHAM A.C. BOYS OPEN ROAD RELAY Report of the Mitcham A.C. boys' open road relay, where Belgrave's A team, coached by Tom Carter, finished 3rd and the club was the only one to finish three teams, with results and individual times. I was pleased that I decided to see this event for I witnessed, on a cold and breezy Sunday morning the results of the coaching of our past International Tom Carter, of the boys who will without a doubt form the nucleus of our Senior teams in a few year's time. Thirteen lads between the ages of fourteen and sixteen turned up anxious to run in any position and any team to which they were allocated-there was no arguing about who should go first or last- they were there to run and they left it to their coach to decide where their best efforts could be used- the discipline was of the highest order and the running was also first class standard. Hartup a new member took the first leg in the 'A' team and finished a creditable sixth in good company, about one minute down on the leaders. David Cocks one of our most consistent performers took the second leg and with one of the fastest times of the day (10.57) gained one place but brought us to only twenty one seconds behind Mitcham A.C. who had gone into the lead. Redwood took over and brought us to second with an excellent run of 10.45 (second fastest of the day). We were then only eleven seconds in arrears when Morrison took over for the last leg. Despite a gallant effort Morrison was forced back to third but in finishing only fourteen seconds behind Guildford & Godalming and six behind Mitcham we can consider our team to have performed admirably; especially when we were without Jack Hampshire. The 'B' team finished eighth and the 'C' team 13th-this lowly position was due to Dawson unfortunately going off course which added about five minutes to his time. We were the only club to start and finish three teams. RESULT: INDIVIDUAL TIMES:- Also running; in Wimbledon A.C. team, as a guest, Davidson 13.13. items.label: May 1960
items.sum: The cross-country secretary's review of the 1959-60 winter season, from poor championship showings to the late revival with the Ilford Relay win and 4th in the National Relay, and hopes for 1960/61.
items.s: X-CTY. HON. SEC'S. REVIEW: The cross-country secretary's review of the 1959-60 winter season, from poor championship showings to the late revival with the Ilford Relay win and 4th in the National Relay, and hopes for 1960/61. If I had written these notes four weeks earlier I would have declared that this winter season was the worst we had experienced for thirty years, but in the latter weeks we have won the Ilford Relay in near record time, our road championship course record has been shattered by two men, and we have secured fourth place in the National Relay in the face of very heavy opposition and certainly to the surprise of the majority of the athletic world. I realise that fourth is still a long way from a victory in this "blue riband" event but when it is considered that we were eleventh in both 1958 and 1959 the improvement is so pronounced as to make even me exuberant for our future. We started the season way back in September with a moderate performance in the Surrey Road Relay which was followed by a much improved effort in the Polytechnic Relay at Chiswick in which we took fourth place against strong opposition. Our next major competition was the Brighton Relay for Southern Clubs on October 10th in which we finished sixth to qualify narrowly for the National race in April 1960. The following weeks were devoted to cross country training and inter-club competition and on November 7th we endeavoured to field five teams in the cross country relay at Reigate Priory. As with most of our away fixtures the attendance was poor and we could muster only sufficient runners for two teams which finished tenth and thirty-fourth. On November 14th we started five teams in the South of Thames Junior race at Caterham of which four closed in taking 5th, 30th, 35th, and 40th positions. On November 28th in the L.C.C. Championship we kept our third position of 1958 despite an improved score. If we could have scored six instead of four we would have taken first place. Our first club championships, the "Seven", was a triumph for Charlie Dabbs enjoying his first year as a senior. The County Championships were held on January 2nd and as always our forces were split between Surrey and Middlesex; although our main strength lies in the former. Sixth place in the team race must however be considered as a very poor performance for a club of our size and standing. Charlie Dabbs again ran well and was included in Surrey's entries for the Inter Counties—an injury however prevented him from running. On January 23rd we held our second Club Championship, the "Ten", and Charlie Dabbs again proved successful in a good time. This same young man showed that he was at the top of his form by securing fifth place in the South of Thames Senior at West Wickham on January 30th and assisted in the team taking a similar position. We narrowly missed the Colman Cup for the lowest score for all twelve runners. From this race emerged a new name which will I am sure appear in all our teams for some time. David Jones, who had finished third in our championship the previous week to surprise us all, again ran well. The next major event was the Southern at Parliament Hill but our running was nothing to raise any enthusiasm over although we did secure the 'twelve' cup for Surrey clubs. A few weeks later we travelled to West Bromwich for the National, without such stars as Newell (unfit) Bhatia and Moore; both of whom are ineligible for birth reasons. The least we say about our 21st position the better. And so to the road relay season once more and a complete transformation in the outlook of our runners. The half hearted attitude toward cross country took on a new look and in the Ilford we proved victorious in excellent time. This win provided the fillup needed after a dismal winter and led to our fourth position in the National Relay. It is difficult to reconcile such a performance with our showing at West Bromwich but at least it proves we have the talent. Unfortunately we lose Ranjit Bhatia in a few months time, when he returns home to India. Our best wishes go with him-he has proved a most valuable asset and is on the threshold of becoming an international class athlete-we shall miss him greatly. We have however the prospect of the return of Jack Brown and the further improvement of many of our runners such as David Jones, Malcolm Robinson, Clive Shippen and Charlie Dabbs, plus juniors Alan Black and Ken Miller who move up to the senior ranks to inspire our hopes for 1960/61. I view the next few years with great anticipation and see signs of a great revival in all spheres of our running activities. I hope I will not be disappointed. W.E.L. items.label: September 1960
items.sum: Editorial saluting Stan Vickers' Olympic 20 km walk bronze in Rome, Eric Hall's tenth place, Ranjit Bhatia's selection for India, and former member Ted Cronk's kayak appearance.
items.s: EDITORIAL Editorial saluting Stan Vickers' Olympic 20 km walk bronze in Rome, Eric Hall's tenth place, Ranjit Bhatia's selection for India, and former member Ted Cronk's kayak appearance. Dear Fellow Members, Salute STANLEY F. VICKERS! Britain's most reliable athletics competitor brings home to his Club and Country an Olympic bronze medal to rest alongside the European Gold Medal he already holds. His heroic effort in the heat and dust of the Roman roads has earned him the enthusiastic admiration of all British Athletics supporters. Compared with the results of the Great Britain team as a whole, his achievement must surely rank alongside his European Games triumph. At the time of Stan's race Britain's "stamina" athletes had produced a string of most uncharacteristic performances; performances which appeared to have been affected by some outside factor rather than loss of form----hardly the ideal circumstances in which to toe the line. What ease of mind he had could not have been improved when after 10 Kilos he passed team-mate Matthews, who had dropped back from a 19secs lead to fifth place in a state of exhaustion, and was indeed taken to hospital shortly afterwards. To hold world record holder GOLUBNICHIY to a 49.2sec margin in these circumstances is a tribute to Stan's tremendous fighting ability. Our congratulations also go out to Eric Hall whose tenth place in the same event was an excellent performance. The six dividing places were filled by men of high renown and Eric can feel well pleased with his effort. Our third member to compete at the Olympics was Ranjit Bhatia, who represented India in the 5,000 and 10,000metres events. The last Belgravian to run in either of these races was Bill Lucas at the 1948 Olympiad in LONDON. At the time of writing we have no details of Ranjit's performances but we are sure he acquitted himself well. The great honour bestowed on him by his country is a fitting reward to the tremendous improvement and great efforts he has made this year. Belgrave are proud of their sporting ambassadors. Three Belgravians at the Olympics is a Club record, but many eyes were also on a fourth competitor whose ties with Belgrave were parted but a few years ago----TED CRONK. Ted was a promising half-miler who, as a result of two motor-cycle accidents, was forced to give up athletics. Determined to continue with some form of physical exercise he took to Kayakking and after only 2yrs was selected to represent his country in the Kayak relay event. No medals were earned, but Belgrave's sporting ties had been widened still further. Stanley F. Vickers STANLEY F. VICKERS STANLEY F. items.s: HON. SEC'S NOTES The Hon. Secretary's notes promoting the A.L.A.C. floodlit meeting at the White City on 28 September, the club's Weekly Football Scheme and the A.A.A. Christmas draw. The Association of London Athletic Clubs (of which we are members, and of which our Hon. Secretary is Chairman and Hon. Treasurer) holds its annual Floodlit Meeting at the White City Stadium on Sept 28th, at 6.30pm, with a 5 miles Walk preceding the main meeting at 5.45pm. The Meeting which is as usual sponsored by "THE EVENING NEWS" promises a view of the Olympic stars of many lands, and also includes a match London v Pan-American Cities in which athletes from the West Indies and others will show their paces. This Meeting promises to live up to the very high standards of the past (remember four men inside 4mins in the 1957 mile?, remember Chataway v Kuts?, remember Herb Elliotts mile in 3mins 55.4secs?) and every Club member should make up his mind to be there and take his friends. For the last ten years we have shared in the proceeds of this meeting---so do yourself a good turn in seeing one of the finest Meetings of the year and help your Club at the same time. Members wishing to reserve seats should make early application with cheque or cash to A.A.S.A., P.O.Box No.1, Hoddesdon Herts, stating "Belgrave Harriers" and deducting 10% discount. A stamped addressed envelope should also be enclosed. Reserved seats are priced at 20/-, 15/-, 10/-, 7/6, 6/-, 5/-, 4/-, and there is unreserved accommodation on the night at 3/-, at the turnstiles. We would also commend our Weekly Football Scheme to those of our members who have not as yet participated in this feature of Club life which has been running for over twenty years. Generous prizes are offered Cont'd. on p.5. Cont'd. from p.3 (and won!) and the proceeds accrueing to the Club assist in the maintenance (and one day, further extension) of our Headquarters, the wealth of competition we are able to provide for our members in every branch of Athletics, and for the encouragement and efficient coaching of the younger element within the Club. Individuals wishing to take up tickets for the season, or agents (ten or more tickets) should get in touch with L.J. Cohen, 54, Lower Kenwood Ave, Enfield, Middx for further details. Your committee has decided to support the A.A.A.'s Xmas Draw, which not only offers bumper prizes (1st prize £1,000) but allows Clubs to retain 25% of the revenue. You will shortly receive further details and we appeal for your staunch support. A.A.H. Chataway Chataway Kuts Kuts Herb Elliott Herb Elliott L.J. Cohen L.J. Cohen A.A.H. A.A.H. A.L.A.C. items.label: September 1960
items.sum: Obituary of walker Len Fletcher, who died aged 54 after 37 years with Belgrave, winning ten Surrey County titles and many club championships.
items.s: A. L. FLETCHER Obituary of walker Len Fletcher, who died aged 54 after 37 years with Belgrave, winning ten Surrey County titles and many club championships. Regretfully we have to record the death of Len Fletcher, after a long illness, at the early age of 54 years. Our sincere condolences are extended to Mrs. Fletcher, and to brother Jack on their great loss—a loss we share. Len joined Belgrave in 1923 at the age of 18 and had a season over the country, but the following year took to walking when he won a novices mile race, promoted by the Club, in 8min 3.4secs. He was nursed along carefully and in 1926 was third in the Surrey County 2 miles Championship and won the Club Championship at the same distance. In 1927 he began to show his maturing strength and in the National Junior 10 miles Championship at Sheffield, over a hilly course, he was narrowly beaten into second place by our Tommy Green. In this year he again won the Club '2', and was placed second to Alf Pope in the AAA Championship. From this time onwards Len had few superiors over his favourite distances of 7 and 10 miles on the road. In 1930/1/2 he had many successes at these distances beating well known walkers of the day in C.W. Hyde, A.H.G. Pope and A.E. Plumb most convincingly, and leading on teams to victories galore. In 1932 he retired from active competition but reappeared in 1936 to win Club and Surrey County titles at 10 miles. During the war Len served with the RAF and saw service abroad, and on his return was again out on the road until 1948. He then served as a Judge, and as Coach, and gave excellent services in these capacities. In all Len won ten Surrey County titles, and won Belgrave Championships at 7 miles (Horwood Cup), 10 miles (four times), 20 miles (once) and 2 miles (six times) and an Inter Counties Track Race at 3 miles, and numerous other events. Len was a tall athlete with long stride and excellent style, but lacked that little extra weight which would have helped him considerably to carry the strain of a succession of races. By nature he was extremely conscientious, a Belgrave man through and through; at times a little grave in manner; and a great lover of classical and operatic music, possessing great talent as a pianist. He served both as Track and Road Captain and inspired many team successes. Len became a first class walker at the time Belgrave was establishing its right to be regarded as one of the finest athletic clubs in the country; and he did much to help the Club both by his ability and sportsmanlike bearing to its present proud position. We mourn his passing and think gratefully of those 37 years in association with us. A.A.H. Len Fletcher Len Fletcher A. L. items.sum: Reports of two early-season track matches: the Carshalton Coronation Trophy on Easter Monday 18 April, where Belgrave were last, and a winning home match at Battersea on 23 April.
items.s: CARSHALTON TROPHIES Reports of two early-season track matches: the Carshalton Coronation Trophy on Easter Monday 18 April, where Belgrave were last, and a winning home match at Battersea on 23 April. EASTER MONDAY-APRIL 18th Our opening fixture of the season could attract no more than a handful of Belgravians, with the result that we were a well-deserved last in the premier match---the "Coronation Trophy". Our eclipse was made to look all the more decisive by the way our opponents enthusiastically supported the meeting. If invited next year we might well find ourselves relegated to the "Grove Trophy" match. Peter Eldridge ran well in the 200 metres, finishing a very close second to A. Breacker (Mitcham) in 22.2 secs. In the 3,000 metres team event our only starter was David Jones who had travelled all the way from Chichester. He was well up with the leaders until 2 laps to go when he faded rather badly, finishing in an equivalent 2 mile time of 9-34.0. Dave Ansell, still not completely free from injury, finished third in the long jump with a plus 21 feet leap. Alan Black and Clive Shippen ran in the 3,000 metres steeplechase, but with 3 laps to go Alan dropped out when in 2nd place, leaving Clive to finish third in 9-57.0. TROPHY RESULT: BATTERSEA-APRIL 23rd A much improved turn-out for this our first home match resulted in our scoring a convincing victory. Dave Carter scored a sprint double (10.5 and 23.2), his runners-up being S. Deane and G. Leroy respectively. A blanket finish in the 880 yds placed Alan Black 3rd (2-0.6) and Ken Venton 4th (2-0.9). Our long-jump team Jim Mc Grath and Dave Ansell scooped the long jump with 21'1" and 20'8", whilst second-claim member Hollingsworth won the discus with 151'-0½" ( what a great prospect this fellow is!) items.h: SWARD TROPHY: BELGRAVE WIN SOUTHERN 4X 110 TITLE
items.sum: Report of the Sward Trophy meeting, where Belgrave's sprint relay team were awarded the Southern Counties 4x110 yards title after Woodford's disqualification and the club finished 7th of 12 in the trophy, with E.D. Lacey's photograph of the relay winners.
items.s: SWARD TROPHY: BELGRAVE WIN SOUTHERN 4X 110 TITLE Report of the Sward Trophy meeting, where Belgrave's sprint relay team were awarded the Southern Counties 4x110 yards title after Woodford's disqualification and the club finished 7th of 12 in the trophy, with E.D. Lacey's photograph of the relay winners. From a Belgrave point of view, the star performers of the day were undoubtedly our sprint relay team. Although Woodford Green A.C. beat them to the tape in the final of the Southern Counties 4X 110 relay, the Bels were the adjudged winners; Woodford being disqualified thro' a faulty take-over involving ex Belgravian C.R. Jones-- a fine "gesture" by Charlie!! However, in an Invitation 4X 110 event held later in the meeting the Bels endorsed their previous win by showing both Blackheath and Woodford the way home. Our only winner in the trophy events was Norman Caves, who took the HSJ with a distance of 45'-0". But there was a definite all-round improvement on last year's effort, for every one of our team was placed in the first six in his event; we thus gained 21 points against last year's total of nine. High hurdler, R. Tolson, battled with his opponents against a near gale-force wind to gain fifth place in both the high and low hurdle events, recording 16.2 and 27.0 respectively. His performance in the "highs" was particularly noteworthy, for the first three were P.B. Hildreth (15.3), J. Taitt (15.3) and V.C. Matthews (15.8). Pat Fox ran in the 440yds hurdles, qualified for the final, and finished sixth in 61.0secs. Tolson and Fox were not the only Belgravians to battle over the hurdles. Clive Shippen, running in his usual gritty fashion, face contorted, head rolling-- was still with the tail-enders after 2 laps of fast pace setting by Woodford's D.G. Chapman. But, hurdling well and gaining ground at each "splash" Clive gradually pegged back the positions to finish a very tired third in a personal best of 9-28.0. Meanwhile, Jim McGrath was doing his usual stirling work in the field finishing fifth in the pole vault with 11'-6" and sixth in the long jump with 22'-2¼"---only 5¼" short of third place! Bill Couzens achieved a personal best performance in the javelin event recording 161'-9" to finish sixth and Jock Whyte's 144'-4" hammer throw was good enough to place him 5th. There is no doubt that all of our representatives performed well, but the field events section is pretty thin on the ground, and could well do with more recruits. On the other hand our runners continue to improve, for in the 2 miles Invitation team race Newell (9-18.4), Dabbs (9-23.8) and Robinson (9-30.2) were only 5 points behind the winners, Polytechnic. This trio could well become an outstanding track team. items.sum: Round-up of Belgrave athletes in the 1960 county championships (Surrey, Bedfordshire, Yorks, Oxfordshire, Middlesex), including titles for Percy Porter, George Williams, Randy Glen, Peter Eldridge, Trevor Tolson and Ranjit Bhatia; the Middlesex note says '1961' though the season is 1960.
items.s: AROUND THE COUNTIES Round-up of Belgrave athletes in the 1960 county championships (Surrey, Bedfordshire, Yorks, Oxfordshire, Middlesex), including titles for Percy Porter, George Williams, Randy Glen, Peter Eldridge, Trevor Tolson and Ranjit Bhatia; the Middlesex note says '1961' though the season is 1960. SURREY Moving from Essex to Surrey has had little effect on the performances of hammer-thrower Percy Porter. Our former Essex champion still proved too strong for the opposition and won the Surrey title with a throw of 154'-1". George Williams had already notched up our first title the previous evening, outclassing the opposition to win in 14-51.2. The field was somewhat depleted here owing to the abstention of several walkers who did not approve of the walk being moved from the main day's events. One thing is certain, this year's championships could hardly be called a success from the programming angle. Many ardent supporters of this annual event were most disappointed. An urgent reappraisal of the programme is called for. Friday evening's mile heats produced the usual fast times. Of our three entrants, Mal Robinson finished a close second to P. Milner (Walton) in 4-17.2; Alan Black was 5th in the same heat with 4-23.6 and Eric Penny, in a later heat, 8th in 4-38.5. Saturday's final saw Mal an unwilling leader on the first lap, and when a group of four moved past in an attempt to break away he was unable to respond. A gap was formed, and although he tried desperately to close it, he had to be content with 5th place in 4-17.8. All the Belgravians in the 880 yds failed to reach the final. The unlucky trio were Peter Pepe 2:0.2, Pete Mitchell 2:2.1 and Randy Glen 2:3.1. In no way deterred by the reputations enjoyed by his opponents, Charlie Dabbs clung to the redoubtable Pirie and title-holder Ernie Earl sufficiently well to gain a notable 3rd place in the 3 miles, clocking 14:21.8---a personal best. Only other entrant was Clive Shippen who finished 1[illegible]th with 14-48.0. The Championship events were completed at Battersea Park on July 23rd. Randy Glen became our 3rd title-holder by winning the 440 yds hurdles in 57.6, and was ably backed up by Peter Pepe who was only inches short of second place with 58.6. Alan Black produced a personal best time of 9-33.6 in the 3,000 metres steeplechase, finishing 4th. BEDFORDSHIRE The ever improving Peter Eldridge was the outstanding performer of the day. In a full afternoon's running he successfully defended all three sprint titles. This year's effort read, 100 yds---10.2, 220yds---22.2, 440yds---49.4---great running, from a fine athlete. Norman Caves, HSJ title holder, did not compete this year as he wishes to exercise a Surrey residential qualification in 1961. YORKS Trevor Tolson, who is hurdling extremely well these days, turned out to be a surprise winner of the 120 yds hurdles title in a time of 15.7secs. OXFORDSHIRE Ranjit Bhatia, Oxford Blue and Club mile record-holder, scored a comfortable victory here in the mile event, finishing well clear of his opponents in 4-16.4. MIDDLESEX The only Belgrave medal-winner in this year's championships was Ted Smith whose 15:28.6 placed him 3rd in the two mile walk. Dave Carter performed well to finish 4th in the 220yds final, and Terry Newell and Dave Mitchell both qualified for the final of the 880yds; but nothing of note was produced. 1961 showed us a marked absence of "Claret and Gold". EDS: No performances are available of Club athletes who competed in the Kent, Sussex, Hampshire and Devonshire Championships, but who do you think we are?........REUTER?!! items.s: KINNAIRD TROPHY: CHISWICK- JUNE 11th Report of the Kinnaird Trophy meeting at Chiswick on 11 June 1960, where Gerry LeRoy won the 440 yards in 48.5 and Belgrave finished 5th of nine teams, with a photograph of LeRoy's win. In his first serious "quarter" of the season Gerry LeRoy ran out a close winner of the Kinnaird Trophy 440 yards. His time of 48.5 was just one tenth better than Polytechnic's Mike Potter, with Internationals Metcalf and Salisbury a further 0.4 and 0.9 secs in arrears. Gerry ran a confident race. Drawn in the fifth lane, he ran within himself for the first furlong and stormed ahead over the last 100yds. Another intelligent run involving a last home sprint was by Ranjit Bhatia in the three miles. Nearly all the distance was led by Browning (Birchfield) but on the penultimate lap Thames Valley's Scottish International and Oxford colleague of Ranjit, Alistair Wood, sprinted ahead to cover the last 660 yards in 95 secs. This was too fast for Ranjit but he clung tenaciously to Turner (Poly) who had attempted to go with Wood, and sprinted past him up the final straight for second place, and a 14:20 clocking. Close behind in fifth place was Charlie Dabbs with a personal best of 14:21.2. He had also found the final sprint too speedy. The "Hurdlers Strike" obviously favoured Trevor Tolson and Alan Spicer (Hildreth and Matthews withdrew claiming that the fierce 30 mph wind was to great to run into). In the straight final they finished 4th and 5th respectively, but their times of 16.8 and 17.0secs are an indication of the wind's hindrance. In the final stages of the mile it looked very much as though Belgrave were, for the first time, going to finish both their runners in the first six; but although Mal Robinson clung to his fifth spot and a personal best of 4:15.2, John Davies had to give ground and with 4:17.1 finished seventh. The winner was Wiggs (TVH) in 4:08.8. Woodford Green's international David Jones running into the wind was first past the post in both sprints with 10.1 and 22.3. Peter Eldridge looked none to happy and was fifth in the longer race with 23.1. Neither of our two half-milers reached the 880yds final. In his heat Terry Newell showed little use of tactics and with 1:58.4 was sixth. However, it should be noted that this is his first season in trophy competition. Dave Mitchell was another to have an off day recording a mediocre 2:1.7. Jim McGrath reached the long jump final and with a leap of 22'3¾" finished sixth. items.s: MATCH v LT (CRS) SA v MPAA v 1st BN WELSH GDS: BATTERSEA- 1st JUNE Report of a four-way track match at Battersea on 1 June 1960, in which Belgrave finished second to the Metropolitan Police. Despite winning both 440yds events, the 100yds 'A', the mile and placing second in most other events we still only managed to finish second to the Met. Police. The sprints up to the quarter were run in strings A and B. Gerry LeRoy opened with a win in the "A" 100 in 10secs and later added the 440, when he convincingly defeated Brian Morris (running for his second claim club) in 49.3. Terry Newell with a time of 51.7secs won the 'B' event. Alan Black was an easy winner of the mile. John Davies in an attempt to push Alan through to a fast time ran to the ¾ mile mark with 64, 2:12, 3:18, but although Alan had little left for a fast last lap, he broke the tape a clear winner in 4:27.8. Second was Pryor (Met.Police) a junior who had previously beaten home John Davies (1:58.0) and Mal Robinson (1:59.0) with a 1:56.2 half-mile. Our field events section for the day was Mike Smithers and Roy Shuter who both took second place in their events. Mike leapt 19'9" and Roy heaved the shot 40'-2". RESULT: Pos Team Points 1 Met. items.h: MATCH v SLH v WIMBLEDON AC v ST. MARY'S COLLEGE: MONDAY 13th JUNE- TOOTING
items.sum: Report of an evening match at Tooting on 13 June 1960 hosted by South London Harriers, in which Belgrave won both the senior and youth matches.
items.s: MATCH v SLH v WIMBLEDON AC v ST. MARY'S COLLEGE: MONDAY 13th JUNE- TOOTING Report of an evening match at Tooting on 13 June 1960 hosted by South London Harriers, in which Belgrave won both the senior and youth matches. In a well organised and keenly contested evening's programme, Belgrave ran out fine winners of both Senior and Youth matches. Our hosts, South London Harriers, did a great job in running off a mammoth total of 26 events, but only managed to finish third in each match themselves. However, the Bels were out in force, and ace sprinter Gerry LeRoy scored a sprint double by winning the 'A' string races in 10.8 and 23.5 against a strong wind. In a tactical half-mile, Robinson and Newell were placed second and third in 1:59.9 and 2:00.2 respectively, and in a similarly run 1500 metres Shipley (second claim) was second in 4:6.2. South London had five of the first six in the 3,000 metres event, but with only two to score Davies (8:54.4) and Black (9:11.6) were able to total 10 pts against the 15 of SLH, and thus kept our noses well to the front. Cornelius (24.3) and Mitchell (52.7) each won their events, as did Hollingsworth (second claim) in both the shot and discus-40'9" and 151'1½". After a winning leap of 19'6½" in the long jump Norman Caves also came near to a double, clearing 5'5" for second place in the high jump. Details of the Youth's match can be found with the rest of their news on Page 9. items.sum: Boys' and youths' section notes on a record season, with the final standings of the youths' and boys' medal competitions (David Cocks and Derek Wade tied for the youths, Roger Hudson won the boys) and notable performances including Jackie Hampshire's and David Cocks' club youth records.
items.s: BOYS AND YOUTHS Boys' and youths' section notes on a record season, with the final standings of the youths' and boys' medal competitions (David Cocks and Derek Wade tied for the youths, Roger Hudson won the boys) and notable performances including Jackie Hampshire's and David Cocks' club youth records. The past season has undoubtedly been the most successful in the Club's history. The enthusiastic support our fixtures received from the boys and youths is in itself a mark of success, and our opponents must have been psychologically defeated on many occasions at the very sight of these swarms of eager claret and gold-clad Belgravians. It is even rumoured in certain quarters that they never remove their Club vests! As Tom Carter so rightly says "One could write many pages on the talent and achievments of the various members who are at present setting the pace. But who can tell at this stage who the champions of the future will be? Those at the back now can so easily be those at the front by the time Senior status is reached". We heartily endorse Tom's remarks, for there are many International stars of today who were no better than average when Youths, and some indeed who had not entered athletics at this age. Patience is a necessary virtue of the successful athlete. Regular and conscientious training will eventually produce the desired results, but no one can yet say how long it will take—so keep at it, be patient, for who knows? You may be a star in the making. The Medal Competitions have drawn to a close once more, and what an exciting finish there was to both sections. David Cocks and Derek Wade tied for first place in the Youth's competition, and Roger Hudson took the Boys competition by only one point from Peter Hawkins. A record number of competitors took part, but many were unable to compete in the required minimum of 5 events, and thus did not qualify for the final count. The scoring system is as follows. There are a total of eight events, of which, the best five are recorded for each athlete. Twenty points are awarded for first place, nineteen for second, eighteen for third, and so on; but these positions are only determined when the final qualifiers are known at the end of the competition. YOUTHS RESULT Also competed:- Morrison, Hampshire, Yeo, Startup, Rendle, Finn, Satchell, Sturgess, Crosbie, Pearce, Williams, Dawson. BOYS RESULT Many notable performances have been produced during the season. Bespectacled miler Jackie Hampshire achieved an outstanding performance in the Intermediate mile final of the All-England Schools Championships by finishing sixth in a new Club Youths record of 4:30.4. Another to break a Club record at the same meeting was David Cocks, whose 2:0.8 clocking in the Intermediate 880 final was 0.2 secs inside Dave Mitchell's four year old mark, but was still not good enough to place him in the result! In a late season handicap race, off scratch, David showed his great potential by recording 1:59.0. Fifteen year old Dave Pottinger's long jump mark of 20'2½" is worthy of special mention, as are the all-round performances of Derek Wade—and so the list goes on! items.sum: Report and full results of the 1960 Belgrave club track and field championships at Tooting Bec on 18 June, with Gerry LeRoy and Jim McGrath triple champions and Malcolm Robinson's championship-record mile; the text puts Dabbs fourth, Hampshire's mile at 4:46.0 and Redwood and Wade both at 2:7.8, while the results show 5th, 4:46.4, 2:7.3 and 2:7.5.
items.s: THE 1960 CHAMPIONSHIPS: TOOTING BEC TRACK-JUNE 18th Report and full results of the 1960 Belgrave club track and field championships at Tooting Bec on 18 June, with Gerry LeRoy and Jim McGrath triple champions and Malcolm Robinson's championship-record mile; the text puts Dabbs fourth, Hampshire's mile at 4:46.0 and Redwood and Wade both at 2:7.8, while the results show 5th, 4:46.4, 2:7.3 and 2:7.5. In a long-lasting battle for supremacy as Belgrave's best sprint man, Gerry LeRoy hoisted his penant high with a triple victory over close rival Peter Eldridge. But, oh! how close it was! At no time in this keenly contested duel did more than a yard separate the combatants; but although Peter was adjudged an unlucky loser of the short sprint, Gerry's performances in the 220 and 440 events were sufficient to rank him best on the day. Their next meeting will be followed with great interest. The Tooting track always seems to provide a pleasant atmosphere and setting for a Championship meeting, and it was no less so on this occasion. The day was blessed with fine weather, and the traditionally high standard of marking set by 'Harry', the late groundsman, had obviously had been maintained by his successors. Everything seemed to be conducive to fast times; although it was felt in certain quarters that the track was too soft underfoot for this to be so. Whichever school of thought was right, the long-awaited clash between Ranjit Bhatia and Malcolm Robinson in the mile brought about a new Championship Record! Mal's winning time of 4:15.8 bettered Jack Brown's nine year old mark by 2.2secs, and with six men inside 4.20 this was surely the fastest ever Club mile. Ranjit had previously run in the 880, but it is mean conjecture to muse on how Mal's sprint kick would have fared had this not been so, or even perhaps if the pace had been faster, for Mal and his 59.4 last lap appeared capable of holding off anything this particular day. Pat Newell, who has been concentrating more on the shorter middle-distance events this season, ran well in gaining 3rd place, but the surprise of the race was the remarkable 4:19.0 of Charlie Dabbs who finished fourth. His was a perfect example of how sheer strength in itself produces speed. Running alongside the lithe Bhatia, a smooth Newell, a relaxed Davies and the nimble high-stepping Robinson, Charlie looked much like a fighting carthorse- but never before has a carthorse been seen to travel at such speed! Chas. is well aware of his unusual gait, but realises that power and strength are the main prerequisites of the successful runner, and he is rapidly proceeding to prove this. Gerry LeRoy was not the only triple champion of the day. Jim McGrath, that stalwart athlete who is the backbone of our field events section, was in fine "decathlon" form, winning the long jump, high jump and discus, and finishing third in the javelin: a fine afternoon's effort. His victory in the long jump was no surprise, for with the absence of his "twin", Dave Ansell, Jim's only serious rival was Norman Caves; although young Derek Wade gave them both a scare by recording six valid jumps between 18'3½" and 18'10". Jim cleared 5'7" first time in the high jump to place Norman second yet again. However, Norman did get a 1960 Club Championship by winning his favourite event, the triple jump; Brian Jones (out of serious training) and George Edwards (who hardly, if ever, trains!! ) had little to offer against his 43'6½". With half a lap to go in the 880yds, defending champion John Davies looked an odds-on winner, but in the final straight first Terry Newell and then Dave Mitchell sprinted past, leaving a surprised John to finish fourth just behind Bhatia who had made up a tremendous amount of ground in the last 220yds. With large numbers of our youngsters competing in qualifying heats of their Schools' Area Championships during the morning, the prospect of a good afternoon's Junior sport was not promising. But this was without reckoning on the enthusiasm of our younger athletes, many of whom made the double journey. Derek Wade, after running a personal best 880yds in his schools race, ran even faster in the afternoon to finish inches behind Ken Redwood, both recording new personal bests of 2:7.8. As if this wasn't enough, he then produced the excellent sequence of jumps previously mentioned to gain third place in the Senior long jump and then rounded off the afternoon by winning the Junior high jump with 5'3". Another to make the double journey was Jack Hampshire also still a Youth, who strolled casually round the track to take the Junior mile title in 4:46.0. As expected, the short sprint went to John Peters, but it was only by a short head, for both he and David Crosby were credited with the same time of 11.1secs. The longer sprint produced a blanket finish and a real head-ache for the judges, before they eventually awarded the title to Alan Mead from Mikes Sturgess and Smithers; all three being timed at 24.8 secs. Young Sturgess was also involved in a close finish in the Boys 100yds, but this time was given the verdict over D. Wiseman. The meeting was undoubtedly a success and full marks should go to Dave Shepherd, Bob Taylor and Co. for their efforts. The Junior events were dominated by Youths and Boys, and it was quite apparent that in a few seasons time nearly all of our seniors will be encountering pretty hot and enthusiastic opposition from these youngsters. Our 75th Anniversary Meeting could well be the hottest Championships in our history. items.label: September 1960
items.h: WALKING NEWS: A.A.A. 7 MILES CHAMPIONSHIP-HURLINGHAM APRIL 16TH
items.sum: Introduction to the walking news celebrating the walkers' second triple of National 10, National 20 and R.W.A. 50 km titles in four years, followed by Eric Hall's fifth place in the A.A.A. 7 miles walk at Hurlingham on 16 April 1960.
items.s: WALKING NEWS: A.A.A. 7 MILES CHAMPIONSHIP-HURLINGHAM APRIL 16TH Introduction to the walking news celebrating the walkers' second triple of National 10, National 20 and R.W.A. 50 km titles in four years, followed by Eric Hall's fifth place in the A.A.A. 7 miles walk at Hurlingham on 16 April 1960. The bronze medal performance of Stan Vickers in Rome obviously overshadows any other news we care to print. But his wonderful performance has in fact provided a fitting climax to one of our most successful seasons ever. For the second time in 4 years we are Triple Champions, having won the National '10', National '20' and RWA 50 Kilos. We are indeed proud that Stan Vickers and Eric Hall should have played as big a part in this as they did for the Great Britain team at the Olympics. The following diary of events will be something of an anti-climax after the tremendous excitement of the XVII Olympiad, but success in any form makes pleasant reading, so in an effort to stir your pride still further we take you back to April, when athletes the world over were making extra serious preparation to meet their day of destiny 5 months hence. A.A.A. 7 MILES CHAMPIONSHIP-HURLINGHAM APRIL 16TH Eric Hall, in a tremendously hard fought battle, recorded a personal best of 51:52 to finish in what must surely have been the fastest fifth place this event has ever seen. Stan Vickers was unable to race owing to leg trouble, so Eric played Sister Anna and carried the Belgrave banner alone. The manner in which he did this was truly heroic, for his opposition included a peak-form Matthews and five East Germans: all reputed to be very fast, which indeed they were. Matthews led from start to finish and was at no time challenged. Eric was third at 1 mile with 7:21. second at 2 miles (14:41)- one second ahead of Weber (E.G.), but at 3 miles had dropped 8 secs on the German. By no means finished, Eric gritted his teeth once more and at 4 miles had closed the gap only to be joined by two more Germans, Koch and Zefanczik. For four more laps these four battled it out neck and neck, but in the last mile Eric had to give way and finished fifth; an excellent performance. items.label: September 1960
items.h: THE R.W.A. '20' or General Goswell and the Gomersal Campaign
items.sum: Report of the R.W.A. 20 miles championship at Gomersal near Leeds on 14 May 1960, won by Stan Vickers in his first race at the distance, with Belgrave winning the team title and Nijmegen Shield, and tributes to organiser Jack Goswell.
items.s: THE R.W.A. '20' or General Goswell and the Gomersal Campaign Report of the R.W.A. 20 miles championship at Gomersal near Leeds on 14 May 1960, won by Stan Vickers in his first race at the distance, with Belgrave winning the team title and Nijmegen Shield, and tributes to organiser Jack Goswell. All the great military leaders of the past have shown a sense of strategy and a knowledge of tactics, and have appreciated the advantage—nay neccessity—of high morale, the value of surprise, the need for consolidation, the immeasurable value of strength in reserve, the essentials of sound and consistent training, and the Napoleonic dictum that "any army marches on its stomach". All these things were borne in mind by Jack Goswell when he planned the Campaign of the Yorkshire Dales from Gomersal (near Leeds) on May 14th- and inevitably, victory utter and complete, was the result. This year we were without the services of Terry Clark at present in Australia, and we knew the holders, Metropolitan W.C. would pay us the compliment of fighting every inch of the way. Twenty four hours before the race Ray Middleton had to cry-off on doctor's instructions. We had expected much of him, but his turn will come. Veteran Dave McMullen was unable to travel and our team began to take on an attenuated appearance. However ten of our walkers plus General Goswell and others made the long journey to Leeds from whence coaches conveyed the party to Gomersal. Let it be said right away that the Gomersal people surpassed themselves in the local arrangements. There was splendid dressing accommodation, ample cars for the officials, extended licences for those with an interest in such things!, a uniformed brass band to cheer everybody on their way, an M.P. and civic dignitaries to play their part, magnificent pointing and feeding arrangements-in fact, almost perfect organisation. Did anyone mention the course? Well, it must be said that this was just about the most severe course possibly, with the steepest and unyielding hills that twenty mile walkers have ever been called upon to face in a Championship. True it was typical of the Yorkshire countryside. Whichever way the course had been planned there would have been hills in plenty! At the start of the Championship five Olympic walkers were quickly into the lead. They were our own Stan Vickers (was he the Surprise!) and Eric Hall; Met's Don Thompson and Tom Misson (the holder) and Sheffield's Albert Johnson. The first four named kept well together for many a long mile but gradually our two managed to draw away and at half way had taken command. Our third man at this point was George Williams, and his light frame seemed to be trickling uphill with the greatest of ease as he took over fifth place. At 12½ miles everything seemed lovely and we were scoring 20 points to the 34 of Met. W.C., 44 of Sheffield, and 53 of Leicester. Soon after 15 miles, however, our smiles were somewhat disturbed. George Williams was experiencing leg trouble and had yielded fifth place to Sheffield's International, and seemed likely to lose more places. At the head of the race, Eric Hall had now found the cumulative effect of so much hill - climbing having its effect and Stan Vickers had to carry on alone, as the Metropolitan challengers were drawing ominously near. So came the end, with Stan Vickers still tackling this most difficult course with the greatest of ease, a comfortable and most worthy winner in 2 hours 41 min 41 secs. It was a devastating performance and called forth the highest of praise from everyone who witnessed it. Having regard to the nature of the course it must surely be the finest 20 mile road performance yet. A most worthy champion, in his first race at this distance! Then followed Met's great couple Don Thompson and Tom Misson, with our Eric fourth. Our sympathies were with Eric for he could so easily have filled a higher position had the luck been with him. As it was he finished fresh in body but the legs had lost their rhythm on so much uphill gradient. However 2 hours 45 mins 8 secs for such a punishing course is certainly not failure-it would be full value for victory on many another occasion; and he need not be dismayed. Ray Hall came through splendidly in the closing stages of the race to sixth position-a great team effort on his part. The excellence of Ray's strongly sustained last five miles counter-balanced George Williams loss of positions over the same section. Our Club had its complete team of four home in the first eleven scoring positions with 22 points, against Mets 32 points. Their's was a fine performance—to score 32 points and be placed second seems scant justice! Leicester and Sheffield battled for third place with the last named club prevailing. Interest in this Championship is continued to the complete team of eight men by provision of the Nijmegen Shield, the destination of which is decided by the position of the eighth team man. Once again we made sure of this by having our eight in 31 scoring positions- a most excellent result. Hugh Mc Greechan was almost back to his very best form, George Beecham turned in his usual reliable Championship performance, Jim Morris did splendidly on his first effort, and George Checkley whipped in a really excellent team of eight men. Outside the eight, Harry Shields and John McKeown also did well and we had ten walkers in the first 39 positions- which was most creditable to everyone concerned. Undoubtedly the entry would have been better had the rail fare been cheaper and the train times more convenient. However, Belgrave had an excellent week-end, with Stan Vickers- a most worthy Champion; our winning team—one of the greatest that has ever represented us, and that's saying something; our Nijmegen Shield team, a new record to go on the books. Three trophies and all went Belgrave-wards! There was a fourth, the Hammond Cup, for inter-area competition and Jack Goswell was very fittingly, as Vice Chairman of RWA Southern Area, called upon to receive this. So it was Belgrave, Belgrave all the way! And let's finish as we began by a tribute to a great little man, Jack Goswell, who worked as hard as anyone to ensure victory for our teams both before and during the race. Lets promote him-hes probably got a Field Marshal's baton in his pannier-bag! He seems to have most things! A.A.H. RESULT Pos Name Team Time 1 S.F. Vickers Bel A 2:41:41 2 D.J.
