items.label: September 1960
items.sum: Report of the R.W.A. National 50 km walk at Chigwell Row on 18 June 1960, where Belgrave beat Metropolitan W.C. for the team title to become triple national road walking champions, with George Beecham winning the club's Bellchamber Cup.
items.s: BELGRAVE TRIPLE CHAMPIONS Report of the R.W.A. National 50 km walk at Chigwell Row on 18 June 1960, where Belgrave beat Metropolitan W.C. for the team title to become triple national road walking champions, with George Beecham winning the club's Bellchamber Cup. In conditions which might well be comparable with those anticipated for the Olympic Games in Rome later in the year, The R.W.A. National 50 Kilometres Championship was held from the excellent new quarters of Essex Beagles at Chigwell Row, Essex on 18th June; the same day as the Club Track Championships. In the absence of Eric Hall, who is now concentrating on the 20 Kilometres, and Hugh McGreechan who had just been presented with a further addition to his family, the team championship looked all set for Metropolitan Walking Club with their now well known quartet of Thompson, Misson, Thompson and Thompson (sounds like a firm of solicitors!) but although none of our walkers were quite good enough to warrant consideration for Rome, by grim determination they brought off one of the most creditable performances for many years. The course, consisting of two laps of just over five miles and two of just under 10 miles, could not be described as an easy one and although passing through quite pleasant country lanes, there was very little shade. From the start, Don Thompson and Tom Misson soon opened up a gap with Albert Johnson of Sheffield close to hand. The two Met. boys over the early stages were closely supported by the other two Thompsons whilst our team, led by Ray Hall, were well spread out over the field. The heat, however, soon began to take its toll and Met. lost one man before the race was half way through. In the meantime, Ray Hall was holding a good position and George Beecham slowly making up ground. George, who always walks better in the heat, had started off slowly and George Checkley was keeping close to hand. Alittle further back John Morris and John Keown, both competing for the first time in the "A" team were walking steadily together, followed by Harry Shields and Percy Wilson. It seemed at 30 Kms. we should get a place. Ray Hall then developed a spot of trouble and George Beecham passed him to go up to 6th place at 40 Kms. After a tussle with Dicky Green of Surrey WC George had to let him go and he eventually finished 4th. At this point, the score was Met. W.C. 38 pts, Belgrave 43 pts. Woodford, Sheffield and Leicester had all dropped places and we looked set for 2nd team medals. Over the last few Kms. however, Met's 3rd man went back to 12th position (10th in the team race) and was passed by Ray Hall. Alittle further back in the field Georg Checkley was holding his position at 11th place and Morris, 18th, had left Keown and was gradually moving up, egged on by Jack Goswell and Ben Knifton, having threatened to retire. At the same time the 4th Met. man was struggling to keep in the race. Over this vital 10 Kms. we succeeded in reducing our score by three points, whilst Met. went up by five and with our 4th man finishing in 16th position we had a final total of 40 points to Met's 43, with Woodford 3rd with 54 pts; Met. having to wait almost to the last man in to complete their team. Of Harry Shields and Percy Wilson, Percy, suffering from lack of training, retired at the end of the first big lap whilst Harry battled through to finish 23rd and gain a certificate for inside 5hrs 45 mins. The most creditable performance was undoubtedly that of John Morris, who without the experience of our first three men, and aided by the coaxing and cajoling of Jack Goswell & Co., walked an excellent race considering the climatic conditions, and made up vital places at a critical stage. So we once again become triple champions on the road with eight of our members sharing the honours. Stan Vickers, Eric Hall, George Williams and Ray Middleton in the "Ten", Stan Vickers, Eric Hall, George Williams and Ray Hall in the "Twenty" and George Beecham, Ray Hall, George Checkley and John Morris in the "Kilos", with John Morris gaining his first National Medal. The Club Championship for the "Bellchamber" Cup was held in conjunction with the race and the trophy goes to George Beecham for the first time, with place medals to Ray Hall and George Checkley. items.sum: Account of Stan Vickers' run of 2 miles walk records in summer 1960, culminating in his United Kingdom All-Comers Record of 13:02.4 beating Ken Matthews at the A.A.A. Championships on 16 July.
items.s: the record breaker: Account of Stan Vickers' run of 2 miles walk records in summer 1960, culminating in his United Kingdom All-Comers Record of 13:02.4 beating Ken Matthews at the A.A.A. Championships on 16 July. At the Southern Championships at Motspur Park on June 25th, Stan Vickers won the 2 mile event in a record 13:30:4---a personal best at the time. Four days later Stan was out again; this time on home ground, at Battersea Park track. In a match versus the Stock Exchange, Stan, walking for the Exchange, improved his personal best time of the previous Saturday by four seconds with 13:26:4; over a minute ahead of George Williams. Stan, off scratch, also took the handicap award. But Stan had by no means finished his succession of sprints, for on July 2nd he was in action again. This time on a grass track at Peterborough, where he equalled a 56yr old record by clocking a remarkable 13:11:4, a personal best yet again---at the time! Four days later he stepped on to the Battersea-track again, on the occasion of the inter-club walks. Stan was out to crack the British record and only failed by the narrowest of margins. His time was only one fifth of a second slower than that at Peterborough. On July 16th at the A.A.A. Championships Stan faced his arch rival Ken Matthews. Belgravians were convinced that Matthews's presence would take Stan to his record, but would Stan break the tape first? Matthews was in great form, and smarting from his defeat at Peterborough. The starter's gun broke the hush of expectancy and 19 competitors scuffled to the first bend, the principal combatants already to the fore. Matthews tore through the first lap in 92secs, Vickers clinging like a leech to the quick moving frame ahead. After six and a half minutes of sweating toil the mile post was reached, and still they were locked in desperate combat. The excitement of the battle was no longer confined to the walking fraternity---the White City crowd were building up a tremendous atmosphere of anticipation. All eyes, within and without the circuit, became centred on the white vest of Matthews and the claret and gold of Vickers---could they break this fantastic record of Larner's which had stood for so long? The sound of the bell was almost lost in the ever-increasing roar of the crowd, and as these "Siamese Twins" approached the back straight it seemed certain that they would finish in the same order as throughout, for how could any human walk past a Matthews travelling at this speed. As the back straight was hit Matthews hesitated momentarily. Vickers, like an animal awaiting a mistake by it's prey, seized the initiative with a vicious sprint, and before Matthews had recovered sufficiently to start closing the gap Stan was well on his way to a new United Kingdom All-Comers Record of 13:02:4, 7.2secs ahead of his rival. The time of that last lap?--------90.4secs!!.... Stan does not always win----believe it or not! but can there be a more reliable competitor in existence----anywhere? The bigger the occasion the more he rises to it. It's a pity Stan can't perform in the very first event of all Great Britain's fixtures. As in the European Games, his effort and example always gives a fillip to team morale. items.h: VANCOUVER TROPHY: BHATIA AND TOLSON SHINE
items.sum: Report of the Vancouver Trophy meeting promoted by Woodford Green on 2 July 1960, with Ranjit Bhatia winning the 5,000 metres and Trevor Tolson setting a club 110 metres hurdles record.
items.s: VANCOUVER TROPHY: BHATIA AND TOLSON SHINE Report of the Vancouver Trophy meeting promoted by Woodford Green on 2 July 1960, with Ranjit Bhatia winning the 5,000 metres and Trevor Tolson setting a club 110 metres hurdles record. Ranjit Bhatia, with a last lap sprint of 61secs, was a convincing winner of the 5,000 metres in 14:44:8 at this Woodford Green promotion on July 2nd. Valuable points were gained by Mal Robinson who backed up well with third place in 14:51.2. At the start W.L. Card (TVH) set up a 50yd lead, but this gradually dwindled, until at 7 laps Mal took a group of five into the lead. The mile had been passed in 4.40, and this fast-moving group went through two miles in 9.31. With two laps to go Ranjit piled on the pressure and only Jeffs (Essex Beagles) managed to stay with him. With 100yds to go Ranjit kicked even harder to break the tape 5yds clear of his rival. Another star performer was Trevor Tolson who won the 110 metres hurdles in a new Club record of 15.3secs. Trevor's morning had been spent travelling down from Liverpool, but he certainly proved his journey was worthwhile. He had taken the lead by half way and crossed the line 3yds clear of his nearest rival Surety of Ilford. After a bad start in the 200metres, in which he lay last at half-way, Peter Eldridge stormed thro' the field to take 2nd place in a fine 22.1secs. D.H. Segal (TVH) was the winner in a meeting record of 21.2secs. Earlier Peter had finished fifth in the 100metres, which was won by ex-Belgravian C.R. Jones! Jim McGrath's 11'6" gave him second place in the Pole Vault, but his jumping was affected by a badly ricked ankle. Despite this, he still took part in his usual "double", and finished 6th in the long jump with 20'11". Our only representative in the 1500metres was the fast improving John Thresher. Running in the 'B' race, he was badly baulked at the final bend yet still turned in 3:59.7 for second place. His time was equivalent to a 4.18 mile—a personal best. items.sum: Report and result of the Club 3 miles championship (Griffin Cup) at Battersea on 27 July 1960, retained by Mal Robinson in 14:19 from Pat Newell and Chas. Dabbs; Newell's time is printed 14:21:6 in the report but 14:21:5 in the result.
items.s: THE CLUB '3': FINE "DOUBLE" BY ROBINSON Report and result of the Club 3 miles championship (Griffin Cup) at Battersea on 27 July 1960, retained by Mal Robinson in 14:19 from Pat Newell and Chas. Dabbs; Newell's time is printed 14:21:6 in the report but 14:21:5 in the result. Defending champion Mal Robinson successfully retained the "Griffin" Cup when he defeated Pat Newell at Battersea on July 27th. A scorching last lap of 59secs produced a winning time of 14:19:0; against 14:21:6 by Newell and 14:28:0 by Dabbs. He thus holds both the one and three mile titles for the second year in succession. An exciting race would have been highlighted even further if Ranjit Bhatia had been able to run, but Ranjit was reserving himself for an Invitation 5,000metres to be held 3 days later at the Great-Britain v France match, and so our top quartet was reduced to a trio. Over twenty starters toed the line on this rather dull and overcast evening. Bill Bird, as is his wont, was soon setting the pace with Bob Norton at his shoulder, and at 3 laps a group of eight had detached itself from the field. Approaching the mile post, John Moore began to fade, and a little afterwards Norton retired. On the fifth lap Bill was still leading, but noticeably struggling, and it was no surprise when Dabbs shot ahead in an effort to break up the pack—with two fast-finishing rivals alongside his only hope was to run out their finish. A fifteen yard gap quickly appeared, with Newell following up five yards ahead of Robinson; but Chas. did not sustain his burst sufficiently long and within 300yds the other two runners had renewed contact. However, Walker had been left trailing and Moore and Maclean were out of it, so the first three places were already decided. Dabbs battled on in his familar fashion and on three more occasions attempted to lose the tenacious hold of Newell and Robinson, but although they were often taken unawares they generally had the measure of their opponent. And so it was proved at the "bell". Pat tore ahead in an effort to get away, for it was his turn now to worry about blunting his opponent's finish, and at 200yds to go he was still ahead, but Mal's final kick was most decisive and he romped home an impressive winner. The race had gone just as the pundits forecast! Result: Pos Name Time 1 M.E. Robinson 14:19 2 P. Newell 14:21:5 3 C. Dabbs 14:28 4 C. Walker 15:06 5 D. Maclean 15:43 6 B. Sawyer 15:44 7 R. items.sum: Report and result of the Club 6 miles championship on 17 August 1960, won by Ranjit Bhatia from Pat Newell in his last club race before returning to India.
items.s: THE CLUB '6': Bhatia's last Club Championship Report and result of the Club 6 miles championship on 17 August 1960, won by Ranjit Bhatia from Pat Newell in his last club race before returning to India. On August 17th, Ranjit Bhatia took a leaf out of Mal Robinson's copy-book when he treated poor Pat Newell to yet another dose of last-lap upmanship! Pat himself did not bemoan his fate though, for Ranjit had won his only Club title in the last Championship race before he leaves for his Indian homeland next month. Our "top four" were soon away from the rest of the field, with the lead changing hands almost lap by lap. Not until 4½miles was reached did the situation change, when Mal found the pace of his first "six" too much and was gradually dropped. Chas Dabbs made strenuous efforts to break away over the last few laps, but was unsuccessful and once more was beaten for speed on the last circuit. As in the Club '3', Newell still had his nose in front with 200yds to go, and when the final straight was reached must have thought his day had arrived. Bhatia, however, had other ideas and his dark loping figure strode past his short-stepping rival, to cross the line ten yards clear. Of the other fifteen runners, Derek Crookes's performance of 32:12 in this his first 'six' was perhaps the most meritorious. items.h: THE BELGRAVE OPEN '20': NORRIS AND PAWSEY SMASH RECORD
items.sum: Report and result of Belgrave's ninth annual open 20 miles road race on 20 August 1960, won in a record 1:47:26 by Fred Norris, with Ron Linstead setting a club record and Belgrave A winning the team race.
items.s: THE BELGRAVE OPEN '20': NORRIS AND PAWSEY SMASH RECORD Report and result of Belgrave's ninth annual open 20 miles road race on 20 August 1960, won in a record 1:47:26 by Fred Norris, with Ron Linstead setting a club record and Belgrave A winning the team race. Fred Norris, the marathon star who so unluckily missed selection for Rome set about the opposition in revengeful manner at Belgrave's ninth annual 20 miles road race on August 20th to smash R. Clark's 4yr old record by 2½mins. Norris's time was 1:47:26. The 78 starters set off at a brisk rate, with Norris setting the pace right away. The "funnel" of runners rapidly lengthened and soon broke up into the usual groups. Ron Linstead spearheaded the Bels contingent running comfortably in one of the leading groups, and at 10miles had drawn clear to take up 7th place. At 15 miles Norris, running splendidly, was 2mins clear of Llewellyn who in turn was 1¼mins ahead of Pawsey(Mitcham) and Towl (HHH). Linstead was maintaining his pace well and had advanced to sixth, a further 1¾mins back. Over the last 5 miles Norris and Llewellyn both faded, and a supreme effort by Pawsey took him to the line in 2nd place, 90secs down on the winner. His time over the last 5 miles (27:35) was the only one to beat our own Ron Linstead's, Norris's included!, and Ron crossed the line in fine fettle with a new Club record to his credit. With the team race in the balance, Belgrave, TVH, Bristol and Walton anxiously awaited their next scoring man. When Len Bishop our next scorer arrived we were last of the four, but the very next man to arrive in was find-of-the-season N. Stairs whose effort took us to a narrow team win—four points covering the first four teams. Apart from the individual winner, Belgrave swept the board, for Linstead Sawyer and Stairs also took the three handicap awards. The organisation was first class and bouquets must go to Bill Bird and his many helpers for staging yet another successful promotion. items.label: January 1961
items.sum: New Year editorial urging Belgravians to train harder and more purposefully for the longer 1961 season after the Olympic year raised standards.
items.s: EDITORIAL New Year editorial urging Belgravians to train harder and more purposefully for the longer 1961 season after the Olympic year raised standards. Dear Fellow Members, May we wish you all a happy, prosperous and successful New Year. 1960 produced a year of tremendous activity in the world of athletics. At all levels the sport was boosted by an Olympic Games which raised standards on to yet another 4 year plateau. The established International star, if such a person exists, may well find the coming season something of an anti-climax, but the club athlete who aspires to any representative honours will face his contemporaries in a year which will reflect the effect of new Olympic marks in no uncertain manner. The fixture-congested "summer" season now spans from April to Sept., and whether or not this is a good thing, the athlete must be fit early on to make any headway on the athletic scene. He should make his mark long before the arrival of the A.A.A.'s Championships, and then hold his form for most of the season. To do this, it should be realised that a more determined and scientific approach must be made towards training. No longer is it possibl to ignore hard training in the Winter and Spring months if one wishes to score in the Summer. It is not necessary, and indeed inadvisable, for the athlete to become the slave of a schedule, but it is important that he undertakes a training programme and adheres to it's general pattern. Any intelligent programme, thoroughly followed will bring forth a high degree of success, provided it's essence is hard work at regular intervals. We hope the Belgravian of 1961 will show a greater sense of purpose in his training, more determination in his racing, and the desire to bring many individual and team awards back to Belgrave. items.s: HON. SEC'S NOTES The Hon. Secretary's notes (continued on page 18) on the London-Brighton relay, a farewell to Ranjit Bhatia, thanks for the Open Youths Road Relay, Handbook corrections, the South London Schools championships at headquarters, Stan Vickers' Harvey Memorial and RWA Coronation Cups, and the 1961 club track championships date. What a great thrill it was to see our team once again in the lead in a London-Brighton Relay race! True, we could'nt sustain it to the end but we were less than a minute behind the winners when Brighton was reached, and proved to ourselves that all we needed was "a little bit of luck" to give us the premier awards, as of yore. How much extra effort is needed before history repeats itself with a Belgrave win? In truth, not very much! A second gained in every mile would have given us a win! Still further reduced; one extra stride in each minute's running by all our men would have carried us to victory. By such small margins are races won or lost--and knowing this secret we can assuredly win, win, win! All we need is that one extra stride per minute from a fit, determined team! x x x x X X x x x x One of the sad things about the London-Brighton Relay was saying "good-bye" to Ranjit Bhatia after his last run in our colours, and we wish him a safe return and many years of happiness in his native India. Cont'd.on P.18 Cont'd. from P.2 A hearty vote of thanks goes to Arthur Whitehead and all who helped in any way with the promotion and carrying through of our fourth annual Open Youths Road Relay. Once again it was a great success and drew support from all over the country. The first six clubs, viz. Hallamshire H, Hercules AC, Coventry Godiva H, Mitcham AC, Sheffield United H, Belgrave H, give evidence of the national appeal the race now has, with two Northern clubs and one from the Midlands in the first six placings out of the 47 teams that competed. It was gratifying too, to see our own boys--not all of them in the "A" team--showing up well in this promotion of ours, which has surely already become one of the classic races for Youths. * * * * * Those b***y asterisks again! Three have escaped from our new Handbook where they should have reposed against the times recorded in the 1 mile, 3 miles and 6 miles Club Championships; indicating that they were Club Best Championship performances. Please amend accordingly! * * * * * Early in November, on a Wednesday afternoon, nearly 400 boys managed to change in our Headquarters and compete in two races for the South London Schools Championships, and the Shields given by our Vice President, Mr. E. Ryan. How encouraging to see Belgrave vests proudly and prominently worn by so many of the runners; and what a testimony to the Club's future that Belgrave boys should win both the races. Well done, Hudson and Morrison! * * * * * Stan Vickers' great 2 miles Walk in the A.A.A. Championships, when a 54 year old record was eliminated, has won for him the Harvey Memorial Gold Cup for the best Champion of the year; and Stan's name rightly joins those of the Immortals who have preceded him. This trophy is a wealth of athletic history in itself. The RWA "Coronation" Cup has also been awarded to Stan for the same performance. * * * * * Our Club Track Championships in 1961 will take place at Hurlingham Park Track on Saturday May 27th. Every Club member is asked to note this date and give his support. The date is a little earlier than usual but only precedes the County Championships by a week. A.A.H. items.sum: Profile of the new club President Leslie (Les) Cohen, from his running days with Ashcombe AC and Belgrave to his many senior roles in athletics administration.
items.s: THE PRESIDENT ~ L.J. Cohen Profile of the new club President Leslie (Les) Cohen, from his running days with Ashcombe AC and Belgrave to his many senior roles in athletics administration. Between the wars a great feature of our Winter programme was the series of three-sided cross country fixtures between Ashcombe AC, Thames Valley Harriers and ourselves which took place from the quarters of all three clubs in turn. These were "mob" matches, and everyone who had two legs turned out, and great was the sport and pleasure thereof. In the very early days after World War 1, Thames Valley had prevailed, but gradually Belgrave became stronger and stronger and eventually dominated the competitions. In 1928 we travelled(over thirty of us) to the Valley's quarters at Feltham, and the race was won by Percy Bicknell of TVH, with the long-legged hairpin-thin subject of this article, running in Ashcombe AC colour in second place. Then came the Bels- Pyer, Penny, Duffett, Bill Webb and so on, and we won with 77pts, to the 275 of Ashcombe and 276 of TVH. A fortnight later the event moved to Wimbledon where there were over 100 starters, 60 of them Belgravians. The winner on this occasion-Les Cohen, followed by Footer, Jack Flower, Duffett, Penny, Allum, Rice, Pyer, with, needless to say, a Belgrave team win of convincing proportions. In the same month Les won the South of the Thames junior race at Epsom, and incidentally, Belgrave had a very satisfying team win! So we continued to meet and admire "Leslie's" running ability and his sporting qualities for many years, as he did his utmost to keep Ashcombe's colours prominent. When it was apparent that the club could no longer effectively carry on, what was more natural than that Putney-born Leslie Cohen should pull a Belgrave vest over his head? He served us well on track and over the country and figured in our scoring teams in both the cross country races held just outside Paris, to which our club was invited. He gained Club Championship medals, and was to be found playing his part in the numerous team successes that came our way at that time. He also took an interest in the financial side of the Club's affairs, and that interest has continued throughout the years and still continues. It is largely through his efforts that we own Belgrave Hall and have been able to add the various amenities that we possess today. After the war, Les decided to play his part on the administrative side of Amateur Athletics, and to serve the sport which had given him so much pleasure. He did this so well that he soon became one of the best-known and certainly best-liked officials in the game. Most years he heads the poll in the election of the Southern Committee of the A.A.A., and the number of honorary positions he holds is legion. He is at the moment President of the English Cross Country Union and of the Southern Counties Cross Country Assoch. He is Championships Hon Secretary of the A.A.A. and Counties Athletic Union, Hon Secretary to the London Business Houses S.A, Championships Hon Secretary to the London County Council and with many another job in addition! Recently he visited Lagos, in Nigeria, to advise on track layout and technical matters generally; and with his usual mixture of good humour and hard work, order was resolved out of chaos! And now we honour Les as President of the Belgrave Harriers. There has never been a Club member with the same status and influence that Leslie wields within the Athletic circle- and the Club can take a lot of credit from this. At the same time and concurrently with all these activities there have been very few within the Club who have done so much for Belgrave. It is a great privelege to have Leslie in the Presidential chair. We have done ourselves great honour; and we wish him many years ahead of continuing health and strength to carry on doing those things he does so well, and with so much personal charm. A.A.H. items.sum: Report of the 1960 club dinner at the Ardington Rooms, Clapham Junction, on 5 November, with speeches by guests, the handover from T.C. Jones to new President L.J. Cohen, and Stan Vickers receiving the Tommy Green Cup and the A.A.A. Harvey Memorial Gold Cup.
items.s: THE CLUB DINNER ~ 1960 Report of the 1960 club dinner at the Ardington Rooms, Clapham Junction, on 5 November, with speeches by guests, the handover from T.C. Jones to new President L.J. Cohen, and Stan Vickers receiving the Tommy Green Cup and the A.A.A. Harvey Memorial Gold Cup. In an admirable speech proposing the toast of Belgrave Harriers, Mr. J.C. Crump, Honorary Secretary of the B.A.A.B., paid tribute to the Club's struggle in earlier years, and It's present wide representation on the governing bodies of athletics in Britain. This year's dinner was held at the Ardington Rooms, Clapham Junction, on Nov.5th. Perhaps this would have been an appropriate occasion for the fireworks to fly, but the only controversial issue touched upon was a reference to the International Athletes Club. Mr. Crump referred to "---a Sunday Newspaper journalist, known to us all" who had criticised the A.A.A. for not accepting an Athletes Registration scheme put to them by the I.A.C. "I sometimes wonder", Mr. Crump, "whether we are organising athletics for the thousands of Club athletes throughout the country, or for a handful of stars". Our own Secretary had supported the proposal's rejection. President L.J. Cohen and Secretary A.A. Harley were spoken of in glowing terms by Mr. Crump, who was given a great ovation. In his response, Dave Shepherd mentioned the impressive lists of past performances and trophies shown in the Club Handbook, and thanked the many Club officials who carried out their duties"--at their wives' sufferance and employers' expense!!! Our newest vice-President, Ranjit Bhatia, was now back home in India, but our thoughts were with him on this occasion for he would certainly have joined fellow Olympians Stan Vickers and Eric Hall as a Club guest. In his conclusion, Mr. Shepherd thanked the Social Committee for their year's work and related several amusing incidents that occurred during the Belgrave party's stay in Rome. In proposing a toast to "Our Guests", our Secretary paid tribute to our Olympic representatives who had performed so well in Rome, and Mr. R. Savage who now had 50 years of membership behind him. We were indeed honoured that our guests should also include such distinguished men as J.C.G. Crump (Hon.Sec.B.A.A.B.), E.H. Clynes (Hon.Sec.A.A.A.), W.Harris (E.C.C.U.), L.W. Woodcock (Hon. Sec.Assocn.London Clubs), P.S. Gale(Treasurer A.A.A.) organiser of the now famous yellow draw tickets!, R. Bacchus of the "News of the World", who had been responsible for so many athletic promotions, and H. Hathway (SLH) whose timekeeping had been of such great assistance. In his response, Mr. Clynes said he hoped that our new President would emulate a certain well known public figure by ringing home the Bels on the Brighton front to a London-Brighton Relay success, during his term of office. Our retiring President, T.C. Jones, then gave an account of Les Cohen's successes in active athletics and his rise to the top of the administrative ladder. This year he would also be President of the English Cross Country Union--a great honour for the Club. After thanking everyone in his typically modest manner, Les Cohen said "I got a great deal out of athletics, and I get a lot of fun putting something back into it. I hope a lot of you will one day do likewise". (These were words that could well have been spoken to the International Athletes Club). Mr. Cohen presented the "Tommy Green" Cup to S.F. Vickers for the year's most meritorious performance by a Club athlete, and called on Mr. Crump to present the same athlete with the A.A.A.'s "Harvey Memorial" Gold Cup; awarded to the year's best A.A.A. Champion. Stan Vickers, after remarking how dangerous it was to give gold to a member of the Stock Exchange, promptly "dropped the gold standard" by allowing the Cup's base to fall to the floor! But in his usual pleasant and unruffled manner he was soon paying tribute to his "many helpers"; Ray Hall, Harry Shields and "Old Man" Goswell. "You runners", said Stan, "don't know how lucky you are not to have a man like Goswell around!" But his tongue was stuck firmly into his cheek whilst he spoke. Dancing was underway by 9pm, and the tinkling of glasses and merriment of the company continued in full swing until midnight. Thus ended one of the most successful Club dinners ever----thanks to A.T. items.sum: Frank Jarvis's report of the 1960 Annual General Meeting at Belgrave Hall on 23 September, covering the Secretary's and Treasurer's reports, R.T. Taylor's life membership, Les Cohen's election as President, a short-handed committee election, Ranjit Bhatia's election as Vice-President and a debate on police athletes' first-claim status.
items.s: THE A.G.M. Frank Jarvis's report of the 1960 Annual General Meeting at Belgrave Hall on 23 September, covering the Secretary's and Treasurer's reports, R.T. Taylor's life membership, Les Cohen's election as President, a short-handed committee election, Ranjit Bhatia's election as Vice-President and a debate on police athletes' first-claim status. FRANK JARVIS REPORTS: The building is Belgrave Hall, time 6.30 p.m., Friday, 23rd September 1960. The occasion was not an Open Run nor an Open Walk, but an open night for all Belgravians- the Annual General Meeting for 1960. Were you there? If you were, these few words will refresh your memory If you were not able to be there, this report of the proceedings will attempt to show what you missed. The number present was small compared with the actual members, there is no doubt that a way will have to be devised to encourage attendance at the A.G.M., maybe a 'whipper-in' for each section. The President T.C. Jones, opened the meeting, and the Secretary in presenting his report, spoke of the respect with which the 'Belgrave' are viewed by other clubs and officials in the athletic world. We in Belgrave may criticise the Club, but all outside admire the Club and its activities and know that within a short period the 'Bels' will win the events that seem to count. Then Syd Roberts, as the Treasurer, presented the Balance Sheet. What accounts! What figures! What an athletic club! This surely, was a balance sheet suitable for a company in the City. It made visible the amount of work that is necessary to organise the Belgrave Harriers, and, maybe, we accept this effort on the part of the officials too easily. After this financial wizardy, it was pleasant to hear Dave Shepherd's proposal that R.T. Taylor be elected a Life member of the club, and its adoption. The election of Officers commenced with the retiring President nominating as his successor, Les Cohen, a man, who, perhaps above all others, has contributed to keep Belgrave Harriers financially strong with his football scheme; and he still finds time to do this invaluable work. It is significant that he has also been elected President of the E.C.C.U. Cont'd. on P.26 Cont'd. from P.5. The election of other officers followed the normal course, some sections had their plans made with members willing to serve, others had difficulty in finding members to act as officials. The election of the Committee was notable in the fact that only nine names were nominated to fill the ten positions on the committee. Is this the first time that this has occurred? In many ways this seems to be 'missing the opportunity'. Criticism is aimed at the Committee (and maybe rightly so) for lack of understanding, but, on election night, there are no volunteers to assist in this matter. Members can learn so much from Committee work-Club adminstration, it's finance, arranging meetings and so forth. A good club committee man is the equal of a champion runner or walker, within the Club. A man who became a good Belgravian in a short time, Ranjit Bhatia, was proposed by Clive Shippen to be made a Vice-President of the Club, and this was adopted amidst acclamation from the members. Then came that item on the agenda, when anything can happen-"Other business". And it happened. A member asked what action the Officials were going to take about Police competitors running for the Police at open meetings; the status of their 'first claim', including the fact that Police members were not running for the Club. The opinions expressed seemed to indicate that the Police athlete was running for the Police Club instead of his private club at his own request. That there was a definite misunderstanding of the Policeman's position, as an athlete actually competing on behalf of the Police Authority, was apparent. Each man selected to represent the Police Authority in a sporting event of whatever nature is entitled to four hours time off for the event once a week. If for any reason he is unable to attend the event he cannot claim the four hours privilege time off under any circumstances. It can be seen that an athlete selected to represent the Police Authority in an athletic event, for which his duty has been facilitated by the grant of the four hours time-off privilege, could be at an event at which his private club have entered a team. The athlete must represent the Police Authority, he must not use the four hours for his private purposes. As a general rule, however, a policeman athlete who is willing to help himself will obtain assistance from his senior officers to attend events, bearing in mind, though, that Police Duty must come first. The Chairman then informed the meeting that the matter of Police athletes at Open meetings was being investigated, and there being no other business, closed a successful A.G.M. In retrospect, it is to be regretted that more members were not there to give their views, and we, all of us, should endeavour to be at the Belgrave Harriers Annual General Meeting next year. F.J. items.s: Surrey Road Relay: Short report of the 1960 Surrey Road Relay, where a depleted Belgrave team finished 5th, with team times. Holidays and the Rome trip caused a surprising shortage of Belgrave "Surrey"men for this year's event. At the halfway mark we still required two more runners to complete the team, but Don Maclean appeared in the nick of time to run 5th stage. Mike Stearman who had come only as a supporter, was press-ganged into running the last leg after 5 months of inactivity! His fine effort in a complete set of borrowed kit (by no means fresh!) enabled us to finish 5th out of 12 teams. RESULT. Ten teams finished. items.s: THE POLY. ROAD RELAY Report of the Polytechnic Road Relay in which Pat Newell set a club stage record of 13:00 and the Belgrave B team won medals as first B team; the text says the A team finished 4th but the result lists Belgrave H 5th. Record upon record was the outstanding feature of the Poly Road Relay. A new Club record of 13:30 set by Jack Brown on the first leg did not survive the afternoon; 30 seconds was lopped off it by Pat Newell on the 5th leg. Pat's 13:00 mins beat the relay record by 2 secs; but this was not enough to erase Bob Roath's new mark of 12:55 set on the first stage. To complete the records our agregate time was our fastest ever. First off was Jack Brown. This was his first race since leaving Cyprus and running him with the 'fast-boys' was a gamble--a calulated one. But come off it did, for Jack handed over in third place--behind Roath (Walton) and Day (Ponders End). Eleventh was Eric Gebbett for the 'B' team. Chas Walker with a personal best, replaced Ponders End for second place, whilst Dick Shackleford, although dropping to fifteenth, turned in a surprising 14:19 for the 'B'. On the third leg Jim Radford had to give best to Poly's Ralph Dunkley (13:21) and Rooke of Essex Beagles (13:36) and handed over to Derek Crookes fourth. Derek on his first run for the 'A' team maintained his position well. Poly and Essex had taken over the second and third places, with Walton still in the lead. By the time Clive Shippen handed over to Pat Newell the leading positions had altered drastically. Brian Turner (13:17) had taken the Poly into a 22sec lead over Essex Beagles, with the deposed leaders, Walton, a further 16 secs in arrears. Ellis (TVH), had moved ahead of us; but the 'Hill' were our nearest rivals, 45 secs behind. The splendid run by Pat Newell gained us one place--that of TVH, but there were still 20 secs separating us from the Beagles; whilst Proffitt (Poly) and Llewellyn (Walton) were beyond capture. Jumbo Masters, with a time better than two of our 'A' team had gained the 'B' team two places. Don Maclean ran well, despite the agonised look on his face and the jack-tar sway of his body near the finish, but Terry Stacey had taken the Valley back into fourth place. The leaders were unchanged. Mal Robinson on the last lap was clearly not at his best; but with Card (TVH) chasing George Knight (Essex) ahead it was a tough proposition, and we finished 4th. Our 'B' team ran well to finish 10th and collected a set of medals for the first 'B' team to close in; the third time they have gained this award in five years. RESULT. Day's fastest:- 1. items.s: BROWN WINS 5¾ ROAD RACE Report and result of the club 5¾ miles road race at Wimbledon, the last-but-one trial before the October 1960 London to Brighton relay, won by Jack Brown from Ranjit Bhatia, with Brian Sawyer winning the handicap. A field of about 37 faced the starter for this, the last but one, trial before the London to Brighton Relay on October 8th. Amongst the runners were Ranjit Bhatia, on his last outing from Wimbledon before returning home, Jack Brown, recently returned from Cyprus and already re-establishing himself as a danger man and Cliff Roffey, home on furlough from Kenya. John Thresher set the pace with Charlie Walker for 2 miles but decided that two laps of the common was far enough and left Charlie to hold the baby! Jack Brown by this time had moved up and Ranjit who had taken a steady start was also prominent. Hallowell, Gebbett, Roffey and Shippen were in close attendance and Peter Shipley, our 2nd claim member from Farnham, was about 20yds further back with Jim Masters. Down Copse Hill the situation was much the same, but when Cambridge Road was reached Jack Brown went ahead followed by Ranjit; Charlie Walker dropped back to 3rd. This was the order when the Common was again in sight but Cliff Roffey had moved through to 4th. Gebbett, Hallowell and Shippen were still in the hunt, close behind. Jack came away well to win a good race from Ranjit, who seemed to have suffered from his heavy summer season culminating in two races in the Rome Olympics. He was certainly lacking the fire which produced a club record over this course last April. Charlie Walker had held on to take 3rd place, only 30yds ahead of Roffey who had 60yds to spare on Gebbett. Generally speaking the race had run to the form book, although it is difficult to reconcile Don Maclean's 35:14 in 30th place with some of his better performances. Brian Sawyer a greatly improving runner, more at home over longer distances, took the first handicap prize with Brian Johnston, John Collier and Charlie Henn sharing second place- how's that for handicapping?!! items.label: January 1961
items.h: SOUTHERN LONDON-BRIGHTON RELAY: VICTORY ELUDES BEST BELGRAVE TEAM FOR YRS.
items.sum: Stage-by-stage report of the Southern London to Brighton relay on 8 October 1960, in which Belgrave led for several stages and finished 3rd, 51 seconds behind T.V.H., with club records from Ron Linstead and Alan Black and two photographs of changeovers.
items.s: SOUTHERN LONDON-BRIGHTON RELAY: VICTORY ELUDES BEST BELGRAVE TEAM FOR YRS. Stage-by-stage report of the Southern London to Brighton relay on 8 October 1960, in which Belgrave led for several stages and finished 3rd, 51 seconds behind T.V.H., with club records from Ron Linstead and Alan Black and two photographs of changeovers. The sight of claret and gold vests leading the field on the Brighton road once again gave Belgrave supporters a deserved "shot in the arm". It may not have lasted for long, (about 8 miles) but it provided us with the brightest spot of the day. The Bels eventually came 3rd, putting up one of their best performances on this course for many years, and finishing a mere 51secs behind the winners (TVH) and 41 secs down on the runners up and holders (Portsmouth). It all began at 10am in Old Palace Yard, Westminster where twenty runners including Eric Gebbett lined up to await the first stroke of Big Ben. We have become used to seeing Eric taking our first stage and as in April he performed well. Nothing detracts Eric from his steady running and this time he managed to arrive at Clapham Common without mishap in 5th place, 27 secs behind Portsmouth, who had taken a good lead which they were destined to keep most of the way to Brighton (Gebbett 21:25; 5th fastest time). Charlie Walker set off on the second leg in great style with Eddie Ellis of TVH breathing down his neck. These two battled throughout and soon disposed of Walton, Blackheath and Highgate but Ealing represented by Blagrove, Brighton with Briault, and Woodford with Chapman were making faster progress from behind and eventually passed our runner. Charlie eventually gave over to Pat Newell in sixth place with a deficit of 42 secs on Portsmouth (Walker, 25:58; 10th fastest time). Pat Newell, who seems to like this third leg, set about closing the gaps and soon took us up to 2nd place in grand style. By the time the roundabout at the beginning of Purley Way had been reached he was joined by Reeve of Poly who was also running a blinder. These two fought neck and neck up the aerodrome straight and Pat eventually had to give away a few yards. Reeve however had "shot his bolt" and was forced to walk the last half mile, thus dropping his club back to 14th. Pat went on to take 2nd place only 13 secs behind Portsmouth. (Newell, 29:23; 2nd fastest time). Jack Brown, making a welcome return to the team, took the fourth stage to Merstham and although losing ground on the leader kept us in 2nd place. Thames Valley, who had had a bad leg on the 3rd, were again coming back in the picture and were in 4th place, behind Mitcham. (Brown, 25:56; 6th fastest time). Next came Ron Linstead fresh(!) from his success in the full London to Brighton run. In devastating style Ron reduced Portsmouth's ½ min lead to a mere 4 secs and was the only man to break 22 mins. Despite the bad conditions his time was a new Club record. His long distance rival, Elderfield of TVH, was left trailing by almost a minute. (Linstead. 21:49; fastest) Malcolm Robinson soon shot into first place and showing fine form opened up a lead of 40 secs. His time was only 4 secs outside the stage record and well inside Alan Black's Club mark. The exuberance of our supporters was a joy in itself to behold-this was the first time we had led in a Brighton relay for many years. (Robinson 13:30:fastest). Next came Alan Black on the flat leg across Gatwick Airport. Completely exposed to gale-force winds and torrential rain he stuck to his task so well that he broke Robinson's club record for this stage by 8 secs. However our lead had been reduced to 24 secs. (Black, 19:02; 3rd fastest.) The next leg is probably the hardest and certainly the most crucial and Charlie Dabbs was again our runner. As in April Martin Hyman was performing for Portsmouth and in similar manner was behind us. Soon after Crawley Hyman was up with Charlie and was running far too well for our man to hold on. Wiggs of TVH was also making rapid headway and it seemed as though we were destined to drop back to 3rd. Charlie managed to keep Wiggs at bay but we were now forty-six secs down on Portsmouth at the end of the leg. (Dabbs, 31:28; 7th fastest) Ranjit Bhatia was again on the leg from Handcross, on which he had run so well in the previous National race. This was to be his last outing for Belgrave before returning to India. Our hopes of a repetition of his time of 28:56 were not to be granted. Ranjit ran well and steadily but his activities in Rome had taken their toll and the fire was gone. He was forced to give way to Card of Thames Valley and we finished the leg in 3rd place, 1 min and 44 secs behind Portsmouth(Tulloh) and 15 secs behind TVH. (Bhatia, 30:20, 5th fastest). Cliff Roffey who was spending a few weeks in England on furlough from Kenya, and who had regained the form he showed when with us regularly, was on the 10th stage, and with a fine performance shattered the Valley opposition and took us back to 2nd place, 67 secs behind Portsmouth. Could we pick up this deficiency over the last two legs? (Roffey, 21:28; fastest) Clive Shippen again took the Dale Hill leg, but it was soon obvious that he was not in his best condition and slowly Hicks of TVH gained to eventually pass him and give the Valley a 180 yds lead over us. Clive had run well enough, however, to take 26 secs off Portsmouth's lead, so at the final change—over the spacing between the 3 teams was 17secs and 24 secs. (Shippen, 22:18, 5th fastest). When Brian Hallowell set off on the last leg we still had hopes of a higher position than third but the two boys ahead were soon fighting out the lead together and Brian was unable to get to grips. We therefore had to be content with 3rd. (Hallowell, 18:54, 2nd fastest). We should be quite satisfied with this result- it shows we are back in the picture. Although we will be without Bhatia and Roffey next time we have good substitutes in Miller, Radford and David Jones, and can expect Jack Brown to be fitter and Ron Linstead to take a longer leg. items.sum: Introduction of Jack Hampshire as the new Junior Hon. Secretary, with his notes on the boys' and youths' winter season and the difficulties of school-leavers.
items.s: BOYS AND YOUTHS Introduction of Jack Hampshire as the new Junior Hon. Secretary, with his notes on the boys' and youths' winter season and the difficulties of school-leavers. Jack Hampshire (Senior) is our new Junior Hon. Secretary and we extend to him our congratulations on his election to this most important post and trust he will stir our younger members to even greater heights. Jack writes:- "After a most successful track season the Boys and Youths are now engaged in their winter fixtures. The usual faces are still to the front, but there are one or two newcomers, notably A. Fairclough, who should soon be fighting it out with them. Of those just leaving school we should not expect too much. The transition from school(with it's orderly way of life) to outside employment, is a difficult one. They have to reorganise their training to suit their changed lives, which invariably include evening classes and the inevitable homework. We can only hope that they adapt themselves to suit both vocations" Jack Hampshire (Senior) Jack Hampshire (Senior) A. Fairclough A. Fairclough

items.sum: Report and results of the Belgrave Open Youths Road Relay at Wimbledon on 15 October 1960, won by Hallamshire Harriers, with Belgrave A 6th.
items.s: THE BELGRAVE OPEN YOUTHS ROAD RELAY Report and results of the Belgrave Open Youths Road Relay at Wimbledon on 15 October 1960, won by Hallamshire Harriers, with Belgrave A 6th. Hallamshire Harriers, national youth cross-country champions, were convincing winners of this years race at Wimbledon on October 15th. The race was started by South Africa's star distance-runner, Jackie Mekler, in wet, blustery conditions; and by the last stage the rain simply poured down. Nevertheless, the race was yet another success for the Race Hon. Sec., Arthur Whitehead. Hallamshire shot into the lead on the first leg with a fine run by A. Evans, who, with a time of 11 mins 11 secs, was only three seconds off the course record. He handed over 50 yds clear of Rushman (Oldbury) and O'Sullivan (Herne Hill H.) In fifth place was the Belgrave 'B' team, through an excellent effort by new member Tony Fairclough; and an unfit David Cocks brought the 'A' team home in 19th place. On the second of the four 2 mile legs Hallamshire were still way ahead, but Belgrave 'A', after a fighting run by Ken Redwood, had moved up to sixth place. Just behind was Manning (Mitcham) who handed over one second behind. H.H.H. had dropped out of the first ten and third place was now filled by Hercules with Sheffield and Coventry 4th and 5th. These teams were altogether in a tight finish at the end of the third stage. Mitcham's 4:17 miler Malcolm Burton had moved his club into 2nd place after a sprint finish with Halliday (Hercules) and Jackie Hampshire, after fighting hard all thr way with Burton, lost a little ground on the run-in but had moved Belgrave into fourth place. In striking distance were Sheffield and Coventry. Oldbury after lying 2nd at the first change-over were dropping out of the running. Hallamshire were 20 secs clear at the finish, but it was a fight for the place teams. With little more than a mile to go the team positions were unchanged; although they were now fairly bunched together. On the final half-mile Holt (Hercules) caught and passed Colwell (Mitcham) to take second place. Colwell was also involved in a sprint finish when Hammond (Coventry), with the 3rd fastest time of the day, went past with barely fifty yards to go. In fifth place was D. Barden (Sheffield) with A. Morrison bringing the Bels home in sixth place. items.h: SOUTH LONDON SCHOOLS' CHAMPIONSHIPS: WINS FOR MORRISON & HUDSON:
items.sum: Alan Morrison and Roger Hudson of Belgrave and Aristotle School won the intermediate and junior South London Schools cross-country titles at Wimbledon on 9 November 1960, both in course records.
items.s: SOUTH LONDON SCHOOLS' CHAMPIONSHIPS: WINS FOR MORRISON & HUDSON: Alan Morrison and Roger Hudson of Belgrave and Aristotle School won the intermediate and junior South London Schools cross-country titles at Wimbledon on 9 November 1960, both in course records. The activities of our younger runners are not only confined to inter-club fixtures. On Nov 9th at Wimbledon, Alan Morrison and Roger Hudson---both members of Belgrave Harriers!---both members of the Aristotle school!---both won their Championship races, Intermediate and Junior!---both set new course records! A great afternoon's running. In the Intermediate event Alan was up against last year's Junior winner, Garcia of St. Gerards and Mitcham AC; but showing great form he fought off all his rivals to win a very close finish (only 4 secs separated the first 4 home) in a record time no less than 20secs inside the previous mark, held by our own Jackie Hampshire. Tulse Hill School's winning team included Belgravians, Edwards (6th) and Leaver (20th)---both fine performances. Roger Hudson was a comfortable winner of the Junior event. After lying in fifth place for most of the way he took the lead with half a mile to go and drew away to a comfortable win. Backing up well in 11th place was Garvey of Aristotle. items.s: THE BELGRAVE INVITATION BOYS X-CTY. RACE Result of Belgrave's invitation boys' cross-country race at Wimbledon in November 1960, won by P. Fuller of Watford, with Mitcham taking the team title and Belgrave 4th. Two outstanding boy athletes, Fuller(Watford) and Blake (Walton) tussled for the lead in Belgrave's Invitation race at Wimbledon on a dank, murky November day. Back down the field, away from this exceptional pair, Mitcham were packing in the old Belgrave style to clinch the team title, and Hudson and Edwards were spear-heading a gallant Belgrave effort to gain a place. The Bels were eventually placed 4th but when the present team become used to the idea of being without last year's leading boys, now Youths, then we can expect their potential to show itself. items.sum: Report and results of a youths' and boys' cross-country match at Sutton & Cheam on 26 November 1960, the youths' first win of the season, with an editors' quip about washing kit.
items.s: Match at Sutton & Cheam — Nov.26th Report and results of a youths' and boys' cross-country match at Sutton & Cheam on 26 November 1960, the youths' first win of the season, with an editors' quip about washing kit. This resulted in the first win for the Youths over the country this season, and a well deserved one too. The course was over two laps of 1½ miles each. Conditions were ideal other than loads of mud; this the boys revel in, including may I say, Tom Carter, who in track suit ran twice as far as the competitors! The first lap ended with Jackie Hampshire and T. Naish (Sutton) in the lead together, with Cocks, Fairclough and Morrison, packing well, close behind; giving Belgrave 5 in 6 at the half way stage. Jackie pulled away about half way through the final lap to finish one second in front of his rival. On this form our team can feel confident of many future successes, but I fear that they will soon have a strike on their hands, seeing the condition of their running kit after each outing. I feel sure we will have a "Mum's" strike! Is the Hon. Treasurer prepared to buy a Washing Machine? J.H. Eds. It would rarely be used Jack. Most Cross Country runners find it more convenient to be able to stand their kit up against the wall. When it gets badly "cracked" they buy some more! RESULT At the same meeting Roger Hudson was our first lad home in the Boy's race, followed by J.Allan and young Pearson, whose action looks more like father Geoff's each time out. This was the first time these lads had run in this standard, and with further races behind them they are sure to show the improvement that enthusiasm and club spirit invariably bring. items.label: January 1961
items.sum: Report of the London to Brighton walk on 17 September 1960, where Belgrave were 4th in a close team race and Ray Hall retained the club's Belgrave Cup.
items.s: THE LONDON-BRIGHTON WALK Report of the London to Brighton walk on 17 September 1960, where Belgrave were 4th in a close team race and Ray Hall retained the club's Belgrave Cup. In what must have been the most exciting team race for years (only 10 points covered the first 5 teams) Belgrave were edged to an uncharacteristic 4th. Why has this race glamour? Why has this race such popularity? Why?----because it's quicker and more comfortable to go by train, and the competitors who lined up at 7am on the 17th Sept. to await the first stroke of Big Ben don't like doing things the easy way. Amongst the competitors were seven Belgravians who were also contesting amongst themselves for the Belgrave Cup. The early pace of Don Thompson was amazing to watch---especially from behind! and he soon moved well away and out of sight. With the individual winner decided so soon most interest centred on the team race; and with each of the first 4 teams taking a turn in the lead this interest was sustained throughout. Poor George Beecham had one of those very rare races (for him) where the distance must have seemed like 100 miles. Between Crawley and Brighton he was forced to drop 11 places. It was ironical that his misfortune should contribute towards the excitement of the team contest. The "Belgrave" Cup was retained by Ray Hall, rather unfit after his Roman holiday, with John Morris gaining his first runners-up medal in a Club Championship. George held on to gain the 3rd medal, and John Keown made up the scoring four. Has anybody a spare pair of legs for Harry Shields still suffering from a large slice of Roman history?! RESULTS R.C.H. items.s: BELS. WIN HIGHGATE OPEN '7': Middleton in form: Report and results of the Highgate Open 7 miles walk, the first of the London sevens, won by Belgrave A, level on 55 points with Met. W.C., with Ray Middleton 6th. Despite being without Stan Vickers, Eric Hall and George Williams---all taking a well earned rest---Belgrave still managed to notch up another victory in this premier event. This was the first of the London "sevens" and 21 Belgravians turned out in the field of 192 starters. The job of leading the team to victory went to Ray Middleton who was in great form. His sixth place was an excellent performance only one second behind 5th and 19 secs behind 4th places. Ray Hall and John Knifton walked steadily throughout and Bobby Barnes, taking one step to everbody else's two, backed up well. When John Knifton finished, each of the 3 leading teams were awaiting their last scoring man. For Belgrave to win "Boots" Barnes had to finish at least 9 places ahead of his rivals' opposite numbers. He did just that-exactly; and the Bels clinched another title. RESULT SCRATCH TEAM RESULT 1. BELGRAVE H "A"....(Middleton 6,Hall 11,Knifton 16,Barnes 22)......55 pts 2. Met. Although still without our Internationals the 'A' team made a gallant attempt to repeat their Highgate win, but had to give best to Met.W.C. this time. Our scoring four were Ray Middleton 6th, over a minute faster than last year; Ray Hall 14th, rumour says he's past it!!; John Knifton 20th, carrying more hair around the chin than on top; and London Transport Champion Ted Smith 34th, having (some say) "hopped on a bus"!! The 'B' and 'C' teams walked very well and Terry Scott improved yet again. Vic Townsend and Gerry Cameron showed what pack training can do, and Don Bartliff walked well for his first "Open" in Belgrave colours. What? no Belgrave man or team in the handicap?---shame! perhaps they are saving it! RESULT SCRATCH TEAM RESULT 1. Met. W.C. "A".....(2,5,13,24)...........44 pts 2. items.sum: Report and results of the 41st Belgrave Open 7 miles walk at Wimbledon on 26 November 1960, won by Ken Matthews, with Belgrave retaining the Berman Cup and winning the team handicap.
items.s: THE 41ST BELGRAVE OPEN '7' Report and results of the 41st Belgrave Open 7 miles walk at Wimbledon on 26 November 1960, won by Ken Matthews, with Belgrave retaining the Berman Cup and winning the team handicap. It was Matthews, Matthews, Matthews all the way in the Belgrave Open '7' at Wimbledon on November 26th. Ken Matthews (Royal Sutton Coldfield W.C.), the A.A.A. 7 mile track champion, was an easy winner; though his time of 52:30 was 3 mins. slower than his record of 3 years ago. In second place was the much improved Bob Clark (Poly) with Eric Hall occupying the same position as last year, third. Fourth was Stan Vickers and fifth, the Olympic 50 Kilos gold medallist Don Thompson (Met.W.C.)----a nap hand of considerable note! Matthews went into an immediate lead and after barely half a mile led the 180 competitors by nearly 100 yds! a few eyebrows were raised but as far as could be seen------no feet. About his victory there was little doubt. The interesting battle was the second place duel between Eric Hall and Polytechnic's Clark. These two were fighting it out together for about 3 miles when, just short of Pepys Hill, Clark moved ahead increasing his lead up the hill. Stan Vickers was a short distance behind, a few yards up on Thompson, with Rays, Middleton and Hall, within the next six places. Lapping the Common for the second time, the leading position was unaltered and interest turned to the handicap award. Bob Barnes was trying hard to catch John Knifton and was six places clear of Ted Smith 30th. Around the 70 mark D. Fotheringham was maintaining a short lead over Cyril Yescombe and Johnny Morris, and a little further back still, Bert East had his eyes set on catching George Checkley and another handicap award! The only change amongst the leaders at the finish was that A.G. Thomson (Met.W.C.) had passed Ray Middleton, and the young Surrey walker M. Fullager had moved ahead of Ray Hall. John Knifton had displaced three, with Bob Barnes maintaining his place. With four in the first eleven we were assured of retaining the BERMAN Cup; whilst our 'B' team took the handicap award. In the individual handicap we took second and third places with D. Fotheringham and ----yes! -----Bert East!! RESULT 172 finished. items.label: January 1961
items.sum: Spotlight profile of Ranjit Bhatia, from his birth in London and early running in India through his Oxford and Belgrave records to his selection for India at the 1960 Rome Olympics and election as a Belgrave Vice-President; it gives his Club 6 miles time as 29:50.6 (29:50.4 in issue 143).
items.s: SPOTLIGHT: RANJIT BHATIA Spotlight profile of Ranjit Bhatia, from his birth in London and early running in India through his Oxford and Belgrave records to his selection for India at the 1960 Rome Olympics and election as a Belgrave Vice-President; it gives his Club 6 miles time as 29:50.6 (29:50.4 in issue 143). As the hot Roman sun sank to the west, casting the Stadia Olympia into shadow, Ranjit Bhatia stepped on to the brick-red track for an Olympic 5,000 metres heat. At 24 years of age Ranjit had gained the highest award attainable by an athlete-that of representing his country at an Olympic Games. Ranjit Bhatia was born in the Middlesex hospital on the 27th May 1936. A year later he had moved to Eastern India where he lived until 1948, when that part of the country became Pakistan. Those troubled times forced him to depart to Delhi in great haste, where, four years later, his athletics career commenced. When in 1957, he left India for a two-year mathematics scholarship at Oxford he had already won the Indian Universities' 1500 metres (4:10.6) and placed second in the 800 metres (1:58.4); but these times were no real guide to his future. During his first year he did not find the change of climate to his liking-and in any event studies came first-but even so he reduced his best mile time to 4:16.0 when running for O.U.A.C. v Middx and had won his first Club medal when finishing third in Belgrave's one mile championship. Contrary to popular belief about Asian athletes, Ranjit seemed to prefer the longer middle-distance events, and after a winter season of rather mixed fortunes he was a member of our second placed team in the Ilford Road Relay, April 1959. Most of his winter training had been done on the track and by May he had reached his peak with 52.3, 1:57.1, 4:15.5 and 9:16.0. It was fortunate for Belgrave, and India too for that matter, that the next 2 months were spent at intensive study; for Ranjit did so well in his finals that he was awarded a year's continuation for research at Oxford. For the remainder of the summer he left the track alone, "I was bored with racing, so I left it and went to Sweden for a holiday". In the autumn of 1959 he changed his training methods and in the company of such notable athletes as Stephen James, Paddy Montague and Alistair Wood, trained exclusively on the country. Each day he lapped round a circuit which included several steep hills, and by the New Year he was considerably strengthened. In the early months of 1960 he established himself as one of our leading country runners, being our second man home in both the South of Thames Senior (39th) and Southern (61st) and winning the Oxfordshire County Championship. He steadily improved and came into his own when the road relay season arrived. In the Ilford Road Relay he was the fastest man of our winning team and became the second ever Belgravian to break 18 mins in that race. The following week he reduced Pat Newell's record by the fantastic margin of 25secs in the Club 5¾ mile Road Race Championship, recording 27:56.6--a time that should stand for many years. Then came the "National" London Brighton Relay. Commenting on the previous autumn's Southern race "Olympian" had written"---a moderate performance with a few bright spots in the form of Bhatia, Black and Dabbs." Ranjit had raced in third on the first leg. Six months later he was promoted to the 9th stage of the "National", and Olympian's report read"---with a time of 28:56 (third fastest of the day) sliced off half a minute from the Club record, besides being faster than such seasoned stars as Gordon Pirie and Bruce Tulloh". Most will remember this as his finest performance; it was a lesson in relaxed, even-paced running. And so to the Olympic year's track season. Initially he had no thoughts towards Olympic selection, but a 4:08.7 and 13:57 on successive days in the Oxford University Championships in April had many thinking otherwise. In the space of the next four months he had run 3 miles thirteen consecutive times under 14:12--a time only one other Belgravian had ever beaten!! During this period he set a new record in the U.A.U. Championships with 13:56, recorded 13:57 in the inter-Counties, was runner-up in the "Kinnaird" to Alistair Wood with 14:02, and on several occasions raced two "threes" in one week---consistency of running which many faster three-milers would envy. When told he was Asia's fastest miler Ranjit realised that Olympic selection was more than just a possibility; but on learning that the team had already been nominated he gave up the idea. Bob Taylor thought otherwise and advised him to contact Les Cohen whose communication to the Indian Olympic Committee resulted in Ranjit being selected for the 5,000 metres. A vacancy existed in the 10,000 metres event as well, so Ranjit decided to use the Club '6' as a trial, instead of competing in Scotland over the shorter distance. He readily agreed to run alternate laps with Dabbs and Robinson, but although winning the race in a new Championship best performance of 29:50.6 he apologised to one of the competitors for not running his laps fast enough!---such is his modesty. Three weeks later he ran in Rome. It would be nice to record that he won through his heat, but he didn't. His peformance dropped in the same sort of proportion as did those of Britain's 5,000 metres runners; although his only comment was "I didn't feel up to it" and the matter closed! Thus we say goodbye to an athlete who endeared himself to us all. It was to honour not only his running prowess but also his modesty and love of Belgrave Harriers that at the A.G.M. 1960 he was elected a Vice-President. L.E.R. items.sum: Report of the 13th Chelmsford road relay, where Belgrave finished 3rd behind Aylesford P.M. and Woodford Green, with Jack Brown briefly taking the lead and Cliff Roffey in his last race in England.
items.s: BELS. PLACED IN CHELMSFORD RELAY Report of the 13th Chelmsford road relay, where Belgrave finished 3rd behind Aylesford P.M. and Woodford Green, with Jack Brown briefly taking the lead and Cliff Roffey in his last race in England. It was third nearly all the way in this the 13th Chelmsford promotion. The exception was Jack Brown, now running with much of the fire shown in his pre-Cyprus days, who moved up to 1st place on the fourth of the six stages. Taking over from Cliff Roffey in 3rd place, he soon put St. Albans behind him and moved steadily up to Woodford. Meanwhile, H. Minshall(A.P.M) was sweeping past Thurrock & St Albans and with little under a mile to go was on Jack's heels. But at this point Jack moved away, catching Crump (Woodford) to hand over to Charlie Dabbs in the lead. Eric Gebbett, running his now customary stage 1, had got us off to a good start by finishing third. Using the "mile to go" post as did Jack, he split the leading group--only Hempstead and Ponders End staying with him. It was only up the finishing straight that they re-passed him. Although passed by T. Smith (Ipswich) and W. Heiburg (Woodford) Jumbo Masters, on the next stage, pegged back the previous leaders and so retained 3rd place. Aylesford, after an excellent run by Frank Sando had moved up from 17th to 4th, just behind. Cliff Roffey ran a well judged stage in this his last race in England. He soon passed Ipswich, although Woodford (Chapman 15.05) had moved further away and Denis O'Gorman with 15.02 had taken St. Albans through to 2nd place. We were still third! It was at this point that Jack Brown took command. On the penultimate leg Charlie Dabbs moved away from Woodford in excellent fashion but eventually had to give way to Mayatt (APM). Mal Robinson, super-confident after his "Brighton" run, set off after the leader as though determined to break the course record, but paid heavily for his too fast a start when he was passed by Woodford (Garrett 14.56) in the last mile. We thus finished, as we had started, third. But our performance was far better than those of the previous two years. RESULT 1. Aylesford P.M. 91:44 2. Woodford Grd. 92:22 3. items.s: Match at Epsom ~ Oct. 15th Belgrave's winning opening cross-country match at Epsom on 15 October 1960, in which American Olympic marathoner Gordon Mackenzie made his Belgrave debut. Our opening cross-country fixture produced a convincing win for Belgrave. Although we had 12 members competing in the Walton '10', and several more assisting with the Open Youths Road Relay at Wimbledon, we were still able to field 14 at this event-a fine start. First man home for Belgrave was Gordon Mackenzie. America's Olympic marathon star was making his debut in Belgrave colours, and although well below his usual form, was too good for all but one of the opposition-D. Brown of the Navy. Gordon was well backed up by Shipley (3rd), Maclean & Shippen (6th), Forey (8th) and Miller (12th). RESULT. items.sum: Report and result of the club's opening home 5 miles cross-country race at Wimbledon, won by Alan Black after Gordon Mackenzie tore a calf muscle, with Joe Dooley third and handicap winner.
items.s: THE 5 MILES X-CTY. RACE ~ Wimbledon Report and result of the club's opening home 5 miles cross-country race at Wimbledon, won by Alan Black after Gordon Mackenzie tore a calf muscle, with Joe Dooley third and handicap winner. Belgrave's Gordon Mackenzie (once known as America's Gordon Mackenzie!) had to be content with second place for the second successive week in this our opening home event of the season. However, it was only due to an unfortunate injury that he allowed Alan Black to gain such a comfortable win. Although six of our leading runners were at Chelmsford the 36 starters were quite capable of producing an exciting race, especially as George Williams, one of our noted walkers, had chosen this race to return to the runners' fold. Black, Mackenzie, Miller and Maclean were soon ahead, but at the "Brook" ( in full flood!) the first two were well clear. Sawyer and Dooley were 5th and 6th through the water, with Jones, Peckings, Williams(!), Penny, Shippen and Mallott in a group 100 yds or so behind. With a mile to go Alan and Gordon were still shoulder to shoulder a full 1½ mins ahead of the next man. It was here that Gordon tore a calf muscle negotiating a ditch and was forced to finish at a mere trot. On reaching the hills Joe Dooley made very rapid headway to gain three vital places and finish a worthy third. This effort gave him a convincing handicap win also. George Williams held his own throughout and should feel well pleased with his first outing. RESULT. Handicap:-1. J.Dooley 26:28 2.R. Bolem 27:25 3. F. Paget 27:27. Pos Name Time Hcp 1 A. items.s: Match at Addington ~ Oct.29th Report of a cross-country match at Addington on 29 October 1960 in heavy going, lost to H.H.H. in both senior and junior races; the text gives the senior score as 96-80 while the result shows 80 to 91. Rain, which had fallen continously for 24 hours, produced stretches of very heavy going on the Addington plough, and caused the rapid obliteration of the powdered-chalk course marks. Ken Miller, Jumbo Masters and Symons of Hercules as a result lost 200 yds or so through going off course. Towl (HHH) was a comfortable winner in 29:53, with Shippen (31:30), Miller (31:35) and Masters (31:40), 3rd, 4th, 5th, Charlie Dabbs (34:40) could not overcome the going and finished an uncharacteristic 15th. Hercules were unable to close in a team, so in a straight fight with HHH we went down by 96-80. The home club were also winners of the Junior match. items.s: BELS. DISAPPOINT IN STH. OF THAMES JNR. Report and result of the South of Thames Junior cross-country championship near Windsor, where Belgrave finished only 8th with Ken Miller their first man in 31st. With Ken Miller and Alan Black in the first four after half a mile and Cyril Forey and Mike Heck backing up well, our team chances looked very reasonable. Then first Alan, and later Ken, dropped to the forties, where, at 2 miles they were joined by Cyril Forey, our new Junior member, who had been steadily making ground. A mile later, with their backs to Windsor Castle, Ken had moved on to 39th, with Cyril four places back; Mike Heck was beginning to move through strongly from the 60's, but Alan was still fading with an attack of stitch, and Brian Sawyer took over as 4th scoring man. Over the last mile all of the team moved forward. Miller up to 31st and Heck passing Forey to 35th place, but we had to wait for Sawyer 93rd, before the team closed in. items.sum: Report of the L.C.C. cross-country championship, where Belgrave took bronze medals after Herne Hill's disqualification, led by Alan Black in 4th.
items.s: PLACED AGAIN IN L.C.C. Report of the L.C.C. cross-country championship, where Belgrave took bronze medals after Herne Hill's disqualification, led by Alan Black in 4th. The bronze medals went to Belgrave again in this year's race, but it was only by a stroke of good fortune, and at the expense of Herne Hill Harriers, that they were gained. Herne Hill suffered the misfortune of disqualification from 3rd place over a technicality involving pacing by one of their ineligible members. We thus maintained our unbroken run of gaining awards in every Championship that has been held. Conditions were probably as bad underfoot as they could have been although we were lucky that the rain abated before the race began. Our boys got away to a good start and Black, Miller, Brown, Dabbs and Johnston were soon prominent, with Masters and Dooley further back but well positioned. At 2½ miles, Alan Black was seen to be running very well and easily in 7th place with Ken Miller on his heels in 9th position. Jack Brown was 21st, Charlie Dabbs (without shoes, à la Tulloh) 32nd, Masters 47th, Dooley 57th, Gebbett(recovering from gastric trouble) 60th and Johnston 64th. A mile further on Alan had moved up to 5th but Ken had fallen to 10th. Charlie Dabbs had found that his lack of shoes was too much of a handicap, and retired. The remainder, with the exception of Jumbo, had made progress-especially Joe Dooley who was enjoying himself immensely making place after place. With less than a mile to go our positions were Black(4), Miller(10), Brown, also without shoes but maintaining his position,(17), Dooley (34), Gebbett (51), Masters (62), Johnston (63). There was little or no change at the finish and our score (with individuals deleted) was 59 which to all intents gave us fourth place. Later we were to learn of Herne Hill's disqualification. It was grand to see Alan Black performing so well- this young man has a wealth of talent and if only he can change his attitude towards racing and convince himself that his rightful position is much higher than he normally finishes, we shall have yet another international in our ranks. Ken Miller can also congratulate himself on a grand effort and Joe Dooley again surprised us all by the progress he makes after a slow start. If his legs could "twinkle" a little harder in the early stages he would be much better placed. Three of our runners lost their shoes during the race. Let us hope they have learnt their lesson before the major championships come round. W.E.L. RESULT 1. Highgate Harriers.....(2,3,8,13)............26 pts. 2.
