items.h: 'IT'S ALL A PROBLEM'.....OR.. When in Rome do as the Belgravians do!
items.sum: M.E.R.'s account of a Belgrave supporters' party's trip to the 1960 Rome Olympics, covering accommodation mishaps, the athletics they watched including Stan Vickers' walk bronze and Eric Hall's tenth place, and sightseeing.
items.s: 'IT'S ALL A PROBLEM'.....OR.. When in Rome do as the Belgravians do! M.E.R.'s account of a Belgrave supporters' party's trip to the 1960 Rome Olympics, covering accommodation mishaps, the athletics they watched including Stan Vickers' walk bronze and Eric Hall's tenth place, and sightseeing. As our train gathered speed and Dennis Logan gave a last cry of "arevederci" to the fast disappearing figure of his daughter on the platform, we settled into our seats to see what the newspaper pundits had to say of the XVIII Olympiad. Our trip to Rome had begun. According to our schedule it should take 36 hours to reach the "City of the seven hills"; and exactly to the minute we arrived. Having got there trouble-free we näiveley assumed there would be no difficulties, but it was in Rome that trouble reared it's ugly head. "Your accommodation" said the most genial, but rascally, Italian ever to be an assistant agent, "has been moved to a lovely villa, not far away". The Villa Gracia was indeed lovely, but over two miles from the City centre and quite out of the way for the stadia. After two nights of Tom Carter and friend Reggie initiating us into the art of late night habits, and giddy climbing over 10 feet high barred gates at 2 a.m., we moved to the Pensione Adriana. This was just outside the station(a magnificent example of modern architecture) and was indeed very comfortable. "Black Wednesday" was our first day at the Stadia Olympica. Hewson out---Rowe out---Salvat and Ranjit Bhatia out; what a start! and then Bruce Tulloh, after a tremendous fight, was also eliminated. But saddest of all we saw the slender, loping figure of Gordon Pirie----the only man to stop the incessant "RA!RA!RA! GERMANIA!" chant of the Germans----finish outside the first six. As we trooped out of the Stadium, a dejected band, the confusion over transport did little to improve our feelings. However, we couldn't remain glum for long, there was so much to see and do. This, Harry Shields emphasised each morning when he mapped out the day's schedule for his family. St. Peter's by 11am, then the Vatican, the Castel S.Angelo and lunch, and then on to the Stadium. "Can we get in the Parthean? we'll see; it's all a problem"!! A problem it was. A night visit to the Colloseum was a must. One's imagination could easily cast off the ruined appearance and visualise a vast marble stadium housing thousands of Romans clad in white togas, gesticulating at the figures in the arena to the accompaniment of lions roaring in the dungeons below; whilst Nero (fiddle and all!) turned down his thumb. Rome is not all ruins, or rather, out of the ruins there often rises beauty. The open air performance of Verdi's opera "Aide" at the Baths of Caracala was indeed spell-binding. Spell-binding too was the view seen from the flat roof of St. Peters, where, looking over the stone balustrade of small sculptured figures, could be seen the Tiber meandering past Castel and hill. The inside of St. Peter's was in itself a wonder. Every stone, mural or font was studded with history. "Christ leant against that colonnade whilst preaching; this mural Michaelangelo painted for his life; this stone------; that window-------," so much for a lay-man to absorb. But all roads led to the Stadia when the noon-day heat was down. "Gee! burn those cinders Morton!", "Come on Radford!", "Viva Berrutti!" could be distinguished from the cheers of the many Nationalities all fervently pleading for their favourites; and each athlete strained even harder to do justice to his support, eager to gain a coveted Olympic medal and all aware that only one man can be the winner. As the evening drew on the hot sun slipped behind the Stadium walls and the ensuing darkness was relieved only by the electric scoreboard and the Olympic flame which fluttered continuously through rain and shine. In a two weeks athletics programme there was so much to see that it is difficult to bring forward all the memorable moments. Though, Thompson striding to a great win in the 50 Kilos walk; Radford flashing to a bronze medal in the 100 metres; Elliott toying with the world's best over 1500 metres; "wild-man" Cerutty running on to the track; Avril Williams throwing the javelin beyond the Olympic record and into second place, only in her excitement, to step over the line and be disqualified; Halberg jumping the 5,000 metres field for a 3:11:0 last 3 laps (60,65,66); Kryzkowiak winning the steeplechase exactly how he wished; the three Americans, after taking all three medals in the "shot", parading around the arena in complete disregard of the officials; the tall lithe negro Otis Davis jumping with abandon when hearing that his winning time in the 400 metres was a world record, and Robbie Brightwell with a new British record failing by the narrowest of margins to qualify for the 400 metres final, come instantly to mind. Most memorable, of course, was the sight of our own Stan Vickers striding gamely into the Stadium to take third place in the 20 Kilos walk. Our 6'X 3' Union Jack which had not been seen very frequently during the Games was waved till the shaft broke! We cheered and cheered, and before there was any quietning Eric Hall appeared in 10th place, his Legionare cap hiding his distorted face as he finished his final effort. It was difficult to know who caused the most attraction, Stan and Eric, or ourselves. Our neighbours were not quite certain for whom we cheered "Up the Bels., B-E-L-G-R-A-V-E, Belgrave!" but their cameras clicked and their movies whirred just the same. And so to those evergreen moments on the social side. Dave Shepherd and Win with Harry Shields and family in the land of spectacle, romance, music and delicious wines, crowding round a small parafin stove on the marble floor for a "brew-up"!; a certain gentleman choosing this particular fortnight in this particular country to have 4 stitches inserted in his head, when no free health-service existed; the look of utter surprise on the face of the East German 1500 metres star S.Valentin, as we galloped past during a hard training session on the sands of the Lido, and the sight of Valentin getting up from his reclining position to train in the opposite direction----mad dogs and Englishmen etc! These, and many more memories come crowding in. As always our last day soon arrived, and as we filed past the beaming Pensione woman, the rascally agent Angelo (what a name!) and on to the Continental Express, our Roman holiday was brought to an end. items.sum: Club news notes: the London Clubs' floodlit meeting at the White City, London vests for Peter Eldridge and Ron Holtum, Len Coleman's chefs' competition, new fathers, a correction about John Bromley's record, and co-editor Clive Shippen's second son.
items.s: HERE & THERE Club news notes: the London Clubs' floodlit meeting at the White City, London vests for Peter Eldridge and Ron Holtum, Len Coleman's chefs' competition, new fathers, a correction about John Bromley's record, and co-editor Clive Shippen's second son. In the London Clubs' Floodlit meeting at the White City on Sept 28th, Belgrave were placed third with Pat Newell (9:7:8) 8th, Ranjit Bhatia (9:9:0) 10th, and Mal Robinson (9:13:4) 13th being our scoring three. In the 5 miles Invitation walk Vickers and Hall were placed 2nd and 4th respectively behind a record-breaking Ken Matthews. * * * * * At the same meeting Peter Eldridge and Ron Holtum gained their "London" vests; Peter doing 48.8 and Ron anchoring the relay team. * * * * * Len "Ginger" Coleman was a member of the triumphant British team in the International Chefs'(!) competition held recently in Germany. * * * * * The Editors have been taken to task for withholding vital information re our increased membership. Both Archie Bedford and Eddie Short claim they were daddies before the issue of our last gazette. Their word is not doubted. After all Archie is capable of almost anything! It is rumoured that Mrs Bedford now has difficulty in deciding who should have the milk (stout!) bottle first!! * * * * * The item of news at the foot of Page 11 in September's Belgravian should have read "------John Bromleys 3 mile record of 15 minutes odd still stands, and-------". * * * * * In attempting to keep track of the recent spate of newly-born Belgravians, your co-Editor, Clive Shippen, almost overlooked that his own second son had arrived!---with 14 years to go before they are even Youths, this newly acquired 2-man paarlauf team has great prospects!! items.s: THE CLUB SEVEN Report and result of the Club 7 miles cross-country championship, won by Alan Black from Malcolm Robinson and Charlie Dabbs, with A. Bishop winning the handicap. A field of 28 took part in this event held on one of the most miserable afternoons of the winter. The start was fairly fast with first Mike Stearman and then Eric Gebbett enjoying a brief few seconds of glory. By 600 yards however Charlie Dabbs was in command with a fair sized bunch of runners all lying handy. Alan Black and Mal Robinson were soon level with Charlie and for the first two miles these three fought it out with never more than a few yards in it. At two miles Alan gradually crept in front with Mal and Charlie only a few yards down. At the end of the first lap Alan (20.53) led Mal (20.55) with Charlie a further 4 secs down. Jack Brown (21.10) was also fairly well up. After these four the field became rather strung out with Hallowell, Johnson and Gebbett filling the next three positions. Stearman, the initial leader, was back in 14th place, and our old friend Macdonald although well down the field was in fine form, vocally that is, and let fly a sizzling stream of abuse at Bill Lucas who will in future know better than to offer "Mac" any advice in the middle of a race! Another to distinguish himself in an unorthodox way was Bob Glover who retired simply because he wanted to watch the leaders finish! Over the final lap the positions remained practically the same except that the gaps increased but Eric Gebbett, now getting fit again after a bout of gastro-enteritis, made up two places. At the finish both Alan and Malcolm appeared to be quiet fit and strong and one can only hope that this result will give Alan a little bit of confidence; which he seems to have lacked in the past. On the debit side mention must be made of the gap between the first four and the remainder of the field; four good men unsupported will get us nowhere in the major races R.L. RESULT Handicap:-1. A. items.s: Match at Blackheath ~ Dec.10th A poorly supported Belgrave team finished last of three in a cross-country match at Blackheath on 10 December 1960. Although we had several runners competing in both the Civil Service and Insurance Championships our turn-out at this fixture was decidedly poor. The already long list of incapacitated Belgravians must have lengthened still further on the day, for the majority of our leading athletes failed to appear. Of the eleven Bels that started only Ken Miller produced anything worthwhile, and it was no surprise when we were placed last in the team result; especially so when five of the eleven were in the last eight to finish. items.sum: The cross-country captain's review of the 1960-61 winter so far: Gordon McKenzie's brief stay, Ron Linstead's emergence, Pat Newell's form, injuries, poor turn-outs and hopes for the Inter-Counties; it says Ranjit Bhatia ran in the Olympic marathon, whereas the Spotlight in this issue mentions only the 5,000 metres.
items.s: CROSS-COUNTRY CAPTAIN'S REVIEW The cross-country captain's review of the 1960-61 winter so far: Gordon McKenzie's brief stay, Ron Linstead's emergence, Pat Newell's form, injuries, poor turn-outs and hopes for the Inter-Counties; it says Ranjit Bhatia ran in the Olympic marathon, whereas the Spotlight in this issue mentions only the 5,000 metres. Since the last issue of the Belgravian we have both welcomed and bade farewell to Gordon McKenzie of the United States. Belgrave Harriers were not exactly unknown to Gordon. How could they be when his wife is none other than the former Chris Slemon of Selsonia Ladies A.C., and close friend of Betty Jones, our immediate past-president's wife. Although their post-Olympic stay with Belgrave lasted but 4 weeks, most active Belgravians have had the pleasure of the McKenzies' acquaintance We hope Gordon's memories of the London-Brighton Relay, two races in Belgrave colours, a Saturday evening social, a Sunday ramble, and the Club dinner will be sufficiently pleasant to persuade him to visit us again soon. Ranjit Bhatia, who ran against Gordon in the Olympic marathon is now teaching at St. Stephen's College, Delhi; and Cliff Roffey, who ran so well in the "Brighton" is now back in Kenya for another 3 year tour of duty. Talking of the "Brighton", what a heartening sight it was to see Jack Brown handing over to Ron Linstead! The former has got back into his running most impressively after his 3 year absence whilst Ron has burst into the limelight in most sensational fashion. Many of us were aware of his potential, but his reluctance to compete unless he considered himself 100% fit and at the height of form led one to believe his intentions were not really serious----until the Belgrave "Open 20" that is. His 6th place in 1:51:49 was a definite warning to the Country's distance runners-----a warning which he underlined, in no uncertain fashion, with 3rd places in the "S.LH. 30" and "London/Brighton" runs. The shorter distance athletes were not exempt from this treatment either, for he chalked up fastest time by far on the Redhill stage of the "Brighton" relay, and was only 3 secs slower than Alan Black in our own Yacht '3'. Unfortunately, Ron is rather injury-prone and will miss the chance of gaining his county colours this January. However, the main part of the season is yet to come and he should find some tough cross-country races a valuable background to his road-running, as have Jack Holden, Jim Peters and Fred Norris before him! We hope to see Charlie Walker out again in the New Year. The tragic loss of his 4 year old daughter in October has naturally curtailed his activities. Several of the lads contributed towards a floral tribute and sent their sincerest condolences to Chas. and Betty, whose young son Stephen helped them magnificently in their time of sorrow. Pat Newell had his first outing of the season in the Match against Mitcham and in his first race for 11 weeks completely pulverised a strong field. His excellent form during the track and road-relay seasons suggests he could well occupy forward positions in the Southern and National Championships. Pat has helped a great deal in "carrying" the Bels through their lean spell these last few years. It rather looks as though he'll be getting the support he deserves---perhaps this will raise him to new heights. Turn-outs for our fixtures have so far not been very pleasing. If 35 can regularly appear in our own closed races, surely we should average 25 at our inter-club fixtures; the present figure is more like 15. Those who rarely miss a fixture include George Piddington, Chris Fairfield Dennis Jones, Eric Penny and Mike Stearman, with another half-dozen not far behind. It is to be hoped that this nucleus will shortly be supplemented by most of our leading runners, who should now be tuning up for the Southern and National events. Charlie Dabbs is another to have joined our long list of "temporarily inactive" runners. Suspected pleurisy has restricted Chas's training for at least 8 weeks, but he should be back in form for the Southern. Most improved runners of the season are at present Ken Miller, Alan Black and, Junior Cyril Forey; but perhaps there are some dark horses waiting for the final run-in before they show their hand---Mike Heck, Jim Radford, David Jones and John Thresher for example. By the time you read this the County Championships will have been decided. We could well have Jack Brown (Kent), Pat Newell (Middx) and one of our Surrey team competing in the Inter-Counties at Bingley. May 1961 bring to you all, the greatest of success-----this, of course will call for a little harder work all round! C.S. items.s: Match at Wimbledon ~ Dec.17th Senior and junior results of the four-age-group cross-country match at Wimbledon on 17 December 1960 against Mitcham, Watford and Hercules, with Pat Newell winning the senior race and Cyril Forey the junior. With Seniors, Juniors, Youths and Boys taking part in one afternoon, there was plenty of entertainment for the many spectators. Arthur Whitehead's new 3 lap course was ideal for the occasion; Boys and Youths doing one lap, Juniors two and the Seniors three. The Bels performed in all four contests, Mitcham and Watford in three, and Hercules in one; and in a very friendly afternoon's sport each club won one match, Mitcham the Senior, Hercules the Junior, the Youth by Belgrave and the Boy by Watford—an ideal way of exchanging Christmas presents! Pat Newell was in a class of his own in the Senior event, with Jack Brown a good second; team support was poor however. Cyril Forey (a great prospect) was a comfortable winner of the Junior race with John Thresher third; and our Youth success was due to Hampshire and Fairclough being 2nd and 3rd. items.label: January 1961
items.sum: Report of the Surrey County cross-country championship at Wimbledon on 7 January 1961, where Alan Black (8th) and Malcolm Robinson (10th) won Surrey places for the Inter-Counties and Belgrave took third team; a stop-press notes Surrey's 6th at Bingley.
items.s: BLACK & ROBINSON MAKE SURREY TEAM Report of the Surrey County cross-country championship at Wimbledon on 7 January 1961, where Alan Black (8th) and Malcolm Robinson (10th) won Surrey places for the Inter-Counties and Belgrave took third team; a stop-press notes Surrey's 6th at Bingley. Running on home ground, over a fast three lap course, Alan Black and Malcolm Robinson ran themselves into the Surrey County team at Bingley with 8th and 10th places respectively, at Wimbledon on January 7th. After one mile Ken Miller, Mal and Alan were together around 10th position; and at the end of the first lap these three were still with the leaders, Mal in 2nd place, Alan 10th with Ken just behind; but for fourth scoring man we had to go back to Clive Shippen in 52nd place - seemingly ruling us out of any team award. With one lap to go the leading group had consolidated, but dropping Ken; but Clive had made up nineteen places and Eddie Short and Eric Gebbett were pegging back places also. On the final lap, R.Langridge (S.L.H.) got away from the field to win by ten seconds; but the next nine places were sorted out only after a desperate fighting finish - 10 seconds covering all nine. Ken held on for 16th place and the Bels took third team award, after a 5 year spell of being "also-rans". items.label: July 1961
items.sum: Editorial apologising for the late issue, appealing for editorial helpers, and urging the A.G.M. to revive Belgrave's struggling field events section.
items.s: EDITORIAL Editorial apologising for the late issue, appealing for editorial helpers, and urging the A.G.M. to revive Belgrave's struggling field events section. Dear Fellow Members, We apologise for the belated appearance of this issue, but since our last publication we have run into many difficulties, not least of which is lack of suitable assistance. It has become increasingly apparent that to produce the sort of gazette we desire, an editorial staff is essential. Offers of help would, therefore, be welcomed from an experienced typist, reporters willing to cover a few events each month, writers able to submit articles or features occasionally and any other enthusiast who is keen enough to take an active part in the gazette's production. We would also like to see members making greater use of this gazette for airing their grievances, contacting old friends, making suggestions or reporting items of interest - whether they be of present or past. Remember, this is your Gazette. * * * * * The most urgent matter requiring attention by our General Committee and the approaching A.G.M. is the state of Belgrave's field events section. It could be argued that no section in fact exists, but this would be unfair to that handful of members (if indeed they number five!) who endeavour to hold this beleaguered fort. Field events Men are naturally more individualistic in their approach to athletics and are, therefore, harder to hold together as a team. They have no common denominator as the track section have; that is - running, and they have greater training difficulties. We are forever hearing the call for more and more tracks, yet compared with the needs of the field events man these calls are trifling. For instance, is there anywhere in England where the hammer, javelin, discus and weight men can train together ? Are there any special field events arenas where there are sufficient jumping pits to satisfy the requirements of the club athlete and the International athlete at the same time ? The answer is NO. It is therefore all the more important that those responsible for Belgrave's field events men should keep in very close contact with the individuals of their section. Each man should feel that an interest is being taken in both his training and competition. Efforts should be made to organise gatherings so that the athletes become more closely acquainted with each other. Enthusiasm is the most important factor in producing a successful athletics team and it is the ability to import this that is the essence of the successful coach or official. For every part of technical knowledge he needs ten parts enthusiasm. Enthusiasm must abound through and through, and until the team look forward to meeting each other again and the coaches and officials take a personal interest in all their doings, success will not be forthcoming. We hope that at the A.G.M. members will make an effort to pick up the remains of this section, instil some life into it and devise some means of building it up over the next few years - a task of no mean proportions. It can be done, however, just as Tom Carter did it with the Boys and Youths, and Jack Goswell with the walkers. Tom Carter Tom Carter Jack Goswell Jack Goswell

items.label: July 1961
items.sum: Obituary of Allan Peckings, a 23-year-old Belgrave runner killed in a road accident while on holiday in Switzerland.
items.s: ALLAN PECKINGS Obituary of Allan Peckings, a 23-year-old Belgrave runner killed in a road accident while on holiday in Switzerland. It is with deep regret that we learn of the death of Allan Peckings, who was killed in a road accident whilst holidaying in Switzerland. Allan, who was 23 years old, had just completed his final examinations as a Work Study Engineer and was hoping to devote more time to running activities. On restricted training he was already beginning to show promise and showed good form at the T.V.H. and Watford relays. He was also an active member of the Boy Scouts Association, being a cubmaster and editor of his Group's magazine "The Echo". Allan, who was cremated at Lugano on Saturday July 8th, will long be remembered by Club members for his pleasant personality and loyalty to Belgrave; our cross-country secretary could always rely upon him. Those members not actively associated with Allan will no doubt recall his forthright remarks at last year's Annual General Meeting, and it was hoped he would soon find his way on to the Club's General Committee. We are indeed sad to suffer such a loss, and convey our sincere condolences to his family. Allan Peckings Allan Peckings Allan Peckings Allan T.V.H. items.label: July 1961
items.sum: Hon. Secretary's notes praising Tom Carter's work with the Boys and Youths and his own running career, a gift towards the Dick Murphy walking shield, Harry Evans's eightieth birthday and gifts from Ed Lacey and Ken O'Kell.
items.s: HON. SEC'S NOTES Hon. Secretary's notes praising Tom Carter's work with the Boys and Youths and his own running career, a gift towards the Dick Murphy walking shield, Harry Evans's eightieth birthday and gifts from Ed Lacey and Ken O'Kell. A feature of all our Meetings these days, both on Track and Cross-country, is the tremendous promise of our Boys and Youths. Their neat appearance, evident enthusiasm and undoubted ability lead us to wonder to what heights they will carry Belgrave in the years ahead. It certainly is a grand sight to see such convincing evidence of a great Belgrave future. The personality who has done more than anyone else to bring about this pleasing state of affairs is Tom Carter. His great experience combined with ever-present humour, and his conscientious and self-less work with the lads has really produced first-class results. Tom first came on the Belgrave scene in 1930, when his stylish striding around Battersea Park Track caused all the experts to predict a great future for him. Tom quickly had his minor successes, and he will be the first to admit that his size in hats increased somewhat for a short while! but the Belgrave "treatment" and Tom's innate good sense quickly corrected that! Suffice it to say that in 1931 he scored in our winning Surrey County cross-country team and from then on it took a very good man indeed to keep him out of our victorious teams. In 1936 he achieved every cross-country runner's goal by gaining his International vest and in the same year he was third in the A.A.A. 10 miles Championship. He was the winner of the Southern Counties C.C. Association's 10 miles title in 1946 and had dual wins in the Surrey and Southern 6 miles Championship in 1939. In 1937 and 1938 he had been placed second in the Southern 2 miles Steeplechase, and second place was his in the Surrey County Cross-country Championships of 1935 and 1946. As a team man Tom's record will require some beating. Three times he was in our winning English C.C. teams (1935, 1946, 1948), four times in winning Southern teams, five times in winning London to Brighton Relay teams, and seven times in winning Surrey County C.C. Championship teams. In addition he has been a member of many other winning and placed teams. Tom's likeable personality with his quick wit and irrepressible good humour has always been most popular. His poker-faced comedy acts at the Club Socials in the '30's can still be remembered with a smile, and Tom has served us well in many capacities, not least as President, and his generosity in presenting a Cup for the Club 6 miles Championship some years ago is still fresh in our minds. Despite all his great work for the Club over thirty years - and it has indeed been great work - Tom may find his present services rate even higher, and if we find but a few amongst Tom's lads to contribute only half as much as Tom has done in his time we shall be glad indeed, and we know Tom will be a very happy man! * * * * * Back in 1916 Past President, the late Dick Murphy, presented the Club with a Shield for a walking event at nine miles, and this later became our 10 miles Championship Shield and now carries many illustrious names. During Dick's lifetime it was always his pleasure to come along and present the Shield, and to take care of any alterations as they became necessary. In January Dick's son came along and was prevailed upon to make the presentation and we now acknowledge with grateful thanks a generous donation from Mrs. Murphy which will enable the existing small shields to be regrouped and new silver shields added to cover the next fifteen years. Mrs. Murphy can recall the Club's earlier days when there was little in reserve; a time when she made toffee for sale among the members for the benefit of Club funds! * * * * * All our readers will join in rather belated congratulations to our popular Past President Harry Evans, who attained his eightieth birthday in May. Harry joined the Club in 1906 and won a Walking Championship in our name in 1908. Harry never seems to miss a fixture, Summer or Winter, and we all hope his health will continue and enable him to be with us actively for many years to come. * * * * * We are pleased to acknowledge the gift of a framed coloured photograph of STAN VICKERS by ED LACEY which will adorn the wall at Belgrave Hall. KEN O'KELL, our Captain and champion of years ago, has also promised us something of an endearing nature to mark his pleasure at being a Belgrave Harrier for so many years and your Finance Sub-Committee has the job of considering various possibilities. items.label: July 1961
items.h: THE X-CTY. SECTION: Reflections and Forecasts.
items.sum: The cross-country section's look ahead to the coming season, contrasting Belgrave's road relay form with its cross-country record and naming the young runners expected to improve the team.
items.s: THE X-CTY. SECTION: Reflections and Forecasts. The cross-country section's look ahead to the coming season, contrasting Belgrave's road relay form with its cross-country record and naming the young runners expected to improve the team. Midsummer is hardly an appropriate time of year to discuss activities synonymous with mud and slush but a new season will be upon us very shortly and our prospects are worthy of comment. If a resumé of last season's efforts over the country amounted to anything worth relating I would do so. But it does not - so I won't! Instead, I would rather look ahead, reflecting only when it is not too painful! Why is it that Belgrave's performances in the road relays are so superior to those over the country ? The immense popularity of these events obviously has something to do with it, but other clubs manage to do well at both, notably Portsmouth, TVH and Woodford, in the South. Perhaps it is because we have never stopped tasting the fruits of success in one, whilst in the other few can recall our last victory of note. One thing is certain, the mental approach of our lads at the start of a cross-country championship is entirely different from that of a road relay. In the former it is taken for granted we shall be unplaced, whilst in the latter it is accepted that we will always be fighting it out with the leaders - each man striving to make the team and on doing so giving his "all" so that the next runner can have every yard of advantage possible. A bad run by one of the team seems to produce even more fire and determination from the remaining runners. What a different story from the country. Perhaps we are in need of an Honorary Psychiatrist! In time I think this "road relay enthusiasm" will spread to the tougher cross country events, simply because the right men are working their way into our teams. Ken Miller, John Thresher, Mal Robinson and Bill Kerr are no respecters of reputation and will fight tooth and nail for Belgrave in any race going. This young nucleus will soon be attracting other "bodies" and the "energy" given off will be well worth following. What of the coming season ? Well, as usual, it consists mainly of "ifs" and "buts". However, the acquisition of Bill Kerr will almost certainly ensure an all round improvement. This popular scotsman, formerly with Victoria PK.AC., has shown tremendous improvement over the last year, and his bounding enthusiasm and singular sense of humour should be of as much value to our teams as his unquestioned running ability. "Evergreen" Pat Newell is running as well as ever these days and we can no doubt look forward to another consistent season from him, while Jack Brown, although getting no younger, is still likely to show a clean pair of heels to his rivals, especially when it comes to relay running. These two should provide the experience a young team must have, particularly as the younger element is quite rightly growing fast. The average age of Messrs. Kerr, Robinson, Miller, Thresher Black & Forey is only 22 yrs., so bearing in mind the success they have already shown this could become a Championship-winning combination for many years to come. This encouraging picture could become even more exciting if there were added to this group two of athletics' fittest performers - Dabbs & Limstead. Both Chas. and Ron have already proved themselves in dazzling fashion and when fit and free from injury their addition to the team improves it immeasurably. Unfortunately, they have both had more than their ration of illness and injury and we rarely enjoy the sight of seeing them together in the same team, but when we do - what a difference it makes! The London - Brighton Relay of October 1960 was a good example. At present, they are tremendously fit and have their troubles well behind them. This could be the turning point. The strength of every team is governed by its weakest man, but with experienced men like Charlie Walker, John Davies and Eric Gebbett to complete our teams it is difficult to see where our weakest link can lie. However, as I said last year, "Rome was not built in a day", and although the foundations are nearing completion we cannot yet enjoy the luxury of the finished product. A lot of hard work and determination to do what is best for the team is still called for, but, given a fair share of good fortune, the coming season should show an all-round improvement, especially over the country. items.s: SOUTH OF THAMES SENIOR RESULT: Brief report of Belgrave's poor showing, 16th team, at the South of Thames senior cross-country championship at Stanmer Park, Brighton. Held at Stanmer Park, Brighton, on February 4th, this must have been our worst performance ever. Ken Miller led the field after a quarter mile, but faded to finish 37th. Ventor (98th) ran below form and Joe Dooley, although making considerable ground in the latter stages, could only reach 106th. The remaining finishers were Stearman (127), Johnston (136), Jones D.W. (139), Collier (146), and an unfit Sawyer (148). Surrey A.C., S.L.H. and Reading A.C. took first three team places with 117, 145, and 179 points respectively. items.label: July 1961
items.h: THE CLUB '10' : Easy Win for Newell.
items.sum: Report and result of the club 10 miles cross-country championship on 28 January 1961, won by Pat Newell in miserable conditions.
items.s: THE CLUB '10' : Easy Win for Newell. Report and result of the club 10 miles cross-country championship on 28 January 1961, won by Pat Newell in miserable conditions. Held on January 28th, this championship was held in the most miserable conditions imaginable. Not only was it almost dark, but few could remember the area in the vicinity of the brook being so muddy. Walker was an early leader, but was soon joined by Newell, with Brown and Shippen close behind. On approaching the brook Newell forged ahead and was never troubled thereafter. Brown overhauled Walker at 4 miles and the first five positions were already determined. Joe Dooley produced some strong running over the last 2 miles and gained four places. items.label: July 1961
items.sum: Report on Belgrave's senior and junior teams at the 1961 Southern cross-country championship at Ewell (10th senior team) and the National at Parliament Hill Fields (23rd senior, 32nd junior).
items.s: THE SOUTHERN & NATIONAL 1961 Report on Belgrave's senior and junior teams at the 1961 Southern cross-country championship at Ewell (10th senior team) and the National at Parliament Hill Fields (23rd senior, 32nd junior). "We've not a ghost of a chance in the National, but with a bit of luck, and if everybody turns out, we might get placed in the Southern", so said Jack Brown just after the Club '10'. But the Southern "place" did not materialise. Our 577 points secured us (if that is the right word!) TENTH position. Pat Newell and Malcolm Robinson started well and were soon up in the first twenty, but after one of three laps over this fast Ewell course Pat had dropped to 27th, which he maintained to the finish, while Mal was fading rapidly some way behind. Jack Brown was eventually our second man home, having moved steadily through the field to gain 60th position. Thereafter, the rot had set in. Chas. Walker, vociferous before the start, revised his views after sampling the fast start and finished 100th, just ahead of Ken Miller (116), whilst Eric Gebbett (136) finished two places ahead of our recent county "vest" (!) Mal Robinson. Jack's view of our chances in the National was borne out when at Parliament Hill Fields we finished 23rd with a new club "record" points total of 1386! With this type of performance it was of little consolation to find our old rivals Birchfield Harriers just behind. Little can be said of credit, though Eric Gebett having lost both shoes gained 70-odd places on the last lap to take the "Harry Parker Memorial Bowl" with 129th, and Clive Shippen, after some hard work in the previous few weeks, improved on recent form to finish 196th. Walker (230) and Robinson (285), like Gebbett, ran barefoot after losing their shoes in the heavy mud. Sawyer made his National debut with 256th place and the evergreen Eddie Short completed the side with 290 - non-scorers being Joe Dooley (326) and an injury-stricken Ken Miller (401). Over 700 started. The Juniors faced much the same. After a false start in the Southern, John Thresher and Cyril Forey fell back from 25th and 60th to 95th and 96th, leaving Mike Heck to carry our colours up front and finish 25th. Ted Churchard was 130th and our 346 points total gave us 17th place. Mike Heck was unavailable for the National and our first man was John Thresher (103). The other three scoring members were, a much improved Eric Penny (207), a below form Cyril Forey (211) and the promising Ted Churchard (241). The team finished 32nd with 762 points. items.s: SUMMARY OF MISCELLANEOUS FIXTURES 1960/61. Round-up of Belgrave's inter-club cross-country matches in early 1961 against the 9th Independent Parachute Brigade, Polytechnic, Walton, Aylesford, Surrey A.C. and Hercules A.C. On January 14th we visited the 9th Independent Parachute Brigade at Farnborough for a match against the Brigade team and S.L.H. Pirie was an easy winner for S.L.H. smashing previous course records set by Hyman and Foord by nearly a minute. Ken Miller was a good third, with Thresher 7th, Walker 8th and Shippen 10th. The home teams were close winners from ourselves with S.L.H. third. Highlight of this fixture is the excellent meal the parachute boys always provide! The following week we met Polytechnic, Walton and Aylesford over a course in Richmond Park. Walker showed much improved form to finish a good 6th, but although we had Shippen (9th) and Sawyer (12th) we could only manage third place with six to score, and second with ten to score. On February 11th a match against Surrey A.C. was held from Belgrave Hall and a good turn-out ensured us of an easy win. Hercules A.C. were invited to take part in the Junior race a little before the start and duly won from ourselves with Surrey third. Two weeks later we were entertained by Walton over their course at Esher. This was the season's last inter-club fixture and the Senior match went to Belgrave; Ken Miller being first home in 44.34 with Eric Gebbett third in 45.34. John Thresher was second in the Junior match but the team were defeated. items.label: July 1961
items.sum: Profile of Belgrave sprinter Ronald Holtum, covering his late start in athletics, his wins over McDonald Bailey, his relay record and his club service, with a photograph of him taking a baton.
items.s: SPOTLIGHT: RONALD HOLTUM Profile of Belgrave sprinter Ronald Holtum, covering his late start in athletics, his wins over McDonald Bailey, his relay record and his club service, with a photograph of him taking a baton. "I run because I like running, and I shall continue to do so all the while I get enjoyment from it". Yet this light-hearted comment was by an athlete whose introduction to the sport was via a medical consultant's table. Born 33 years ago at Dover, Kent, RONALD HOLTUM, was advised by Dr. Woodward to run "as far and as often as you can", in an endeavour to heal an injury which threatened to leave him with a permanent limp. This injury had been sustained whilst playing football. For one who entered athletics so late - he was 23 years old - his path to the top was exceptionally rapid. Within a year he had taken second place in the Middlesex County 100 yards and had won the Brockman Trophy short sprint. The following year he startled everybody by defeating the almost invincible "black flash", McDonald Bailey. The positions were reversed a few weeks later in Scotland where, on a grass track, Ron was beaten 9.6 to 9.8 (Unfortunately, not an official A.A.A. time). In 1954 he had his most successful season, recording 9.9 on several occasions to eventually take 4th place in the final of the A.A.A.'s 100 yards event at the White City. But it is as a member of our winning relay teams that he is best remembered. Wherever, and whenever, we entered a team Ron was an automatic choice; usually on the last leg, where his fast pick-up never failed to gain those extra few yards which would take us to a win or place. He was a member of our 4 x 110 yards relay teams which won the Middlesex County Championship in 1954 and 1958, the Southern Counties in 1954 and 1960 and the A.A.A. title in 1954. The teams of 1954, which included such athletes as Ivan Mayers and Clay Gibbs, have long since retired - excepting Ron of course, who is still most active. His consistency year by year has not been due solely to his natural ability, for at 9 stone 4 lbs. this 6'1" tall athlete was far too light to absorb the strain of a full season's top class competition. To remedy this initial weakness he began weight training during the winter months to help build himself up. He now scales around 12 stones, which is an ideal weight for a sprinter. Unfortunately, domestic difficulties and a crushed foot have prevented him from racing this season, but he assures everyone that he has not hung up his racing shoes and will continue to don the "claret and gold" for a good while yet. At a time when the Club is lacking in sprinters this is most welcome news, for his experience will prove invaluable to our younger members. For Ron has often asserted that the only way to get a well-blended and healthy team for the future is to go all out for the youngsters. He has always shown an interest in the youth of the Club and is not one for words only. In 1959 when Frank Simmons was in hospital Ron took over the weight-training classes at Chelsea Barracks and did so again last year when sessions were held at Ravenstone Road School. He has been actively interested in Club activities as a whole and in his time has been a member of the General Committee, Track Secretary and Track Captain, and has rarely missed supporting our teams in the London - Brighton Road Relay. Ron, married and with a five year old daughter, now lives in Wandsworth Bridge Road, Fulham. He is a Chartered Structural Engineer by profession, having managed to combine many years of study with his running activities. Most successful men owe part of their success to admirable wives, and as Ron is no exception it is all the more regrettable that Mrs. Holtum is at present in hospital for a period of several months. Fortunately it will not be long before the Holtums are back to normal again, so we can expect to see RONALD HOLTUM amongst our entries once more and, who knows, he might well anchor the London sprint relay team again as he did last year at 32 years of age! items.sum: Stage-by-stage report of the Ilford Road Relay on 18 March 1961, where Belgrave, the 1960 holders, finished fourth behind T.V.H., Woodford and Mitcham.
items.s: BELGRAVE LOSE TITLE AT ILFORD Stage-by-stage report of the Ilford Road Relay on 18 March 1961, where Belgrave, the 1960 holders, finished fourth behind T.V.H., Woodford and Mitcham. March 18th, 1961. We travelled to Ilford as the holders of the Ilford Road Relay Cup, which we won in 1960, but left with neither trophy no place medals this year. Our 4th place was by no means a disgrace, however, for despite being without the services of Newell and Miller our time was only a minute slower than last year's and was our third best ever. Had Pat and Ken been available we would certainly have been contesting the lead with T.V.H., Woodford, and Mitcham, who finished ahead of us. The proof that we had the beating of these clubs was demonstrated a few weeks later when we finished ahead of both T.V.H. and Mitcham in the National relay (Woodford had not qualified). The story of the race is one of improvement throughout. Eric Gebbett faced stiff opposition on the first leg and although putting up the good time of 18.27 could do not better than 12th - 38 seconds in arrears. Charlie Walker took the second leg and in doing 18.25 improved to 9th place - a good solid effort. We were then 42 seconds down on Polytechnic, who had gone into the lead by virtue of an excellent run by B. Fernee. John Davies, pursuing his even-paced running theme, gained another place to 8th, but his time of 18.45 was below the standard we would expect from a man of his capabilities. Mitcham had taken the lead at this stage and we were now 53 seconds down. Alan Black brought us up three places with an excellent run of 18.26 but we still lost ground on the leader. Polytechnic had once more taken up the running through a first class performance by Brian Turner (17.44). We were, however, within striking distance of the 3rd and 4th teams. Clive Shippen, who has had a poor season owing to domestic troubles which have reduced his training to a minimum, came into the team in the absence of Pat Newell and on the whole ran well to do 19.06. He was forced to give way to Collins of Shaftesbury who went from 6th to 2nd and Lewis of Woodford (10th to 4th), but was able to displace Blackheath. Mitcham at this stage had regained the lead - our deficit now being 80 seconds. Charlie Dabbs, still recovering from a chest complaint, was competing for the first time for some months and was an unknown quantity. He beat 19 minutes by just 2 seconds, but was obviously far from his best and was forced to give way to "Kipper" Herring who put up the second fastest time of the day in taking Blackheath back to 3rd. Next came Ron Linstead, also an unknown quantity, but with a time of 18.31 he showed that he was regaining his form. His fine effort took us back to 6th as Polytechnic were now falling back. We were, however, over 2 minutes behind the leaders who were now T.V.H. John Thresher took the eighth stage and gained a further place although his time of 19.07 was a little disappointing. T.V.H. had gone further ahead and our deficit had increased to 2 minutes 43 seconds. We still had some big guns to come though, so were still hopeful of a place. Malcolm Robinson on the 9th, with a time of 18.29, took us up to 4th and gained 18 seconds on the leaders. We were, however, out of touch with the teams ahead and this left little chance for our last runner. Jack Brown had the place of honour, but despite the excellent time of 17.53 could do little more than gain on all the teams ahead except Woodford. Jack is certainly happier on the road than on the country and we look to him to strengthen our relay teams for some time to come. T.V.H. ran out the winners in record time and Woodford who finished a close second were also inside the previous best time. Mitcham in third position showed they are again a force to be reckoned with. W.E.L. Pos Team Time 1. T.V.H. (rec.) 3 : 04 : 06 2. Woodford Gn. A.C. 3 : 04 : 08 3. Mitcham A.C. 3 : 05 : 01 4. Our main rivals, T.V.H. and Blackheath, were left trailing by 21 seconds and 39 seconds respectively. Eric Gebbett ran with great determination to hold off the opposition on Stage 2, but had to give way to T.V.H (Stacey) by 14 seconds, with Blackheath (Sibley) moving to third 11 seconds away. Unfortunately, Alan Black had to contend with messrs. Haith and Herring, who took their clubs well away, but he held off the remainder - handing over to John Davies in third place with Reading 11 seconds behind. John ran a nicely paced race, but eased noticeably near the end allowing Reading and Walton to all but catch him. Walker set off on the last stage, in the company of Sale and Milner, to gain third place, but was well below his best and not only did he have to give way to his two opponents but Chelmsford (Hill - Cottingham) and Ponders End (McIntyre) rubbed it in by passing him in the last half-mile. items.s: CLUB 5¾ MILES CHAMPIONSHIP Report and result of the club 5¾ miles championship for the Wimbledon Cup on 25 March 1961, won by Jack Brown, with guest Bill Kerr fastest on the day. Held on March 25th, this was the club championship race for the "Wimbledon" Cup, and Jack Brown was the name to be inscribed under that of Ramjit Bhatia - who set such a hot record last year. Although Jack beat Mal Robinson and Pat Newell well enough, he was in turn beaten by a guest runner who has since become a familiar figure to most Belgravians - Bill Kerr. This was Bill's first race since leaving Scotland and no sooner had he finished than he was signed on! On leaving the Common, after 2 miles, a group of three - Kerr, Brown and Robinson - broke away from the main bunch and were still together half way up Cambridge Road. It was here that Mal fell back, leaving the other two to dispute the lead. It was soon apparent, however, that Bill was holding back simply because he was unsure of the way, but on reaching the monument he raced for home in powerful fashion to score an impressive win. Mal regained some lost ground in the final stages, as did Pat Newell, who has been unhappy with his running for some time, but now looked considerably better. The most encouraging run of the day was that of Cyril Forey who showed what a great prospect he is by finishing 5th in 29:22 in his first crack at the event! items.s: WATFORD ROAD RELAY (6 x 3 miles) Report of the Watford Road Relay a week before the London to Brighton, used as a trial for the 'big 12', in which Belgrave finished seventh. Held one week before the "Brighton" relay our 'A' team consisted mainly of runners who had just failed to make the "big 12". Exception was Black who needed a sharpener, and a possible exception, Crookes, who was asked to elaborate on his "5¾" form, so that the selectors could decide whether he or the much-raced Thresher should fill the twelth place the following week. Shippen took first stage and although only 14th after a mile showed a belated return to form by taking eight places to hand over in sixth position. Crookes, who had suffered with some stomach trouble that week, threw caution to the winds and took a further place within 300 yards. Unfortunately he paid the penalty; not only dropping back seven places, but running himself out of the "Brighton" team. Black righted matters somewhat by bringing us back to sixth, but the first three teams were already out of touch and it was now a race for 4th place. Sawyer showed a good turn of speed for a man who does "double marathon" stuff and maintained our position, but Masters, whose first race this was for 4 months because of injury, was forced to give a place on the run in for the final change-over. The ever improving Peckings soon regained this, but stood no chance when Eldon came storming past, and had to be content with seventh place. Maclean, who had not had a happy winter season, showed how much better he performs over the shorter distances by recording 14.53 for the 'B' team. Pos Team Time 1. Blackheath H. 87.49 2. items.h: BELS. 5th IN NATIONAL RELAY: ANOTHER FINE PERFORMANCE ON BRIGHTON ROAD
items.sum: Stage-by-stage report by 'Olympian' of Belgrave's fifth place in the 1961 London to Brighton (National) Road Relay, with a photograph of John Davies finishing on the last stage and the top-ten result (continued from page 10 to page 11; the winner's time is partly misprinted).
items.s: BELS. 5th IN NATIONAL RELAY: ANOTHER FINE PERFORMANCE ON BRIGHTON ROAD Stage-by-stage report by 'Olympian' of Belgrave's fifth place in the 1961 London to Brighton (National) Road Relay, with a photograph of John Davies finishing on the last stage and the top-ten result (continued from page 10 to page 11; the winner's time is partly misprinted). Many clubs never cease to wonder how Belgrave maintain their high standard in this race. Over a period of many years our record is second to none and this year proved to be no exception. Our opponents look down our list of entries, which is usually devoid of "star" names, and write us off as "also rans" but we pop up in the leading places with amazing regularity to confound the critics and surprise the forecasters. Why this is I cannot say for our form over the country for many years has been deteriorating, culminating in an all time low at Parliament Hill Fields in 1961. As soon as the National is past our runners take on a new lease of life and in the Ilford Relay, traditionally held the week after the premier cross country event, we begin to show signs of the strength and depth of our middle distance runners. A new spirit arises and the sole topic of conversation is "The Brighton". The nerves of the team selectors become frayed and the telephone wires between Purley and Shepherds Bush hum with the up-to-date rumours of injury, sickness, loss of form, and other prevalent ailments common to all athletes prior to important events. This year seemed to be worse than most - the running order was changed with alarming regularity - the permutations to be used to cater for every eventuality were more extensive than any football syndicate could devise! In the end it all turned out for the best and those added grey hairs produced by the Running Hon. Secretary during the two weeks prior to the race proved to be quite unnecessary. To finish fifth in such company was a great performance. Even the most optimistic of our supporters gave us no chance against Derby and Portsmouth, so the best we could hope for was third, and there were many clubs who could also lay claim to such a position. Coventry eventually took this place and South London managed to hold us off to take fourth spot. However, these events were unknown to the 20 starters in Old Palace Yard, Westminster, that morning. Not until the first stroke of Big Ben at 10 a.m. did the story begin to unfold. STAGE 1 - Malcolm Robinson (20.32, 3rd fastest). Sheffield's Ken Wood set a brisk pace right from the start but not until Chelsea Bridge was crossed did the pace really step up. We were delighted to see Malcolm respond in a convincing manner and maintain an excellent run right to the end. Ken Wood broke the lap record to give Sheffield a lead of 18 seconds, but Malcolm was close up to the second man and failed to beat the club record held by George Flanagan by just one second. STAGE 2 - Alan Black (25.28, 8th fastest). Alan is one of our most stylish runners and has a great athletic future, so we knew this stage was in good hands. He ran steadily throughout and although forced to give way to Derby and Tipton he managed to catch and pass the Coventry boy to finish his run in fourth position. Derby, through one of the Keily brothers, had established a lead at Mitcham of 51 seconds over Tipton and we were 64 seconds in arrears. STAGE 3 - Pat Newell (28.57, 8th fastest). It had needed the diplomacy of our General Hon. Secretary to get Pat on his mark for the run to Purley. Great fears of a printing strike had hung over our heads during the preceding week as the price for Pat's presence, but Alf's negotiations with a leading "daily" proved successful and a fit and happy Newell set off to fight every inch of the way on this crucial part of the race. The whole pattern changed in a few miles. Heatley came up from ninth to take over the lead and to lower the course record by 17 seconds, whilst Pat, despite an excellent run, was pushed back to eighth by other "big-guns", namely Connolly, Craig, Langridge, and Herring. However, we were still only 63 seconds behind the leaders! STAGE 4 - Eric Gebbett (25.47, 12th fastest). Eric had been given this leg following his return to form over the preceding few weeks, during which he had performed so well in the Wigmore '15'. Unfortunately he was not at his very best and although running steadily throughout and giving a plucky display we had to drop some ground - although still maintaining our eighth position. At Mersthan we were 1 minute 40 seconds in arrears. It was on this leg that Portsmouth became prominent for the first time. STAGE 5 - Charlie Dabbs (22.19, 8th fastest). Owing to illness which had curtailed his training for many weeks during the Winter, Charlie was only a shadow of his best and had to relinquish the later leg on which we have been accustomed to seeing him run so well. The fast downhill start on the stretch into Redhill did not really suit the Dabbs' style but nevertheless he gained a place and although not covering himself with glory can be said to have performed up to expectations. STAGE 6 - John Thresher (13.55, 9th fastest). This is the shortest leg of the race and John, still a junior, was running in his first "Brighton". His performance was above average and compared most favourably with his predecessors on this stage; a good effort which will undoubtedly be the forerunner of many more outings in this race. At the end of this leg Derby were out in front with a 40 second lead and we were lagging by 2 minutes 46 seconds in 7th place. STAGE 7 - Cyril Forey (19.01, 10th fastest). Cyril is a relatively new member of Belgrave and one of our brightest prospects; a lad who gets fit very quickly, has a good judge of pace and can be a champion if he makes up his mind to stick to the hard work needed to take him to the top. This was his first run on the Brighton Road yet he established himself by taking Alan Black's club record for this leg, by one second! and moved us up to 6th just behind TVH. The distance from the leaders, Derby, had, however, widened to over 3 minutes. STAGE 8 - Jack Brown (30.25, 10th fastest). Jack protests that he is getting old, but there are few in Belgrave who can hold him on the road; as he proved by lowering Charlie Dabbs stage record by 18 seconds to maintain our sixth position in the face of heavy opposition. This is the leg where the race can be won and lost, and names such as Hyman (who produced a fantastic new record - 34 seconds better than his own previous best), Wilkinson, Perry, North, Reed, Edmonds, Hogan and Foord appeared - enough to frighten the stoutest of hearts. Portsmouth at this point had built up a lead of 1 minute 11 seconds and we were 4 minutes, 28 seconds behind them. STAGE 9 - Bill Kerr (29.07, 6th fastest). To the uninitiated Belgrave appeared to have gone from the face of the earth at this stage, for the claret and gold vest was nowhere to be seen. Not only that but we were running a comparative stranger, for Bill had only been in our ranks just long enough to gain entry to this event. Unfortunately the club vest which had been provided for him and which was resplendent with his correct numbers had been whisked away in the official coach whilst he was warming up and he could do no more than run in what he wore. How well he ran is shown in his time of 29.07, beaten only once by a Belgravian and that non other than our Indian Olympic runner Ranjit Bhatia just one year earlier. When Bill Kerr passed Mick Firth of S.L.H. to take us up to 5th place we knew that the form he had shown in our road race two weeks earlier was no flash in the pan and our confidence in entrusting him with this crucial leg was justified. This was our greatest "find" for many years and we welcome our new Scottish friend to our midst. STAGE 10 - Ron Linstead (20.55, 9th fastest). How Ron suffered on this day in driving himself over this stage, and the state of nerves he built up is known only to himself. Sufficient to say he spared himself nothing and although losing one place he put up a most courageous effort. The subsequent reaction concerned us greatly but we are glad to know the effects were not lasting. Ron must indeed have been pleased to see Charlie Walker waiting for him at the foot of Dale Hill. STAGE 11 - Charlie Walker (20.54, 5th fastest). With only two legs to go we were now sixth and nearly 5½ minutes behind Derby who had again taken the lead. Charles set off up Dale Hill in his indominatable manner and ran a well judged race throughout, shaking off the persistent Roberts of TVH. Unfortunately the S.L.H. boy, Barber, was in full cry and forced Charles back into 7th place despite the encouragement of our supporters. Nevertheless the three clubs immediately ahead were not out of reach and all depended on the last leg. STAGE 12 - John Davis (17.42, 3rd fastest). John had the dubious pleasure of watching Gordon Pirie set off exactly 30 seconds ahead with Bristol and Blackpool in close attendance. Not only that but T.V.H. (Nottage) were on John's shoulder after 300 yards. Our runner had built up over a period of months a judgement of pace which, although not always to the liking of supporters in its early stages, invariably produces a first-class performance. Showing interminable patience John drew slowly away from T.V.H. and with our supporters suffering every agony imaginable gradually closed the gap on Bristol and Blackpool, who were fighting together some 100 yards ahead. A great effort over the last mile took John into the finishing funnel ahead of his rivals by just 4 seconds and 9 seconds respectively - the best judged race we have seen for a long time. Although our 5th place was far better than many had expected, the gap of 6 minutes between us and the leaders (½ minute per leg) indicates just how much we must improve, but we can anticipate being much closer next year with men like Dabbs and Linstead in fitter condition and our younger runners older in both age and experience. items.h: JUNIOR ~ SECTION Incorporating Boys & Youths: Cross-Country
items.sum: Review of the Youths' and Boys' cross-country season, including third place in the Southern Youths Championships at Ewell, 18th in the National and third in the Ilford Youth Road Relay, with results of seven races (continued on page 12).
items.s: JUNIOR ~ SECTION Incorporating Boys & Youths: Cross-Country Review of the Youths' and Boys' cross-country season, including third place in the Southern Youths Championships at Ewell, 18th in the National and third in the Ilford Youth Road Relay, with results of seven races (continued on page 12). "Of four inter-club matches this season our Youths had three wins," writes Junior Secretary Jack Hampshire Snr. "These were over Sutton, Surrey and close rivals Mitcham." After such a start, and more especially beating Mitcham for the first time, hopes for a good performance in the Surrey Youths were high. However, the race at Guildford proved a disappointment. We were sixth. But the course was very much unsuited to the track style of our leading runners, save Jackie Hampshire, involving three laps of stiff hill-climbing. Next came the highlight of the season - the Southern Championships, at Ewell, where we finished third of the thirty-eight teams. Over 400 started on the one lap three-mile course. After a mile only Tony Fairclough was anywhere near the leaders, but after a further half mile he had been joined by Hampshire and was in the twenties. Alan Morrison, Ken Redwood and David Cocks were together in the forties and Chris Steer near the seventy mark. The leaders had separated from the field as they came down the farm yard and turned sharp right to cross over the plough. Fairclough and Hampshire were still together, with Morrison and Redwood drawing clear of Cocks. With little more than a half-mile to go, up the football field across the stubble and onto the finish, Jack began a powerful stride which swept him past seven runners for 13th position. Six behind was Tony. Ken was 47th and Alan, who just beat in David after a hundred yard sprint for last scoring man, was 68th. We have to go back to 1952 for when the Youths were last placed in these Championships. It reflected credit not only on the lads' but also on the methods of training carried out by Tom Carter, (Combined PACK training of both the good and the not so good boy). Secretary Jack Hampshire says it was a wonderful tonic to all those associated with the club who were present. Parliament Hill Fields was the next venue - for the National. The lads did not take too kindly to the heavy mud. That is, all with the exception of Jack Hampshire. Jack ran his usual strong race, face set in concentration, arms swinging vigorously to come in 25th - and so gain his club 'honours' badge. Next to make the short sharp climb to the finish was Chris Steer (123), just ahead of Mitcham's sub 4.20 miler, Malcolm Burton, with Tony Fairclough 150, closely followed in by Ken Redwood 159. A notable absentee was Alan Morrison who had been confined to bed during the week. The team took 18th of the 66 places. All in all the Youths can be said to have had a good season. The team has been considerably stregthened by the inclusion of both Tony Fairclough and Chris Steer, and with the seasoned Hampshire, Redwood, Cocks and Morrison, not forgetting 'near misses' Howard Satchell and John Jarvis, they can be expected to improve on their performances next winter. Tony Fairclough took his place on the starting line just ten seconds before the race started! Due to fixture 'mix-up' the two cars which set off for Ilford landed (!) elsewhere; arriving just prior to the referee closing-in the teams. The excitement experienced getting to the venue was maintained by the lads in their running when they very narrowly failed to take second place - closer than the time suggests. Pos Name Time 1. J. items.s: Track & Field : Junior section track and field notes on Roger Hudson's record-breaking season and the youths' Southern Championships results, with results of four junior, youth and boys' matches. This has been a record-breaking season for Roger Hudson. Aristotle School, South London and London Schools 440 yards records have all fallen to him this year. His latest time being 52.9! He and Edwin Hawkins represent London in the All-England meeting to be held at Cherterfield; Roger in the quarter and Edwin in the Long Jump. For the first time in many a day we had six competitors in the Southern Championships. The most successful was Jack Hampshire who finished 7th in the Youth mile final with 4:32.3. He finished second in his heat with a time of 4:33.6. Pushed out in the heats were David Cocks, Junior 880, 5th 1:59.7 (!); Chris Steer, also Junior 880, 2:10.1; Ken Redwood, 5th in Youth mile in 4:43.5 and R. Sturgess, Youths 220 yards in 24.4. Continuing his winning streak Roger Hudson ran 2:05 in an Invitation 880 yards on 16th July during the Veterans' Championships. In a special 2 mile race, put on during the inter-club walks, Jack Hampshire had an easy victory over half-miler David Cocks. Event Pos Name Performance 100 yards 2. A. Mead 11.1 3. D. items.s: BELGRAVE OPEN FIELD EVENTS MEETING Charlie Jones reports on the poorly supported Belgrave Open Field Events Meeting at Tooting Bec track on 4 March 1961, with results of six events. CHARLIE JONES WRITES: This year's meeting was held at Tooting Bec track on March 4th, and was the least successful so far. The entries were below those of previous years, and in spite of the fine weather not more than 50% of those entered turned up to compete. As far as the Club are concerned, our entry was so poor one wondered if members wish to support Club promotions. In fact just three members troubled to send entries and appear. items.s: From 'THE BELGRAVIAN' 25 years ago Reprint from The Belgravian of 1936 describing the comic "Belgravian Nights" or "East of Wapping" show at the club's third social of that season. 1936: "BELGRAVIAN NIGHTS" or "EAST OF WAPPING" was the star attraction of the season's third social. "The curtain rose depicting the splendour of the East, with Sheik El Red (A.A.Harley) reclining on a divan, looking a veritable Bluebeard all gone bloodshot. (Note: in our last presentation, "Love in Bloom" it will be remembered that our esteemed Hon. Editor was then only a back-row girl. Well done, Red!). At the Sheik's side towered his Nubian (bleached) slave, Ali Ben Mail, a colossal heap of flesh, but none the less an honest fellow, who calls a blade a blade. At the Master's bidding, Ali ushered in the Court musicians (Jack and Charlie) who gave a good account of themselves on the accordions, and were awarded long and uproarious applause. Next came a slave girl (Percy Wright), a beautiful maiden from the East (End!), but with Ali it was a case of see blondes and bust! Sallying forth, he literally proceeded to knock the stuffing out of the maiden. After this bout (which Ali won by three throws to nil), the slave girl entertained us with a snake dance using a string of best beef sausages. To keep the Royal pot-a-boiling, Ali, with a few passes of his (t)rusty blade, persuaded the Court singer (T. Cotton) to entertain. Of course, Tom always goes down well. Unfortunately, you can't keep a good man down long! After this, the Court musicians got busy again, and to the strains of Eastern music, the Neverwere Dancers entered, presenting a very native dance dedicated to their patron, St. Vitus. This part of the show was under the personal supervision of Miss J. Parsons, whom we all thank for her patience and interest. An easier task would be training elephants to walk the tight-rope, and the chances of success would be greater! Alf. Taylor and A.A. Bird should go far; I am on safe ground in saying the like has never been seen before! "Mick" Walker and "Snaky" Webb, whose dancing reputations are far-flung, should play opposite one another, more often. Ring, the Ruthless, gave a great exhibition of Eastern passion in contrast to his partner, Cecil Penny, who danced with utter abandon. La Josephine, and our friend Ali, put in some fine work, although I am inclined to think the scales were faked when they weighed in!". A.A. items.s: WALKING NEWS Walking section news praising Ray Middleton's form, with results from the Cambridge Open 7, the Boxing Day Handicap, a 31 December 1960 race, the Essex Beagles youths race and the Metropolitan Police 7 miles at Imber Court (printed "Anber Court"). The walking section have, during the period under review, suffered the agonies and frustrations of seeing a re-built team struggle against re-juvenated opposition. The "easing off" of Eric Hall, the temporary retirement of Stan Vickers and the absence of George Williams seemed to give our rival clubs a moral uplift and a feeling that they were no longer fighting for second place. Team results have thus become very close affairs, and both enthusiasm and walking standards improved as a result. However, our boys are still fighting it out up front, and it is only a matter of time before they forge ahead once more. The feature of the last six months has been the walking of Ray Middleton, whatever the distance. Much admiration has come from other clubs about his style. Ray has come to the forefront just when he has been most needed and proved himself a worthy spearhead to Belgrave team efforts. * * * * * The following results were omitted from our previous issue:- Our opening event for 1961 was the Essex Beagles Open Youths & Juniors 3¾ miles at Chigwell on January 7th. Our two representatives were Barnes (10th - 31:22) and Cameron (26th - 33:44). The latter, only a youth, was 7th man home in his age group. On January 14th at Anber Court, the Metropolitan Police held their popular 7 miles event, with 208 starters. Favourable weather conditions meant fast times and Ken Matthews broke his own course record of 48.14. The Belgrave 'A' team seemed to have the race nicely sewn up when, at 3 miles, one of the team was ruled out (he shall be nameless!) Thus Cyril Yescombe, for what must be the first time, was called on to complete what still proved to be a winning 7 miles team. Eric Hall, already showing his old form, was a good second. items.s: Round-up of February 1961 ten-mile walks: the Garnet Cup at Brighton, the London County championship at Battersea Park (team title retained), the Metropolitan Police 10 miles at Imber Court and a narrow match defeat by Surrey W.C. at Banstead. The month of February heralded in the numerous 10 miles events. First of all there was the "Garnet Cup", whose barring clauses prevent the entry of leading walkers. Held at Brighton in perfect weather only John Knifton and Ken Bailey showed good form, with the team having to be content with 6th place. Surrey W.C. took the title, thanks to Fullager and Nihill who were 1st and 2nd! Belgrave placings were, 5. J. Knifton; 22. K. Bailey; 26. C. Yescombe; 34. R. Barnes; 37. G. Townsend; 40. T. Scott; 44. D. Fotheringham; 52. J. Keown; 55. J. Belderson; 72. J. Wilson; 79. P. Wilson. 105 started. The London County 10 miles championship found Belgrave on home ground - Battersea Park. Our team certainly looked at home, and although without Eric Hall they retained their team title. That man from the "Green Belt", Ray Middleton, walked his usual fine race to finish 4th (79.01) behind Clark (Poly.) 76.07, D. Thompson (Met.) 76.11, and Godbeer (Camb.) 76.23. Bob Barnes showed rather better form than in his previous races to clinch our scoring four. Belgrave placings were, 4. R. Middleton; 8. J. Knifton; 9. R. Hall; 16. R. Barnes; 26. C. Yescombe; 27. K. Shields. 85 started. Belgrave members were prominent in the Metropolitan Police 10 miles championship held at Imber Court on February 16th. 'A' Division won the team race and the successful quartette were our own H. McGreechan 10th, D. Fotheringham 11th, W. Belderson 12th, and D. Bartliff 13th - how's that for packing! Cyril Yescombe was first Belgravian home, in 5th position, with G. Checkley (14th), T. Bates (17th), R. McAuliffe (21st), and B. Stevenson (26th) also amongst the 46 finishers. On February 18th we were involved in a tremendous tussle with Surrey W.C. in a straight fight over 11¾ miles at Banstead. items.s: BELS. LOSE NATIONAL '10' TITLE Report and result of the 1961 National 10 miles walk at Loughborough, where Belgrave lost the team title after five years, finishing fourth, with Eric Hall second and Ray Middleton fifth. So Belgrave's name does not go on this National trophy for the 5th consecutive year after all. Even though we were without "Bones" Vickers (saving his energy for other things!) and Ray Hall (stricken with marriage nerves!) we were still in with a good chance. However, "Lady Luck" completely deserted us and John Knifton was ruled out within the first 100 yards. He had but to finish a little ahead of Bob Barnes in the 40's for us to retain our title, whereas a close scoring result pushed us back to 4th. This year's event was held on March 18th over a hilly course at Loughborough, and a field of nearly 200 started. Eric Hall and Ray Middleton walked extremely well to hold 2nd and 5th places throughout. Eric must surely rank amongst the greatest clubman Belgrave has ever had. Over any distance from 2 miles to 50 kilometers he turns out performances of International quality, yet he will always walk for the Bels. however small the race may be. Ray Middleton's superb walking gave him his highest National position to date and it should not be long before he gains an international vest. Bobby Barnes, carrying the Middlesex colours for the first time, was our third scoring man and walked steadily throughout. George Williams completed the quartette, and despite being short of training walked a gallant race. Pos Name (Club) Time 1. K. Matthews (R.S.C.) 74.21 2. E. W. Hall (Belgrave H.) 76.54 3. R. A. items.sum: Walking reports for April 1961: the Met. W.C. 20 km in Regents Park, Ray Middleton's Civil Service win and A.A.A. 7 miles track walk, the Croydon to Godstone race, and the Club 20 miles championship won by Ray Middleton with full result.
items.s: Walking reports for April 1961: the Met. W.C. 20 km in Regents Park, Ray Middleton's Civil Service win and A.A.A. 7 miles track walk, the Croydon to Godstone race, and the Club 20 miles championship won by Ray Middleton with full result. The April fixtures commenced with Belgrave sending 3 teams to the Met. W.C. Open 20 Kilometers event in Regents Park on Saturday the 8th. For various reasons we were without Eric Hall, George Williams, John Knifton & Ray Hall, so we were well under strength. The 'A' team finished 10th, with Ray Middleton 6th (97.04), Ken Bailey 32nd (109-13), Cyril Yescombe 33rd (109-27), and George Bates 44th (111.24); 111 finished. Young Barry Freeman walked well in the 2 miles boys race to record 19.05. The following Wednesday Ray Middleton won the Civil Service v R.A.F. v M.P.A.A. fixture over 10 miles, recording 79.06. George Beecham was also a member of the Civil Service team. Ray Middleton was out again on the next Saturday, this time acting as our sole representative in the A.A.A. 7 miles track championship at Hurlingham. Ray's 54:03.2 was just 3.2 seconds outside 1st class standard, thus missing a possible style award by the narrowest margin. However, only 3 men proved themselves better on the day; these were the near-invincible Matthews (49.43.6), Ilford's Williams (53.08.1) and Cambridge Harriers' Godbeer (53.20). Meanwhile Messrs. Bailey, Bate, Bartliff, Belderson, Fotheringham and Wilson (J) were battling it out in Surrey W.C.'s "Croydon to Godstone & back" race over 18¾ miles. They finished in the aforementioned order 16th, 22nd, 29th, 41st, 42nd and 43rd, respectively. April 22nd brought us the Club 20 miles championship. From the word "go" the ever-present Middleton and Eric Hall (holder) fought out the lead for 10 tough miles, before Ray pulled ahead to win in convincing style and thus allow a new name to be inscribed on the "R. W. Ricketts" shield. Eric, whose work has moved him to the North of England, was not as fit as earlier this year but even if he had been he would have needed all his old form and skill to hold off Ray Middleton in his present mood. Eric kept plugging away in his inimitable style to finish a good second, 1½ miles ahead of George Beecham in 3rd place. Further down the field battle was joined in many quarters. The most forward of these involved Cyril Yescombe, John Knifton and George Beecham, with Ken Bailey a little behind. A dramatic change took place on reaching the cemetery gates (an appropriate place after all!) for John retired and Cyril left the road for a while, thus leaving George to take full advantage of the situation. This he did, piling on the pressure to drop Bailey and finish 3rd. The handicap was won by J. Keown (37.00), with D. Bartliff (38.00) second and J. Morris (36.30) 3rd. Pos Name Time 1. R. C.
