items.s: More X-Country : Match at Epsom - December 9th Report and result of a cross-country match at Epsom on 9 December 1961 over the Surrey championship course, a convincing Belgrave win led home by Charlie Walker and Ron Linstead. Run over the Surrey County Championship course of 7½ miles this match reminded our older supporters of Belgrave's halcyon days of team-running. Although the turn-out was poor our claret and gold colours were well to the front, and with six in nine at the finish we scored a convincing win. After the first 500 yds of this 3 lap course, Charlie Walker, showing something like his old form, shot into the lead and opened up a gap of 20 yds., hotly pursued by Shippen, Miller, Thresher and our ever-improving junior Tony Fairclough. At the end of the first lap he had increased this slightly, with Shippen and Linstead fighting it out with Scurr of Epsom for second place. A lap later Ron had joined Charlie in the lead and Clive had moved away from the Epsom man. It was here that young Fairclough completed the junior distance when lying in the forward position of 6th. The last lap saw little change, apart from the widening of margins, and our two leaders ran in together, well ahead of the field. Pos Name Time 1. C. Walker 44:03 1. R. Linstead 44:03 3. C. Walker Shipley and Linstead took over for the second lap but the last named faded badly on the last circuit and Shipley dropped Walker in the last mile to secure a fairly comfortable win. items.s: JUNIOR - SECTION Incorporating Youths & Boys Junior section review of 1961 by Jack Hampshire Sen.: Roger Hudson's schools titles, David Cocks's junior 440 record, Edwin Hawkins, honours badges, the club road handicap and the 1960 Ryan and H.W. Shields medal competition tables. The 1961 track season did not bring the overall success I had hoped for, writes Jack Hampshire Sen., but perhaps I expected too much, too soon after our successes of 1960. We only had moderate performances in the County and other Championships, but with the experience gained in these races, I feel sure we will have a better season in 1962. It must be remembered that a lot of the lads are now at work and in the throes of adapting themselves to their new routines. Belgrave's strength in quarter miling also extends to the Clubs younger members. Roger Hudson had a remarkable season, winning both the All England and London Schools' Championships. A 52.9 quarter at 15 years of age stamps him as a great prospect. David Cocks, a first year junior has also shown great form over the single circuit, clocking 50.4 in the London County Championships for a new Club junior record - watch out Messrs. Morris, Eldridge and Leroy, you will soon have to face opposition from within. Edwin Hawkins was another to excel in the London Schools' Championships, finishing 2nd in the Long Jump, and thus gaining his London badge. When representing London in the All England meeting he had the mis-fortune to record three 'no-jumps'. Never mind Edwin, international jumpers suffer similar disappointments. Three Belgrave Honours Badges were awarded to members of the Junior Section during the 1960/61 season - two youths and one junior. Tom Carter and Jack Hampshire are very proud of their protegés' achievements and ask our many statisticians, is this a record? The Cross-country season will soon be approaching its height and our Youths' team in particular are looking forward to the big events. Apart from the accession of Chris Steer and Tony Fairclough to the Junior ranks, last year's team is intact. In the Club road race handicap, held from Belgrave Hall on September 21st, fastest times were recorded by J. Hampshire (11.38), A. Fairclough (11.45) and K. Redwood (11.54) The 1960 Medal competitions for the 'Ryan' cup and 'H.W.Shields' cup were another great success. items.label: January 1962
items.h: THE BELGRAVE OPEN YOUTHS ROAD RELAY
items.sum: Olympian's report of the Belgrave Open Youths Road Relay on 21 October 1961 (4 x 2¼ miles, 37 teams), where Belgrave 'A' finished second to Luton by three seconds after some teams went off course.
items.s: THE BELGRAVE OPEN YOUTHS ROAD RELAY Olympian's report of the Belgrave Open Youths Road Relay on 21 October 1961 (4 x 2¼ miles, 37 teams), where Belgrave 'A' finished second to Luton by three seconds after some teams went off course. October 21st 1961. Facing the starter this year were some 37 teams, certain of whom had travelled from places as far afield as Sheffield, Coventry, Luton, Reading, Oldbury, Brighton and Chelmsford to compete in this 4 x 2¼ mile event. This fact offers some indication of the increasing popularity of the event. Belgrave were fielding the strongest team and the first leg was entrusted to Alan Morrison, who brought us home in 9th place - somewhat disappointing but nevertheless a good effort in the face of such strong opposition. Next came Ken Redwood, who set about the teams ahead in no uncertain fashion, moving up to fifth position by the time the village had been reached. Unfortunately, a section of the field went off course and about 10 runners took a short cut which sliced off some 500 yds. and brought them into the early places. Redwood therefore found himself handing over with no less than 13 teams ahead. Jackie Hampshire thoroughly enjoyed himself and passed 10 of those ahead to bring us up to 4th - an excellent performance which gave him one of the fastest times of the day. David Cocks running the race of his life, gave everything he possessed and took us up to 2nd only 3 secs. behind the Luton boy Hyde, who had previously caught and passed him to put up a first-class performance. The confusion caused by those teams mistaking the course presented a most difficult problem for the officials to resolve. In view of the high standard of organisation this was a most unfortunate incident and it can only be hoped that it will not occur again. The result from the Belgrave viewpoint was most satisfactory and points to a good season for our ever improving youths. Their success will be almost entirely due to the guiding hand of Tom Carter. items.sum: Report and result of the Boreham Wood youths relay on 28 October 1961, where Belgrave finished third behind Luton and Surrey A.C.
items.s: 'Bels.' placed in Boreham Wood youths relay : Report and result of the Boreham Wood youths relay on 28 October 1961, where Belgrave finished third behind Luton and Surrey A.C. OCTOBER 28th. We again entered two teams for this event, and were again amongst the medals. We finished 3rd, the winners again being Luton, who this year seemed to have taken over from Hallamshire as the leading Youth team. It is interesting to note that the first three teams home beat the time of last year's winners Mitcham A.C. Our first leg runner, Alan Morrison, followed the pattern of the previous week and handed over once again to Ken Redwood in 9th position. Ken then ran a "blinder" to take us up to third. This was his best performance to date in a team race. The hilly course seemed to be to his liking and his time of 11:23 was ranked 7th fastest of the day - in this company really something! Jackie Hampshire took over for the 3rd leg and held 3rd position; not an outstanding run but he appeared to be feeling the effect of the previous week's outing. More training needed Jack? David Cocks ran the last leg and as usual ran a very well-judged race to bring us home in a creditable 3rd place. The performance of our 'B' team proved that we are at last developing a certain amount of strength at depth. Pos Team Time 1. Luton H & H. 45:36 2. Surrey A.C. 46:08 3. Belgrave H. 46:19 Name Time A. items.s: THE 'OVERSEAS' CUP Report and result of the youths' Overseas Cup race before the club 7 miles, won by Jackie Hampshire for the third successive year; guest J. Bicourt fourth and Alan Morrison taken to hospital with a spike wound. HAMPSHIRE'S HAT-TRICK This race preceded the 7 miles cross-country championships and was held on a crisp sunny day with conditions under foot quite good. After a good start, the leading bunch began to draw away from the rest of the field. A.Morrison was the early leader, followed by J. Hampshire, bent on winning the championship for the third successive year, then came D. Cocks and K. Redwood in close attendance. Before long however, Alan Morrison was spiked, an unfortunate accident which sorely affected his running and consequently he was forced to drop several places. Going down to the polo field Hampshire and Cocks were still contesting the lead with Redwood hanging on gamely. This was still the pattern at the Windmill. Then,however, Hampshire drew away to win by quite comfortable margin, although Cocks, who finished second, was making up ground again towards the finish. Third place went to Redwood, Bicourt, running as a guest, was fourth, and Morrison finished fifth only to be rushed immediately to hospital where he had five stitches in the gash on his foot. All in all, this was a most keenly contested race and congratulations are due to Jackie Hampshire becoming the first youth to complete a hat-trick of wins in this championship. A.W.P. items.label: January 1962
items.sum: Members' news column: Eddie Lacey's views on training, Ranjit Bhatia's news from Delhi University and Mal Robinson's news from the University of Southern Louisiana.
items.s: We hear from people: Members' news column: Eddie Lacey's views on training, Ranjit Bhatia's news from Delhi University and Mal Robinson's news from the University of Southern Louisiana. Have you ever thought what photographer Eddie Lacey thinks about this training and racing business? Well Eddie, following hard upon our appeal for magazine material sent us some jottings that summarised his views. In his time, Eddie must have met a great number of athletes and it seems fairly obvious that his opinion cannot be dismissed as mere pipe-dreaming. Whether or not the pained expressions and agonised features that he usually snaps led him to his conclusion is not clear, but he maintains that training does help! "Some of us are blessed with natural ability. Some have none. To those who have it and can compete on little training, I say train harder. To those who have no natural ability, I say you are the ones who have to train harder than harder." Furthermore Eddie suggests that a great many athletes train in too stereo-typed manner - "experiment with your training" he suggests - and although your resolution and determination must always remain unchanged, your training methods should be adopted and possibly discarded in a quest for the ideal schedule and routine. Senior or Junior, champion or scrubber, runner or walker, however we are all Belgravians and that means we are proud of wearing the claret and gold. Above all it means that we shall never be content with our racing or our final positions until the 'Bels' are once again in the rightful position at the top of the athletics tree. Thanks Eddie for writing to us! We now know at least a couple of things about you. Firstly that you're not just a sadist delighting in candid camera shots of athletes wallowing in the "slough of despond" at Parliament Hill. Secondly that you are a true Belgravian with the interests of the Club always at heart. * * * * * Ranjit Bhatia, now at St. Stephen's College, Delhi University, tells us he is beginning to find form again after a lengthy ankle injury which prevented him from running for a large part of the Indian C.C. season. He recommenced racing on September 23rd when he finished 2nd in the Delhi 6 ml. road race championship. A fortnight later, in the Delhi state track relays, Ranjit ran an excellent 1,600 metres leg in which he gave the state champion 30 metres and a beating! He says however, that he is nowhere near his 1960 peak of fitness yet. On September 28th he won a 3,000 metres in 9 min. 32 secs. and followed this nine days later with a 56.1 victory over 400 metres. Two wins in one afternoon - 1,500 metres (4:8.6) and 5000 metres (15:16.0) - were chalked up on November 18th and a month later he reduced his metric mile time to 4:5.8 in the annual fixture between Delhi University and Aligarh University. These performances are most encouraging after a lengthy lay-off and we look forward to return of the scintillating form he produced in 1960. Ranjit has been endeavouring to change the fixed ideas Indian distance runners have on training. He tells us "the local athletes used to think I was quite wrong when I suggested that distance runners ought to do most of their training in parks and on hills and not on the track. Our coaches in India have got their ideas on distance running from the Americans,anyway after two of our men from St. Stephen's - at my suggestion - took to the English type training and improved by fantastic margin, they are beginning to feel that I am not off my head after all!" Both these men are now the top performers at Delhi University - a fitting tribute to Ranjit's guidance. Ranjit himself is still wearing Belgrave Colours and hopes he will be able to run " a Brighton or two" within the next few years. Nothing would delight us more than to see his hopes materialise. To all at Belgrave Ranjit Bhatia sends New Year greetings. * * * * * Your Co-Editor of many recent Belgravians, Mal Robinson, writes from the University of Southern Louisiana, U.S.A. where he is taking a four year course to further his ambitions as a journalist. Mal tells us he is locally in a class of his own when it comes to miling and over and he has taken over the coaching of the section himself - introducing a new method known as hard work he is already beginning to show good form. In a 3½ miles race he lapped even paced throughout to win in en excellent 16:59.8. The time of the runner up? - 18:04! In a time trial over a fast road course of 20.3 miles he is reputed to have done 1 hr 49 minutes. Mal has been in contact with Fred Morris at nearby McNeese College and between them, they hope to "dust up" the State of Louisiana. May we wish them every success. Eddie Lacey Eddie Lacey Eddie Lacey Eddie Ranjit Bhatia Ranjit Bhatia Ranjit Bhatia Ranjit Mal Robinson Mal Robinson Mal Robinson Mal Fred Morris Fred Morris Dave Mitchell Dave Mitchell Delhi 6 Miles Road Championship 1961 Delhi State Track Relays 1961 Delhi University v Aligarh University 1961 Belgrave Harriers 10 Miles Cross Country Championship 1961 Parliament Hill Delhi India Louisiana, U.S.A. items.sum: Letter from Dave Mitchell, held over from the previous issue, urging changes to the brook crossing on the Club 10 course after accidents, with an Arthur Bruce cartoon of a runner in flippers.
items.s: Letter from Dave Mitchell, held over from the previous issue, urging changes to the brook crossing on the Club 10 course after accidents, with an Arthur Bruce cartoon of a runner in flippers. Immediately after last year's Club '10', your new Co-Editor, Dave Mitchell sent us the following letter which was not then included in the current Belgravian as that was essentially a track and Summer issue and cross-country matters were hardly topical. Since the present issue, however, should be in your hands at about the time this year's event, we consider the merits of this letter can best be judged with close reference to the Club '10' of 1962. Dear Sir, "What's good enough for Elliott ought to be good enough for us!" So retorted an onlooking Belgravian when several competitors in the Club 10 had the effrontery to complain of the hazards and difficulties presented by the crossing of the brook. Ignoring the rather infantile Elliott argument - for I'm sure that Jazy, Waern, Hewson, Lincoln et. al. will maintain that what's good for 'our Herbie' is most definitely not good for everybody else - I most certainly would suggest that some alteration of the course might be seriously considered to obviate any chances of the accident that annually threatens to take place. I know that Messrs. Penny, Carter, Allum and Footer also in their time contended with this "natural obstacle", but the retention of this section of the course can only be prompted nowadays in the cause of sentimentality or tradition or pure sadism - (blow you Jack, I have my Wellington boots on) - I am also fully aware that after ten, or, in the case of Juniors, five very wearisome and distressing miles, reports from competitors as to the state of the course (*@!!*?*)are prone to fantasy and exaggeration. I do know for certain, however, that in the past two years the Junior '5' has been seriously marred as a race by two unfortunate mishaps at Beverley, the wonder is, moreover, that neither of these accidents resulted in injuries of too serious a nature. Cross country, sir, is essentially a trial of speed, strength, stamina, and determination, not I might add a test of agility in which failure might well mean disability. " Horses for courses" might well be an apt adage in this case - but I beg to remind you that unlike our equine counterparts, we have only two legs and furthermore we should like to remain that way. NO DIVING SUITS ALLOWED Dave Mitchell Dave Mitchell Elliott Elliott Elliott Herbie Jazy Jazy Waern Waern Hewson Hewson Lincoln Lincoln Penny Penny Carter Carter Allum Allum Footer Footer Belgrave Harriers 10 Miles Cross Country Championship 1961 Belgrave Harriers 10 Miles Cross Country Championship 1962 Belgrave Harriers Junior 5 Miles Cross Country Championship Beverley the brook, Wimbledon Common

items.s: Welcome to new member Derek Bousey, India's leading triple jumper, introduced by Ranjit Bhatia. We extend a hearty welcome to new member Derek Bousey who was introduced to the Club by our old friend Ranjit Bhatia whilst in India. Derek was India's most promising athlete last season, having leapt over 50 feet in the triple jump on no less than six occasions - he is not yet 21!! We wish him the greatest of success this coming season and hope to see him carry Belgrave's colours through the 50 feet barrier for the first time. items.s: ROAD - RUNNING Distance captain Arthur Penstone on the poor turn-out for road races in the second half of 1961, with praise for several runners and forthcoming fixtures. ARTHUR PENSTONE WRITES:- I would like to say that the second half of the road season was not very bright. Our road runners express a desire to compete in most of the events and I enter teams accordingly, only to find on the day that we are lucky to close in one team. Could it be that Saturday afternoon Bingo is claiming them? Cheers to Ron Linstead, Barry Sawyer, and the terrible twins Joe D. and D. Jones who have shown good form this year, also to Brian Johnston who had an excellent run in his first '10' at Walton. Lastly, about next season, I hope we shall see more of Eric Gebbett and Charlie Walker in the lesser road races. Forthcoming attractions:- Mitcham '15', Wigmore '15', and Finchley '20'. items.s: The Witney '12' : R.L.'s report and result of the Witney 12, where Ron Linstead (5th), Eric Gebbett and Barry Sawyer gave Belgrave third team behind two Bristol teams (result on page 27). A field of 60 runners took part in this event, run over three circuits of a 4 mile lap. Eric Gebbett was soon up among the leaders battling gamely, at this stage Kilby (Godiva)and Edwards (Bristol) were running first and second. What a tenacious runner Eric is, he went through one mile in 4:45 - not much outside his best for the distance - in an effort to hold his rivals. The most improved Belgravian of the year, Barry Sawyer, also started in one of the leading groups, whilst Ron Linstead was once more holding back. Over the later stages Eric tired somewhat and only held off Barry by 3 secs. Ron went by them both, to demonstrate the effectiveness of even-paced running. He overtook Barry at 6 miles and Eric at 9, although he fought hard. The final positions gave us third place in the team race behind two strong Bristol teams. It is interesting to note that our three runners were more than likely be the backbone of our Southern and National teams; thank heavens for plodding(?) marathon runners! R.L. Pos Name (Club) Time 1. items.s: THE BELGRAVE OPEN '20' Report and result of the 10th Belgrave Open 20 on 19 August 1961, won by Ken Honney of Walton, with a record low 49 finishers and Belgrave third team. August 19th Walton's Ken Honney was a fine winner of the 10th Belgrave Open '20', scoring a well-deserved victory over Hicks of T.V.H. in 1hr. 50mins 13 secs. - the fifth fastest time on record. This year's promotion was poorly supported, however, and there was a record 'low' of 49 finishers. This was probably due to the ever-increasing number of road-running fixtures and the previous week's Enschede Marathon which was supported by many home runners. After the usual fast start a group of five runners detached themselves from the field and it was quite apparent that they would not be troubled by the mass behind. With 3 miles to go, Ken Honney broke clear to score a popular win, with Gobey (H.H.H) just pushed into third place. Belgrave were without Sawyer and Linstead, but Denis Jones ran very well and with the support of Norman Stairs and Len Bishop, we were placed third. Pos Name (Club) Time 1. K. items.s: Hogs Back 9½ : Report and result of the Hogs Back 9½ on 16 December 1961 finishing in Guildford, where a depleted Belgrave 'A' team was 11th and Barry Sawyer 14th as part of a 140-mile training week. Held on December 16th over a one-way course finishing in Guildford a depleated Belgrave "A" team could only manage to finish 11th of the 40 teams competing. At the half-way mark, with the long uphill drag over, Barry Sawyer was still in contact with the leaders and Clive Shippen was making steady progress through the field with a group in the forties. Our new Australian member Doug Chugg, was in the sixties having faded after a fast start but this was his first race of the season so a few more races should give him that competitive edge. Following up were Johnston and Jones neither quite at their best. With 2½ miles to go and only the long downhill run to come, Barry was lying ninth and Clive 29th but neither was happy with steep descent and they faded 5 and 8 places respectively. Although disappointed with his run, Barry had held his own against top class opposition for a large part of the way. Yet this race was used only as part of his strenuous training schedule - for not only had he run 15 miles the previous day, but also 8 on the morning of the race. Add to this a two mile run from home to the start, the race itself, and an 11½ mile run home and you can see how this great prospect gets in his 140 miles a week. Pos Name (Club) Time 1. M. items.s: SURREY COUNTY SENIOR ~ Epsom Report and result of the 1962 Surrey County senior cross-country championship at Epsom, where captain Clive Shippen's 11th place earned an Inter-Counties reserve spot and Belgrave were fourth team. Highlight of the day from our point of view was the determined running of our captain - Clive Shippen. Along with our other boys he had a comparatively steady start but moved rapidly through the field to reach the 'teens until on the last laps, he had the unenviable task of leading a tightly packed bunch. His final position of eleventh gained him a place as reserve for the Inter-Counties and a county vest would be a fitting reward for all Clive's endeavours. Chas. Walker, John Thresher and Ron Linstead supported well but we had to wait some 20 places before Charlie Dabbs and Ken Miller appeared. Unfortunately Ken suffered a recurrence of his troublesome back injury. Belgrave finished fourth behind S.L.H., Walton, and Mitcham. Pos Name (Club) 1. M. Gillett (Mitcham) 2. R. items.s: From THE BELGRAVIAN 25 years ago Reprint from 1937 of the Surrey County cross-country championship at Epsom Downs, which Belgrave won for the tenth time in twelve years. 1937: The Surrey County Championship was held at Epsom Downs again this year, on the 2nd January. We were well placed at the start, and after about a mile and a half Hines, of Surrey, was leading, with about nine of ours in the first thirty.At three miles Bert Footer was on Hines' shoulder, having apparently done a bit of "snaky" running when out of the sight of spectators. Penny was next, followed by Carter, Cohen, Ring, and Wood (who won the Surrey Junior Race the week after) in the first twenty places. Our hopes of repeating our win of last year were now very bright; and we next saw the field coming round Tattenham Corner led by Bert Footer. Then came Penny, fifth, Carter sixth, Cohen seventh, Ring thirteenth, and Wood seventeenth. This scoring enabled us to win comfortable from Surrey A.C., thus making our tenth win in the last twelve years. Pos Team Points 1. Belgrave Harriers 49 points 2. Surrey A.C. 98 points 3. items.s: BELS. WIN MITCHAM '15' Report and result of the Mitcham 15, where Barry Sawyer, Charlie Walker and Bill Kerr won the Jim Peters Trophy and Belgrave won the Fry Trophy by one point after a recount, with an Arthur Bruce cartoon of Bill Kerr. Our three 'A' team runners in this event Barry Sawyer, Chas. Walker and Bill Kerr had a most successful afternoon's competition. Barry Sawyer was up with the leading bunch in the early stages and although he dropped back for a while in the mid part of the race, his final position of 5th is ample testimony to the steady improvement he is making. Chas. and Bill ran together throughout the race and although a minute behind Barry were placed 7th and 8th close on the heels of Ted Caiger of Hercules. With three to score for the Jim Peters Trophy our boys beat the Bristol leading trio by 16 points, and in the Fry Trophy competition for six runners our first three boys together with D.W.Jones (55) Len (64) and Alan Bishop (67) beat Epsom & Ewell Harriers by one point after a recount. All round, this was a most satisfactory afternoon's running from the Belgrave viewpoint, and one which we hope heralds in future successes on the road. Pos Name (Club) Time 1. items.label: May 1962
items.sum: Editorial announcing full-page photographs on the inside covers as a permanent feature, thanking photographer Eddie Lacey, and urging members to try the club's weaker 'Cinderella' events.
items.s: EDITORIAL Editorial announcing full-page photographs on the inside covers as a permanent feature, thanking photographer Eddie Lacey, and urging members to try the club's weaker 'Cinderella' events. In scanning through the pages of some old'Belgravians' we realised that virtually none of those early gazettes carried pictures of the athletes whose names became by-words within the club, and whose performances established Belgrave in the fore-front of athletic clubs.We feel that photographs can play a most important part in a magazine of this nature, one of whose primary objects should be the recording of club history. To this end we hope to make a permanent feature of the full page photos on the inside covers. This will also give us ample opportunity to make full use of the generous contributions made by our fine photographer Eddie Lacey. Incidentally anyone wishing to purchase copies of photographs can obtain them from Eddie at 55 Graham Road, Mitcham Surrey. In view of our weakness in certain of the "Cinderella" events we wonder how many prospective Prince Charmings there may be in the club. We therefore urge that the club should attach greater significance to those events at which we do not excel and give them something of a star billing. Let us stage a field event in which everyone can compete and let us see sprinters and middle distance men, particularly the youngsters, having a crack at such events as the javelin or triple jump. Only then shall we discover what potential does exist within the club and only then can we begin to hope to become a great athletic force once again. Eddie Lacey Eddie Lacey Mitcham

items.label: May 1962
items.sum: The Hon. Secretary's notes on the club's approaching 75th anniversary, Frank Simmons' illness, committee elections, Mrs. Savage's honorary membership, the Macher Shield, proposed honours boards, the A.A.S.A. Derby Draw, the club championships at Hurlingham and Tom Carter's record.
items.s: HON. SEC'S NOTES The Hon. Secretary's notes on the club's approaching 75th anniversary, Frank Simmons' illness, committee elections, Mrs. Savage's honorary membership, the Macher Shield, proposed honours boards, the A.A.S.A. Derby Draw, the club championships at Hurlingham and Tom Carter's record. Seventy-five years young this Autumn - that's us! Little is known of our Foundation meeting or of the Club's early days - and if any of our readers have recollections, records, press cuttings or photographs of three-quarters of a century ago, the Hon.Secretary would be glad to have a sight of them. 1887 must have been a busy year for the birth of Athletic clubs for in addition to ourselves, Thames Valley Harriers, Essex Beagles and Queens Park Harriers in the Metropolitan area were also formed that year. Incidentally, at the T.V.H. 75th Anniversary Dinner held a few weeks ago, their original Hon. Secretary was an honoured guest at the age of 91! * * * * * All Belgravians will join with us in wishing our former Chief Coach Frank Simmons, a quick return to normal health after many difficult months of hospital treatment. Frank has done tremendous work for the Club over a long period, and whilst severely critical at times, his loyalty to, and regard for, Belgrave has always been on the highest plane. He is determined to win his present battle and we sincerely hope he will be back with us soon, eager to do everything possible for the Club which means so much to him. * * * * * In the elections for Committee of the Southern Counties Amateur Athletic Association members of our Club were elected as follows:- 1st Les Cohen; equal 4th Alf Harley; 17th Harry Shields. In addition Frank Jarvis serves as a delegate from Race Walking Association and Bill Lucas represents the Southern Counties C.C.Association. Cohen (A.A.A.Championships Hon. Sec.) and Harley (elected) serve on General Committee of A.A.A. * * * * * Your Committee have invited Mrs. Savage to become an Hon. Member of the Club in appreciation of the help she gave to Dick in his work for the Club over fifty years and for the very real assistance she herself has given us over the whole of the period. We are happy to advise that she has accepted our invitation and expressed her desire to carry on helping the Club. * * * * * Our congratulations go to Mrs. Wyn Shepherd, wife of our Dave, on the Presidency of the Surrey Womens A.A.A. * * * * * We are greatly indebted to our two Vice-Presidents Albert and Gus Macher for a generous donation which will renew the useful life of the Macher shield for another generation. This Shield, awarded for our 10 miles Cross Country Championship, was jointly presented by Albert and Gus and their late father (a former Club President) in a successful endeavour to change the emphasis of cross country running. Until that time, most of the smaller clubs never ran beyond seven miles with the possible exception of an outing in the "Southern" when they could not expect to do well. The introduction of a Club 10 miles Championship changed this outlook and introduced a new mental approach which, with fullness of time, gave us our run of Championship wins and placings; and our host of International cross country runners. * * * * * A former Club Captain and Champion over country and on track, Ken O'Kell, has generously promised to defray the cost of an endearing addition to our Headquarters; and your Committee, with Ken's approval, are exploring the possibility of installing two Honours Boards - one to carry the names of Club Presidents since 1887, the other of our Internationals through the years. * * * * * Our past President, Frank Webb, will have advised you all of the Club's intention to give full support to the A.A.S.A.Derby Draw, and of the benefits which will derive to Athletics generally and on our Club in particular. We do ask that every member will do his best for the common weal - that if he can sell that extra book he will not hesitate to get in touch with Frank and do so; that he will really exert himself in his own sphere and see that counterfoils and cash (only) go back to Frank Webb at 50 Longford Avenue, Southall before Monday May 14th. But for additions to our funds of this nature, our standard subscription would need to be between £3.3.0d. and £4.4.0d. per annum, otherwise our activities would be curtailed, Headquarters allowed to deteriorate, and our facilities whittled away. We look to everyone of you to give maximum assistance in this vital matter of finance. * * * * * The Club Track and Field Championships will take place at Hurlingham Track on Saturday May 26th - a week before the main County Championships take place - and we expect first class entries and performances. It is unfortunate that Surrey County have for the first time arranged certain Relay Championships and other events on our Championship Day. This we regret, but obviously our full and undivided support from competitors officials and supporters belongs to our own Club Championships. * * * * * Tom Carter has the wonderful record of being in all four of our winning English Cross country championship teams in 1935, 1939, 1946 and 1948. With the great improvement and success our younger runners are now showing, under Tom's inspiration and guidance, it is safe to say that our next winning team will include his spirit and example even if he is only looking on approvingly. items.s: THE CLUB '10' Arthur Penny's report of the Club 10 miles cross-country championship won by Ron Linstead, with the full result and handicap placings. ARTHUR PENNY REPORTS:- A field of 28 lined up for the start and after a few ribald remarks to the President (!) they were away to a good start over 10 miles of wet going and a pretty full brook. At the end of the first lap Barry Sawyer had a slight lead over Davies, Linstead, Walker & Kerr; the latter giving the impression of only coasting. Shippen, Dabbs and Gebbett were also well to the fore at this stage. Several big gaps opened up during the second and final lap, and when the runners came into sight at the Village. Ron Linstead had built up a useful lead over a limping Barry Sawyer who, in turn, was a comfortable distance ahead of Charlie Walker. David Jones, making a welcome return to the running scene was 9th and John Moore, also fighting his way back, 10th. A gap of nearly 3 minutes separated these 10 from the rest of the field. An interesting race all round and a well-deserved and popular victory for Ron Linstead. HANDICAP:- 1.R.Linstead (1:15) 2.J.Moore (4:30) 3. J.Davies (1:30) Pos Name Time 1. R.Linstead 58:29 2. items.sum: C.S.'s review of the 1961/62 cross-country and road-relay season comparing placings with 1960/61, noting injuries and departures, welcoming Gerry North and assessing the club's runners, with a forecast for next season (continued on page 17).
items.s: THE X-CTY. SECTION C.S.'s review of the 1961/62 cross-country and road-relay season comparing placings with 1960/61, noting injuries and departures, welcoming Gerry North and assessing the club's runners, with a forecast for next season (continued on page 17). Reflections and Forecasts. So we come to the end of another cross-country and road-relay season. some of the team (or should I say teams, for we have seldom run the same team twice) will seek their fortunes on the cinders, some on the Macadam and others, no doubt, in the more pleasurable recreations associated with the summer months. But just how did we fare this winter? Perhaps the kindest way of measuring our performances is to compare them with the corresponding events of 1960/61. This is what we find:- [table] The most significant feature of those results is, of course, the lack of victory in either season, but the total number of positions for season 60/61 is 95, and for the season just ended, 81 which must be considered as an improvement. The last four results undoubtedly spoiled this season's record, and as those are freshest in our minds, we tend to overlook the earlier improvements. I am sure that the many critics who have been so quick to sieze upon these recent disappointments will be effectively silenced next October. Bill Kerr and Barry Sawyer have been most unfortunate with injuries and we did not have them both fully fit for any race. Ken Miller has been completely out of training with severe back trouble, Alan Black with a fractured foot, and Charlie Dabbs is still travelling the long road back to fitness. Other sad losses, both temporary we hope, are Mal Robinson who is now in America and Pat Newell who when settled down to married life, expects to make a come-back. Now for the faces who are going to appear, or re-appear, in our future teams. Gerry North. This is a name that I hope will inspire all of our runners to great efforts, to increase their training, to improve their team spirit and to give them the determination to provide this great runner with the support he deserves. Gerry is the first ready-made runner to have joined Belgrave since the war, and is already very popular with the team. He and Bill Kerr will provide the spear-head that has been missing for so long, and with our great depth behind them, there is no reason why we should not enjoy a positive glut of medals! The end of the season coincided with the return to fitness of a previous'5¾' winner - John Moore. John is determined to make a successful come-back and hopes to do some road racing this summer for the first time in order to continue his progress. He is at his best on the country and I expect to see him in the fore front of our supporting runners next season. It would indeed be a joy to see Pat Newell return and gain support of the North/Kerr calibre. How about it Pat? Talking of Pat reminds me of a runner of very similar style who is blessed with tremendous natural ability Laurie O'Hara. Although he has run for some time as a means of keeping fit primarily for football, his racing experience is negligible. The form he showed in the Ilford, '5¾' and Brighton indicate that he has a potential of considerable proportions. If he decides to devote himself to realising his potential he should certainly become one of our leading athletes. Any support provided for our front runners must have a young core to provide for future seasons and it is to this group of youngsters that I now turn. John Thresher (22) Chris Steer (19) Cyril Forey (20) Tony Fairclough (19) Alan Black (22) are all runners of great promise. John has already proved himself and shows grit and determination when the going is toughest; Chris I consider to be one of our best prospects; Cyril, blessed with so much natural ability, could well become another Ray Tooby; Tony on his day could beat them all; whilst Alan is at the moment the most experienced of this young nucleus. Our leading youths will be moving up to the Junior ranks next season so it will not be long before our Senior teams will be having a very young look about them! Cont'd. on P.17 Cont'd. from P.5 The experienced element has been, and will be for a while yet, provided by Ron Linstead and Charlie Walker. Ron and Chas. supported almost every one of our winter fixtures and can be relied upon to do likewise next year. Excellent support also came from Barry Sawyer, Eric Gebbett and John Davies but it is difficult to accurately assess the future of these three. Barry expects to emigrate to New Zealand in October, Eric is now a family-man living at Leighton Buzzard and John frequently speaks of retirement - it will be a pleasant 'bonus' if they continue their form through next season also. We are very proud indeed that Ron Linstead should be selected by the Road Runners Club for their four-man team to compete in the Comrades Marathon in South Africa this summer. Ron, I feel sure, will be a worthy representative both athletically and socially. Elsewhere in this Gazette a spotlight has been thrown upon the career of that fine athlete Jack Brown. This was prepared on hearing of Jack's retirement, but he has since told me that the urge to compete again is very strong. In fact, only a foot injury kept him out of our trials for the Brighton Relay, so it is quite probable that a summer's work will see him back into our team again. It will be a while yet before we can afford to lose men of his calibre. In the preceeding paragraphs I have mentioned as many as 18 names, all of whom, on their day, could be runners of considerable class. I should like to see all 18 runners determined to make next season their best ever, for it might well have to be if they are going to make the teams. Others like David Jones, Don Maclean, Ken Venton and our newly promoted Youths will be endeavouring to reach that "top 12" also, so a few fireworks would not be amiss! All sportsmen like a long range forecast, so what about next season's positions in the events I mentioned at the beginning? I think the score will read (top to bottom) 3,1,2,2,1,1,3,2,4,6,4,2,5. Who said I was a pessimist? C.S. items.h: BELS. SECOND IN STH. OF THAMES SENIOR
items.sum: Report of the South of Thames Senior cross-country championship at Maidenhead where Belgrave, starting only nine runners, finished second team to Reading A.C.
items.s: BELS. SECOND IN STH. OF THAMES SENIOR Report of the South of Thames Senior cross-country championship at Maidenhead where Belgrave, starting only nine runners, finished second team to Reading A.C. PACKING NOT FORWARD ENOUGH AT MAIDENHEAD The few supporters who journeyed to this Berkshire beauty spot were well rewarded by a glimpse - somewhat rare these days - of Belgrave's team packing as it used to be. It was a grand sight to see the claret and gold vests massing at the finish and the only regret was that we met Reading A.C. on "their day" which robbed us of first place in the team race. On paper we had the strongest team of the day but through injury Barry Sawyer was forced to withdraw and for various reasons best known only to themselves others who had been carded failed to appear and we could start only 9 runners which precluded us from winning the Cup for the lowest score for a full team of twelve. Don Maclean in inimitable fashion appeared immediately after the start - it is a pity he cannot find a jalopy which could do the distance in a little faster time, we could then depend upon him reaching the starting line with at least a minute or two to spare! Bill Kerr and John Davies got away well and after the first half mile were contesting the lead whilst our other runners were all well-placed. The field disappeared along muddy tracks and over ploughed fields to be seen again in the far distance slowly wending their way up a tough climb which took them onto a ridge high above the surrounding country. The next appearance was at 3½ miles where a particularly rugged piece of plough had to be traversed John Thresher was our leading runner in 18th place with Bill Kerr 20th Ron Linstead 21st John Davies 24th and Clive Shippen not far away 30th. Our 6th scoring man was Ken Miller in 48th position. Ken was suffering agonies with a back injury but managed to keep going very pluckily. Again the field climbed the long slope to the ridge, but were too far away to be distinguished and we had to be content to wait till the finish to see whether the positions had been maintained. We were not to be disappointed. The close packing of our leading runners had served them in good stead and little or no change took place except that John Thresher found the distance a little too much and had to concede a few places. The final total of 167 points gave us second place to Reading who scored 100 points. What a different picture it might have been with Barry Sawyer, Pat Newell, Mike Heck and Brian Johnston in the team! W.E.L. Pos Name Club Time 1. H.Foorde Brighton 41:51 2. M.Baker Horsham 42:12 3. Walton —Wimbledon Ron Linstead's report of the inter-club match with T.V.H. and Walton at Wimbledon, in which Belgrave lost their unbeaten home record, finishing third. Our last inter-club match of the winter saw us lose our unbeaten home record, for both TVH (109 pts) and Walton (203 pts) finished in front of ourselves, who totalled 206 - 10 a side scoring. Leading our lads in was Clive Shippen who ran well to finish 5th, 22 secs. down on the winners. In coming 7th John Davies set up a club record by going slightly off-course on Wimbledon Common for the second time this winter, whilst leading. A pity you couldn't have done the hat-trick John! Close behind were John Thresher and Mr. Erratic himself. In what was for us a not too encouraging afternoon's sport, Chris Steer stood out. Only 18 years of age, he was 15th out of 46 finishers and beat in such men as Phil Vivian, Ken Honney and Geoff Winchester. Ron Linstead. Pos Name Club Time 1. E. Ellis TVH 29:47 5. C. items.sum: Alf Harley's review of the Southern Counties cross-country championships at Caversham Park, Reading, recalling Belgrave's first win in 1934 and reporting sixth senior, third youths and 21st junior team placings, with full results.
items.s: SOUTHERN COUNTIES C.C. CHAMPS. Alf Harley's review of the Southern Counties cross-country championships at Caversham Park, Reading, recalling Belgrave's first win in 1934 and reporting sixth senior, third youths and 21st junior team placings, with full results. ALF HARLEY REVIEWS THE CHAMPIONSHIPS AT CAVERSHAM PARK,READING. On the rail journey to Reading, passing through Taplow my mind went back to 1934 when our first-ever Southern Championships was won. On that occasion, this year's President Arthur Penny finished second, Arthur Allum was 8th and Bert Footer 13th. Close behind were Jack Flower 15th, and Tom Carter 16th; Alf Taylor 27th, completed our scoring team, passing man after man including team-mates, in the last half mile. Close support was given by Micky Walker (33) Bill Rice (40) Albert Shaw (43) and Cecil Penny (70) who had been brought into the team at the last moment. Our winning score was 81 points to the 97 of Surrey A.C. and 111 of Wycombe Phoenix H & A.C., and our joy was great at being first of the 26 competing clubs. Before the Senior event that year, the Junior Championship had been decided and in this race Harry Shields finished fourth, supported by Dave Shepherd (none other than our present Track Hon. Sec.) 20th, E.G.Saunders (38) and G. Chantler (51). We were placed fourth of the 28 supporting teams. A fortnight later, with the 'National' Championship at Hemley Park our Club was placed for the first time. Birchfield were the winners with 88 points, Salford H. second with 112 points, and we were third, with one point more; our six men scoring in 36 positions and Arthur Penny and Bert Footer receiving International selection for the second time. So much for the past - now for the present. The Youths' Race over 3 miles was the first race to be held and we had high hopes of being prominent and so we were! But our third position of the 33 teams closing in disappointed our lads, which is a measure of the high standard they have set themselves. With such an outlook, how can they be denied premier places soon? Of our lads, David Cocks was first home in 13th position, Ken Redwood 22nd, Jackie Hampshire, suffering from vaccination effects, 41st and the team was completed by Peter Edwards in 96th position. In winning a set of team medals our team did well, but we had this feeling that had the luck been with us, we could have halved our score and won the event. In the Senior race we knew we should give a good account of ourselves without getting into the first three placed teams. Portsmouth with six scoring men in 32 positions won from Woodford Green (6 in 41), and South London H. (6 in 82). Our position was sixth of the 46 teams competing with our sixth man in 131st position - a result which certainly did not disgrace us. Bill Kerr was our star man. Early on he took up a position in the twenties, and as the race progressed, so did Bill, eventually running home 15th. Our Captain Clive Shippen gained places over the last lap to be our second man home, passing Barry Sawyer, still suffering from the injury which had kept him out of the South of Thames race three weeks earlier. Experience in the shape of Charlie Walker, was our fourth scorer in the 84th position, closely followed by Ron Linstead (88th) and Eric Gebbett (131st). So we totalled 450 points. We must aim at trimming a third off this as aprelude to a set of place medals. Of our non-scoring runners, it was pleasing to see John Moore out again. Charlie Dabbs is fighting his way back and should he among the scorers next time. John Thresher was not at his best following an injury, and injury kept John Davis out of the team. Joe Dooley and Don MacLean completed our runners. Mac, not for the first time, tried to give the whole field a four minutes start and did well to finish where he did. The third race of the day, the Junior over six miles,now took place. In this Championship our prospects were not bright, and we eventually finished 21st of the 32 teams closing in. Chris Steer led our men home in 57th place, closely followed by Tony Fairclough. Eric Penny 127th and an under-trained Cyril Forey 178th completed our team. We shall do much better in this Championship in future years. Taking the three Championships together, of the Clubs who finished teams in all three races, probably only South London Harriers and Thames Valley Harriers could show a superior record to us on aggregate - and with this we must be well content. I started off with a little history. May I conclude with a little more? In 1928 in the Senior Championship our first man home was Bert Footer in 33rd position. In 1934, the year of our first win as recounted in earlier paragraphs, our seventh man was 33rd. Our improvement in the next few years can be even more dramatic. A. A. H. Results overleaf. items.sum: Reprint from 1937 describing the abandoned Southern cross-country championship of 1937, when the trail was blown away, and Belgrave's decision not to contest the re-run at Dartford.
items.s: From 'THE BELGRAVIAN' 25 years ago Reprint from 1937 describing the abandoned Southern cross-country championship of 1937, when the trail was blown away, and Belgrave's decision not to contest the re-run at Dartford. THE SOUTHERN 1937:....... at halfway our chances of winning the title from Surrey A.C., not to mention a possible individual winner, appeared very bright and all we could do was to wait until the runners had been out in the country again. Then followed a long suspense. Suddenly the runners were sighted, but in the wrong direction. The funnel was reversed, but again they disappeared. It was soon evident that the trail had been lost. Meanwhile, an observer from round the course had reported that the 'Bels' had 6 in 12. Then there was a shout and everybody dashed to a barbed wire fence to see the field come straggling uphill over a cabbage field, running from all directions. It was immediately decided to call the race off. It transpired that the high wind had blown the trail away, but, surely, for a Championship Race, something more definite and not subject to the mercy of the elements as is a paper trail is necessary. Or shall each runner be provided with a map and compass? However, the sad fact remains that the entire field ran about twelve miles over very tough country for nothing; and as for many of the runners the "Southern" is their only 10 miles race, it must have been a very galling reward for their winter's training. No less mortifying was the lot of those clubs who had hoped to have earned a high position in the finishing list. For our own part we feel that Fate has robbed us of what appeared to be a potentially phenomenal win - first two men home, two in the next three positions and the other two scoring men inside the dozen. All of our men had gained ground, including Pat and Jim, who at a short distance from the finish, had increased their lead to 100 yards. Our complete team of twelve would have closed in by the time that the 60th man was home - surely a performance of which even the wildest optimist would never have dreamed. In the annals of the sport the event will go down as "Race Postponed", but to those who were there (whilst hoping that a similar fate will never befall a race again), I think that it will go down as a moral victory for the Bels. It was decided some days later to re-run the Senior race on Easter Saturday, at Dartford. In view of the strenuous programme facing our men, some having Service and International engagements in addition to the normal fixture list, and the unsuitability of the date, we decided not to compete. Our feelings were shared by most other clubs and eventually only 32 individuals comprising four teams (as against 33 teams originally entered) competed in the re-run race - a truly farcical state of affairs. It is to be hoped that suitable reference is made in the records as to the conditions size of field etc., of the re-run race, as there can be no credit in a success of this kind, and it is only fair that future generations shall be reminded that no serious "Southern" Senior Championship was decided in 1937. Pat Pat Jim Jim Southern Counties Cross Country Championships 1937 Dartford Surrey A.C.

items.label: May 1962
items.sum: Profile of Jack W. Brown, Belgrave's most consistently successful post-war runner, tracing his career on track, road and country from his Southern Junior 880 yds win in 1944 to the 1957 Mitcham '15' record and his retirement.
items.s: SPOTLIGHT Profile of Jack W. Brown, Belgrave's most consistently successful post-war runner, tracing his career on track, road and country from his Southern Junior 880 yds win in 1944 to the 1957 Mitcham '15' record and his retirement. JACK W. BROWN Jack Brown has been the most consistently successful Belgrave runner of the post-war years. He has always had more than one string to his athletic bow, and, although he declared a preference for track miling, his performances on track, road, and country have been equally meritorious. Yet he has remained something of a quiet man, gained more self-knowledge, and enjoyed more personal satisfaction than he has publicity. We feel, however, that his retirement from the competitive scene merits a few verbal handshakes and also that there are certain facets of his career and personal philosophy that could serve as an inspiration to athletes, young and not so young alike, The mid 1920s were not the most pleasant years that this country has known and Jack William Brown was born in 1925, a year before the General Strike. Patience and resilience were essential in these years and it is probably more than mere coincidence that these two qualities were so much in evidence throughout his career. Furthermore of course, war broke out at a crucial period in Jack's young life and possibly it is to these unsettled times, that we must attribute his comparative late start as a serious athlete. In fact, although he won the Southern Junior 880 yds. in 1944, his best performance for the mile in 1948 was only 4:30 and he admits to having only started training thoroughly and concientiously in 1950. When Jack did eventually get down to hard training, he brought to each work-out great concentration and intense determination, attributes which were usually obscured to the casual spectator by the flowing relaxation of his naturally athletic style. Jack's rise in the athletic world could hardly be described as meteoric but above all it was relentlessly consistent and from season to season persistence could be seen paying dividends. Progress in the mile for instance was quite gradual. In each of his first two years of training he sliced some 5 secs. off his best performance, being a 4:18 miler at the age of 26. It took him a further 3 years to reach his best performance for the distance of 4:11.8. In competition, too, Jack had often to wait patiently for the victor's laurels. From 1949 to 1952 he finished second (1950 3rd) in the Kent County mile and it was not until 1953 that he won the title. Can you imagine the satisfaction in that victory? Also in 1953 he won the Civil Service mile title in a photo finish with Len Eyre, the Northern Champion, after finishing second on no less than four previous occasions. Can you envisage the faith Jack must have had in his own abilities and training methods? He had set his sights high and he was going to reap the just rewards of diligent and intelligent training. In fact in 1953 and 1955 he gained international honours by running for the Great Britain 'B' 4 x 1 mile relay team in matches against France, and Germany. In addition, for four consecutive years, '51 - '54 he reached the A.A.A mile final - his best finishing position being 5th in 1952. If we now consider, just to quote one example, that the Club 10 mile Cross Country Trophy, the Macher Shield, graced the sideboard of the Brown household for 8 consecutive years (1950 - 1957) it will be seen that our Spotlight falls not only on a greyhound of the track but on a man who could combat the heavy going of the horse rides, the terrors of the Brook and the general "blood and guts" conditions of the country. It is one of his greatest unfulfilled ambitions that he never actually represented Great Britain in any cross country International. In 1957, his best season, he finished 10th in the Southern, 11th in the National and was selected as reserve for the International. This fine form, however, was completely overshadowed by his magnificent performances on the road during the first four months of 1957. During this period he ran five road races and in each of them broke the course record. Dividends were now being paid in full! Those long years of sheer hard work were paying off. His star was now in the ascendant, he went from success to success. It was at this time that Denis O'Gorman was also enjoying an unbeaten run of success on the road and enthusiasts eagerly awaited the clash between the pocket-sized Irishman and our own 'Brown Bomber'. They met in the 1957 Mitcham '15'. For all but the last 400 yds. Jack followed hard upon O'Gorman's heels and his finishing burst carried him to a clear and convincing victory and a record which has resisted all subsequent assaults. This race in the eyes of many Belgravians was the peak of Jack's athletic achievements and certainly established him as one of the foremost road runners in the country. Without a doubt he would soon be collecting marathon titles and he might even achieve his real ambition of a place in an Olympic., European or Empire championship team! But there other things in life besides athletics and Jack, a Civil Servant by profession, had a career to pursue and he was posted for three years to that comparative athletic backwater and world trouble spot, Cyprus. Who in fact knows what this interlude cost him? Admittedly he competed when and where he could and on his return he quickly showed that the old ability still remained by winning the Club 5¾ (strangely enough this was his first ever run in the race) but much of the old incentive had gone and the beginning of this current winter season saw his departure from competitive athletics. He assures us that we have not heard the last of him, and he has agreed to write certain articles for us on his theories on athletics. We are certain that if his writings spring from the knowledge that he has gained in the only way possible from athletics, that is the hard way, they will serve as an inspiration and help to any aspiring athlete, no less we hope than do these details of his wonderful career in athletics. items.s: T.V.H. Relay (cranford): Report of the T.V.H. 5 x 4⅓ mile road relay at Cranford on 3 March where Belgrave's 'A' team was eighth, with stage times for three Belgrave teams. MARCH 3rd A rather mixed bag of performances gave our five 'A' team runners a poor 8th place in this road relay of 5 x 4⅓ miles. On the first stage John Thresher ran with his usual tenacity, and although not yet back to fitness after the injury he sustained at Maidenhead, handed over to Clive Shippen in close contact with the main bunch. Clive showed fine form in gaining five places and handed over to Ron Linstead in 8th position, about 100 yds. behind the 3rd team (Walton). Ron had a tremendous tussle with Haith (T.V.H) but the Valley star was in great form and took his club ahead of us. However, Ron gained three further places and showing all of his old fire and determination brought us to the change-over in 6th position. A below-form Barry Sawyer ran Stage 4 for us, and lost considerable ground on the teams ahead, but his recent injury came thro' this test satisfactorily and this was a welcome consolation. That ever-present member of our team Charlie Walker, set off on the last stage in 8th place and it was fully expected he would take us to 5th, however, Chas. unfortunately had a domestic burden on his mind that day and could do no better than hold his place. Thus Belgrave had to be content with 8th place, four and three-quarter minutes behind the winners, Portsmouth. Day's fastest 1. Hogan (Poly)20:32 2. Eldon (Winds) 20:35 3. items.sum: Ron Linstead suggests reviving the old Belgrave custom of Sunday country rambles, illustrated by a photograph of a January ramble from Faygate, Sussex.
items.s: WHY NOT A RAMBLE? Ron Linstead suggests reviving the old Belgrave custom of Sunday country rambles, illustrated by a photograph of a January ramble from Faygate, Sussex. RON LINSTEAD SUGGESTS A RETURN TO THIS OLD BELGRAVE CUSTOM Bored on Sundays? Had an extra hard race on Saturday? Fed up with training? Then the best remedy for you is a Sunday ramble through the countryside which is in such easy reach. What better tonic is there than 10 hours or so in the freshest of air, getting the City 'fug' out of your lungs? Places like Boxhill or Dorking are just over half an hour's journey from Clapham Junction, and the cost is only about 6/-d. In addition British Railways run frequent excursions to the South Coast and a resort like Littlehampton can be reached in 1½ hours for 12/-d. These rambles can be most enjoyable.They produce a spirit of comradeship, provide a refreshing break from the week's training routine and give ample opportunity to discuss a wide variety of topics. A short break (say from noon to 2p.m.) is usually made to acquire liquid refreshment which is all some of us go for! items.s: MIDDLETON WINS CLUB '10' Report of the Club 10 miles walking championship at Wimbledon on 27 January, won by Ray Middleton for the first time, incorporating a match won against the Police. WIMBLEDON - Saturday 27th January. A good field contested this annual championship which again incorporated a match with our friends of the Police. After a brisk start it looked like a battle between Ray Middleton and George Williams for the individual championship, but from just before half-way, Ray opened up a 16 sec. lead and continued to increase this to 1 min. 17 secs. at the finish to annex this Trophy for the first time. George Williams was not fully fit but walked well to take second place with John Knifton capturing third place by easing out Bob Barnes shortly after half-way with Belderson finishing fifth in a good time of 85:40. It was encouraging to see Gerry Cameron finish so well in this his first try-out over 10 miles and also to have Bernard Eglinton back home again after three years abroad and pushing the lads once more. We were unfortunately without the previous holder Eric Hall who was unable to travel down from Manchester. After a good afternoon's sport we won the match against the Police 148 points to 203 (13 a side). "Evergreen"Joe Wilson popped up yet again to win the Club Handicap from Will Belderson with Bob Barnes third. Our thanks are due to the officials judges and helpers who once again on a cold day enabled us to hold another Championship. MATCH RESULT (scoring 13 a side) 1. BELGRAVE HARRIERS 148 points 2. items.s: 11¾ Miles Walk Match v.Surrey Walking Club. Report of an 11¾ mile walking match against Surrey Walking Club at Banstead on 17 February, lost by Belgrave, with John Knifton second behind Paul Nihill. BANSTEAD - 17th February. Lacking some of our faster men, we lost the team match in this race because of the solid packing of S.W.C. in the middle places. On the outward journey Ray Hall and John Knifton led the field with Paul Nihill (S.W.C) in close attendance. After the turn at Banstead Ray Hall took the lead from John Knifton, but in the later stages Nihill came through strongly and finished a worthy winner while John managed to snatch second place by a few yards, but Ray Hall in third place showing a four-minute improvement on his previous fastest time won the handicap race. Don Bartliff walked a good race with a well-sustained effort over the return journey. Ken Bailey seemed to be doing a steady training spin, while the extra miles suited Bernard Eglinton who shows steady improvement on each outing since his return from abroad. Joe Wilson made a strong effort to beat the handicapper once again, but this was not to be his day. RESULT; 1. P.Nihill (S.W.C) 96:36 2. J.Knifton (B.H.) 97:12 3. R.C.Hall " 97:18 MATCH RESULT; 1. items.s: THE COUNTY '10' Report of the county 10 mile walking championships on 24 February: Ray Middleton won the Surrey title and Belgrave retained the team title, with notes on the Middlesex and Kent championships. Saturday 24th February. We were primarily interested in the Surrey Championship which was held at the Canons, Mitcham. The title holder Eric Hall was not defending his title and Ray Middleton walked extremely well to finish first in the individual championship in 77:26. Ray was in very fine form and he managed to pull back Paul Nihill who was leading at one stage, and then went on to beat him by 1:41. Ray Hall (4th) John Knifton (5th) W.Belderson (7th) backed extremely well and we managed to retain the County Team Championship by the narrow margin of 2 points from Surrey W.C. Our 'B' team of Keown, Morris, Beecham, and Stevenson walked exceedingly well and only lost 3rd team position by 2 points. Will Belderson was awarded the Sir J.Coleman Cup. Unfortunately, George Williams was affected by the cold, never appeared to settle down and was disqualified in the first mile. RESULT. 1. R. Middleton (Belgrave) 77:26 2. P. Nihill (Surrey) 79:07 3. P. Selby (Surrey) 80:24 4. R.Hall (Belgrave) 81:53 5. J.Knifton " 83:03 7. W.Belderson " 84:29 Teams:- 1. Belgrave Harriers 17 pts. 2. Surrey W.C. 19 pts. * * * * * Over the Enfield course in the Middlesex Championships we were not to prove quite so successful. items.s: Battersea Park, Saturday 3rd March, Southern Counties 7 mile Track Championship Report of the Southern Counties 7 mile track walk at Battersea Park on 3 March, where Ray Middleton was disqualified and George Williams finished second to Clark of Poly. This race at one stage threatened to produce something of a sensation. By the two-mile stage, two County Champions of the previous week came under the Judges' ban, Arthur Thomson (Mddx) and our own Ray Middleton (Surrey), while others who were disqualified included Godbeer, (Cambridge). It was not surprising therefore the times were a little slower than last year. George Williams took the lead at 2 miles in 14:47 and was leading Clark by 11 secs. at 3 miles. In the next mile, however, Clark cut down this lead and was 1 sec. ahead of the Belgravian at 6 miles. Then in the last three laps the Poly man opened up considerably to finish in 53:05, some 20 secs. ahead of George. Will Belderson recorded his best time ever (58:00) to finish 11th whilst Don Bartliff finished 20th in 59:05 and gained his 7 mile star for the first time. G. Beecham (23rd in 60:43), J. Keown (27th in 61:11), and J. Morris (28th in 61:11) were our other finishers. In the supporting road events, Gerry Cameron walked very well in the Junior 6 miles, to finish 5th in 51 minutes. items.s: NATIONAL 'IO' LOST 200yds. FROM FINISH! Report of the National and Inter-County 10 mile walk at New Southgate on 17 March, won by Ken Matthews, where George Williams' disqualification 200 yards from the finish cost Belgrave the team title and left them third. NEW SOUTHGATE , Saturday 17th March. It goes almost without saying that Ken Matthews scored his fourth successive win in this National and Inter-County 10 Mile Championship, held from the Standard Telephones Works over a tough 4 - lap course. On this occasion however, he was unusually hard-pressed, for Bob Clark was only 90secs away. From the Belgrave viewpoint however, this was a day of bitter disappointment. Only 200 yards from the finish George Williams was in 5th position and we were virtually assured of carrying off the team Championship.Unfortunately the effort was telling on George and during a bout of sickness, he was disqualified, and this decision apart from ruining our chances of first team placing, also provoked quite a storm of controversy and no inconsiderable amount of coarse comment from some of the more partisan Belgrave supporters. This mishap to George meant that Ray Middleton who finish 6th in 79:18 was in fact our first man home, and was therefore awarded the Frank Thomson Cup. Eric Hall proved as reliable, if not as fit, as ever to finish 14th, with Ray Hall once again revealing his worth by finishing 19th. We had to be content with third team position behind Highgate and Surrey W.C. This was indeed a sore disappointment to us, when it had seemed inevitable that we should regain the National Title. In particular our sympathies were with George Williams, who after walking such a game race became the victim of a somewhat harsh and hasty decision. Pos Name Club/Team Time 1. items.label: May 1962
items.sum: Bill True, the club's walking handicapper, describes the trials of handicapping race walkers.
items.s: VERY 'TRUE'! Bill True, the club's walking handicapper, describes the trials of handicapping race walkers. OUR CARTOONIST INTRODUCED YOU TO "THE HANDICAPPER" IN OUR LAST ISSUE. THIS TIME, BILL TRUE TELLS OF THE TRIALS AND TRIBULATIONS OF THIS HANDICAPPING "LARK"! To me, one of the most mysterious things in athletics is the fact that all athletes consider themselves better handicappers than the appointed official, yet at any A.G.M. no-one volunteers for the job. Why? When I agreed to become walking handicapper to ease the burden of work from Sid Roberts, I knew nothing about the job and had no idea of the amount of work required to produce a good handicap. I awaited the result of my first effort with very mixed feelings, but a reasonable result produced congratulations from the prize-winners and cheeky back-chat from the unsuccessful. In those early days I discovered that a good handicap went virtually un-noticed by most of the competitors. One effort, when with some luck I placed 15 men in 23 seconds in a two-mile match v. Surrey Walking Club, was noticed by the grand total of 1 solitary walker. Now handicap results are discussed, marks commented upon and the promise readily given to try to do better next time. I have accumulated an enormous amount of paper showing race results from all parts of the country. I have been forced to make an intensive study of walkers and walking. I have been pointed out to newspaper reporters as someone able to give the 'gen' on all the competitors. I have even received a letter addressed 'To the man who knows most about Race Walking Fame at last! What I have not found is how to produce the perfect handicap, the perfect system to assess the improving,whilst giving everybody a fair chance, how to give a fair mark to the man who turns up once in two years. But then, that I suppose is a challenge of handicapping and what in fact makes it such a worth while job. Bill True BILL TRUE Sid Roberts Sid Roberts Surrey Walking Club

items.sum: Introduction to the junior section praising the youths' best-ever season, including fourth place in the National, and urging more self-reliance away from coach Tom Carter.
items.s: JUNIOR ~ SECTION Incorporating Boys & Youths Introduction to the junior section praising the youths' best-ever season, including fourth place in the National, and urging more self-reliance away from coach Tom Carter. The Youths have just completed the best season this section has ever known. Their 4th place in the National was a great effort and as we consider them all to be the "sticker" type of lad, a great future seems assured amongst the leading seniors of their day. Only sweat, toil and tears complete with supreme self-confidence and knowledge of oneself will get them there though, and they must therefore lean less heavily upon Tom Carter and use their Junior status to prepare for entry to the Senior ranks. Whilst we do not suggest that Tom should forsake the Juniors altogether, we feel that it might be in their own athletic interests if they were treated a little less as fledglings and taught a little more self-reliance. items.s: YOUTHS EXCEL IN NATIONAL CHAMPS. Report of the youths' and juniors' races at the National cross-country championships, where the Belgrave youths were briefly announced third before being pushed to fourth, and the juniors were 48th. As a prelude to the Senior Championship our youngsters gave us a most heartening display in the Youths event; indeed it was rather unfortunate that some of their more experienced club-mates didn't follow their wonderful example. The field was away quickly and it soon became clear that the Bels meant business for after some three quarters of a mile Cocks, Hampshire, Morrison and Redwood were all grouped in the first two dozen runners. At this stage, Simmons of Derby had opened up a considerable lead which he gamely maintained right to the finish,although at one stage another Midland youngster, Hammond of Coventry, looked as if he might close the gap. At 1½ miles we were still in the Championship hunt when Ken Redwood struck a bad patch and began to lose places. Now there was consternation in the Belgrave camp - it is even reported that Tom Carter stopped talking for once. Then, however, 'Noddy' Edwards, who had been strolling somewhere in the seventies began to make up places at a most alarming rate. He passed Ken and flogged himself until the funnel was reached to complete our scoring four and,as it at first appeared, to provide us with a Championship place. Birchfield were announced as winners, Coventry were placed second and Belgrave third! Tom Carter started talking and there was jubilation amongst our Belgrave supporters. But to our dismay, and to the bitter disappointment of our game youngsters, Sale Harriers handed in their result rather late and their points score managed to push us back to fourth. This was the first occasion that the boys had been out of the medals and in the circumstances it came as something of a bitter pill. We were, however, first Southern Club home and all our lads showed just those qualities that we need in all Belgrave teams. Well done lads! * * * * * The Juniors, over the two lap course, did not seem to be particularly inspired by their younger brethren and all seemed to run well below their usual form. Chris Steer finished first for us but after his recent good form was rather disappointing, Eric Penny and Tony Fairclough battled gamely on, whilst Cyril Forey gave us ample proof of his lack of training.
