items.label: November 1962
items.sum: Olympian's stage-by-stage report of the Southern London to Brighton road relay on 13 October, where Belgrave finished third behind Portsmouth and T.V.H. to qualify for the National relay, with Gerry North fastest of the day and two changeover photos.
items.s: 'BELS' BACK ON TARGET! SOUTHERN 'BRIGHTON' Olympian's stage-by-stage report of the Southern London to Brighton road relay on 13 October, where Belgrave finished third behind Portsmouth and T.V.H. to qualify for the National relay, with Gerry North fastest of the day and two changeover photos. Was the 13th to be an unlucky day for us or were we to run up to our proper form, secure a place, and so qualify again for the National Relay next April? This was the thought in most of our minds as the runners went to the start in Old Palace Yard, Westminster just before 10 o'clock on a cool Autumnal morning. If confidence was anything to go by we were certain to finish amongst the first three because the spirit of the team was higher than for many a long day and competition for team places had been keen throughout the previous weeks. No-one in their right mind could see Portsmouth being beaten but the second spot was thought generally to be between T.V.H., Woodford and ourselves with S.L.H. and possibly Walton providing opposition. Woodford were without three of their leading runners due to committments on the Continent and we were without the services of Kerr, Linstead and Black all of whom were injured. The race in fact soon resolved itself into a fight between the above-mentioned Clubs and we eventually took third position behind Portsmouth and T.V.H. Walton fought us every inch of the way and this rivalry produced plenty of fireworks on the last few stages. The race itself was outstanding from our point of view for a number of reasons. Firstly Charlie Walker was performing yet again,in his 25th consecutive Brighton Relay, an achievement of which he can be justly proud and which the Press duly noted with some complimentary comments. Secondly, Gerry North was leading the team for the first of what we hope will be many Brighton races and just how well he did it is indicated by his time of 27:27 on the 9th stage, only 2 secs. outside the record set up by Brian Kilby last April and 68 secs. faster than Bill Kerr's Club record. Then we had John Davies producing the form of which we know he is capable to take the fastest time of the day on the 6th stage. Also Pat Newell returned to the team to record another first-class performance and so lower the Belgrave record for the 10th stage by 13 secs. Pat now holds two Club stage records against Jack Brown's three - this can surely be changed next April Pat! The story of the race is one that almost excludes the winners Portsmouth for they took the lead on the third stage and from then on it was only a question as to how far ahead they would be at Brighton. In fact, it was something more than a mile, which in some way illustrates the strength of the Club. Eric Gebbett had been given yet again the task of bringing us near to the front on the first stage and again he did not fail - his 7th position was performed against good opposition and his time was a personal best for this leg. (21:12. 7th) John Thresher took the second stage and was anxious to redeem himself for his moderate run last April. Starting perhaps a little too fast, he ran nevertheless, very well to take us up to 6th position without losing any ground on the leaders, Woodford,who had entrusted this stage to one of their stalwarts Eric Major.(25:07. 5th) At Mitcham Jack Brown took over 43 sec behind the leading club on what is probably his favourite leg. How well we remember his grand performances of a few years ago,one of which earned him the record that still stands as a Club best. The encroaching years have slowed Jack down a little but have not dampened his enthusiasm and he put in a steady run which took us up to fifth place although the distanc between us and the leaders, now Portsmouth, had widened.(29:51. 14th) Charlie Walker made a further place on the run to Merstham, chased all the way by Roly Langridge of S.L.H. and producing a sprint finish with what he himself describes as "a desperate effort". (25:32. 5th fastest) Next came George Williams the International Walker who only a few months ago was making a great name for himself by helping Great Britain to a win in the Europa Trophy. George has turned to running and may well be the first to achieve National honours at both walking and running. Despite his inexperience of relay running he performed very well. Taking over with Harvey of S.L.H. he was unfortunate to meet a younger man who was running a little above his normal form. George did the only thing possible, he went with him and later had to suffer for a slightly too fast start.(22:33. 10th) John Davies set off with a gap of 30 secs. between himself and S.L.H. and a deficit of 3½ minutes on the leaders. John ran his best ever Brighton leg and just missed Mal Robinson's Club record by 3 secs.(13:33.1st) Cyril Forey was making a welcome return to the team on the Gatwick leg. He had the unenviable task of trailing Mick Firth on this windswept stage and it was only towards the end of the leg that Firth's greater experience and fitness took him away from Cyril. (18:48. 5th. fastest) Barry Sawyer took over in 5th place and he quickly passed his S.L.H. rival and whilst running steadily did not quite manage to produce the same spark that he had shown in recent weeks although it must be conceded that he was very much on his own and so was not hard pressed. At Handcross, Barry handed over 5 mins. behind Pompey but within striking distance of T.V.H. and Walton.(31:27. 10th. fastest) This was the position that faced Gerry North and how well he tackled it is illustrated by the fact that after 6 miles he had reduced Portsmouth's lead by 10 secs. ( their runner being non other than Martin Hyman), brought us to within 13 secs. of T.V.H. and 4 secs. of Walton. This was the fastest time of the day but unfortunately missed the stage record by a mere 2 secs.(27:27.1st) On the next leg T.V.H. pulled out their trump card in the form of Mike Wiggs who with a great run knocked off 10 secs. from Jim Peters's stage record set in 1953 and this time in turn was bettered by Bruce Tulloh running in the lead position who ran even 30 secs. faster than Wiggs. Meanwhile our own Pat Newell, not in the least deterred by the class of the opposition, was putting pressure upon Peter Milner of Walton and ended up in third position only 45 secs. behind T.V.H. and 29 secs. ahead of Walton. (19:56. 4th. fastest) On the penultimate leg we had Laurie O'Hara running in only his second Brighton. He took Dale Hill in admirable fashion and although losing a little ground on the two leading clubs made sure that Walton were not in a position to challenge over the last leg.(21:01. 5th. fastest) Don Maclean has this year been entrusted with last leg in all the relays in which we have competed and has aquitted himself admirably. This was to be no exception for although he could not catch T.V.H. he certainly gave Walton no chance of 3rd place. As it was Don only missed Jack Brown's stage record by 10 secs. (17:25. 4th. fastest) Thus we arrived at the Aquarium in 3rd place to ensure that we compete in next April's National Race. We hope that by then we have Bill Kerr Ron Linstead and Alan Black back with us, and also see such people as Miller Moore and our up-and-coming Juniors making competition for those coveted team positions really hot. With that proverbial 'bit of luck' we shall certainly be pushing the mighty Portsmouth and Derby teams very hard next spring. Supporters please book the date now - you are promised an exciting day's sport. Pos Team Time 1. Portsmouth A.C 4:27:04 2. T.V.H. 4:32:47 3. BELGRAVE H. 4:33:52 4. Walton A.C 4:34:57 5. items.s: SAWYER WINS '5¾' Report and result of the Club 5¾ miles race on 22 September, won by Barry Sawyer in 28:43, with John Baker winning the handicap. September 22nd. - A smaller field than usual faced the Starter, our newly elected President Dave Shepherd. It took only the length of Lauriston Road to separate the"fast men" from the rest of the field and round the first lap of the Common a group comprising Sawyer, Brown, Gebbett, Walker Williams and Fairclough battled for the lead with the steadier types trailing along behind the most prominent of which were Forey, Crooks and Moore. Down Copse Hill Williams dropped away a little but Tony Fairclough keen as mustard to prove himself as good as the Seniors, hung on for grim death. Forey, Crooks and Moore were all making progress behind the forward group and were getting into position to pounce on any of the leaders who showed signs of flagging. Cambridge Road as usual, sorted the sheep from the goats and Barry Sawyer returning once more to the form he showed about a year ago, pulled away from Eric Gebbett and Jack Brown who were renewing the battle they enjoyed in the Poly Relay only a week before. Chas. Walker was showing signs of tiredness at this stage and young Fairclough was finding the hills just a little too much. George Williams who seems to have renounced walking for good, was showing good form and sound pace judgment only to be forced to drop back temporarily thro' an attack of catarrh soon after passing the church. Meanwhile Barry was going further ahead and looked a certain winner with just one lap of the common separating him from victory. Eric and Jack were still locked in deadly combat and Chas was obviously contenting himself with 4th place. George Williams got going again after the "dip" and set off at great pace to recoup his losses. John Baker excelled himself at the tail end of the field with his fastest run to date over this course which secured him the first position in the handicap. George Piddington also achieved a personal best to take 2nd place and the race winner Barry Sawyer, with an excellent 28:43, faster than is normal for the autumn race, snapped up 3rd prize. Overall the result augured well for the imminent Brighton Relay. Handicap: 1.J. Baker 27:40, 2.G. Piddington 27:49, 3.B. Sawyer 27:58. Pos Name Handicap Time 1. B. Sawyer (0:45) 28:43 2. E. items.s: HAYES WINS Yacht '3' Report and result of the club 'Yacht' 3 miles handicap, won by boy R. Hayes, with scratch man Gerry North setting a course record of 14:15. First two places in this year's race went to boys. Young Hayes, who has been showing good form of late, made the most of a generous mark to romp home over half a minute ahead of the next man, Bicourt. The next 33 men arrived home in the space of a minute and with several back markers racing through the field the finish produced much excitement. The scratch man this year was Gerry North who was having his first crack at the event. Gerry celebrated his initiation by slicing a full ½ minute off the existing course record with 14:15. Other notable runs were made by Fairclough, O'Hara and Don Maclean; the latter's 15:11 being 2nd fastest of the day. (cont'd overleaf) Pos Name Handicap Time 1. R. Hayes (3:50) 13:19 2. J. items.sum: Ron Langheim's humorous account of four Belgravians' trip with the Athletics Weekly party to the European Championships in Belgrade.
items.s: BELGRADE Ron Langheim's humorous account of four Belgravians' trip with the Athletics Weekly party to the European Championships in Belgrade. We have all read Hackett, Moor, and Allen on the Championships. We have all thrilled to the films of Messrs. Tulloh, Brightwell and Kilby winning gold medals. Now read the unpublicised story of the exploits of four Belgravians in Belgrade!! "West London air terminal was the meeting point for the 'Athletics Weekly' party to the European Games. A motley crowd had assembled all keen to set out on a journey which was to provide most of us with our first glimpse of life behind the Iron Curtain. The Belgravians present were Mike Shingles, Fred Paget, 'Glimpy' Jones (Keeping a tight grip on his two main possessions in life, stopwatch and camera) and myself. After a five hour flight we arrived in Zagreb where we boarded a coach for the trip to Bled, a lake near the Austrian border. Here we joined the party who had made the long train journey. The next stage of the journey was a twelve hour coach trip to Belgrade that soon had all concerned well and truly 'Shattered'. The only person who seemed to be enjoying himself was 'Glimpy' Jones who had armed himself with meat-pies and tablets of all colours. We arrived very tired and just in time to fall into bed - oh what a night! The bed was like iron and we were just nodding off when angry voices could be heard on the staircase - 'Travel 12 hours and find no bed!' In burst Brian Nott of Ranelagh, a room-mate of Glimpy's, struggling up to the top floor with a bed under his arm. Apart from the sleeping arrangements in the hotel, our stay here was most enjoyable and there was even an English-speaking waiter keeping a beady eye open for those who dodged paying for their beer at meal-times. We travelled on to the Adriatic coast and it was here that we ran in an epic road relay - started on the sea front at seven in the morning by Jimmy Green of A.W., it managed to convince the local inhabitants that the English visitors really were 'bonkers.' We arrived home with empty pockets although Glimpy managed to bring home some samples of Yugoslave meat-pies, whilst 'keep-fit' enthusiast Fred Paget smuggled home a jar of local honey. All in all, a hectic holiday, but nevertheless a really enjoyable time was had by all concerned." items.sum: Arthur Penstone's comments on the improving road-running season, new members of the road squad and the County and Southern 20s.
items.s: ROAD RUNNING Arthur Penstone's comments on the improving road-running season, new members of the road squad and the County and Southern 20s. ARTHUR PENSTONE COMMENTS:- Once again this past road racing season has seen Belgrave Harriers competing in most of the major road races of the South - or most of the older established ones anyway. A brief glance at the results is sufficient to indicate the improvement shown. New faces are always welcome and this season the road running ranks have been swelled by Gerry North, Bill Kerr, Charlie Walker, George Williams John Moore and Peter Wrench; and with Jack Brown showing a return to form, things look good for next season. I would like to thank all the lads who helped out on the day of the Belgrave '20' also those who generously contributed towards the cost. This assistance helps to make our own '20' the best of them all. One important reminder - watch out for the dates of your County and Southern '20s' and contact me for your entry forms. These races must be supported. items.sum: Report and result of the 11th Belgrave open 20 miles on 21 July, incorporating the Surrey championship, won by Ron Linstead from Gerry North with Belgrave winning both team races.
items.s: BELGRAVE OPEN '20' Report and result of the 11th Belgrave open 20 miles on 21 July, incorporating the Surrey championship, won by Ron Linstead from Gerry North with Belgrave winning both team races. JULY 21st - This was the 11th annual 'Bels 20' and before all else, credit must be given to Arthur Penstone for the admirable way in which he organised the race. His Worship The Mayor of Wimbledon (Alderman T.H.Metcalfe J.P.) acted as starter and Ernest Neville presented the Surrey County awards as this championship was incorporated into the overall race. On the first of three laps the leaders were our own Gerry North; Tony Towl and Ted Richardson with other Belgrave athletes such as Gebbett, Dabbs and Linstead also moving well a little lower down the field. At about 11 miles Gerry went out alone - passed 12 miles in 63:30 and was leading in fine style at 15. But at this point, Ron (Best-Bitter!) Linstead was beginning to make his presence felt and at the 15 miles mark he was only some 50 secs. behind North. The strain of leading now began to tell and as the wind on the third lap hit Gerry again, Ron relentlessly closed the gap. At the finish Ron was a clear winner by some 52 seconds and his winning time ranks 2nd to Fred Norris's all time best (1:47:26) whilst Gerry's time is the fourth best ever recorded. Eric Gebbett ran his usual evenly-paced race to finish seventh with Chas. Dabbs making a most welcome return to something like his old form, eighth. In the team events the Bels. did very well indeed winning both the open and the Surrey County events. In the final analysis, therefore, Belgrave were successful on two scores; their athletes performed excellently and the event was organised in the best Belgrave traditions of hospitality and efficiency. items.sum: Description of the Road Runners Club, founded 16 April 1952, its membership rules, subscription and newsletter.
items.s: ROAD RUNNERS CLUB Description of the Road Runners Club, founded 16 April 1952, its membership rules, subscription and newsletter. Road Runners Club was formed in an attempt to channel the abundant enthusiasm that existed, and still does, into an Association uniquely qualified to cater for this branch of the sport as well as to know and foster the interests of the runners themselves who constituted the Club. The Association was actually founded on April 16th 1952 with the object of encouraging running and in particular road running. Membership is confined to amateurs who are members of clubs affiliated to the A.A.As or to the governing body of the country in which the athlete resides. The minimum subscription is 5/-d. per annum payable on April 1st in each year. A News Letter is published and sent to all members F.O.C. on average 3 times a year. Besides giving detailed results of R.R.C. sponsored races, it gives results of other major long-distance road races held in this country and abroad; articles are often written by runners themselves describing their training and experiences in races. Road Runners Club R.R.C. A.A.A.

items.label: November 1962
items.sum: Ron Linstead's account of travelling with the Road Runners Club team to the 54-mile Comrades Marathon in South Africa on 30 May 1962, where John Smith won and Linstead was fifth, with a South African newspaper cartoon and the result.
items.s: SOUTH AFRICAN JOURNEY Ron Linstead's account of travelling with the Road Runners Club team to the 54-mile Comrades Marathon in South Africa on 30 May 1962, where John Smith won and Linstead was fifth, with a South African newspaper cartoon and the result. At 7.p.m. on Saturday 19th May, the R.R.C. team of John Smith, Don Turner, Tom Buckingham and myself, boarded a B.O.A.C. Comet 4 which was to take us to Johannesburg in some 18 hours. We were off to compete in the world's longest, hottest and hilliest road run - the 54 miles Durban to Pietermaritzburg 'Comrades Marathon'. The flight was really thrilling. We had views of the Eiffel Tower, the Alps, the Nile, Mt. Kilimanjaro, the Victoria Falls and the great forests of Equatorial Africa. We stopped en route at Rome, Khartoum, Nairobi and Salisbury. On the plane we fed and drank well, the meals being superb. We arrived at Jo'burg at 2.p.m. on Sunday and some two hours later John and myself were out training. We found it tough going in the rarified atmosphere, for Jo'burg is at an elevation of 6,000'. The next day we did a hard 23 miles over a very hilly course. The sun, of course, was shining brightly and Tom Buckingham became severely sunburnt. On the Tuesday we were taken by car to Pietermaritzburg some 300 miles away; this was to be our pre-race H.Q. P'burg is in the beautiful province of Natal, an area rather like the Scottish Highlands except that the sun is always out and there are no lochs - only winding rivers. You can guess what an ideal situation it was for training. In the eight days prior to the race we did one run of 30 miles and six of between ten and 17, with perhaps the occasional stride out. It was sheer joy to run in that hot sun through such lovely scenery. Sometimes we left the roads and went over the dirt and gravel mountain tracks and had superb views. We felt that we were hundreds of miles away from civilization. Occasionally we encountered native kraals and villages where our appearance would cause a sensation. Often barefooted children would run with us for a mile or more, seemingly untroubled by the rocky flinty surfaces. It was all so very peaceful - there was no sound of traffic, no golfers, horseriders, dogs or any of the encumbrances one encounters on Wimbledon Common and in Richmond Park. In P'burg, we stayed with 'Toppy' Fanver a 40 year old Accountant who was also to take part in the race. In common with many other South Africans he was no one-sport man, for golf, cricket, tennis and carpet bowls were among his interests. Thoughtfully, he kept a fridge stacked with lager. It was great to sit in the bath after a run and have a 'nice cool beer'. We ate well, too well in fact, as I was to learn to my cost. Food is so cheap. A sack of oranges, for example, costs only 31/-d. Spirits and cigarettes are other cheap commodities being only 50% of the price they are here. It must be hard for the South African distance man to keep fit. The time passed quickly and and 6.a.m. on Wednesday 30th May, we found ourselves lined up with 150 others for the start of the race outside the Durban Post Office. Many of the entrants were just running to finish the gruelling course and so win a Comrades Silver Medal and the right to wear the distinctive blazer and tie. Some were rugby players, canoeists, etc. who were starting because they had strictly unofficial bets on! Bets made, one suspects, when the lads were concerned were full of beer! The ages ranged from 18 to 60; one runner was the blind 60 year old Ian Jardine, for whom two others had unselfishly agreed to act as guides. All competitors had until 5 p.m. to finish - eleven hours. In those who were just running to finish, the true spirit of the aptly named 'Comrades Marathon' was exemplified for they would be out in the cruel sun longer than any of us, helping and encouraging each other. The start was very fast, with the green vested South African Marathon Club runners Jackie Mekler, Fritz Madel and Frikkie Steyn opening up an immediate lead. Tom Buckingham was the only R.R.C. man to go with them. The first twenty five miles was a steady climb reaching an elevation of 2,500 feet. Just picture it, Copse Hill lasting for almost the length of a marathon! Here briefly is how the race progressed - the distances and altitudes are approximate. PINETOWN 12½ miles (1,400' alt) 1. Mekler 1.21 2. Madel, Steyn, Buckingham 1.23 5. Smith 1.24 6.Linstead 1.28 10.Turner 1.30 HILLCREST 21 miles (2,000' alt) Sun was really hot now. 1. Mekler 2.13 2. Smith and Buckingham 2.19 4. Madel and Steyn 2.20 6. Linstead 2.24 8. Turner 2.30 DRUMMOND 28 miles (2,500' alt) 1. Mekler 2.57 2. Smith 3.3 3.Buckingham 3.4 4. Madel and Steyn 6. Linstead 7. Turner. At 31 miles came the gruelling 2 miles long 800 feet high climb up Inchanga. I moved up past Madel and Steyn here. From this point on, Mekler started to tire, and Smith eventually caught him at 44 miles. I took a bashing down this stretch and spent time off the road with stomach trouble (every time the grass rustled I suspected a snake was approaching!) At 45 miles I went by Tom Buckingham and moved into 3rd place and I now felt really hopeful. By 48 miles however, I 'blew up' weakened by stomach pains and cramp around the kidneys. Here Turner went by me, looking for all the world as though he was on a normal Sunday session round the gentle Surrey roads. At 49 miles came the nastiest hill it has ever been my misfortune to run up. 1½ miles long and 500 feet high, it was the notorious Polly Shorts Cutting, named after the man in charge of the road construction gang. Just picture yourself going up a hill four times as long and twice as steep as Wimbledon Hill, with legs battered by some 49 miles of hard going (about 50,000 strides) and on top of it all a midday sun beating down, the temperature being about 90°F. Macdonald and Footer couldn't have supplied enough superlatives to sum up my feelings. Each stride felt as though it would be my last, I resolved this would be my final road race, wished I had never been a runner and cursed myself for ever getting into the team. How thankful I was to reach the top! I was now feeling half-dead and Buckingham went by me. However, with the nearest South African four miles behind, I now had just to concentrate on finishing. Ahead lay four miles of gentle down gradient, where I was able to recover somewhat. Over this part the crowds lined the roads two or three deep. They were delighted at our success - those of British origin having little love for the Boer descendents. Natal is very pro-British. As I ran , came remarks like "Come on Limey, you've b-----ed up Republic Day!" One woman was heard to say "He looks nice and fresh". Miraculously, I didn't stop to belt her one! Eventually I got there, and did the final 300 yards over the soft grass of the Collegians A.C. ground. It was a great relief to stop. Someone, whom I would remember in my Will if I had anything to leave, thrust an opened bottle of beer into my hand. It was just great and the contents disappeared in a few seconds. I recovered quickly after that and after a bath and more beer, I felt quite O.K., although some photos I have seen since, show that I looked tremendously gaunt. John Smith finished first in 5 hours 57 minutes and 5 seconds. Mekler did 6 h. 4 mins 4 secs. Turner, Buckingham and myself recorded 6:7.8; 6:8.26; and 6:10.39 respectively. These times placed us 2nd 4th 5th and 6th on the all-time list, ahead of anything Hayward, Walsh, Newton and Allan had ever done. The sixth man, Charley Chase of J'burg did 6:30.42 - he hadn't been nominated for the S.A. team and spent four days before the race drinking in Durban bars! (Cont'd. on back page) (Cont'd. from p.30) There was a great social after the race. Having spent 6 hours in the hot sun chasing my team mates and Mekler it was a welcome change to chase the local talent round a dance floor! Lack of space, I feel, must forgive me to curtail detail of the last ten days of the trip. The day after the race we went back to Jo'burg and thence to the Krugu National Park Game Reserve for a long weekend. Here we saw the wild animals in their natural surroundings, from the safety of a car. During this trip we covered hundreds of miles over crude roads, passing through breath-taking mountain scenery. We saw tobacco, oranges and sugar cane being grown. Back in Jo'burg for the last few days we were entertained at many parties and dinners. Usually on such occasions I had to get up and make a speech - indeed, I became fairly proficient for the last one. Inevitable we were shown down a gold mine, which proved most interesting. Friendly as our miner guides were though, we weren't given any free samples. On Friday 8th June, our stay in South Africa ended and we left Jan Smuts Airport for the long journey home. We were by then very tired but quite contented. Our stay had been a happy one, for the people we met had been friendly, generous and hospitable. It had been a great experience made possible only by the generosity of those who had contributed to the R.R.C. appeal, and here I must thank all those in Belgrave for their donations. items.label: February 1963
items.sum: Editorial welcoming the Courage, Barclay and Simonds grant for British field events and arguing that schools must introduce boys to field events if clubs and the national team are to find talent.
items.s: EDITORIAL Editorial welcoming the Courage, Barclay and Simonds grant for British field events and arguing that schools must introduce boys to field events if clubs and the national team are to find talent. The New Year was heralded in by the announcement that British field athletes were to benefit from a generous £10,000 grant by Messrs. Courage, Barclay and Simonds Ltd. to boost jumping and throwing standards over the next five years. Athletics Weekly commented "----it will certainly be a great help to many athletes and give them every chance to reach the top IF THE RIGHT MATERIAL IS THERE". Is the right material, in fact, finding it's way to the National team? The B.A.A.B. use the Athletic Clubs of this country as their source for Internationals but to whom must the Clubs look for their material? Mainly, of course, the schools. It is this end of the scale that needs the attention. Every schoolboy plays soccer or rugby but how many have had the opportunity of pole-vaulting or even seeing a hammer? How many good-class rugby players have ever handled a shot or discus?-- They might have well missed their true vocation. When the majority of schools in this country can field a team of two strings in all recognised events then the real cream will surely filter through to the top. Army units can find 2 men per event for the Inter-Unit Team Championships, and from the rawest of materials too, so the schools surely can. If 100 boys all throw the hammer for the first time, however crudely it may be, the best two or three are very likely to follow up their prowess if given the right encouragement. The seeds of enthusiasm must already be sown before a youngster will join an athletic club to improve his ability and seek competition. The field events sections of most Athletic Clubs are in dire need of recruits,---and it is upon school-leavers that most clubs depend. The number of Clubs in this country that can field 2 men in all field events can be counted on the fingers of one hand. It is no wonder that the National team suffers in turn. If all schools, particularly those at the lower levels, would take a bigger interest in field events then they would be doing as big a service to the sport as the "Courage Awards". Perhaps our schoolteacher members are the best equipped to campaign for this end. Courage Awards Inter-Unit Team Championships

items.label: February 1963
items.sum: Report of the club Children's Party at Belgrave Hall on 6 January, with games, a puppet show, a conjuror and Father Christmas.
items.s: THE CHILDRENS' PARTY Report of the club Children's Party at Belgrave Hall on 6 January, with games, a puppet show, a conjuror and Father Christmas. JANUARY 6th - BELGRAVE HALL Crackers, jellies, balloons, sweets, ice-cream, cakes - games with 'Uncle' Bill Lucas and 'Uncle' Bob Taylor - music, dancing, more sweets, more balloons and, inevitably, more and more noise! Phew! Training is needed for this type of event just as much as the athletic kind and, thanks to Ted Pallan and his social committee, everything was kept under some sort of control by the many adult helpers. The deafening din reached a crescendo when the puppet show got under way and 'Mr. Punch' went home eventually with an inferiority complex - there is no hope for the clown. When the conjuror had finished his penal task, there was barely time to clear the chairs away before the floor was taken by the children once more. More noise. Then silence! Father 'Nutty' Christmas had arrived. The children watched his slow plod with an air of apprehension as though they feared he might not approve ( having been kept hanging around for 12 days; but their fears were quickly dispelled when the lights went up and the presents were handed out. By the same token, Santa Claus himself was forgotten (for the next 11 months at any rate) when the presents were opened. Bedlam broke loose once more; this time accompanied by the roar, rattle and crash of the new toys. It was a joy to see so many senior member[illegible] scuttling across the floor with aeroplanes, cars and balloons - to see Ron Linstead engrossed in the puppet show and Bob Taylor leading the 'conga'. Ye[illegible] for the sake of our Senior members, we must keep the children's party going. Bill Lucas Bill Lucas Bob Taylor Bob Taylor Ted Pallan Ted Pallan Ron Linstead Ron Linstead C.S. C.S. Belgrave Harriers Children's Party 1963 Belgrave Hall

items.label: February 1963
items.sum: Countryman's gossip column on Gerry North's Inter-Counties run, the first North Surrey League season, Cliff Roffey's visit from Kenya, Clive Shippen's comeback, promising newcomers and a reprinted Indian newspaper report on Ranjit Bhatia, with Eddie Lacey's photograph of Charlie Walker in the Club '7'.
items.s: A COUNTRYMAN'S Jottings Countryman's gossip column on Gerry North's Inter-Counties run, the first North Surrey League season, Cliff Roffey's visit from Kenya, Clive Shippen's comeback, promising newcomers and a reprinted Indian newspaper report on Ranjit Bhatia, with Eddie Lacey's photograph of Charlie Walker in the Club '7'. Gerry North, the holder, was given little hope by the Press of obtaining a forward position in the Inter-Counties race at Reading. His defeat by Snowdon in a Surrey League match and sixth place in the Lancashire County were the basis of these views. When, seven days before the big race, Gerry only just held off Shelley (N.Staffs) in the Mitcham '15' it was said he was not the force of last year. How wrong they were. Despite suffering from a bad cold he beat all the recognised opposition only to lose his title to Portsmouth's T.K. Johnston who, revelling in the Artic conditions, chose this day to make the biggest break-through of his career. I wonder how many of our senior athletes have noticed that Gerry can race week in and week out yet still produce the big effort for the big occasion. Perhaps, if the lesson is learned, we will soon field our strongest team more than once a season. * * * The first season of North Surrey League fixtures has ended, and was undoubtedly a success. These matches give the bulk of club athletes a chance to experience the big race atmostphere and, with 10 to score, an opportunity of counting for their team. The league was born at the "3 Kings" Mitcham in May of last year. The proposal was put forward by Mitcham AC but, because of traditional fixtures being affected, it was not over-enthusiastically received by the other six clubs present who were, Belgrave, Walton, Surrey, Hercules, Herne Hill and South London. Eventually,however, all except SLH agreed to give it a trial. I understand that South London are now looking for a "Mr Heath" to negotiate their entry to the "six". I wonder if Bill Lucas would make a good "De Gaulle"! * * * Cliff Roffey arrived in this country a few weeks ago for a spot of leave from business in Kenya. I saw Cliff before the Club '10' and he said he did not feel as fit as on his last visit. Personally, I think his effort in the Championship compared favourably with the first race of his last visit. Few will need reminding of the success he enjoyed last time. He went from strength to strength and in his final outing clocked fastest time of the day on Stage 10 of the Brighton Relay. That other overseas stalwart, Ranjit Bhatia, handed over to Cliff that day and for both that was the last time they ran on the Brighton Road. Unfortunately, Cliff returns to Kenya just 2 weeks before the National relay in April, so must undergo another period away before he can return to the Belgrave team. Our other exiles, Mal Robinson (U.S.A.) and Ranjit Bhatia (India) are also keen to return for a spell. Who knows? they might all arrive together. * * * Clive Shippen, who we have not seen competitively since last August, tells me he is making a determined come-back. Clive, who is 31, is not satisfied with what he calls "a career of near misses". Although he gained a Surrey Co vest in 1962, not a single team winners medal has come his way. He has a silver and bronze for the South of Thames Junior, silver and bronze for the London County, silver for the South of Thames Senior, bronze for the Surrey County, bronzes for the London/Brighton National and Southern Relays and narrowly missed a Club Honours Badge when he ran a 9:28 steeplechase the very season the AAA reduced their Grade 1 standard from 9:30 to 9:25! Should he be successful in adding some "golds" to his collection an interesting set would be the South of Thames medals, for, to obtain a complete set, the gold must be won last of all-- the winning team being barred for good. * * * Of the newer members that have been appearing at our recent fixtures Pat Bradley is perhaps the most promising addition. Pat, a Scot, was introduced into the Club by Bill Kerr and has already shown useful form. Next season could see him amongst our leading runners. Paul Binns, still a junior, is not yet as advanced as Bradley and our other Juniors, but after speaking to him recently I am convinced he will make the grade. He has been running for nearly 2 years now but has only just started seriously. if he can stick to his 40 miles a week training he should reap the benefit in a year or two. Martin Edwards, a junior also, has wasted little time in carving a niche for himself in the ranks of our Junior team---a team which can be expected to perform well against the tough opposition they will meet in the Southern and National. Before these jottings are read the former event will be over and I shall not be surprised if a set of medals comes their way;nor for that matter the senior team also. * * * SIX MORE MARKS IN DELHI STATE ATHLETICS RANJIT BHATIA SETS THE PATTERN BY A STAFF REPORTER You can't keep a good man down! The headline you see here is reproduced from an Indian newspaper, and reads on as follows:- "Indeed, the day's outstanding performer was a Senior---Ranjit Bhatia of St. Stephen's College, who represented India at the Rome Olympics It was Bhatia who began Saturday's record-smashing---and in conditions hardly conducive to such a feat. Bhatia began a "dead-cert" for the 5,000 metres. In fact, he had to race all the way against himself---his nearest rival was more than 400 metres behind---but he did this so splendidly that the whole Railway Stadium had to applaud him. He had clocked 15:4.1, 10.3 secs better than the old mark, yet he looked still fresh at the finish. Later, he was still fit enough to help his team take second place in the 4X400 metres relay--------" Ranjit, who lectures at St. Stephen's, introduced cross-country running to the College team and their runners have improved immeasurably, winning the state title. He tells me he also ran 1:56.7 (800 m) and 4:02.7 (1500 m) at the same meeting---surprising many pundits who regard him as semi-retired. International politics rarely affect the affairs of Belgrave Harriers yet India's border dispute with China is an exception. Ranjit was planning to spend next summer's holiday in London but will now have to do a 4 month spell of military training instead. Thus, a reunion to which we all look forward must be postponed once more. * * * HEY!------WHAT'S THAT?-----'OUR CHAS' TAKING A PEP PILL? Eddie Lacey's action picture seems to catch Charlie Walker in the act during the Club '7' with 2½ miles to go. He certainly needed it, for Gerry North (no pill) passed him shortly after to win by over a minute. COUNTRYMAN HEY!------WHAT'S THAT?-----'OUR CHAS' TAKING A PEP PILL? This was the 9th year the race had been held and its popularity grows on each occasion. It is customary for the Belgrave runners to draw for partners - one from the better half with one from the lesser - but with our first couple finishing only 8th the time has probably come for our stars to partner each other. items.s: BOXING DAY HANDICAPS Report and results of the Boxing Day handicaps at Battersea Park: 120 yards, shot, two-mile run and three-mile walk handicaps. Held at Battersea Park on a bitterly cold day this meeting was still able to command a fair turnout. It was as though those in attendance had friends in the Met. Office who had informed them that this would be their last chance of performing on firm going before the snow storms and freeze-up which arrived that afternoon. There were 7 starters in the 120 yards sprint and Pat Cornelius (off five yards) steamed home in a brisk 12.7. Later he made full use of his 5ft. 6" allowance in the shot to beat all but one of the 8 competitors with 33'0". Not a performance to worry Dallas Long but not a bad effort after all that Plum Pud, Turkey, and cigars! A grand total of 25 starters went to their respective marks for the 2 mile run handicap and John Leaver, a youth, emerged a popular winner by 7 seconds from Dudley Gordon who manages to find time between his continental jaunts to'get up' in these handicaps. Chris Steer and John Bicourt had a really ding-dong battle with Chris just getting the edge over his younger rival for 5th place. One of the most heartening features of this event was the fine running and encouraging support of our younger members. In the 3 mile Walk Handicap there were 10 starters. Eric Hall was back marker with an allowance of a minute and P. Wilson was first away with 7:30. Wilson held on to his lead and finished almost a minute ahead of Hall who had worked his way through the remainder of the field with deceptive ease. J. Wilson came under the Judges' eye on the 2nd lap and George Piddington better known in the cross-country section, decided to stick to running after 6 tough laps of " heel and toe". items.s: BELS. PIPPED IN REIGATE RELAY Report and result of the Reigate 6x2½ miles road relay on 3 November, where Gerry North's course record last leg left Belgrave three seconds behind Surrey AC. NOV 3rd----6X2½ MILES When Gerry North set off on the final leg 19secs down on Surrey AC and 17secs down on Mitcham AC, fireworks were eagerly awaited by the excited supporters. They were not disappointed, for Surrey's runner was no less than John Snowden who had every intention of holding his lead. Slowly the gap closed, but when North passed Mitcham's Rogers the Surrey man was still way ahead. In the final storming finish Snowden got home by 3secs, but Gerry had set a new course record of 9:21 which will take some beating. The foundation was laid on Stage 1 when Bill Kerr came home 5yds down on Harris of Mitcham. John Davies consolidated our second place and John Thresher took us into the lead at the half way mark. "Charlie boy" didn't look very happy leading Stage 4 with the result that Don Maclean took over with opponents hard on his heels. items.sum: Bill Lucas's report of the South of Thames Junior cross-country at the Guards Depot, Caterham, where a depleted Belgrave A team finished 12th, with team and individual placings.
items.s: South of Thames Junior Bill Lucas's report of the South of Thames Junior cross-country at the Guards Depot, Caterham, where a depleted Belgrave A team finished 12th, with team and individual placings. BILL LUCAS REPORTS: The race was held this year from one of the regular venues for this event, namely The Guards Depot Caterham where the dressing, bathing and catering facilities are somewhat better than usual. The conditions were very damp and slippery underfoot after continuous rain in the morning which had hampered the operations of the officials in preparing the course. Our teams were very depleted and although fifty two names had been entered for five teams only twenty two went to the start. This was most disappointing as this race is designed to give a chance to the "lesser lights" of appearing in open competition. Belgrave accept this opportunity with open hands and enter everyone able to put one leg in front of the other. In the absence of Barry Sawyer, Ken Miller, Clive Shippen, Laurie O'Hara, Derek Crookes and George Williams from the A team our hopes of a place as in the 1961 race were reduced to nil and the best we could do was to take 12th position out of the 69 teams that finished. Tony Fairclough confirmed his early season form by running a steady race throughout to finish 19th and be our first finisher. Another junior, Chris Steer, also performed well to finish 55th with John Moore 59th and David Jones 89th. These were the scoring four who amassed 222 points as compared with Guildford and Godalming's 81. Many of our runners were short of training and probably the most disappointing position was that of Cyril Forey who after a fair start fell right back to 195th whereas he should have been up with the leaders. What a pity Cyril is wasting his natural ability by lack of concentration on training. Good performances were put up by Alan Morrison (115th) and Fred Paget(148th) and Keith Angus a new member showed great promise in finishing 170th. It was interesting to note that four juniors were amongst our first seven finishers--a good omen for the future. The B and E teams were incomplete to score . items.s: THE L.C.C. Report and result of the L.C.C. cross-country championships at Parliament Hill Fields, where Belgrave finished second to Polytechnic Harriers, led by Charlie Walker in 6th. Polytechnic Harriers and Thames Valley Harriers chose this year to enter teams for the first time and whilst we were able to conquer the latter we had to give best to a strong Poly team. The race was run as usual at Parliament Hill Fields and only competitors who had worked or resided in the London area for a minimum of two years were eligible. Gerry North and Bill Kerr, therefore, were unable to compete. Walker, Black and Davies got an excellent start and at 3 miles had settled down into 13th, 15th and 17th places with Sawyer in the 20s and Brown in about 30th spot. A long drag and some heavy going in the next mile took its toll of John who dropped several places but Walker and Black (now 10th and 11th) and Sawyer (19th) were going very well and were ably supported by Brown and Gebbett who were now both inside the first 30. With the exception of Charlie Walker our boys made little improvement in the final stages. Chas. however, must have produced the fastest last 880 of the race in his effort to make every place count. In the finishing straight a floundering Ken Harland ( Cambridge H.) was all but knocked over by Charlie's slip-stream! Pos Name Club Time 1. W. Card T.V.H. 30:15 2. J. Hogan Poly 30:21 3. E. items.sum: Report of the Club 7 mile cross-country championship at Wimbledon on 1 December, won by Gerry North for the 'Black Staffe' Shield, with a photograph of the start and the full handicap result continued on page 25.
items.s: THE CLUB '7' Report of the Club 7 mile cross-country championship at Wimbledon on 1 December, won by Gerry North for the 'Black Staffe' Shield, with a photograph of the start and the full handicap result continued on page 25. Gerry North earned the right to hold the magnificent 'Black Staffe' Shield for 12 months, when he won the Club 7 mile cross-country championships at Wimbledon on December 1st. Although the winner finished over a minute ahead of the field, the race was full of interest throughout and many observers were speculating as to the humdinger that would ensue if the absent Kerr and Newell were able to get amongst 'this lot'. Thirty-five runners set off in the murk of the afternoon over the three lap course with Walker, Black and Thresher forcing the pace. After one circuit these three, with North, Davies and Sawyer tucked in behind were clear of the field. Another half lap saw the fading of Davies and Sawyer and by the time the final circuit was under way a revitalised Walker had shaken off all but North. It was at this stage that Gerry moved away like a Rolls-Royce in a scooter rally and it says great things for Charlie's temperament that he battled on undeterred never allowing his pursuers to gain an inch when many lesser men would have been thoroughly demoralised. Gerry stormed round that last lap finished 63 seconds clear of Chas. John Thresher was troubled with a minor leg injury and did not appear to be his usual fiery self but he nevertheless, finished a comparatively close 4th. Jack Brown had to make full use of his experience to pull back Tony Fairclough and John Davies in the later stages but eventually he got away from them and was fast catching Barry Sawyer in the run in. Thirty runners completed the course and the handicap was won by Niel Aston from Chas. Walker and Alan Black who finished equal second. (Cont'd. at foot of page 25.) Cont'd. from page 8. items.label: February 1963
items.h: SURREY Co. CHAMPIONSHIPS — Great Win For Juniors
items.sum: Report and results of the Surrey County cross-country championships in deep snow at Reigate Priory on 5 January 1963, where Belgrave won the junior team title and the seniors were 4th.
items.s: SURREY Co. CHAMPIONSHIPS — Great Win For Juniors Report and results of the Surrey County cross-country championships in deep snow at Reigate Priory on 5 January 1963, where Belgrave won the junior team title and the seniors were 4th. REIGATE PRIORY---JANUARY 5TH 1963 Heavy falls of snow during Christmas and New Year covered the course to a depth of 8/9inches with deeper drifts in parts--this, with a bitter cold wind, made conditions far from attractive for both runners and spectators although the latter were able to obtain some inner warmth from a welcome stall selling hot Oxo (no advertising intended). The afternoon's activities started with the Junior race for which we were fielding our strongest team made up of a number of the runners who had in 1962 taken the Youths championship and the remnants of last years Junior team. It soon became evident that we were possible winners for Tony Fairclough was with the leaders followed closely by Chris Steer with David Cocks and Jackie Hampshire not far behind. Tony ran a gallant race in atrocious conditions and fought every inch of the way with Stebbings of Croydon and Gregory of Walton before being forced back in 3rd position which he held at the finish. The others also held on to the early places and we took the team honours from Herne Hill, the favourites, by a mere two points. Martin Edwards, a new member, ran very well in finishing 32nd. Next came the Senior race in which we were hoping for a place despite the fact that our best runners are so spread that they do not qualify for Surrey In fact we had runners in the Lancashire, Middlesex, Hampshire, Kent and Sussex championships on the same day. Alan Black set off at a great pace in an endeavour to secure an early good position but a slip sent him sprawling in the snow and it took two miles before he settled down again. It says much for his fitness that he worked his way up to 8th to again secure his County vest which he was first awarded in 1961. Charlie Walker confirmed his good form by running a steady race to take 11th place. Our next runner was John Thresher in 25th position; a little disappointing as he had been running very well in earlier races, but perhaps understandable for a track man in such conditions. Don Maclean excelled himself to be our fourth scorer only a short distance behind John. Then came a gap before Ken Miller appeared--Ken is slowly working his way back afer a long lay off through injury and by the time the big races come round should be a great force again. Our sixth scorer was Eric Gebbett with Ron Linstead (placed 70th) just behind--this was too far back for a runner of Ron's calibre in a field of only 120 runners, but it was obvious that the deep snow was not to his liking. In the end we took 4th position in the team event in a race where form went by the board. W.E.L. Pos Name Club Time 1. F. Stebbings Croydon 29:08 2. M. Gregory Walton 29:20 3. A. items.h: MATCH AT CHISWICK V POLY AND WALTON--JAN 19TH
items.sum: Chris Steer's report of a road race at Chiswick against Poly and Walton, held instead of the snowbound cross-country match, won by O'Gorman of Poly with Bill Kerr second and Belgrave taking the team match easily.
items.s: MATCH AT CHISWICK V POLY AND WALTON--JAN 19TH Chris Steer's report of a road race at Chiswick against Poly and Walton, held instead of the snowbound cross-country match, won by O'Gorman of Poly with Bill Kerr second and Belgrave taking the team match easily. CHRIS STEER REPORTS:- In Artic conditions with a gale-force wind blowing, eight intrepid Belgravians braved the weather (and the Poly) in a road race consisting of two laps of the Road Relay Course. The scheduled Cross-country match was cancelled owing to the "state of the course";two feet of frozen snow. Soon after the start a group of about 8, including some Bels who were indistinguishable in an assortment of track suits, jerseys and even tights, separated themselves from the rest of the field. This group stayed together for most of the first lap when Steer made a break pursued by O'Gorman of Poly. These two opened up a lead of 50 yards over Bill Kerr, Laurie O'Hara and Pat Bradley, amongst others. However, Bill then started to get moving and caught the leaders about half a mile from the finish. O'Gorman went with him and with about 400 yds to go drew away to win by about 20 yds in 29 mins 03secs. Bill Kerr came in 4secs later, with Chris Steer 3rd in 29mins 16secs. Laurie O'Hara was 5th, Pat Bradley 6th and Don Maclean 7th. Belgrave scored 16 pts to win easily from Poly, 28pts.and a team consisting of two Walton runners and a couple of Bank runners who scored 44 pts. items.s: Linstead Retains 'MACHER' Shield Report and result of the Club 10 miles cross-country championship on 26 January 1963 on a snow and ice covered course, won by Ron Linstead who retained the Macher Shield. CLUB '10'----JAN 26TH Ron Linstead, the holder, scored a fine win in this year's ten miles championship beating Pat Newell by 300yds over a snow and ice covered course of 4 laps. Ron went straight into the lead and was never headed. Mile by mile he edged further away from Pat Newell and after 3 laps was 150yds ahead----a distance he doubled over the last circuit. Pat, in turn, got well away from Alan Black who was taking part in this Championship for the first time. A most welcome competitor was Cliff Roffey, home on a spell of leave from Kenya, whose sun-tanned form was decidedly out of character with the surroundings. Cliff's 5th place was most noteworthy for he seemed to have greater difficulty with the conditions than anyone----conditions that caused several retirements including Kerr, Bradley and O'Hara; although the latter went off course when in the first six. The first 3 home also got the corresponding handicap prizes. It must be a long time since the "back-markers" had such a field day. Handicap 1. R. Linstead (3:00) 2. P.Newell (2:45) 3. A. items.sum: Report and results of the South of Thames Senior cross-country at Sparrows Den, West Wickham, on 2 February, where Belgrave finished third and second in the Colman Cup.
items.s: South of Thames Senior Report and results of the South of Thames Senior cross-country at Sparrows Den, West Wickham, on 2 February, where Belgrave finished third and second in the Colman Cup. WEST WICKHAM----FEB 2ND As the winning team is barred from future races the runners-up in this 7½miles championship should become favourites for the ensuing year's title. This was the position we held at the start. Only four of last year's men were included in our 12 starters---Linstead, Kerr, Thresher and Moore---yet for all that this was our strongest eligible team. A heavy fall of snow on the preceding day led the officials to shorten the course to 6¾ miles. With snow beginning to fall once again, and a cold easterly wind cutting across the Sparrows Den playing fields, the 286 starters set off on the first small lap. Alan Black got his usual fine start and at 1 mile was in 4th place. John Thresher was 22nd, with Ron Linstead near at hand, but it was disappointing to see Kerr, Gebbett, and Maclean outside the first 100. However, at the half-way mark Mitcham and ourselves were scoring about 150 points each and it was obvious that every place was needed. Unfortunately many of our runners were unhappy with the going and our total score steadily increased whilst the Mitcham men made ground. Black and Thresher were unable to hold their places and it was left to Linstead in 14th place, to lead the team home, as he did last year. Tony Fairclough ran another excellent race to finish 34th and was our fifth scorer. Our sixth man closed in too far back to prevent Walton AC pipping us for 2nd place. Walton, therefore, have the privilege of starting favourites next year---perhaps that gives us a better chance of winning the title that has eluded us since 1955. Pos Name Club 1. P. Barber S.L.H. 2. items.label: February 1963
items.h: Is AMERICA'S College Set-Up The Answer?
items.sum: Mal Robinson, writing from the University of Southern Louisiana, describes American high school and college sport, coaching and scholarships and compares them with the British club system.
items.s: Is AMERICA'S College Set-Up The Answer? Mal Robinson, writing from the University of Southern Louisiana, describes American high school and college sport, coaching and scholarships and compares them with the British club system. MAL ROBINSON WRITES FROM UNIVERSITY OF SOUTHERN LOUISIANA, U.S.A. The fact that the United States of America produces so many sports stars is no accident. But it is hard for the lay-man to understand why the U.S. can head the world list at so many sports. A look at its High School and College set-up provides some of the answers. In American schools sport has an important place. There is no time for a "playing is the important thing" attitude. Each school maintains a sports department with a specialist coach for each sport for the express purpose of providing a winning team. Usually a school has its own stadium ( often better in quality than most British First Division Football Stadia) and each football game is attended by upwards of 10,000 spectators. The coach is normally a College graduate holding a degree in Physical Education as well as some other academic subject. All this is made possible by alumni (old boys) and local businessmen. They provide the money to run the athletic programme but as is often the case, " he who pays the piper, calls the tune" and a non winning coach will often find that his contract is not renewed at the end of the season. A coach of a state championship team, however, can bargain for his contract. Old boys( sometimes for tax exemption purposes) donate money to obtain a winning team and local merchants do so because a winning ball-team provides publicity for the locality. Every state is divided into areas, and within these schools are graded according to pupils strength. Normally any school will confine its competition to schools within its group. At the end of the season each area classification champion plays off on a knockout basis to determine overall state supremacy. The newspaper reporters then draw upon all teams in any one classification to determine a state team - similar to an England representative side. This is further developed with regard to area and then national teams - "All-American High School Team of '62". For the individual school there is great prestige in being respective class champion, for the individual it is a great honour to be picked for a representative side. Also at season's close a certain number of the school team will be selected by the coach for a letter award. This is the letter of the school (I am an S man of Southwestern). This is a great honour and one which if properly earned is of considerable value to a high school or college graduate. One of the biggest high school advantages takes the form of college scholarships. There are however, different types of scholarship awarded with varying degrees of coverage with regard to the payment of fees. To ensure that the college secures the best boys for its various teams an elaborate talent scouting system is operated and in some cases "under the counter" inducements are even offered. Once the boy is at college he is expected to concentrate on two things - training and study (often in that order). During the season the athlete will train hard each day and this continues, though admittedly with less intensity, in the off-season. He is expected to be in his dormitory by 10.30p.m. and no smaking and no drinking is the general rule. Contrary to general belief in the U.K. a certain scholastic standard must be maintained and theoretically a student is not allowed to compete in the college team if he does not maintain a C average. Therefore the coach is expected to keep an eye not only upon athletic progress but also their studies. Bearing all this in mind it is not difficult to see the sort of environment that has produced so many Olympic and world champions. The essential difference between the American and British sports systems is the comparative absence in the U.S. of the small amateur clubs and district associations and the concentration of athletic activity in highly subsidised and professional-minded colleges. In Britain we used to depend upon Oxbridge as our source of National Champions but whilst we still find our Metcalfes, Richard Sharps, and Chris Davidges, the amateur clubs throughout the country are now producing the lion's share of our stars. Ineviteably there is a different approach resulting from each system. Despite the insistence on the maintenance of academic studies the American athlete is at least semi-professional and as such has a far greater need to win, whilst his English counter part, although perhaps nowadays not an amateur of true blue quality, treats his sport more as a hobby and this would probably account for his not having quite the same 'killer' streak as his Trans-Atlantic rivals. Mal Robinson MAL ROBINSON Metcalfe Metcalfes Richard Sharp Richard Sharps Chris Davidge Chris Davidges U.S.A. Louisiana Oxbridge University of Southern Louisiana Southwestern

items.sum: Walking section overview praising Vaughan Thomas's winter form and noting the contributions of Ray Hall, Ray Middleton, John Knifton, Eric Hall and newcomer Dave King.
items.s: WALKING Walking section overview praising Vaughan Thomas's winter form and noting the contributions of Ray Hall, Ray Middleton, John Knifton, Eric Hall and newcomer Dave King. There was a time when any talk of Belgrave walking centred upon Hall and Vickers. Then came Williams and Middleton to hog the limelight. It was almost like a procession of music-hall names---rumour has it that Morecombe and Wise even considered joining our walking section. But this winter it's fair to say that one name more than any other has made Belgrave walking news---Vaughan Thomas.Vaughan is yet another walker who looks like gaining regular international honours before very long. He has led the way home for our boys in all the 'sevens' so far this season and obviously is a born fighter. The two Rays, Hall and Middleton, have also walked extremely well, and this part of the season,with its relatively short races,is not Ray Hall's particular favourite. John Knifton and Eric Hall have also been in winning teams and illustrate two ends of a scale---the enthusiasm and fire of the youngster and the determination and experience of the older man. There are many who are worthy of mention but for the sake of brevity we would conclude by mentioning a name to look out for in future---Dave King. He's provided a few upsets already and looks likely to unseat a few more established favourites before he's finished. The cross-country section certainly seems to be emerging out of the depths again and successes have not been comong so frequently to the walkers as they have in the past five years. But the talent is still there and certainly the spirit has not disappeared. If Thomas maintains his form, Middleton gets really fit, Ray Hall gets going over the slightly longer distances, and our youngsters Barnes, Knifton, King etc. continue to improve then we shall be taking the gold instead of the silver and bronze. items.s: "The Sport Of Race Walking" Notice of the Race Walking Association's new 161-page book 'The Sport of Race Walking', largely compiled by the club's General Hon. Secretary, with ordering details from Jack Goswell. The Race Walking Association have just published a 161-page book "with 24 illustrations" bearing the above title. It has been largely compiled by our own General Hon. Secretary and traces the growth of competitive walking up to the present day, has many informative and indeed instructive chapters, and includes the results of all the past A.A.A. and R.W.A. Walking Championships and many other events. Naturally, as Belgrave has played such an important part in race walking history the pages of the book are scattered with well-known Belgravian names, not to mention three of the full-page illustrations. In all, over 2,500 athletes names appear and there are hours of pleasure in store for all Belgravians who have a genuine interest in athletics in general and walking in particular. Copies ( 6/-d. each including p. & c.) may be obtained from Jack Goswell, 7, Faversham Court, Faversham Road, S.E.6. Jack Goswell Jack Goswell A.A.A. Walking Championships R.W.A. Belgrave Open 'Seven' Ben Knifton's report and full result of the 43rd Belgrave Open 7 miles walk, won by Paul Nihill, with Metropolitan WC taking the Berman Cup and Belgrave 'B' the team handicap. BEN KNIFTON REPORTS This our 43rd annual event attracted the best entry since 1956 and some 26 teams contested the team competition. The individual race was well and truly won by Paul Nihill (Surrey WC) who had a margin of some 47 secs on the second man home Bob Clark (Poly) with Arthur Thomson (Met.WC) just easing himself into third spot. Once again Eric Hall was our first finisher although needless to say he is now just that little bit slower than he was a couple of years back. But this was great walking and Eric revealed his enthusiasm for the sport and the club by travelling down from the North for the event. Unfortunately Vaughan Thomas was 'pulled' after 2½ miles whilst doing battle with the leaders and this spoiled any Belgrave hopes of winning the team trophy. All praise, however, to Metropolitan WC on their fine packing which enabled them to carry off the Berman Cup. Needless to say our lads didn't go home empty-handed for they got right up amidst the handicap prizes carrying off ten of the awards. INDIVIDUAL HANDICAP 1. G. Farley. 2. D. King. items.s: L.C.C. '10' Report and result of the L.C.C. 10 miles walking championship at Battersea Park on 9 February, where Belgrave finished third after three wins in four years. BATTERSEA PARK----FEB 9TH The Bels were all out for their third consecutive win in this, the 5th L.C.C. Championship, but finished a disappointing third. Yet, for all that, the first 3 teams had a battle royal, finishing their twelve scorers in the first 13 team places, with Surrey W.C. getting home by 4 points from a full-strength Poly quartet and ourselves a further 7 points behind. A record number of 92 starters set off on the first of the Battersea Park laps with the B.B.C., I.T.A. and the press in close attendance. Nihill (S.W.C.) shot straight into the lead with Polytechnic's Clarke close behind--both held their places to the end. For 6 miles Ray Hall and John Knifton, walking together, were our leading men in the early 'teens but Ray Middleton, who had been moving through steadily took over the mantle of spearhead and eventually took 8th place. In the closing stages Hall went ahead of Knifton in a vain attempt to catch Surrey's Bale. Our supporters were hoping that Will Belderson, our 4th scorer, would make considerable ground on the last lap but he was unable to make much impression on those counting in the team-race and, in any case, Surrey W.C. were already out of reach, so, after 3 wins from the 4 previous championships we dropped to third, and although by no means disgraced you can be certain that next year the Bels will be out for vengeance! items.s: The flying BelgRAFians: Feature on RAF sergeants Vaughan Thomas and Bob Farley, with Thomas winning the R.A.F. 7 miles walk title in a record 52:06, two photographs of them training at Carshalton, and a footnote on a letter from George Towers in North Africa. In the R.A.F. 7 miles championship at Lindholme on January 30th, Vaughan Thomas took the title in the excellent record time of 52:06. Bob Farley was 4th in his best time of 56:14. Vaughan and Bob are both sergeants at the Chessington RAF station and both have sporting interests other than walking. Vaughan is a basket-ball international and still makes full use of the gymnasium, whilst Bob is a football referee and coach.---this keeps him busy most Saturdays in the Winter but he should be a force in our distance walking teams this Summer. As can be seen from this photograph our two Airforce members help each other a great deal in training. Both are dead keen and the pair can often be seen at 6 o'clock on cold winter mornings legging it out on the Chessington roads. Thomas is leading Farley here in a time-trial at Carshalton track and these pictures are 2 of several taken at Vaughan's request to show where his style-faults lie. Ken Matthews had some difficulty with his style at one time and was "pulled" by the judges in 3 consecutive races----nearly quitting for good as a result. Our own Harry Evans, one of the judges concerned, persuaded Matthews to persevere, and we all know to what effect. Vaughan intends to follow in his footsteps (figuratively speaking of course!) Yes, this man means business. FOOTNOTE: Fame travels fast! Jack Goswell recently received a letter from George Towers of Leicester W.C. who is currently stationed with the RAF near Tobruk, North Africa. Towers sent his congratulations and regards to Thomas and Farley on their recent results and added "I only hope they will be posted abroad before I return home!"----Whose side is he on?. items.sum: Junior section review of the season for Fairclough, Bicourt and Hayes, with encouragement on patience and training for younger runners and a look ahead to the National at Cambridge.
items.s: Junior Section Junior section review of the season for Fairclough, Bicourt and Hayes, with encouragement on patience and training for younger runners and a look ahead to the National at Cambridge. Fairclough heads the Juniors---Bicourt the Youths------Hayes the Boys. This is the position at the present time, but who knows how long it will last when we have so many other youngsters striving to depose them? Hayes is expected to show some pretty hot form when he gets amongst youths next season, for this lad could well be a worthy successor to Bicourt. But this season has seen Fairclough and Bicourt fighting it out for honours in their respective divisions with Fairclough perhaps having the edge by virtue of his excellent 3rd place in the Surrey County Junior Championship. Then came the "Southern" at Parliament Hill. With a beautifully timed run Bicourt took 3rd place-----an effort of great merit. He thus becomes our 'Cover-Boy' for this issue;the first Youth to grace the front page. Fairclough's 18th place was also a fine effort and endorsed the consistency this scraggy fleet-footed hope for the future has shown this season. Bicourt has received admirable support this year from Simmons, Edwards and Leaver. John Leaver is not yet quite a match for Eugene and "Noddy" but this tall, stylish runner seems to have temporarily outgrown his strength (a common occurrence amongst tall young athletes), but once his strength has been built up to match his physique then we could well see some startling progress from this likeable youngster. Patience is the key, and this applies to all of our younger runners. Remember, you all develop at different rates and if your rival appears to be improving more rapidly than yourself it doesn't necessarily mean it will remain that way. Many of you, after a period of encouraging progress, will find yourselves "marking time" for anything up to a whole season---dont be discouraged, for this is merely a period of consolidation. You cannot climb to a higher plateau until you have established a firm foothold on the lower one. Routine plays an important part here. Hang on to your fitness by resolving never to miss a training run--and if you don't feel like training? give yourself the luxury of an "easy" until you do, but still go out! The National Championship, to be held on March 2nd at Cambridge will conclude the 1962/3 season and we look to our Youths and Juniors to round off this season on a high note. items.s: The North Surrey League — Youths & Boys Final positions and race-by-race reports and results of the first North Surrey League youths and boys season, in which Belgrave finished third behind Mitcham and Walton. FINAL POSITIONS (subject to confirmation) The four fixtures of this North Surrey League season were held in conjunction with the Senior/Junior league matches---each race being over a 2¾ mile course. As in the Senior league, Mitcham, Walton and ourselves were predominant throughout. Scoring was based on 5 to count,University scoring. RACE NO.1---Wimbledon, Oct 27th In a tremendous finish John Bicourt gained second place, fractionally ahead of Walton's Blake and Mitcham's Cope. Simmons ran well, as indeed did Major, but with Mitcham finishing 5 and Walton 4 before our second man was home we stood little chance in the team race. RACE NO.2---Esher, Dec 15th Bicourt put himself out of the running for the League's individual award when he missed the start rather foolishly. He joined in the race after a short distance and finished fourth but did not, of course, score. "Noddy" Edwards and 15 years old Ron Hayes filled the breach admirably, however, and we finished third once again. RACE NO.3---Kingston, Dec 29th John Bicourt made sure he was at the start this time, but found the snow-covered course not at all to his liking and finished a struggling 7th. We were still no match for Mitcham and Walton and remained in our third place niche. RACE NO.4.---Addington, Feb 9th A mixture of frozen-plough, ice and knee-deep snow faced the starters in this final league match. And Bicourt faced his second disappointment in four matches when, after drawing away into the lead, he went off course at the half way mark and re-joined the field in 3rd place. With 300 yds to go he was second once more and only 10 yds down on the leader, but his effort had cost him dear and his two closest rivals raced away from him at the finish. The rest of the team ran very well and we were only 2 points short of turning the tables on Mitcham with our lowest yet score of 51. (Cont'd overleaf) Pos Team Points 1. MITCHAM A.C 156 points 2. items.s: "SAVAGE" SHIELD WIN FOR FAIRCLOUGH. Report and result of the club junior cross-country championship for the Savage Shield on 26 January, won by A. Fairclough from D. Cocks and J. Bicourt. Held on the same day as the Senior "10", Jan 26th, this Junior Championship was run over two 2½ miles laps of a partly-thawed icy course. On the previous day it seemed very likely the race would be off, for the frozen course was particularly dangerous, but a thaw came along on the morning of the race softening up the surface enough to make racing possible. John Bicourt went straight into the lead with Fairclough, Cocks and Morrison tucked in behind. John, running against athletes age-group above himself, was still in front at the half-way mark, his 3 pursuers close behind. On the final lap Cocks and Fairclough piled on the pressure, dropping Morrison and moving ahead of Bicourt. Fairclough had the race well in hand and drew away steadily with no sign of strain to win by 120yds from Cocks with a gallant Bicourt 50yds away, third. It was good to see Keith Angus getting back to form again, this 19yrs old Sheffield runner has lots of potential. Pos Name Time 1. A. Fairclough 33:06 2. D. Cocks. 33:28 3. J. Bicourt 33:36 4. A. items.s: THE SOUTHERN — Juniors 4th.—Youths 6th Report and results of the Southern junior and youth cross-country championships at Parliament Hill Fields on 16 February, with John Bicourt third youth, the juniors fourth and youths sixth team, and a photograph of E. Simmons finishing. PARLIAMENT HILL FIELDS----FEB 16TH Bicourt gained 3rd place by 1 second---the Junior team lost 3rd place by 1 point. By such margins are honours won and lost. John Bicourt really rose to the occasion on this dangerous icy course. He never let the leading group get right away, although at times it was touch and go. With ¾ of a mile to go he was 11th and then made a big effort up the last hill before the final long descent to the finish. His lengthy stride soon took him up to 3rd place on the downhill stretch and just as it looked as though he would get well clear of the pack the tremendous effort began to tell and our supporters shared every agonising step down the long finishing straight----but John held on and was a worthy winner of the bronze medal. He said afterwards "The crowd at the top of that last hill made me think it was the finish, that was why I took it so hard. When I saw the finish was nearly another half mile away I just hung on and tried to keep my effort going". Perhaps that crowd did him a good turn! As expected, Tony Fairclough was our first Junior to finish and his 18th place was a pretty good guide to his season's form. Surprise of the day was the grand form shown by Keith Angus, whose 35th place was far above expectations. The determined running of this young athlete was a joy to watch, and his rapid improvement after a long lay-off augurs well for the National when David Cocks hopes to have overcome the effects of his recent injury. David ran his heart out but could barely raise a gallop down the finishing straight. Two weeks of hard training should see him right for the National. Jack Hampshire,as usual in the big races, really pulled his weight and was our third scorer in 61st position. Our Youths team packed in their usual order with Simmons (31) Edwards (41) and Leaver (103) being Bicourt's supporting string yet again. All in all, both teams acquitted themselves well. Tom Carter and Jack Hampshire (Senior) can feel proud of these reliable youngsters for, lets face it, its the club with reliable men that makes its mark, not the one with "flash-in-the-pan" results gained by an occasional collection of their best runners. items.s: ROAD RUNNING Road running column on the promise of Pat Newell and Derek Crookes, with Arthur Penstone's appeal to road runners for their plans and County '20' entries. Pat Newell and Derek Crookes, who have always looked ideally suited to road running, have shown by recent performances that 'life on the road' might well bring them considerable success - providing, of course, they can find time to reel off the extra mileage in training. Pat had his first long-distance outing in the Mitcham '15', and although he faded a bit in the last mile or so, it was a useful debut to finish as high up as 8th in a race of this class. His smooth, effortless action suggests he could 'purr' on for ever. It will be interesting to see if he can. Derek ran in the Faversham '5', Hogs Back '9½' and the Mitcham '15', but found the distance a little too much in the latter. His efforts in the first two races were most encouraging and we look forward to seeing him in our future road running teams. Arthur Penstone appeals to all road runners to let him have some idea of their plans for the coming season. All should make a point of running in their County '20'.
