items.label: February 1965
items.h: BELS FAIL BY 14secs / TITLE LOST IN "SOUTHERN" RELAY
items.sum: Stage-by-stage report of the October 1964 News of the World London-Brighton relay (Southern clubs), where holders Belgrave lost to Portsmouth by 14 seconds, with Tony Fairclough becoming the first Belgravian under twenty minutes on his leg.
items.s: BELS FAIL BY 14secs / TITLE LOST IN "SOUTHERN" RELAY Stage-by-stage report of the October 1964 News of the World London-Brighton relay (Southern clubs), where holders Belgrave lost to Portsmouth by 14 seconds, with Tony Fairclough becoming the first Belgravian under twenty minutes on his leg. BELS FAIL BY 14secs TITLE LOST IN "SOUTHERN" RELAY We started last October's "News of the World" London-Brighton relay race (Southern clubs)as holders of the trophy,and the pundits gave us a good chance of retaining the title - although Portsmouth were at almost full strength. We found the opposition to be a little too strong but it was a close thing - in fact only fourteen seconds separated us in the end and we were catching up rapidly. The lads ran extremely well. Laurie O'Hara taking the first leg for the first time gave us a good start with third place only seven seconds behind the leaders,Walton; and John Thresher, who now knows every inch of the second stage,made no mistake and put us into the lead at Mitcham. At this point Portsmouth,through John Lindsell,had moved up to our heels. Trevor Hart,however, soon sorted out this position and ran away from Fudge, the Portsmouth runner,to put us into a thirty eight second lead at the Wallington take-over. The fourth stage is a new and crucial leg being one of the longest and Charlie Dabbs tackled it in workmanlike manner with the knowledge that Dave Cooke,one of the Portsmouth twins,was chasing him.Charles ran well to keep out in front although our lead was now cut back to five seconds. Mel Thorpe,running in Belgrave colours for the first time on the Brighton road,was faced with the problem of dealing with Reynolds of Portsmouth and John Snowden of Surrey. Both were in good form and were in fact the first and second fastest of the day,so there was no disgrace for Mel in having to give way. Our deficit at Earlswood was forty three seconds. Pat Newell,back into the team again,ran a fast sixth stage and just caught the Surrey boy at the end of the leg. He had to share the fastest time with the Portsmouth runner so we were still forty three seconds behind. Alan Black pulled back nineteen seconds across Gatwick Airport with a stylish performance which gained him the second fastest time of the day, and Gerry North set of on the long trek to Handcross to Handcross with Martin Hyman in sight. Unfortunately Gerry was not at his absolute best and instead of picking up Hyman as we had hoped,he was forced to drop back ten seconds leaving Bill Kerr the invidious task of chasing the other and better of the Cooke boys. Bill set off slowly whilst Cooke went like a bomb. and the gap widened rapidly. Our spirits dropped but were raised again when we found that the fast start was telling badly on the Portsmouth runner.Bill slowly pulled back and we had visions of him finishing close, but a great effort over the last mile kept Portsmouth in the lead by sixty five seconds. This lead was further increased with a fast run by Bruce Tulloh on stage ten despite a great effort by Geoff North and with only two stages to go we were almost one and a half minutes behind - practically an impossible position. Tony Fairclough had different ideas on the subject and caring little for the reputation of Frank Salvat,produced the best ever run by a Belgrave Harrier on this leg;and in knocking four seconds from Dave Baulch's club record became the first Belgravian to beat twenty minutes. This excellent effort reduced Portsmouths lead to fifty seconds and put new heart into the Belgrave supporters. Although Jack Brown (back into the team again after missing a number of Brightons) was our oldest runner;his great experience soon became apparent,for against a Portsmouth newcomer on his first Brighton, he closed the gap rapidly. The leeway was just too much,however,and Portsmouth got home by a mere 100 yards. Jack ran his heart out and was only thirteen seconds outside his own club record set up twelve years ago when he was at his very best. Obviously there is life in the old dog yet - we shall look forward to a repetition next April. items.label: February 1965
items.sum: Note on Derek Crookes's recovery from major surgery in 1963 and his election as Road Running Secretary.
items.s: ROAD RUNNING Note on Derek Crookes's recovery from major surgery in 1963 and his election as Road Running Secretary. In the summer of 1963 Derek Crookes was stricken with a stomach ailment which necessitated major surgery. From an active athlete at all distances up to a marathon this keen Belgravian became a pale shadow of his former self. Prospects for a continued athletics career were decidedly remote. Thanks to a fighting spirit though,and faith in the human frame,Derek was running again within 6 months. He is now keener than ever,and at our last AGM Derek Crookes was elected Road Running Secretary. He not only enters names,organises teams and keeps in touch with the road running world,but also competes himself and writes reports and results for your Hon.Editors! It is on this latter score that we are particularly indebted to Derek,but we feel sure that on all scores he will serve Belgrave well. Derek Crookes Derek Crookes Derek Crookes Derek

items.label: February 1965

items.s: THE '5¾' ROAD RACE Report and handicap result of the club 5¾ mile road race at Wimbledon on 26 September, an autumn Brighton relay trial won by Bill Kerr from Tony Fairclough and C. Dabbs. Wimbledon - September 26th Bill Kerr showed a welcome return to form when he took the Autumn "trial" in convincing style from Fairclough and Dabbs. Several of our leading runners were not taking part and it was apparent that any potential "Brighton" man would have to make the first eight to be worthy of further consideration. By the time Copse Hill had been reached the eight were sorted out from the rest. Fairclough set the pace for a fair time and the opposition gradually dropped away until only Kerr and Dabbs were with him. Kerr then made his effort, and although Tony hung on for a while the scotsman proved the stronger, crossing the line with an 11 second margin. Dabbs pulled back ground on young Fairclough, but Tony's courage held off the assault and he preserved a well-run second place. Jack Brown ran himself back into the Brighton team in convincing fashion and Bicourt, in only his second crack at the event, showed he will be well to the fore next time. items.label: February 1965
items.sum: Report of the Nos Galan New Year's Eve races at Mountain Ash, where Gerry North was 5th in the mile and 2nd in the midnight 4 miles and Belgrave's team finished 7th (the report puts John Bicourt 16th, while the result lists him as '3.').
items.s: NOS GALAN Report of the Nos Galan New Year's Eve races at Mountain Ash, where Gerry North was 5th in the mile and 2nd in the midnight 4 miles and Belgrave's team finished 7th (the report puts John Bicourt 16th, while the result lists him as '3.'). At long last Belgrave managed to field a team in the 4 miles team race which starts in the old year and finishes in the early minutes of the new year. The Nos Galan races( 100yds, 1 mile, 4 miles and womens mile) are held at Mountain Ash in Wales. The celebration started in the afternoon when Brian Lee (Roath H) arrived with a goodwill message from the Mayor of Cardif 20 footsore miles away,for the Chairman of the Mountain Ash Council. The mile started at 4pm. on Dec.31st and Gerry North thought this would be a good warm up for the midnight '4'. After a flat out sprint over the far from flat course he finished 5th behind Whetton,Simpson and D.Taylor in a field of 31 and only 2.6 seconds behind the winner - some warm up! The torch bearing mystery runner of 1964 was Stan Eldon,who ran down the mountainside in all white to light the Nos Galan beacon and start the midnight race. At 11:46 pm. the verey rocket let loose 240 runners on the start of the Mountain Ash. Gerry got with the leaders right away and John Bicourt also made an impressive start. Lt soon became a Simpson/North duel and,to Gerry's surprise,the Rotherham runner proved stronger up th hills. After several efforts Simpson eventually got away near the end to win with a 4 secs margin. The rest of the field led by O'Riordan (Donore H),were nearly half a minute away but it was not long after that John Bicourt crossed the line in 16th place after a very fine run. Gerry and John were our only top men present and Bels had to wait until 88th position for their 3rd scorer to appear (Derek Crookes). Joe. MacDonald completed the Belgrave contingent in 131st place,with nearly half the field behind him. With another of our better runners Belgrave would certainly have got amongst the team prizes but,as it was, they could only finish but 7th. Perhaps next year we will be able to get that extra man along and stamp our name on a celebration of increasing prestige. There were 258 finishers and 28 teams closed in. items.sum: Junior Section notes on the youths' cross-country season, promising juniors such as Adrian Major, and the return of Ron Hayes and Derek Hurd after illness and injury.
items.s: Junior Section Junior Section notes on the youths' cross-country season, promising juniors such as Adrian Major, and the return of Ron Hayes and Derek Hurd after illness and injury. The Youth's section,in cross country competition,have not hit the headlines so far this season. But as all members know,these things go in cycles and I am hoping that the track season this year will compensate.New members of late seem more interested in the shorter track events,and I know that our coaches will supply the necessary knowhow. Ben Lulham is full of enthusiasm for the sprint relays and Frank Simmons, I feel sure,will come up with some material. So all in all it should be an interesting track season. Back again to the winter,Adrian Major has had a very good season and it is most noticeable that in this section a potential star emerges each year. Recent instances have been D.Cocks,A.Fairclough,J.Bicourt,J.Vivian,J.Barnard and J.Mitchell;and there are numerous others good enough to rate first team selection in the Seniors when coming of age. I was very pleased indeed to see two of our boys back again fit and well after a long absence - Ron Hayes and Derek Hurd.Ron has recovered from a serious illness,and tells me that he has now resumed full time work. Derek, who spent a month in hospital after a cycle accident,also looks well and hopes to resume light training soon. These two have been missed this season and I feel sure they have the very best wishes of the club. Jack Hampshire Snr. Jack Hampshire Snr. Jack Hampshire Snr. Juniors:- The team were well pleased with their 2nd place over the tough two-lap course which included several ploughed fields and ditches. John Bicourt ran a great race in finishing 4th - especially considering that he had run in the Nos Galan only two days previously. Next year he will still be eligible and could quite well be the individual winner. The rest of our scoring team were all high up in the field but nothing could have beaten Hercules AC who won the team event easily,even without one of their star men - Dave Holt. Howard Satchell nearly caused an upset when he was only narrowly beaten by Alan Morrison;thus just missing a team medal. items.sum: Chris Steer's humorous account of the season's socials at Belgrave Hall: a Pyramus and Thisbe sketch, a darts and photographic competition, and the New Year's Eve Carnival, crediting Charlie Manning.
items.s: SOCIALLY YOURS Chris Steer's humorous account of the season's socials at Belgrave Hall: a Pyramus and Thisbe sketch, a darts and photographic competition, and the New Year's Eve Carnival, crediting Charlie Manning. What! Shakespeare at Belgrave Hall? The Bard's immortal poetry echoing around the showers? Could this be the Belgrave of old ? It certainly could,and the occasion was,strangely enough,the first social of the year. By way of an added attraction,a group of itinerant Thespians,with a thirst for bringing culture to the masses (and an even greater thirst for beer)were hired,at great expense,to squeeze a dramatic interlude between Joe Loss and the Beatles. Dramatic was the word! Before a spellbound audience the tragic story of Pyramus and Thisbe unfolded. The star studded cast threw everything into the performance: Mel Thorpe(Pyramus) and Brian Nott (Thisbe) made as fine a pair of lovers as ever graced the stage of the Old Vic and the supporting players,Ted Stimpson (Moonshine), Alan Mead (Wall),Howerd Satchell (Lion)and Chris Steer (producer,director, stage manager,prompter,etc.)would have done justice to the National Theatre. In fact contracts and film rights had to be turned down as these would interfere with training. The next social gave other specialists in the club a chance to exhibit their skills,this time the darts players and photographers. The darts contest,held in the hallowed precincts of the 'King of Denmark' turned out to be a victory for Bill Cousins,who defeated Bob Taylor in the final. The photographic competition aroused a terrific interest(especially the unclothed lady in the 'sports and pastimes' section). The variety and quality of the photographs displayed the latent talent in Belgrave. The New Years Eve Carnival proved to be another revelation. Could that really be Clive Shippen looking like the Count of Monte Cristo ? Was that dusky skinned gentleman Mr.Kenyatta bearing a striking resemblence to Alan Mead? Who ever thought of Mr.and Mrs Collis as Neanderthal man and woman ? As for Charley Manning - he looked like a decadent Nureyev. There were 1920 flappers,South Sea Islanders,Arabs,Barrow Boys,a pantomime cow and Geoff North as Cassius Clay - or was he just being himself ? The occasion was a great novelty and a great success,and was enhanced by the presence of a real live band. Need one add that the tremendous success of socials this year can be attributed directly to the enthusiasm and dynamism of one person - Charles Manning. Although officially titled Social Secretary this usually involves being a carpenter,electrician,sweeper and doorman. Needless to say Charlie has executed all these functions with his usual good humour. Remember though there are TWO MORE socials yet to come. Details are,of course,top secret at this stage,but of one thing you may be sure..... ...... IT'LL BE A GAS,MAN. Chris Steer. items.label: February 1965
items.sum: A humorous child's-eye account of the club children's party at Belgrave Hall on 10 January.
items.s: THE CHILDRENS' PARTY A humorous child's-eye account of the club children's party at Belgrave Hall on 10 January. JANUARY 10th - BELGRAVE HALL My sister and I have been asked to write a short report on the childrens' party held at Belgrave Hall. I ask you;how conceited can grown-ups get? Always wanting to be in the limelight. Of course they always insist on dressing us up;then the instructions before we go."Don't show off,don't eat too much, don't fight." That puts you off for a start. When we got there my mum insisted that we put a blindfold on and try to put a tail on a donkey. I soon put a stop to that lark,I stuck the pin in her tail. I don't know why we had to wait 'till everyone arrived before we started tea though. First come,first served,I say. I ate 14 sandwiches,8 cakes and 2 jellies(I pinched the boy's next to me when he wasn't looking;well he should have been quicker). Someone came and whipped the table cloth before I could eat any more,so I stuck a couple of chocolate cakes in my pocket for later. Then they wanted to organise a lot of soppy games. Ugh!! Do you suffer with grown-ups? I enjoyed myself the best way I could in this,I trod on some girls skirt just as she was about to stand up. That caused a bit of a stir. It was smashing in the sing-song with Uncle Reg Hopkins on the guitar. I kept pinching the girl in front and everyone thought she was singing.I had a good laugh at Uncle Bernard Merry when he poured water down Uncle Chris Steer's trousers. Of course it didn't fool me when they pretended to pour water over all of us. As if they would after dressing us up like that. Was I embarrassed when my dad came in dressed as a wizard. Well! How would you feel if your dad made a fool of himself in front of all those kids. Then a ghost kept appearing. How daft do they think we are? It was Uncle Howard Satchell with a sheet over his head. I liked the ice-cream. I queued up three times,but nobody noticed. Father Christmas came and gave us all smashing presents. I expect he gets fed up with grown-ups too,always singing "Jingle Bells" every time he arrives, and turning the lights low just as he is struggling down the stairs with that big sack. When he had gone we were all given a bag of sweets,a blower and a big sticky coconut sweet. When we got home though what happened?Dad took away the blowers 'cos he couldn't stand the noise,and Mum gave me a good hiding for having two squashed chocolate cakes in my pocket. Anyway,I had my own back,I was sick all over the kitchen floor! Reg Hopkins Uncle Reg Hopkins Bernard Merry Uncle Bernard Merry Chris Steer Uncle Chris Steer Howard Satchell Uncle Howard Satchell Belgrave Harriers Children's Party 1965 Belgrave Hall

items.label: February 1965
items.sum: Mock-heroic account of the club jumble sale at the Hall in Wimbledon on 12 December, which raised twenty-five pounds, with a cartoon of the crowd.
items.s: I was there... Mock-heroic account of the club jumble sale at the Hall in Wimbledon on 12 December, which raised twenty-five pounds, with a cartoon of the crowd. "JUMBLE SALE, SATURDAY 12th DECEMBER......", read the gay little sign that graced the salubrious portals of several derelict shops, neatly covering the "bill posters will be prosecuted" notice, in and around Wimbledon. Some wooden fences, that had previously been of a strictly utilitarian purpose and used by late night revellers from the "Denmark" and "Swan" to wet their initials on were similarly decorated. The local paper carried the same succint message. So, with the advertising done and the stage set we awoke to a windy, cold and squally winter's day - the glorious 12th. Arriving at the Hall just after 9.30 we were puzzled to see a knot of people outside, we subsequently learned that they had been there since 9.o'clock Inside had a true Dickensian flavour, the stage was obscured by rows of gent's suits; ladies' hats and mirrors were within this wall of loths. Trestles were sagging from the weight of toys, skirts, roller skates, cigarette lighters and coal scuttles; umbrellas and football boots were beautifully arranged to show off the washing machine and a King George V Coronation Cup to their best advantage. There were fire fenders and car bumpers plus a fine copy of Moriarty's Law. A tandem, a carpet from one of our stately homes and a Ming dynasty vase sat shoulder to shoulder with pictures in frames and pictures out of frames or just frames, in this Fagin-like warehouse. Outside,the knot had lengthened to the Ridgway, and so, as the hour drew nigh and reports filtered through it was apparent that the old adage "The pen is mightier than the sword" took on a more frightful aspect. Just the two words, "jumble sale", had awakened something savage in the breast of man. with a minute to go the fiends were hammering on the door. The few Belgravian stalwarts were sheltering behind their women folk waiting for the onslaught. We started the count down, the air was pregnant with awe, with wonder, and at zero with fear. Never, from my invincible position locked in the corner kitchen, have I before seen the look of terror written on the faces of those whom I call friends. Win Penny mesmerised like a rabbit before a snake, Arthur Penny crouching behind the bannisters and pretending it was a bad dream which would soon go away. Gwenda Lucas throwing her arms in the air in sheer horror and screaming a question at Jean Manning who was inarticulate in the face of this tidal wave of warriors armed with handfuls of 3d bits and a variety of bags for the plunder. The enemy were devastatingly efficient, their consumption insatiable, their brazen contempt for accepted commercial traffic was evident by the looting we were powerless to stop. How had the thin claret and gold line held round the hall with only the stalls for defence? Although I had so far remained undetected in the lift shaft - my heart went out to them. I remembered when Ted Stimpson and I had cantered gaily over the Common together;would he now at best be only maimed for life ? Alan Mead - that hair- they'd have that for certain.What of Bill Lucas? he really hadn't been such a bad chap; just misunderstood. The noise of battle was still raging when I considered our other flank. George Piddington and Ben Lulham were old campaigners; had they prevented the rape of Evelyn Stimpson?- would we ever see her smile again? We had lost Bernard Merry in the first few seconds - of this I was convinced and had crossed myself earlier. Almost as suddendly as it began the tumult ceased.....it was over.... gradually we emerged.....Belgrave had triumphed....weary and slightly dazed we took stock.....we'd won.... twenty-five tax free pounds! C.M. This brave Belgravian was posthumously awarded an Honours Badge after saving the club piano from being sold! This brave Belgravian was posthumously awarded an Honours Badge after saving the club piano from being sold! C.M. C.M. items.label: February 1965
items.sum: Clive Shippen's history of the International Cross-Country Championship from 1898 to 1964 ahead of the 1965 race at Ostende, with Belgrave's international runners, the leading individuals, a country-by-country summary table and five photographs (four England teams and the 1952 first three).
items.s: The International Championship Clive Shippen's history of the International Cross-Country Championship from 1898 to 1964 ahead of the 1965 race at Ostende, with Belgrave's international runners, the leading individuals, a country-by-country summary table and five photographs (four England teams and the 1952 first three). Clive Shippen reviews the history of...... The International Championship On March 20th, 1965,a dozen teams of the world's best cross-country runners will line up in Ostende, Belgium, to fight out the 52nd International Championship. It could be anyone's race. Arizmendi (Spain) holds the individual title and England the team award, but the Spaniard is unlikely to start favourite and the English team will be hard pushed to defeat the home side, all out to regain the title England took from them last year in Dublin. In 1963 only 3 points covered the first three teams - such is the standard that has made this event the Mecca of cross-country running. It was a different story in 1898. The French Athletic Federation challenged the first eight in the English 'National'. The race was held over a 9 miles course in France and the English team filled the first eight places! The first Frenchman, A. Touquet, fell unconscious as he crossed the line and, to rub it in, their second man was an Englishman, H. Freeman. Enthusiasm died down in the following three or four years. Then, in 1903, enthusiasts in the Welsh and Irish Associations planned the first International cross-country race. How confident were the organisers of success? Well, it was not until after the race that the LUMLEY Shield came into being and it was agreed to form an International Cross-Country Union. The Welsh/ Irish secretaries approached Scotland first of all, who readily adopted the idea, and it is not surprising to hear that the English were against it. After all, wasn't our own 'National' open to all amateur teams. "I do not see the good to be gained by such a race. It will be almost as much a farce .... as our unfortunate trial with France a few years ago" - so spoke an English official. It is significant, however, that France was not invited. Eventually England agreed to compete providing, of course, that the race was postponed a week to enable the great Alfred Shrubb to run! Shrubb duly won and England's scoring 6 were split only by the Irishman Daly, who was 3rd. The inaugural meeting of the Union was held on the morning of the 1904 race where it was agreed that the venue for the succeeding year's event should be decided on the morning of each Championship. The race would be 'open to the world'. The 1904 race went the same way as the previous year's, except a second 'intruder' split England's six. France got its invitation two years later and raced for the first time in 1907 at Scotstown. This was the occasion when a swarthy, thick-set Frenchman named Jean Bouin made his first appearance on British soil; it was not his last, and England's runners were to see a lot more of him in subsequent years - mainly from behind. The first hiatus was brought about by World War I. England had won all 12 Championships and Bouin was the first to score a hat-trick of individual titles. Contests were resumed in 1920 and the following year the England team notched up its 14th successive title. All good things come to an end, and it was fitting that France should be the country to end them. The memory of that 1898 "whitewash" was erased in 1922 and future championships became a France/ England battle. 1937, Winning Team, ENGLAND L. to R. G.W. Bailey(26), A.Bourton(13),J.T. Holden(-),J.H. Potts (4), T. Lee(18),R.V. Draper(19) J. Ginty(3),H.D. Clark(12),J.A. Burns(5). In 1923, at Maisons-Lafitte, near Paris, the local Mayor presented to the Union a bronze statuette known as the Maisons-Lafitte trophy, to be awarded to the individual winner for 12 months. This year also saw the admission of Belgium and the temporary withdrawal of Ireland, who were sorting out North v South domestic squabbles amongst their officials. Perhaps it was fortunate that the Union met but once only a year; more frequent meetings might well have magnified the difficulties. France and Scotland were not happy with the venue "going the round". The French wanted it every 3rd year in France and the Scots every year in the north of England and the result was "no change", whereupon the French delegate proposed that the 1924 race, to be held in England, should be held as near the French coast as possible - it was staged at Newcastle! France was on a hat-trick at Newcastle but England chose this occasion to be the first team to score minimum points in the official championship (21) by having the first six men home. However, the French got their hat-trick plus a bonus win in 1926/7/8/9. In the latter year non-member nations competed for the first time; Spain, Italy, Switzerland, and Luxembourg, boosting the entry to ten. England, however, were ready once more for a long run of victories and replied by notching up the next nine; leaving France the last one before World War II (1939). Jack Holden was the individual winner in the last pre-war race and thus became the first man to score 4 wins. Belgravians were notable contributors to this period of England supremacy. The roll of honour reads as follows:- 1931 Arthur Allum 9th 1933 Bert Footer 4th 1933 Arthur Penny 9th 1934 Arthur Penny 3rd 1934 Bert Footer 4th 1936 Tom Carter 37th 1937 Jim Ginty 3rd 1939 Arthur Penny 18th 1939 Ted Stimpson - 1939, Second Team, ENGLAND E. STIMPSON (-) next to official, with A.W. Penny (18) on his right. J.T. Holden (1st) is 6th from left. Now to the post-war era - food rationing, austerity everywhere, and the need to mould new teams. The effects of war had stimulated the desire for friendship and little time was lost in resuming contacts within the International Cross-Country Union. Even the Irish settled their differences and entered a combined team for the first time since 1932. As in many other spheres of the immediate post-war era, England appeared to suffer more than her continental friends. For 3 years, the Championship was exclusively a French/Belgian contest and in 1949, France had 5 in 8, with Alain Mimoun scoring his first of 4 wins. Most of Belgrave's post-war contributions were made during this period. 1946 Len Herbert 21st 1947 Len Herbert 40th 1948 Verne Blowfield 35th To those who do not remember the days of food rationing, it might be of interest to quote the following minute from the E.C.C.U's A.G.M. of 1948. "The Manager of the English International Team in Paris last March referred to the very generous action of the officials of the Eire A.A.U. in providing necessitous food to the members of the team, without which they would have been insufficiently nourished." Belgium won the championship for the first time in 1948 and provided the first two home in J. Doms and E. Renson. Holland entered for the first time in 1950 and Yugoslavia in 1953 when their No. 1, F. Mihalic, took the individual title. This latter year was the Jubilee Year of the I.C.C.U. The Championship was held in Paris and over 20,000 people were present, including the President of the French Republic M. Vincent Auriol. The heat was intense and 13 runners retired with sunstroke. England celebrated the jubilee in the best possible way - by beating their old rivals and recording their 27th win in 40 appearances. Surprisingly this was Gordon Pirie's only outing in the International Championship - his 19th position being 11 places better than his father's effort in 1926. 1948, Third Team, ENGLAND L. to R. S.C. Wooderson (14), J.A. Carrick (32) V.S. BLOWFIELD(35),R.C. Adams (34) A. Shorrocks(11),J. Corfield(30),J.Charlesworth(39)R.V.Hughes(19) The early nineteen-fifties were notable for the emergence of England's finest cross-country runner since Jack Holden - Frank Sando. His remarkable sense of judgment and a "wise old head" on a young and supremely fit body enabled him to finish inside the first two places on five occasions in seven years. He was 9th in his first championship (1952) and 8th in his last (1960) - a record of consistency that can only be matched by Holden and Mimoun. Mimoun had his first outing in 1949 when he took the individual title by inches from team-mate Pujazon, who was chasing his 3rd consecutive victory. The latter made no bones about how he felt! Mimoun was beaten in the Jubilee race by Lucien Theys of Belgium but in 1954 at Birmingham he regained the title at the expense of Ken Norris. Nevertheless, England finished 6 in 8 and retained the Lumley Shield. In 1955, Portugal became the 13th country to compete in the race and their 5th place out of eight teams was a fine start. England completed yet another trio of victories with 6 in 8 and Sando recorded his first win. France's 4th place was their lowest since 1920. Mimoun did not compete this year, but he came back with a vengeance in 1956 at Belfast where he beat Sando and K. Norris by 60 yds. and led the French team to victory; despite England having 3 in 4! These extremes of form in the England teams were even more apparent the following year when we had Sando 1st, Heatley 2nd, K. Norris 3rd, Chorlton 5th yet could only finish 3rd! Firth and Driver who finished 4th and 2nd in the English 'National' could only manage 52nd and 60th and it was left to Perkins 34th and reserve Humphreys 39th to complete the six. Belgrave's Jack Brown was next reserve on call and would certainly not have done worse than this supporting cast. His absence from the race also meant that the Club had gone 9 years without gaining an international vest over the country. 1958 saw the entrance of Tunisia and the start of another England hat-trick. The race was held at Cardiff and Eldon, Sando and Mimoun entered the final straight together. Mimoun forged ahead 50 yards from the tape but in a last desperate effort, Eldon stormed home to a win that prevented the Frenchman from being the only man to score five victories. In 1959, at Lisbon, Morrocco became the 15th country to have competed in the Championship and England turned out another of their 4 in 5 efforts. In the following year, Gerry North had his first I.C.C.U. outing finishing 15th (3 ahead of Mimoun) and was England's sixth scorer. Excellent packing by Belgium in 1961 at Nantes prevented England from gaining a 4th consecutive victory, but we had the consolation of seeing that fine cross-country runner Basil Heatley, gain his first International title. At Sheffield in 1962, Gerry North was hoping to be the first man to win the Inter-Counties, National and International titles - the first two were already his. Early in the race he fell at a sharp bend and lost a dozen places. The effort in fighting his way back to 3rd at half-way brought on a 'stitch' and he had great difficulty in holding on to a gallant 8th place. However, England re-gained the title and Gerry gained his second team-winners' medal. The South Africans, who were over here for the London/Brighton road run and who had stayed at Arthur Whitehead's cottage for many weeks, entered a team; the 16th country to do so. They ran exceptionally well to finish 6th and had great pleasure in beating France by virtue of their last scoring man. This was France's lowest ever position. 1963 saw Belgium, France and England within 3 points of each other - Fowler the individual champion - a record entry of 11 teams - and last, but not least, the 18th consecutive appearance of that amazing Belgian Marcel Vandewattyn. Last year he made it 19; will he make it 20 at Ostende? I have purposely left this 40 [?] years old veteran until last; although this is not the position to which he is accustomed. Vandewattyne's first international was at Ayr Racecourse in 1946, when he finished 2nd to Pujazon. Scottish conditions must have agreed with him, for 6 years later at Hamilton Park Racecourse, he was 2nd again; this time to Mimoun. Ten more I.C.C.U. appearances went by until at Sheffield in 1962, team-mate Roelants became the 3rd man to push the unfortunate Vandewattyne into 2nd position. To be a runner-up in this class of competition at each end of a 16 years' span is an achievement that even Jack Holden couldn't match. It is ironical though that, unlike Holden, Vandewattyne has not recorded a single win in his 19 outings. The sands of time are now running out for this remarkable Belgian and his 26th position of last year is just about as high as he can now aim. All lovers of cross-country will be hoping to see the familiar figure of Marcel Vandewattyne in the 1965 line up in Ostende and, should he appear, I've an inkling that it will not be just Belgian supporters cheering him on. To produce a ranking list of the top individuals is too difficult a task to attempt, but I have no hesitation in noting the performances of the four runners that stand out above all others. They are:- JACK HOLDEN ( England) 12 appearances. 1st (four times) 2nd (twice) 6th (three times) 7th, 18th and on one occasion did not finish (1937) ALAIN MIMOUN (France) 9 appearances 1st (four times) 2nd (twice) 6th, 18th and 26th. FRANK SANDO (England) 9 appearances 1st (twice) 2nd (three times) 3rd, 4th, 8th and 9th. MARCEL VANDEWATTYNE.(Belgium) 19 appearances 2nd (three times) 5th, 7th, 9th. 10th, 13th (three times), 14th, 15th, 16th, 17th (twice), 24th, 26th, 29th and 30th. 1952 First Three Individuals L. to R. B. Driss (F)3rd, A. Mimoun (F) 1st, M. Vandewattyne (B) 2nd. (Cont'd. on p.17) Cont'd. from p.22 No Belgravian has run for England over the country more than 3 times (Arthur Penny) nor finished higher than 3rd (J. Ginty, A. Penny). Gerry North's 4th came close to beating the latter record at Dublin and, in time, he should beat the former too. Belgrave appearances for the other home countries were:- J. Parker (N.I) 1937 and 1938, D.J. Main (Ireland) 1946. W. Kerr was selected for Scotland in 1962 but was unable to compete. So, thanks to that small band of Welsh and Irish stalwarts 61 years ago, the International Championship is now a red-letter day on the cross-country calendars of Europe. Sixteen countries have contributed to this success and it is fitting perhaps that I should conclude with a summary of their efforts. NOTE Italy has competed once (6th), S. Africa once (6th) and Luxembourg twice (10th each time). Eire and N. Ireland sent their own teams on 3 and 7 occasions respectively - the former finishing 4th and 7th (twice), and the latter 6th (six times) and 7th. items.label: February 1965
items.sum: Reprinted 1950s training article by walker Len Fletcher on style-first race-walking training for track and road, continued on page 13.
items.s: HOW I TRAINED Reprinted 1950s training article by walker Len Fletcher on style-first race-walking training for track and road, continued on page 13. We continue our series of training articles from Belgrave Newsletters of the early 1950's (2) LEN FLETCHER Next to judging I know of no more controversial subject apertaining to race walking. It is like asking a tobacconist which is the best tobacco,or a piano salesman which is the best piano. In short there is no best way;it all comes down to a point of suitability,and from my own experience,athletic training,or should I say the correct training methods used depend largely on the physique and temperament of the individual. I commenced race walking at the tender age of 18 years;a tall,lanky and much too thin youth,and I was fortunate to be coached by my late father and his brother;two athletes of the old school who always deplored the general tendency to burn up youngsters before they even learned a good style. Style comes first and if you show a tendency to push the pace,check yourself;speed will come if you are going to be a walker. This was hammered into me continuously. So remember,develop a good easy natural style and a natural stride and let anyone win the training spins. Such do not win races, as you leave your speed and consequent exhaustion in a spin,whereas you will want all your energy for the race. For the walker of the thin physique who must preserve his strength,I recommend the following methods:- TRAINING FOR THE TRACK. Once you have developed a good style,approved by your coach,approach your training in a campaign attitude.First I recommend a very slow trot of two or three laps thus loosening the muscles in a similar manner to the runners,and at the same time indulging in deep breathing exercises. Then commence a walk of two miles starting very steadily and concentrating on your style and balance. On commencing the second mile,warm up the pace but still walk within yourself,but when you enter the last lap speed up and finish fast. This method I used for the first 4 to 6 weeks of track training,thus making sure I could stay the distance. As I got fitter and consequently faster, I reduced the steady pace to the first mile and speeded the second mile. Once fit and fast,my training was reduced to fast miles or at the most 6 laps. Eventually I got to a 6:52 mile and 14:2 for 2 miles. These performances on the tracks of Battersea Park and Stamford Bridge would have meant faster performances on the fast White City track. Once again I emphasise that the methods quoted here are those I recommend for the slight physique type of walker who must preserve his weight and husband his strength to last the season. ROAD TRAINING FOR 7 TO 10 MILES. Road walking requires a combination of speed,staying power and judgement,particularly over the longer distances. First and foremost I do not recommend a walker under the age of 21 attempting any distances over 7 miles. Cont'd. on p.13 Cont'd. from p.24 For training over a 7 to 10 mile course: Again walk a steady 6 miles not forgetting your style and getting that feeling of good balance,making the 6th mile faster and finishing over the last 400 yds fast. I found this a good stamina build up and had confidence in staying the distance. At any stage of road training there should be no fast-all-the-way methods. That is a sheer waste of energy and leads to staleness before the end of the season. For a 10 mile race a distance of 8 or 9 miles is sufficient at moderate speed until the last two miles; then warm up the pace to the finish. Finally remember. STYLE FIRST.speed will come, Len Fletcher LEN FLETCHER Battersea Park Stamford Bridge White City

items.sum: Countryman's gossip column on Hugh Barrow joining as first claim, the North Surrey League, Arthur Whitehead's pack runs, members abroad (Barry Sawyer, Fred Paget), forthcoming relays and the North brothers' races at Lille and in the Sefton Brancker Trophy (continued on page 4).
items.s: A COUNTRYMAN'S Jottings Countryman's gossip column on Hugh Barrow joining as first claim, the North Surrey League, Arthur Whitehead's pack runs, members abroad (Barry Sawyer, Fred Paget), forthcoming relays and the North brothers' races at Lille and in the Sefton Brancker Trophy (continued on page 4). A COUNTRYMAN'S Jottings ...... Hugh Barrow completes his 14 months qualification period in March and thereafter will be first claim Belgrave. At one time Hugh had anticipated moving to London permanantly but finally decided to remain in Glasgow and travel as often as possible - hence his 14 months wait. In Scotland he is first claim Victoria Park AAC, which is Bill Kerr's home club. Hugh is a dedicated runner from whom great things can be expected. He already holds the British Junior mile record. For 2 years now he has been a keen follower of Belgrave, going to considerable expense to get down here as often as possible. Now he is first claim we can expect to see even more of him. * * * For the past two years Walton AC have taken the North Surrey League title with Belgrave runners-up each time. This year, with one fixture to come, we are well ahead of them. Unfortunately there is another team which has jumped right to the top and is almost certain of winning the trophy - Hercules AC. Their runners are good friends with Belgravians and I think they would admit that part of their success this last year or so is due to the collective pack runs of the two teams over Wimbledon Common and Richmond Park. * * * On the subject of pack runs, the Sunday morning outing from Arthur Whitehead's cottage sometimes numbers as many as fifty. Up to six clubs are represented. I sometimes wonder how Arthur manages to cope with such numbers and still provide hot showers, tea and biscuits. The Lauriston Cottage rendezvous is of great value to the runners but perhaps they would do well to ponder the moral of this issue's Editorial. * * * Barry Sawyer still seems to be getting in plenty of running in South-Africa. He is now living in Cape Town where he will remain until he moves to New Zealand in November. Unfortunately his running career is threatened by chronic trammatic teno-synovitis which occasionally pulls him up when an achilles tendon refuses to function. Although I would question his wisdom in running 11 miles flat out each night "to brutalize myself a little more and ignore the pain", his determination to win this year's Comrades Marathon is worthy of admiration. Barry had a crack at the South African National Cross-country championship He led for the first 1½ miles but his leg trouble put him back to 34th at the end. Belgravians will be interested to know that Mike Coningham was 13th and Rex Chugg - a former Australian member - was also competing. Rex's brother Doug is now back in Australia running his own business but finds little time for training. Barry is soon hoping to see Henk Altmann who goes up to Oxford this year, so with any luck there should soon be another Belgravian on his way. * * * Fred Paget, a familiar figure at our cross country, road and track fixtures these last eight years, has moved to Australia. So yet another Belgravian takes his claret and gold vest overseas. Now nearing his 35th birthday, Fred had for some time been dogged with injury and it is a while since we saw him show promising form. He was also an accomplished cyclist and used this medium to keep fit when injury prevented his running. We shall miss his noisy, but determined, running - so adeptly called "fiery locomotion!" Good luck Fred! * * * Speaking of Fred Paget reminds me of that well known address, 4, Gowan Avenue, S.W.6. which he recently vacated. Several Belgravians have lived there at some time or other; two in particular being Pat Newell and Bill Kerr. It is odd that all the runners who have stayed there produced thier best form when at No. 4. Current lodgers are John Roberts and Ferdie Gilson of SLH, who are also running better than ever. What is the secret of Gowan Avenue? * * * The Southampton - Bournemouth relay and the Ilford relay both fall on March 13th. Our best six will be running at Southampton and our next twenty in the 'A' and 'B' teams at Ilford. Belgrave hold the Ilford trophy and are still capable of winning it for the third successive year, despite being without their first five in the "Southern" and Thresher. After all, how is this for a depleted ten? - Black, Brown, Barrow, Kerr, O'Hara, Newell, Bicourt, Thorpe, Moore and Walker. It would be an even greater feat to win both trophies! * * * Geoff North is running into fine form and stands every chance of equalling his 14th place of 1962 in this year's "National" at Parliament Hill Fields on 6th March. If he can keep his enthusiasm going for longer periods - and this seems more likely now he is settled - then he will soon have "big brother" watching him very carefully! (cont'd on p.4) Cont'd. from p.25. On the day of the Inter-Counties the North brothers were picked to join Derek Ibbottson in "La Voix du Nord" race at Lille. Winner was Allonsius (Belgium) in 29 : 51.5 with Gerry only 24.5 seconds down in 4th place. Ibbottson was 29th and Geoff (off-colour) 54th. Gerry missed the Inter-Counties out as he intends to adopt a Surrey qualification next season. He will be a great boost to the steadily improving Surrey team. Three Belgravians helped to boost this year's effort at Coldhams Common, Cambridge - John Thresher 34th, Tony Fairclough 54th and Charlie Dabbs 90th. On February 3rd at R.A.F. Halton, Geoff finished second to Briault in the Sefton Brancker Trophy match between the Civil Service, Middlesex and the R.A.F In leading the Civil Service team to victory Geoff easily beat Price, Pugh, Presland, Barratt, Cooper, Ellis, Entwistle, Mellor, Lindsell and Holts. ...........COUNTRYMAN Countryman COUNTRYMAN Hugh Barrow Hugh Barrow Hugh Barrow Hugh Barrow Bill Kerr Bill Kerr Bill Kerr Kerr Arthur Whitehead Arthur Whitehead Barry Sawyer Barry Sawyer Barry Sawyer Barry Mike Coningham Mike Coningham Rex Chugg Rex Chugg Doug Chugg Doug Henk Altmann Henk Altmann Fred Paget Fred Paget Fred Paget Fred Pat Newell Pat Newell Pat Newell Newell John Roberts John Roberts Ferdie Gilson Ferdie Gilson John Thresher Thresher Thresher John Thresher Black Black Brown Brown O'Hara O'Hara Bicourt Bicourt Thorpe Thorpe Moore Moore Walker Walker Geoff North Geoff North Geoff North Geoff Gerry North Gerry Gerry "big brother" Derek Ibbottson Derek Ibbottson Derek Ibbottson Ibbottson Allonsius Allonsius Tony Fairclough Tony Fairclough Charlie Dabbs Charlie Dabbs Briault Briault Price Price Pugh Pugh Presland Presland Barratt Barratt Cooper Cooper Ellis Ellis Entwistle Entwistle Mellor Mellor Lindsell Lindsell Holts Holts Surrey League (North Surrey League) 1964-65 Comrades Marathon 1965 South African National Cross Country Championships 1965 Southampton - Bournemouth Relay 1965 Ilford Relay 1965 National Cross Country Championships 1965 La Voix du Nord race, Lille 1965 Inter-Counties 1965 Sefton Brancker Trophy 1965 Glasgow Wimbledon Common Richmond Park Lauriston Cottage Cape Town New Zealand Australia Oxford 4, Gowan Avenue, S.W.6 Southampton Ilford Parliament Hill Fields Lille Coldhams Common, Cambridge R.A.F. items.s: PRIORY RELAY Report and result of the Priory Relay at Redhill and Reigate on 7 November, where a weak Belgrave turnout finished 6th. WEAK TEAM AT REDHILL AND REIGATE - November 7th Although only ranked as a minor event the turnout of claret and gold was still surprisingly poor. Bicourt, who ran first stage, was our fastest runner, finishing 8th, and thereafter our position hovered between 6th and 9th before settling for the former after nearly an hour. items.sum: Note that Belgrave, holders of the London County cross-country title, gave it away by failing to turn out a full team, with only Hart, Fairclough and Dear running.
items.s: SANTA BELGRAVE ! Note that Belgrave, holders of the London County cross-country title, gave it away by failing to turn out a full team, with only Hart, Fairclough and Dear running. As Holders of the London County C.C. Championship for 1963, one would think it reasonable to expect our runners to hang on to the trophy for all they were worth. Not on your life! Freshly endowed with lashings of Christmas Spirit and Goodwill to all men (particularly other athletes) we actually GAVE AWAY the title by failing to turn out a full team. Perhaps those runners who fail to answer cards will substitute courtesy for generosity in 1965 - perhaps. Those who did what they could to salvage the situation were Trevor Hart (13th), Tony Fairclough (29th) and John Dear (49th). items.s: The North Surrey League Reports and results of the first three senior North Surrey League matches (Wimbledon, Esher, Addington), with Belgrave winning the first two and lying second to Hercules AC with one race left, illustrated by P. Pepe's photograph from Wimbledon. MATCH No. 1 - Wimbledon,October 24th This first fixture,of the four making up the annual contest,was held from our own HQ in conjunction with our opening '5'. Walton,the holders, were dead keen to retain their title but many Belgravians thought that Hercules AC,our frequent training companions,presented a far greater threat this season. Gerry North had not been at his best since before the "Brighton" and it was all he could do to hold Snowdon until the run-in,when the Surrey AC man sprinted to a good win. Only 7 of our Brighton 12 were running but they finished well enough up to take our scoring 10 to a narrow win. Jack Brown followed up his memorable relay effort with a fine 17th place,only 17secs behind Tony Fairclough (18 years his junior). RESULT: (scorers only) (150 finished) Teams:(10 only to score - University scoring) Photo: P. Pepe. Geoff North (10) leads Gowan (110), Presland (211) and Thresher (3) in the opening match at Wimbledon. MATCH No. 2.- Esher,December 12th. Surprisingly,both individual and team wins went to the same clubs as in the opening fixture. Even more surprising was the inept display of the home club and trophy holders - Walton AC. They could only field eight runners and were therefore obliged to include the last two available positions in their score,namely,69 and 70. Even unluckier were Hercules AC who,after 8 in 43 ,also had to take places 69 and 70 into their score through being two men short. Belgrave were also poorly represented (it must have been the Christmas "spirit") but still had sufficient numbers to take them through to another win which increased their league lead to 33 [?] points over Hercules and 44 points over Mitcham. RESULT: (Scorers only) (83 finished) Teams: MATCH No.3 - Addington,January 16th Herne Hill Harriers were hosts for the third fixture which was held over their tough course,with its gruelling stretch of heavy "plough". Unfortunately the fixture clashed with Inter-Counties Championships and an international race on the continent,which meant we were without the North brothers,Thresher,Dabbs and Fairclough. To rub it in Walker and Maclean missed the start. Our main rivals,Hercules AC, were at full strength and,as if to drive home this advantage, decided to hold their 5 miles club championship in conjunction. They ran out convincing winners and little would have held them on this day. Our depleted team ran very well,almost every man doing better than he expected,and we still managed to salvage third place. John Bicourt showed great form and has obviously hit the Junior ranks as a real force. He could well cause some upsets in the Southern and National. The forward running of Hampshire and Dear also did a great deal towards keeping us in the Championship 'race'. RESULT: (Scorers only) (97 finished) Teams. items.sum: Reports on Belgravians in the Surrey (Guildford), Middlesex (Cockfosters) and Warwickshire (Baddesley) cross-country championships, with John Thresher 2nd in Surrey and Geoff North and Mel Thorpe running for Warwickshire.
items.s: County Championships Reports on Belgravians in the Surrey (Guildford), Middlesex (Cockfosters) and Warwickshire (Baddesley) cross-country championships, with John Thresher 2nd in Surrey and Geoff North and Mel Thorpe running for Warwickshire. SURREY - Guildford. This was the first time for a long while that three Belgravians ran themselves into the County team with such ease. Roberts (SLH) got away right from the start and it was soon evident that John Thresher would be second. Tony Fairclough,although still below peak,was third until the last mile when he was overhauled by a fast finishing trio,but was well pleased with the result - as indeed was Dabbs who was surprised to make the team so easily. Unfortunately the rest of the team were not up to the same standard and we had to go back to positions 68,80 and 84 to close in. Our 6th place was one of our worst ever performances. MIDDLESEX - Cockfosters. For once the going at Cockfosters was fast and firm and should have suited our runners. It was a fine effort for our team,Cadogan AC,to turn out twelve men,even though they did not rank high in club form. Mike Shingles and Trevor Hart were both "under the weather" and trailed in 65th and 68th positions. Laurie O'HAra was only 43 seconds outside the county team,in 20th place,and this fast improving runner should soon obtain a red and gold vest. All twelve Cadogan runners finished,with the scoring six placed 8th. WARWICKSHIRE - Baddesley. We had two "first timers" in the Midland event - Geoff North and Mel Thorpe. Both were previously Lancashire thro' residence,but since moving South decided to adopt their County of birth - Warwickshire. Geoff split the Coventry team most convincingly,beating Kilby,Taylor and Heatley,but had to give best to Adcocks (an easy winner) and Horne who beat Geoff in the run in. Mel Thorpe also ran particularly well finishing 16th and only 39 seconds outside one of the strongest County teams. items.s: MATCH v United Banks v Epsom and Ewell H.- Wimbledon, January 9th. Report and result of the cross-country match with United Banks and Epsom and Ewell at Wimbledon on 9 January, narrowly won by Belgrave thanks to Laurie O'Hara's late-start run. With Brian Nott and Alan Morrison representing the Banks on this occasion and finishing 3rd and 5th into the bargain, Belgrave only scraped home in the match result by their 6th man's position. It was Laurie O'Hara though who really saved the day. After a spell in bed during the week he only decided to run at the last minute, setting off after the field 2mins 10secs behind in a 5 miles race! The first two miles was spent catching the field, Thereafter he went among them like a knife thro' butter passing 43 rivals before crossing the line in 10th position. But for that delayed start he would have been a certain second - but for his keenness we would not have won. RESULT: (53 finished) (Scoring 20 a side) 1. Banks 419 pts. 2. BELGRAVE 527 pts. items.s: CLUB '10' to NORTH Report and handicap result of the club 10 miles cross-country championship (Macher Shield) on 23 January, won by Gerry North from his brother Geoff, with R. Linstead's photograph of the start. GERRY TAKES "MACHER" SHIELD - January 23rd. In marked contrast to last year, when Gerry finished 13th and brother Geoff retired, the North brothers set about the field with a fine display of determined running to take first two places well inside last year's winning time. Gerry stormed into the lead at the start and was obviously out for a good time in his last race before the "Southern", three weeks away. At 2 miles he was 25 seconds ahead of the field and at halfway a full minute. Churning out mile after mile at a relentless pace he eventually finished almost 2½ mins. in the lead, having completed his second 5 miles only 15 seconds slower than the first. Although the Championship was never in doubt there was an interesting race for the minor placings. After 2 miles Geoff North, Fairclough, Thorpe, Black, Dabbs and O'Hara were closely bunched with Black and Geoff North setting the pace; Bill Kerr was already finding their speed too fast. At halfway Geoff and Tony were still pushing the pace with Mel Thorpe hanging on extremely well. Black and O'Hara were dropping and the defending champion, Dabbs, did not look his usual self but was managing to hold his 5th place. With one lap to go Fairclough was leading from Geoff N. with Thorpe 20 seconds down, then Dabbs, Black and O'Hara (7th). Bill Kerr retired at this point when 8th, as did Bromley(9th) - who had the misfortune of a shoe spike penetrating thro' his inner sole - after some good running. Photo: R. Linstead Gerry North and Alan Black lead Geoff North (1), O'Hara (5), Thorpe (18), Fairclough (16) and Dabbs (27) shortly after the start. Geoff N. dropped Fairclough on the last circuit who was in danger of being caught by Thorpe in the closing stages. The only other change was O'Hara passing Black and moving up on Dabbs, who was not sorry to see the finish on this occasion. Of the others Chris Keavey and Bob Glover ran well and it was good to see Bob enjoying his racing once again. The Hon. Handicapper once again did a good job - the first three, Mel Thorpe, Gerry,and Chris Keavey being the most deserving prize winners of the day. It is interesting to note that of the 24 runners to finish this 4 x 2½ miles course the winner lapped all but the first 13! RESULT: Pos Name Handicap Time 1. Gerry North (Scr) 54:28 2. items.s: South of Thames Report and result of the South of Thames senior cross-country championship at Bracknell on 30 January, with Belgrave fifth (equal on points with Cambridge H). "Senior" Championship, Bracknell - January 30th. Having won the 1964 Championship our winning team became barred from future races. It is usually very difficult, as a result, to show up well in the following year so it is a credit to the 1965 team that they finished as high as 5th. In fact, with 5 in 49 they looked well set for a sensational 2nd place if their closing runner could finish near at hand, but Mike Shingles is still struggling to regain his old form and could only make 98th,so in a close contest we had to be content with 5th - the same position we made in the "Junior". Tony Fairclough and John Dear got a very good start but the latter paid dearly(!) for his effort and went back steadily down the field to a below-form 102nd. Tony also faded in the latter stages going from 6th to 14th. Trevor Hart in his first race for 5 weeks, produced a tremendous sprint finish with Beard (Hercules). Their impetus took them to the neck of the funnel full tilt and Hart's opponent was sent flying across the ropes; however, Trevor gave him the benefit of the doubt and sportingly let him take the forward placing. Kerr, Hart and Thorpe are all capable of better things and, with any luck, they should run into top form again in time for the National. RESULT: (25 teams finished) Pos Name Time 1. P. items.label: August 1965
items.sum: Editorial announcing that Belgrave will promote a new Invitation Road Relay from Belgrave Hall, Wimbledon on 9 October to replace the cancelled Southern clubs Brighton relay, and listing the club's annual open promotions.
items.s: EDITORIAL Editorial announcing that Belgrave will promote a new Invitation Road Relay from Belgrave Hall, Wimbledon on 9 October to replace the cancelled Southern clubs Brighton relay, and listing the club's annual open promotions. In February last we commented on the "News of the World's" decision to reprieve the National London - Brighton relay race and cancel the Southern Clubs "Brighton" instead. This decision was well received by the majority of people but two questions remained unanswered. Firstly,how will the ten southern clubs for the National event be selected ? Secondly,what will replace the premier autumnal relay ? Those questions were uppermost in the minds of most relay enthusiasts - not least those of Belgrave Harriers' officers. This Club has always regarded its object as the encouragement of amateur athletics (see Rule 4) and there was unanimity amongst the Committee that we should make every effort to plug this gap in the athletics calendar. After considerable lobbying it was found that the vast majority of Southern Clubs would welcome a subsitute event providing it was of sufficient stature. On the strength of this Belgrave Harriers have decided to promote an Invitation Road Relay on Saturday,October 9th,from Belgrave Hall,Wimbledon. It is a tribute to our reputation in the Athletics world for efficient organisation that,of the twenty-five clubs invited, twenty-four promptly accepted;and we are indeed honoured that they should endorse the view that our proposals were the best of many put up at the time. Twenty-five clubs will compete,each fielding teams of 12. There will be two laps - a "red"circuit and a "green" circuit;the former will be 5½miles and the latter 3 miles. Each will be run alternately,giving a race distance of 51 miles. The race commences at 12 noon and all Belgravians (whatever their sectional interests) are asked to come along and support the inaugural race of an event certain to become a red-letter day in the athletics calendar. Our Annual promotions are now as follows:- Open Field Events Meeting (March) Open 20 Miles Road Race (July) Invitation Road Relay (October) Open Youths Road Relay (October) Open 7 Miles Walk (November). London to Brighton Road Relay 1965 Belgrave Harriers Invitation Road Relay 1965 Belgrave Harriers Open Field Events Meeting Belgrave Harriers Open 20 Miles Road Race Belgrave Harriers Open Youths Road Relay Belgrave Harriers Open 7 Miles Walk Belgrave Hall Wimbledon

items.label: August 1965
items.sum: Hon. Secretary's notes on the club's new London Borough of Merton status, road construction at Tibbett's Corner, Syd Roberts's illness, fixture changes, E.T. Ryan's new Belgrave Shield for schools, reviving the Football Competition Scheme, the new Belgrave Road Relay and the AGM notice.
items.s: Hon Sec's Notes Hon. Secretary's notes on the club's new London Borough of Merton status, road construction at Tibbett's Corner, Syd Roberts's illness, fixture changes, E.T. Ryan's new Belgrave Shield for schools, reviving the Football Competition Scheme, the new Belgrave Road Relay and the AGM notice. Our Headquarters at Wimbledon now falls within the new Greater London Council area of the London Borough of Merton; and details of our Club and activities have been passed to the new Council who will make them available at Public Libraries etc. Our association with Wimbledon now goes back a very long way; the Club first using cross-country courses in the vicinity as far back as 1911-12. * * * We view with very great interest the road construction work which is imminent at Tibbett's Corner and thereabouts; and are hopeful that there will be no great interference with our running and walking road courses. Everywhere, particularly in urban and suburban areas the menace of increased traffic accompanied by the demands for more and more roads makes life difficult for the athlete using the roads and for Clubs responsible for promotion of road events. Some of us recall when our 5, 7 and 10 miles Cross-Country Championships were held over courses which involved the crossing of the main road and entering Robin Hood Gate into Richmond Park to run round Spanker's Hill Copse and Pen Ponds - but wider roads and increased traffic ended all that. Our Past-President, Syd Roberts and former holder of a number of offices in the Club extending over many years, has recently had an extremely severe illness. Fortunately he is now home again and progressing well and after a period of convalescence should be back with us again. We wish him a speedy return to normal health. * * * The change of August Bank Holiday to the end of the month has given rise to some fixture alterations and members should amend their Summer fixture list accordingly. The London Fire Brigade Meeting will take place on September 18th and this programme will include two A.A.A Relay Championships as usual; and a special Relays Programme with several newly-instituted A.A.A Championship relay events will be held on August 28th at Hurlingham Track. * * * We regret that our German friends from TURNVEREIN 1862, LANGEN were not able to confirm acceptance of our invitation to come to London this year. * * * The Track season is well on its way and we shall soon be back in force at Wimbledon once again retracing our courses on and around the Common. It is now the time to resolve to have a set of place medals - or even winning - in the E.C.C.U. Championship next March. We have the men - all we need is the will and determination and just a little bit of luck in the way of health and injuries. * * * We once again acknowledge the generosity of Vice President E.T. RYAN in providing a further Shield - the Belgrave Shield - for competition in the cross-country Championships promoted by the South London School Association. Thus all three groups into which schoolboys are now divided have a trophy thro' the Belgrave Harriers, at the expense of Eddie Ryan. * * * For many years past we have conducted a Football Competition Scheme which has gone a long way towards providing us with amenities well above average among athletic clubs; and enabled us to participate in practically every Championship and major events held, to a greater extent than any other club. In recent years with the retirement of some of our older members and changing circumstances; interest has waned somewhat in our money-raising activities and we now seek to fan it into flame again. We ask that every senior member should take a personal interest himself, and in addition that those able to do so should enlist the aid of their friends to take part in what is generally accorded to be one of the most generous competitions of its kind. Our Hon. Treasurer will gladly give further information - lets have our Supporter's Scheme back where it was years ago. * * * Our Belgrave Road Relay over twelve stages to be held at Wimbledon on October, 9th promises to be most successful, and twenty five clubs - the maximum permissible - have accepted invitations comprising the best in the South. Whilst the glamour associated with the Brighton Road will be missing- nevertheless the racing will be as keen as ever. * * * To economise on postage,etc.,the Notice of Annual General Meeting is included in this issue of the Belgravian on page 5,and no other notice will be circulated. It is hoped that all members will make an effort to attend. A.A.H. A.A.H. A.A.H. Syd Roberts Syd Roberts E.T. Ryan E.T. RYAN E.T. RYAN Eddie Ryan London Fire Brigade Meeting 1965 AAA Relay Championships 1965 E.C.C.U. items.sum: Report and result of the National Cross Country Championships at Parliament Hill on 6 March, where Belgrave were 6th and Gerry North 10th to make the International team.
items.s: BELS 6th in NATIONAL C.C. Report and result of the National Cross Country Championships at Parliament Hill on 6 March, where Belgrave were 6th and Gerry North 10th to make the International team. Parliament Hill-March 6th Although 6th is certainly no disgrace in an event of such stature, Belgravians were generally disappointed with a team which had promised so much. The margin between glory and mediocrity in these championships becomes increasingly narrower as the years go by. The smallest slip and half a dozen places are lost. Unfortunatley Geoff North and Trevor Hart, who had been showing great form in the preceding weeks, both dropped out. To lose two such runners and still finish 6th was a tribute to the rest of the team. Gerry North once again made the international team but this time had his supporters' hearts in their mouths. After one lap he was still in the twenties and although he began to make ground on the second circuit it was a slow and painful business against such opposition as Adcocks and Kilby (Coventry), Rose, Wheeler and Wyatt (New Zealand), Tulloh, Roberts and Barlow. With one lap to go it was fairly certain that the first 9 were decided; as these included two New Zealanders the next two Englishmen would make the "International". With two miles left Gerry was on his own with Tulloh and Roberts fighting it out 50yds ahead and Mike Wiggs moving up very fast through the field behind. The runners were next seen with half a mile to go. North had put in a tremendous effort over the back of the course to catch and pass Tulloh and Roberts and was now 30yds clear. However, the race for 10th place was by no means over and with 600yds to go Wiggs also caught the Pompey/SLH pair---"picking them up" in a long sprint for home. Gerry's 30yds had dwindled to five by the time the final straight was reached but after a desperate final effort he held off Wiggs by 1 second, Tulloh by 5 seconds and Roberts by 7seconds---quite a sprint! Dabbs and Fairclough had good runs and were very consistent; Kerr and O'Hara made considerable ground in the closing stages and John Thresher showed great courage in fighting on, despite losing 40-odd places in the final lap. If the experience of this occasion is put to good use and our team can keep free of illness and injury then Belgrave stand every chance of being amongst the medals at the next "National". RESULT 49. items.label: August 1965
items.sum: Report and result of the Ilford Road Relay on 13 March, where a second-string Belgrave team finished 4th and lost the trophy they had held for two years.
items.s: BELS lose title at ILFORD Report and result of the Ilford Road Relay on 13 March, where a second-string Belgrave team finished 4th and lost the trophy they had held for two years. ROAD RELAYS Ilford Road Relay--March 13th Unfortunately this race clashed with the Southampton/Bournemouth Relay which nowadays attracts a better class field. We therefore sent a strong team of our best six runners (too strong as it happened!) to Southampton and endeavoured to win the Ilford trophy for the third successive year with our next best 10 men. It almost worked. Many "ifs" come to mind, particularly those affecting Alan Black (unable to get away from Loughborough), John Bicourt(Junior Cross Country Race) and Pat Newell (shift working), but it is a lot to hope for--getting our top 16 men out in one day--and the question still remains "which fixture should have had the top priority?". The New Zealand cross-country team competed as guests and "won" by 7 minutes, but can be discounted as far as race description is concerned. Laurie O'Hara gave us a great start by winning the first stage from Dellar(Camb. H) by 1 second--the third man, King (Essex Beagles), being over half a minute behind. O'Hara thus became only the 4th Belgravian to break 18 mins round the course. Mike Shingles, who had been below his best for several weeks, was unable to break through the spell and dropped us to 4th on the next stage- a position maintained by Jack Brown on the 3rd leg, and who regained much lost ground in closing up to within 13secs of the runner ahead. Mitcham were in the lead at this point, 41secs ahead of Cambridge H and 53secs on Romford. Charlie Walker had not had a good winter season, and although he gave of his utmost on stage 4 it was nowhere near his old best, and he handed over to Jackie Hampshire a full minute behind 3rd place and 2 mins 11secs behind the new leaders--Cambridge H. Jackie must have picked up Charlie's trouble at the hand-over for he also was nowhere near his best and dropped us even further behind, in time (3:02), and position 8th. The revival commenced on Stage 6 with Mel Thorpe. Displaying scintillating form he scorched round the lap to take nearly a minute off the Cambridge man and move us up to 5th place. At this point Baldwin took Blackheath into the lead--a position they held to the end. Bill Kerr tried to continue the good work but, for him, his run was not spectacular. John Dear passed Mitcham on stage 8 but had to allow Poly to pass. We were still 4th, 1½mins behind the second team and 28secs behind the third--Blackheath were certain winners and the race was on for second place. The penultimate leg was taken by John Moore, another to have had a below-form winter, and although he recorded a mediocre time he took us past Polytechnic into 3rd place only 46seconds behind Cambridge Harriers. Everything depended on Don Maclean over the last stage and no-one envied him his task--Maynard of Cambridge H. 46seconds ahead and Malcolm Browne, the Essex Beagle miler, just 20seconds behind. Don made a great fight of it, and although Browne went right through to 2nd place and Belgrave had to be content with 4th position, Mac was fast closing on the Cambridge man at the finish, ending up only 13secs behind. items.s: Note that Vice-President Ranjit Bhatia may return to Oxford for postgraduate study and has donated, on behalf of Belgrave, to the first Indian Athletic Youth Festival. RANJIT BHATIA tells us there is a likelihood of his returning to Oxford in September for post graduate study. Although his stay would only be for about 8 months he is hoping to turn out for the Bels at every opportunity. As one of our Vice-Presidents, Ranjit still waves the claret and gold flag in India. In furtherance of our object to encourage Amateur athletics Ranjit made a donation, on behalf of Belgrave Harriers, to the first ever Indian Athletic Youth Festival, and we were pleased to receive a note from the organisers thanking us for our help. items.s: POMPEY ARE THRASHED Report and result of the Southampton/Bournemouth Relay, won by Belgrave in a course record 2 minutes 40 seconds ahead of Portsmouth, with three stage records. Great Win in Southampton/Bournemouth Relay Belgrave gained sweet revenge for their defeat last year by Portsmouth, by smashing the Hampshire club's course record by no less than 2½ minutes and beating them by 2 minutes 40seconds into the bargain. Of our six runners, three broke stage records and none was outside the fastest two for a leg. This fixture is growing in popularity and it was a pity it clashed with the Ilford Relay, for this team with our best six at Ilford would have run the New Zealanders very close in that race. John Thresher shadowed Gibson (Surrey AC) for most of the first stage but let him get away in the closing stages by a six second margin. John was still 54seconds inside the stage record though! Trevor Hart went off like a man possessed and put Belgrave in a commanding lead--a lead they opened up more and more over the next three legs. Gerry North was in grand form in stage 3, increasing our lead to 2 minutes and adding another record to his collection. Charlie Dabbs was first off into the second half of the race and although he was 8 seconds slower than Lonnen(Bristol) he was only 10secs away from Martin Hyman's stage record. The Bels really had their tails up now and Geoff North collected a 3rd stage record for the North family (Gerry holds two), and thrashed Dave Cooke of Pompy (2nd fastest) by no less than 45seconds, giving Tony Fairclough an invincible lead of 3:22 for the final stage. John Cooke reversed the treatment his brother received on the previous stage but it had little effect. This was undoubtedly the most decisive relay win we have had for years and augered well for the forthcoming "Brighton". RESULT Stage 1: J. Thresher(25:15) 2nd fastest. Stage 2: T. items.s: PIPPED AT BEXLEY Report and result of the Cambridge Harriers Relay at Bexley on 20 March, where Belgrave were third behind Blackheath and SLH, with Geoff North equalling the course record. Cambridge H. Relay--March 20th After our fine double outing of the previous week, at Ilford and Southampton, when we had 16 'A' team runners performing, there should have been little difficulty in getting 6 of our best dozen runners out at Bexley and thus clinch another convincing win. But it was not to be. Only 4 of our expected six appeared and Jack Brown and Don Maclean were moved up to fill the gap. Both ran very well, but we were obliged to concede 53 seconds to Blackheath at the end and had to be content with 3rd place. This was another case of key runners not notifying the team manager when unable to appear. Laurie O'Hara gave the opposition another dose of his 'Ilford' treatment on the first stage and romped home with a 5 seconds lead over a surprised Roseman(SLH). John Thresher increased the lead to 17secs but Trevor Hart met Baldwin(B/Heath) in record breaking form and converted this to a deficit of 32secs. Jack Brown held second place but Blackheath doubled their lead and SLH were moving up close behind. Geoff. North put us bang into the running again by equalling Baldwin's new course record and regaining the lead by a 10seconds margin. Poor Don Maclean. For the second successive week he had the unenviable task of being our last man with the race in a precarious state. Mac made a tremendous effort to stay with Herring of Blackheath but was dropped after 1½miles. Second place seemed assured, but a storming finish by Avila(SLH) took his club into second place a few yards before the line and a possible Belgrave win had become a 3rd place.
