items.s: THE NORTH SURREY LEAGUE — YOUTHS & BOYS Final table and race-by-race reports of the 1965-66 North Surrey League youths and boys competition, in which Belgrave finished fourth, with two photographs of young runners. YOUTHS & BOYS FINAL TABLE 1. Mitcham Athletic Club.......101 points 2. Croydon Harriers............201 points 3. Hercules Athletic Club......335 points 4. BELGRAVE HARRIERS...........377 points 5. Surrey Athletic Club........407 points 6. Walton Athletic Club........582 points 7. Herne Hill Harriers.........619 points The loss this season of Adrian Major to the Senior/Junior league hit any hopes we might have had of improving on last year's 3rd place. Once again Mitcham and Croydon took first two places whilst Hercules jumped from their bottom place of last year into third position. Our only runner to take part in all four races was J. Kelly, who was our first man home in three of the fixtures. The individual trophy went to D. Faircloth of Croydon, who had 3 wins and a second place. RACE NO.1 (omitted from November BELGRAVIAN) Held on our own course last October we had our best turn-out of the competitions. Kelly, Chandler and Geary packed well in the early twenties and were supported by Tony Brooks and the Hamilton twins in the late thirties; but these were positions that were unlikely to give us a forward placing and it was no surprise to learn we had come 4th. RESULT Teams:- 1. Mitcham 24 pts, 2, Croydon 49 pts, 3. Hercules 53 pts, 4. BELS 104 pts 5. Surrey 111 pts, 6. HHH 143 pts, 7. Walton 152 pts. RACE NO.2. (Walton AC ---Esher)---December 11th Run through heavy mud and deep water, over a course that included a very steep hill, this was a true test of strength for everyone. Our lads were not deterred by the conditions and, led once again by Kelly, were able to achieve fourth place again. Our runners finished in a similar order to the first race except that Iqbal turned the tables on Bondonno and thus closed in our scoring five. RESULT Teams:- 1. Mitcham 27 pts, 2. Croydon 53 pts, 3. Surrey 67pts, 4. BELS 83 pts 5. Hercules 117pts, 6. HHH 156 pts, 7. Walton 165 pts. RACE NO.3. (Surrey AC, Richmond Park)---January 15th From the sloppy going at Walton we went to the extreme of rock hard going at Kingston. Bitterly cold weather and a hard frost had made the course too hard for comfort. The occasion did not suit Kelly and Chandler, our first scorers in the previous two matches, neither of whom scored this time. But for this unfortunate setback we would certainly have made third place, but due credit should go to the rest of the team---particularly R. Young--who salvaged the situation to gain us a close 5th position. John Hamilton got the better of his brother Bob for the first time in three races; the margin?---one second! RESULT Teams:- 1. items.s: JUNIOR & YOUTH 'NATIONAL' Report and results of the National junior and youth cross-country championships on 5th March 1966, where John Bicourt (43rd) and Adrian Major (48th) were Belgrave's only forward placings. Bicourt and Major only forward placings---March 5th Our Surrey County Junior champion, John Bicourt, who was 7th in the Southern was, together with our supporters, hopeful of making the first dozen---after all he was 22nd last year---and even possibly making the Junior International team. But it was not to be. He got a resonable start and the three hill climbs at the beginning should have suited him, but he was unable to reproduce his County and Southern form and fought a losing battle to hold his place---slipping to 26th at 1½, 33rd at 3, 39th at 4½ and 50th at 5½. Team mate Adrian Major ran to form, making enough ground on the final lap to pass John a mile from home, but his lack of a finish enabled Bicourt to re-pass him 200 yards out. Our other two scorers were Mike Baker, whose 195th place was a good effort in his first year of running, and Jim Rimmer who, when ahead of Baker, had two heavy falls that cost him 100 places in half a mile. Our score of 564 points failed to place us in the first twelve teams. Our Youths' team is not up to the strength we have previously known, but the lads are keen and we did better than some clubs in starting a team. Tony Brooks, Richard Moody and John Kelly packed well to be our first three home and if they keep at it could be doing likewise in our future senior teams. JUNIOR RESULT Teams:- 1. Sale H. 167pts, 2. items.s: DON'T FORGET THE JUMBLE SALE Appeal for jumble, to be given to Ted Stimpson, and notice of the club jumble sale on Saturday 26th March. Have you any jumble? Old clothes, books, records, toys, bric-a-brac--anything you feel you could part with without too much heart-rending is just what we need. Just telephone Ted Stimpson at MAL 3893 and he will do the rest. Now, don't read on, look NOW and telephone right away. Oh! and by the way, if you should wish to replace any of those valuables you are going to send us why not come along to our jumble sale on Saturday, March 26th (10a.m to 11 a.m.)-- you might find something there you need. Ted Stimpson Ted Stimpson Belgrave Harriers Jumble Sale 1966

items.sum: Geoff and Gerry North's account of their November 1965 trip to Mexico City with a team investigating the effects of high-altitude competition, with portraits and the results of four weekly races, concluding that the Mexico venue is unfair to sea-level athletes.
items.s: MEXICAN TRACK DANCE Geoff and Gerry North's account of their November 1965 trip to Mexico City with a team investigating the effects of high-altitude competition, with portraits and the results of four weekly races, concluding that the Mexico venue is unfair to sea-level athletes. Geoff and Gerry North write of their trip to Mexico as part of the team investigating the effects of high altitude competition; with the 1968 Olympics in mind. (Photos: Monitor Press Features Ltd.) GERRY GEOFF We arrived in Mexico City on November 7th 1965 accompanied by Martin Hyman and John Cooke (Portsmouth), Dominic Keily (Derby) and Mike Turner (Liverpool) together with John Le Masurier, the team coach, and Doctors Pugh and Owen. Prior to embarking on the trip we had taken part in a programme of physical fitness tests and racing that enabled direct comparison of results to be made. Mexico struck us immediately as a beautiful country, with captivating scenery and exciting little market towns, whilst Mexico City itself was very modern with buildings of striking architectural merit. Whilst there we paid a visit to a bull-fight at the 80,000 capacity stadium - the largest bull ring in the world. The Mexicans have a very cheerful outlook on life and we found them easy to get on with. We stuck to English food throughout and took regular doses of "Streptoriad" tablets - these safeguards kept all members of the team free from stomach ailments. Our hotel was well away from the main traffic and was in a pleasant and relaxing situation. We made several trips to outlying places during the days and in the evenings we found many other places of interest ! The beer was very good and the people always very friendly - particularly the senoritas ! The first few days of training were most uncomfortable. The rarified air made us feel as though we were just unfit, with laboured breathing, a tightness in the chest and heaviness in the legs. A race was held after 3½ days, Gerry finishing 4th and Geoff 6th, and our performances were about 1¼ minutes down on our current sea-level times. As one would expect, our pace judgement was bad and in the early races there was a noticeable slowing-up after about a mile. Recovery afterwards also took longer than usual to begin with but, as with everything else, it felt normal once we had become acclimatised. Four races were held during our stay in Mexico and these resulted in average percentages down on sea-level times by 8%, 6.9%, 6.6% and 5.7% respectively - a clear indication of the benefits of an acclimatisation period of 4 weeks. The results of each weekly race were as follows, (the figures in brackets give seconds down on mean sea-level times) Throughout our stay we continued the laboratory tests that were held during our final few weeks in England. Doctors Pugh and Owen collected data on heart rate, respiration rate, blood pressure, oxygen consumption rate, oxygen debt and other functions. It was proved conclusively on this trip that no harm would come to the fit distance athlete training or racing at this altitude, and that an acclimatisation period of four weeks (minimum) is essential - we were both continuing to feel fitter and faster right up to the moment of our departure. We are agreed on one vital point. No thought could have been given to the middle and long distance athletes by those delegates who voted Mexico for the 1968 'Games'. It is evident from all tests so far carried out that the highland athlete will always retain an advantage over his sea-level counterpart when competin at high altitude. With the latter also having to spend a month or so beforehand to only partly close the gap, it seems distinctly unfair. Another factor of course is professionalism. With many countries setting up training camps at high altitudes and most sportsmen requiring even more time off from work when 1968 arrives, the Mexican venue will mean yet another step in the direction of non-amateur sport. items.sum: Walking notes on pack training, new walkers, Ray Middleton's build-up, Gerry Cameron's Commonwealth Games hopes and Middlesex colours, summer fixtures, and the Southern Counties track 7 (the column's continuation is printed on page 13 headed 'Cont'd from page 17').
items.s: WALKING Walking notes on pack training, new walkers, Ray Middleton's build-up, Gerry Cameron's Commonwealth Games hopes and Middlesex colours, summer fixtures, and the Southern Counties track 7 (the column's continuation is printed on page 13 headed 'Cont'd from page 17'). Ray Hall is still persevering with the pack outings from Belgrave Hall on Tuesday evenings, and appeals to the non-regulars to support these training sessions. It is far more enjoyable training in company and is almost certain to produce better results. More important it stimulates team spirit and gives the individual the enthusiasm to go away and follow up the work done. New blood is continueing to flow into our membership and there is a good chance that McGrath and Saunders (both Juniors) and Morrison (just a Senior) will blend with our more established walkers and play a leading part in Belgrave's resurgence. Ray Middleton is working up to full training again now his annual period of light training has ended, and will undoubtedly reach peak for the 50 Kilos championship which will be held this year at the Essex Beagles HQ, Chigwell Row. Incidently, last time the race was held at this venue Belgrave won the team title! Ray has recently been giving encouragement to Charlie Capener, who is also in the postal service, by joining him twice a week for training. Chas. has the ability to put this help to very good use and his progress will be watched with interest. Gerry Cameron is riding high these days and is sufficiently self-confident to take the Editors to task for suggesting that Eric Hall had helped him along at Leicester. "Why, I had that old man hanging on in our training sessions!" was his reply---a comment that should draw an appropriate retort from Eric. For those who do not know it, Gerry is a Scotsman and is one of three whose names have been put forward to the Scottish selectors by the RWA as possibles for the Commonwealth Games in Jamaica later this year. The two others named are Sutherland (Highgate) and Munroe (Southampton). Gerry does not underate this opposition, but has high hopes of a Jamaica trip all the same. Mike Hamlin has moved from North-East London to Battersea and is ideally placed for full participation in race-walking, but we have not yet had the benefit of his support. Another whom we have counted on in the past is Steve Laker-Jones who is only just getting out again after two severe bouts of tonsillitis. With Mike and Steve at their best our teams would receive a boost. WALKING:(Cont'd from page 17) In the Middlesex County Championship, Gerry Cameron did very well in a good class field. His 5th position earned him his Middlesex colours for the first time. The course times were very similar to those in the "Surrey" so Gerry's time of 81:00 was exceptionally good and could well have gained him a medal in the Wimbledon event. * * * This summer the Club is incorporating a points competition into the usual programme of 2 miles track handicaps. Prizes (value dependent upon support) will be awarded at the end of the season instead of after each event. A point will also be awarded to each starter. The seven miles track championship will be held on Wednesday August 10th instead of the expected May 2nd. Jack Goswell asks all walkers to make an effort to support our inter-club walks promotion on JULY 6TH---please note the date in your diaries now! The National 20 Kilos will be held at Hillsborough, Sheffield over a one-lap course---out to the reservoir and back. This will be the same course as used three years ago. The National 20 miles championship will be held over a two lap course at Hinckley College, Leicester. * * * Our only entries in the Southern Counties AAA track '7' at Battersea Park on March 5th were Ray Middleton and John Morris. The race was won by J. Webb (Basildon), the season's "find", from Don Thompson with times of 53:26 and 53:42.8 respectively. In a very close race, and a particularly tight finish for second place, Ray finished a worthy third---only 2.2 seconds behind Thompson. items.s: Cameron wins 'Horwood' Cup Report and results of the club's 7 mile Horwood Cup junior walking championship and match with the MPAA on 18th December 1965, won by Gerry Cameron. In Conjunction with MPAA match - December 18th Gerry Cameron was in brilliant form over our own 7 mile course the week before Christmas. His four minutes margin over Ray Hall enabled him to win both the match and the Junior Championship. Gerry started very fast and Bob Barnes (temporarily re-vitalised by an all night party) attempted to go with him. He soon paid the penalty though and dropped back steadily, leaving Cameron to disappear into the distance on his own. David Mayo, taking part in his first Club Championship, was another to walk well. Improving each time out, on this occasion he was second in the 'Horwood', third in the match and winner of the handicap. New member, R.Morrison, had a promising debut at the Belgrave Hall. Although walking for the Police on this occasion he will be wearing claret and gold regularly soon and could shake up several of our regular members. items.s: G.L.C. '10' Report and result of the first G.L.C. London 10 miles road walking championship at Battersea Park on 12th February 1966, with Belgrave seventh team after a poor turn-out. POOR TURN OUT BY BELS---Battersea Park, February 12th This was the first London 10 mile Road Walking Championship to be promoted by the new Greater London Council, and the new conditions enabled the large number of 190 entries to be made. Held over five laps of the familar Battersea Park circuit, it was obvious right from the start that Belgrave could hope for very little. With two teams entered we could barely field one, and our six starters represented our poorest turn-out yet in this annual event. Ray Middleton and Ray Hall were, once again, the stalwarts that continued to keep our colours to the fore and although the supporting cast of Keown and Cook did their utmost to make our score respectable, they could not make amends for the non-appearance of six established walkers. Our captain, Ray Hall, was there as usual to give the lads a lead, and but for a badly blistered heel which he picked up about 2 or 3 miles from the finish he would have been placed higher than his eventual 12th. items.label: March 1966
items.sum: Reprint from early-1950s Belgrave newsletters of Schwab jnr.'s training schedule for the 1948 Olympic 10,000 metres walk.
items.s: HOW I TRAINED Reprint from early-1950s Belgrave newsletters of Schwab jnr.'s training schedule for the 1948 Olympic 10,000 metres walk. We continue our extracts from Belgrave Newsletters of the early 1950's Here is the schedule of Schwab jnr. the 1950 European 10,000 metres Champion and silver medallist in the 1948 Olympic Games. TRAINING FOR THE 1948 OLYMPIC 10,000 METRES. Commencing with the winter season 47/48 a training stroll of 1½ to 2 hours was taken every Sunday. During the stroll special care and attention was taken to exercise and strengthen the inner organs, and deep breathing was always practised with a view to improving the lymph and blood circulation and to fully exercise the lungs, the digestive organs and the heart. This strolling was done in all weathers thus getting the body used to any climatic changes, or inclement weather. Practise long swinging strides from the hips, to improve the length of pace and exaggerate the arm action far forward and well back, so that the body is carried alternately straight, up, a little back and a little bent forward. This is practised in rhythm with the breathing. Four paces in and four paces out, and the whole can be practised at varying speeds, but must be as easily and as smoothly as possible and without strain. Following this take a hot and cold shower, massage and relax in the gymnasium. On Wednesday,the same training on a smooth road, but only for about ¾ of an hour duration. From the middle of March to the middle of May continue with style work and increased speed. By the middle of May the following programme and times should be worked:- Tuesday ½ hour style work: Thursday three times 1,000 metres. These 1,000 metres should be done separately thus:- starting on the hour do the first, then the second,15 minutes from the start of the first, then the third, 15 minutes from the start of the second, in each case trying to come down to a time of 4 minutes 10 secs. and then to 4 minutes 15 secs. per 1,000 metres. This should be watched by an experienced walker or a judge. Sunday One hour on the track with the second and fourth quarters of an hour used for lapping at 1 minute 53 secs to 1 minute 47 secs. lap speed for 400 metre laps. items.s: THE SURREY '10' Report and result of the Surrey 10 miles walking championship from Belgrave's headquarters at Wimbledon on 26th February 1966, where Surrey WC retained the title with Belgrave second and Ray Middleton runner-up to Paul Nihill. SWC RETAIN COUNTY TITLE---Wimbledon, February 26th Held from our own Headquarters this year's Championship produced a field of 30 starters, 10 of them from Belgrave. Ray Middleton and Surrey's Olympic medallist Paul Nihill made a fight of it for a large part of the way with Nihill only 22 secs ahead at half-way and the threat of a strong Middleton finish, but Nihill drew away half way up Copse Hill near the end and increased his lead to a minute. Ray Hall took third place, holding that position throughout, but Bob Farley who had not long recovered from flu dropped from 5th to 8th in the latter stages. John Morris caught George Beecham during the second half of the race and these two had a battle right up to the line when they were both given the same time. Middleton, Hall and Farley have been selected for the County team which will defend it's Inter-County title at Copthall Stadium, Hendon on March 19th. RESULT Pos Name Club Time 1. P. items.label: March 1966
items.sum: Charlie Manning's humorous piece on sightings in Richmond Park of a mysterious athlete resembling the comic-strip runner Wilson of 'The Wizard', with a newspaper-cutting collage 'Has Wilson come back?'.
items.s: HAS HE RETURNED......? Charlie Manning's humorous piece on sightings in Richmond Park of a mysterious athlete resembling the comic-strip runner Wilson of 'The Wizard', with a newspaper-cutting collage 'Has Wilson come back?'. Of course, if you are reading this sitting in a deck-chair whilst the wife is mowing the lawn, or sun-bathing on a beach to the delightful squeals of children dancing through the waves,or just being jerked along in a bus that allows 54 sitting, 5 standing but has, in fact, 618 on board, then this article will lose its point. You see, in the warmth of human contact (that includes the wife), little fears can be laughed at, but for just a few minutes try to discard your modern cynicism, cast off the mantle of sophistication and look again through the eyes of youth. Turn the leaves with frantic haste, with excitement and finally gaze with awe at the two pages in the middle of "The Wizard". "The Truth About Wilson". Who'd ever have thought that in our sphere we would seriously concern ourselves with such ficticious nonsense...with so much data recorded.. performances observed....sagacious timekeepers..impossible.. and yet.. he HAS been observed. A few whispers to close friends have spread gentle ripples across the black bottomless minds of the Titans that run around Richmond Park. "Is it him...?". "Can it really be...?" . "I wonder...". This phantom, if that is what it is, does not materialise when there is a large pack or the green-sward is littered with picnickers, or more restricted parties are agitating the ferns. No. It manifests itself, except in one rather singular case reported below, to lone runners. It is most likely to occur when the "Park" has one of her moods; she can make the conditions right, fatigue prepares the susceptible athlete's mind and inclement weather catalyses the whole action. "The world is a stage and we but actors..." etc., so wrote the bast.., sorry bard from Stratford, but, upon what apron in this global theatre are there charged such forces that would a Hercules quake as now forgather within the gates of Richmond Park. (If you read from the word "but" in a sort of iambic pentameter it sounds rather good, don't you think). However, we digress - let us return to our backcloth loaded with atmosphere. One of our actors is a well known Belgravian - accountant - holder of the Blackstaff Shield - we are with-holding his name in case he is charged with heresy. A noble, astute and uncompromising reason lies in this voter's head - which is why we believe his story more than the others. The fleet footed figure has been observed definately on three occasions. The first reports were early spring in 1965; secondly, in December of that year and again in January of this year. The facts are simply that the man is lean and drawn with lank hair. He moves at great speed with all the effort registered in his countenance. He appears to be naked from the waist up and his trousers are tight, black and stop just below the knees. Sifting through all the information is an arduous task. There are those who make ridiculously extravagant claims, some who just don't want to be left out and others who are pure romancers. Now we have irrevocable proof .... that there is a mysterious athlete.. but, is it HIM. The evidence will be exhibited at our next social in April. At the moment it is being covetously guarded in the vaults of the Westminster Bank, Hampstead. It happened this way.- The sky was a dull monotone grey, torn into great jagged pieces and moving rapidly across the heavens. The trees cracked their leafless icy fingers in the biting wind. Two figures struggled up the north face of Spankers. One was the intrepid Belgravian already mentioned, the other was the equally talented winner of the Inter-Counties last year. Their speed and strength confirmed their rankings until quite suddenly they looked relative scrubbers to the runner that flashed past....it was him...it must be...no ordinary man could dwarf such giants ..His athletic prowess was immediately evident...as quickly as had been his devastating appearance, so was he out of sight amongst the forbidding tangle of black bushes. This story would have remained untold but for what followed... About thirty cold minutes later, having circumscribed the park without meeting a soul abroad, they once again approached the forbidding copse. Having traversed the ridge with the "White House" behind them, they began the descent when they saw him again, swinging through the trees with surprising agility. He was naked; it all happened so fast. They shouted a friendly "Hallo". he dropped to the frozen ground, glared malevolently, grunted and disappeared into the wood. For every fact there are a dozen rumours, perhaps you can decide. Myself, I must now have my wild honey, selected herbs and spring water, to sleep for 10 hours under a roof of stars for tomorrow's exploration to the limit of my endeavours. Charlie Manning Stop Press:- In an interview with the Author of our article - "Has he returned..." he said, "if they don't like it, they should make their own contribution. You should tell them that sometimes you are so short of copy you will be commissioning Enid Blyton next." -- Eds. HAS WILSON COME BACK? Collage of newspaper cuttings: "HAS WILSON COME BACK?" with Peter Wilson ('This has been a sporting boob of the greatest magnitude'), Daily Mail, The Daily Telegraph, Standard, News Chronicle, Evening Standard, Morning Post, James Coote, Desmond Hackett, J.L. Manning ('The Last Word') and a speech bubble 'Tom Pollock's missed another scoop'...... items.s: BELS win Hogs Back race Report and result of the Hog's Back road race on 18th December 1965, where Belgrave won the team race for the first time with only five runners, led by Geoff North in 6th. December 18th 1965 When the first Hog's Back race was held in 1958 Belgrave just scraped up a team of the bare scoring three:- Derek Crookes, Jim Radford and Alan Bishop. We were placed 15th of the 22 teams. This year we did only a little better in quantity (5 runners) but a lot better in quality - 1st of the 62 teams. Although winning the team race was clearly a great achievement in a field of 390 starters, the fact that a club of this size only had five runners was a perfect disgrace; especially as we turned out 14 last year ! There were at least two or three 'A' team runners watching and the usually everfaithful "supporting cast" was completely missing except for Philip King. One possible reason may be that individual entry as well as team entry had to be made and the majority have got too lazy to write out an entry form. Anyhow, as stated above, thanks to the North brothers and the latest find from over the border, Joe Reilly, we won the team race for the first time. Geoff North led the team home with a very good 6th place, only 40 secs behind the winner, Mel Batty. Gerry North, perhaps feeling some after effects of Mexico City,was a little off colour but still finished 13th. Joe Reilly was a very creditable 30th (just in front of last years runner up, Mike Gowan). Mel Thorpe suffered a little and fell to 72nd compared to his 40th position last year. That stalwart of the long distance section, Philip King, completed our team in 267th place. 390 started, 334 finished and 62 teams (3 to score) closed in: RESULT Pos Name Club Time 1. January 8th 1966 This performance by Belgrave was in some ways better than the win in the Hog's Back '9½'. Instead of having the stars and nobody else, we managed to find eight runners with most of the stars away (resting for the coming Inter-Counties Cross Country). It was good to see Pat Newell back in the distance ranks, running an excellent race to gain 12th place. Chris Steer ran quite well in 35th place but perhaps could have been a little higher. Our 3rd scorer was Charlie Walker in 50th place. These three together with Charlie Dabbs should form the basis of a good team for the summer races. Of the others Doug Brew ran very well in his first attempt at the distance to finish in 67th place. Mike Bullivant broke Jack Brown's course record by over a minute but it should be remembered that conditions were ideal. items.s: CROSS-COUNTRY — Thresher wins Club '7' Report and handicap result of the club 7 miles cross-country championship for the Blackstaffe Shield at Wimbledon on 4th December 1965, won by John Thresher from Laurie O'Hara. December 4th - Wimbledon John Thresher made the most of the North brothers' absence by winning the Club Championship race for the "Blackstaffe Shield" by a 7 sec. margin over Laurie O'Hara. Run over three laps of our 2½ mile circuit, the race produced many interesting contests and the spectators had the pleasure of watching several races in one as the field split up into isolated groups. The first four were soon clear of the field and after one lap were followed by a trio of Fairclough, Hart and Reilly - the latter only a first year senior. A quartet of Steer, Dear, Walker and Brown then passed by and, after a further gap, another pack of five. As the race progressed the groups moved further apart. John Thresher was in fine form, pulling away from his rivals over the last lap and showing style that augured well for the County Championship just four weeks away. O'Hara and Thorpe also ran well to chase John home but the star of the race was undoubtedly John Bicourt, our leading Junior, who split these two and by running something like a minute faster than the handicapper expected also took the handicap award. Winner of the second 'race', for 5th place, was Tony Fairclough who just held off Trevor Hart and Joe Reilly. Finishing behind 20 years old Reilly was a runner exactly twice Joe's age - that elder statesman of the running fraternity, Jack Brown. Jack moved well away from his immediate rivals on the final lap and clocked a time that placed him 5th in the handicap - form that suggests he will be running yet again for Belgrave in the Southern Championships in February. Mel Thorpe, recent runner-up in the South of Thames Junior, took 2nd handicap prize and John Dear 3rd. RESULT: Pos Name Handicap Time 1. J.Thresher (0:45) 42:30 2. L.O'Hara (1:00) 42:37 3. items.sum: Report of the Surrey senior cross-country championship on Wimbledon Common on 1st January 1966, won individually by Gerry North with Belgrave taking the team title, with two photographs by P. Hilliar.
items.s: BELGRAVE WIN SURREY C.C. Report of the Surrey senior cross-country championship on Wimbledon Common on 1st January 1966, won individually by Gerry North with Belgrave taking the team title, with two photographs by P. Hilliar. January 1st 1966 - Wimbledon Common Held this year over three laps of our own course at Wimbledon, the Surrey County Cross Country Champ. had been eagerly awaited for many weeks. How would our team (the strongest for many years) fare against the holders, South London Harriers? Would John Roberts (SLH) beat Gerry North for the individual title? As the 138 runners were sent on their way, Roberts went straight into the lead and after 2 miles he was still there, followed closely by Gerry, who was in turn pursued by a small pack including Gowan (HHH), Robinson (Guildford) and Thresher (Belgrave). At the halfway mark the two leaders were running shoulder to shoulder, neither runner giving an inch. Tony Fairclough was working his way through in the teens and with Alan Black and Chris Steer also fairly well positioned, we were confident of a team place, although Mitcham AC were packing well. With a couple of miles left Roberts could hang on no longer (he had in all fairness been suffering with a severe cold earlier in the week). It was just a matter of whether he could hold off Thresher and Collins (Surrey AC) who was tearing through the field after taking it easy for the first two laps. Chris Steer, not at his best, had dropped back somewhat but Chas. Dabbs, entering our scoring six for the first time in the race, soon took both him and Charlie Walker - things were looking very rosy. (Photo: P. Hilliar) LEFT: Gerry North and John Roberts in the lead after one lap. RIGHT: Charlie Dabbs negotiates one of the "lakes" on lap 2. Gerry ran out a clear winner, 62 seconds ahead of the second man home Collins (Roberts having dived into the bushes not far from the finish). John Thresher was pleased with his 3rd place as was Tony Fairclough with his 8th, thus making it three Bels. out of the ten athletes selected to run for Surrey in the Inter-Counties event at Blackpool. The race was no sooner over when Charlie Walker, collecting his 'umpteenth' county medal in being our 6th man home, was heard to be talking about the 'Brighton' - What do you think ! items.label: March 1966
items.sum: Countryman's cross-country column previewing the National at Sheffield, with notes on Gerry North's new son, Ranjit Bhatia, veteran Charlie Smart, Mel Thorpe's move to Coventry, new member Bill Dance and Laurie O'Hara's county selection, with two photographs.
items.s: A COUNTRYMAN'S Jottings Countryman's cross-country column previewing the National at Sheffield, with notes on Gerry North's new son, Ranjit Bhatia, veteran Charlie Smart, Mel Thorpe's move to Coventry, new member Bill Dance and Laurie O'Hara's county selection, with two photographs. At the time of writing these notes the National Championships have not been held. After the 'Southern' at Parliament Hill Fields it looked as though we would be fielding our strongest team since we last won the title in 1948. Our first eight, Gerry North, Thresher, Fairclough, Geoff. North, O'Hara, Dabbs, Thorpe and Black were to be joined by Hugh Barrow for the "National" at Sheffield, leaving runners of the class of Steer, Reilly and Hart as reserves. Since then our hopes of winning the coveted National title have taken a severe jolt. Barrow is certain not to run, Thresher will be doubtful right up to the last day or so, and Thorpe is also touch and go. Our reserves are so strong that they ought to be selected if there are doubts still lingering in the final week. Either way, I expect our sixth man will be just too far back to put us amongst the medals and that we will finish 4th or 5th. * * * Gerry North is now the proud father of a second son, Alistair Stuart. Alistair obviously has a keen interest in his father's running career for, due on the week-end of the National, he had the good sense to arrive a week early! Perhaps this will inspire Gerry to great things in the big race. * * * Ranjit Bhatia has been enjoying his return to English cross-country running, but does not expect to return to the form he showed when he was last over here. He ran for us in the league match at Walton last November and finished a modest 60th, but in his later appearances for local club Oxford City he has shown improved form. Unfortunately he missed the start in the final league match at Shirley, so is determined to show his paces in the forthcoming road-relays. * * * Dark horses for the '5¾'? My picture shows Arthur Bruce trailing Charlie Smart in some special (?) training for the Club road championship in April In a year or two Arthur will be joining the veteran ranks (40) yet the man leading him here was a veteran when Bruce had barely left our Junior team!! Yes, 57 years old this year, Charlie Smart can show a turn of speed on track or road that would shake many of our young members. With a 5:10 mile to his credit last year he makes Percy Cerutty seem quite mediocre. Is there anyone of similar age anywhere who can match this remarkable runner over three miles on track or road? (Photo: R.Linstead) * * * In 2½ years Mel Thorpe has raised himself from a very unfit athlete to a runner who is virtually an automatic selection for our Championship teams. After joining us in August 1963 this popular Warwickshire-born runner was soon accepted as "one of the boys" and in return has given Belgrave valuable service. It was no easy task to regain the form he had shewn with Sale Harriers earlier in his career but with perseverance and a year's hard work, he made our "Brighton" team and has not looked back since. It was quite a shock therefore, to learn that Mel is shortly moving to Coventry; but there was no need for alarm for Mary Thorpe is as loyal a Belgravian as anyone and I'm sure that if Mel had any doubts about continuing his allegiance, Mary would be swift to dispel them! G.W. "Bill" Dance, who has only been a Belgravian for a few months is no newcomer to cross-country running. For many years he was a member of Benwell Harriers and gained several vests for Northumberland and Durham; being 4th scorer in that county's 7th placed team of 1960 with his best ever position of 66th. Although Bill has had thousands of individual tussles during his racing career, he certainly did'nt realise at the time that two of them would be with future club mates. In 1961 he was pipped by Malcolm Robinson in the Inter-Counties and the following year he turned the tables by doing a similar thing to Clive Shippen in the National of 1962. Since then he has not done a great deal, but being with the Bels has restored his enthusiasm and he tells me he is training harder than ever before and that next Autumn and Winter should see him showing good form. Judging by his improvement these last 3 months, I believe him. (Photo: C. Shippen) My picture shows Bill (far right) alongside Chris Steer, our President Bob Taylor, Trevor Hart and Alan Black; with the two Norths and Dabbs in the front row. * * * Laurie O'Hara was very unlucky to miss selection for the Middlesex Inter-County team in January. Over the tough Cockfosters course, which must surely be the most difficult there is after heavy rain, Laurie finished 9th but was not named in the County nine, as the Junior winner M. Beevor, was brought in. However, justice was done when the Middlesex team was picked for the "Sefton Branker" match, and Laurie finished as 5th scoring man---beating 3 of those that beat him at Cockfosters. This will not be the last County vest he will gain. Countryman Dark horses for the '5¾'? items.label: March 1966
items.sum: Amanuensis's report of the New Year Carnival Social at Belgrave Hall on 1st January 1966, with the fancy-dress awards.
items.s: CARNIVAL NIGHT Amanuensis's report of the New Year Carnival Social at Belgrave Hall on 1st January 1966, with the fancy-dress awards. For many years the activities of the Belgrave Harriers in the athletic world have been front-page news. It is possible that this developement was not envisaged by those far-seeing Belgravians when they founded the Club in 1887. For a certainty the Belgrave New Year Social would not have been imagined. A long time ago, someone said "The hand that rocks the cradle, rules the world", this would seem to indicate that females play an important part in the affairs of men. It is a fact, no doubt, that the female supporters of the Belgrave Harriers play an important part in the well-being of the Club. Mothers, wives and girl friends have become a feature of any Belgrave meeting; encouraging the athlete and committee-man to greater endeavours. For some years the Belgrave Harriers have recognised the value of Social gatherings and some splendid functions have been organised for the enjoyment of the members such as 'Jazz Festival', Jumble Sales (rather hectic) Week-End at Butlins (Indoor Sports), with the Saturday Socials and the Belgrave Annual Dinner. One of the finest of these functions was held on 1st January, 1966, when the members of the Bels. in the company of athletes from a large number of other clubs met in Belgrave Hall to celebrate the commencement of the New Year and literally competed in a Carnival Social. The Fancy dress and period costumes seen on the ballroom floor as the wearers swirled and twisted was a most colourful sight. It appeared that the history of the nations was being paraded for the purpose of comparison; the togas of the Romans, the wisdom of the Greeks, the gaiety of the French, the piracy of the seas, the joys of Pantomime, the misery of doom (or was it departed Pussyfoot), Grimms fairy tales, the grossness of the Middle Ages, the hope of a newly born baby. To so much colour, to the carefree laughter of this 'Get With It' congregation should be added the music that seemed to capture the mood of the moment; Jazz, Old-Time, The Blues and of course the Twist. Truly an evening of relaxation and enjoyment with the thoughts of training and performances on the road forgotten. During the interval some clever miming to records was performed by various groups and the efforts of B.Merry & Co. is worthy of repetition. The costume parade by the ladies provided the selection committee (or Judges) with a most difficult task, it was only after five circuits of the Hall that the judges agreed to give the award to the 1966 Baby (Pat Balaam) for being so apposite. The Principal Boy (Jean Manning) and Aladdin (Mrs Lucas) were noted. The costume award for the gentleman was a little easier, but it is said that the winner did not know that he was King Henry VIII, he thought he was a pirate. Mention was made of 'David Crockett' (Hacking Col.), the Victorian Barman (Ted Stimpson). The award for the best lady and gentleman pair was gained by an Indian and his squaw, their costumes were perfect (two of the judges thought they were 'Sioux'), It was later established that these 'Indians' were John Bicourt and Val Harper. Ted Stimpson and his assistants on the Social Committee should be well satisfied with their efforts in providing a wonderful social gathering for the enjoyment of the Belgrave Harriers and their Ladies. items.sum: Jean Manning's report of the pirate-themed Belgrave children's party at Belgrave Hall on 9th January 1966.
items.s: CHILDREN'S PARTY Jean Manning's report of the pirate-themed Belgrave children's party at Belgrave Hall on 9th January 1966. This year Belgrave Harriers' Children's Party took on a salty flavour and under the captaincy of "Long John Reg Hopkins" and a motley crew, the S.S."Belgrave Hall" set sail on 9th January. During the voyage the passengers were served a delicious tea by Aunty Win Shepherd and her "Galley Slaves". Various deck games were organised by the captain with the help of his ferocious looking pirates and a red indian brave and his squaw. At the crossing of the equator, King Neptune came aboard and conducted the usual initiation ceremony. As to be expected on a pirate's ship several of the crew mutineered and after a fierce sword fight the culprits were forced to "walk the plank" and came to a wet end. The passengers were very lucky in having on board a celebrity from T.V., 'Saveen' with his very lovable friends including Daisy May. There was also John Wenk who sang folk songs and accompanied himself on the guitar. At the last port of call our old friend Father Christmas was piped aboard and as usual gave every child a present. We would like to thank Admiral Ted Stimpson for organising such a wonderful trip which I am sure all the children thoroughly enjoyed. items.s: Major prominent in South of Thames Senior Report and result of the South of Thames senior cross-country championship in Windsor Great Park on 29th January 1966, where Belgrave were fifth team and first-year junior Adrian Major finished 31st, with A. Mead's photograph of Mel Thorpe and John Bicourt. January 29th - Windsor Running his best race to date, Adrian Major, who is only a first year Junior, finished 31st in the South of the Thames Senior cross-country race at Windsor. This was the first time he had raced over more than 5 miles on the country, in fact only this season, since leaving the Youth ranks, did he step up from 3 mile races. The event was held over three 2½ mile laps of muddy grassland in Windsor Great Park and although we had many of our team barred, due to a win in 1964, we hoped to take home a set of medals. Baldwin (Blackheath) went straight into the lead and after one lap was well clear of Yates (Windsor & Eton) and Gowan (HHH) who were fighting off a small pack. Mel Thorpe and John Bicourt were fairly well placed but with the exception of Adrian in the early 50's, we were having to wait too long for our other scoring men. (Photo: A. Mead) Mel Thorpe leads John Bicourt in the South of Thames At 5 miles John Bicourt had dropped back but Adrian, running steadily through the field, soon took him and was chasing hard behind Mel. Joe Reilly was starting to make some impression after a slowish start and Howard Satchell, who was originally only reserve, had dispatched Chris Keavey etc. and for a few glorious miles had his sights trained on Ranjit Bhatia and John Dear. Apart from Mel Thorpe and Joe Reilly (who must have been the fastest in the field over the last lap) our boys all felt the heavy conditions towards the end and we had to be content with a team position of 5th. items.s: THE NORTH SURREY LEAGUE Final senior table and reports of races 2-4 of the 1965-66 North Surrey League, which Belgrave won for the first time at the fourth attempt, with a page of five photographs from the final match at Shirley; race 3 is described in text only. FINAL TABLE 1. BELGRAVE HARRIERS..............868 points 2. Hercules Athletic Club........1248 points 3. Mitcham Athletic Club.........1282 points 4. Herne Hill Harriers...........1380 points 5. Walton Athletic Club..........1579 points 6. Croydon Harriers..............1682 points 7. Surrey Athletic Club..........2041 points So, after the fourth attempt, we have at last won the League title. In 1963 and 1964 Walton pushed us into the runners-up position and last year Hercules did likewise. Our ever-increasing depth in numbers of good class runners and the consequent better turn-outs were instrumental in gaining us this win. The competition is really a test of reserve strength as the top runners are rarely able to compete in all four fixtures. Belgrave had 23 different runners filling the ten scoring positions in the four fixtures---a reassuring thought when one considers that each combination was good enough to give us a win in 3 races out of 4, and a second place in the other. The individual title (only those who compete in all four races are eligible) went to Dave Bagshaw (Hercules) with 46 points and the runner-up our own promising Junior Adrian Major with 68 points---an exceptionally good start in his first year of the competition. The first race was covered in the November issue of the Belgravian. This is how the remaining three went:- RACE NO.2 (Walton AC---Esher)---December 11th The Esher Common course was at it's worst. Muddy at the best of times on the outgoing and homeward stretch, the continuous rain of the preceding weeks had left it a veritable quagmire. A brown healthy looking Gerry North---freshly returned from Mexico---was out to see whether he could do a "Keino"; having descended over 17,000 feet a few days earlier. Although not as 'tanned' as the famous Kenyan when he started, he must have matched him for both performance and appearance by the time he had finished! His mud-covered figure crossed the line over a minute ahead of the next man, John Thresher; despite going off course during the first lap and losing his initial lead. Bicourt and Fairclough ran very well to give us 4 in 6, and with such a good start we had little difficulty in winning the match and moving into an overall lead of 111 points, at the expense of Hercules the holders who had won the first race at Wimbledon. New member Bill Dance did well in his first league run, and it was good to see our old friend Ranjit Bhatia out again in Belgrave colours. RESULT Teams:- 1. BELGRAVE H.( 1,2,5,6,15,20,22,25,29,53)........178 points 2. Mitcham AC (7,8,9,11,18,26,32,34,39,42).........226 points 3. Walton AC (16,17,23,30,33,47,48,49,55,62)........380 points 4. Hercules AC. 383 pts, 5. H.H.H. 390 pts, 6, Croydon H. 418 pts 7. Surrey AC 515 pts. RACE NO. 3. (Surrey AC---Richmond Park)---January 15th Held on the same day as the Inter-Counties Championship at Blackpool, this third league match found us with our points lead in jeopardy, as Gerry and Geoff North, John Thresher, Tony Fairclough and Trevor Hart were on call by their Counties and Mel Thorpe, Alan Black, and John Dear were also away. Maybe it was because many of our leading runners were away that the remainder supported the race so well, but it was certainly a magnificent effort for 26 to turn out and support this away fixture as they did. Despite his disappointing exclusion from the Middlesex team, Laurie O'Hara was there to lead our team into the fray, nobly abetted by John Bicourt and Ferdie Gilson (in his first outing as a second-claim member). Ferdie went straight to the front, with Bicourt, O'Hara and Steer well placed. Laurie soon worked his way up to third and entered into a lengthy battle with Presland of Surrey AC. Gilson faded a little and soon had Major and Reilly closing on him. At halfway there was nothing to choose between ourselves, Mitcham and Herne Hill but the latter appeared to have a slender lead. We were doing far better than expected; particularly as John Bicourt had been forced to retire at this point. The lads held their own admirably on the final circuit, and with the Mitcham late-scorers making ground at the expense of their Herne Hill counterparts we ended up tying for first place in the closest team result yet. RACE NO.4.---(Croydon H---Shirley)---February 26th We went into the final race at Lloyd Park with a lead of 111 points in the Competition, and although only four of our intended "National" nine decided to run the week preceding the E.C.C.U. Championships we were still able to turn out a useful ten.. The North brothers forced the pace right from the start and at halfway Gerry was half a minute clear of Geoff, who was about 15 seconds ahead of Gowan (HHH). Alan Black was showing excellent form, leading the remainder of the field a short distance behind. With Adrian Major making Dabbs and Hart work hard, and Bill Dance chasing Chris Steer we had no less than eight in the first thirteen! Gerry showed he was hitting form just right for the National the following week by going right away to the time of 1:35. Geoff had little difficulty in holding his second place, and Alan was only 9 seconds short of catching Gowan. Dabbs's superior strength had the edge on young Major and both dropped Trevor Hart. Bill Dance (11th) and Junior Michael Baker (39th) both ran particularly well and we should be seeing a lot more of these two. RESULT Teams:- 1. BELGRAVE H. items.s: FAIRCLOUGH BY A YARD ! Report and handicap result of the club 10 miles cross-country championship (Macher Shield) at Wimbledon on 22nd January 1966, won by Tony Fairclough by a yard from Laurie O'Hara. 'MACHER' Shield win over O'Hara - January 22nd - Wimbledon What a finish to this year's Club 10 miles Championship! Just when Fairclough appeared to have got a safe lead over O'Hara in the closing stages Laurie turned on a final sprint that took him to within a stride of victory and to dreams of "what might have been". Nevertheless, Tony went at the right psychological moment and justified his decision by taking the title - a fine win by a fine runner. Charlie Dabbs was another to re-run the race many times in his thoughts. First up the final climb to the Windmill he could do little to stop his speedier opponents draw away over the last flat ¼ mile, and must also have thought "If only I'd gone earlier". In what must have been the closest finish for years in this race, 40secs covered the first five runners. These five were so superior to the remainder that they also occupied the first five positions in the handicap - an occurence that must be unprecedented in the annals of Belgrave handicapping. John Bicourt's 4th place was particularly good for a Junior and he did well to finish just ahead of Alan Black, who is getting back to top form once again. Only 15 of the 20 odd starters finished - so much for a 4 lap course and willpower! RESULT: Pos Name Handicap Time 1. A.Fairclough (1:45) 58:15 2. L.O'Hara (1:45) 58:16 3. C.Dabbs (2:15) 58:36 4. items.sum: Olympian's report of the Southern senior cross-country championship at Parliament Hill in February 1966, where Belgrave were again second to Portsmouth, with a photograph of Gerry North leading Baldwin; the text gives Portsmouth's score as 106 but the printed result says 105pts.
items.s: BELS. 2nd again in 'SOUTHERN' Olympian's report of the Southern senior cross-country championship at Parliament Hill in February 1966, where Belgrave were again second to Portsmouth, with a photograph of Gerry North leading Baldwin; the text gives Portsmouth's score as 106 but the printed result says 105pts. Although the weather was not unduly cold and we were spared the promised snow the conditions under foot were worse than had ever been experienced,even at Parliament Hill. The whole area was sodden with water and it needed very little to turn the ground into a sea of mud. On paper our team looked very strong indeed and we had every hope of reversing the 1965 result when Portsmouth beat us by 42 points. However, the Hampshire club were at the top of their form and the result turned out to be almost identical to that at Brighton the preceding year, with the same margin of points. It was not our team captain's day for he was up-ended before even getting out of the starting pens and deposited ignominously on his bottom. This gave him the extra task of catching up with the leaders, a difficult job in normal conditions but infinitely worse in the sloppy mud of today's race.Nevertheless after 2½ miles Gerry was our first man in 7th place followed by Thresher 19th Geoff North (fully confident that he was to beat his brother at last in a cross-country race) 31st, Fairclough 35th, Thorpe 46th and Black 54th well backed up by O'Hara 55th and Dabbs 56th. The score at this stage was 192 and Portsmouth, despite having four men in the first eleven places, were approximately 180. One mile further on all our lads had improved considerably except Black who had fallen back to 87, his 6th scoring place having been taken by Dabbs who had come up to 47. Score now 169 as against Portsmouth's 155, for whom Martin Hyman was moving through the field from 80th place at a great speed. Towards the end of the 2nd lap Gerry had moved up to 3rd with Thresher 17th, Geoff North 22nd, Fairclough 26th, Thorpe 39th and Dabbs 45th,totalling 152. Hyman for Portsmouth was now up to 33rd and their score was down to 130. As the field went up the hill at the beginning of the third lap we had made up a few more places to score 147 but Portsmouth had drawn away a little and were now totalling only 115. Over the last lap our fortunes wavered for Mel Thorpe,who had been running very well, dropped back twelve places,but Laurie O'Hara who had been late arriving and started without a warm-up, was coming through fast and gained fourteen positions to pass both Thorpe and Dabbs. Gerry was finding the going tough and had to give way to John Roberts (SLH) and Peter Yates (Windsor & Eton) and brother Geoff also lost some ground. The final reckoning gave us a total score of 148 as against Portsmouth's 106 so we must wait another year before we displace them from the leading position in Southern cross-country circles which they have held for six years Perhaps we could do it in this year's National at Sheffield. items.label: March 1966
items.sum: Report of the 1966 National cross-country championship at Graves Park, Sheffield, on 5th March, won by Ron Hill, with Gerry North fourth and Belgrave fourth team, their best since 1948.
items.s: THE 1966 NATIONAL Report of the 1966 National cross-country championship at Graves Park, Sheffield, on 5th March, won by Ron Hill, with Gerry North fourth and Belgrave fourth team, their best since 1948. National Championships, Graves Park, Sheffield---March 5th What a race! What a finish! After Hill (Bolton) and Turner (Liverpool) had been locked in combat for the whole race, alternately pushing the pace and out on their own, Hill made a frantic effort to shake off his rival 1½ miles from the finish but 2 yards was all he could get. With just 600 yds left Turner made his 'final' effort and when a gap of 4 yards appeared it seemed all over, but the Bolton man showed a new lease of life 100 yards from the line and produced a second sprint that momentarily carried him sailing past Turner; but with the finish drawing nearer at increasing speed the Liverpool Harrier responded yet again and as they crossed the line in a blanket sprint finish it seemed there could be no justice in a result other than a tie. However, inches do count in the end and on this score the verdict went to Ron Hill who, surprisingly, is National Champion for the first time. Our own Gerry North had an excellent run, proving the forecasters wrong again---none of them considering Gerry for the International team yet alone the first four. After the usual fast start, up a steep hill, the field had to negotiate 2 laps of a miniature ½ mile circuit---hardly fair to the outside positions in a field sometimes 15 abreast. Gerry and Geoff got a good start though and were both in the first six after 600 yards. With only 1¼ miles gone the steep climb from the start had been covered three times and the field well and truly sorted out. Geoff began to drop back the second time up and Gerry was dangerously near losing contact on the third ascent. Briault was pushing the pace at this stage, but the pace slackened for the only time in the race on the flat, zig-zagged portion of the course farthest away from the finish. For a short distance the runners were 5 abreast and the leading group had consolidated itself to 10 strong. It was at this point that Turner decided to break up the 'pally' gathering and with Hill the only one to hang on the leaders were soon strung out in Indian file. Gerry's effort in regaining contact with the leaders left him little with which to respond but he still managed to carve himself a niche in 5th position, a place he slowly but surely improved upon--reaching 3rd at 6 miles and for a spell pulling back the leading pair. Unfortunately the steep slope down to the start caused him serious discomfort each of the four times it was covered, due to a lingering stitch, and on each occasion he lost ground. Hogan, who was running in his first English "National" and who had been trailing Gerry throughout, probably noticed this for on the last descent just prior to commencing the final large lap he made his effort disposing of a 10 yards deficit and opening up a 20 yards lead. For a further mile Hogan kept the pace going and it seemed for a spell that he might well catch the leaders but after getting 50 yards clear of Gerry he could make no further impression Gerry held his form well and finished strongly, though his pursuers were making ground over the final circuit. Geoff also suffered on those first 3 steep climbs. he was not quite strong enough to maintain his excellent start but he deserves full credit for the way he battled over the whole distance to hold a slipping position From 9th place at ½ mile to 17th at 1¼ miles, he was 28th at the half distance. His tenacity over the final 4½ miles enabled him to finish 38th and be our second scorer. Of the remainder, none was inside the first 150 after a ½ mile and, except for Fairclough, none inside the first 120 after 3 miles. Tony worked very hard to make ground over the first large lap and at 3 miles had reached 68th position, but the final stages of the race were a bit too much for him, most of his slip to 81st occurring in the final mile or so. Charlie Dabbs showed his strength after being outpaced at the start. He worked his way through to 145th at 3 miles and then forged through the field at the rate of 10 places a mile; just failing to catch Tony at the finish. Laurie O'Hara also progressed steadily and gained more valuable places with his usual final burst. Our sixth scorer was 20 years old Joe Reilly, who had only come in as reserve but rose to the occasion in great style--taking 30 places in the final lap and finishing a creditable 134th. Mel Thorpe had great difficulty in getting to the start on time. A fast car drive from Blackburn and a sprint from the dressing-room enabled him to just make it, but this, together with the effects of his present move to Coventry must have left him with precious little nervous energy for an event of this stature. As it was Mel felt unable to continue when well down the field and retired from the race. Whether or not it would have made any difference no one will ever know but Trevor Hart, who had been told to stand by, didn't even report to the team manager who, when teams were declared entered Mel's name more in hope than design. In the normal course of events Hart would have been declared as a runner. So much for our growing band of runners who consider reserve status beneath their dignity. The team race was very interesting. With five men home Portsmouth led Coventry and North Staffs, but the position was reversed on the close-in with N. Staffs' 6th man 90th, Coventry's 132nd and Pompey's 173rd. Our 4th place was our best effort since 1948 and with Thresher and Barrow still to come our chances of further improvement next year are very good. Have you seen who were 5th? Is it likely that a renewal of the great Birchfield/Belgrave battles of the past is imminent? RESULT Teams: 1. N. Staffs & Stone AC (8,18,19,31,59,90)..............225 pts 2. Coventry God. H. items.label: August 1966
items.sum: Editorial congratulating Ray Middleton on his Commonwealth Games 20 miles walk silver and praising Geoff North's world-class season.
items.s: EDITORIAL Editorial congratulating Ray Middleton on his Commonwealth Games 20 miles walk silver and praising Geoff North's world-class season. Congratulations! Ray Middleton. Our leading walker continued the tradition of Belgravians being amongst Games walking medals by winning a well-earned "silver" in the 20 miles walk at the British Empire and Commonwealth Games in Jamaica. His usual steady start left him in 5th place at the 9 miles mark. "I then knew I was in with a good chance for a medal" he said, "I made my effort, moved through and I knew I'd got one". It all sounded so simple. What he didn't say was how he felt about getting within 30 seconds of the winner, team mate Ron Wallwork! As a medal winner,Ray now joins that illustrious pair of Belgravians Tommy Green (Olympic Gold) and Stan Vickers (Olympic Bronze and European Gold). He must also be hottest favourite for this year's"Tommy Green" Cup award. Whilst appreciating Middleton's grand performance, a thought should be spared for another Belgravian who narrowly missed going to Jamaica and whose performances this season have put him in World class. We speak of Geoff North. Geoff scored a fine win in the Inter-counties 3 miles in a Championship Best Performance time of 13 minutes 18.8 seconds and deservedly represented Britain against U.S.S.R. Two disappointing performances afterwards were just sufficient to squeeze him out by the narrowest of margins. With next season to consolidate his new form, he stands every chance of renewing his acquaintance with the Mexican senoritas in 1968! We are sure he can do it. Meanwhile our thoughts remain with Ray Middleton, who will shortly carry our flag again in the European Championships at Budapest, where the competition will be much tougher. items.label: August 1966
items.sum: The Hon. Secretary's notes (signed A.A.H.): tributes to Jack Crump and former secretary F.A. Bool, a 1901 club news sheet, AGM and money appeals, news of several members, and hopes for the cross-country and walking teams.
items.s: HON SEC'S NOTES The Hon. Secretary's notes (signed A.A.H.): tributes to Jack Crump and former secretary F.A. Bool, a 1901 club news sheet, AGM and money appeals, news of several members, and hopes for the cross-country and walking teams. We were indeed sorry to learn of Jack Crump's death in April and Athletics has lost one of its greatest workers. In his very early days Jack, with his brother Bob, was a member of Belgrave until they decided to throw in their lot with a club nearer their home, London Vidarians W.C. Some months ago Jack confided to the writer that he had been inspired and encouraged throughout his long career in athletics by the thought of some of our earlier Belgrave enthusiasts - men like Parker, Belchamber and Horwood - who had impressed him in those early 1920 days with their love of the sport and their Club. Belgrave owed much to Jack Crump's efforts in so many ways. He was always very welcome at our Meetings and functions, and always helpful to us. We mourn his passing. We have recently been advised that one of our oldest Life-Members died earlier this year on the eve of his 91st birthday. F.A.Bool was Hon.Secretary of the Club from 1898 to 1903 and was made a Life-Member in 1905. He lived in Chelsea all his life and his daughter tells us that he followed the fortunes of Belgrave until the end. A copy of a Club News Sheet issued in May 1901 has recently been sent to us - and this was written and issued by the above mentioned F.A.Bool. It tells of the fine entry of 30 for the Club race of the month, a half-mile handicap, held, of course, on the road along the Embankment. 27 runners started and the winner proved to be W.Berridge, off 35 yards. Scratch man was an old friend of many of us, the late George Still. One item reads "members will be pleased to hear that Sgt.J.Cox is on his way home from the front"! We are indebted to the son of W.Berridge for this News Letter, found among his fathers papers. All members should note the formal Notice of Annual General Meeting, given on another page, as required by ruling of our constitution. No other notice of this Meeting will be circulated. We hope for the usual good attendance of members to demonstrate the vitality of the Club and the interest of its members in all its activities. As a Club with freehold Headquarters to maintain and improve, and a record of competition in Championships and other events wider than that of any other club, we must give thought to MONEY . We do ask for (a) the prompt payment of Subscriptions, which become due at the Annual General Meeting, (b) generous donations from our Life-Members, Vice-Presidents and others, (c) support of our excellent and rewarding Football Scheme details of which may be had from our Hon.Treasurer and (d) full blooded co-operation with Frank Webb in his efforts on behalf of the Club when he circulates details of our Derby and Christmas Draws. Greetings to all members come from Bernard Eglington now serving in Malta where between duties he is acting as "talent-spotter" for Belgrave. George Piddington's imminent move into Hampshire will rob us (partially at any rate) of one who has made great efforts for our Boys and for coaching within the Club. We do thank him most sincerely for all his hard work and honest endeavour,and we hope to see him quite regularly in the future. Our revered Harry Evans, now in his 86th year, has had a patch of ill-health, but is now happily recovering. He was able to be with us at the Club Track and Field Championships and again at our Inter-Club Walking Competition at Battersea Park. Harry's regularity of attendance at our races, both Summer and Winter, is proverbial; and an example to younger generations of officials and athletes. A Club Champion of former days (1927 and 1928 to be explicit) Jim Cooper Clark showed up recently and promptly requested re-election. We hope to see him frequently at our events although he no longer moves with the speed that astounded us at one time ! Incidently we do like to keep in touch with former members; and welcome them as Honorary or full members, so if you know of any, sign them on the dotted line ! When this copy of the "Belgravian" reaches you, we shall be about to begin a new winter season. Can our cross-country runners reach a peak next March to win the English Championship? It could be. We certainly have the men, and if all could and would give of their best at the same time, the title could once again be Belgraves. Our walkers haven't the same strength in depth as obtained in recent years but with the return of Eric Hall to the South, and with the help of our two other Internationals in Ray Middleton and Ray Hall, we hope to remedy affairs and build up as powerful a team as ever we have known in the past. What about it Stan Vickers ? We understand there's no surplus weight! A corner to acknowledge George Beecham's solid worth to our walking teams over many years. Again this year he scored in our winning team for the NIJMEGEN Shield (teams of eight), the ninth occasion he has done so. A.A.H. items.label: August 1966
items.sum: Round-up of Belgrave's 1966 spring road relay season (three wins, two seconds and a fifth) in a year without the London-Brighton relay, with a results summary.
items.s: ROAD RELAY ROUND-UP Round-up of Belgrave's 1966 spring road relay season (three wins, two seconds and a fifth) in a year without the London-Brighton relay, with a results summary. 3 FIRSTS — 2 SECONDS — 1 FIFTH What an anti-climax the 1966 Spring road relay season proved to be ! The loss of the revered National London - Brighton road relay knocked the bottom out of the usual "spring spirit" and most leading club men were unable to conjure up the enthusiasm for events that were once used as valuable pointers to Brighton form. The excitement of seeing two dozen athletes fighting to prove their worthiness for inclusion in the select twelve was, alone, an occasion worth waiting for. But this year there was nothing at the end of it and the short season seemed to fizzle out like a damp squib. Perhaps next year a new form of National road relay will help to remedy the situation. As usual, the Ilford and Southampton/Bournemouth relays clashed the week following the National cross country championships. Last year we stretched our resources in an endeavour to win both, but although taking the Southampton event by a 2½ minutes margin could only finish a close 4th at Ilford. Re-arranged teams could certainly have won both. Because of this we attempted to do the same this year but finished one place further down in each event; both teams being affected by injuries and Thresher, Hart and Reilly all being unavailable. At Ilford, Clive Shippen and Gordon Biscoe were called up into the 'A' team and this alone meant the difference between 1st and 5th places. It was good to see Ranjit Bhatia showing some of his old form again and with Jack Brown and Pat Newell also putting in useful appearances the team was not unlike those of 7 or 8 years ago. At Southampton Chris Steer produced some of his best running to date, being within 3 seconds of fastest time on stage 2 and taking us from 7th to 3rd. Gerry North was also in great form, taking nearly a minute off Hyman, and Belgrave to within 20 seconds of the lead. Despite the acquisition of Dai Davies the Welsh Champion, and fastest stage times by Wiggs and Ellis, our old rivals TVH could still only get within 47 seconds of us at the finish. At the Cambridge Harriers relay at Bexley, a great effort by Geoff North (who for the second successive year shared the fastest time of the day) helped Belgrave to a good win over the two teams who pipped us on the final stage last year - Blackheath and SLH. The following week we beat both Portsmouth and TVH at Cranford in the "Valley's" annual promotion but a full strength Bristolian quintet rose above their Bournemouth form to beat all three of their former conquerors. Geoff North was second fastest of the day, ahead of Strong,Tulloh and Wiggs, and Adrian Major proved himself capable of holding his own in any of our first teams by turning in a notable sub-17 minute run. Our best outing was undoubtedly at Blackpool where we won against tough opposition for the 3rd consecutive year. In 1964 and 1965 the race was for teams of six runners but this year the number was reduced to four and it was felt that this would tend to favour our rivals. However, which ever runners we pair with the North brothers it seems to make little difference and this time Steer and Fairclough paved the way for Geoff and Gerry to clinch another win. Of the remaining runners Bill Dance was the fastest. The rate of this man's improvement since joining us is most gratifying and he has surely now run himself into our 'A' teams. The road relay season closed on April 30th with the Boro' of Enfield relay, which resulted in another victory for the BELS in record time. Our 'B' team were 5th, and with Bill Kerr doing a great 17:46 "come back" and Bill Dance anchoring in 17:55 we had two men faster than Major and Steer in the 'A' team So with three wins in six races our runners showed they were in their usual tip-top Spring form. Had there been a "Brighton" this year the selectors would have had their usual difficult task, but the ironical thing is that this year the collective form of our best twelve runners was so much better than our leading rivals. If the abandonment of the race had been postponed for a year we would have had an excellent chance of being the first and last holders of the National Relay Title (1951 and 1966). items.label: August 1966
items.sum: Report of the club 5¾ miles road championship on 2 April 1966, won by Geoff North in a club record one second inside brother Gerry's time, with the full handicap result.
items.s: GEOFF WINS WIMBLEDON CUP Report of the club 5¾ miles road championship on 2 April 1966, won by Geoff North in a club record one second inside brother Gerry's time, with the full handicap result. '5¾' victory in record time At one minute to 3 o'clock on April 2nd 1966 the Club Record for the 5¾ miles road race championship stood at 27 mins 15 secs. - credited to Gerry North. During those tense moments before the 50 starters poured down Lauriston Road, one athlete appeared to be extraordinarily on edge - even wanting to know the exact position of the start line; it was plain to see he really meant business this day, for when it was suggested he might like someone to knock in some starting blocks for him, it failed to raise even the merest smile. When Geoff North reacts this way he is either about to cane all and sundry or, less frequently, has just been caned; as he had not yet run, it became apparent to everyone that he was gunning for brother Gerry's record - an excellent time, set a few weeks after the elder North had won the National Cross-Country title in 1962. No sooner had Bob Taylor's starting arm dropped than Geoff was clear of the field and 10 yards to the good at the end of the road. After the two small laps had been completed and the Copse Hill stretch approached, North was 100 yards clear and still going away. He was in great form, and providing he could overcome the hills on the return journey, stood a fair chance of clipping the record. At this point a group of five (Hart, Dabbs, Major, O'Hara and Fairclough) were being led along by Chris Steer. Chris and young Adrian Major looked in fine fettle but Laurie O'Hara was showing the effects of recent 'flu'. Geoff kept his form well on the homeward run and a "break it or bust" sprint down the finishing straight sent up an "ooh!" from the watchers that, momentarily, did not indicate which side of the record his time was. Relief all round (Gerry of course wasn't there!) as it was announced that Geoff had beaten the record by just ONE SECOND! His fast pace had really kept the others at it and the battle reached its climax up Cambridge Road and the steep "kiss of death" where Adrian Major romped past Fairclough, Steer and O'Hara like a 2yrs old only to find the experienced Dabbs and Hart just out of reach. After a hard fight over the last mile Trevor got the advantage over Chas. and Adrian clung to his well earned 4th place. The field had certainly stretched out, but never before have we had as many as eight men under 28:30. With Gerry North, Thresher and Barrow not running (besides other possibles like Newell, Reilly, Dance and Kerr) this surely would have produced our fastest "Brighton" team. Once again veteran Jack Brown put in another of his stirling performances, shaking up many first team aspirants with his 29:27; and Ranjit Bhatia made the most of his years stay in England by re-appearing in the race for which he once held the record (27:56 in 1960). Another distinguished record-holder to re-appear was Ron Linstead whose 28:25, set 12 years ago when he was 17, stood for 5 years. Geoff.North's fast run also earnt him 3rd place in the handicap - Chris Fairfield having risen above his usual form to take first prize and Adrian Major a well earned second. items.sum: Extracts from the Belgravian of June 1941 and September 1926 and a club circular of May 1901, on the football-forecast building fund, a javelin title and a half-mile handicap.
items.s: 25 YEARS AGO.... Extracts from the Belgravian of June 1941 and September 1926 and a club circular of May 1901, on the football-forecast building fund, a javelin title and a half-mile handicap. From the BELGRAVIAN June 1941: Previous to the winter 1935/36 Frank Elson had run a small competition in which one forecast how many goals would be scored in the first and sedond divisions of the English Leagues. Each forecast cost one penny and the prizes began at 10/- and then increased to £1 as the scheme grew. This, though seemingly a small thing, proved to be a very valuable addition to our "Building Fund" ........ a committee was formed ........; so it was that in season 1935/36 a very large competition was launched. ....... our wildest dreams were surpassed and the future, as well as the present, Belgravians will owe much to those who so heartily supported us in those days. As soon as this bad dream (the war) has ended and we get back to civilian life, we are going all out to put Belgrave in such a financial position that we will have the finest headquarters of any club, equipped with baths and showers, indoor excercise facilities, massage room,etc.,etc. and all our very own, by our own efforts. That independence is very dear to all Belgravians and we shall insist on maintaining it. .... and 40 YEARS AGO From the BELGRAVIAN September 1926: We have had one great disappointment owing to the General Strike. We did not have the opportunity to defend our title of "National Champions" of road walking. That race being eventually abandoned. We always must have a champion of some kind in the Club and, as Len Smith disappointed, our energetic field event member G.H.Powell came along and obliged. He is now the holder of the "Southern" Javelin Championship. This he won at Chatham, in June, with a throw of 145'2". (Eds. note: George Powell had just one throw (98'-7") in the 1966 Club Championships!) .... even 65 YEARS AGO From the monthly circular, May 1901: The fixture for the month was a half mile handicap, first prize presented by Mr.W.Gurves, taking the form of a handsome brass column lamp. The record entry of 30 for an evening race was obtained and it was saying something for the popularity of Mr.Wilcox's handicap when 27 faced the starter. The race ended in a win for W.Berridge off the short mark, for him, of 35yds. G.Still won the 2 miles handicap at Hertford off virtual scratch (65yds) in the fast time of 9:40.6 seconds. Please note evening meeting, July 17th. Events: 100 yards h'cap, 880 yards steeplechase, 1 mile h'cap, scratch Long Jump.
