items.h: BERNARD MERRY rewarded for aiding Police
items.sum: Bernard Merry and a workmate are rewarded for helping an off-duty policeman catch two young criminals, one armed.
items.s: BERNARD MERRY rewarded for aiding Police Bernard Merry and a workmate are rewarded for helping an off-duty policeman catch two young criminals, one armed. Supt.W.Gibson presented Bernard and his work-mate Mr Percy Gray with £10 each after they helped capture two youths, one of them armed, some months ago. P.c.Dawson of Morden was off duty at his home when he saw the two young criminals attempting to break into a house. While police reinforcements were on the way, Bernard and his friend helped P.c.Dawson collar the two and during the scuffle a gun was produced and threatened to be used. Bernard and Mr Gray were also presented with letters of praise for their spirited action from the Assistant Commissioner for Crime, Sir Ralph Bacon. items.s: Three short club notes: the Walker Brothers, Len Bishop in Belgium, and Jack Brown's son. We feel that we should point out that there is no connection between the current well known 'Pop' group, 'The Walker Brothers', and two Belgravians of the same name ! —— apart from the noise that is !! Belgrave's ex-marathon champion Len Bishop is now living and working in Belgium. He expects to be there for 2 or 3 years. He sends best wishes to all Belgravians. Overheard in the dressing room:- "The reason that Jack Brown remains so fit is that his son is now running so well over half a mile that Jack has to make sure he doesn't beat him! items.s: TRACK & FIELD ROUNDUP — OPEN Field Events MEETING Report and results of the open field events meeting at Tooting on 26 March 1966, with John Mitchell winning the long jump. March 26th - Tooting This meeting was well supported and appreciated by 44 competitors from a variety of clubs; there being 7 Belgravians. There were very good performances from John Mitchell, who won the Long Jump with 22'7¾", and Bob Jones who was 3rd with 21'0"; both first year seniors and still at the height of arduous winter training schedules. A hearty welcome to Bob Couillaut who was just pipped into 4th place in the Triple Jump with 41'2¼". He is also in his first year as a senior. New member Ricky Raffan competed in the High Jump and Long Jump and also has interests in the Shot, Discus and Hammer. He is just getting back into training and will be a very useful club member. Hard luck for Brian King who slipped at his 2nd attempt in the Javelin, badly cutting his knee and spoiling his chance of the big throw he has been training all winter for. John Martin should be pleased with his 32'4" with the 16lb weight as he insists on using the junior size in training for sentimental reasons! RESULTS: Event Pos Name Club Performance High Jump 1. items.sum: Belgrave win their first track match of 1966 at Battersea Park on 23 April against St. Lukes, Met. Police, Ealing/Southall and Hercules.
items.s: v St.Lukes,Met.Police,Ealing/Southall,Hercules Belgrave win their first track match of 1966 at Battersea Park on 23 April against St. Lukes, Met. Police, Ealing/Southall and Hercules. April 23rd - Battersea Park - v St.Lukes,Met.Police,Ealing/Southall,Hercules In spite of being rather short of middle-distance men, due to our teams in the Blackpool Road Relay, we won our first track match of the season with a strong turnout in the sprints and field events. The very gusty weather spoilt some of the times but Chris Martin's furlong looked very strong, although he later expressed disappointment at it being so slow. Barry Townsend was well up in the Long Jump and Javelin in which he was closely beaten by Brian King. An unusual sight was that of a Belgrave senior team winning the 4 x 110y but of course our quartet were all first year seniors, fresh out of the junior ranks where Belgrave sprinters are amongst the strongest in the country. Coach Dave Ansell achieved a lifetime best in the shot and with his generous handicap mark of 15'3" took 1st prize from Tony Brooks and John Kelly. items.sum: Report of the Leyton invitation floodlit meeting at Eton Manor on 4 May 1966: John Bicourt's club steeplechase record and a Belgrave team win in the 3 miles led by the North brothers (the text puts O'Hara 11th, the results 8th).
items.s: GREAT CHASING BY BICOURT Report of the Leyton invitation floodlit meeting at Eton Manor on 4 May 1966: John Bicourt's club steeplechase record and a Belgrave team win in the 3 miles led by the North brothers (the text puts O'Hara 11th, the results 8th). May 4th - Eton Manor - LEYTON INVITATION FLOODLIT MEETING John Bicourt made a magnificent start to the season by finishing 3rd in the 3000m Steeplechase with 9:15.4 - a personal best by 13 seconds and a new Club Record. After hovering in 3rd or 4th place for the first three laps he moved into the lead, shadowed by Moxsom(Woodford G) and Pymm(TVH), looking far more confident than he has done for some while. Moxsom moved away with two laps to go, never to be headed again, John dropping back to 4th, but a last effort carried him back to 3rd place and, what is more, a probable Surrey team place in the Inter-Counties match at Whitsun. The 3 miles promised to be an interesting race with Batty(Thurrock), having recently regained his old form; the North brothers, fresh from the recent road-relay victories, and the London based Australian, Ian Wheeler(HHH) all taking part. Laurie O'Hara and Adrian Major completed the Belgrave team. Batty made the early running, passing the mile in 4:27.0 - well on the way to a track record but the pace dropped somewhat during the following couple of laps. Two miles was reached in 9:05 and here Geoff North decisively strode out into the lead, quickly opening a large gap on Wheeler and Gerry, Batty having dropped back. Laurie O'Hara, still suffering from the after effects of 'flu', was our 3rd scorer in 11th place with Adrian Major not far behind. Two laps left and Gerry dropped Wheeler for good, really making up some ground on brother Geoff. He had left it too late though, finishing full of running but only 4 secs down on his best time. Laurie clinched the team race for us, making it our third win in succession. The 100 yards was a disappointment for Jim Vivian who pulled up with leg trouble some 20y from the tape but still managed to record 10.4. Let's hope it is not too serious. items.s: VANCOUVER TROPHY Report and results of the Vancouver Trophy match at Woodford Bridge on 7 May 1966, with Ray Middleton winning the 2 mile walk in a meeting record and Belgrave sixth. May 7th - Woodford Bridge As usual, the Surrey Relay Champs at Wimbledon clashed with this meeting but we were able to field at least one man in practically every event at Woodford for the first time in several years. Most of our points were scored by decathlon man Barry Townsend with a 2nd in the 110m Hurdles, 3rd in the Pole Vault and 6th in the High Jump. Lyle Moar and Bob Couillaut both scored in the Triple Jump, in which Fred Alsop(Hornchurch) was only 2nd, and Laurie O'Hara ran his best ever 1500m in finishing 3rd to Maxwell(Woodford) and Blakesley(LCAT); as did Adrian Major in 8th position. It was good to see Bill Kerr out of hibernation to run a sound 5000m. Our only win of the afternoon came when Ray Middleton thrashed the opposition in the 2 mile walk for a meeting record time of 14:47.2 . items.s: SURREY CHAMPS. (Part 1) First part of the Surrey Championships report (Wimbledon Park, 7-8 May 1966): John Bicourt wins the steeplechase and Gerry North the 6 miles in a county record. May 7th/8th - Wimbledon Park Confirming his recent good form, John Bicourt won the 3000 metres Steeplechase in 9:17.2 from Halliday(Hercules) 9:20.8. It was disappointing to see only three athletes lining up for the start of this race (the other being Alan Black who dropped out anyway) but this does not detract anything from John's performance for John Halliday is no mean athlete. We did not expect too much of our sprint relay team but one thing that did stand out was the running of Chris Martin. On the last leg he brought the team up into 4th place and it looks as if we shall see great things from him this season. The 6 miles was held on the Sunday afternoon in extremely trying conditions. Constant squalls of rain made the track very sticky and the wind made the leaders task even worse. At the start Barry Collins (Surrey) went to the front with Roberts (SLH), Robinson (Achilles) and Gerry North all content to sit in and let him do the early work. Catcallers in the stand were answered by Roberts and North, both showing great presemce of mind; simultaneously making a rude gesture. Suddenly Collins was in trouble and dropped back, the others each trying bursts to break away but not succeeding. The halfway mark was reached in 14:21. With 2½ miles Gerry put in a 67 sec lap, streaking away and still improving on his lead right through to the finish. The time of 28:34.2 broke his own County Record by 14 seconds. John Roberts was a worthy 2nd just outside 29 minutes and Robinson 3rd. RESULTS: Event Pos Name Club Performance 3000m SC 1. J.Bicourt BELGRAVE 9:17.2 2. J.Halliday Hercules 9:20.8 6m. 1. items.sum: Surrey County Championships finals at Motspur Park on 21 May 1966: Chris Martin second in the 220 yards, Gerry North losing his 3 miles title to Robinson, with results and a photo.
items.s: Chris Martin 2nd in SURREY CO. CHAMPS. Surrey County Championships finals at Motspur Park on 21 May 1966: Chris Martin second in the 220 yards, Gerry North losing his 3 miles title to Robinson, with results and a photo. May 21st - Motspur Park A great display of sprinting was put up by Chris Martin, our only Senior sprinter in the Championships, the climax coming when he chased the international Mel Cheskin (Poly) home in the final of the 220yds. Having already run in the heat and final of the 100yds (10.5/2nd - 10.4/5th) Chris was drawn in the outside lane of the furlong with Cheskin right on the inside. At the gun it was obvious that nobody would be able to touch the Polytechnic Harrier as he steamed through the field to win by 10yds in a new record but Chris fought off the rest to finish a brilliant 2nd in 22.2 - his best ever time. John Thresher was 5th in the mile, having only been training in spikes for little more than a week. With a bit of luck he should be in top line for the major championship meetings later in the season. Seventh was our 2nd claim Poly member Derek Fernee with 4:15.1 . The 3 miles was a very tactical affair with no one wishing to take the lead and the field bunching up to three or four deep. After 3½ laps of this Gerry North shot to the front and within 220yds the field was strung right out - the first mile being reached in 4:36. Once again the leading pack slowed up and Roberts (SLH) took the initiative with Bob Holt (Hercules) and Robinson (Achilles) close behind. With all this chopping and changing the inevitable happened and unhappily, Mick Gowan (HHH) was badly spiked and had to drop out. At 2 miles (9:13.8) Gerry took the lead again and this time only Robinson followed. Adrian Major, running steadily near the rear of the field improved his best 2 mile time yet again with 9:32. One and a half laps left and Robinson made his effort and although Gerry closed in the final straight, he had to let his title go to the athlete who so nearly won it last year. items.s: v Polytechnic H., London AC Belgrave beat Polytechnic Harriers and London AC in a match at Chiswick on 25 May 1966, with John Thresher winning the 2 miles and placing 2nd in the mile. May 25th - Chiswick v Polytechnic H., London AC Once again this meeting at the Poly H home ground was held in dreary, rainy conditions with a blustery wind to boot. The line-up for the 100yds (specially run with the wind) was incredible. Poly had three internationals in Campbell, Frith and Cheskin - LAC had Winbolt-Lewis and Marsh - and running in "claret and gold" were John Mitchell and Chris Martin. Frith won in 9.8 but John was 3rd in the official time of 9.9 with Chris breathing down his neck! Unfortunately the timekeepers had the times all mixed up (not unusual at Chiswick where Frith and Ronay were both once given 10.2 for 100m) and the Bels times as taken by Dave Ansell were a more realistic but unofficial 10.2. Adrian Major improved on his best half mile clocking as did Philip Smith in the'quarter', but the hardest worked athlete of the meeting was John Thresher who took the 2 miles in 9:03.1 and no more than 10 minutes later lined up for the mile , this time finishing 2nd. items.h: Fabulous 3miles by North — Derek Boosey 2nd in Triple Jump
items.sum: Inter-Counties Championships at White City, 28-30 May 1966: Geoff North wins the 3 miles for Warwickshire in a championship best and club record 13:18.8, with Derek Boosey second in the triple jump.
items.s: Fabulous 3miles by North — Derek Boosey 2nd in Triple Jump Inter-Counties Championships at White City, 28-30 May 1966: Geoff North wins the 3 miles for Warwickshire in a championship best and club record 13:18.8, with Derek Boosey second in the triple jump. May 28th/30th - White City - INTER-COUNTIES CHAMPS. All the usual barracking in the "three-bobs" between Middlesex and Surrey supporters was completely forgotten as Geoff North, running in the blue and gold vest of Warwickshire, sailed past Bill Wilkinson to win the Inter- Counties 3 miles title in a championship best, personal best by a phenomenal 13.6 secs. and Belgrave Club Record. What a reply to Mal Robinson's 13:27.4! Geoff always looked in command of the situation, leading through the mile in 4:25.6 and thereafter hovering just behind the leader.Wilkinson was in front as 2 miles came up in 8:55.6 with Freary(Lancs), Geoff, McGrow(Yorks) and Briault(Mddx) all close up behind. With half a mile to go 'Wilkie' put in a fast lap and dropped all but Freary and 'our kid' . Then with a furlong left Freary slipped back. Forty yards from the tape and Geoff strode away to win - his final lap approximately 59.5 . Derek Boosey took the lead in the Triple Jump during the 2nd round with 49'5¾". But the next round saw Fred Alsop clearing 50'11¼" and try as he could, Derek could not close the gap on the Hornchurch Harrier; still holding 2nd place by 9" . In the '6' Gerry North stayed with the leaders gamely for nearly 5 miles but didn't look at his best in the heat, eventually finishing 7th in his fastest time this year. All hoped that our top Steeplechaser, John Bicourt, would improve again in his speciality but he was unfortunately spiked and fell on the very first lap at the second barrier. He was quickly up but instead of being well positioned he found himself trailing at the back of the field. Pluckily working his way through, John was still improving on his position at the finish and despite his injury he still beat, amongst others, his victor at Leyton - Colin Moxsom. Quite a number of Bels turned up for this meeting and the result was a fairly good 3rd place in the match to strong LAC and SLH teams. One of the best races was the 220yds in which Martin Winbolt-Lewis of LAC just got the better of our Jim Vivian with Nigel Rice, also LAC, close behind. Chris Martin in the "B" race had no trouble in disposing of John Marsh (LAC). Adrian Major, now enjoying track running even more than cross-country, gave a great display of uninhibited running, leading past the bell in the 880yds in 57.0 .but unfortunately slipping back during the 2nd lap. In the Long Jump, John Mitchell was forced to take 2nd place behind Kelly (HHH) with Bob Couillaut 4th and Barry Townsend 6th, only 1'7" covering the first six competitors. It is just as well that we have Derek Fernee running occaisionally for us otherwise our points in one of our strong events - the 2 miles - would have totalled nil. items.s: CLUB CHAMPIONSHIPS Report and full results of the Belgrave Club Championships at Hurlingham Park on 4 June 1966, with championship bests for Bob Jones, Alan Black and John Thresher. June 4th - Hurlingham Park Saturday, 4th June at the Hurlingham Park Track saw the Belgrave Club Championships Meeting. There was a welcome return of the children's races and this together with the customary efficiency of our "top brass" officials created the ideal setting for our best Championships in years. Blessed with fine weather, although the wind was quite gusty, blowing up clouds of dust from the track, there was a good turn-out of spectators and athletes. It was obvious we were in for an exciting afternoon when with his very first jump in the first event, Bob Jones upped the Champ.Best with a Long Jump of 23'2½". No sooner had the commotion died down when we were informed by the announcer that Bob, on his second leap, had improved again - this time to the winning mark of 23'5½". Derek Wade held 2nd place for most of the competition until John Mitchell, unable to produce his best form, displaced him with a 22 footer. Chris Martin started a busy couple of hours by chasing home John in the 100yds, later reversing the result in the furlong. Both were very close races. The next event on his schedule was the quarter-mile for which there were heats. By the time the final came around he was practically dead on his feet but his turn of speed around the final bend was still too much for Bob Nelson and Alan Mead, so he gained himself a second 'pot'. In the Javelin, Brian King threw over 9'0" further than before to beat Colin Clair by only 1" with Barry Townsend 3rd. Brian's magnificent effort just halted Colin's bid for a treble as he took the discus and shot, both with best distances by Belgravians so far this year. Geoff North, after one false and one very doubtful start, made all the running in the 880yds, finishing well ahead of Dick Calderwood and Lionel Mann, both of whom had excellent runs. John Bicourt, who ran in 4th, had decided in view of his injury sustained in the Inter-Counties,not to compete in the Steeplechase leaving Alan Black to go it alone for a Meeting Record of 9:30.4 . Bill Dance was 2nd in exactly 10 minutes with John Dear close behind. Another solo effort for a record was John Thresher's very even paced mile of 4:13.2 . The battle for the positions was much closer, however, Adrian Major fading towards the end with Pat Newell and John Bicourt both getting away from him. Bob Jones made it a double by winning the Triple Jump from Bob Couillaut and Barry Townsend was an inch too good for Derek Wade in the high jump. RESULTS: Event Pos Name Performance 100yds 1. items.s: SPOTLIGHT ON C. T. CARTER Spotlight profile by C.S. of Tom Carter, Belgrave's great cross-country runner of the 1930s and 40s: his discovery by Bert Footer in 1930, National and Southern successes, wartime winning run, and later coaching and presidency. The scene: Battersea Park Track. The year : 1930. A young blond runner has just finished lapping the track several times and pauses for a walk. His stylish running has not gone un-noticed and a small man with a walking stick hobbles up and enquires "Do you belong to a Club ?" The rosy cheeked youth stops, wondering whether the fellow means football club, youth club or Christmas club. "Er, not a running club,why ?" he replies. The enquirer screws his eyes up yet again, leans heavily on his stick and says "Well you ought to take up running properly, and join one now". This conversation heralded the association of two men whose names were synonymous with Belgrave in the 30's and 40's. The man with the stick was Bert Footer, Belgrave's greatest ever Captain (then injured) and the fair headed novice Tom Carter - the subject of this article. Tom Carter was born on 18th May 1908 in Putney and was raised, under the care of his grandparents, in Chelsea. Although his grandfather's brother had been a member of Ranelagh Harriers and a contemporary of the well known Sid Thomas, Tom had no aspirations towards athletics. In fact the only competitive event he took part in at school was a walking race, which he duly won ! At the end of 1922 he left school and was apprenticed to a joiner. Keen on football, he belonged to a youth club where he played a game every Saturday and Sunday, soon becoming an established team player. During these early years Tom also became a proficient ballroom dancer and five times a week danced his way into the night. His urge for competition gained him many successes, but these events were few and far between then and Tom was obliged to engineer his way into closed events. On one occasion he reached the final of the London British Legion Championships, but was disqualified when it was discovered that none of his relatives were members ! Dancing, Football and walking were his main preoccupations and it was not until 1928 that his athletic ability became apparent. The occasion was the Sports Day for Chelsea Youth Clubs, and on the strength of Tom's lasting ability on the soccer pitch his rector suggested he represented the Club in the mile. Not one for half measures, Tom borrowed a pair of spikes,("a little too big") from a work-mate and dutifully appeared at the meeting. After two laps he lost a shoe, but he continued to "just follow the leaders" until the final straight, when he came thro' to win feeling highly elated and none too concerned about his blistered foot. He had won his first mile in fraction under 5 minutes. This display of natural ability led his club friends to persuade him to "gather an odd point" in the 440 yards. Strapping his shoes on more securely this time,he sprinted to the first bend, got the inside berth (no lanes then) and held off the opposition all the way round to score a second win. Carter's canniness had already made it's mark But, most important, these results encouraged Tom to do a little training. During this year he joined the "Young Imperials", soon becoming their Social Secretary, a position for which his extrovert sense of humour was well suited. It was at the London Sports Day of the Young Imperials that Tom first rubbed shoulders with a Belgravian - our own Norman Dewberry, who a few days earlier had been placed in the Belgrave 1 mile Championship. Once again Tom produced a final flourish, passing Norman in the straight to finish second and go forward with the winner to the All England Championship at the Crystal Palace. Tom was not over-awed by this premier event and, rising to the occasion, finished 4th, beating the London first string and clocking 4:46 - an excellent time for a novice, particularly in 1929. Further encouraged, Tom began to visit Battersea Park track and it was here that he met the "little man with the stick", as previously related. He was not sure which club to join, if one at all; but under some pressure from Tommy Scrimshaw and Ernie Duffett he decided on Belgrave, "mainly because I liked their vest". On 29th August 1930 Tom Carter was formally elected a member of Belgrave Harriers - a date of great significance for the Club. Only a few weeks after joining he made his mark. Off only 40 seconds in the Yacht 3 miles handicap he finished second! From then on he went from strength to strength, and in 1934 ran his first "National"; Belgrave finishing 3rd and Tom 95th. The following year he was walking on air; a "National" team-winners medal was his, thanks to his 19th position; but there was still the little matter of the four Belgravians that finished in front! In 1936 he put it right by being first Belgrave man home (12th) and gaining a place in the International team The successes of his long career are too numerous to mention in full. Suffice it to say that wherever Belgrave went Carter went also, and the Club was all-conquering in the 1933-48 era. He obtained his Surrey County Colours at the first attempt and represented the County over the country on 19 occasions. During one of these trips to the"Inter-Counties" an argument developed between the late Jack Crump (team manager) and George Pallett (then Herne Hill) over which of two runners to drop from the team. Tom who was Captain on this occasion, heard all the arguments for and against, and with typical unselfishness stepped in and insisted on dropping himself as he was not yet back to his best after injury. Footer and Penny were his close rivals for most of the time, but Tom is the proud owner of the rare AAA vest of early design, which neither of the others managed to obtain - and he still raises a chuckle over this..Many of our present active members will be surprised to learn that Carter actually turned down his first ever invite from the AAA because it clashed with an important Club event. He is sorry to see the present clamour for "over-rated" races outside Club fixtures and firmly believes that many"stars" are losing their sense of values. It is fascinating to hear him reminisce and to relate anecdotes concerning innumerable Belgravians, but the one for whom he had most admiration was Bert Footer,"his great determination and personal example put our Club on the map". In 1938 Tom married Ethel the girl who had keenly supported him and the Club for many years. It is an indication of their keenness that, because of a mix-up in dates and the clash of their wedding day with the well known Plymouth track meeting, they (?) put their wedding back a day! It was not long after this that Europe became embroiled in war, and the organisation of athletics took a severe knock. Tom had now become a proficient mill-wright and being in a totally reserved occupation was able to help hold together those few members that were left behind. Despite difficulties with the "blitz" and "black-out" he still kept training, and in season 1940/41 had a remarkable sequence of nine wins in nine weeks, generally against the best opposition in the South. His coverage in the newspapers increased week by week. The run of wins was broken on the 10th outing thro' going off course and failing to get back to the front by a mere 2 seconds. Eventually the war ended and the 1945/46 season found Tom running as well as ever. The "National" was staged once more, with Belgrave defending champions after their win in 1939. Carter had won the Southern title and was expected to make the International team quite easily but, as in 1937 when he was also tipped for a place, he contracted 'flu', ill-advisedly ran, and finished 16th. Nevertheless he had helped Belgrave to retain their title and it was this that mattered most to him. What were his most satisfying moments? Well,there were many, but one was undoubtedly being a scoring member of our last winning National team (1948) at the age of 40 years. He continued to make our National teams for two further years, but it was perhaps symbolic that as Tom faded so did our team (6th in 1949, 8th in 1950). The second experience he most likes to recount was his win in the "Southern" of 1946. He was invincible at this time, particularly over our own course where the race was held, but he had heard that Doug Wilson (Poly) was planning to run one lap only and use his well known miling speed to break Tom and let in Bingham (Finchley) - Carter was always a very fast starter and would not ease up until he had got clear of the field. Doug Wilson remembers to this day how Tom went out and ran him off his feet after 2 miles - going on to win the title by 32 seconds. The retirement of Carter from competition coincided with the start of a ten-year lean spell for our runners. It was particularly galling for Tom to witness this, having been a key figure for so long during Belgrave's superiority. He resolved to do something about it personally and embarked on a scheme to nurture a group of boys and youths and to coach them through to Senior status. He was elected Junior Captain and in 1956 became our President. The first of his pupils included Fairclough, Steer and Cocks, who have since proved their worth in the Senior ranks. Tom's coaching school is still going strong at Battersea Park,where he appears each Tuesday to give them their week's programme. He enjoys being amongst our young members and its quite apparent that they like him to be there too - not just so they can be one of the dozen bodies that are frequently transported home in his car, but because he is young at heart, has a sense of humour, and most of all, understands them. Tom is now in his 59th year (though he looks 10 years younger) and has a business of his own. His bubbling enthusiasm and Carterian humour are as active now as they ever were, whether it be at track or committee room. He still does a little running, but that irrepressible competitive urge now has to be satiated by the frustrations of golf! It is 36 years since that fair headed youngster met Bert Footer at Battersea track - Belgrave Harriers have been richer for every one of them. C.S. items.sum: Review of the junior section's excellent 1966 summer, with five match wins out of six and notable performances by Jim Vivian, Tony Brooks, John Kelly, Derek Thorogate and Arnold Bent.
items.s: JUNIOR SECTION Review of the junior section's excellent 1966 summer, with five match wins out of six and notable performances by Jim Vivian, Tony Brooks, John Kelly, Derek Thorogate and Arnold Bent. Our Junior Section has performed exceptionally well this season, notching up five match wins out of a possible six (the one they lost was by just 1 point). Main points scorers have been John Kelly, Tony Brooks and Philip Gee - all first year Juniors, and Stevie White who is only a first year Youth and one of the most promising young athletes we have. Many times this summer these athletes together with Jim Vivian have scored a goodly amount of points in our Senior matches. Jim, so far, has picked up a double championship win in the Surrey County (100y/220y), successfully defended his 'Southern' 100y and is now set to improve on last years 2nd and 4th places in the AAA Junior event at Hurlingham on 13th August. Tony Brooks is another to compete at Hurlingham, hoping to cut down on his 51.2 'quarter' set up in an S.C.A.A.A. race at Battersea on 12th June. John Kelly failed by the narrowest of margins to break 2 minutes for the 880y, his closest mark being 2:00.0 on a running watch - heartbreaking! Both John and Tony also perform well on the field, backing up Derek Thorogate whose Discus throw of 139'7" in the County Champs was worth a new Club Record (Yths) and a bronze medal. He also placed 3rd in the shot, this time just missing the record mark by 3". Youth jumper Arnold Bent has been bugged by injury lately but still regularly notches up wins for us, his best clearances being a 5'8" High Jump (Junior and Youth Records) and a Long Jump of 20'6½". So, with the AAA Junior and one or two other matches to come, we can look back on one of the best ever seasons we have had from our younger members. items.s: v Ealing & Southall, Hercules AC Junior and Youth match at Battersea Park on 23 April 1966: Belgrave win the Junior match and are third in the Youths. April 23rd - Battersea Park v Ealing & Southall, Hercules AC Belgrave won the Junior match and were third in the Youth match on this windy afternoon at Battersea. Tony Brooks took the 'quarter' comfortably in 54.2 having already competed in three field events plus the LAC Schools 44oy (53.0) the evening before. John Kelly, another versatile athlete, was 2nd in the Javelin and 880y, having led for 660y, dropped to a 10y deficit and then all but winning with a final desperate effort. Our leading points scorer in the Youths section was Steve White who won the two sprints and the Long Jump. He was another who had competed in the LAC meeting.. John Hamilton ran a good 440y, being well up for half a lap. He had taken too much out of himself, however, and was just pipped in the straight by a very strong Hercules boy who had taken his first furlong somewhat easier. items.sum: Belgrave junior and youth relay teams at the Surrey Relay Championships, Wimbledon Park, 7-8 May 1966: third, third and a close second.
items.s: SURREY RELAY CHAMPS. Belgrave junior and youth relay teams at the Surrey Relay Championships, Wimbledon Park, 7-8 May 1966: third, third and a close second. May 7th/8th - Wimbledon Park Junior 4 x 110yds - In this race we had felt quite confident of victory. However, our star performer, Jim Vivian, pulled a muscle two days before the race and Geoff Hale missed his train. So we fielded a team with that well known half-miler - Schhhh.... you know who.. running first leg. Starting in the wrong lane, he craftily switched to an inside lane after the start and gained a five yard advantage. Being a middle-distance runner though, even with a five yard advantage he could not be expected to be leading, so Philip Gee took over second leg in 4th position. A very good leg by Philip brought us to within reach of the leaders and on the next leg Tony Brooks caught up even more. Kevin Finn did well on the last stretch to pursue the leaders right to the finish but we could only manage 3rd place. 1.KCS Wimbledon 46.1, 2.Bishop Grant School 46.6, 3.BELGRAVE H 46.8 . Youths 4 x 110yds - Composed of three Tulse Hill school mates and John Hamilton, the Youth team looked promising. It is obvious that with a little extra training, John, Eric Wickens, Geoff Shaw and Steve White will end up with performances equalling those of last years Junior team. The changeovers were perfect and the team managed a very creditable 3rd. It must be remembered that they all have another year in this section. Junior 4 x 220yds - With the arrival of Geoff Hale, we felt more confident. After a good first leg by Geoff we were well positioned and our place was held on to by Kevin Finn. A brilliant third leg by Philip Gee brought us up into 2nd place. Tony Brooks proved to be too eager to take the lead and this led to some bumping on the bend. As he and the Mitcham runner Ian Hill hit the straight they gave the crowd a good exhibition of boxing and whilst engaged in this, failed to notice Kings College on the outside. The final result was extremely close. 1.KCS Wimbledon 1:37.0, 2.BELGRAVE H 1:37.0, 3.Mitcham AC 1:37.1 Jim Vivian Jim Vivian Geoff Hale Geoff Hale Geoff Hale Geoff Philip Gee Philip Gee Philip Gee Philip Tony Brooks Tony Brooks Kevin Finn Kevin Finn John Hamilton John Hamilton John Hamilton John Eric Wickens Eric Wickens Geoff Shaw Geoff Shaw Steve White Steve White Ian Hill Ian Hill Surrey Relay Championships 1966 Wimbledon Park KCS Wimbledon Bishop Grant School Tulse Hill school Mitcham Kings College Mitcham AC

items.s: THOROGATE GAINS TWO COUNTY MEDALS Surrey County Championship heats at Motspur Park on 17 May 1966: Derek Thorogate wins two Youth bronze medals with a club record discus, and Jim Vivian and Philip Gee qualify in the 220 yards. May 17th - Motspur Park - SURREY COUNTY CHAMP.HEATS Derek Thorogate gained us our first medals of the meeting by placing 3rd in both the Youth shot and Discus. His Shot Putt mark was 47'9½" whilst his discus reached 139'7" . A new Youth Club Record . After treatment from Ted Chappell it was hoped that Jim Vivian's leg injury was fully recovered and sure enough it was. Cruising around the turn in the furlong in 4th place, he didn't open up until 50yds from the tape but still finished 5yds ahead of the second man. Philip Gee ran his best ever time to qualify in the other heat in 3rd position. John Kelly found himself run out of the final in the half-mile during a tactical race. The first lap was taken at 61.4 and the result was a fast second lap of 59.0 odd - too fast for John,but better luck next year. Qualifiers for finals: 220y P.Gee 23.7, J.Vivian 22.9 . items.s: CLUB CHAMPIONSHIPS Junior and boys' events at the Belgrave Club Championships at Hurlingham on 4 June 1966, with Jim Vivian and Tony Brooks winning two titles each. June 4th - Hurlingham Jim Vivian took both sprints as expected from Philip Gee in the 100yds and Tony Brooks in the 220yds. Tony also won the 'quarter' and 'half' in good times with Philip 2nd again and John Hamilton, only a first year Youth, putting up a great performance for 3rd place in the shorter event. The 880y promised to be an interesting race and,as in the Senior event,there was a false start as John Kelly prepared to tear away from his faster finishing rival Tony. The second time away though, he was much slower and had to fight through the field in the back straight. Tony led at his own pace all the way and John never really got on terms with him. John Lewis was a worthy 3rd. and Robert Hamilton 4th. Arnold Bent was the only competitor in the High Jump. Perhaps it is his reputation that scares all the opposition away. items.label: August 1966
items.sum: Walking notes for summer 1966: Ray Middleton's Commonwealth silver and string of second places, Belgrave's win in the R.W.A. 50 kilometres team race, and news of the club's walkers; with an uncaptioned photograph of a walker wearing number 12.
items.s: WALKING Walking notes for summer 1966: Ray Middleton's Commonwealth silver and string of second places, Belgrave's win in the R.W.A. 50 kilometres team race, and news of the club's walkers; with an uncaptioned photograph of a walker wearing number 12. What a great effort by Ray Middleton (see Editorial). His Empire Games silver medal was a just reward for his performances this season and, dare we say it, symbolic of his runner-up record this year. Every time Ray beats the race favourites, someone else seems to pop up and steal the limelight. In the R.W.A. 20 miles he beat Wallwork and Thompson, only for Norman Read of New Zealand to beat him by just half a minute; in the R.W.A. 50 kilos he cracked Nihill, only for Thompson to come through and win; and to crown it all in Jamaica he beat both his former victors, only for Wallwork to take his turn at winning. Altogether this happened on eight occasions between April 20th and August 6th, the victors being Nihill (twice), Read (twice), Thompson, McCullagh, Brooks and Wallwork. Everyone,except Wallwork so far, has been soundly beaten by Ray since their wins. Ray will not have Ronnie along side him in Budapest so will have to wait for an opportunity to continue the trend; perhaps he could try willing himself to believe that every competitor in Budapest is Wallwork - you never know! Ray Middleton had his usual steady start to the season and, in the four "National" races, improved with each performance - clinching his Empire and European Games places. After the 10 miles, 20 kilos and 20 miles races it looked as if Belgrave were in danger of a complete shut-out for medals in 1966. Team positions of 5th, 4th and 4th did not auger well for the 50 kilos on July 23rd, but rising to the occasion on an oppressively hot day our boys romped home to an excellent win, placing 7 in 23. Middleton was still working up to peak form when the 10 miles and 20 kilos were held, but he began to come into his own on June 11th when the R.W.A. 20 miles was held in the Midlands. Holding the leaders to within a minute for three-quarters of the race, he made his effort over the final 5 miles, permitting only Norman Read the Olympic Gold Medallist to head him home. Some felt that if he'd made his effort earlier he would have clinched a win - who can tell ? There were "ifs and buts" also at Chigwell Row after the 50 kilos, but no-one begrudged the diminutive Don Thompson his win. Jack Goswell is as shrewd a tactician as any and he advised Ray to go out gunning for Nihill right from the start, as he knew that the S.W.C. man was not himself when under pressure It worked. Nihill stretched his lead to 43 seconds at 10 kilos, lost it over the next 10 kilos, and was 75 seconds down at the 30 kilos mark; Thompson being over a minute further behind. It was here that Ray began to blister badly, and his blood soaked sock at the finish was adequate evidence of the courage he had shown during the final stages when he had to fight against pain, the effects of his fast start and his old rival Thompson. Compensation was provided to the full though by our team's great win. On a day when half the field couldn't take it we had Ray Middleton (2nd), Ray Hall (5th), Dave King (9th), Bob Farley (11th), Pat Duncan (19th), George Beecham (20th) and John Keown (23rd) - heroes all! It is good to see George Beecham getting back to his old form. Now living at Canvey Island, George has established a routine of walking home from work (11 miles) and he is already feeling the benefit. By the time these notes are read he will have completed the Hastings - Brighton — a race Jack Goswell regards as a reliable yardstick for form in the London - Brighton on September 3rd. Belgravians will be watching George's performance in the latter race with interest as our stalwart over that famous course, Ray Hall, is a non-starter. Our road walking captain has had a long season of distance work - The Stock Exchange events starting early in March- and felt obliged to ease off after the 50 kilos. The demands of the "Exchange" and family life make his efforts to lead the team in support of Middleton all the more creditable. The walkers are in luck! That bespectacled Surrey man, with Leicestershire sympathies, a Cheshire vest and a Belgravian-bred wife is back down South. Yes, who else! Eric Hall. Our team could certainly do with him again, just as the Editors could do with some more of his "journalism"! Turn-outs have been disappointing this summer and some faces rarely seen Steve Laker-Jones, David Mayo and Mick Hamlin for instance. We understand the latter is shortly going abroad. David is now teaching at a U.S. station in East Anglia and Bob Barnes,who is in Cambridge, is hoping David will be able to join him for some training sessions. Bob has managed to find some training companions and is now training more regularly; the effects may well show up this winter. Dave King, who did well in the 50 kilos, has moved from Bournemouth to Uppingham, near Hull, which means he will not be able to compete for us very often. He is still getting in the mileage and we hope he will keep in touch with us. Bob Farley, who has been a P.E. instructor at Loughborough College for some time now will be moving from there shortly. His work has kept him very fit and we shall be delighted if his move brings him nearer to Belgrave Hall. Jack Goswell would like to see our walkers stepping up their mileage, particularly those who are just not doing enough to tackle races of over 10 miles. Time is the enemy of us all, but you will only chop it down in the races if you add it on to the training. Obtain the strength to compete at the longer distances and the short ones will look after themselves. By the way, don't forget that the secret of our past great teams was pack training from Belgrave Hall. Ray Middleton won the Ipswich Open '10' in a new course record of 77:54. Fogg (Enfield) was the early leader but Ray moved up in his usual way over the second half of the course and was a comfortable winner. After leading Wales to the basketball championship of the Home Countries in April, Vaughan Thomas was back in training again for walking competition hoping to get into the Welsh Empire Games team. If he did take part in the trial he was not placed in the first 6, so was unsuccessful The Belgrave 1966 20 miles Club Champion is Ray Middleton (2:41:43) who won from Ray Hall (2:55:29) and Gerry Cameron (2:56:43). Ray Hall was a good winner of the Stock Exchange 25 miles championship at Hayes on April 2nd, winning by over 8 minutes (3:41:21) from his old rival Dicky Green (SWC). The R.W.A. Annual General Meeting will be held at the Polytechnic, 309 Regent Street, W.1. on Saturday 17th September. The Barking to Southend Police walk could not be held owing to the seamen's strike which necessitated the police being available for duty. Ray Middleton won the Open race at the Wiltshire County 20 miles on May 21st at Swindon. He won by nearly 4 minutes in a time of 2:35:55. Gerry Cameron produced a good performance in the Leicester "Mercury" Open '20', finishing 9th in a hot field with 2:59:59 - easily under 3 hours! The Bradford Open 50 Kilos was absolutely dominated by Ray Middleton. He won by a QUARTER OF AN HOUR! Runner up was A.Johnson (Sheffield). Ray's time ? - 4:38:59. items.s: HOW I TRAINED Extract from an early-1950s Belgrave newsletter on strolling versus stripped training for the London to Brighton walk, with checkpoint times from the 1950 race and pre-war record holders. We continue our extracts from Belgrave Newsletters of the early 1950's Here is a summary of a debate on the merits of strolling vis-a-vis stripped training. The main arguments appeared to be whether strolling should take precedence over stripped training and how fast the strolling should be. Our Brighton cup-holder confesses to a preference for speeds of well over five miles per hour. The ex-holder favoured Alf Pope's preference for a steady 4¾ mph (13 minute miles) in which he is supported by Harold Whitlock. Other and equally important considerations which might have been discussed had time permitted are:- (a) That strolling training can be done from home and is much less likely to attract small children, dogs and offers of a lift, and (b) that it is not always easy for a family man to find time for all day strolling. Those out to reach Brighton in the first three must of course study seriously the strolling school plan, but those whose aim is as yet less ambitious may take comfort from the fact that most of the men who walked in our team last September, which was certainly the finest eight we have ever fielded, did most of their preparation in stripped training and racing over shorter distances, with very little high speed or long distance strolling. For those who like to collect statistics and those wise enough to rely not too much on schedules, the following times of the first dozen at the principal check-points in the 1950 Brighton race will prove interesting. For purposes of comparison we have given calculated times for speeds varying from 5½ to 6¾ mph together with the actual times of the Green - Ludlow - H.Whitlock record holders of pre-war days. items.sum: Report of the Belgrave open 20 miles on 16 July 1966, won by Graham Taylor of Cambridge Harriers in a course record 1:39:47, with Charlie Dabbs sixth in a club record.
items.s: BELGRAVE '20' — TAYLOR SMASHES RECORD. Report of the Belgrave open 20 miles on 16 July 1966, won by Graham Taylor of Cambridge Harriers in a course record 1:39:47, with Charlie Dabbs sixth in a club record. TAYLOR SMASHES RECORD. Those that showed surprise last year when Bob Roath chopped our course record down to 1:45:53 were simply astounded on July 16th this year when 21 years old Graham Taylor of Cambridge Harriers re-wrote the record book with a truly outstanding 1:39:47. This sub 1:40 effort (equivalent to sub 5 minute miles throughout) came just 10 years after the first sub 1:50 performance round this course. What then in 1976?! Taylor was in a class of his own and his performance will have done our promotion a lot of good. He had a 1:10 lead after one lap, 2:59 after two and a winning margin of 3:42 at the end of the three lap course. His lap times were 32:49, 32:49 and 34:09 - with 2 miles of "stitch" on the final circuit! Conditions were cool and windy when our President, Bob Taylor, sent the 108 starters on their way and for 2½ miles a sizeable group held the lead; including our Charlie Dabbs. It was at this point that Graham Taylor set off on his lonely way, stretching out the field behind him. Dabbs passed through the first lap in 8th position with 35:06 and was still holding his place a lap later after a second circuit in 36:23. Chris Steer was still well placed after two laps in 35:30 and 37:13 but did not look happy when embarking on his final lap. Our potential third scorer was Doug Brew, running in his first ever '20' and with laps of 37:38 and 38:28 he was sufficiently well up for us to be leading a close fight for second team place. A lot happened on the final lap. Cambridge Harriers edged up to take second team place and Ranelagh 'B' simply raced through the field to snatch third. For Belgrave, Charlie Dabbs held his form well to finish 6th in Club Record time, but Chris and Doug dropped nearly 20 places each to put us out of the team reckoning. Charlie Dabbs took the "Lady Fell" shield for the first time but he must have had quite a fright; for Bill Dance joined the race just after the start and made his way through the field to finish an unofficial 6th in 1:47:36 . But for missing out that first 50 yards he would have undoubtedly been Club Champion at his first attempt. Once again Gordon Biscoe handled the race arrangements, and once again everything went off very well. RESULT: Pos Name Club Time 1. G.Taylor Camb.H 1:39:47 2. B.Collins Surrey 1:43:29 3. items.sum: Report of the Polytechnic Marathon on 11 June 1966 in hot conditions, with Gerry North 17th as first Belgravian, plus photographs by P. Hilliar.
items.s: The 'POLY' Marathon Report of the Polytechnic Marathon on 11 June 1966 in hot conditions, with Gerry North 17th as first Belgravian, plus photographs by P. Hilliar. By the time June 11th arrived the large number of runners who earlier in the year had proclaimed that "they were going to do the 'Poly' " had for various reasons been reduced to our usual small band of stalwarts plus Gerry North; who although lacking the distance training had his eyes on the forthcoming European and Empire Games and was not passing up any chances of selection. The weather turned out to be hot and humid and more than ever 'proceed with caution' was to be the order of the day. In the early stages it was Charlie Dabbs who led the Bels contingent but, after going through 10 miles in 45th position it was Gerry complete with hat, dark glasses and handkerchief, looking every bit like Belgrave's Don Thompson; who proceeded to pass Charlie and run steadily through the field to lead the Bels home and comment "I wish I'd trained for this earlier". Unfortunately Charlie was forced to retire at 20 miles and join the other victims, Norman Stairs and John Hilton thus leaving Geoff Pearson and Ken Stimpson to close in the team. Ken, who ran extremely well in these conditions considering it was his first marathon, commented before the race, "I shouldn't be here you know, I've been talked into it by Geoff". If it brings this type of result let's hope Geoff Pearson talks to a few more! RESULT: 165 finished (Photos:P.Hilliar)LEFT:Taylor leads Hogan at 22 miles. items.sum: Report of the Cheltenham 7 miles road race on 9 July 1966, where Gerry North finished fourth.
items.s: CHELTENHAM '7' Report of the Cheltenham 7 miles road race on 9 July 1966, where Gerry North finished fourth. On July 9th the road runners went slightly further afield than usual when a small team travelled to Cheltenham for the annual 7 mile race. This race held in conjunction with the Cheltenham Festival takes place in the early evening, thus on arrival in the afternoon Gerry North and family soon led the search for a T.V. shop to see what was happening in the AAA Champs. at the White City. A strong field assembled for the start and having been introduced as one of the 'stars' present, Gerry found himself in the company of such names as Adcocks, Price, Ingleton and Yates as they sped off on the first of three laps. With his entry in the AAA '6' the previous evening obviously having some effect Gerry ran well to finish 4th being just unable to hold on to a very much on form Bill Adcocks. Charlie Dabbs turned in another of his fine performances to take 18th place while, with Mel Thorpe kept out of the race because of 'flu', a private battle ensued further down the field between Chris Keavey and Gordon Biscoe to decide who should complete the scoring three. Don Maclean who completed the team had one of his off days and was mot amused on entering the straight to hear himself announced as - "Another runner wearing those well known colours of that famous club - Coventry Godiva". However, with Don compensated by the award of a can of beer; Gerry winning the prize his wife Phil had ordered; and Gordon restraining Chris from jumping into the town's fountains to ease his feet, it was fish and chip suppers all round before heading back to home. items.s: Bracknell '5' Report of the Bracknell 5 miles road race in pouring rain, with Laurie O'Hara fifth. As if pouring rain was not enough to contend with, and although split into four different cars for various reasons, the whole of the Bels team arrived within ten minutes of the start of this race, consequently no one was able to get any warm up. In spite of this Laurie O'Hara and Mel Thorpe ran extremely well to take 5th and 20th places respectively in a very strong field. It was good to see Eric Penny back in action again and we hope to see more of him on the road. 'Glimpy' Jones is also enjoying a new lease of life at present and "out to get" the elusive Charlie Smart. Team-wise it was the old story, another good 'A' team member backing up Laurie and Mel would have put Belgrave amongst the pots as well as making Mel's 2½ hour dash from Coventry in rotten weather a little more worth while. items.s: GEOFF NORTH'S International Debut Geoff North's international debut for Great Britain against Russia at White City on 18 June 1966, third in the 5000 metres in a best of 13:49.4, with Jim Vivian second in a junior 100 metres. June 18th - White City GREAT BRITAIN v RUSSIA Geoff North partnered "Big D" Derek Graham in the 5000m returning his best time over the distance of 13:49.4 . Both the Britons followed in the wake of the mighty Soviet steeplechaser Viktor Kudinskiy until 300yds to go when Geoff attempted to outsprint the field, leading through 3 miles in 13:23.8 . However, he could not hold off the Russian's finishing spurt and Graham also got past before the tape was reached. In the Junior Invitation 100m Jim Vivian was 3yards down on Ralph Banthorpe at the finish but easily had the measure of the rest of the field. Pos Name Team Time 1. V.Kudinskiy USSR 13:47.0 2. items.sum: Ryder Trophy meeting at Southampton on 2 July 1966: Brian King throws the javelin 185'2" and Barry Townsend sets pole vault and high jump bests, with Belgrave equal sixth.
items.s: 185 foot Javelin throw by KING — TOWNSEND — 11'4" Pole Vault — RYDER TROPHY Ryder Trophy meeting at Southampton on 2 July 1966: Brian King throws the javelin 185'2" and Barry Townsend sets pole vault and high jump bests, with Belgrave equal sixth. July 2nd - Southampton Sports Centre Our field events men performed exceptionally well in the 'Ryder'Trophy meeting but unfortunately we lost many valuable points due to a shortage of sprinters. Barry Townsend was in top form and set up personal bests in the Pole Vault(2nd with 11'4") and High Jump(3rd with 5'11"). His potential decathlon score is now quite impressive as he has already reached a 16.5/110mH, 20'10"/LJ, 155'11"/Jav, 33'5"/Shot and 99'8"Discus - all this year. Another to break new ground was Brian King , who rose to the occasion in the Club Championships with a Javelin throw of 9'0" farther than ever before, now topping that mark by a further 9'0" for 185'2" to gain 4th place. Performances in the Triple Jump show how we are gaining depth in events which only recently have we had anyone competing. Bob Couillaut, in the 'A' event, cleared 43'0" for 2nd place whilst R.Bennett broke the sand at a promising 42'7" for 3rd place amongst the 'B' competitors. The run-up was in a terrible state and was very nearly as soft as the pit itself. Kelly of Herne Hill H., who won, was a couple of feet short of his normal distance so our boys, jumping close to their best should be well pleased. On the track John Thresher put up our best performance in sharpening up for next weeks AAA Champs., clocking a useful 1:54.7 half-mile in 4th place. In the 3 miles Gerry North was soundly beaten by Tulloh (Portsmouth) who looked as if he was running very easily for 13:32.0 . items.sum: Belgravians at the AAA Championships at White City, 8-9 July 1966: John Thresher eighth in the mile final in 4:04.6, with disappointing results elsewhere.
items.s: Thresher down to 4:04·6 in A.A.A. Belgravians at the AAA Championships at White City, 8-9 July 1966: John Thresher eighth in the mile final in 4:04.6, with disappointing results elsewhere. July 8th/9th - White City There were no fewer than nine Belgravians taking part in this year's AAA Championships but,on the whole,performances were disappointing. On the Friday night we saw Jim Vivian running well below his best in the 100y, looking as if his leg injury was playing him up again. Derek Boosey, who must be in line for a trip to Trinidad or Budapest (or both) had three no-jumps in the Triple Jump, so he didn't make the final six and lost a chance to really show his mettle. Gerry North never looked comfortable in the '6' and was forced to drop out. The one bright spot of the evening was put up by John Thresher in qualifying for the mile final. With only the first two in each heat plus the fastest two losers to qualify, John was drawn in the first race with Simpson(Rotherham), McKim(Kettering), Tagg(Norfolk G.) and that grand old man Derek Ibbotson(Longwood); so things looked pretty tough. After being last away, John got up to 5th at 440y in about 61 secs. and at 660y he moved into the lead, deliberately keeping the pace warm. Simpson took over after the half-mile mark (2:03.8) going on to win in 4:04.2 with John 4th in 4:05.6 - his fastest of the season. As the other heats came and went it was realised that with only one race left, John's time was still 4th fastest With fingers crossed we watched Booth(Longwood) and Duggan(Sparkhill) qualify easily with 4:06 and John was through by the skin of his teeth. In the Long Jump, held on Saturday, John Mitchell (best of 23'2½") and Bob Jones (23'5½") were competing and we hoped that the presence of Lynn Davies, R.Stenius, etc. might inspire our duo to something really spectacular. It was not to be. John, who recently injured his ankle, didn't seem to have a really full out effort and only reached 20'8" whilst Bob hit 22'1" at his second attempt. Their best jumps would have placed them 7th and 4th respectively. The field in the mile final included five sub-four minute milers and all John Thresher had to do was to hang on for a fast time but we were out of luck. The race was slowly run, all watching one another until the bell was reached and then a 54.1 last lap. All the same, in spite of the odds being stacked against him, John ran very creditably for 8th place and 4:04.6 beating Tagg and McKim. A sound Steeplechase was run by John Bicourt but the standard was very high and he only managed to keep with the bunch during the early laps; nevertheless recording his third fastest time. items.label: August 1966
items.h: BROCKMAN TROPHY — COLIN CLAIR EQUALS JAVELIN RECORD
items.sum: Report and results of the 18th H.G. Brockman Trophy at Wimbledon Park on 16 July 1966, where Colin Clair threw the javelin 210'2" and Belgrave finished fifth.
items.s: BROCKMAN TROPHY — COLIN CLAIR EQUALS JAVELIN RECORD Report and results of the 18th H.G. Brockman Trophy at Wimbledon Park on 16 July 1966, where Colin Clair threw the javelin 210'2" and Belgrave finished fifth. July 16th - Wimbledon Park The 18th Annual H.G.Brockman Trophy meeting was held in cold, showery conditions at the Wimbledon Park track. Our field events section continued the trend started a fortnight ago at the 'Ryder' by scoring 27 points to our track men's 15 points. Hurdles events (11 points) not being included in either score. Our overall position was an improvement on the 1965 result by three places and 31 points. Prior to the Javelin competition Colin Clair had joked about the possibility of his gaining a AAA Grade I Standard. No one was more suprised than he when on his 5th effort the spear reached well over the 200' line and was later measured at 210'2" - a standard and Club Honours Badge by 2" . The most amazing thing was that his other throws were all around his normal distance of 170'- 180'. This one was completely out of the blue. He was placed 3rd behind Travis (Surrey) and Fitzsimmons (Poly) and ahead of R.Lane (Croydon) 204'2" and Colin Smith (TVH) 199'1" . In the sprints Chris Martin ran only one-tenth slower than his best in the final of the furlong, won by Steane (TVH) with 21.5, and also finished 4th in the heats of the 100yds in 10.4 . Tony Brooks clocked 51.7 and finished 2nd in his heat of the 440yds but could only manage 52.6 and 5th in the final, 45 minutes later. Our high hurdler Pete Pepe was 4th behind G.Tymms (Surrey) 14.8, Howell (HHH) 15.7 and Wilmshurst (Walton) 15.9 and was unlucky to be given 16.0 when he was inseparable with the 3rd man. Four men cleared 5'9" in the High Jump but Barry Townsend was placed 6th on the count-back of failures. The Long Jump also produced a close finish with Howell (HHH) winning with 22'8" and Bob Jones and Hudson (TVH) both reaching 22'3½". This time the Belgrave man got the best of the verdict with a superior second best distance. In actual fact Bob only fractionally fouled a 22'11" jump. The middle-distance record was not so good. After originally having a strong team, the 'phone calls started to come in towards the end of the week with one runner after another crying off. Gerry North tried hard to break away in the '6' but after 2 miles Ellis (TVH) and Gevers (SLH) caught him. He tried desperately to hold on but they got away from him towards the end, Ellis winning in 28:44.8 . items.sum: Club 3 miles and 120 yards hurdles championships at Battersea Park on 20 July 1966: Alan Black wins the 3 miles, Pete Pepe the hurdles for the fourth year, and John Martin the four-event handicap.
items.s: Club '3' win for Alan Black Club 3 miles and 120 yards hurdles championships at Battersea Park on 20 July 1966: Alan Black wins the 3 miles, Pete Pepe the hurdles for the fourth year, and John Martin the four-event handicap. July 20th - Battersea Park - CLUB 3 MILES and 120 YDS HURDLES CHAMPIONSHIPS The rain started just in time for the 3 miles and before long, the already soaked track was covered in ever widening stretches of water. At the gun Bill Dance roared off into the lead at a pace that strung the field right out after one lap. Only three runners were with him at half a mile (2:15/13:30 pace!) - Joe Reilly, Adrian Major and Alan Black. It was obvious that he could not maintain this sort of speed for long and as he tired Joe strode out in front. Farther back John Dear was sticking on John Bicourt's tail as they strove to regain contact with the leading quartet. With two laps to go Joe had dropped and only Alan and Adrian were left in the championship battle,and at 660 yds the former struck out for home, opening up his winning margin of 15 yds within half a lap. John Bicourt and Bill Dance (recovering from his early pace) were fighting it out for third place and in the process made up some ground on Adrian during the last circuit although the younger man still had a good 30 yds in hand at the finish. The versatile Lionel Mann added 3 miling to his repertoire (having already notched up a run in the Belgrave '20' and a 2:00.2 'half' this season) and it was pleasing to see Bob Glover, a little overweight maybe, out on the track again. The High Hurdles were won for the fourth consecutive year by Pete Pepe but it was a much closer thing this time. Barry Townsend was with him over the first five flights but lost ground towards the finish. Another who was well up, until a near fall almost put him out of the race, was Bob Jones. Later, in the four event handicap, Bob produced a massive leap of 22'11½" (from 5" back) and underlined his ability to pull out great Long Jumps no matter what the conditions. John Mitchell showed his superiority in the sprint, giving away 12 yds to the front markers and still winning his heat. The handicap was won with good all-round performances by John Martin, half a point ahead of Barry Townsend. RESULTS: Event Pos Name Performance 1. P.Pepe 17.0 2. B.Townsend 17.5 3. R.Jones 19.3 4. items.s: v Wimbledon AC Belgrave beat Wimbledon AC at Wimbledon Park on 27 July 1966, with Chris Martin's club-best 440 yards of 51.1 and a mile win for new member Anthony Heath. July 27th - Wimbledon Park v Wimbledon AC The best performances in this light hearted match against our local rivals came from Chris Martin in the 'quarter' and Anthony Heath in the mile. Tony, who is only recently joined and is a member of Achilles, took the lead with a lap to go from Laurie O'Hara and Alan Black, striding away to win fairly comfortably in 4:17.7. Chris Martin was beating Tony Harris (Wimbledon) all the way round in the 440 yds but just failed to hold him off 20 yds from the tape. The Belgrave man's time of 51.1 was his best and the fastest in the Club this year. The Triple Jump saw a rare defeat for Bob Couillaut by fellow club man Barry Townsend who cleared his previous best by over a foot. There were no fewer than six Bels. competing in this event. items.s: v LAC, Blackheath Harriers. Belgrave beat Blackheath and London AC in a close match at Crystal Palace on 3 August 1966, with Jim Vivian winning both sprints. August 3rd - Crystal Palace v LAC, Blackheath Harriers. This was one of our best results of the season for we defeated London AC again plus Blackheath , who are rated as one of the best all round clubs in the South, after an extremely close match. The final result was not certain until the last event, the Javelin, was finished and here Brian King did his duty by beating the nearest Blackheath rival by 4 feet. The sprints were run into a stiff wind and the times suffered considerably but Jim Vivian romped home in both, looking most impressive in the furlong where he beat a good man in Shurmer of the 'Heath. Bob Couillaut and Lyle Moar filled first two places in the Hop, Step and Jump, held yet again into the wind. These two should both be heading for 45 feet with a little more help from the weather. In the mile race, Chris Wade(LAC) led all the way with Alan Black lying 2nd and a member of Blackheath 3rd. The LAC runner piled on the pressure over the last lap and beat Alan by 10yds but the 3rd man faded and it looked really impressive as Belgrave men streamed past him in the final 100yds to fill 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 5th places. items.sum: Club gossip column: invitation races versus club fixtures, the autumn road relay fixture list, late cross-country results, Ranjit Bhatia's book on Otto Peltzer, John Thresher's races in Vienna and La Baule, and news of Mike Shingles and Arthur Bruce (continued from p.38 to p.37).
items.s: HERE AND THERE Club gossip column: invitation races versus club fixtures, the autumn road relay fixture list, late cross-country results, Ranjit Bhatia's book on Otto Peltzer, John Thresher's races in Vienna and La Baule, and news of Mike Shingles and Arthur Bruce (continued from p.38 to p.37). With so much competition available outside Club fixtures it has been a rare sight to see more than 2 or 3 of our middle and long-distance men at one time. The better runners get these days the quicker they are to plan their season around the multitude of so-called "Invitation" races that are fired, as from a shot gun, right through the Club's fixture lists each year. These races are now so frequent that one wonders whether it will soon go full cycle and be "the trend" to appear at Club fixtures ! It is presumed that our road relay performers do occasionally meet each other during the summer, so it is hoped that many of them will get together during the latter part of the season to prepare for an intense Autumn Road Season (you can always ease off during November!). The fixtures are as follows. September 10th - Surrey Road Relay (Woking) September 17th - Blackheath Road Relay (Hayes) / Club 5¾ miles road race (non-championship) September 25th (Sun) - "Johnstone" Open Road Relay, 12 stages (Hornchurch) October 1st - Walton Road Relay / Club 3 miles Yacht Handicap October 8th - BELGRAVE H & S.C.A.A.A. ROAD RELAY, 12 stages October 22nd - Bristol — Weston Road Relay Excluded from the March issue of the "Belgravian" was the result of the International Cross-Country Championship. Although he did not quite repeat his "National" form Gerry North once again scored for the winning England team being 6th scorer in 19th position. On the following Saturday Gerry was the third Englishman to finish in the Martini cross-country classic in Brussells, his 11th place being 46 secs. behind Khlistov (USSR). Another late cross-country result was the Junior Inter-County race , in which John Bicourt (15th) and Adrian Major (22nd) were the first two Surrey men to finish. Ranjit Bhatia is endeavouring to collect material, in connection with a book he is hoping to have published next year, on the life of Dr. Otto Peltzer, the controversial German distance runner of the 1920's, as a tribute to his 10 years work in India as an outstanding coach. If any of our members have any published information or personal recollections of Otto Peltzer the Editors will gladly pass on to Ranjit the details, however minor they may seem. It was the day after Geoff North's excellent win in the Inter-Counties '3'. The Sunday morning pack were dressing after their showers and were very full of their activities of the previous night. Geoff listened. His happy face slowly saddened, as he said with a sigh "With all this dedication I can't even remember when I last stayed up to see the dawn break"____ Tough! John Thresher produced his best ever 5,000 metres performance when he raced in a special invitation event in Vienna on July 14th. Conditions were atrocious and the track waterlogged. Ron Clark was the winner in the slow time (for him) of 13:41.4; Mecsar and Kiss of Hungary were 2nd and 3rd in 13:55 and 13:59 respectively. John was still with Kiss with 600 metres to go but was unable to hold his own in the final rush for the line. Vasic (Yugoslavia), Gerlach(W.Germany), Coyle (Australia) and Dick Taylor (Coventry) all passed him and John finished in 14:05.8; 4.8 seconds behind Taylor and only fractionally outside the European Games qualifying standard. Latest news of Mike Shingles now happily married in New Zealand is that he is enjoying the life out there and is now back in full training. He certainly won't be able to get the 'Bels' out of his system as he is now employed as a fireman in Wanganui. Mike adds that he and Beverley are expecting their first little 'Kiwi' at the end of this year - shows you what speed training can do!! Following the photograph in the last'Belgravian' of Arthur Bruce doing some 'shady' training with Charlie Smart, it has now been reported that Arthur has bought himself a new club vest - "My first since 1945", as well as new road shoes. Those who are used to Arthur's normal immaculate appearance are not sure whether this is a sign of a determined'come back' or just to help keep Gerry North in business. (Cont'd on p.37) HERE AND THERE (Cont'd from p.38) Thresher had a second B.A.A.B. trip to the Continent on July 30th.This time to La Baulle, a popular sea-side resort in France. Accompanying him was Geoff North. It was intended that John would run in the 1500 metres and Geoff in the 3,000, but on arrival it was found there was no 1500 only a 1000. John plumped for the 3,000, where our boys clashed with the redoubtable Michel Jazy. Geoff led the field for 2½ laps and then John took over, dropping all except Jazy. With 800 metres to go the Frenchman sprinted away to an easy win with Thresher 2nd in 8:14.0 and North 4th in 8:27.0 . Not out for a fast time, Gerry North was content to tuck in behind the leading pack for 4½ miles and then do a solo for home. Joe Reilly did the donkey work for the first 3 miles, with Alan Black then taking over. When North broke away Reilly, Fairclough and O'Hara chased hard, dropping Alan in the process, but Black recovered well and showing great determination ran through again only to fail by a mere inch to add a "silver" to his 3 miles "gold". Jack Brown went through the field like a dose of salts with 3 mile splits of 15:40 and 15:31 to beat Ranjit Bhatia who was competing in his last track race before leaving again for India in October. items.label: December 1966
items.sum: Editorial opposing the A.A.A.'s proposed 10/- annual registration fee for athletes and suggesting a per-capita levy through club affiliation fees instead.
items.s: EDITORIAL Editorial opposing the A.A.A.'s proposed 10/- annual registration fee for athletes and suggesting a per-capita levy through club affiliation fees instead. At the Annual General Meeting of the A.A.A. on October 29th the following resolution was passed on a card vote:"It is the opinion of this meeting that in order to raise the finance needed to ensure the continued development of our sport a registration scheme should be introduced as from 1st January 1967, or as soon as possible thereafter, which would require each active athlete in open competition under A.A.A.laws to pay a registration fee of maximum 10/- per year." The ever increasing problem of financing athletics has been frequently commented upon in these columns, and only last March we asked you the question "Do we pay enough for our athletics?" The all too obvious answer is now with us. During the fifteen months ending last March the A.A.A.lost over £6,000, despite Ministry of Education assistance to the tune of £28,000. Furthermore the Ministry has indicated that Athletics must take steps to augment it's own income (It is ironical that Governmental legislation prevented the late Phil Gale from expanding his money-spinning draws). It is fair to say that everyone is agreed that more money must be found but it is equally fair to say (in the South at any rate) that the proposed method is regarded as impracticable. In fact after a lengthy debate, the A.G.M.meeting itself was overwhelmingly against the proposal, but was obliged to bow to the large proxy vote of "non-active" clubs, as we know them. It is the view of the Belgrave General Committee that the clubs should retain control over their members and that to have two creeds within their membership - the "registered" and the"unregistered"- would be highly undesirable. To begin with, it must be left to the individual to decide whether he wishes to register and be eligible for open competition. In which case, how on earth can sectional secretaries be expected to keep track of their members' personal status when entering teams? What fun for race organisers or competitors stewards checking on registration before each event! How would the numerous offers of paying registration fees on the day of the race be dealt with, without causing a) a lot of work in the event of their being accepted or b) open rebellion if not? Anyone concerned with collecting subscriptions would appreciate this point. There are many technical points that need thrashing out and an A.A.A. sub-committee has the matter in hand, but are there not easier ways of raising £6,000 without spending about £2,500 in the process? Rather than tax the enterprising athlete who wishes to carry his club colours in open competition, it would be fairer to exercise a levy through the club affiliation fees on a "per capita" basis. If there is concern about losing the affiliations of the closed clubs then two, or even three scales, could be introduced. Each club would simply declare it's membership each year and pay the appropiate figure. Five shillings a head would certainly amass a larger net sum than the present 10/- proposal and, most important of all, full control would still remain in club hands. "Declaration of membership" would require careful study but there would seem to be fewer evils in such a proposal. Further developments must be awaited and, quite possibly, some will have materialised before you read this column. For instance the English Cross Country Union have yet to express their views and, similarly, fireworks are likely to fly at the Southern A.A.A. meeting— due at time of going to print. One thing arises out of all this. The athlete must face up to the fact that his annual subscription is less than in almost any other sport. Thirty shillings a year is only sevenpence a week - a penny more than the unattached member would pay going to a subsidised public dressing room once a week. For every thirty shillings of subscriptions that come into this club, thirty-five shillings is able to go out - thanks to your Committee's efforts in other directions. We feel sure that the Amateur Athletic Association's need for additional revenue is fully appreciated by most Belgravians, but are equally sure that our members would wish to see such revenue pass through the hands of the club - and thereby serve just one master. Phil Gale Phil Gale A.A.A. Annual General Meeting 1966 Southern A.A.A. meeting 1966 A.A.A. English Cross Country Union Amateur Athletic Association
