items.label: December 1966
items.sum: Cross-country column by 'Countryman' previewing the 1966/7 season: Belgrave's National progression, rival teams, member news, the Andy Gibb relay controversy, the new National Relay, and the North brothers' records.
items.s: A COUNTRYMAN'S JOTTINGS........ Cross-country column by 'Countryman' previewing the 1966/7 season: Belgrave's National progression, rival teams, member news, the Andy Gibb relay controversy, the new National Relay, and the North brothers' records. ........ It is with a sense of real purpose that the cross-country runners enter the 1966/7 season. For the fourth successive year they approach our main fixtures with a team even stronger than last years. Our depth, always good, is now the strongest in the land and it would not surprise me if our 12th man was inside the first 90 in the Southern Championships at Parliament Hill Fields on February 11th. The premier event is of course the National Championships, to be held this year at Norwich. This surely must be our year to make the first three. Just look at our progression over the last five years:- 1962 ...... 17th (1218 points) ....... 6 in 426 1963 ...... 11th ( 706 points) ....... 6 in 231 1964 ...... 8th (607 points ) ....... 6 in 160 1965 ...... 6th ( 484 points) ....... 6 in 140 1966 ...... 4th ( 447 points) ....... 6 in 134 Could there be a better challenge for 1967? Our runners have enough time to condition themselves both physically and mentally to go out with the confidence needed to lift the title. Six in 100 and nine in 150 is a distinct possibility. This could be the year! What of our rivals for the main events of the season? Well Portsmouth, 3rd in the last National, appear to have the strongest potential with only six to score. Their performances will greatly depend on how injury free they can keep their teams. They finished 5 in 37 in the 1966 National but had to wait until 173 for their sixth scorer. Since then Ingleton has joined them and,on his day, could well make the first 50. The two Cookes are both in trim again after lay-offs and should reach peak just at the right time. With Johnstone and Tulloh to lead them and Hyman marshalling the remainder Pompey could well be the biggest threat unless.............. unless the holders North Staffs and Stone think otherwise. They will not let their title go easily. Their rise to fame has been little less than meteoric,with National placings over the last four years of 41st, 12th, 5th, and 1st. Their depth is questionable, but with the stalwart Fowler, Shelley and Walker to boost runners with flair such as Jackson, Dean and Boyden they have a powerful half dozen - and there is always Billington on the fringe. As good as these two teams are there is another that commands more respect than all our rivals put together, and that is Coventry Godiva Harriers. With one first, one second and two thirds in the last four years their consistency makes them the most formidable team of all. Basil Heatley, although "retired" from representative running, is still a very consistent performer and provides the Godiva team with the stability it sometimes needs. Dick Taylor, their fast improving 5,000 metres runner will be a useful pacemaker for those marathon medallists Adcocks and Kilby. In addition,there is every chance that their cross country internationals Juan Taylor (only once outside the'teens in the last four Nationals) and John Hammond will be well to the fore. This is a formidable sextet, and they still have Horne, Lancaster and Dowall to provide strong support. This is the team that needs watching most of all. What good news it is that Bill Kerr is running into form again. After showing tremendous promise in his early days with us - he was our No.1 before Gerry North arrived on the scene - he has since had his ups and downs and many thought we had seen the last of him. But you can't keep a good Scot down and Bill's present form suggests he could be a real threat to the opposition in the New Year. Talking of Scots, we have had the pleasure of Albert Smith's company during the latter months of 1966. Albert is a friend of Bill Kerr and Hugh Barrow. He ran for us in the Banks match at Epsom, splitting Bicourt and Dance, and displayed a keenness that we were sorry to lose so soon. We were, indeed, even sorrier to lose that other Scotsman Joe Reilly. Joe has turned in some excellent performances for Belgrave and his support for the club was always greatly appreciated. He is now studying and training at Liverpool University to become a P.E. teacher. We wish him all the success possible and trust he will spread forth the gospel of Belgrave Harriers. No club can easily afford to lose someone of Reilly's calibre and it was fortuitous that within days of his departure we had the pleasure of welcoming Brian Buxton to our ranks. Brian (formerly of Grafton AC) has led something of a lone-wolf existance to date. This has not deterred him from turning in some good performances though, and he has shown himself to be in the 9 minute 2 miler class. He ran very well in the South of Thames Junior race at West Wickham to gain 3rd place and he is very likely to revel in the competition our fixture list provides. David Davies, a City of London Policeman and son of Stan Davies, took part in the recent Barking - Southend 34 miles walk. In only his second appearance he finished 25th of the 139 starters. But walking, apparently, is no longer for him and he has set himself the initial target of a Belgrave running handicap. Not content to "go it alone" he has cajoled two of his police colleagues Joe McMahon and Peter Cooper into becoming Belgravians and presented two others with membership forms, all interested in running - hard luck walking section ! Those that take "Athletics Weekly" will have read the letter written by Portsmouth's secretary Andy Gibb following our Open Relay promotion . This year the Southern AAA gave official backing to our race so that it could be used as a qualifier for next year's new National Relay. The aim was to get the strongest teams in the South together. This it achieved. What was overlooked by both Southern and Belgrave officials was that by giving the race Championship status the rules for S.C.A.A.A. track applied and that individuals who had competed in other area track championships in the previous 12 months were ineligible. This defeated the whole purpose of the support and resulted in the declaration of an Open result and a Southern result. No one really minded, least of all the athletes and officials, and every runner was eligible for the National event anyway. However, Andy Gibb was prompted to write "..... I am amazed that the officials running these two clubs (Belgrave and TVH) should see fit to cheapen the Championship by fielding teams not qualified to compete in it and seem to be so parochial minded about the prestige of their clubs that they have slighted the officials of the Area Association......." Hmm! Sounds like sour grapes to me! Although few details are yet to be had there is certain to be an official inaugural National Relay Championship at Leicester on April 1st. There will probably be 12 stages, alternate long and short as in our own event, and the course is likely to be over a relatively traffic free circuit The idea is for the Championship to be held at the same venue each year, thus enabling all clubs to make it a one day outing It is 10 years since Gerry North won the National Junior title at Parliament Hill Fields by more than a minute. His career as a Senior, apart from those early years when he was dogged by stomach trouble, has been a model of consistency. Since that great Junior win he has run in eight consecutive Senior Nationals, finishing in the first twelve on every occasion, His record is One 1st, one 3rd, two 4ths, one 6th, one 10th and two 12ths - a run that will take a lot of beating. Geoff North proved this summer that he is no longer running in the shadow of his brother. His international vest on the track could be a prelude to one on the country. Bearing in mind that Geoff was 12th in the 1962 National that Gerry won, he stands every chance in 1967 of an E.C.C.U. vest at least. items.s: Match v Combined Banks - Epsom, 15th October. Belgrave beat the Combined Banks in a cross-country match at Epsom on 15 October 1966, won by John Bicourt with newcomer Albert Smith second. A friendly atmosphere prevailed in our opening match of the season at Epsom, with our opponents having a Belgravian flavour in the form of Alan Morrison, Geoff Pearson and Stan Bradshaw. The match had several interesting features, none more than the appearance of Albert Smith - a 23 yrs old Scot who should prove to be in the Barrow/Reilly mould. Albert split our first team men Bicourt and Dance easily but found John in scintillating form. The winner was in a class of his own and has the prospect of a great season before him. Don Maclean started about 12 minutes behind the feild but was unable to catch any tail-enders in the next 42 minutes. At least he must have enjoyed it more than Bob Glover and Peter Wrench who went off course and were not recorded in! RESULT: Teams:- 1. items.s: NORTH SURREY LEAGUE First North Surrey League race of 1966/67 at Wimbledon on 22 October, with Belgrave only fourth of seven teams and Howard Satchell winning the club handicap. RACE No.1 - Wimbledon,October 22nd Belgrave got off to a bad start in the 1966/67 4- match programme finishing only 4th of the seven teams. Granted we had our best eight competing in the Bristol/Weston Relay, but there were still several good class runners who failed to appear. As last year, we shall now have to pull all the stops out to retain our title - perhaps we like it tough! Of the 130 starters, 39 were Belgravians competing for the Club Handicap prizes, giving our runners an added incentive. Charlie Dabbs was always well placed and ran to form, and Pat Newell produced his usual reliable performance. Bob Holt of Hercules led Presland (Surrey) and Smallbone (Mitcham) at the half-distance with the Hercules and Mitcham teams pressing hard. There was virtually no change over the second lap, and with Belgrave well out of the running all that remained of interest was the handicap result. This resulted in a good win for Howard Satchell with John Martin, who ran exceptionally well, second and the fast improving Alan Morrison third. items.sum: Report by 'Olympian' of the senior Priory Relay at Reigate on 5 November 1966, where Belgrave 'A' finished second, nine seconds behind Windsor & Eton.
items.s: PRIORY RELAY Report by 'Olympian' of the senior Priory Relay at Reigate on 5 November 1966, where Belgrave 'A' finished second, nine seconds behind Windsor & Eton. November 5th In past years we have not been able to field a really strong team at Reigate but this year it should have been good enough to get first place. Unfortunately we found Windsor & Eton at their very best and we followed them home 9 seconds behind. John Bicourt gave us 6th place on the first leg (13:41) and Chris Steer moved us up to 5th with 13:39 just to prove to John that he cannot always do better times. Bill Dance kept us in 5th place but closed up on the leaders with 13:36. Then came Tony Fairclough to prove that the Bristol - Weston relay was all a bad dream with a great run of 13:20 which took us up to 3rd leaving our captain Gerry North in a good position for an excellent performance, as always, in which he just beat 13 minutes (12:59) and brought us into 2nd place. Laurie O'Hara tried valiantly to catch Barton of Windsor but running on tricky ground in almost darkness (due to the race starting half an hour late) is not conducive to fast times and he could not get us into the lead. On the whole a satisfactory performance but being beaten is always disappointing - we no longer expect this to happen to us Olympian RESULT: Pos Team Time 1. Windsor & Eton 80:44 2. items.sum: Peter Hilliar's report of the Lauriston Runners Club 30 km track race at Walton on 12 November 1966: Jim Hogan sets a world record and Trevor Hart is fourth, within two minutes of Zatopek's former record.
items.s: HART NEAR ZATOPEK'S BEST Peter Hilliar's report of the Lauriston Runners Club 30 km track race at Walton on 12 November 1966: Jim Hogan sets a world record and Trevor Hart is fourth, within two minutes of Zatopek's former record. November 12th - 30 Kilometres Track Race - Walton-on-Thames Peter Hilliar reports:- On a mild autumnal day in mid-November the scene was set for the inaugural promotion of the Lauriston Runners Club at Stompond Lane track, Walton. Among the eight starters who toed the line was Trevor Hart. It was on this track last year that Tim Johnston (Ports) set the world record for 30 kilos. After an opening lap of 76 seconds Jim Hogan, the European Marathon Champion, took the lead followed by Graham Taylor, the Polytechnic marathon victor, and the rest of the field. A first mile of 4:53.6 saw Taylor leadin[illegible] with the rest of the field splitting up. At 2 miles, reached in 9:42, Hogan was in the lead never to be challenged again. At 10 miles, times wer[illegible] Hogan 48:46 (Johnston 49:01), Taylor 50:17, Smallbone 51:16, Hart and Watson 51:36. Hogan continued inexorably on to 15 miles in 1hr13:52 (Johnston 1hr 13[illegible] 55) and by this time had lapped the other four competitors still in the rac[illegible] at least once. It was abundantly clear that a well merited world record was his if he could keep going. This he did, finishing 9.2 seconds faster than the present mark. Trevor Hart's effort in finishing 4th was quite outstanding. His time was under 2 minutes slower than an erstwhile world record set by none other than Emil Zatopek; and this in his first race over 10 miles! Trevor ran through three miles in 15:18, six in 30:35, ten in 51:36, approx. 11 miles 1,040 yds in one hour, fifteen in 78:15 and eighteen in 94:54. items.label: December 1966
items.sum: Belgrave win the South of Thames senior cross-country team title at West Wickham on 12 November 1966, with Brian Buxton third and photos by R. Linstead.
items.s: BELS WIN SOUTH OF THAMES Belgrave win the South of Thames senior cross-country team title at West Wickham on 12 November 1966, with Brian Buxton third and photos by R. Linstead. November 12th - West Wickham Although a day late, November 12th will be Bill Lucas's remembrance day in future years. 1966/67 season is his year of office as President of the South of Thames C.C.A. and his election must have seemed especially rewarding on this occasion for, as a previous winner himself, he had the pleasure of presenting third individual medal to Brian Buxton and team winners medals to Belgrave Harriers. It would be interesting to know when a S.T.C.C.A. President last presented 5 of the 8 medals to his own club. It was at 3-15 pm that Bill Lucas sent over 300 runners on their way over the 5 mile course at Sparrows Den, West Wickham, and it was with some suprise that after a small lap of 1 mile Brian Buxton was seen to be leading the field followed closely by Bill Dance, Mel Thorpe, Adrian Major and John Dear. It is many years since we had 5 in the first 20 at this stage. Photos: R.Linstead LEFT: Brian Buxton approaches the finish in 3rd place. RIGHT: Bill Dance making ground on the second circuit. At the half way mark Brian had slipped to 3rd with Mitcham's Badgery out in front, a clear leader. Bill Dance had taken a fall and dropped back to the 20 mark with Mel alongside. Adrian was fading and John Dear had completely blown up - the picture was no longer so rosy. Windsor had 2 in 6 and Hercules 3 in 20. In the final stages of the race Bill recovered very well to reach 8th position and his re-vitalisation went a long way to securing us a team win. Brian held on doggedly to his forward position and a strong finish secured him the 3rd place he thoroughly deserved. Mel was not at his best (he was 2nd last year) but fought well all the way and Adrian Major, only just getting back to form after a bad foot injury, suffered a recurrence of the trouble, but despite the physical and psychological effects of such a setback grimly continued on to close in our scoring four. Of our other runners, and we had 25 out all together, the bouquets went to Bob Glover and Eric Penny. Bob was showing some of his old fire again and moved very well to finish 96th, and Eric continued his steady improvement to record a best ever placing of 118th. items.sum: Belgrave win the Essex Beagles cross-country relay at Chigwell on 12 November 1966 by 42 seconds, with Gerry North fastest of the day.
items.s: Belgrave all the way Belgrave win the Essex Beagles cross-country relay at Chigwell on 12 November 1966 by 42 seconds, with Gerry North fastest of the day. November 12th - Comfortable win in Essex Beagles X-cty Relay Whilst our South of Thames team was winning a hard fought battle at West Wickham, six of our best runners were having a comfortable outing at Chigwell. As usual, Laurie O'Hara did all that was expected of him - and more - by winning the first stage. This provided a real test for Bill Kerr, who has just got back to fitness after a long lay off, but he displayed quite a large slice of his old form and had little difficulty in holding our lead. Our Captain decided to run in the first half of the race for a change, but found the position very much as usual in these smaller relays - Belgrave in front. Gerry built a 1½ minute lead and Bicourt and Steer found it difficult to show their normal sense of urgency, allowing over half the margin to slip back to our opponents. Although the race was never really in doubt Tony Fairclough stepped up the pace just to make sure, giving Belgrave a winning margin of 42 seconds. items.sum: Gerry North wins the G.L.C. cross-country title at Parliament Hill Fields on 26 November 1966 and Belgrave 'A' take the team title.
items.s: G.L.C. Champs Gerry North wins the G.L.C. cross-country title at Parliament Hill Fields on 26 November 1966 and Belgrave 'A' take the team title. Gerry Wins Individual Title---Parliament Hill Fields, November 26th. With Parliament Hill living up to it's reputation for tough conditions with even more sticky muddy going than usual, one was reminded of those days when our runners succumbed to such testing courses. Not any longer though. Running with the right kind of fitness and confidence our scoring quartet forged their way through the mud, leaving their rivals well and truly bogged down. Gerry North ran with Enfield's T.J. Briault for the first of the two 3 mile laps, but when he decided to go it alone the Enfield runner was unable to respond, leaving Gerry to build up a full half minute's lead. Tony Fairclough showed great determination. Hard pressed in 6th place after the first circuit he fought off the opposition to move into a final 4th placing. Meanwhile Laurie O'Hara and Trevor Hart were providing excellent support, running together the whole way with the team result in their pocket, RESULT Teams 1. BELGRAVE 'A'(1,3,7,8)------- 19pts 2. items.s: CLUB 7½ Club 7½ miles cross-country championship on 3 December 1966, won by Gerry North seven seconds ahead of brother Geoff. December 3rd Although the margin was only 7 secs, Gerry North's win over brother Geoffrey was quite an easy affair. After John Thresher had led for the first of the 3 laps the North brothers moved 50 yards clear and ran shoulder to shoulderfor the rest of the race; but Gerry had plenty in hand and had no desire to over extend himself. Thresher stuck doggedly to the Norths' trail and, but for Gerry 's prescence, would probably have joined Geoff on the last lap. Hart ran solo throughout and Fairclough, O'Hara and Dance had "easys ", finishing together. RESULT Pos Name Handicap Time 1. Gerry North (SCR) 41:53 2. Geoff. North (0:30) 42:00 3. J. items.label: March 1967
items.sum: Editorial arguing that British track and field is waning and calling for a National A.A.A. Club Championship, followed by a note that the individual athlete registration scheme is dead but members may face higher subscriptions to fund the A.A.A.
items.s: EDITORIAL Editorial arguing that British track and field is waning and calling for a National A.A.A. Club Championship, followed by a note that the individual athlete registration scheme is dead but members may face higher subscriptions to fund the A.A.A. There has been much talk in recent months of the need for an inter-club competition during the summer season. Many views put forward seem to favour a league system with, we presume, promotion and relegation; or a super-league including the top clubs in the unofficial ranking list - a list insufficiently broad to reflect true team strength. Whilst we do not agree with the form of the proposals so far presented we fully understand the motives that prompt them. Despite the excellent, conscientious work of our National and Area coaches and the efforts of those many others who endeavour to produce medal-winning Britons, British Athletics is waning. And when compared with many other sports, waning fast. At a recent symposium on Recreational Planning, representatives of the Sports Council and National Playing Fields Association claimed that participation in Track and Field had shown little increase in recent years while the progress of many other sports was described as no less than "explosive". It was also revealed that some local authorities are being advised against constructing running tracks - many of which, to date, have been nothing more than "white elephants". In our view cross-country, long-distance and road-relay running are not suffering to the same degree because they are more closely identified with team participation. But Track and Field is a sport of many activities, and here lies it's weakness at club level. Furthermore, because of a chaotic summer programme of trophy meetings, inter-club events, various championships "invitation" events (of which there are hundreds) in the midst of which another programme of races is fitted to facilitate selection of our International teams, it is no wonder that team competition in the summer months is little short of farcical. Which is the most important event for the Club to win? Everyone has his own idea and club spirit during this period is at its lowest ebb; yet it is the clubs that form the base of the Athletics Pyramid. It is at club level then that the interest, indeed fervour, for Athletics should be engendered and thus enable the pyramid's apex to be pushed higher. A NATIONAL A.A.A. CLUB CHAMPIONSHIP is urgently needed. All events, except perhaps the walks, marathon and six miles, should be included. All flat races could be relays, except the 3 miles (decided on Cross-country scoring) and all the remaining events have 2 men per team. Field events could be decided on the aggregate best heights or distances of each pair. Similar competitions are held in other countries and the Army A.A. has held their inter-unit Championships on this basis for many years, and with great success. The Area Associations of the South, Midland and North would need to stage one or, at the most, two eliminating rounds with the three winners going through to the final and the three remaining places being decided, perhaps, on performance scoring tables. Studded with some quality invitation events such a "Cup Final" would attract a large following - and if it attracted the bell-ringing, flag-waving, football-type support the "Brighton" knew (and it could) then it would be a certain success. As for venue, well let us say that last August's British Games could have done with such a Championship around which to frame it's programme. It is our belief that this prestige event would persuade clubs to pay more attention to the Cinderella events, create at least one TEAM red-letter day in the summer and be a useful first step in a long overdue re-appraisal of the British Athletics scene. * * * * * We may take it that the much-discussed and much-reviled Individual athlete registration scheme is now dead. The A.A.A. have accepted that there are many inherent difficulties in such a scheme as originally planned,- not least being the interference with Club life and activity and the heavy expense ratio involved - but the fact remains that the A.A.A. needs more finance to carry through its programmes. It is probable that we shall all be asked to give more financial support to the A.A.A. than in the past; and it is possible that all members may be asked to pay a higher Club subscription permitting a per capita payment to be made to the A.A.A. on behalf of each subscribing first-claim member. This would be in accord with the A.A.A. and Area Associations' need for more finance; and the Government Department's (from which considerable grant-aid has been forthcoming) suggestion that athletes themselves should provide more money for their Sport than heretofore. London to Brighton Road Relay British Games 1966 A.A.A. Army A.A. Sports Council National Playing Fields Association

items.label: March 1967
items.sum: Obituary and career history of Harry Evans (1881-1967), Belgrave walker from 1907, R.W.A. judge and Club President in 1942-43, with E.D. Lacey's portrait photograph.
items.s: HARRY EVANS Obituary and career history of Harry Evans (1881-1967), Belgrave walker from 1907, R.W.A. judge and Club President in 1942-43, with E.D. Lacey's portrait photograph. HARRY EVANS (Born 5.5.1881, died 27.1.1967) It is with profound regret that we advise the passing of Harry Evans in his sixtieth year of membership; and it is with gratitude that we recall his many years of service to the Club and the Sport. His unfailing good humour, his contempt of the overcoat, his absolute dependability and complete integrity and high degree of competence endeared him to us all. To be disqualified by Harry Evans was to put the issue beyond all doubt; his decisions were accepted without the merest shadow of a protest for everyone accepted that his judgements could not be improved upon. He was without malice or guile. Uprighteousness, integrity and sincerity were to us synonymous with Harry Evans; and we shall miss him tremendously, whilst thankful for those very full years from 1907 to 1967 when Belgrave meant so much to him and he gave so much of himself to us. It was in 1907 that Harry was approached by a fellow baker and asked to support the Baker's Charity Athletic Meeting at the old Kensal Rise Track by competing in a walking race. Harry agreed, and surprised himself by finishing a close second to the trade champion. Another baker named Savage, who had been the World's professional champion and whose records made under the name of "Billy Franks" in 1882 still stand, thereupon became interested in Harry and, having a son in Belgrave, he introduced Harry to our club. Up till this time the Bels had never been a power to be reckoned with in Championships of any kind. It is true that their stationery and Entry Forms showed that once they had been placed third in the South of the Thames Cross Country Championship, but that was their sole team honour. In those days the betting element had invaded the world of Amateur Athletics and became fairly well rooted there. The Authorities were striving to suppress it but despite their efforts it was easily possible to back one's self or one's fancy at any athletic meeting of note. At Stamford Bridge itself there was a spot near the rails in the back straight where, despite both Police and Authorities, a brisk business was done for many years. In most of the prominent clubs there was a betting coterie and many young athletes found teachers willing to supervise their training who expected them to run or hold back as ordered. Now it is undeniable that this canker had eaten deep in the Belgrave Harriers as in many other clubs; and where handicap wins and odds as long as possible are the objective, it naturally follows that the attainment of high team honours is extremely unlikely. The aim is not high enough. From the outset, Harry fought openly and strenuously against this, and in my opinion, any tribute of thanks we pay him should commence with the acknowledgement of this, as the club's numerous team victories have all been achieved since the days when he showed his fellow clubmen that true sportsmanship demanded that one should give of his utmost in every race. The Walking Captain of the club at that time was F.W. Coomber, a fine walker and a good sportsman, who quickly realised Harry's potential ability. He taught Harry so thoroughly that in the next club race to be decided the pupil walked away from the teacher. So Harry was urged to enter for the two-mile handicap at the Stamford Bridge Open "Good Friday" meeting. Hot Cross Buns, being a National necessity at that time, Harry had to put in a stretch of 36 hours on them. During this period he had only two short rests. The race commenced only a few hours after he left the Bakery but Harry won the race by 75 yards. The Belgrave urging and cheering throughout the race was insistent and incessant, and he learned afterwards the Bels had backed him very heavily. The results recorded later will show that he kept on winning despite the frowns of those who wanted his wins to be accompanied with bets at favourable odds. Harry certainly had no time for the athlete who was not in the game for the love of it and for the glory of winning or fighting to do so. Shortly after the Good Friday race Harry competed at Herne Hill and was a close third in the very fast time of 13mins.32secs. Next he won a 2 mile Walk at Redhill. Here Tommy Eaton, whom many of you will know as our pre-war masseur was the virtual scratch man together with Alf Pateman. Harry followed with a 2nd prize at the Tottenham Hospital Sports and a first prize at Sutton. This Sutton race was memorable in as much as Harry was receiving a small start from A.E. Rowlands, the New Zealand Champion, who was over here for the 1908 Olympic Games and who had been recording some very fast times. He was a strong favourite for the race and actually caught Harry, but Harry fought on to gain the victory by a yard. This race was followed by a second place race at Epsom. During this season Harry had won every Club handicap from the scratch mark. During the Winter Season he won the club 10 miles Championship in 78 minutes. Following this he walked in the A.A.A. 7 Miles Championship and recorded the fast time of 54 mins.30secs., and in the 2 miles Championship recording 14mins.10secs. He followed this up with a win at 2 miles on the old White City track of 3 laps to the mile. This was a very fast track, certainly faster than Stamford Bridge, but not quite so fast as the present track there. A second place in the L.A.C. Open Walk at Stamford Bridge came next and this was followed by a first at Clapton. This was undoubtedly one of Harry's finest performances. E.J. Webb, a winner of five A.A.A. Championships gave Harry a short start and caught him with a lap to go. Harry held him and one of the judges ran the whole of the lap in case either broke contact. It was neck and neck all the way with Harry just winning. By now we have got to the Winter Season of 1909 and here we find Harry winning the first Junior Individual and Team Race promoted by the Road Walking Association. Belgrave lost the team race by one point, but hereafter there was another honour recorded on our letter headings. This race started at Brentford and the Course mapped out was one passing Gunnersbury Park, crossing Ealing Common, climbing Hanger Hill, dipping down to Alperton and climbing part of the way to Wembley before returning. The road over Hanger Hill was then narrow with a very second-class surface. About two miles of tar-macadam and eight miles of rolled granite were generally to be expected in a ten mile race at this time, and in this race the course was typical. In winning Harry recorded the splendid time of 81mins.37secs. Harry was more than disappointed with the team's position of 2nd as earlier in the day there had been a two mile handicap at Stamford Bridge and several of the team had raced there before participating in the longer race for their club. Following this, the club arranged a fair number of inter-club races and in these, although Harry was generally first man home, our successes were few as usually only three or four Belgravians turned out. In the years 1909 to 1911, Harry gained six first class standard medals in the A.A.A. Championships, three at seven miles and three at two miles, and did well against the Champions of the day who included G.E. LARNER, E.J. WEBB and H.V.L. ROSS. Now came a long break in Harry's athletic career. He married, and a growing family, his wife's ill-health and night work kept him out of the sport for some time. This period of inactivity was followed by the 1914-18 World War. Harry was an early volunteer for the forces. He was captured and spent a long while in a German prison camp. On returning to England in 1919 he was talked into training again by Jimmy Belchamber. Although he did not get back the pace that had formerly made him so formidable he soon became a very sound and reliable team man at seven and ten miles. In the Winter seasons of 1919-20 and 1920-21 Belgrave were the winners of most of the seven and ten miles scratch team races. We had seven walkers who could be relied upon to finish well up. Usually we could rely upon at least six of the seven turning up. These seven were Jimmy Belchamber, Harry Evans, Harry Hanger, Bill Hawker, Bob Ricketts, Alec Spendlove and Charlie Wells. Amongst these Harry was at a disadvantage in respect of age, but he was in our scoring four many times. He found pace enough also to win some more prizes at 2 miles on the track, a 1st at Paddington just after the 1920 Olympic Games being especially commendable. In this race the British, Australian and South African Olympic walkers were competing. Harry's handicap mark was by no means a long one. He also won a first prize at Writtle and a second at Hornsey. On the road he was awarded the style prize in the Islington Borough Walk in March 1920. Twice Harry attempted the 20 Miles R.W.A.Championship but found that this was not his distance. This was before 1914. When he made his post-war come-back he could not be persuaded to try this distance. As a walking judge Harry had no superior. He had been on the R.W.A. list since early 1921 and officiated at many A.A.A.Championships, the 1948 Olympic Games, and at thousands of races on track and on the road. His worth to the Club as an adviser on style and fair walking was inestimable. As a committee man he served a life-time and held the Presidency of the Club worthily for two years, 1942 and 1943, in addition to being a Life Member. He was a great believer in breathing exercises and in physical exercise for the developement of the stomach muscles, and in his earlier days profited by weight lifting. Harry was acutely aware as a young baker of the high mortality rate in the trade, largely due to chills etc. developed by working at high temperatures during the night and then going out into the early morning cold; and he sought to protect himself by being physically fit. Indirectly this brought him into sport and the Belgrave Harriers, where generations of us have learned to regard him with great affection. And so we take our leave of one of Belgrave's noblest sons....... R.I.P. A.A.H. items.sum: Obituary of Belgrave walker and Metropolitan Police inspector Cyril Yescombe, who died of a heart attack after the club 10 miles championship.
items.s: CYRIL YESCOMBE Obituary of Belgrave walker and Metropolitan Police inspector Cyril Yescombe, who died of a heart attack after the club 10 miles championship. CYRIL YESCOMBE (BORN 9.10.1919, DIED 21.1.1967) We mourn the passing of Cyril Yescombe, aged 47, and our sincere condolences are extended to Mrs Yescombe, who has helped us so often, and her family. Cyril joined us in early 1955 and we had come to know him as a great hearted walker who whilst not aspiring to the higher placings, yet gave stability in the middle reaches, and was a source of encouragement to us all. Cyril competed in the club 10 miles Championship on January 21st and covered the course in 92 minutes. Two or three hours later a heart attack seized him whilst at the wheel of his car on his way home, from which he died almost immediately. We are indeed sorry to have lost such a good Belgravian. Among his best walking performances were his eleventh place in the RWA 50 Kilometres Championship at Leyland in 1957, in sub-tropical conditions, which gained him his Club Honours Badge; and his 100 miles walk recorded in our current Handbook. Inspector Cyril Yescombe was very popular indeed amongst his Metropolitan Police colleagues and was one of the two Vice-Chairman of the Metropolitan Police Walking Club. In recent months he had done valuable work in training the young Police Cadets and his splendid example will have left lasting impressions for the good on a new generation of policeman. He will be sorely missed by us all. R.I.P. items.s: HON SEC'S NOTES Hon. Secretary's notes on the centenary of cross-country running (quoting Walter Rye), the search for early club records, the 1967 track fixture dates, news of past members, the club's football pool scheme versus the new Atlas Pool, and Belgrave officials on the Southern Counties AAA committee. This year sees the Centenary of Cross-Country Running and no doubt more will be heard of this when the Autumn comes again. It is interesting to read the words of WALTER RYE, the first President of Thames Hare and Hounds. He wrote in 1894: "At the end of 1867 a few members (of whom the writer was one) of the Thames Rowing Club at Putney conceived the idea of holding some cross-country steeplechase during the winter season with the idea of keeping themselves more or less in condition until rowing began again. As may well be imagined the arrangements of Thames Handicap Steeplechase No 1, as it was called, were primitive in the extreme and indeed the whole affair was treated more as a joke than anything else. The competitors were taken up to the starting place on Wimbledon Common, the edge of the Beverley Brook by the bridge in a bus, and had to dress how they could, and the race was run in the dark over 2¼ miles of the roughest and boggiest part of the Common, then very different indeed as to its surface from what it has now become after recent drainage. Still there were a dozen starters out of twenty entries, and the affair being the first cross-country steeplechase (not being at a school) attracted much attention". In the following winter (1868) it was decided to try paper-chasing and Walter Rye continues:- "Our first run took place on October 17th 1868 from the 'Kings Head', Roehampton, then as it still is, our headquarters, and the beau ideal in many respects of a paper-chaser's home, being a quaint old wooden built inn, squatted behind a great wych elm, covered with creepers, and in the middle of real open country. We had secured the written leave of Earl Spencer, who then owned Wimbledon Common, to run over it, and still claim to be the only club who can drop paper over the heath, as having the right before there were such things as conservators and their bye-laws; and all existing rights were saved by the Act." Rye writes on the first championship races thus:- "It was not till 1870 that the first real championship race was started though this attempt to bring it off in the wilds of Epping Forest proved a great failure, everyone losing his way separately on his own account. Next year a carefully laid out course was chosen from Roehampton, over the Common by Merton and Morden, West Barnes and Crooked Billet Lane, about 11¾ miles. The Thames H & H won the first time scoring 35 as against South London H. 58 and the Spartans 94" Much more of a fascinating nature follows but we must conclude....... "When the run is over, the tub - lukewarm if it can be had - is in universal request, followed, if possible, by a cold douche by means of a bucketful of water from the hands of a stable-helper. If the run has been extra wet or cold, a steaming glass of port negus may be wisely taken as a precaution, but it is a singular thing that both before and after the meal which terminates the evening, 'ginger beer and gin' is the favourite drink, having probably been found by long experience to best carry off the extra heat of the body caused by a long run." * * * * * Our own eighty years of history have been much in mind lately, and a letter published in "Athletics Weekly" and many local newspapers asking for details and relics of our very early days, whilst widely seen and noted by many interested persons has, as yet, added nothing to the sum total of knowledge of our first twenty years or so. Not that this surprises, for a stripling of 20 years in the Clubs earliest Embankment races, would now be awaiting his 100th birthday! It may be, however, that a second or third generation have preserved details of Belgrave of the late 1800's; and if this is so we should be glad if they could find their way to the Hon. Secretary, and so assist in his researches. If you know of any such persons please try and obtain their co-operation, for time is all too short. * * * * * One reads of the recent discovery of Chaucerian manuscripts, and of lost and unknown works of Leonardo da Vinci coming to light after centuries- and wonders what happened to the Belgrave Harriers Minute Books, 1887-1907! * * * * * Thanks to a succession of conscientious Hon. Editors our story from 1920 onwards has been lovingly recorded in the pages of the Belgravian in its sporting results, its comments, its humour, and its exhortations. The historian of the future has bricks in plenty from which to fashion his edifice - lets hope he doesn't drop too many of them! * * * * * The Track season will soon be with us once again and below is given a list of the dates for which permits have been granted to us. You are asked to note these dates in your diaries and ensure that the programmes arranged have your full support whether you are an active athlete, an official or an onlooker. In addition to these dates we shall of course be engaged in the usual multiplicity of fixtures, full details of which will be available in due course: Saturday, 18th March - Tooting Track (Invitation Field Events) Saturday, 29th April - Battersea Park Monday, 1st May - Battersea Park Wednesday, 10th May - Battersea Park SATURDAY, 3rd JUNE - HURLINGHAM PARK (CLUB TRACK AND FIELD CHAMPIONSHIPS) Wednesday, 14th June - Battersea Park Wednesday, 28th June - Battersea Park Wednesday, 5th July - Battersea Park (Invitation Inter-Club Walks) Wednesday, 12th July - Battersea Park Wednesday, 26th July - Battersea Park Wednesday, 9th August - Battersea Park * * * * * We shall hope for greatly improved track performances this coming Summer, and our Field Event specialists are already fitting themselves to secure their generous quota of points in trophy events. Remember! our President has requested at least one Trophy during the Summer. It could be the "Brockman", the "Sward", the "Cecil Fry", even an A.A.A. Relay Championship - he won't worry overmuch which it is! * * * * * We were delighted to have a visit from Wally Bayliss at Headquarters in December when the 7 Miles Championship was held. Wally is a Past-President - a former Hon. Secretary for eleven years, a former Club Captain and a Life Member - and we hope to see him with increasing regularity in the future. * * * * * News comes from Albert Macher that he is progressing after a period of ill-health which prevented him from coming along recently to present the Macher Shield for the 10 Miles Championship, Albert and his brother Gus, belong to that very select band of members who joined the Club prior to World War I - in 1912 to be precise. * * * * * Greetings have been received from Edmund Donovan, O.B.E., of New York, who was a very active Club member in 1912, and subsequent years. It is possible that he may be present at our Club Track and Field Championships at Hurlingham in June. * * * * * Many members will know that the Amateur Athletic Association has recently entered into an arrangement with a professional football pools organisation whereby Amateur Athletics will receive some monetary benefit, the participating clubs also receive an addition to their funds; and of course the individual subscriber have his chance of winning one of the prizes offered. We in Belgrave have, of course, enjoyed the fruits of our own scheme and the work of many dedicated members for over thirty years; and our own freehold Headquarters is a monument to the many Club helpers who have participated in this great Club effort since the 1930's. We now have the task of maintenance and improvement. A sense of duty and a wish to help the AAA and BAAB in their financial problems prompted your Finance Committee and General Committee to give detailed consideration in all its aspects to the new Atlas Pool; and thought was given to the possible termination of our own scheme and the transfer of interested members - if they so wished - into the newly introduced Pool. However, a conscientious and unbiased appraisal of the merits of the two main money-raising schemes under discussion (and of other subsidiary competitions) and their detailed workings convinced your Committee that we should continue with our own scheme; and intensify our efforts within the Club to ensure the maximum efficiency of our own Belgrave Supporters Scheme. This decision was agreed unanimously and it is intended to continue our existing scheme at least until the end of the 1968 Football Season. Meantime the situation will be kept under review. Les Cohen, in addition to his AAA Championship Hon Secretary's duties and hundreds of other official chores, still finds time with the assistance of his wife, to conduct our scheme and has agreed enthusiastically to carry on. To Les and Mary our very great thanks are due and also to those members who have given such loyal support, which has resulted in our unrivalled facilities and activities. There is room for much more support and Les Cohen our Hon Treasurer will be pleased to give further information - addresses are in our Handbook. We have also decided to give token support to the newly introduced Pool and members who would like to participate in this Pool should contact Frank Webb - another great worker for the Club and its finances. * * * * * At the recent AGM of the Southern Counties AAA Les Cohen and Alf Harley were confirmed in office as two of the five Vice-Presidents and Harry Shields was elected to the Committee on the nomination of the South of the Thames C.C.Association. In addition Bill Lucas (Southern Counties C.C.Association) and Frank Jarvis (Race Walkin Association - Southern Area) serve on the Committee as delegates. A.A.H. items.sum: Junior Section notes on Sunday boys' training at Battersea Park, welcomes to William Curtin and Ray Gale, Robert Poole's move to Reading and an appeal for more Youths.
items.s: JUNIOR SECTION Junior Section notes on Sunday boys' training at Battersea Park, welcomes to William Curtin and Ray Gale, Robert Poole's move to Reading and an appeal for more Youths. We have a large group of Boys meeting for training and competition at Battersea Park track every Sunday morning. Why don't you join us? Every three weeks a field events meeting is organised by Bill Couzens and Dave Ansell in which all the boys take part. Regular events that are most popular are the Shot, Javelin and High Jump. We intend in the coming weeks to put on some races over most distances, including relays. We even have our own Bamboo pole for vaulting, must admit nobody does it very well yet, but it does cause a few laughs. Welcome to William Curtin who has just joined us. We hear he recently won the London Schools Cross Country Champs. so he will certainly help to strengthen our team. No less a welcome to Ray Gale who although only a novice, looks promising. He certainly must be keen for he cycles all the way from Bethnal Green, East London to be present at our Sunday morning meetings. We are sorry to hear that Robert Poole has gone to live in Reading. He wishes to remain a member of Belgrave and will get down to race for us whenever he can. Good for you Bob! Although we have built up quite a large Boys Section in the Club, we have fallen low in numbers of Youths. We are now canvassing for new members so put the word about and see if there are any friends at school you can introduce into the Club. They don't have to be good, that they will become when they have been in Belgrave for a short time. REG.HOPKINS Reg Hopkins REG.HOPKINS Bill Couzens Bill Couzens Dave Ansell Dave Ansell William Curtin William Curtin Ray Gale Ray Gale Robert Poole Robert Poole Robert Poole Bob London Schools Cross Country Championships 1967 Battersea Park Bethnal Green Reading

items.s: November 26th Under 15 match v Wimbledon College Report of an under-15 cross-country match narrowly won by Belgrave over Wimbledon College, 101 points to 109. This was a friendly match against our neighbours and we just managed to beat them by 101 points to 109. The individual winner was M.Geary of the College but the Bels filled second and third places with Robert Poole and John Hamilton. There were 34 boys in the race - more than half of them being Bels. Youngest of these was Ian Gillings who was only eight years old at the time and yet managed to place 27th - a tremendous little runner! The College gave us a fine tea afterwards and we were waited upon by some of the older boys. This was very much appreciated by all of us and helped make it a most enjoyable afternoon. M. items.s: NORTH SURREY LEAGUE (YOUTHS & BOYS) Final table and race-by-race results of the 1966-67 North Surrey League for Youths and Boys, in which Belgrave were second to Mitcham, their best ever placing hoped for. NORTH SURREY LEAGUE (YOUTHS & BOYS) This was an excellent performance by our younger members. Fourth last year and third the year before we did not, at the beginning of the season, expect to better either of these results. Mitcham retained their title, as expected, and although their winning margin was 166 points against last year's 100, Belgrave gained ground on them. Next year we look to our promising young team for a further closing of the gap. FINAL RACE - Croydon H (Lloyd Park), February 25th We went into the fourth match knowing that the favourites, Mitcham, would retain their title but with a great chance of gaining a best ever 2nd place. Croydon were our main rivals for the runners-up position, already holding the same number of points as ourselves (250), but Surrey (291) were also uncomfortably close. John Kelly set off at a fiery pace which he was unable to maintain but, nevertheless, held on well to finish a creditable 9th. Good support by Poole, Curtin and Bacon - all with the makings of future first team men - and the "experienced" backing of Tony Brooks was too much for our main rivals both of whom finished behind us. COSTESSEY, NORWICH----March 4th Our Juniors and Youths did not enjoy the success of our Seniors but, nevertheless, put all they had into their running. Our leading performer was Adrian Major who, still not fully fit after persistent ankle trouble, forged through the field on the second lap to finish 52nd in the Junior event. John Kelly led the Youths home, with the team hitting exactly 1,000 points-- 19 fewer than their Junior friends---but this essentially track team look all set to reap the benefit of their winter's work this coming summer. A word of encouragement to both teams. Tony Fairclough ran in the National Junior for the first time in 1962 and finished 272nd! Trevor Hart did likewise in 1961 and finished 310th! Look AT THEM NOW. items.s: Harry Hare reminisces Harry Hare recalls the club's 1921 photograph at the Swan Hotel, Ridgway, taken at the 7 mile C.C. Championship for the H.T. Blackstaffe Shield, with a numbered key to the group and memories of the old winter headquarters. This Club photograph was taken in the early days of 1921 on the occasion of the 7 mile C.C.Championship for the"H.T.BLACKSTAFFE" Shield, This was the ninth contest. First competed for in 1910 with a lapse during part of the 1914-18 War. The winner was J.F.Gray, with H.Parker second and R. Savage third. 1 F.FORD 2 "THE HOST" 3 C.COOK 4 E.GORDON 5 C.C.ARNOLD 6 A.F.W.MACHER 7 H.WRIGHT 8 H.FEARN 9 BOY (?SON OF) 10 J.B.BELCHAMBER 11 - 12 A.E.MACHER 13 H.GOODFELLOW 14 G.STILL 15 - 16 R.J.SAVAGE 17 J.F.GRAY 18 H.PARKER 19 A.L.PORTER 20 J.W.MACHER 21 C.H.SPEECHLEY 22 - 23 C.P.SEXTON 24 - 25 J.F.SATCHELL 26 - 27 - 28 W.D.PRITCHARD 29 - 30 J.PRITCHARD 31 A.E.CHORLEY 32 - 33 - 34 R.W.RICKETTS 35 J.W.GILBERT 36 C.C.HARRIS 37 J.K.CHALK 38 - 39 "THE POTMAN" 40 J.J.CRICHTON 41 W.H.HARE 42 E.G.COOPER As can readily be seen, the group is in the foreground of "The Swan Hotel", Ridgway, which was "Winter Headquarters". At this period, part of the premises was fitted up as a Skittle Alley of the old type; nine pins and bowls of heavy wood, flat and rounded in the form of old Dutch cheeses. Along the sides of the narrow alley, plain wooden seating provided the dressing facilities. At the end it opened out to a small room where the pins were set up. This provided further accommodation which on busy days would overflow into the adjoining Saloon bar (closed of course for normal business). A sash-corded window looked out onto a small open yard beyond which was a small wash house or old coach house. Here the Potman would set up a couple of zinc hip baths topped up with a few pints of hot water. So it was a case of up with the bottom sash, hop out and dash across for the after-run or walk wash down. Needless perhaps to mention that on a busy or wet afternoon the density of the water rose and the temperature fell at depressingly rapid rates. My most lasting impression of this era was a 10 mile, time started handicap walk. As a comparative new member and novice, and favoured with a generous allowance, I entered the last 3 mile lap with only the fear of the unknown pack of fast backmarkers after skin, and won, literally by a "street and a half". With unchecked haste home, I was through the window and (with the absence of runners on an away fixture) into the luxury of near constant hot water. This I thought was sufficient reward. I was however to receive the unusual Club pot, a small hot-water jug E.P.N.S. - Happy days. It may be wondered "Why did we leave this home with the "Beer and Skittles?" Why? items.s: BELS RETAIN SURREY TITLE Report and result of the Surrey senior cross-country championship in Richmond Park, where Gerry North retained the individual title and Belgrave the team title, with R. Linstead's photograph of the race. Richmond Park - January 7th Although we were successful in beating off some strong Hercules and Mitcham opposition our retention was in no small way due to Derek Fernee, our second-claim member from Polytechnic. The only championships in which he can represent us are those of Surrey County, and with our being short of good Surrey men he stepped into the breach to be our fifth scorer and help retain the title. His absence would have relegated us to second. In keeping with the mood of the afternoon, Gerry North ran out a convincing winner of the individual championship, thus retaining his title also. Gerry set the pace throughout, but after the first of the three 2½ mile laps still had Robinson (Guildford) and R.Holt (Hercules) at his shoulder - the latter looking particularly relaxed. A mile later though, Robinson was shaken off and it was not long before Holt also had to give way. Gerry went into the last lap with a 50 yard lead, which he increased steadily to the finish. John Thresher, in a personal duel with Mick Gowan (HHH), forced the pace all the way and took 6 miles to increase his lead from one to five yards! With 300 yards remaining Gowan sprinted hard, caught John 50 yards from the line but was unable to resist Thresher's final surge. Tony Fairclough and John Bicourt supported well, the latter finishing faster probably than anyone and beating team-mate Fernee on the line (perhaps he was just practising for the Southern!). items.s: OTHER COUNTIES Notes on Belgrave runners in other county cross-country championships: Middlesex, Warwickshire and Hertfordshire. MIDDLESEX. Trevor Hart was only 17 seconds away from another County vest when he all but mastered the treacherous conditions at Cockfosters. His 11th placing was an excellent effort considering the County team placed 5th at Leicester. Laurie O'Hara was very unhappy with the going and his 20th position, although creditable, belied his true form. John Dear finished 36th and Bill Kerr 41st, but Cadogan could not close in a team. WARWICKSHIRE. Geoff North, now free of injury but still not fully fit, showed up quite well at Sutton Coldfield where he placed 6th behind a Coventry quartet and Herriott. Mel Thorpe also appeared and placed 24th, 2mins 31secs. behind Geoff. Unfortunately, further illness prevented Geoff from competing at Leicester. HERTFORDSHIRE. Gerry Williams gained selection for the County team and finished an excellent 58th at Leicester, ahead of such runners as Hyman, Heatley and Bullivant. items.s: O'HARA Gets His REVENGE! Report and handicap result of the club 10 miles cross-country championship at Wimbledon, won by Laurie O'Hara from Tony Fairclough and Trevor Hart, with C. Shippen's photographs. Club 10 miles Championship - Wimbledon, January 21st It was as though Laurie O'Hara had had this race on his mind for 12 months. In a race which is perhaps a little over-distance for him, he shot straight to the front and set a fast pace 30 yards clear of the field - displaying a courage and determination that made one wonder whether last year's inches defeat was still on his mind. Within striking distance was his victor on that occasion, Tony Fairclough, closely accompanied by an equally determined Trevor Hart. Both these runners narrowly missed representing their counties in the inter-county event at Leicester the same day and on current form were thought to have the edge on Laurie. All praise then to O'Hara for his courageous front running. For three of the four laps the gap remained the same with Hart striving to shake off his fellow pursuer, but on the final circuit Fairclough moved away and provided O'Hara with company for the first time. Such reserves suggested that Tony would retain the "Macher"Shield, but to beat this man O'Hara you have to draw his sting before the finish and Tony just couldn't shake him off - the last 150 yards settled it. Laurie was a deserved winner and a worthy champion and both runners should be congratulated for making this contest so exciting on two consecutive occasions. Photos: C.Shippen LEFT: Hart leads Fairclough in the chase for O'Hara. RIGHT: Bill Kerr paces "World Sports" star Charlie Walker! Bill Dance had his first outing since a bout of achilles trouble and performed surprisingly well, but Bicourt, Steer (retired) and Kerr disappointed. It was a fair reflection on the excellent form they displayed that the handicap awards should go to the first three home; with O'Hara proving a double winner and Hart getting the better of Fairclough on this occasion. items.s: BELS 3rd in SOUTH of THAMES Report and result of the South of Thames senior cross-country championship hosted by Belgrave on Wimbledon Common, where Belgrave were third team behind Blackheath and Ranelagh, with E.D. Lacey's photograph of John Dear and Howard Satchell. Wimbledon Common - January 28th With Belgrave Harriers acting as hosts for this year's Championship, and Bill Lucas as S.O.T.President hoping to award winner's medals to the Bels., as he did in the Junior race last November, hopes ran very high among home club supporters - particularly as we won convincingly three years ago when the event was last held at Wimbledon - but it was not to be. Although our team were the first to close in, our scorers were not forward enough to clinch the title in a close race. The cards were stacked against us early on when Brian Buxton, running barefooted, retired after hitting an extra rough patch of ground when in the 'teens. Gerry Williams ran very well, lying between 4th and 7th throughout, and was well supported by John Bicourt. Bill Dance, now free from his achilles trouble, was all out for a trip to Belgium and forged through the field in the later stages. Blackheath and Ranelagh were almost at full strength yet only managed to beat our restricted team by 46 points and 6 points respectively. This is one page of the Belgravian that will, censor permitting, cover some of the fringe aspects of our sport. We hope to recruit some of the more avanteguard writers from within our ranks not just to knock the establishment but to stir the stagnation that is mistakenly referred to as solid and respectable - contributions from any depraved Bel who has something to air gratefully received by this supplement's editor, KILROY. Daily Dsilx SEX & PERFOMANCE WHAT ARE THE EFFECTS ? BY DUNG (SHOCKING - DISGUSTED ETC.) WILSON Having rivetted your attention with the headline, I can now reveal the inside story I overheard whilst drinking in the Stadium Bar well away from all that horrid activity of the arena. A couple of N.U.T.S were comparing the times of the 100 yards dash and it was patently obvious that the women's event was 9/10 second slower than the corresponding Men's race. With my natural ear for a story, I waited until they discussed the furlong; with the same difference, the women's time was slower. Meanwhile, back at the Bodleian, I was checking other events. This was the startling revelation. At all distances from 100 yards up men were consistantly faster than women. In both the long and high jump, women jumped shorter and lower. THIS HAS GOT TO STOP! What is Mr. D. Howell doing about it? As Labour Minister for Sport he should not allow this discrimination. In today's emancipation and equality, why can't women perform so well? AFTER THE BALL WAS OVER Reliable reports say that several runners looked decidedly jaded at a Kensington party the evening of the "Southern". Quote from Geoff North, watching colleagues staggering out, "These guys just can't take it'". Geoff, of course, is not running these days. HANNUT All was sweetness and light when it was found that nobody would have to foot the bill for the additional travellers. Pity it wasn't discovered earlier - a lot of bad feeling could have been avoided. Note: J. Thresher voted the most sociable fellow abroad a broad. items.s: BIG GEAR HOIST AT 'SOUTHERN' Spoof crime report (continuing the satirical supplement) on G. North's car being robbed at Parliament Hill Fields during the Southern championship, with a mock footnote about Bob Glover. Parliament Hill Fields was the scene of a most audacious raid during the "Southern" C.C.C. when G. North who made an equally successful raid on the title was robbed of his car and contents. The car was subsequently recovered but the gear apparently uninsured, was gone. It has been suggested that a collection be taken up to reimburse him for his loss. FOOTNOTE: By Marjory Poops. Is this the gesture of comradeship that prompted the same authors to help Bob Glover when he was homeless, living in his car parked at a lonely copse somewhere in Surrey? G. North G. North Marjory Poops Marjory Poops Bob Glover Bob Glover Southern Counties Cross Country Championships 1967 Parliament Hill Fields Surrey

items.label: March 1967
items.h: GREAT WIN BY GERRY ! ..... but BELS fail to topple POMPEY
items.sum: Report and result of the Southern Counties cross-country championship at Parliament Hill Fields, where Gerry North won his first Southern title and Belgrave were second team to Portsmouth, with R. Linstead's photographs on the following page.
items.s: GREAT WIN BY GERRY ! ..... but BELS fail to topple POMPEY Report and result of the Southern Counties cross-country championship at Parliament Hill Fields, where Gerry North won his first Southern title and Belgrave were second team to Portsmouth, with R. Linstead's photographs on the following page. SOUTHERN CHAMPIONSHIPS, Parliament Hill Fields, February 11th. "His best ever", "outstanding", "scintillating", "devastating", "a great champion". These were just a few of the superlatives heard at Parliament Hill when Gerry North won his first Southern Counties C.C.Championship by a margin that would have made an hour-glass more appropriate than a stop-watch! Surging through the quagmires and gliding over the firm stretches this veritable power house of a runner made the opposition look mediocre. So impressive did he look that even when Johnston was at his shoulder half way round the first lap one had no doubt that their company couldn't last. And so it proved to be. In the space of a mile a gap of 50 yards appeared and despite a fall on the second lap Gerry increased this lead to 200 yards. A final circuit of undiminished power doubled the gap and North crossed the line to the applause of a fair sized crowd, who then settled down to await the arrival of the competitors who had been left struggling in the wake of the new Champion. Belgrave got off to a fine start when the large field raced up the first hill. Bill Dance was first to hit the top, with Gerry and Chris Steer close at hand; Bill and Ghris were to pay for their fast beginning, but we still had 8 in 25 and things looked well. The field soon sorted itself out and it was clear that our hopes depended on forward packing to offset the superior individual performances of the leading Portsmouth men. At 2 miles Thresher was 13th, with O'Hara, Williams, Hart and Bicourt all in the twenties. Fairclough was 35th, not at all happy, but John Dear who ran only because of Alan Black's last minute withdrawal, was running the race of his life in 59th spot. Bill Dance had not yet recovered from his fast start and was already in the sights of Bill Kerr in the eighties. Brian Buxton looked quite distressed and it was unfortunate that our "twelve cup" chances should disappear with his withdrawal early in the second lap. With only 15 points separating the Portsmouth and Belgrave teams, the battle really hotted up on the second circuit but our rivals got the better of the exchanges - mainly due to that fine team runner, Martin Hyman. Continuously making ground, he rallied his last three scorers, particularly J. Cooke and Plumpton who were not looking too good, and promptly doubled his team's lead. So, although we went into the last lap with eleven runners in seventy-six, team chances looked bleak. Thresher suffered with a bout of stitch on the final circuit and conceded ten places, but with O'Hara and Fairclough producing strong finishes the loss was offset. With 2 miles to go Tony was only our 7th man, running along side Pompey's 6th man, Plumpton, but at the finish Fairclough had shot through to 4th scorer (25th) and the Portsmouth man faded to 44th - but even this could not shake Portsmouth's command of the situation and they ran out deserved team winners, with their reputation for being a formidible team with six to score considerably enhanced. FOOTNOTE: Gerry North's penalty for being such a good winner was to have his Great Britain tracksuit top stolen and then, after the presentation, to find his car and £200 worth of sports goods also stolen. items.label: March 1967
items.sum: Coach Dave Ansell tells how Snowy Brooks trained on an aircraft carrier, and reminds members of the club's winter training facilities at Belgrave Hall and Battersea Park.
items.s: DAVE ANSELL WRITES: Coach Dave Ansell tells how Snowy Brooks trained on an aircraft carrier, and reminds members of the club's winter training facilities at Belgrave Hall and Battersea Park. There are always some athletes who continually complain about lack of facilities and to them I would tell this story:- Snowy Brooks - one of our first class track and field men - wrote for a training schedule a couple of months ago and it was duly worked out for him. As he is serving in the Royal Navy, on an aircraft carrier, certain alterations had to be made from a normal routine. Firstly he could only train in the open air when there was no flying as I suppose he didn't fancy being sucked into a jet engine or chopped in half by an aircraft's wing during his warm-up jog. Then again he couldn't train on the flight deck in very bad weather (participants in the Boxing Day 2 Miles handicap will understand best what this must be like, only this time he keeps still and the "ground" moves). Jumping was also dodgy, for if you jump up when the boat goes down then a simple hop could send you soaring up in the air and when you come down - Ouch! Any running he could manage would have to be at irregular times and spikes, of course, were out, so all his sprinting has to take place on solid steel in plimsoles - not to be recommended. I thought his weight training would prove to be the only part of his schedule which would follow a normal course, as there is a fully equipped gym below decks. I had made allowances and adaptions for all of these drawbacks except for one thing - the consequence of my ignorance was a letter from him thanking me for the training plans but he was going to have to leave out the various jumping and jump squats in the gym, as he would hit his head on the low ceiling if he attempted them! Well I don't know how many of you have as much trouble in trying to carry out your training but I can tell you that Snowy has shown the true Belgrave spirit and is somehow training every day and is now in Australia where he hopes to compete in some local meetings. I am sure that you will join me in wishing him Good Luck with his athletics, and if his performances compare with the way he has overcome the lack of facilities for training which he has experienced then I am sure that he will be carrying Belgrave colours to victory on many occasions. * * * * * I shouldn't think that anybody has every training facility on their doorstep so we must make our training schedules fit in with what is available. We in Belgrave Harriers have an immediate advantage over other clubs because of the existence of Belgrave Hall. This is ideal for the sprinters and field events men to train from in the winter and we meet there on Saturdays at 2.30 p.m. and of course we are also at Battersea Park track on Sunday mornings at 10.30 a.m. There are usually four coaches passing on their personal experience and know-how to the wise members who take advantage of all these facilities. We have an exciting season ahead of us and everybody will have to do their best if we are to fulfill the President's desire for a triumph in a Trophy match. If you put in the groundwork then you must surely get the results. Good Luck for the coming season. DAVE ANSELL. Dave Ansell DAVE ANSELL Snowy Brooks Snowy Brooks Snowy Brooks Snowy Belgrave Harriers Boxing Day Meeting 1966 Australia Belgrave Hall Battersea Park

The usually strong field assembled in almost ideal conditions at Farnham this year for the tough race over the Hog's Back to Guildford. John Bicourt was the first Bel home after having been pushed hard by ever-green Pat Newall making one of his all too infrequent performances. John Dear turned in another good performance, considering the company, to complete our scoring team, it being unfortunate that Gerry Williams arrived too late to be declared. Bill Kerr, still on the come-back trail, ran steadily through the field, no doubt under strict orders from his adviser - Charlie Walker !! - who finished just behind him. items.s: January 14th - MITCHAM 15¾ [?] MILES Report and result of the Mitcham 15¾ [?] miles road race, with John Bicourt first Belgrave in 44th, and R. Linstead's photograph of Chris Steer and Doug Brew (result printed on page 28 under 'Road Running (Cont'd)'). Once again good conditions prevailed when the large field set out on the first of three laps over a new course. John Bicourt, running for the first time over the distance, put in a very good run to lead our team home after having been 'caught in the act' of dropping out by Chris Steer and Doug Brew who were following behind. However, it was Chris who was forced to retire at 10 miles, leaving Doug to forge on alone to complete a very good run after a long lay-off. items.s: Postbag: Dear Mr. Editor, Letter from W.H. Hare correcting the names and details of the 1925 and 1926 club photographs in the December issue, and dating the club's first South of Thames Junior win to 1929. Postbag: Dear Mr. Editor, The original photo of that reproduced on page 35 of the December 'Belgravian' was taken on Easter Saturday, 10th April, 1925, previous to the start of the third contest for the Club's 20 mile Championship. The complete and corrected names should read:- Back row - J.N. THOMAS, R.E. WILLS, C.A. WATTAM, W.H. HARE, J. RATHBONE, J. MILES, E.L. REEVE, W.J. HAWKER, T. EATON. Front row - F. RICKARDS, E.A. WALL, R.W. RICKETTS, E.G. COOPER, R.D. McMULLEN. (A.P. Spendlove and J.K. Chalk were not in attendance). F. Rickards, holding the R.W. Ricketts Club Trophy, retained this, with E.G. Cooper second and E.A. Wall third. R.W. Ricketts (President) displays the R.W.A. 20 Mile National Championship Shield, won by the Club in 1924 for the first time, at Windsor. Bob was to retain this trophy for the Club, in a unique way, in the next race held at Derby on May 8th. Walking as a member of our 'B' team, he finished in front of the fourth scoring member of the Surrey Walking Club and thereby gave our 'A' team the vital one point by which our victory was won. The upper photo was, in fact, the start of the fourth Club 10 Mile C.C. Championship for the 'Macher Shield', held on 27th March 1926. Of the five unidentified runners, M. Hasler is on the inside of H.E. Footer, and C.J. Davis on the inside of J.G. Flatt. The runner in the background is probably L. Hartland, who finished fourth. Of the remaining two, one is O.L. Borrett. George Still, who finished third, was the veteran of the field and it seems difficult now to realise that 25 years or so previoulsy, at the turn of the century, he was in winning teams of the Southern Counties and National C.C. Championships when he ran as a member of the long defunct UNITY A.C. and later the HIGHGATE HARRIERS. The report of the South of Thames Junior, of November last, reads "It would be interesting to know....". The short answer would be the 9th February 1929, when the Club won the Championship for the first time, at Gatton Park, Merstham. Yours sincerely, W.H. HARE. W.H. Hare W.H. HARE J.N. Thomas J.N. items.s: Dear Mr.Editor, Letter from A.A. Harley recalling that Harry Hare, the first Belgrave president of the S.T.C.C.A., presented the club's first South of Thames Junior team awards in 1929 and earlier medals in 1928. Dear Mr.Editor, May I congratulate you on an excellent December issue of the Belgravian? And may the many future successes in store jostle and fight for inclusion in the pages to come! On page 40, in your description of the South of Thames Junior event you point out that our Bill Lucas as this years Association President, had felicity of handing five awards to Belgrave runners and ask rhetorically if any other President of the S.T.C.C.A. has had similar pleasure in the past. Yes, indeed! In 1929 Harry Hare, the first Belgrave President ever of the S.T.C.C.A., handed to his club mates the DEWAR Shield for winning the Championship (for the first time), and the six team winners medals to:- BILL MITCHELL (4), ARTHUR PENNY (7), ARTHUR ALLUM (12), BILL WEBB (16), PAUL KHLOPIN (23) and ALEC ROBERTSHAW (26). In addition Belgrave also won the COLMAN Cup as the first club to finish its complete team of twelve men, and great was the satisfaction when Harry called forward STANLEY DRAKE, our twelfth scoring man, to receive this trophy - also for the first time. Yours Sincerely, A.A.HARLEY P.S. Further research would also indicate that on November 7th 1928 at Epsom Downs, Harry Hare also had the pleasure (in advance of the above mentioned triumphs) of presenting winning medals to another Belgrave team in the Junior race, with two place medals in addition. The team was:- BILL MITCHELL (2), ARTHUR PENNY (3), ARTHUR ALLUM (4), BILL RICE (13). Actual winner of this event was LES COHEN , then running in Ashcombe colours and the writer was 97th! A.A.H. A.A. items.sum: Report of the New Year's Eve carnival night at Belgrave Hall with Tim Healy's Jazz Band and fancy dress winners.
items.s: SOCIAL - December 31st CARNIVAL NIGHT Report of the New Year's Eve carnival night at Belgrave Hall with Tim Healy's Jazz Band and fancy dress winners. SOCIAL December 31st CARNIVAL NIGHT New Year's Eve at Belgrave Hall saw one of our best ever social nights. We had a new group - Tim Healy's Jazz Band - lined up for the evening's entertainment and they proved to be so popular, joining in with the spirit of things and at one time even marching round the hall playing their instruments for all they were worth, that you can rest assured we will see them again. The fancy dress competition was disappointing, only a dozen or so making the effort. Those who did bother, though, had really gone to town.- Charlie Manning won the men's competition as an Egyptian mummy (Tutan Khamen/Tooting Common!) whilst his wife, Jean, took the ladies prize in a topical prisoners garb with the caption "It's in to be out". Bill and June Laws made it another family double by being voted the best "group" in some fabulous Elizabethan gear. Tim Healy was by now obviously feeling the heat and stripped to the waist, wearing a pith helmet, he led his band into the 'Hokey Cokey' with a very merry Gerry North dancing like a dervish in the centre and looking suspiciously as if he was trying to 'nobble' Bob Holt of Hercules (the County Champs were the next week-end). 'Auld Lang Syne' took about twenty minutes with each member of the band taking a solo, and the night finished gloriously on a patriotic note as all Belgravians joined Tim in a doubtful rendering of 'God Save The Queen'. Great stuff! "LAURISTON RUNNERS CLUB WIN NATIONAL"----well, it's a headline that's not possible but interesting all the same.
