items.sum: Walking section notes: an appeal for a walking reporter, tributes to Cyril Yescombe and Harry Evans, news of the club's walkers, Bob Barnes 10th in the Metropolitan Police Open 7, and (continued on page 34) Belgravians in the 1966 British top-ten walking lists.
items.s: WALKING Walking section notes: an appeal for a walking reporter, tributes to Cyril Yescombe and Harry Evans, news of the club's walkers, Bob Barnes 10th in the Metropolitan Police Open 7, and (continued on page 34) Belgravians in the 1966 British top-ten walking lists. It has become increasingly difficult of late to obtain any results, news or information relating to Walking matters. Your Editors are well used to prodding, persuading, cajoling, pleading and even begging for material from some contributors to your Gazette and what success we have, coupled with our own personal knowledge of track, field, cross-country and road-relays, enables a fairly thorough coverage to be made. Unfortunately it is not possible for us to attend walking fixtures as well, so if the bare result even is unobtainable then we can publish nothing. Such is the case for much that has happened since our last issue. For many years the walking section kept Belgrave's name to the forefront when their fellow-Belgravians were struggling thro' a lean spell. Now the wheel has turned half circle and, relatively, the roles are reversed---yet Belgrave's walkers are still amongst the most feared and respected of teams and are still enjoying some success. Those halcyon days of the late fifties and early sixties should not be forgotten. Members should be continually reminded of their rightful place in the Walking World--- i.e. the TOP. Space is also needed to record our current successes and to give encouragement to those promising walkers who are only too eager to get amongst the medals. Our General Honorary Secretary has said on many occasions that we should do our utmost to avoid becoming too sectionalised; that members should feel they are party to Club activities in all spheres; that we are first and foremost Belgravians all, that this is best fostered through our social functions and the medium of this Gazette. Your Editors are not happy with the coverage our walkers are getting and therefore appeal for someone to come forward and provide us with the news we require. He will not be obliged to write reports but, merely, every few weeks or so provide us with results and, if he prefers, only report verbally on the latest happenings in the Walking World. Articles, reminiscences and tit-bits of information are still welcome from any others but, most importanty we need that "Walking" reporter. Any offers? * * * * * The tragic loss of Cyril Yescombe is a blow to us all. It is men like Cyril that carry a club through it's lean years, and his sense of humour and loyalty to Belgrave will be sadly missed. His concern in the training of Police cadets played a large part in the latter years of his life and one felt sure that on Belgrave's behalf he had one eye open for possoble walking potential. With the loss of Cyril fresh in our minds, and only six days gone, we suffered another loss with the passing away of Harry Evans, our most revered Past-President. No words need be added to our coverage in earlier pages except perhaps, those few that make up that brief, but fitting, epilogue of Edward Nazen Parker: "Life's race well run, Life's work well done, Life's victory won, Now cameth rest". * * * * * Eric Hall, Ray Hall and Ray Middleton have all had bouts of sickness since Christmas but are now recovered and 'rarin' to go for the R.W.A. and Inter-Counties '10' on March 18th. Eric hopes to have a pre-race work-out in the "Ipswich" the previous week. Well settled down South again, he is now training regularly with Ray Hall. They manage to get to Belgrave Hall on some training nights, but the real regular there these days is Pat Duncan who is in attendance every Tuesday and Thursday. How about getting a real "Duncan" pack out those evenings? Bob Barnes is walking very well these days and could surprise in the National '10' With Gerry Cameron also walking into form the teams could well click at the right time. We do not see a great deal of Doug Fotheringham and Bert Stevenson these days. Both Inspectors, Police duties seem to have restricted their appearances. Dave King has faded into obscurity, temporarily we hope, but living as far distant as Hull must make it difficult for him. Unfortunately, no new members have yet appeared that can fill these gaps but if Messrs. Hall (E), Hall (R), Middleton, Barnes, Cameron, Duncan and Farley can "bring home the bacon" then our problems will look after themselves. * * * * * Bob Barnes was our only walker to show up in the Metropolitan Police Open'7' on January 14th. After a fast start by the 257 competitors Bob soon settled into 10th place and showing good style and determination held on to his niche to record a speedy 53:07---1:56 behind Empire Games Champion Ronnie Wallwork. Illness pushed our team right out of the medals. Walking (Cont'd from p.33) In the British "Top Ten" ranking lists for 1966 Belgravians failed to make the lists in the 2 miles track, 7 miles track, 10miles road and 20 Kms. road. When it came to the longer stuff we fared much better. The County results were generally disappointing. Bright spot was Ray Middleton's second place in the Surrey event. items.sum: Final table and reports of races 2-4 of the senior North Surrey League, which Belgrave retained by 174 points after trailing with one race to go.
items.s: NORTH SURREY LEAGUE Final table and reports of races 2-4 of the senior North Surrey League, which Belgrave retained by 174 points after trailing with one race to go. Belgrave retained their League Title by what at first appears to be a comfortable margin; but with one race to go they were placed only 3rd! Last year we went into the last fixture with a lead of 111 pts and increased this to 380 pts. This year we changed a 101 pts deficit into a winning 174 pts margin, thanks to a repeat of last year's excellent turn-out. Once again, well over twenty different runners scored for us in the four matches and our depth should carry us through to a succession of titles in the coming years. None of our top runners was able to take part in all four fixtures so the individual award went to Fred Stebbings of Croydon. The first race held at Wimbledon was reported in our last issue. The remaining three fixtures went as follows:- RACE NO. 2 - WALTON (ESHER), DECEMBER 10th. Belgrave went into the second match of the series no less than 200 points down on Hercules and 100 odd on Mitcham and Surrey. This had been caused by the first race clashing with the Bristol/Weston Relay where we had sent our strongest eight. Now the battle was on to put things right - but where had all our supporting runners gone? Whilst Gerry North, Williams, Thresher, Fairclough and Bicourt produced great efforts to spearhead our team, the burden of support fell upon runners who would not normally have filled such a role. The missing men (and their were nine or ten who could have occupied the space between 12th and 37th) ensured that Surrey A.C. and Mitcham A.C. remained ahead of us in the overall table. The Course was at it's muddiest best and, after a comfortable first lap, Gerry North moved well away over the last circuit. Feature of the race was the running of that other Gerry - Gerry Williams. Revelling in the conditions he finished ahead of those seasoned campaigners Thresher and Fairclough; there will be many dust-ups (or mud-ups!) to come. RACE NO. 3 - MITCHAM (MORDEN PARK), DECEMBER 31st. The fight-back continued over the fast grassland course of Morden Park but just to make it more difficult for us, seven of our scoring ten at Walton did not appear, but were fortunately replaced by another seven who found themselves in a similar boat - 7 in 25 and then a long wait to close in. Perhaps the shift system has arrived to stay! Thresher tuned himself nicely for the county event the following week and O'Hara showed his liking for a fast 5 miles course. Bill Dance produced an excellent run, but broke down with achilles trouble next day so will have his work cut out to regain this form in time for the "Southern". Our final score was sufficient to push Hercules further behind us but, with one match to come, Surrey and Mitcham are 105pts and 2pts respectively ahead of us. The final race is a week before the "National" so many runners will probably miss out. The League can be won though if all those runners on the fringe of the National team turn out at Lloyd Park. FINAL RACE - CROYDON H.(LLOYD PARK), FEBRUARY 25th With seven of our National '9' turning out, and no less than a further 20 providing support, Belgrave swept to a match win and an overall league win in devastating fashion. Any hopes Surrey AC had of clinging to their 100 pts lead were soon dashed as the claret and gold phalanx swept to the front providing, at one stage, ten in twenty. It was great to see such team spirit - "National" next week or not, we were going to retain our title and to indicate our confidence our captain did not even bring the trophy along! Gerry North was out for nothing more than a training run but, just to shake up the leading group during the race he put in a half-mile spurt to open up a lead of 100 yards and then eased up to await training companion Bob Holt of Hercules, whereupon they crossed the line together. items.label: March 1967
items.sum: 'Countryman' column on the 1967 National (Belgrave 4th again), New Zealand runners in the National, Mel Thorpe leaving for Coventry Godiva, Charlie Dabbs, Trevor Hart's transformation, Gerry North's stolen car, horse-riders at Wimbledon, World Sports cuttings by Neil Allen, and a predicted National Road Relay team.
items.s: A COUNTRYMAN'S JOTTINGS.............. 'Countryman' column on the 1967 National (Belgrave 4th again), New Zealand runners in the National, Mel Thorpe leaving for Coventry Godiva, Charlie Dabbs, Trevor Hart's transformation, Gerry North's stolen car, horse-riders at Wimbledon, World Sports cuttings by Neil Allen, and a predicted National Road Relay team. What a National! What a course! What a pace! I cannot recall the premier event of the season ever being run at such a pace. At times, the leading runners appeared to be almost sprinting. It was certainly a track man's course and it was a pity that this venue should have coincided with Gerry North's best year since 1962. After his great win in the "Southern", one is tempted to say "If only the National had been at Parliament Hill" but I somehow feel that March 4th was not Gerry's day, whatever the course. As for the team, well, they did at least improve marginally on last year's performance. 1966........4th (447 points).............6 in 134 1967........4th (443 points).............6 in 114 Once again, Portsmouth AC, the team that has so often stood between us and major honours, were deserved Champions. By a remarkable coincidence they finished 5 in 37, exactly as in 1966, but this time their sixth man (Meadows) was 102nd against the previous year's 173rd. Even with 9 to score Pompey had the edge on us 765/838. Shock pressure came from Longwood and Reading. The potential of these teams was realised but no-one expected the former to pip us by 24 points nor the latter to force us to a decision on last scoring man. Belgravians you have been warned!---Longwood could take over from Pompey for, without the redoubtable Ibbottson, they still finished 9 in 174. * * * * * As last year, certain sections of the Press spoke in terms of a New Zealand team victory at Norwich whereas, of course, they 'lost' 62/34 to the England team. Whilst I am all for allowing visitors to compete in our domestic racing programme I do have reservations when it comes to the "National". This is a championship where a great deal is at stake and I forecast a furore of no small magnitude when the team title is decided by a New Zealander's position---particularly if it is their tenth man! When our Honours Badge qualifications were laid down no account was taken for the "intrusion" of ten foreign internationals. Tony Fairclough's 42nd place was two positions outside an Honours Badge yet only 21 places away from inclusion in the England team. Morally, he is intitled to that badge. * * * * * I suppose it was inevitable. To hope to hang on to Mel Thorpe indefinately when he now lives as distant as Coventry was too good to be true. Perhaps it might have been different if it were not such a struggle to make the team these days. However, Mel has resigned his first-claim membership (retaining second-claim status) and will now probably run against us in the National Road Relay wearing the colours of COVENTRY GODIVA HARRIERS. Mel writes "I thank all those at Belgrave for the happiest four years of my life" It was a pleasure to have you Mel! * * * * * Charlie Dabbs, who seems to have been running all my life yet, remarkably, is still only 29 years old has been plagued with injury again this winter. The best medicament for Charlie's injuries, though, is the smell of the "5¾ [?]". As our bi-annual road race draws nigh his injuries are overcome, his resolution returns and Charles S.Dabbs is all set for another "come-back" Perhaps it's just Spring! * * * * * It must have been nearly ten years ago that I saw Trevor Hart storm down the straight at Tooting Bec track to win the Belgrave Youths' 100 yards Championship - in case you are staggered by the man's versatility, it was a lean year for sprinters! For several years after, he was just 'around', and my memory of him then was the runner who enquired of everyone what it was they would be doing that training session and then tagging along with the slowest. Then Trevor grew up - overnight he became a masochist. He could be seen at the Duke of York's track revelling in the pain of repetition running and hanging on to our fast boys for grim death. And after a few months the break came; and then the jutting jaw of Hart was a symbol to be feared by those scrubbers who had had the audacity to beat him in earlier times. Why the sudden transformation? Had Trevor discovered "the truth about Wilson"? Was it a secret training schedule? A special diet? Or ........... a woman? Well, Trevor gets married on September 30th ....... look out for the next instalment of "THE HART SAGA"!! .................. Gerry North's impressive first win of the Southern Cross Country Championship proved to be a very expensive outing. After annihilating his rivals to the tune of a minute, his high spirits fell when he discovered his Great Britain track suit top had been stolen, sank further when he remembered he had left his car keys in the pocket, and were finally devastated when he found his car had been stolen with £200 worth of athletics gear. What a price to pay! Only the car has so far been recovered so if anyone discovers running shoes, quality track suits, vests, etc. being sold cheaply they should advise Gerry, who may be in a position to identify such goods. * * * * * Belgrave were hosts this year to the South of Thames Senior Championship and as such were responsible for choosing and marking a course. In an effort to make a partial return to the tougher courses of old we put in a large 5 miles lap to supplement our usual 2½ miles circuit. The larger lap took in the horse-ride along the back of the cemetery and the one that climbs from the farm to the golf course. On the former stretch our equestrian friends showed open hostility towards the use of the horse-rides for races and persistantly pulled up flags and threw them into the bushes. On a previous occasion a woman rider endeavoured to block the watersplash bridge claiming it was "for horses only"! One rider asked if the South of Thames field would slow down if requested! Ours are not the only races to be held on the common and we may be paying the penalty of indiscretions by others; either way, feuding of this sort does no-one any good and it might be wise for our course planners to try and keep horse-ride running down to a minimum, if not completely avoided. * * * * * "When it comes to cross-country runners of the past and present I would just as soon pick, perhaps surprisingly, on one Charlie Walker of Belgrave Harriers, who seems to have been running since the mid-1940s without ever looking much older as the years go by. This season, big-chested and legs driving, he came shooting up the slopes of Parliament Hill Fields and I shouted, as I have done so many times before, "Go on Charlie." We have never met, but to do so might, I sometimes think, destroy the aura of immortality he has for me. It is one of the joys of cross-country running that we followers can all look out for our favourite Charlie Walkers in the struggling pack far behind the men who will run for their country at Barry. For me there is Ferdie Gilson of South London Harriers, George Knight of Essex Beagles ..." "... way traffic of our top men over there. But our domestic races have their own attraction for the regular follower as I have been for more than 15 years. Les Cohen, in his gum-boots, cheerfully shouting at everyone in sight, is the official I associate most quickly with the very worst weather---and readers from many other countries will have just no idea of how bad the rains, snow and ice can sometimes become in Britain for the major races." "Mike Hryciw, a 9.5sec man for 100yd, provides the sort of problem of pronunciation which phlegmatic White City announcer Bill Lucas must be hoping will not arise when the Americans meet Britain next August, but if a certain 13.8sec high hurdler makes the team and beats his British opponents, there will be an obvious accolade. His name? Marcellous (with a "c" not a "y") Reed." As can be seen from the above cuttings Belgravians were well represented in the March issue of "World Sports". On reading that Neil Allen had shouted to Charlie Walker "Go on Charlie" many times I couldn't help wondering how often our Chas. has shouted back his famous catch phrase "What d'ye think, Neil?" As for that "aura of immortality" well, inviting as it is to crack jokes about it, I think Neil Allen's words were very well chosen and few in the know would dispute his choice of Charlie Walker - a runner whose enthusiasm is as great now as it was in the days when he led them all home. * * * * * Who will win the National Road Relay on April 1st? Well, I believe it will be Belgrave if the following team is turned out;- LONG STAGES: Gerry North, Fairclough, Thresher, Barrow, Hart, Kerr,. SHORT STAGES: Geoff North, O'Hara, Williams, Bicourt, Dance, Major,. With Black, Dabbs, Steer, Buxton, Dear and a host of others itching to get in, the lads should really be on their Mettle. A coach is being run to Leicester. Why not come along and see an exciting contest? ... items.label: March 1967
items.sum: Ernie Duffett recalls Belgrave's 1948 National cross-country team win at Graves Park, Sheffield, where Vic Blowfield was second to Sydney Wooderson, with E.D. Lacey's photograph of Tom Carter.
items.s: "I Was There" NO.2 Ernie Duffett recalls Belgrave's 1948 National cross-country team win at Graves Park, Sheffield, where Vic Blowfield was second to Sydney Wooderson, with E.D. Lacey's photograph of Tom Carter. NO.2 - by Ernie Duffett. When your Editors asked me to write the second of these mementous occasions, my mind fairly 'boggled' at the thought. After serving for 25 years as Running Hon. Sec. of the 'Bels' I was present at so many of our most famous victories. After consideration I selected our 'National' win at Sheffield in March, 1948, when we regained the title from the holders, Sutton Harriers. We knew we had more strength in depth than our rivals, and so it proved after a most exciting race both for the individual and team prizes. It was a fine afternoon in Graves Park and many thousands of people who came to see some great racing, paid over £500 for admission. Sydney Wooderson, the one-time holder of the 880 yards and 1 mile world records, was a firm favourite, but before he eventually won his first 'National' title over the country, he had to contend with one of the severest races of his career. His challenger was none other than our own Vic Blowfield who was always up with the leaders, and when they came round for the last of the three large laps, Blowfield and Wooderson were together with Shorrocks of Hailesowen some 25 yards behind in 3rd place. With barely half a mile to go, Blowfield went away from his rival and Wooderson was looking very tired, and Vic opened a lead of about 25 yards with only 400 yards of the undulating course to be covered. Then the large crowd broke onto the course in their excitement, and Blowfield literally had to fight his way through them. In the 'rugger' scrum Wooderson came again and managed to pass Vic and being the faster finisher he came home just four seconds in front of Blowfield. If the course could have been kept clear it is uncertain whether our man would have been the winner, as Wooderson naturally had the greater speed on the flat. Then came the fight for the team title, and with Len Herbert running one of his finest races to finish in 12th team position, and well backed up by Ted Stimpson in 15th place, we had three men home to Sutton's two. Then they had four home to our three, but Frank Abberton scored 27th to make it four each. But Sutton still had five in before our 5th man (Tom Carter 41st) and then praise be, Tommy Clinton came along in 57th place to complete our scoring six, while Sutton's 6th man finished 65th! We thus won the title with a total of 154 points to Sutton's 174, and Blackheath Harriers were 3rd with 183 points. Our other men to finish, with nine to compete and six to score, were Les Stokell 64th, Albert Frost 95th, and finally Dick Tobin 132nd. It is interesting to note that Denis Brickwood finished in 80th place, and was then running for Mitcham A.C., and it is perhaps sad to reflect that of our team members, only Tom Carter and Ted Stimpson, are still active within the Club in an official capacity. Tom Carter, who was our fifth scoring man. (photo: E.D. Lacey) Tom Carter, who was our fifth scoring man. items.label: March 1967
items.h: International Cross Country Race HANNUT, BELGIUM
items.sum: Account of Belgrave's trip to the international cross-country meeting at Hannut, Belgium, where the club won the club team race and Gerry North was third behind McCafferty and Roelants.
items.s: International Cross Country Race HANNUT, BELGIUM Account of Belgrave's trip to the international cross-country meeting at Hannut, Belgium, where the club won the club team race and Gerry North was third behind McCafferty and Roelants. February 5th 1967 We were delighted to receive an invitation to compete in the club team race associated with the international event at Hannut for this is one of the plum Continental races and attracts representation from Belgium, France, Germany and Holland in addition to England and Scotland. This was our first foreign cross-country race since pre-war days and the boys rose to the occasion to make sure that thirty years would not go by before the next invitation arrives. In the face of strong opposition and scoring five aside, we won by six points to take the beautiful trophy presented by the Belgian newspaper Le Soir. The weekend began with five runners meeting at Wimbledon and four runners and the team manager assembling at London Bridge to converge by road on Dover for a night sea crossing to Ostend. The two cars disembarked at 5.30 am. on Saturday morning and after a quick run on the motorway we arrived in Brussels just as the restaurants were opening and were able to obtain a first class breakfast to set us up for a sight seeing tour of the Belgian capital. The centre of attraction was a shoe shop where most of the team equipped themselves with a continental version of the Chelsea boot in first class (?) suede which no doubt will be proudly displayed en masse at the next Club Social. At midday we set off again for the last fifty miles drive to Hannut which was reached at about 1pm and after reporting to the headquarters (a cafe in the centre of the town) of the Hannut Football Club, who are the organisers of this cross country event, we were taken for a steak lunch with wine and all the trimmings. Thoroughly satisfied with our reception we then strolled off to look at the course for the following day's race before again assembling to be allocated our "digs" for the weekend. Everyone was most comfortably housed with local residents and there is no doubt that we received very hospitable treatment. Saturday evening was spent quietly over a drink or two at the cafe of Roger Gustin the organising secretary and again the kindness and hospitality of the local people was much in evidence, for most of the refreshments consumed, whether coffee or otherwise, were "on the house". As we had had only limited sleep the previous night we were all ready for bed and an early retirement was the order of the day. A briefing for team managers was called for at 10.30 on Sunday morning for team declarations and distribution of numbers. This was followed by a further inspection and a gentle run over the course by all but the team manager who preferred to view rather than sample. The general consensus of opinion was that the race would be fast for although there was a generous helping of plough the weather had been dry and this would soon bed down to a firm surface. By midday the town of Hannut was a mass of people attracted to the afternoons programme of racing which comprised seven races in all for various ages and even for the local tennis players, culminating in the international event at 4.15pm. The number of spectators was estimated at 10,000, swelled no doubt by the fact that this was the 25th promotion and was being honoured by the presence of His Majesty King Baudouin, obviously a popular man with his people. Continental races are generally on short lap courses and this was no exception for the full distance of the big race, which was a little under six miles, was made up of two short laps and six large laps so the spectators who were mainly assembled in the football stadium, where the start and finish were sited, were able to enjoy the racing to the full. The number of starters in 'our' race was about sixty, made up of international teams from the leading cross-country nations of Europe plus club teams from France, Holland, Germany and Belgium in addition to ourselves. The international race scored three a side and the club race five a side. Marcel Vandewattyne, one of Belgium's best ever athletes was the starter and in the field was Gaston Roelants, Belgium's current top runner and present Olympic 3000 metres Steeplechase Champion who was the favourite and himself anxious to win to establish a record of four wins in a row and five wins in all to break the existing record which he held jointly with Vandewattyne. It is interesting to record at this point that the latter was in the first five in this race for every year between 1948 and 1963, an extremely good run of performances. As expected the pace in the early stages of the race was very fast, dictated by Roelants and Scotland's Ian McCafferty who only the previous evening had taken from Roelants his indoor 2 miles European record with a great run at Cosford. Our own boys were not too prominent early on but it was interesting to see John Bicourt just ahead of Gerry North after the first half mile when they were ninth and tenth respectively. Gerry battled on gallantly throughout the whole race and although he never got to grips with the two leaders he slowly worked his way past Jim Alder, Bruce Tulloh, Tim Johnston, Lachie Stewart and the strong foreign opposition to come home a comfortable third which achieved for him the honour of being presented to King Baudouin who showed considerable interest in our own captain. At the half-way stage McCafferty raised a cheer from the British supporters by taking a thirty yard lead over Roelants, who at this stage appeared completely shattered, but two laps later a super human effort took him again to the front and he stayed ahead to run in a popular winner with the crowd by a five second margin. At two miles our runners had established themselves in or about the positions they were to finally occupy and little or no change took place for the remainder of the race. The scoring members other than Gerry who was well ahead were all in the twenties and although this may not appear high in so small a field it should be remembered that the majority of the first twenty-five are established internationals. It was difficult to diagnose the progress of the race from the team scoring angle in view of the wide diversity of vests but it was pleasing to see the claret and gold standing out well and the Belgian crowd obviously appreciated the forward running of our team. They seemed to be very discerning in the arts of cross-country running. Although we thought that five in twenty-eight was good enough we had to wait for some time before the final result was announced and we were proved to be the victors. In the international race Belgium, led by Roelants were at their best and were easy winners over Scotland and England. After the race all the runners assembled at the Town Hall to collect their prizes - everyone in the race gets one. The standard of prizes was very high and they were awarded by choice according to the order of finishing. All our runners were extremely pleased. On the Sunday evening a banquet with plentiful food and drink was held with the usual speeches and our members came into contact with the local "talent" for the first time. It seemed that most were well satisfied - it is thought that Thresher and Williams will almost certainly wish to return - we all hope the telephone numbers they collected are not changed by 1968. After the banquet some of the ladies were persuaded to join our party at the local discotheque where the frivolities were continued until 3am. on Monday morning. A quiet but by no means dispirited team assembled at 8am after only a few hours sleep for the drive back to Ostend for the boat home. Wimbledon was reached late on Monday afternoon with sufficient energy for most to partake of a training session. On the whole a most satisfactory and successful weekend. Belgrave's name is now established in Belgium and we have made many good friends and created much good will. It is hoped we can return in 1968 but there is a possibility that this race may be discontinued. Perhaps we will get an invitation from another town. If we win the National we are assured of other visits to Europe. items.sum: Short notes on Gerry North 12th in the San Sebastian 10,000 metres cross-country and a visit by former member Keith Angus.
items.s: Short notes on Gerry North 12th in the San Sebastian 10,000 metres cross-country and a visit by former member Keith Angus. Gerry North fell heavily during the San Sebastian 10,000 metres X-cty event last January. The heat overcame Maurice Herriott (24th) but Gerry, also uncomfortably hot, recovered well to finish 12th---1½ minutes down on winner Mamo Wolde of Ethiopia. A crowd of 20,000 were in attendance! * * * * * Keith Angus, who ran for us a few years back, visited Lauriston Cottage on Sunday, Feb.19th with Sheffield team-mate Newbie. They were both members of Sheffield University's second placed team in the Imperial College Relay, held the previous day. Keith is showing his best ever form and should do well in the "National". items.sum: Report on the season's three minor inter-club cross-country matches, at Ruislip (Hillingdon), Richmond Park (Polytechnic) and Cranford (TVH), all lost by Belgrave.
items.s: MINOR FIXTURES. Report on the season's three minor inter-club cross-country matches, at Ruislip (Hillingdon), Richmond Park (Polytechnic) and Cranford (TVH), all lost by Belgrave. With so many "major" fixtures in the Winter Calendar these days, and with the North Surrey League occupying a large part of the remaining space, the inter-club mob match is fast fading from its prominence of yesteryear. Apart from SLH, Blackheath and Ranelagh, who have a long tradition of mob match "feuds" and turn out every available able-bodied man, most clubs now use these races as training or social runs. Consequently the home team is always much the stronger. With only three such fixtures in our Winter list many Belgravians chose these occasions to train in the morning and have a "holiday" in the afternoon. Some observers may question whether these races are worth while, but it should be remembered that we have a large number of runners who never make the major races and it is for their sakes that these meetings are arranged. Our first such match was at Hillingdon's HQ, Ruislip on Dec.17th, and although we had five of the first six home we were beaten into third place by the home club and Shaftesbury in a close result, scoring 8 a side. The scores were 105/108/112 respectively. Gerry North was the individual winner by almost 2 minutes from John Thresher. On February 4th, over Polytechnic's course in Richmond Park, a two-sided match was held scoring 12 a side. Being almost on home ground we would normaly have had a strong turn-out, but this was also the day of our Club visit to Belgium and our best nine runners were absent; nevertheless twenty Belgravians toed the starting line. Howard Satchell set off as though deputising for Gerry North but paid dearly for the experience and it was left to Chris Steer and John Dear to lead our men home in 3rd and 6th places respectively. Once again the home team ran out winners - 113/187. The last minor fixture was against TVH at Cranford on February 18th where the Valley scored a 137½/226½ victory. Thirteen Belgravians made the journey but of the first-liners only Bicourt (4th) and Major (6th) and Hart (26th) appeared - the latter obviusly having an "easy", rounding up our supporting runners. items.sum: Reminder of Belgrave's unwritten 15th rule that, unless injured, no Belgravian retires from a race.
items.s: Reminder of Belgrave's unwritten 15th rule that, unless injured, no Belgravian retires from a race. Now the Cross-Country season is over this an opportune moment to remind our runners, of all age groups, of Belgrave's unwritten 15th rule: "Unless injured, no Belgravian shall ever retire from a race, once under starter's orders". There should be no need to elaborate on a philosophy that has been in-bred in Belgravian teams for eighty years.

items.label: March 1967
items.h: BELS MISS THEIR CHANCE 4th in NATIONAL
items.sum: Report and results of the 1967 National cross-country championship at Costessey, Norwich, where Gerry North collapsed after fading to 48th and Belgrave were fourth on a tie-break with Reading, with a backpiece photo montage by Ron Linstead and Eddie Lacey.
items.s: BELS MISS THEIR CHANCE 4th in NATIONAL Report and results of the 1967 National cross-country championship at Costessey, Norwich, where Gerry North collapsed after fading to 48th and Belgrave were fourth on a tie-break with Reading, with a backpiece photo montage by Ron Linstead and Eddie Lacey. COSTESSEY, NORWICH - March 4th This could have been "our year". A fast, dry flat course, a team running into top form and our main rivals seemingly having difficulty to reproduce their strength of last year. But it was not to be. Despite truly excellent packing of 9 in 140 (in a field of 831 ) we barely managed to retain our 4th position of last year. The Tragedy of the race, through Belgrave eyes was the misfortune of Gerry North. The Southern Champion, currently showing his lust form for years, was with the leaders after a mile but then faded. Obviously not feeling his usual self, he fought on with tremendous determination and at 7 miles was still 15th, but with legs wobbling and a strange oblivion taking over only his sixth sense kept him tottering on to the finish as runner after runner swept past. John Thresher caught him 100 yards from the finish and sacrificing 2 or 3 places ushered Gerry to the line where our Captain collapsed for the first time in a long and illustrious career. Although it was only in the last half mile that we slipped from 3rd to 4th, no-one would have blamed Gerry if he had dropped out. It is indicative of the feeling in the team that no one for some time afterwards was concerned with the team result. It was 20 minutes before Gerry was on his feet again and one wonders whether he was in the early stages of illness of whether the considerable shock he suffered after the "Southern" had not cleared from his nervous system. This is the fist time that Gerry has finished the "National" to find himself excluded from the International team. Our team got a good start on the inside of the field when the mass of multi-coloured vests streaked away at exactly 2.30 p.m., but this was offset after 500 yards when a sharp right hand turn meant they were reduced to a walk as they "queued up" to go round the corner! At the mile post we had 3 in 70, with the remainder outside 120 and Bill Kerr trailing around the 200 mark. The positions after one lap are not usually far off the final score and at this point we had North 8, Thresher 35, Fairclough 58, Hart 97, Williams 119, Bicourt 130, Dance 150, O'Hara 154 and Kerr 160. All except North, Thresher, and Williams were making ground and it looked as though only Portsmouth were out of reach, although we had more than a solitary eye cocked at Longwood H. who had too many vests in the first 100 for our comfort. Fairclough showed again that the second circuit is always his best by gaining 15 places. Bicourt tried to follow suit but after an early gain of 8 positions lost some ground. Meanwhile Hart ploughed on in his steady, reliable way while O'Hara and Kerr mopped up the rear guard. We had now consolidated to 9 in 149 and with one lap to go we had North 12, Thresher 34, Fairclough 43, Hart 88, Williams 122, Bicourt 132, Kerr 136, O'Hara 137 and Dance 149. The final circuit was the crucial one. As Gerry suffered, John Thresher was stricken with the most ghastly blisters on both feet and battled his way to the finish with blood soaked shoes. Fortunately incidents like these are exceptions, and there was obviously nothing wrong with the rest of the team as they stormed through to the finish picking up 67 places amongst them, but it was all too late and none knew, of course, what had happened to our two leading men. Bouquets go to Tony Fairclough who takes the "H. Parker Memorial Bowl" for the first Belgravian to finish, to Laurie O'Hara who came staight from night-work to make the long trip and indeed, to the whole team who, with Geoff North's inclusion must be on the verge of reaping major honours. * John was really 49th. STOP PRESS! Gerry North shook off the effects of his all-out run in the "National" by turning out against the New Zealanders again just 7 days later at Chigwell Row. And he nearly won! Only man to beat him was Kiwi Eddie Gray---by one second! Gray finished sixth in the National the previous week. Gerry must now feel hopeful that the bad luck that hit him immediately after the "Southern" at Parliament Hill, finished it's run at Norwich. RESULT: 1. E. Gray(N.Z)29:11, 2. Gerry North 29:12, 3. T. items.s: BELGRAVE WIN SOUTHAMPTON/BOURNEMOUTH RELAY. Report and result of the Southampton/Bournemouth road relay, won by Belgrave's A team with lap records for Trevor Hart and Gerry North, the B team sixth. Running in atrocious conditions, of driving rain and sleet, our 'A' team ran out good winners in a time only 48 secs outside their own course record. Our 'B' team also did magnificently to finish sixth. After being tripped up in the early stages, Tony Fairclough finished sixth on the first stage, 28 secs down on Heaver of Blackheath. Trevor Hart knocked 17 secs off Pettit's lap record for the next stage to move us up to 2nd and a back-in-form Gerry North followed suit by lopping 24 secs off Ellis's record to put us way out in front. Kerr had no difficulty in holding the lead with a very good time, but the sensation on this stage was the running of Chris Steer who absolutely hammered the opposition to move our 'B' team from 16th to 8th with a time only one second slower than Bill's. Laurie O'Hara had a shock on the penultimate leg when his minute lead was wiped out by new International Bob Holt who sped tp a new lap record, 13 seconds better than Gerry's existing mark. Gerry Williams had no difficulty in restoring our position and ran in a comfortable winner. John Bicourt produced a fine stint for the 'B' team to bring them home sixth and was helped in his effort by his determination to beat the time of his 'A' team counterpart----that's the stuff! items.label: June 1967
items.sum: Editorial calling for all-weather track surfaces in London, especially at Tooting Bec, and urging Belgrave to challenge for summer trophy meetings, praising the boys' section.
items.s: EDITORIAL Editorial calling for all-weather track surfaces in London, especially at Tooting Bec, and urging Belgrave to challenge for summer trophy meetings, praising the boys' section. Already this season torrential rain has caused many of our tracks to post those familiar notices "track closed", "dressing rooms only". When the tracks are back in use again, three or four groundsmen will spend considerable time preparing for the next meeting, rolling, sweeping, marking and then, to protect their handiwork, post that even more familiar notice "outside lanes only". Betwe n times some of these tracks (Tooting Bec in particular) get such a pounding that on occasions the Common horseride is smooth by comparison. If ever a country needed all-weather track surfaces, then this country is it. The National Playing Fields Association is alive to the desirability of such surfaces for play areas in general, but many local authorities appear to be dragging their feet. The capital cost is, of course, higher than the traditional cinder track but maintenance is negligible by present standards, markings are permanent and drainage is immediate, Furthermore, athletes can train in all weathers and only need road shoes for doing so — though needle spikes are advisable for sprints during competition. The En-Tout-Cas "K" surface (a resin-bound rubber chip on a hessian mat over an asphalte sub-base) has been laid down at Queens University, Belfast (1966) and at Leicester (1967). Freedom from maintenance was the prime mover in both cases and, whilst there is difficulty at present in finding a solution for the normally long spiked javelin throwers, each track has proved to be very successfull. The "K" surface is also being laid at the twin sports cities in Tripoli and Benghazi, Libya, which will accommodate the 1969 Pan-Arab Games, and in Montreal the 1967 Pan-American Games will be staged on the fabulous 3M "Tartan" surface - a ½" thick synthetic polymer sheet costing £12 a square yard! The first resilient all-weather track was laid in the U.S.A. in 1958 — 9 years ago. Within a year or two there were dozens, yet London is still awaiting its first. Tooting Bec track is probably the most heavily used track in the country. Many improvements have been made there and it was one of the first to install floodlighting. The G.L.C. would render an even greater service to the athletes in the South London area if it were to lay an all-weather surface at this popular venue, and at the same time ease it's own labour problems. ***** ***** ***** With the summer season only shortly begun there have already been some tremendous individual performances by Belgrave athletes although we have still failed, so far, to click as an all-round track and field team. Four Club records have been written into the books with others being threatened at almost every meeting we attend. We have yet to be beaten in an ordinary club match this year so LET'S HAVE A GO AT THOSE TROPHY MEETS. Amongst our younger members the scene is fantastic. There are literally dozens of Boys between the ages of 8 and 15 years old at Battersea Park on Sunday mornings (similarly at Norbiton) training in all aspects of our sport. All standards are being catered for but some of the performances put up by these lads are truly amazing - after all, how many of our Seniors can Long Jump over 17'0", toss a Javelin out to 120'0" or more, or knock up 2:12 for a"half"? items.s: HON SEC'S NOTES Hon. Secretary's notes: Les Cohen recommended for the AAA Award of Honour, Alf Harley elected Southern Counties AAA Deputy-Chairman, corrections to the 1921 photograph names, AGM date, fixture changes, the boys' section, and a letter from Bill Dodkin. All Belgravians will be delighted to know that the AAA General Committee has unanimously recommended that Les Cohen should be awarded the AAA Award of Honour for his tremendous services to Athletics. This recommendation will require the endorsement of the Anual General Meeting in October when it is certain that everyone connected with the sport will take the opportunity of showing their appreciation of the work Les has done over so many years. * * * * * Our Hon. Secretary, Alf Harley, has been elected Deputy-Chairman of the Southern Counties AAA. * * * * * In our last issue we printed a photograph taken outside "The Swan" in 1921 and Albert Macher (who himself appears in the photograph) has been able to fill in some of the blanks among the names as follows; 38.Mr Gray Snr. (J.F.Gray's father); 32.Frazer; 26.Wyatt; 29.Barrell. He confirms that 23 is H.E.Nice and not C.P.Sexton as printed. * * * * * Our Annual General Meeting will take place on Wednesday, September 20th at our Wimbledon Headquarters, and diaries should be noted accordingly. * * * * * An alteration should be made to the current Summer fixture list. The AAA Marathon Championship will take place on Saturday, August 19th (and not 26th as shown) from Baddesley Colliery, near Nuneaton. Also that the Hastings - Brighton walk will be on August 12th and not as shown. * * * * * One of the heart-gladdening sights at our track meetings at Battersea Park is the number of enthusiastic Boy members, whose keenness is a joy to behold. They tackle all sorts of events arranged for them with such evident pleasure and enthusiasm that Reg Hopkins, Tom Carter, Dave Ansell and others must surely feel well compensated for the terrific volume of work involved in looking after the interests of our young members. * * * * * A letter of good wishes to the present generation of athletes, and to those who may remember him has been received from W.G.("Bill") Dodkin who ran and walked with us in the early 1920's, after three years in the army in the first World War. LERWILL............(Queens Park H) HONORARY MEMBER Victor F. RANGER of CHINGFORD, E.4. An especial welcome is accorded to Peter Whewell, member of the South African cross-country team. Although he now hails from JOHANNESBURG he was in fact born in Cheshire and did not leave these shores until the age of 12 years. That was nearly 15 years ago, and as Peter had every intention of re-visiting the land of his birth he used the South Africa cross-country team as the vehicle! Not an easy way, but a satisfying one. The name of BELGRAVE HARRIERS was not new to him either, for in Johannesburg he shared a flat with former member Mike CONINGHAM (resident at Lauriston Cottage for some time) who also made the Springbok's team.. After the International in March Peter stayed on. An accountant, he took a job with a Auditing firm which has kept him too busy to continue with his normal training. Nevertheless he plans to set personal bests for all his track distances this summer and has already put the six miles behind him with an excellent 28:35 at Walton. The other times awaiting betterment are 1 mile 4:5.0, 2 miles 9:6.0, 3,000 metres 8:27.0, 3 miles 13:59.0 (at an altitude of 6,000 ft). At the beginning of August he commences a two month tour of the Continent and Scandinavia and then, on his return, will weigh up the advantages and disadvantages of prolonging his stay. Whatever his decision, we wish him a happy stay and hope he will make many friends here. Enrique Barragan Enrique BARRAGAN Anthony C. Bianchi Anthony C. BIANCHI Donald R. Bonser Donald R. items.s: From 'The BELGRAVIAN' 25 YEARS AGO..... ....and 40 YEARS AGO Extracts from the Belgravian of May 1942 (on wartime members serving in the Forces) and June 1927 (T.W. Green and A.L. Fletcher first and second in the Road Walking "Junior" Championship at Sheffield). From 'The BELGRAVIAN' 25 YEARS AGO..... MAY 1942---" Each month sees a wider distribution of our members over the Earth's surface---each month lengthens the distances between us---each month makes THE BELGRAVIAN more and more of a necessity. Our Gazette is a reminder of happy times spent together in sporting endeavour and a reminder that the prized friendships we have built against a background of amateur sport and happy associations, still exist; and will continue to exist even when the War is recalled as something rather unpleasant which came our way in the distant past. The great majority of Club members are now serving in the Forces and look forward to the arrival of THE BELGRAVIAN giving news of friends and of the athletic events which continue to be held----We re-live the incidents of past years, we wonder how this one is faring and where the other lays his head in these days of War. ....and 40 YEARS AGO JUNE 1927---"If the eagerly anticipated Road Walking "Junior" Championship at Sheffield failed to provide the expected success to the Club in the team event, ample consolation was forthcoming for any disappointment by the really great performances of T.W. Green (Olympic Gold-medallist 5 years later) and A.L. Fletcher who finished first and second respectively in the actual race after as good and exciting a race as has been witnessed over 10 miles. With a field of over 200 there was naturally some bunching at the start but at a mile Green was ahead with Fletcher behind a pack in close attendance. Shortly after, the two drew out clear ahead and at 4½ miles Green had a nominal lead of some 2 yards---they were having a battle royal and knowing the speed at Fletcher's command we were considering that he would be certain to win when the time came for the final effort, but Green was a sturdy finisher and resisting all challengers held on to win a very fine race by some 6 yards----. We started 17 and all finished. T.W. Green T.W. Green T.W. Green Green A.L. Fletcher A.L. Fletcher A.L. Fletcher Fletcher R.W.A. Junior Championship 1927 Olympic Games 1932 Sheffield

Humorous note suggesting White City announcer Harold Abrahams should give spectators a telephone, stenographer and assistant to follow his announcements. TAILPIECE to the Bank Holiday meeting at White City. If Harold Abrahams intends to persevere with the announcing "game" he might like to note the suggestion that was noisily aired in the "popular" section of the ground. This was to supply each spectator with a telephone, a stenographer and an assistant. The telephone would enable him to reply to Harold's greeting of "Hallo"! before every announcement, the stenographer to enter names while the spectator struggles to get down numbers and times only, and the assistant to discover what the numbers are when names only are given. The latter would also have an additional task---that of recording the results announced while an exciting race is in progress! Harold Abrahams Harold Abrahams Harold Abrahams Harold White City Bank Holiday Meeting 1967 White City

items.s: GERRY REGAINS 'WIMBLEDON CUP' Report and handicap result of the club 5¾ miles road race at Wimbledon, won by Gerry North six seconds outside brother Geoff's record, with Bernard Merry winning the handicap. COMFORTABLE WIN IN '5¾' - MARCH 18th Although Geoff North relinquished his hold on the Club 5¾ road race title, there was little doubt that it was destined to remain in the family. Brother Gerry was back in good form after his set-back at Norwich but surprised even himself to run within six seconds of the record set by Geoff last year. "If I'd known I'd be that close I would have gone for the record" he remarked, ruminating on last year's event when his record was surpassed by just one second! When Frank Jarvis sent the 45 runners on their way it was soon apparent that the best three would have to work very hard for their medals. Following his excellent run in the Southampton - Bournemouth relay the previous week (B team!) Chris Steer was really out to show it was no freak performance. Before the field had realised it his tall stylish figure had raced into a 20 yards lead which he had doubled by the half mile! Bill Dance led the chase and, inevitably, the gap narrowed - but it was not until the runners made their way out to Copse Hill that Gerry moved into the lead he was to hold to the end. Geoff North, Major, Dance, O'Hara and Fairclough joined Chris to form the forward bunch and the contest for second place. On the homeward run Tony Fairclough drew away for a comfortable looking second place but those ace finishers Bill Dance and Laurie O'Hara reduced it to very modest proportions down Lauriston Road and at the same time relegated Chris Steer, the hero of the race, to 5th position. Bill Kerr, fast regaining his form of old, made a lot of ground in the final stages, but John Thresher once again showed his dislike for road races in excess of 4 miles. Pat Newall chivvied up our leading men with a snappy 28:49, just 14 seconds faster than his winning time of 12 years ago! Lionel Mann and Pat O'Connor both ran exceptionally well and you will be hearing a lot more of this fast improving pair. items.sum: Short notes: Adrian Major second Surrey scorer in the Junior Inter-County at Derby, John Barnard signed by Plymouth Argyle, and Ray Middleton the first holder of the Jack Crump trophy.
items.s: Short notes: Adrian Major second Surrey scorer in the Junior Inter-County at Derby, John Barnard signed by Plymouth Argyle, and Ray Middleton the first holder of the Jack Crump trophy. Cross-country item omitted from our March issue. On 11th March at Mark Eaton, Derby, the Junior Inter-County C.C. Championships were held in which the Surrey team were 7th. ADRIAN MAJOR was their second scoring man in 35th place. * * * JOHN BARNARD, one of our most promising youths for the last two seasons, has now turned his attention to soccer in a big way. This talented all-round sportsman has been signed up by Plymouth Argyle and is looking forward to a long professional career. John will not be the first to leave our ranks for the soccer field---nor indeed the first John. Another that comes to mind is our former junior long-jump record holder, JOHN KEY, who made the grade at Fulham F.C. We wish John Barnard similar success and will watch his progress with interest. * * * RAY MIDDLETON became the first holder of the "JACK CRUMP" trophy when this fine silver salver was presented to him at the Surrey County Championships at Motspur Park on May 20th. The trophy was presented jointly by the Surrey Co AAA and the Surrey Co P.F.A. to perpetuate the name of Jack Crump who did so much for Surrey Co athletics. items.sum: Review of Belgrave's 1967 spring road relay season (wins at Southampton-Bournemouth, Brighton and Ponders End, 4th at Cranford, 3rd at Blackpool, 7th in the AAA National) with summary results for each relay.
items.s: ROAD RELAY ROUND-UP Review of Belgrave's 1967 spring road relay season (wins at Southampton-Bournemouth, Brighton and Ponders End, 4th at Cranford, 3rd at Blackpool, 7th in the AAA National) with summary results for each relay. THREE FIRSTS ---------- ONE THIRD ---------- ONE FOURTH ---------- ONE SEVENTH The 1967 Spring Road Relay Season produced three wins in six outings - as in 1966 - but one can't help having mixed feelings about the record. On the credit side, three wins is a performance that many clubs would envy and is, of course, a great morale booster to the lads whose sideboards are becoming heavily laden with prizes. Even our 'B' teams are making their mark with runners clocking times superior to some 'A' team men and giving the selectors a real head-ache! On the debit side, Portsmouth did not defend their Southampton - Bournemouth title and our other two wins were at Enfield and Brighton where the opposition could hardly be termed difficult; and at the latter venue we were closer than was comfortable even then. Our 4th place at Cranford was not really disappointing for we were without the Norths, Thresher and Fairclough, but our limitations are brought home to us when we meet our Midland and Northern rivals. The leading clubs in these areas are surging ahead again in the form books whilst standards in the South (outside Portsmouth and Belgrave) are at a low ebb. The new generation of Midland and Northern runners are already making their mark and are proving harder nuts to crack than their Southern counterparts. With Portsmouth having seen their best days it is up to BELGRAVE to keep the Southern flag flying and to prepare in earnest for a tougher than ever 1967/8 season. The South African cross-country team competed as guests at the T.V.H. road relay, Cranford, and were first to cross the line. Although we won nothing this day we did not come away empty handed. Peter Whewell, who clocked fastest time of the day for the South Africans, signed on the dotted line and hopes to compete for us for the remainder of the year. Our depleted 'A' team had plenty to run for and were never outside the first five. On the final lap John Bicourt stood an outside chance of finishing 2nd to a full strength Poly team but had to concede places to Price (Bristol) and Herring (Blackheath). Trevor Hart was our best performer for the 'A' team and Pat Newall the top 'B' man. The wisdom of racing on the track between the National C.C. and Relay events was shown to be doubtful when both Gerry Williams (strained stomach muscle) and Gerry North (strained calf) were invalids at the A.A.A. inaugural relay at Leicester. Williams withdrew minutes before the start and North broke down during the race. John Dear did everything that was asked of him as reserve but our long stage men found the opposition too much to cope with. There were plenty of "ifs" and "buts" floating around after the race but great teams win despite their set-backs and Coventry had more of these than anyone! With seven days to overcome their disappointment there was a carefree air abouth the eighteen runners that appeared at Brighton for the Front Relay. A warm, sunny, windless day was in complete contrast to the conditions at Leicester the previous week. The usual debate as to who should step down to the 'B' team resulted in Tony Fairclough having his turn as a second team man. This resulted in a fine tussle between Tony and Bill Dance ('A') on the first leg which ended with Bill's usual sprint finish cutting back his rival's 30 yards lead to a mere 1 second margin. Such rivalry between our 'A' and 'B' teams does the Club nothing but good and our runners finished 3rd and 4th to give their colleagues a grand start. S.L.H. proved to be a surprise package here for, without Roberts and Gilson, they led us until the final stages of the last leg when Laurie O'Hara did his usual duty for us. Brian Buxton made his only appearance of the short season and showed how useful he would have been at Leicester. Winners for the last three years, Belgrave sent a useful team up to Blackpool for the four-man relay. Peter Whewell had his first race in our colours finishing 4th behind Ibbottson, Leigh and Ravald and Bill Dance took us up a further place. Geoff North got us to within 8 seconds of Manchester D.L.C. but Gerry, in his first outing after his calf injury, could do nothing to stop the two leading clubs from going away and we had to be content with 3rd place. A name to note in the Manchester team was R.Wilde, who was amongst the day's fastest times and with team-mate Gregory and the whole Longwood quartet , were faster than any of our four men! This illustrates only too well the improvement in standards "up there". Our final outing was at Enfield for the Ponders End Relay where, once again, we went as holders. Last year we led from start to finish and we followed the same pattern this time, except that this year the only team to provide any opposition was our 'B' outfit! Slowest of our ten runners was Bill Kerr whose time was beaten last year by only Gerry North and Laurie O'Hara. This time it was Bill Dance's turn for relegation to the 'B' team and he gave the only sensible answer to such decisions - a time faster than two of our 'A' men! All in all an interesting, though brief, season. Would anyone dare to predict our record next Spring? items.sum: Stage-by-stage report of the inaugural A.A.A. National Road Relay at Whetstone, Leicester, where Belgrave finished 7th behind Coventry after Gerry North's calf injury and Tony Fairclough's stitch.
items.s: Bels slump in National Relay Stage-by-stage report of the inaugural A.A.A. National Road Relay at Whetstone, Leicester, where Belgrave finished 7th behind Coventry after Gerry North's calf injury and Tony Fairclough's stitch. LONG STAGE WEAKNESSES WHETSTONE, LEICESTER - APRIL 1st Once again, when the chips were down against top opposition, we failed to make our mark. Oh yes! It was quite easy to work out afterwards how we would have won if it had been "our day" but such daydreams overlook the fact that other clubs can justifiably do likewise and in several instances have a bigger "time-credit" up their sleeves. Belgrave finished 7th; Coventry are the Champions and the gap was 3mins 14secs. That was the result but the story was much different. There is no doubt that Dick Taylor of Coventry went as near as anyone could to winning a relay on his own. Taking over 3 minutes down and in 8th position the National Cross Country Champion took his club into the lead and they never looked back - but this effort did no more really than offset Coventry's disastrous run on Stage 3, when they dropped from 3rd to 15th. Gerry North, only partially recovered from injury in an ultra-early track race, risked himself on a long stage and broke down halfway through to record a time as slow as Coventry's "failures" on the third and seventh stages - but we had no Dick Taylor or John Hammond to off-set such setbacks and therein lies our weakness at this level. Neither of the Norths were fully fit yet it was still necessary for them to do long stages and although our short stage men performed excellently it is very unlikely that they would have improved on our long stage rankings of 14th, 8th, 10th, 10th, 16th and 16th - figures that tell a great deal. The Championship was held at the English Electric premises at Whetstone Leicester on April 1st. The course was a figure-eight circuit with the large lap measuring 5m 1,600yds and the short one 3m 705yds - an almost perfect venue with all the facilities of the firm available to competitors and officials alike. About sixty Belgravians and supporters turned up for this inaugural championship and in the hour preceding the start there was to be good and bad news for our followers. Spirits sank when Gerry Williams' pre-race "test" confirmed his withdrawal from the team, but rose again when it was understood Gerry North would be taking a long stage after all. The only other change was Bill Kerr to replace Bill Dance on a long stage. STAGE 1: Geoff North (28:45 - 14th fastest) Conditions were cold with a very strong head wind as the 28 runners set off on the first of the long stages. Geoff seemed contented enough for the first mile or so, but when the field strung out before the head wind had been overcome the going became much harder and his absence from competition began to tell. It was generally felt that Coventry and Portsmouth were the main teams to watch so although Hammond brought Godiva home with a useful lead it was gratifying to see Geoff hold Meadows of Portsmouth to one second. STAGE 2: John Bicourt (16:34 - 2nd fastest) Everyone knew that it was up to our short stage men to make progress while the long stages held their own and John set an excellent example of what was required. Only the redoubtable Ibbottson bettered his time. John's effort had hauled us up from 14th to 7th and we were now 39 seconds behind the leaders, Longwood. STAGE 3: Bill Kerr (28:42 - 8th fastest) Bill really did justify the last minute decision to switch him on to a long stage. He passed every one of the six runners ahead, only to be passed in turn by Perry (Birchfield), Wright (Tipton) and in a final sprint Leake (Leicester). Nevertheless we were better placed than at any time in the race, being 33 seconds behind the leaders, 29 seconds ahead of Portsmouth and 1:15 up on Coventry. STAGE 4: John Dear (17:22 - 13th fastest) John was in the unenviable position of being a last minute replacement for Gerry Williams and taking over in 4th place. He kept his head, stuck to the task well and although conceding three places got inside the 17:30 we were looking for. More important, John had drawn 17 seconds further away from Pompey and Coventry were still over a minute behind. STAGE 5: John Thresher (29:03 - 10th fastest) John regained a place and ran to form for a race of this length, but the five clubs ahead all moved away and Entwistle (Man DLC) and Hirons (Coventry) each gained over half a minute in our rear. STAGE 6: Adrian Major (16:44 - 2nd fastest) It was on this stage that Mel Thorpe, who has given us such good service in the past, was to have his first opportunity of crossing swords with his old team-mates. Providing he didn't gain ground at our expense everyone wished him well! Adrian was most helpful, running second fastest time on this leg and thus enabling Mel to finish third fastest (2 seconds slower) and gain the congratulations of both teams - a most diplomatic solution! STAGE 7 Trevor Hart (29:18 - 10th fastest) Trevor held his place well for most of the stage and moved past Polytechnic (Beacham) near the end to take 4th position, only to be passed by Gregory (Man DLC) who had run 37 seconds faster. Hyman had also run 20 secs faster to bring Pompey a little nearer but Coventry had another bad stage with Dowall clocking 30:29 in 10th place - 1:11 slower than Trevor and nearly 4 minutes behind the leaders, Birchfield. At this point we rashly dismissed Coventry from the reckoning; after all, didn't we have Gerry North, Fairclough, Dance, O'Hara and Steer to come? Surely no one could match such power - we thought! STAGE 8 Chris Steer (16:54 - 2nd fastest) Chris was quick to endorse this point of view and followed Adrian Major's example by clocking second fastest time for his stage; only Coventry (Juan Taylor) running faster. Portsmouth slipped back further still while Chris's effort had caught Manchester on the line. STAGE 9 Tony Fairclough (30:16 - 16th fastest) This was the stage that decided it all. When Tony set of with Ravald of Manchester, a man of equal calibre, 1:36 behind the leaders and 1:18 and 1:48 ahead of Coventry and Portsmouth respectively we looked to be in with a good chance still, for it was not unreasonable to hope that Fairclough would hold off the efforts of Taylor and Tulloh. However, Tony chose this day for one of his rare mediocre performances and Dick Taylor picked it for perhaps his greatest run to date. Ravald got away from Tony almost immediately and while the Manchester Lad opened up a minute's lead Taylor simply tore through the field like a half-miler against marathoners and shot from 8th to 1st in 27:08, well over a minute faster than Tulloh and Holt and 37 seconds faster than the next best man of the day, Allan Rushmer (Tipton). So sensational was this performance that when it was announced that Taylor had taken the lead a mile or so from the finish, no one believed it. Surely it was another error over the radio-telephone. But no, in he raced to applause from all sides with a narrow lead over Leicester and Derby and it was nearly two minutes later that the anxious eyes of our supporters spotted a distressed Tony Fairclough struggling to the finish, just 6 seconds ahead of Bruce Tulloh. It was bad enough to get "stitch" in a race of this importance but to have it rubbed in by the two fastest men of the day tearing past was cruel luck for our runner. STAGE 10 Laurie O'Hara (16:45 - fastest) The race had been transformed and things looked black, but not to Laurie O'Hara. Revelling in the situation his rapid stride ate into the deficit and brought us back up to the Manchester club again. He fully deserved his number 1 ranking for stage 10. We had now recovered to 1:29 down on the leaders, but with the first four teams running in a pack during this lap it was a formidable gap to close. If anyone could do it, it would be Gerry North. STAGE 11 Gerry North (30:27 - 16th fastest) Gerry soon caught and passed Ward of Manchester DLC and half way round the lap was over half a minute ahead of his Northern rival and fast closing on the runners ahead. Tim Johnston of Portsmouth was running equally well 37 seconds behind and was making little impression on the gap. Then disaster struck. Gerry's leg failed to stand the strain and he tore his damaged calf again. Reduced to a hobble but with no thought of retiring, he pressed on at a painfully slow pace. First Johnston, then Ward swept past and Gerry's good work was rapidly undone. Instead of finishing a certain third he could do nothing but limp in a gallant 8th, 3 minutes behind the leaders, Derby. Gerry is normally at his best in these relays and it would not be unreasonable to assume he would have matched Johnston's time of 27:59 in normal circumstances. In the final analysis this alone was the difference between 3rd place medals and 7th place. STAGE 12 Bill Dance (16:59 - 5th fastest) With well-wishers from many sides implying that it would all depend on the last stage and that Gerry would probably hand over in 3rd place, it must have been no small shock to wait 2½ minutes longer than expected and see one's rivals disappear into impregnable leads. Bill did enough to gain the only place it was humanly possible to take but certainly would have been higher up the ranking list if he had been in at the kill as expected. Nevertheless he was our 5th runner to break 17 minutes on the short lap - a record that no other club could match. And so we had to be content with 7th place, but whilst we live to fight another day it must be remembered that so too do Manchester, Longwood, Tipton, North Staffs and our old rivals Birchfield, all of whom are growing stronger month by month. It will not get any easier and next year our team will all be a year older - a factor that will soon eclipse the Portsmouth outfit. Our team would no doubt be quite happy to fade away if they could match the record of their south coast rivals! It is not impossible. Pos Team Time 1. Coventry God. H 274:35 2. items.label: June 1967
items.sum: Social notes: a record jumble sale, the Club Dinner at the Wimbledon Hill Hotel on 18 November, children's races on Championship Day, and Chris Steer's 'Freak-Out' disco at Belgrave Hall.
items.s: SOCIAL Social notes: a record jumble sale, the Club Dinner at the Wimbledon Hill Hotel on 18 November, children's races on Championship Day, and Chris Steer's 'Freak-Out' disco at Belgrave Hall. The last Jumble Sale was our most successful so far and we took no less than £28-18-10½. Our thanks go to all those regular helpers who helped to make it a success. For those who have not witnessed the spectacle of jumble being sold, you don't know what you are missing! Come along and help out on a stall at our next sale; students of sociology will find it quite an education. * * * The Club Dinner will be held at the WIMBLEDON HILL HOTEL again this year, November 18th. If you think that is early then you had better note that there are only 240 tickets left---10 were snapped up at the Club Championships on June 3rd! Seriously though folks, it was a full house last year and some late applicants were disappointed. Make a note in those diaries to get your tickets in September and be safe. * * * Club Championship Day, June 3rd, saw our usual programme of Children's races during the interval. Charlie Manning ("Uncle Charlie") was in control(?) and apart from one prize, which disappeared with it's recipient over the track railings, the awards were in fact won by children of bona-fide club members---or should it be bona-fide children of club members! The few races were the "Benger's Benefit" 20 yards for 2 yr olds, the "Dolly Mixture" derby (30yds) for 3 yr olds, the "Lollipop Stakes" 30 yds for 5 yr olds and the "Cow and Gate" handicap hurdle for 5-10 yr olds over 40 yds. The handicapping left a lot to be desired and starting stalls would have been useful for some of the 2 yr olds. The Club's Hon. Handicapper was, nevertheless, still seen to be jotting down some of the form for filing with his 1980 marks! * * * On the evening of the Club Championships a "Freak- Out" was held at Belgrave Hall. The originator of Wimbledon's pirate pop station, Christopher "Carnaby" Steer, was in the "chair" with sufficient record stocks and equipment to rival the B.B.C. (sorry, I mean Caroline). Apart from the incoherent ramblings of the disc jockey, who had difficulty in reading the record titles through dark glasses and hashish smoke, and the aura of purple haze around the set this could have been any radio station. The poor amplification helped to make it sound even more authentic. A good sized crowd got really bouncing as the evening wore on and it might have been an idea to open up the showers at midnight when the evening drew to a close. Everyone had a good time, particularly Bob Taylor who celebrated his birthday with Don Maclean in the bar! Chris put a lot of time into preparation for the evening and deserves commendation for his decor, publicity and presentation---not forgetting, of course, Charlie Manning's witty skits on T.V. advertising during the interval.
