items.s: Harry Hare continues his reminisences:- Harry Hare's reminiscences prompted by a 1923 photograph of members in Denmark Road before the Club walking championship for the R. Murphy Shield, with a numbered key, the history of the race and memories of Joe Sawyer and Battersea Park walks. In his first two articles, W.H. Hare (Past-President, former Hon. Secretary and founder Editor of "The Belgravian") looked back on the last days of our history at "The Swan" and the first days of our move to Belgrave's present H.Q. in Denmark Road, Wimbledon. The photograph shown opposite has stired his memories still further and he tells of the recollections this picture brings. 1.J.SAWYER 2.E.GORDON. 3.T.EATON. 4.D.McLEAN. 5.W.SAVAGE. 6. T.W.CARNE. 7. The photograph was taken in Denmark Road just before the start of the Club walking championship of 1923. This was the 5th contest for the R.Murphy Shield, instituted in 1916, for the trophy presented to the Club by 'Dick Murphy, who appears here (No. 17.) The inaugural race was over a 6 mile course and was won by C.McLellan, a Scots Guardsman at that time. Wounded in France, he returned to Scotland and later won their National Championship and set up a number of individual records. Owing to worsening war time conditions no further race was held until 1920, when the distance was increased to 9 miles and won by R.W. Ricketts (No. 28), who repeated his win in 1921. With new members now coming along, the 1922 race was won by H.F. King (No. 14) who went on to win the R.W.A. 'Junior' Championship at Regents Park; leading the Club to their second team success in this event. Harold retained the Club championship in 1923 and again in 1924 (now standardised at 10 miles) before taking up an appointment on the Gold Coast of Africa. He returned to collect more 'gold' by winning once more, in 1927. Of those in the photo not competing, a very notable personality is J. Sawyer (No. 1). The father of 4 members, of whom two were casualties of the war, he gave to the Club the J.G. Sawyer and the A.J. Sawyer Memorial Cups that remain our oldest track trophies. Joe was a regular attendant and helper in those early days, and was relied upon as the unofficial Clerk of Course; a familiar figure with his yardstick made in the form of a giant pair of dividers. It was the late summer of 1920 that I made my first contact, before coming an active participant in Club proceedings. Attending Battersea Park to watch a 2 Mile Walk Handicap, in which a business colleague was competing, I found the course pegged out on an open field situated between the tennis courts and the S.W. main gateway. To my critical, if inexperienced eyes, the going looked 'distinctly rough' and recalled that line of the poet Gray "Where heaves the turf in many a mouldering heap". It was certainly a 'graveyard' for fast and fair walking, and this may have accounted for the lack of progress that the backmarkers made towards the middlemen who dominated the final placings. There was no lack of spectators who, attracted by the sport provided, gathered in force both outside and inside the circuit. Inevitably, the crowd closed in, and in the closing stages of the race the competitors found themselves walking in a steadily narrowing funnel. ....Cont'd on page 23. (Cont'd. from p.11) All good things, however, come to an end; much to the relief of the Parkkeeper deputed to maintain order. Joe collected his flags and marking pegs and soon "The curfew tolled the knell of parting day" - Closing time. So a page of history was turned; the cinder track in its original form, 3 laps to the mile, was opened for use in 1923. In the interregnum of 1921 and 1922 the Club was able to use the ground of Prices A.C. at Openview, Earlsfield, by kind permission of Price's Patent Candle Company of Battersea. It was here in 1922 that the Club's Track Championships' meeting was instituted with a modest programme that included 4 trophy events, 100 yards (Grosvenor Cup) 440 yards (J.G. Sawyer Memorial Cup) 1 mile (Garnett Cup) and 2 mile walk (A.J. Sawyer Memorial Cup). The Club now has 44 Championship trophies .............. ............. we have travelled a long way in the last 45 years! items.sum: Introduction to the track and field section summarising a season of ten inter-club wins and four trophy wins, with congratulations to Derek Boosey, Alan Lerwill, Jim Vivian and John Thresher.
items.s: TRACK AND FIELD Introduction to the track and field section summarising a season of ten inter-club wins and four trophy wins, with congratulations to Derek Boosey, Alan Lerwill, Jim Vivian and John Thresher. INTER-CLUB MATCHES:- TEN WINS, TWO DRAWN. TROPHY MEETINGS:- FOUR WINS, ONE 5th, ONE 6th. This year has seen one of our best seasons in living memory, our only bad performance coming in the 'Vancouver' (seelast issue). Turning out a competitor in every event is half the battle and with our re-emergence as a strong Field club as well as track the scene is set, we hope, for many years of like success. Congratulations to Derek Boosey for his now regular British team place, to Alan Lerwill and Jim Vivian for their national team places and to John Thresher for his fine 'Southern'win in his first year as a 3 miler. items.h: JUNE 10th - CROYDON 'JACK LEWIS' TROPHY FIRST TROPHY WIN SINCE 1956
items.sum: Report and results of the Jack Lewis Trophy at Croydon Sports Arena, Belgrave's first trophy meeting win in 11 years, edging Cambridge Harriers by 9½ points.
items.s: JUNE 10th - CROYDON 'JACK LEWIS' TROPHY FIRST TROPHY WIN SINCE 1956 Report and results of the Jack Lewis Trophy at Croydon Sports Arena, Belgrave's first trophy meeting win in 11 years, edging Cambridge Harriers by 9½ points. At last a 'trophy' meeting win with some great performances turned in by a great team. It's all of 11 years since we last took home a trophy and Croydon Sports Arena was the scene of our triumph in gusty but warm conditions. The first event started with maximum points for us as Jim Vivian and Terry Derham took both 'A' and 'B' hundred yard events, the former in a meeting and ground record. Cambridge H, who were to prove our strongest opponents throughout the afternoon, were close behind us with second places in each race. This set the trend for nearly all the track races as time and again our boys led the field. John Bicourt kept clear of a fast finishing Mike Fuller (Wimbledon) in the mile with Laurie O'Hara nearby to take the 'B' event (both races were combined). Vivian again outpaced the Cambridge men for an even time furlong with this time Chris Martin providing the backing with another win in the 'B' race. Tony Brooks recorded his fastest 'quarter' of the season after pushing Mike Fleet (Croydon) at the half-way mark but tying up in the finishing straight. The most inspiring event of the afternoon was the 3000m Steeplechase, won by John Dear, but with the amazing Don Maclean only 16 seconds down in 2nd place and beating all the other clubs' 'A' runners., a tremendous feat by our hard working Press Secretary. Our Field Event specialists were short of Nick Head, who had to go abroad at the last moment, and therefore several of our 'B' men had to move up into the 'A' events and we had to start looking around for second string men to fill their places. This gave Cambridge H , who are fairly strong on the field, a chance to gain on us. Barry Townsend was kept busy taking 3rd in the 'A' Long Jump, 2nd in the 'A' High Jump and 2nd in thr 'B' Javelin with a good throw of 158'8½ to beat an off-form Brian King in the 'A' event. The Hammer resulted in another improvement for Bill Couzens who adds a couple of feet every time he competes. The final result was in doubt until the very end when our Javelin men managed to beat the opponents who really mattered and clinch the match by the skin of our teeth and 9½ points. It was pleasing to see the Bels. taking part in the meeting as a real team, track men urging on Field men and vice versa. With a result as close as this all the athletes who competed for us can feel that the points they scored were the vital ones, but three who deserve special mention are ; Don Maclean, with his great 'chasing; Tony Brooks, who filled in his spare time between the 440y and two relay legs with the 'B' Triple Jump where he finished 2nd; and Jim Vivian, who ran four races including a leg of the 4 x 440y in which a highly fancied Cambridge team were beaten and we gained 12 extra points. items.sum: John Thresher sets a Belgrave 2 miles best of 8:38.4 in fourth place at the White City.
items.s: JUNE 13th - WHITE CITY - ANOTHER THRESHER BEST John Thresher sets a Belgrave 2 miles best of 8:38.4 in fourth place at the White City. This race was to have been an attack on the British 2 miles record but although the early pace was too slow for this, it was just right for John Thresher who hung on grimly as the pace quickened over the last few laps to record a Belgrave best of 8:38.4. It surely cannot be long before he improves on another of our best Club marks - Geoff NortHs 13:18.8 for 3 miles. items.s: JUNE 23rd/24th - MOTSPUR PARK SOUTHERN CHAMPS. Report and results of the Southern Championships at Motspur Park, featuring Alan Lerwill's long jump win with Belgravians second and fourth, and John Thresher's 3 miles title. The 'Southern' Long Jump was one of the closest events at this meeting and was a triumph for Dave Ansell. After three rounds Peter Templeton (Bristol), the Inter-Counties winner, led with 23'0½, Alan Lerwill was close behind with 22'9½, John Mitchell was also on this mark and only scraping into the final six after two 'no-jumps, and Derek Wade in 4th spot with 22'5½. So high was the standard that several top class jumpers could not make the final three rounds. As the final began the rain eased - Templeton improved fractionally in Round 4 but it was in Round 5 that things really began to happen. Lerwill, drawn 4th launched out to 23'10½ and next down the runway was Templeton, improving again but now only 2nd in the competition with 23'2½. Now,drawn 6th, came Derek Wade with a magnificent leap of 23'7 - alas! a no-jump. John Mitchell led off on the last round with the distinct possibility of not getting a medal but showing that characteristic fighting quality he tore down the runway and cut the sand at 23'3, 2nd place. He could do nothing now but burn up nervous energy watching his rivals come down one by one. Alan Lerwill also hit 23'3, Templeton in a do or die effort fouled at 23'4 and now it was all up to our Club Champion Derek Wade, poising himself at the end of the run-up, the last competitor to jump and knowing that he was at the top of his form. Alan and John couldn't look - Templeton couldn't look away as Derek soared smoothly away from the board. 23'1 and a good 4th place. The only pity was that Bob Jones who was within 2" of Derek at the Club Champs was unable to compete due to injury. Beating a classy field, a waterlogged track and stringing together three separate miles of 4:32.8, 4:38.0 and 4:25.0, John Thresher took the first major title of his career . Nobody could have forecast the winner with any certainty with only one lap remaining but 220 yards out Thresher struck out for home, reaching the tape fractionally ahead of Tim Johnston (Ports) and the ex-holder Dave Gibson (Surrey). items.s: JULY 1st - SOUTHAMPTON RYDER TROPHY Report and results of the Ryder Trophy meeting at Southampton, where Belgrave finished fifth in a close contest, illustrated by J. Martin's photograph of Nick Head throwing the javelin. At first our 5th place seems to be only an average performance at this Southampton AC sponsored trophy meeting but only 27 points covered the first five clubs and we had more than our share of bad luck. Jim Vivian went down with a throat infection and a mix up in the sprint relay cost us at least 12 points. Our only wins of the afternoon came from Peter Whewell (1m), John Mitchell (L.J) and Alan Black (3000mSC) recording a personal best of 9:15.6. However, we had many runners-up and scored well in most events. On the track John Dear recorded a good 9:37.8 for 4th in the Steeplechase and Peter Hilliar made a welcome return to our trophy team with 3rd in the 'B' 880y. Denzil Winsborrow and Barry Townsend filled 2nd and 4th places in the Pole Vault and also scored heavily in the High Jump. Top points scorer of the day, though, was Nicholas Head with 3rd in the Javelin and 5th in the Shot and Discus, both the latter being close to his best ever. Photo: J. items.sum: Report and results of Herne Hill Harriers' H.G. Brockman Trophy at Wimbledon Park, won by Belgrave with 86 points, including Nick Head's club record javelin of 211'3" (results continued on page 15), with a page of A. Mead's photographs.
items.s: 'Brockman' Win Report and results of Herne Hill Harriers' H.G. Brockman Trophy at Wimbledon Park, won by Belgrave with 86 points, including Nick Head's club record javelin of 211'3" (results continued on page 15), with a page of A. Mead's photographs. JULY 8th - WIMBLEDON PARK In 1965 we were 8th of the twelve clubs that compete annually for Herne Hill Harrier's "H.G.Brockman"Trophy with a measly 12 points. 1966 saw us improve to 5th with 53 points and now in 1967 we have beaten all the top clubs in the London area to win the event with 86 points. A magnificent performance! The afternoon started not too hopefully for us when in the first track final - the '6' - an injured Trevor Hart retired after a quarter of the distance had been covered. Another blow came when Tony Brooks was unable to qualify for the 440yd final although recording a time that would have almost won the other heat. However, the 'Field Boys' were already making up for the unexpected loss of points - Bill Couzens making the final six in the Hammer and Nicholas Head, in great shape, heaving the discus 123'11" for 4th place (a sandwich in his non-throwing hand) The standard in the sprints was amazing, both winning times being faster than those of the Invitation events put on for the visiting South African team. John Mitchell clocked 9.9 to qualify for the final of the '100' which was eventually won by Bob Frith (Poly) with 9.7 into a stiffish wind. John was again timed at 9.9 (the fourth time this year) for 4th place. Mike Hauck (TVH) took the furlong in 21.6 with 'Our Jim' Vivian well ahead of the rest in 22.0. The 1500 metres was a pre-AAA Champs warm up for John Thresher and he absolutely romped away from a field including Hugh Pullan (SLH), two S.African Internationals and arch rival Bob Holt (Herc). Back on the field the 'Bels' were still steadily notching up the points. Derek Wade made 2nd in the Long Jump, Denzil Winsborrow vaulted into 4th place despite a treacherous wind that removed the bar without any help from the competitors, and Barry Townsend recorded his best marks of the season with a 16.5 High Hurdles effort and a 5'11" High Jump. We were now equal 3rd with TVH in the team result behind Surrey AC and Blackheath H but now came two events that drastically altered the points situation. On one of his last throws in his speciality, the Javelin, Nick Head launched a mighty throw of 211'3" - a Club Record and four feet clear of any other thrower. Bill Couzens was sent into ecstasies,and as Peter Whewell ground away the opposition in the 3 miles to knock 20 secs off his best and finish 2nd only to Tim Johnston (Portsmouth) who wasn't scoring anyway, even announcer Bill Lucas had to chime in over the'mike' that the 'Bels' had taken the lead. Only the Steeplechase and the 4 x 440yds to go. An unknown Surrey man forced his way into the lead in a do or die effort for his club but it was soon the 'new style' Alan Black forging away from the field at every barrier with even Dai Davies (TVH) hard pressed. Alan hammered away and was rewarded with a best ever of 9:13.2. It looks as if John Bicourt is not going to have things all his own way. The relay was unfortunately divided into two separate races, the result being decided on times. TVH and Hercules were well clear in the first heat and it was a great pity that we had not been drawn with them for the opposition in our own race was almost nil. Tony Brooks gave us a good lead on the first leg which was steadily improved upon by John Mitchell, Chris Martin and Jim Vivian and we finished streets ahead in our race but 3rd overall in 3:24.5 our best time for ages. The 'Brockman' was in our hands again after 11 years. A happy Bob Taylor was presented with the 'goodies' by the Herne Hill officials and it's the 'Advertiser' and 'Boughey' trophies next on the list! items.s: Humorous comic-paper style letter from 'Bill Sykes' looking forward to the A.G.M. and recalling quips by Albert Footer and Treasurer Sid Roberts. Dear Friends, This week we are getting very excited because we are all going to our A.G.M. - What a jolly time we shall have there. I remember many years ago one of our members, who was very cross, leaping to his feet and crying 'I'm not satisfied!' Albert Footer, who was always so quick cupped his hand to his mouth and replied 'Well - get married!' Ho! Ho! What a little tinker he was. Then on another occasion our Treasurer Sid Roberts, who was most concerned at collecting our pennies, banged his paws together to make sure everyone was sitting up straight and listening, said slowly and deliberately, 'Iwant you all to become subconscious!' Dear me, how we did laugh. So don't forget, come along, we shall have such fun. Lots of love, Bill Sykes (and a thumb print from clink). Bill Sykes Bill Sykes Albert Footer Albert Footer Sid Roberts Sid Roberts Belgrave Harriers Annual General Meeting 1967

items.h: A FAIRY TALE .... by Enid Blighted
items.sum: Satirical fairy tale about two gnome editors of the Bell Glade's news-leaves whose jokes upset the King Elf, apparently alluding to the Belgravian's editors.
items.s: A FAIRY TALE .... by Enid Blighted Satirical fairy tale about two gnome editors of the Bell Glade's news-leaves whose jokes upset the King Elf, apparently alluding to the Belgravian's editors. Once upon a time there were two gnomes. They lived in a big forest. The part of the forest where they lived was called the Bell Glade. The two little gnomes had a special job. You see, because not many of the other fairies and elves could write, our two little friends used to collect all the news of what happened in the Bell Glade and write it all down on big leaves and give it to all their friends. The fairies and elves in the glade looked forward to getting the news and would read it excitedly to see if their names were mentioned. The two gnomes worked very hard. But as time went by the fairies and elves in the glade did not get so excited when they received the leaves with all the news written on them. 'Oh Dear' said the first gnome, whose name was Eddie Tore 'no-one gets excited by our leaves anymore. What are we to do?' 'I know', said his friend, who was called Ass Ed,'Instead of just writing news on our leaves, everyone's heard it anyway, let's give out extra leaves with jokes and things like that.' They both thought this was a splendid idea so they asked another gnome whose name was Charlemagne to write some jokes. Charlemagne was a very witty gnome who spent all his time chasing butterflies and moths round the glade. But he found time to write some jokes and when the next leaves were given out everyone laughed and said'Aren't we lucky to have such clever gnomes in our glade. The fairies in other glades haven't got such good news-leaves.' But the King Elf and some of his friends were angry because they thought that the fairies and elves shouldn't laugh at the affairs of the glade, even if they were sometimes funny. So they called a meeting of all the important folk in the glade and the important fold said that the two gnomes were very naughty and in future they must treat their work more seriously. Of course this made the two gnomes sad because they had only been trying to cheer other people up. They were so sad that they packed their bags and ran away to another glade. So from that time on the fairies and elves of the Bell-Glade didn't get any news at all, and, as the King Elf said, 'No news is good news.' The moral of this story is - Don't worry, you can't please all the people all the time. Enid Blighted Enid Blighted

items.sum: Report and Belgrave results from the AAA Championships at the White City, with Derek Boosey second in the triple jump and Geoff North the leading Belgravian in the 3 miles in 13:23.0.
items.s: A. A. A. CHAMPS Report and Belgrave results from the AAA Championships at the White City, with Derek Boosey second in the triple jump and Geoff North the leading Belgravian in the 3 miles in 13:23.0. JULY 14th/15th - WHITE CITY Fresh back from Nevada University, Derek Boosey looked his fittest yet. On May 20th at San Jose in California he had Triple-Jumped 51'8½ only 2½" behind his own Club Record and with National Record holder Fred Alsop not as fit as he has been, Derek could possibl; have taken his first AAA title. Alsop opened the competition with a leap of 50'4¾ whereas Derek could only reach 48'11½. Neither man improved until in the 5th Round the Belgravian closed right up with 50'3¼. This was just thm spur that Alsop needed and his final effort took him well clear of all the opposition - 51'5. The title clould still be Derek's if he could reproduce the form he has shown in the States on his last leap. It was not to be, he fouled and had to be content with 2nd place but a certain team place in the G.B. v U.S.A match. Derek Wade and John Mitchell both failed to reach the final eight in the Long Jump but had to contend with the toughest of opposition. Alan Lerwill did, however, compete in the final and managed to finish 7th but more significantly 3rd Briton behind Lynn Davies and Peter Reed. John also competed in the 100yds and together with our other ace sprinter Jim Vivian reached the semi-finals. Both were drawn in separate semis, both races called for photo-finishes involving the last places for the final and, unhappily, both our men were ruled out. It was great to see two Bels getting that far. Jim also finished 3rd in a furlong heat with only the first two to qualify. The 3 miles race involved a battle royal to find the top Belgrave man. John Thresher running as he never has before, took another 8 seconds off his best time only to find himself beaten by Geoff North who returned 13:23.0, only 4 seconds down on his Inter-County winning time of last year and coming to hand just at the right time of the season. As if this was not enough a third Belgravian was hot on their heels. Peter Whewell continued his astounding progress over the 12 lap event with 13:36.2, a time that only a couple of years ago would have been a Club Record but now could only take him up to third Bel home! items.s: FAIRCLOUGH takes CLUB '3' Report and results of the Club 3 miles championship at Battersea Park, won by Tony Fairclough from Laurie O'Hara, and the Club 120yds hurdles won by newcomer Peter Vickery. JULY 26th - BATTERSEA PARK Whether over ten miles or three, when Tony Fairclough and Laurie O'Hara cross swords in a Club Championship race you can bank on there being a tight finish. This was to be no exception. Bill Kerr shot away from the start in his typical do or die fashion, only Alan Black and Fairclough hanging on for the ride. Eyebrows were raised when it was noticed that Bill Dance, usually only too keen to take on suicidally fast starts, was taking things more steadily in company with Gerry North and not far from our newly joined Guardsman Dick Piotrowski. At about half-way 'Flying Scotsman' Kerr ran out of steam and was picked up by the main pack at an alarming rate. Now Alan Black started to drop, though not so quickly, and Tony Fairclough seemed to have the race all sewn up. But who was this streaking through through the field as the finish neared - none but 'Little Laurie' O'Hara. He ripped past Alan Black and with 660 yards to go was 35 yards down on Tony. The 'bell' spurred him on even more and one wondered why with this amount of energy left he had let Fairclough get so much lead. With half a lap left the gap was down to about 5 yards but at that it remained, the leader refusing to give another inch. Fairclough was a good winner and unable to contain his elation at winning the championship skipped with glee as he broke the tape. The other championship held on this evening was the 120yds Hurdles. The winner was an athlete who is going to be extremely useful to us in the near future. Note his name - Peter Vickery. Although winning by only one tenth of a second, Peter, who is a junior and therefore used to lower barriers, was never in danger of losing this his first race since joining the Club. Apart from his hurdling (he has already won the Southern Junior 330yds Hurdles) he has Long Jumped 21'9, clocked 10.4 for the 'hundred' and has aspirations towards the Decathlon. 37 started. items.sum: Report and results of the Club 6 miles championship at Battersea Park on 9 August, won by Tony Fairclough from Laurie O'Hara; the text mentions 27 runners while the results say 29 started.
items.s: IT'S FAIRCLOUGH AGAIN Report and results of the Club 6 miles championship at Battersea Park on 9 August, won by Tony Fairclough from Laurie O'Hara; the text mentions 27 runners while the results say 29 started. Battersea Park---August 9th Running in his most relaxed and confident manner, Tony Fairclough shook off all the opposition just after half way to become our 6 mile champion for 1967. Don Maclean may have been last to arrive at the track but the momentum of his speedy change and dash to the start carried him into a first lap lead, closely tailed by the barefooted Trevor Hart. The latter towed the field through the next two laps at a fairly leisurely pace until Gerry North, the holder, livened up the pace with a burst to the front. Laurie O'Hara tagged him closely but Fairclough was nearly caught napping and took half a lap to close up again, whilst Dick Piotrowski failed to get out of the ruck in time to maintain contact. There were many surprised faces 2½ laps later when Laurie and Tony moved away from Gerry. The two leaders looked extremely comfortable, running shoulder to shoulder, with Fairclough in the second lane. The remainder did not look too good, except perhaps Piotrowski who also passed Gerry a lap later. The leaders passed through 2 miles in 9:40 with Dick just 6 seconds down, followed by Hart and North (9:54) and Dance (10:06). The first three steadily drew away and the lapping commenced---an event that called for the full concentration of six or more officials, for some of the 27 runners were to be lapped four times before the end. Three miles saw the leading pair through in 14:43 with Dick now 15 seconds back, followed by Hart (15:06), North (15:17), Dance (15:23), Mann (15:26), Steer (15:32) and Hilliar (15:34). Just one lap later Fairclough decided to go it alone and went into a 2 second lead, but Laurie hung on well and 5 laps later was still only 4 seconds in arrears. Meanwhile Hart had retired ("the pace was too fast"), Bill Dance was another to pass the still unfit North and Peter Hilliar was suffering badly with stitch. Four miles saw the first three through in 19:44, 19:48 and 20:13 and at five miles the leading positions were, Fairclough (24:45), O'Hara (25:00), Piotrowski (25:32), Dance (25:48), Steer and Mann (25:53) and North (25:57). Except for North regaining fifth place from the Steer/Mann partnership the last mile saw no change. Peter Hilliar recovered well after considerable loss of ground in the middle stages whilst Bob Glover showed some excellent form. Those "old stagers" Charlie Walker and Arthur Bruce went round in tandem for most of the race with Chas. having the edge on the last circuit. Young Nigel Bacon, competing in his first "six", did well to put five seniors behind him. What is more, he looked fresher than many of his opponents. Don Maclean faded rapidly in the middle stages with blistered feet, and on noting the lap recorders' confusion as to his position prompted them with his own count-down on each of the remaining circuits! 29 started. ...... In the recent 'Belgrave Baby Stakes' there was a very close finish for the 'Gold Medal' between the Langheim and O'Hara's. Young David Langheim taking after his fathers habit of always being late, just managed to get first place by arriving one day before 'Silver Medallist' Phillip O'Hara. Whilst offering congratulations to the respective Mums and Dads we have to report that there is no foundation to the rumour that Brenda and Bill Dance, not content with a 'Bronze' are hoping for the TEAM award later in August. items.label: September 1967
items.sum: Notice reminding members of a new I.A.A.F. rule under which athletes can lose eligibility for advertising or endorsing merchandise, including carrying branded bags.
items.s: NEW I.A.A.F. RULING. Notice reminding members of a new I.A.A.F. rule under which athletes can lose eligibility for advertising or endorsing merchandise, including carrying branded bags. Members are reminded that under a new I.A.A.F. ruling an athlete can lose his eligibility to compete under I.A.A.F. rules if he:- (a) "Receives, directly or indirectly, any compensation for using or recommending the use of any merchandise whatsoever; 'merchandise' shall include anything sold or any service supplied to the public". (b) "Allows his name or his picture, whether static or moving, to be used directly or indirectly to advertise any merchandise;- NOTE: When and where it is proved that the name or the picture of the athlete was used for the purpose of this paragraph without his knowledge the indemnity to be collected from the person or persons responsible for the injury privately agreed or stipulated by the courts, will revert to the Federation to which the athlete belongs". (c) "While training or competing, displays any advertisement whatsoever. You will note that this rule precludes, among other things, the carrying into the arena of any bag or container bearing the name of any merchandise whatsoever.'Merchandise' includes anything sold or any service supplied to the public. The carrying into the arena of bags displaying the name of makers of running shoes falls within the prohibited category". I.A.A.F.

items.label: September 1967
items.sum: Clive Shippen's 'I Was There' No. 4 recalls the 1960 AAA Championships and Stan Vickers' world record 2 miles walk duel with Ken Matthews at the White City (concluded on page 23).
items.s: I WAS THERE Clive Shippen's 'I Was There' No. 4 recalls the 1960 AAA Championships and Stan Vickers' world record 2 miles walk duel with Ken Matthews at the White City (concluded on page 23). No.4 : by Clive Shippen The A.A.A. Championships of 1960. Do you remember them? It was the year of the Rome Olympics, so you probably do; but I wonder which event stands out in your mind. Perhaps it was the 3 miles where those ace finishers Tulloh, Ibbottsor and Salvat all hit the final 300 yards mark together and when "Ibbo" unleashed his final effort Frankie Salvat stayed with him for 80 yards before letting loose probably the fastest 220 seen before or since in this event. To open up a 25 yards lead during the finishing bursts of two such rivals was a sight few will forget. Or perhaps it was the shot or hammer, where the two champions proved to be in the twilight of youthfull careers. British athletics has never recovered from the early retirements of Arthur Rowe and Mike Ellis. The former's 59'2" shot win and the latter's 210'7" hammer heave make their counterparts of today look modest performers indeed. Field events enthusiasts will no doubt remember those Championships thro' their nostalgia for Rowe and Ellis. It could have been the 100 yards - Radford's 9.5 secs. is still unbeaten - or even the mile where the exiled Hungarian, Lazlo Tabori, beat Wiggs and Michel Jazy and all eight runners bettered the Championship best performance. Many will remember the occasion (Charlie Dabbs in particular) for Gordon Pirie's comfortable win in the six-miles, where his final burst lapped the Belgrave man in the finishing straight. But, for me, none of these memorable incidents matches the event that stood out above all others on July 16th, 1960. I speak of the contest that brought together two men who had, for some time, swept all before them. Two men who, between them, were destined to gain an Olympic gold, a European gold and an Olympic bronze. They were athletes who adopted a "professional" approach to their training and who brought glamour to an event that needed it badly. Yes, their names were Stan Vickers and Ken Matthews and the start of the 2 miles walk at the A.A.A. Championships of 1960 was the signal for the bars to be emptied of their beer-drinking occupants instead of the reverse which is now customary. The Public's imagination had been captured by the clash of two giants both making a bid for the very suspect 56 years old world record of 13:11.4 by George Larner. Both walkers tackled their track training in a similar way to their running counterparts - liberal doses of repetition speedwork - and their faultless styles travelling together at speed were a sheer joy to watch. Few would dare to forecast the result with any certainty, though Vickers had the slightest edge perhaps over this short distance. Two weeks earlier he beat his rival narrowly on a grass track at Peterborough but this was not regarded as a serious pointer to a Championship event at the White City where Matthews was not only the Holder in a best of 13:19.4 but the previous year the Midlander had beaten Stan by a 27.6 seconds margin. There were 18 starters, including four East Germans and two Indians, including Zora Singh who had some good times to his credit. The crowd, fully aware of the record attempt, hushed as the walkers lined up. Eric Hall gave his fellow Belgravian a good luck wish as he stood alongside and the tension mounted rapidly, almost producing a false start. The gun exploded, the watches clicked, the scoreboard clock snapped into motion and the crowd's roar swept the field round the first bend with the turbanned Zora Singh to the fore. Singh scampered thro' the first lap in 94.3 secs. revelling in his moment of glory with Matthews, Vickers, Colin Williams, Adjit Singh and Lindner hard on his heels. A further circuit was sufficient to convince the judges of his faulty style and he was ruled out just after being passed by his followers. The lightning pace also accounted for the departure of two of the East Germans. Matthews refused to let the pace lapse and even at this stage he and Vickers were visibly straining to do the utmost. For every yard of the way it looked as though the Midlander was making "a last desperate effort" to shake off his Belgrave rival; and for every yard of the way it looked as though Vickers would hold on for no longer. "Time at one mile, 6 minutes 30.2 seconds" roared the Tannoy in it's effort to overcome the crowd's cheering, but few heard. All could sense that the record would go but I have never been so uncertain of a result as I was on this occasion. Was it humanly possible to actually walk past a man travelling at Matthew's speed? The mile and a half was reached in 9:51.4, averaging 98.6 a lap! And still the two raced round in tandem a full straight ahead of East Germany's Lindner. (Cont'd. on previous page) (Cont'd. from p 24) A penultimate lap of 99.6 saw them thro' the bell requiring only a 100 second circuit for the record. It must fall. Excitement raced to fever pitch as all attention focussed on the desperate duel to see who would hold the new mark. Matthews appeared to accellerate round the first bend determined to hold off Vickers at all cost but when he hit the back straight he seemed to falter, just momentarily, and that settled it. Vickers was past in a flash. His accelleration was astonishing. All those repetition 220's and 440's at Battersea were now paying off and his initial burst took him into the last bend 20 yards clear. Matthews recovered well and for a spell actually reduced the gap but Vickers gave him no chance as his final burst carried him thro' the tape in a new record of 13:02.4, 9 seconds inside the old mark. It was only justice that Ken Matthews also got inside the old mark, by 1.8 secs. And so our two greatest ever walkers jogged round the track to receive the acclaim of the crowd. Their record will stand for a long long while. Neither would rate this race near the top of their achievements. The Olympic Gold of Matthews and the European Gold and Olympic Bronze of Vickers make it seem very small fry indeed. But, for me, all the qualities of these two fine athletes were displayed to the full in just 13 minutes of this July day seven years ago and only through this contest do I remember the other events of that year. items.s: YOUTHS & BOYS Reg Hopkins reports on the growing Boys Section and gives the final points tables of the H. Shields Cup (Youths), won by Michael Franks, and the Ryan Cup (Boys), won by David Wilkinson, with a photograph of three youths. There are now over fifty active members in our Boys Section, writes REG.HOPKINS, and more are joining every week. The record at the moment stands at twenty-two applications in one week! The fame of our younger members is spreading throughout South London and many local schoolmasters are sending promising youngsters along to Battersea Park to take advantage of our coaching, etc. One person in particular who has introduced us to several young athletes is Charles Elliott, senior AAA coach and Editor of 'Arena'. We are most grateful. An interesting point to note is that many of our Boys are mainly interested in Field Events, a trend which if nation-wide could solve some of Britain's athletic problems. The Youths and Boys Medal Competitions have drawn to a close once again and have had more support than ever before. Congratulations to all who took part. Thirty-one members competed in the Ryan Cup for Boys, the winner being Javelin thrower David Wilkinson 3 points clear of Bill Curtin with Bob Williams 3rd. Michael Franks, the Youths winner, was most impressive scoring the maximum 100 points. items.s: MAY 28th - BRACKNELL - CAMBERLEY YOUNG ATHLETES MEETING Nigel Bacon reports on the Camberley Young Athletes Meeting at Bracknell, where Bill Curtin won the 880y and David Wilkinson placed in the javelin and shot. NIGEL BACON REPORTS:- Over 700 entries had been received from as far apart as Scotland and Cornwall for this, the largest meeting in Britain apart from the All-England Schools. All the Bels. competing did well but the best of the bunch were David Wilkinson who has great potential in the throws and who placed 3rd in the Javelin and 4th in the Shot, and Bill Curtin looking every inch a champion and winning the 'half' with a devastating last 60 yards. The Boys were really grateful to chauffeur Reg.Hopkins and the long trip to Bracknell was even more worth while when certain members of the team made contact with the female members of Coventry Godiva ! items.h: ROAD RUNNING It's that man again!
items.sum: Road running gossip: a letter from Derek Palframan in South Africa about Trevor Hart, a joke about Pat Newell's training and Glimpy Jones beating Brian Hewson over 3000m.
items.s: ROAD RUNNING It's that man again! Road running gossip: a letter from Derek Palframan in South Africa about Trevor Hart, a joke about Pat Newell's training and Glimpy Jones beating Brian Hewson over 3000m. Derek Palframan writes from Pietermaritzburg, South Africa and tells how much he enjoys reading THE BELGRAVIAN. "It is with great interest that I read about all the chaps I met whilst staying at Lauriston Cottage. I still can't believe that the Hart you people talk about is the same bloke I knew!" Well, well. First Australia, now South Africa. We wonder what it is that makes Trevor so well remembered by our overseas members. You tell us. We might even publish the best suggestion! * * * * * We have it on good authority that the reason for Pat Newell being so unfit lately is because he is only doing 60 miles a week in training. * * * * * "EUROPEAN CHAMPION BEATEN BY'UNKNOWN' FULHAM GAS FITTER"........... ......there could have been the headlines when a few weeks ago Glimpy Jones (& Others!!) got the edge on a certain Brian Hewson over 3000m at the Duke of York's, but, as Glimpy himself put it---"I've done it nine b......., years too late"!!!--we feel it is only fair to point out that since this epic run Brian Hewson has got very much fitter with the result that Glimpy (and Co.) have thought it wise not to hold a return match! items.label: September 1967
items.sum: Humorous report of the rain-soaked and badly marked Camberley 5 road race on 24 June, where Brian Bacon of Reading was adjudged the winner, with Trevor Hart first Belgravian and Belgrave third team.
items.s: CAMBERLEY CAPERS Humorous report of the rain-soaked and badly marked Camberley 5 road race on 24 June, where Brian Bacon of Reading was adjudged the winner, with Trevor Hart first Belgravian and Belgrave third team. 24th June - Camberley '5' Black thunder clouds during the early afternoon of June 24th did not augur well for a summer's afternoon sport. Sure enough, as the runners were arriving, the skies opened and the deluge began. This was not the only 'shower' the athletes had to contend with - the organisation of this race was in the hands of people who could politely be called drips (excuse the Sam Ferris type pun). After changing in a (very) small marquee, the runners lined up in pouring rain and after being told to do one lap of the (grass) track set off on their wet way. Immediately the absence of markers became apparent. Half the leading bunch turned to complete a full lap whilst others headed straight out of the nearest gate. The latter proved to be the more popular course. Soon, however, the field sorted itself out with Steer and Hart with the leaders and Dabbs and Mann close by; having started rather less impetuously. O'Connor and Merry were near at hand but Bernard later paid for his fast start. The race progressed and the leaders gradually became more strung out, only pausing occasionally to ask the way. At 3 miles the leaders were Merriman (Reading) and Gevers (SLH) with Hart, Steer and Dabbs in convoy in 7th, 8th and 10th places. At this point the Belgrave runners were suprised to see a car suddenly scream to a halt beside them and the occupant pointing feverishly in the opposite direction. It seemed the leaders had missed a turning. Trevor and John Snowdon (Surrey) gently suggested that the leaders should be informed whereupon the driver set off Surtees style after them - they had a considerable lead by this time. Eventually all the runners were corrected and Trevor was suprised to find himself in the lead since all those in front had to retrace their steps. Needless to say most people had ceased to regard the race with any seriousness and merely ran to finish the course and get in out of the rain. For the record Brian Bacon (Reading) was adjudged to have won and Belgrave were given third team place. The medals were nice though....... items.sum: Report and results of the Polytechnic Marathon, in which Charlie Dabbs was 16th to take the Club Championship and Belgrave fifth in the Southern AAA team race.
items.s: The POLY Report and results of the Polytechnic Marathon, in which Charlie Dabbs was 16th to take the Club Championship and Belgrave fifth in the Southern AAA team race. On paper our prospects looked very good and although our final team positions were much improved on recent years we have still yet to gain any major successes in this event. The weather was very humid at the start and when the first significant time checks were taken at 10m Trevor Hart's position only 1½ minutes behind the leaders posed the problem as to whether he could keep it up in this his first Marathon. Charlie Dabbs, Lionel Mann and Chris Steer were following more cautiously some 3 minutes farther back. At 15m Trevor looked very 'shakey' and was finally forced at 16m to retire, to fight, we hope, another time. By now Chris was leading Charlie by over a minute, a pos- he held till around the 20m mark when Charlie's experience over the longer journey began to tell. He gradually pulled Chris back to take something like 6 minutes off him in the final 2m, to finish in 16th position and take the Club Championship. Chris finished very tired and 'weak at the knees' but had achieved a creditable time in his first ever marathon. Lionel Mann also having his first outing over the distance finished looking just as strong at the end as he had at the start - although he probably didn't feel that way! Alan Bishop was our fourth scoring man in the Open Race just getting the better of ever-green Geoff Pearson, who none the less ensured we had all our runners inside 3hrs. items.s: The Cheltenham 7 Light-hearted report and results of the Cheltenham 7 road race, with Charlie Dabbs first Belgravian in 11th and Belgrave 'A' fifth team. Most of the ten Belgravians who made the long trip to this haven of retired gentlefolk arrived well before the evening start and spent the intervening hours variously drinking beer, sun-bathing and generally loafing about. These activities probably accounted for the poor showing of one or two runners. Gordon Biscoe only just made the start after spending the afternoon on a nature study ramble (that was his story anyway). The large field including strong contingents from several leading Midland clubs, started down the Promenade which was packed with spectators. Encouraged by the cheers from several young ladies from the local 'Comprehensive' Chris Steer went immediately to the front and at 2 miles (9:45) was still with the leaders. The price of such vanity was swift and painful as a large part of the field gradually swept by. Charlie Dabbs ran his usual wily race and held his position well but towards the end of the race was in danger of being caught by the amazingly versatile Lionel Mann (the only man in England who can make crepes suzettes and run a 1hr. 56m. '20'). Don Maclean showed he is returning to fitness by beating drinking partner Chris Keavey and Gordon Biscoe, who was still looking rather flushed after his exertions during the afternoon. items.s: 20% Belgrave Report and results of the Bracknell 5 miles on 5 August, where Belgrave fielded five teams, finishing second team and winning the 'B' team prize. BRACKNELL 5 MILES---5TH AUGUST When reporting this race last year we bemoaned the lack of a good third man to complete our scoring team and put us among the awards. It is therefore now good to report that we made amends this year, by having 5 teams doing battle over this very pleasant traffic--free course, where we succeeded in taking 2nd team and first 'B' team prizes. With a very fast pace set throughout by Bruce Tulloh(Ports) our A team packed in extremely well, with Laurie O'Hara just managing to get the better of Tony Fairclough after they had come back into the track together. Gerry North completed the scoring three, making a welcome return after a prolonged injury to the knee. Dick Piotrowski making his debut for us on the road and his first outing as a first claim member fully justified his 'A' team selection just beating our old friend Mel Thorpe (Coventry G)--our second man home in 1966. Whilst Messrs. Hart, Steer, and Mann quietly set about securing the 'B' team prizes for themselves, other titanic struggles were going on further down the field. Up and coming Pat O'Connor put in another very strong run whilst Eric Penny took nearly two minutes off his last year's time. John Walker, inspite of a recent spell of "special coaching and altitude training" by brother Charlie in the Isle of Wight, found Charlie Smart just too good for him again, as did Glimpy Jones---rumours that Glimpy travelled down overnight and went round the course in the morning have not yet been proved!. 110. items.s: Boxed news of overseas members: Barry Sawyer winning Victoria's 'King of the Mountains' 20 miles in Australia, and Ranjit Bhatia in India congratulating John Thresher and John Bicourt. Barry Sawyer won the Victorian "King of the Mountains" 20 mile race in Australia and now has his name inscribed alongside that of past winner Percy Cerutty. His time was a speedy 1:50:25. The same week(!) he won an open '16' in 84:35 so his form is still pretty good. Barry sends his congratulations to John Thresher but, in true Cerutty fashion, says "It's about time though that John ran that 4 minute mile---he should re-organise his training and set his sights higher". Phew! What do you say about that John? Another to congratulate John on his fine Southern win is Ranjit Bhatia who also acknowledges John Bicourt's excellent run in the Inter-Counties steeplechase. Many Indians probably think Ranjit has gone mad for he has adopted the English practice of training in the midday sun! Even a shade temperate of 111 F has not deterred him. Ranjit finds thirst to be more of a problem than fatigue. Funny---so do Don Maclean and Linstead! items.sum: Report and results of the 16th Belgrave 20 miles road race at Wimbledon on 22 July, won by Jim Wright of Tipton, with Charlie Dabbs seventh and Belgrave 'A' fourth team.
items.s: BELGRAVE 20 Report and results of the 16th Belgrave 20 miles road race at Wimbledon on 22 July, won by Jim Wright of Tipton, with Charlie Dabbs seventh and Belgrave 'A' fourth team. Hard working Gordon Biscoe gained the reward that all race secretaries look for when he received a record entry of 180 runners for the 16th annual Belgrave '20' at Wimbledon on July 22nd. Road works at Tibbet's Corner had made the organisation particularly difficultand required quite a few hours perambulating a surveyors wheel around the course to ensure that the proper distance was covered. Work like this is not only wearying- it can be compromising. What was Gordon to say when interviewed by the long arm of the law in the small hours while busy outside the Vietnamese Embassy with a brush and a bucket of white paint. The conversation can be imagined. It certainly started with the words " 'Allo, 'allo, 'allo. What's all this 'ere then?" Road race secretaries are never taken aback, however. "Aha," says Gordon, "I'm painting mile markers on the road so that the runners in the Belgrave '20' know how much suffering has been and how much is to come." Anyway, a persuasive chap, Gordon. All the marks were there for the race. Graham Taylor, who set a magnificent course record of 1hr.39m.47s. the previous year, was unfortunately prevented from turning out by injury, and with the withdrawal by Peter Yates, the race seemed from the start to lie between Scottish international Jim Wright of Tipton, and Barry Collins of Surrey AC. The 126 starters soon sorted themselves out in three groups of varying speed, and were soon sweating nicely on an oppressively hot day, with Wright and Collins well up and Barry Watson, last year's third man also well to the fore but soon to retire. By the end of the first of the three main laps, the groups had broken up. Every man for himself. At this stage, the Bels chances for the team race looked bright. Charlie Dabbs, Bill Dance, Chris Steer and Lionel Mann were all well placed. In the individual competition, Wright had cut out in front and Collins was a clear second. The individual places at the head of the field showed little change after that - except for a strong breakthrough in the later stages by Dai Davies of T.V.H. and K.Darlow of Reading, who who finished 4th and 5th respectively - D.McFadzean (RNAC South) having sorted out a comfortable third place for himself. The team picture altered drastically, however, as first Chris Steer and then Bill Dance was forced to retire. Thames Valley kept going well to take the race, with Paignton gaining a popular place as runners-up, and Cambridge H third. The Bels "A" squad of Charlie Dabbs - another to move through strongly as the race went on, finishing up in 7th place - Lionel Mann, 15th, and John Hilton, 44th, was fourth. Charlie and Lionel were first and second in the Belgrave Championship, but third place went to the first "B" team runner, John Baker, who was 38th in 2hrs.08m.01s. John has only just switched from walking to running and has made a quick impact. We look forward to even better things from him in the future. items.label: September 1967
items.sum: Clive Shippen previews Belgrave's autumn road relay season, reviewing last year's results, the candidates for selection and the autumn fixture list (continued on page 23).
items.s: Autumn Relay Prospects Clive Shippen previews Belgrave's autumn road relay season, reviewing last year's results, the candidates for selection and the autumn fixture list (continued on page 23). Clive Shippen Reviews the forthcoming Road Relay season Of the six autumn road relay races held last year we chalked up 2 wins (Belgrave and Walton), 2 seconds (Johnstone and Blackheath), 1 fifth (Surrey) and 1 sixth (Bristol/Weston). A fair performance---but there were weaknesses. The Surrey County event at Woking Lido is a notorious one. The holiday season affects it every year and our multi-county membership also restricts our entry, but we could still field stronger teams than hitherto. The venue is in a most pleasant setting with the start and finish in the park, on grass, and the amenities of the Lido available afterwards. Perhaps the atmosphere is not "cut-throat" enough for us! With John Bicourt not expected back from North America until late September, if at all, we are weakened even before Bill Lucas sends out his selection cards. Nevertheless, a team from Gerry North, Thresher, Black, Fairclough, Steer, Major and Dance should stand an excellent chance of pulling off the title---providing no more than one cries off! Non-Surrey men can take part in the 'B' and 'C' teams and with names like Geoff North, O'Hara, Hart, Piotrowski, Kerr, Dear, Williams, and Buxton there could be a ONE/TWO in it for BELGRAVE. Little has been seen of Gerry Williams and Brian Buxton since June and we hope they will be fit and available once more during the coming weeks. With Mel Thorpe's departure to Coventry Godiva Harriers we were doubly pleased to welcome Dick Piotrowski to our ranks. Dick, formerly a member of Bracknell AC, is stationed with the Guards at Chelsea Barracks (just local to ur training tracks at Battersea and the Duke of York's) and has become first-claim Belgrave under the hard-cases rule. He has turned in a 9:16 steeplechase and already proved his worth as a replacement for Mel by beating him in the Bracknell '5' road race--albeit by a few seconds. Another missing from our Belgrave Relay dozen of last year is Joe Reilly, but with Geoff North standing down on that occasion we should be stronger this year, despite the loss of Mel and Joe. If Peter Whewell is still with us in early October and Bill Kerr and Adrian Major can keep free of injury then our depth should carry us through to some big wins. One event we should win for the third successive year is our own Open Relay. With twelve stages involved we have a clear advantage over Portsmouth and TVH, our only serious rivals. But what of that 8-stage classic the Bristol/Weston?. Well, our eight runners will have to run about five minutes faster than last year to win it. Looking at last year's result shows just what they are up against. Gerry has yet to regain his form of 12 months ago and even if he does so in time can Dance, Fairclough, and Bicourt run a joint 4 mins-20secs faster than they did last year when we found ourselves 13th after three stages? Yes, the Bristol/Weston is as tough a nut to crack as the National, but with five weeks of selection ahead of it we have every opportunity of finding the right eight for the job. There is another 12 stage relay, other than our own promotion. This is Hornchurch Harriers' "Johnstone" relay to be held on Sunday September 24th. Our performance last year was better than our "National" effort 6 months later, for we finished second to Coventry by a 1:40 margin and had Tipton, Longwood, Manchester and Derby behind us for good measure. These latter teams have all improved since and we will have to raise ourselves even to maintain a second placing. The Blackheath Road Relay clashes with our non-championship '5¾' again this year, so one team only will be sent to Blackheath to put right that 3 seconds defeat by Portsmouth. Meanwhile our own race will be setting out to establish form for the three big relays and a battle royal can be anticipated from the expected 40 strong field. Each time we approach the Spring or Autumn road-relay season there are a few members who assume they are automatic selections. Be warned! All the dark horses are at peak fitness and there is invariably someone who records a "breakthrough". No one can afford to be complacent. Remember, even Geoff North could only make first reserve position last year in our Open Relay, yet 3 months earlier he was running for Great Britain versus U.S.S.R!. To remind our runners of the competition they might have from within the Club I name just seventeen candidates. Before anyone takes their place for granted I suggest they note the names carefully and assume that all of their rivals are running betterthan ever before---because the twelve that are picked probably will be! A. Black J. Bicourt A. Buxton C. Dabbs W. Dance A. Fairclough T. Hart W. Kerr A. Major Gerry North Geoff North L. O'Hara R. Piotrowski C. Steer J. Thresher P. Whewell G. Williams At least five of these will have to stand down---still confident? With Pat Newell, John Dear, and Lionel Mann (amongst others) also waiting for an opportunity to nip in I would say the position of every runner is precarious to say the least. And remember, experience has shown it unwise to rely on one good effort for selection. (Cont'd. on p.23) (Cont'd. from p.34) The Autumn fixtures are as follows. Why not telephone Bill Lucas now and tell him of your plans and state of fitness? Close contact with Bill (660-2576) will help both you and the selectors. Last year our tally was 2 firsts, 2 seconds, 1 fifth and 1 sixth. This year let us erase the memory of those fifth and sixth positions. items.label: December 1967
items.sum: Editorial welcoming the AAA's proposed national track and field league, hoping Belgrave's trophy wins earn an invitation, and saying farewell to co-editor Alan Mead.
items.s: EDITORIAL Editorial welcoming the AAA's proposed national track and field league, hoping Belgrave's trophy wins earn an invitation, and saying farewell to co-editor Alan Mead. "Good order is the foundation of all good things" Edmund Burke. The newly formed Organisation & Development Committee of the A.A.A. under the secretaryship of Mike Fleet, wasted no time in producing a draft plan for transforming the chaos that is our summer season into a state of highly competitive order. In the March edition of "THE BELGRAVIAN" we referred to "--a chaotic summer programme--little short of farcical" and called for some form of National Championship through the Area Associations. Mike Fleet's outline proposals go much further. A National league of 3 divisions supported by a wide base of local leagues is planned and all recognised track and field events, including the 4 x 110 and 4 x 440 relays but excluding the six miles, staged. What a tonic for the cinderella events this will be. With 2 men per event it is doubtful whether any club will begin the programme with a pair of recognised performers in every field event, but there is no better way of encouraging the emergence of such men. Each division would contain six clubs who would meet each other, all together, on three occasions. Promotion and relegation would be two up and two down. Competition of this sort is almost certain to herald a breakthrough in field events standards and, on this score, Belgrave badly need a recognised hammer thrower. When finalised, the scheme will probably begin to operate in 1969. A pilot scheme is likely in 1968 but Belgrave have received no invitation to take part, despite our enthusiasm. It would seem that the "Birds Eye" trophy rankings will be used as a yardstick to begin with, but these are not a true indication of strength for the competition as planned. The "Birds Eye" rankings are based on a restricted number of events by a restricted number of athletes and in no way reflect the strength of a possibly 40 strong team. We can only hope that our four trophy wins of last season (including the Brockman) will earn us an invitation. If not we all know how to prove them wrong in 1968. * * * * * It is with sincere regret that the longer serving half of your Editorship says farewell to his partner Alan Mead, who has been obliged to resign. Alan's enthusiasm and artistic approach to the Gazette's layout will be sorely missed, to say nothing of his typing ability and knowledge of the younger set. Fortunately he is not lost to the Club, his resignation being due to the commencement of a career in the Metropolitan Police so we are still likely to see his mark from time to time within these pages. In the meantime if anyone feels a post of this sort to be his metier then he will be most welcome. The Editor is indebted to GWEN COUZENS for her help in preparing this issue. Edmund Burke Edmund Burke Mike Fleet Mike Fleet Alan Mead Alan Mead Gwen Couzens GWEN COUZENS AAA National League (proposed) Birds Eye trophy rankings Brockman Trophy 1967 A.A.A.

items.sum: Hon. Secretary's notes: Les Cohen's AAA Award of Merit, Frank Jarvis's RWA (Southern Area) presidency, a tribute to retiring Walking Hon. Secretary Jack Goswell, club colours, the AAA Indoor Championships and higher AAA fees.
items.s: HON SEC'S NOTES Hon. Secretary's notes: Les Cohen's AAA Award of Merit, Frank Jarvis's RWA (Southern Area) presidency, a tribute to retiring Walking Hon. Secretary Jack Goswell, club colours, the AAA Indoor Championships and higher AAA fees. At the Annual General Meeting of the Amateur Athletic Association, Les Cohen was presented with the A.A.A. Award of Merit by the Marquess of Exeter, who discussed the great work Les has carried through for Amateur Athletics over so many years. Needless to say the presentation was received with enthusiasm, and in reply Les said how happy he was to be able to put back into the sport something in return for the years of pleasure he had enjoyed as an active athlete. We heartily congratulate Les on this honour in which we as fellow Belgravians can take great pride, and we hope he will be able to continue making his great contribution to athletics at all levels for many years to come. * * * * * Congratulations also to our immediate Past President Frank Jarvis who now becomes President of the Race Walking Association (Southern Area) and doubles up this position with the Hon Secretaryship of the Association. * * * * * At our recent A.G.M. Jack Goswell (as he had notified us a year earlier) did not seek re-election as Walking Hon Secretary. For fifteen years Jack has done great work for our walkers and the Club and we thank him most sincerely for all his efforts. We are quite sure he will still be there to give a helping hand whenever required, and to assist in the building up of more and more successful Belgrave teams. Jack took over the Walking interests of the Club at a time when our triumphs of a few years earlier had flattened out to something rather more ordinary. Nothing to be ashamed of but just lacking that extra punch and effort which turns the good performance into the unbeatable. This Jack quickly supplied. His enthusiasm, unfailing hard work and selfless labour met with due reward. Numbers increased, quality of performance was raised, organisation of events was perfected and Belgrave stood high in the world of walking. Our recrutment of new walkers and systematic and regular training as organised by Jack gave us individual champions and champion teams. Our Olympic and European Games walkers owed him much, as did every walker wearing a Belgrave vest. Jack's thoroughness was never more evident than on a long distance road event when he never spared himself in the care and encouragment of our teams. And he still had breath - if permitted - to play the piccolo on the way home. Later Jack was the inevitable choice to become Championship Hon. Sec. to the Race Walking Association and right well did he carry through his tasks until resigning in September last. Jack has been a very popular Belgrave President and is an elected Life Member. He has also been President and Chairman of the R.W.A. (Southern Area) and is a Vice President of the Race Walking Association. He has lived intensively for walking for fifteen years without a break (and let us here pay tribute to his wife Joan who has also rendered terrific service) and we know his heart is so much with sport that we shall continue to enjoy his help and support on all possible occasions. Thank you Jack, your work has been immense and our gratitude is boundless. * * * * * Reference was made at the Annual Meeting to the fact that some members wore other than Club vests in training and racing and urging all members to wear the Club colours at all times. It is to be hoped that all members will bear this in mind and show their pride in the Club by wearing its official colours, and also enable the newcomer to identify his club mates to the advantage of all. * * * * * The A.A.A. Indoor Championships will be held at R.A.F. Cosford on Friday & Saturday February 2nd & 3rd. Entries close on January 8th. * * * * * Application fees to the A.A.A. have been increased and as one of the larger clubs we shall now be called upon to pay £20.per annum, and shall be entitled to have five representative members attend an Annual or Special General Meeting. items.label: December 1967
items.sum: New President Ted Stimpson thanks members for electing him and sets out his hopes for the year, including a major cross-country title.
items.s: THE PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE New President Ted Stimpson thanks members for electing him and sets out his hopes for the year, including a major cross-country title. Dear Belgravians, May I say thank you very much for electing me as your President for the coming year. Like all past Presidents I trust that I shall have a successful year of office, and I know that I will have the backing of all members in each section. It is certainly a great help to have such a first class set of officers and committee men to assist me. It would give me great pleasure this year to go one step further than our immediate past President, Frank Jarvis, and win more than one outstanding Championship, and I would very much like to see our cross country men win a major title, either the Southern or the National. The walkers I know will do their best, and the continued success of the track and field events men, I hope will continue. Under the guidance of Tom Carter and Reg Hopkins I am sure our youths and boys will progress still further. Success in any club always comes from having a good social side. We are very fortunate in having this and are, no doubt, the envy of other clubs, so please continue to give your support to our new Social Secretary, and do not forget to bring your wives and girl friends in to this important side of our activities. In closing, I would like to thank the editors of the magazine, and our press reporters for their outstanding work in bringing this great club of ours to the notice of the public. Our press coverage is first class, so would all section officers send their details after all races to the reporters, who will be only too happy to spread our name in the news. Lastly, I would like to welcome all new members to our club, and wish them every success in the future. Ted Stimpson Ted Stimpson Ted Stimpson Frank Jarvis Frank Jarvis Tom Carter Tom Carter Reg Hopkins Reg Hopkins Southern Cross Country Championships 1968 National Cross Country Championships 1968

items.label: December 1967
items.sum: Profile of new President Ted Stimpson, tracing his running career from joining in 1934 through junior cross-country titles and 1939 international selection to his war service and club work.
items.s: Our President - TED STIMPSON Profile of new President Ted Stimpson, tracing his running career from joining in 1934 through junior cross-country titles and 1939 international selection to his war service and club work. TED STIMPSON joined us in June 1934 and quickly made his mark by winning an 880 yds. handicap off 70 yds. in 1 min.56.2 secs. at our Club Track Championships Meeting on August 11th. Our scribe wrote "E.S. Stimpson, 18½ years of age, showed style and ability in taking the 880 yds. handicap. He should develop into a club champion with maturer years." Two or three months later Ted ran in the Club Junior Cross-Country Championship for the SAVAGE Shield and finished third behind George Chandler and our present Hon. Treasurer Joe Flower, always a good judge of a runner wrote at the time "Stimpson ran splendidly. He has nothing like the experience of the other two, but I like his style and determination and feel confident he will make a good name for himself as a cross country runner." A few weeks later Stimpson ran third in the Middlesex County Junior Cross-country Championship at Northolt, and our tame prophet wrote "ran exceedingly well to finish in third place. With another years strength and experience he should win this event." Well Ted did continue to gain strength and experience and on Dec.2nd 1935 he won the Savage Shield. A week or two later, as prophesied above, Ted distinguished himself by winning the Middlesex Junior Championship. His appetite whetted, he won the Southern Counties Junior cross-country championship at Sandown Park "running a clever race, using his head as well as his legs and in perfect style came away in the last mile to win comfortably. Golden opinions were heard everywhere not only on the achievement but on the manner of its performance." Two weeks earlier Ted had led our South of the Thames team to a convincing victory, finishing sixth himself and incidentally we also won the "Colman Cup" for being the first club to finish its complete team of twelve, a habit we must strive to regain. Later in the year he ran in our winning London - Brighton Relay team, our third successive win. 1938 was a quiet year for Ted but in the first few days of January 1939 he finished second in the Middlesex Cross-country championship, and the Cadogan A.C. team (consisting entirely of Belgrave runners as follows:- Stimpson 2, D. Patience 4, Shields 7, Allum 14, Tobin 15, F.R. Webb 17) were easy victors. Third place in the club "10" behind Penny and Carter, was succeded by sixth place in the Southern when Belgrave could only manage third team position in a close fought race. But compensation came a fortnight later when Belgrave beat Birchfield for the English title and Ted Stimpson finished a gallant fourth and gained International selection with Arthur Penny who finished eighteen seconds behind him. Before another season could come round war had overtaken us and Ted Stimpson was serving in the Royal Artillery. Undoubtedly, but for the war, Ted would have recorded many further International selections, but, as for many others, the years when he would have reached his peak performances were given over to more serious matters. News came through in 1943 that he was now married, that he was a sergeant, and was retiring from running as he was now 28 years of age. However later on he was running almost as well as ever with B.A.O.R. Following his return home Ted found, as did so many, the need to concentrate on his career and whilst he still ran, he could not hope to find his old brilliance. Nevertheless, he turned out whenever possible and helped to pass on his experience to the new generation that had grown up. Growing business claims prevented Ted from playing the part in Club life he would have wished for several years, but when circumstances permitted he embraced the opportunity of putting something back and working on Committee and on the Social side of the Club. He was elected a Life Member of the Club and has now been called upon to be President by unanimous vote at the Annual General Meeting. We know he will be a very worthy President, that he will inspire and guide our efforts and that the club year ahead of us will be a memorable one. For our part we offer him all our support and all our good wishes in his year of office. A.A.H. Ted Stimpson TED STIMPSON TED STIMPSON E.S. Stimpson Ted Stimpson Ted Stimpson A.A.H. A.A.H.
