items.label: December 1967
items.sum: Members' letters: Barry Sawyer on Australian athletics and his marathons, George Piddington on becoming Vice President, Derek Boosey's 1967 triple jumps, Percy Wilson's praise and complaints about missing prizes, and Rangit Bhatia's Indian cross-country season (concluded on page 38).
items.s: Postbag: Members' letters: Barry Sawyer on Australian athletics and his marathons, George Piddington on becoming Vice President, Derek Boosey's 1967 triple jumps, Percy Wilson's praise and complaints about missing prizes, and Rangit Bhatia's Indian cross-country season (concluded on page 38). BARRY SAWYER is still very close to that king of the coaches, Percy Cerutty. Barry found himself quite shocked recently when he found the 72 yrs old Cerutty looking tired after a weightlifting exhibition at a sports store. "He has such an air of indestructibility and agelessness that you don't expect him to have normal human failings". Barry writes that athletics like all sports is fiercely competitive in Australia, "quite a contrast to the English garden-party meets". In the track season, clubs are divided into 3 geographical groups to compete weekly in a 3 months competition. Events are arranged into two programmes, held alternate weeks. All events are graded and standards set that must be attained to score points (it's not enough to just win). With this the only inter-club contest available "you either get on or you get out". The top 4 clubs in each area then compete in a knock-out competition for "group premier" and then a "Grand Final" is held between the three winners. There is also a cross-country championship based on three races, at 5 miles, 10,000 metres and 10 miles (6 to score) and a road running title based on three races also, a 6 x 4 miles relay, 10 miles and a 15 mile road runs. Barry is studying hard, but still managed to run 3 marathons in four weeks during August and September. The times tell the story though, 2.28.13 (9th), 2.31.32 (1st) and 2.37.27 (8th). Nevertheless these were times still good enough to put him ahead of Ron Clarke, Dave Power, Ian Sinfield and Fred Howe. * * * * * GEORGE PIDDINGTON writes from Hayling Island expressing his appreciation of the Club's decision to elect him Vice President. "In spite of living a long way away now, I hope I shall still be able to put as much back into the Club as the enjoyment I have had in being a member". George, of course, attends many of our fixtures and functions and on several occassions has had to walk the last 7 miles home late at night. He now has a car though and has passed his driving test " - - - 6th time lucky! At the moment, like Trevor Hart's running, it has broken down and the other evening blew up!" * * * * * Our International triple-jumper DEREK BOOSEY tells us that he recorded no less than 15 leaps over 50'0" this year. Despite this he never quite reached his best ever performance of 51'11". His travels took him to France and America during which time he clocked an "evens" 100 yds. For the record, his leading performances were as follows:- May - San Jose - 51'8½" (2nd) June - A.A.U. Championships (California U.S.A.) - 51'0½" (5th) July - Santa Monica - 50'7½" (2nd) July - A.A.A. Championships - 50'3" (2nd) July - La Baule (France) - 51'0" (1st) Sept - Solihull - 50'5¾" (3rd) Derek is now studying physical education at Madeley College and hopes to wear our colours more often next season. * * * * * Our old friend PERCY WILSON writes to express his pleasure at Ted Stimpson's election as Our President and also his appreciation of another Alan Bishop outing in the R.R.C. London - Brighton Run. "I was present at the Chequers, Horley, and as he came along I could not help shouting "Up the Bels" - after all he was wearing a Belgrave vest - Well done sir!" In throwing out the bouquet Percy also serves a sprinkling of brick-bats. He refers to our President's first handicap presentation. "As Ted stood on the stage he was a very disappointed man - - - the prizes had not arrived. Around me there were cries of 'what again' and 'cor blimey' - not a very nice thing to hear from a Belgravian. I felt sorry for you Ted. On the 7th October one of the handicap winners of the 5 miles road walk was a new member from Guernsey and again there were no prizes to present - a great show down for Belgrave. Why,oh! Why,does this have to go on; it has always been said that Belgrave do things properly,well please let us see it done in the proper way". * * * * * RANGIT BHATIA tells of his promising start in the Indian cross-country season. In the Delhi State Championships he was 10th, just good enough to (Cont'd at foot of opposite page) (Cont'd from opposite) make the State team, but when the National came round he finished a praiseworthy fifth over the 9 miles course. Rangit is trying hard to popularise athletics in India and is always an excellent host to visiting athletes. He hopes his Athletic Association will soon start inviting runners from various parts of the world. "If you should know of anyone planning to visit Delhi in the near future please don't hesitate to let him contact me if he wants a holiday-cum-athletics stop over here". items.sum: Cross-country column by 'Countryman' on Peter Whewell's place in the team, Belgrave's chances in the 1968 National, a cartoon of the flooded Wimbledon Common course by Arthur Bruce, and the team's obligations to fellow members.
items.s: A COUNTRYMAN'S JOTTINGS Cross-country column by 'Countryman' on Peter Whewell's place in the team, Belgrave's chances in the 1968 National, a cartoon of the flooded Wimbledon Common course by Arthur Bruce, and the team's obligations to fellow members. When Peter Whewell joined us just after the last "National" following his appearances here with the South African cross-country team, no one really knew how he would fit in with Belgrave affairs - if at all. After all, he was only going to be here a few months and it is not uncommon for such internationals to merely use club membership as a vehicle for entering certain selected races. Well, not only did he settle in within a matter of days but this popular Chesire-born runner has shown himself to be cast in the true Belgrave mould. Apart from being a reliable runner, he is a good team man who is not frightened to turn out when short of training. Like Gerry North, Bill Dance and Laurie O'Hara his name seems to appear automatically in every team we field these days. The big question is, will he carry a Belgrave vest in the "National" next March ? There is no doubt that none of our team would begrudge him a place, so well has he been received, and he almost certainly would make our nine. Unfortunately, for Belgrave at any rate, Peter starts a university course in Johannesburg the same month and may well have to leave here two weeks or so before cross-country's premier event. I am sure that all Belgravians hope Peter will find some way to stay on and join them in the champagne celebrations after the National. * * * * * Speaking of the National, what are our chances really? Well, last year we were disappointed with our 4th place (nearly 5th) and Gerry North and John Thresher had disappointing runs, yet we still beat Coventry, Derby, Tipton and Manchester. I bet many have forgotten that already. Portsmouth were unbeatable that day, with five home before our first man but now they are a spent force. Runners-up were North Staffs, now reputed to have broken up, and third Longwood, always an unpredictable outfit and undoubtedly suited to last years track-like course. Of the nine we fielded last year, Trevor Hart (4th scorer) is unlikely to make it but with any luck Geoff North, Peter Whewell and Brian Buxton will be fighting for a place which should result in our fielding a peak form outfit. Last year I called for 6 in 100 and 9 in 150. We achieved 6 in 114 and 9 in 140 yet finished fourth. We must obviously aim higher so how about 6 in 60 and 9 in 90 with one man every 10 places ! * * * * * WEATHER FORECAST-----"RAIN AGAIN" As is usual at this time of the year our course has been very wet; though it is never heavy. The "Avenue" looked more suitable for swimming than running a few weeks ago. Arthur Bruce sees it like this;- [cartoon] BELGRAVE TEAM IN TRAINING FOR FUTURE CHAMPIONSHIPS ON WIMBLEDON COMMON. LIFEBELT. GLUG! GLUG! GLUG! GLUG. TIMEKEEPER * * * * * When our team win an open event or championship it is a source of pride to all Belgravians. Those that will never be good enough to make the team and those that are well past appearing in it, together share the joy and satisfaction of those that were actually there. "We won on Saturday" says the scrubber, automatically linking himself to Gerry & Co., and the many readers of this Gazette who have not been to Belgrave Hall for many years find the words so much sweeter when they record a win. Our team would do well to remember from time to time that they have achieved selection from a club of over 500 members and that they are not the only ones with "butterflies" when a big race is on or who suffer bitter disappointments at a loss. Our runners therefore have at least a moral obligation to their fellow members. Perhaps they will bear this in mind next time they consider splitting forces and relinquishing a relay trophy, as happened in the Essex Beagles Relay/Bracknell '10' clash this year. items.s: NORTH SURREY LEAGUE Seniors/Juniors Race No. 1 Report and results of the first North Surrey League senior/junior race at Wimbledon on 28 October, won by Gerry North, with Belgrave adjudged team winners by 90 points and the club handicap result. Wimbledon - October 28th. What a day! Record fields, pouring rain, only two course markers, obliterated or missing numbers and the poorest turn out of officials ever. After two weeks of brain-teasing investigation Belgrave were adjudged winners of the first race by a margin of 90 points. This is a start they should hang on to for the three remaining fixtures. Gerry North showed himself to be approaching top form again and John Thresher indicated he will be a major force this winter. The Hercules/Wimbledon combine showed itself to be at least our match in depth and therefore a threat in succeeding matches. They had 22 in 100 compared with our 19. In the Belgrave Handicap,"old-stagers" Don Maclean and Mike Stearman tied for first place Third was that scourge of the handicapper, Jim Rimmer - he'll have his wings removed altogether soon! items.sum: Report and results of the South of Thames Junior cross-country championship at Swindon on 11 November, where a depleted Belgrave 'A' team were only 13th after winning the previous year.
items.s: SOUTH OF THAMES 'JUNIOR' Report and results of the South of Thames Junior cross-country championship at Swindon on 11 November, where a depleted Belgrave 'A' team were only 13th after winning the previous year. SWINDON 11th November Out of an entry of forty, we could only muster sixteen runners on the day which is a very poor showing when one considers that this is a race carrying barring clauses and thus restricting the competitors to "lesser lights". It is designed to give even the "scrubbers" a chance to run in club colours in large fields under championship conditions and the club must obviously consider whether the wastage of money on team entries, and in this case providing a coach for transport at small cost to the competitors, is warranted in future years. Having won this race last year it was necessary this time to find a completely new team and with Dick Piotrowski, John Dear, Roger Donnison, Lionel Mann, Malcolm Simms, Howard Satchell, Bob Glover and Pat O'Connor eligible we appeared to have a strong team but unfortunately Donnison, Mann, Simms and O'Connor were unable to appear and we lined up with a much depleted team. Dick Piotrowski,looking very strong,was prominent throughout and although dropping back a little on the third leg was easily our first finisher in 21st place. John Dear making a steady start was not able to get up to a good place and although our second scorer was a little disappointing. Howard Satchell shared a welcome return to form to be placed 66th and the fourth scorer was Bob Glover, also a little disappointing after recent performances. When the points were added up they came to 227 and this gave us only 13th place whereas we could well have been in the first six if we had fielded our best team. In the 'B' team Don Maclean set out to prove that he should have been nominated for the 'A' team and this he did very easily by finishing in front of two 'A' team nominees. The best performance in the 'B' team was without doubt John Kelly's who during the road relay season had been running well below his best but on this occasion came up to 136th which should encourage him for future races during the winter. items.s: Slip at Chigwell Report and results of the Essex Beagles cross-country relay at Chigwell Row on 11 November, where Belgrave finished third and lost the New Zealand Cup. Essex Beagles Cross-Country Relay. 11th November Last year, whilst our South of Thames Junior team were winning their title at West Wickham, our relay boys were annexing this Beagle's promotion with a convincing victory over Ealing/Southall & T.V.H. This year, whilst our South of Thames team were being drubbed to a lowly 13th place at Swindon, our relay team were obliged to give best to their two main rivals at Chigwell Row and relinquish their hold on the "New Zealand Cup." Once again, one disappointing run made all the difference. This time it was John Bicourt, who had been unwell the preceeding week, and would have withdrawn had our forces not been dispersed over three fixtures. Adrian Major got us off to a good start in 7th place and Fairclough and Buxton got us up to 3rd and 1st respectively. Bicourt then ran a minute below his normal form to hand over 4th to Whewell who cut back the deficit and gained a place with fourth fastest time of the day. Laurie O'Hara did all he could on the final lap to finish within 10 seconds of T.V.H. and 21 seconds of the winners. Pos Team Time 1. Ealing & Southall A.C. 84.20 2. Thames Valley H. 84.31 3. items.s: REIGATE----November 4th Belgrave win the Redhill & Reigate 6 x 2½ miles cross-country relay for the first time, with Gerry North fastest of the day. In terrible conditions of continuous rain, strong winds, thick mud and steep hills Belgrave pulled off their first ever win in this 6X2½ miles cross-country relay. Adrian Major brought us home in 6th place on the first stage but then Tony Fairclough ran one of his best stints for some time taking us into the lead. Peter Whewell, Bill Dance and Gerry North stretched it to considerable proportions; the latter doing fastest time of the day. Laurie O'Hara finished off as usual, with Gerry Stevens (Reading) chasing him hard, but he had the race well under control and finished comfortably 16 seconds ahead of his rivals. Pos Team Time 1. items.s: Gerry Keeps '7' Title Report and results of the Club 7 miles cross-country championship for the Blackstaffe Shield at Wimbledon on 2 December, retained by Gerry North from Peter Whewell and Laurie O'Hara, with Howard Satchell winning the handicap. Wimbledon--December 2nd Gerry North had no difficulty at all in retaining the "Blackstaffe" Shield from Peter Whewell and Laurie O'Hara. His time was 44 seconds slower than last year's when he was run much closer by brother Geoff and Thresher. These two, plus Hart and Fairclough, were missing this time so Whewell and O'Hara were favourites to gain the place medals. After the first lap the expected medallists still had the close company of Dabbs, Major and Bicourt with O'Hara towing them along at a snappy pace. Another lap was sufficient to shake off the opposition and going into the final circuit Gerry burst ahead to split up the trio for the first time. Gerry's times for the three laps were 14:45, 14:19 and 13:33 which speaks for itself. Peter and Laurie are both going very well and they also gained nearly a minute on their followers during that final lap. Bill Dance started 7 minutes late and there was some excitement to see how far he would get thro' the field. Not to be outdone in this sort of practice,Don Maclean set off no less than 12:15 in arrears! A first circuit of 19:00 indicated that he was not going out for a win and he politely informed the officials that they needn't wait up for him! The handicap went to Howard Satchell, who is showing good form these days,with Bonser second and Whewell a hard-earned third. Pos Name Handicap Time 1. Gerry North (SCR) 42:37 2. P. items.label: March 1968
items.sum: Editorial on governments withdrawing from the Mexico Olympics, warning that state-aided sport brings political strings.
items.s: EDITORIAL Editorial on governments withdrawing from the Mexico Olympics, warning that state-aided sport brings political strings. "He who pays the piper, calls the tune". Have you ever heard athletes talk of anything but athletics?. Are there any wives who doubt what the topic of conversation will be at social gatherings?. And when it comes to the dedicated athlete, is it not true that those outside the understanding atmosphere of the athletic club would regard him as selfish, inward looking?. Athletes may talk politics sometimes but other athletes never hear them do so---it is a non-political world. All the sadder then that international politics should be encroaching into it. Several GOVERNMENTS have recently announced their withdrawal from the Mexico Olympics. No one knows what their own Olympic Committees thought, least of all the athlete's views. In the political arena it doesn't matter what they think. One does not question the reasons for such actions, simply the procedures and their ramifications. Where will it all end? Will the United Nations soon be legislating on where international teams may compete?. Athletic Associations are bound by the laws of their country---those that are state sponsored are bound even tighter. We in Britain may have to hand the cap round at each Olympics, rely on commercial sponsorship and make do by our own efforts; but at least we run our own affairs, and the Government would get short shrift if it tried to speak for the AAA or BAAB. As tempting as it is to have lavish government support for athletics, is it really worth having the political strings that go with it?. On Thursday, March 14th, Mr Denis Howell, Minister of Sport turned down a back-bench suggestion that the Government should not continue to subsidise the British Olympic team for the 1968 Games in Mexico in view of the racially segregated team from South Africa. Mr. Howell told M.P.s, quite rightly, "British participation in the Olympic Games is a matter for the British Olympic Committee----". The significance of such questions being raised in the House of Commons should not be overlooked. State aided sport will soon be widespread. Those who think this will solve all our problems would do well to ponder the events of recent weeks. Denis Howell Mr Denis Howell Mr Denis Howell Mr. Howell Olympic Games 1968 Mexico South Africa AAA BAAB British Olympic Committee

items.s: HON SEC'S NOTES The Hon. Secretary's (A.A.H.) notes on the 1968 track fixtures, the Open 20 miles and a Wandsworth-sponsored 7 miles road run, the loss of the committee's meeting place, Albert Frost's I.C.I. appointment, the pilot athletic leagues, the 1969 move to metric A.A.A. championships, new eligibility rules and Tom Morrell's recovery. The Track Season will be with us very shortly and we would once again ask all members to support our fixtures to the full as active athletes, or as helpers and officials, or as supporters. Particularly we would ask you to note our Championships date - Saturday May 25th at Hurlingham Park Track. Other dates booked are :- Sat. 23rd March - Tooting Track (Field Events Meeting) Sat. 20th April - Battersea Park. Wed. 1st Ma y - " " Wed. 12th June - " " Wed. 26th June - " " Wed. 3rd July - " " (Inter-Club Walk) Wed. 17th July - " " Wed. 31st July - " " Wed. 7th August - " " Please also note Sat.July 20th when our Open 20 miles Run will be held from Belgrave Hall, Wimbledon, and Sat.Sept.7th in the evening, when the Borough of Wandsworth are sponsoring a 7 miles Road Run which we have agreed to promote on their behalf. The prize list looks like dazzling everybody, and refreshments for all competitors are a probability which should guarantee three dozen Belgrave entries at a minimum. There is likely to be a special prize for the first Wandsworth resident not gaining any other award; and now that the Borough of Wandsworth embraces additionally most of the area previously under Battersea Borough Council, we may expect keen competition to take this extra award. In years gone by our Club drew tremendous strength from the district now falling within the London Borough of Wandsworth, and every street name carried recollections of Belgrave members. If, as is possible, their Seven miles run becomes an annual event it may well be the means of bringing a regular supply of new members to the Club. Many will remember that at least three "local lads" BERT FOOTER, ARTHUR PENNY and HARRY CHURCHER became International athletes many times over, in the intervals of assisting Belgrave to win Championship team titles. For many years our Committee met at the "Feathers", Broadway, S.W.1. where we enjoyed adequate facilities in a very central position at no cost to the Club. Our December meeting at this venue was our last, however, for we understand a block of offices is to rise on the present site in the near future. If any member does know of a suitable monthly meeting place with this advantage of centrality, your Hon Secretary would be glad to hear from him. We are always interested to follow the careers of those who have served the Club's teams well in the past; and the recent press announcement that ALBERT FROST, after eight years as Treasurer, has been appointed Financial Director of I.C.I. Ltd., (probably Britains largest company) calls for our congratulations and good wishes. Probably Albert's best run for the Club was in the 1947 "National" at Apsley over a course covered with two feet, and more, of snow, when he finished 17th - not all that far out from being nominated as an International. This however did fall once again to LEN HERBERT (6th); and other members of our team on this most difficult day were :- DICK TOBIN 31, VIC BLOWFIELD 37, TED STIMPSON (this years President - none other) 51, STAN EALES 65. Sutton Harriers, from the North, took our title from us, scoring 160 pts. We were second with 184 pts, and Reading A.C. took third medals. In our last issue we printed a photograph of Club members outside Tom Sullivan's pub at Barnes, supplied by Albert Macher. For the record it should be noted that this photograph was taken in 1913 (not 1912 as stated) and in fact appeared in"LOTINGA'S Weekly" on 26th April 1913. Incidentally we were very glad indeed to see Albert Macher and his daughter at our 10 miles C.C.Championship; and to see Albert present the "MACHER" Shield in the Hall after the race. Charlie Speechley who has been a member of the Club since 1919, has been made Life Honorary Member of the Club to mark his many years support to Belgrave. During the coming Track season it has been decided to promote two "pilot" Leagues of equal precedence, and as one of the major clubs in the country we have received, and accepted, an invitation to compete. This will involve two full scale meetings in the Midlands and one in London, and will demand 100% enthusiasm and support from our track and field athletes if we are to do ourselves justice. Based on the experience and knowledge gained in this years "pilot" Leagues the new official National Leagues, with promotion and relegation, will commence in the 1969 season. Obviously any scheme of this sort will not achieve immediate perfection or be without its critics; and suggestions for possible improvements have been invited. One such that we have made(which was turned down in the pilot League arrangements) is the addition of a 6 miles event. Races at this distance are one of the great attractions of the major White City meetings and lead to tremendous interest. Can the Leagues afford to neglect this event? Any suggestion that the time taken (30 minutes or so) rules this event out is surely invalidated by say the inclusion of the Pole Vault which with twelve competitors or varying standards may take hours and hours. The writer feels, too, that the Leagues should consist of twelve clubs each fielding one man per event, rather than six clubs with two athletes in each event. Twelve clubs would ensure a more widespread national appeal, bring more "star" athletes within the scope of one meeting, create less difficulty for the clubs in that the teams would be half the size. The difficulty here would be in deciding the minor placings in the short distance events; but with the goodwill of the clubs this should not prove insuperable - a system of cross heats should take care of it. This is not the time or place to go into further detail on this matter of Athletic Leagues, but we may be sure there will be plenty of discussion on this subject in the months to come. In 1969 the A.A.A. Championships will move from the time honoured July date to Aug. 1st & 2nd, and all championships are likely to be at metric distances. The equivalent of the mile will be 1600 metres, four laps, and not the usual 1500 metres we have seen hitherto in international events. Four laps of the amended track seems entirely logical, and the translation to metric distances inevitable following the pressures being exerted in governmental and industrial circles. All A.A.A. championships will change, including Youths & Juniors; and Relay championships also and this is calculated to give the Clerk of the Course and groundsmen some worries on old established tracks. Presumably Area and County championships will follow suit when practicable and in the fulness of time our Club Championships may also undergo changes. We shall miss the magic of "All out for the Mile" - but no doubt there will be compensations. Another change which will have much earlier application, (effective April 1st in fact) is that relating to team eligibility. New rules approved give athletes at School, College, Universities etc., opportunities, if desired, to represent their educational establishment in open competition (subject to conditions laid down); but to be eligible for their "open" club if the "closed" club does not compete. The "qualifying" period (which applied to athletes changing their clubs if they had represented their first club in open team competition) of 14 mths is reduced to 9 mths. The County residential qualifying period is also reduced to 9 months, and some help given to athletes born abroad. To come in line with the above an athlete joining a club over twenty miles from his place of residence will now wait only 9 months instead of the 14 months previously required. It will be interesting to see whether this general move to ease restrictive rules (generally speaking, introduced many years ago to avoid various abuses) will be found to function fairly and satisfacorily both for individual athletes and for clubs. It is pleasing to be able to report that PAST - PRESIDENT TOM MORRELL is now making great progress following a heart attack just before Christmas, and should soon be with us again. Tom is one of those quiet workers for the Club who accomplishes so much without ever creating any sense of fuss, or calling attention to himself. His services in connection with prizes, issuing of numbers and collection of fees at our track meetings, recording and keeping account of the points earned by the competing clubs have been most valuable; as are the other duties he carries through unobtrusively but reliably. We shall welcome his return to Club activities with real pleasure. A.A.H. items.s: BOXING DAY MEETING - 1967 Harry Shields' account of the club's 1967 Boxing Day handicap meeting, with results of the 2 miles, 120 yards, shot and 3 miles walk handicaps. HARRY SHIELDS WRITES: After the fug of Christmas activities, to those with energy enough,what compensations there were in this delightful gathering, on a lovely fresh sunny morning with its mixture of young in heart and young in body. The thought of some thirty years ago, Arthur Penny fresh from his reputed Christmas diet of fish, regularly winning the 2 mile handicap, now resplendent in his red starters cap escorted by that epitomé of courage, his wife Winn. Dave Shepherd, Norman Dewberry and many others not looking a day older. Tom Carter acting with the august majesty of a Cohen on the top of the Judges stand. Ted Stimpson, Our President, busily looking after the tape. We all missed the solid presence of Tom Morrell and his unassuming "general factorum" in obtaining the prizes, being competitors steward, results recorder etc., and voiced our hopes to see him speedily restored to health. With the exception of the walk, the events were well supported and very obviously enjoyed. The rich mixture of experience and the product of that academy of young athletes presided over by Reg Hopkins, produced keen and exciting competition. After all the pomposity one hears in connection with the "Byers Report", international athletes and so on, how refreshing it is to be in this atmosphere of true amateur athletics. The whole meeting was suitably rounded off by a typical gesture of our "A.A.A's" timekeeper E. Ryan who by sleight of hand produced two aircraft construction kits to be added to the prize list for the younger athletes. Thank you Ted they were much appreciated. (Cont'd overleaf) RESULTS: Shot Handicap: A very good turnout for this event which could only be started after the tedious job of baling out about 50 gallons of water from the shot putt area, leaving our marker Dave Ansell being regularly splatted as the 16lb weight dropped in the mud! items.sum: Gordon Biscoe's introduction to the road running section asking road runners to plan their season around the races in the summer fixture list.
items.s: ROAD RUNNING Gordon Biscoe's introduction to the road running section asking road runners to plan their season around the races in the summer fixture list. GORDON BISCOE WRITES:- This being the semi-closed season of the year for road running there is not a great deal to report on,but one's attention is drawn towards the coming season and the many races this involves once again. The number of races available still increases and we have now reached the same situation as faces the track man, that there are in fact too many. With this in mind we must be selective in the number of races we support, in order to concentrate our efforts and not split them over different events in the same day. In order to do this it would be appreciated if all road runners when planning their 'campaign" for the coming season, would use the races listed in the summer fixture list as a basis to work on. Gordon Biscoe GORDON BISCOE

items.label: March 1968
items.sum: Report and results of the Hogs Back 9 mile road race on 16 December 1967, where Gerry North was tripped and injured early on and Belgrave 'A' were second team behind Tipton.
items.s: HOGS BACK Report and results of the Hogs Back 9 mile road race on 16 December 1967, where Gerry North was tripped and injured early on and Belgrave 'A' were second team behind Tipton. HOGS BACK 9 MILE---DECEMBER 16th 1967 The old cliché, 'we was robbed' would have been a reasonable comment following our failure to win this annual outing over the Hogs Back. For the second year, near ideal conditions prevailed, only this time our entry was stronger and our hopes higher. However, fate was quick to deal its blow when just after the start Gerry North, whilst leading the field, was accidently tripped from behind and received a badly gashed arm and thigh. After this serious shaking he was faced with the unenviable task of trying to re-catch the leaders in this class field. At around 5 miles there were only about six in front including brother Geoff. and a very strong Alan Rushmer (Tipton H.) leading the field. At seven miles, before the fast run down to the finish, only Rushmer remained in front, but the effort had taken its toll and ,as the results show, by the time those last two miles had been covered Gerry had been forced to concede some of the places so gamely fought for. Geoff. fading a little over the final stages ran a great race,as did Peter Whewell to complete our scoring three. Bill Dance ran well considering he started with hardly any warm up, arriving as did Pat O'Connor just in time to get their numbers. In fact their last minute timing (not for the first time!) prompted the question as to whether Don McLean's 'title' was in jeopardy!!.It was good to see steeple-chasers John Bicourt and Dick Piotrowski out on the road, at what is a slightly longer than usual distance for them,as well as being a tough race. John recorded a time only a few seconds slower than last year (47m26s), when he was our first man home in 36th Position!. 'Old man' Mike Stearman on the come-back trail showed he meant business by giving Pat O'Connor a few uncomfortable moments and some of these watching food for thought. Teams: 1. Tipton H. 32 pts. 2. In the last few years this has not been a very successful race for us, mainly due to lack of support, and this year was to be no exception; with snow and ice in all directions making the thought of 15 miles on the road a rather miserable prospect. Our stalwarts who did come under starters orders were nearly all 'semi invalids' recovering from flu, injury or semi retirement ! and are therefore to be congratulated for turning out at all. Thus, as the results show, whilst athletic honours were not coming our way on this occasion perhaps we should mention that great team work in bulk buying enabled us to carry off a raffle prize for the second year in succession - enough said!! items.sum: Youths and boys section notes: thanks to helpers, a plea for subs, winter track turnouts, club films, and Bill Curtin's and Richard Langley's schools cross-country wins and English Schools selection.
items.s: YOUTHS & BOYS Youths and boys section notes: thanks to helpers, a plea for subs, winter track turnouts, club films, and Bill Curtin's and Richard Langley's schools cross-country wins and English Schools selection. The boys & youths would like to thank those seniors who help our section through the winter by helping to mark and marshal our cross-country races - not forgetting the ladies who serve us with tea and cakes afterwards. An appeal to all boys & youths to pay their subs. It is a costly business running a club,and our postage bill, carding all of you almost every week, comes to quite a large amount. It is our duty as good club members to help pay our way. We have had some grand turn-outs at the track this winter with, on one occasion, 25 boys in attendance. This is most encouraging and augurs well for the coming track season. Training has been quite varied and during the snowy weather included a three hour snowball fight! Ideal for the throwers perhaps and, in Nigel Bacon's case, for his running also! Reg Hopkins and Tom Carter have been taking movie films from time to time, and they hope to put on a show in the near future. Included will be a repeat of that film classic(!) "Belgrave Win the London-Brighton Relay". Bill Curtin once again won the South London Schools Cross-Country Championships held at Wimbledon just before Christmas and so will now represent his area in the All London Champs, this unfortunately for us is on the same day as the final match in the North Surrey League when we would have liked his services in trying to hold our 11 point lead. Never mind, we wish him luck and know he will be out to win his way into the all-England race. Another one of our Boys will be absent for the same reason. Richard Langley was the winner of the East London Schools Cross-Country Championships in 18.35 (180 Runners) helping his school to win the team event. This was a 3 mile cross-country race held at Hanaiult Forest. Bill and Richard will not be meeting in the London Championships however as Bill is in a higher division. We can however hope to have two winners and, perhaps, two winners in the All England? LATER! TWO BELS AT STOKE Bill Curtin and Richard Langley won themselves a trip to the English Schools cross country Championships to be held at Stoke on March 23rd. Bill gained his place by coming third in the intermediate division of the 'London' over four miles at Hainault on Saturday February 23rd. Richard also gained Third place, but in the junior division. items.sum: Account of a sponsored bridge-running charity event for a youth club on 19 December 1967 in which seven Belgrave boys reached 12 bridges in 70-85 minutes.
items.s: A Dozen Bridges Account of a sponsored bridge-running charity event for a youth club on 19 December 1967 in which seven Belgrave boys reached 12 bridges in 70-85 minutes. On Tuesday evening 19th December some of our boys ran in a competition to help raise funds for a youth club who allow us to use their headquarters midweek. This youth club found sponsers to pay a shilling per bridge per boy who then tried to run as many bridges as possible in two hours. The competition was due to start at 8 o'clock but due to the unexpected large entry (75 boys) it was 8:20 before the "off". The finishing time had been fixed for 10 o'clock The organizers and the large number of spectators were amazed at the ability of our boys who reached 12 bridges before 9:30 and at this point were brought to a halt because the organizers did not visualize any one reaching this far in two hours let alone 70 mins. and therefore had no marshals beyond this point. Only one other boy,who was not Belgrave, managed to reach so far before 10 o'clock. N.Bacon 12 Bridges 70 mins. V.Butcher 12 Bridges 70 mins. R.Hopkins 12 Bridges 80 mins. items.s: NORTH SURREY LEAGUE Youths/Boys Belgrave's first win in the North Surrey League youths/boys competition for 1967-68, with the final table and reports and results of races 2 (Esher), 3 (Morden Park) and 4 (Richmond Park). FINAL TABLE Undoubtedly one of the most pleasing features of the season was our first win in this competition. Second last year was beyond our expectations, but to improve on it against the calibre of Mitcham and Walton---particularly when we were only third in our opening home match---hardly beared thinking of; except in the minds of our Youths and Boys of course! We moved up to second at Walton and then, with our tails up, actually won the last two fixtures. You now have something worth fighting for next season. The first race of the season was reported in the last issue of "The Belgravian". The last three races went as follows:- RACE No.2. - (Walton) Esher, December 9th. Run in dangerous, icy conditions and a blizzard thrown in at the end for good measure, our lads really rose to the occasion and, led by Cliff Calderwood, split Walton and Mitcham in the team event - leaving us only 11points down at the halfway stage of the competition. RACE No. 3. - (Mitcham) Morden Park, December 30th This was probably our best performance so far. Ten claret & gold vests in the first twenty four finishers! And Bill Curtin (still 2 yrs away from being a youth) finishing second, nine seconds ahead of the winner at Walton, R. Martin. Cliff Calderwood was well up again and when John Crockford led in a solid pack of Bels in 10th place there was no doubt who the winners were. Of the 52 finishers 25 were Belgravians ! Now to hold that 11 points lead in the final fixture at Petersham. RACE NO.4.------(Ranelagh) Richmond Park, February 24th Once again our lads rose to the occasion and, despite being without Bill Curtin, held on to their precious 11 points lead to lift the title for the first time. They not only held their lead but won the race itself on last scoring man. The Days, Hamiltons, Crockford, Butcher and Bacon all excelled themselves to make the first 17. Pos Club Points 1. items.sum: Report of the Surrey Boys cross-country championships at Morden Park on 17 February 1968, where Bill Curtin was beaten into second by Buckwell of Guildford and Belgrave were fourth team.
items.s: CURTIN 2nd in County Report of the Surrey Boys cross-country championships at Morden Park on 17 February 1968, where Bill Curtin was beaten into second by Buckwell of Guildford and Belgrave were fourth team. SURREY BOYS CHAMPS., MORDEN PARK---February 17th Ten schools and nine club teams provided over 100 runners at the start line, and Belgrave had high hopes that Bill Curtin would be leading our team to victory. Displaying his usual courageous running Bill went straight to the front and only Buckwell of Guildford could stay with him. They stayed locked together all the way until, with the finish close at hand, Buckwell (the elder by one year) swept past to take the lead for the first time and go on to break the tape. Bill's effort to shake off his opponent had left him nothing with which to respond and the winner's margin stretched to 10 seconds. Robert Poole travelled down from Reading and finished eighth but Vic Butcher and Mick Harvey were not at their best and we had to be contant with 4th place. Bill is still eligible for this race next year and must be a hot favourite. To win the team title he will need all the support he can get---if our other runners train hard as a team we can do it. Bill Curtin Bill Curtin Bill Curtin Bill Buckwell Buckwell Robert Poole Robert Poole Vic Butcher Vic Butcher Mick Harvey Mick Harvey Surrey Boys Cross Country Championships 1968 Morden Park Reading Guildford

items.sum: Profile of youth runner Cliff Calderwood, born 1949, covering his training, ambitions, best marks and his win in the Belgrave Junior Cross Country Championship.
items.s: YOUNG PROFILE No:1 CLIFF CALDERWOOD Profile of youth runner Cliff Calderwood, born 1949, covering his training, ambitions, best marks and his win in the Belgrave Junior Cross Country Championship. Clifford Owen Calderwood was born at Isleworth, Middlesex on 17.12.49. But for his brother Dick (also a Belgravian) he would not be carrying a claret & gold vest in our Youth teams today. Cliff, who is a slight 8½ stone and 5'5½" tall, runs daily throughout the year and, apart from pre-race days, each session lasts a good hour. His ambition, in the short term, is to re-write the Belgrave Junior 3 miles and 6 miles records and, in the long term, to win a marathon race. One would expect a youth showing such singleness of purpose to admire most of all the Jim Ryun's, Kip Keino's or Ron Clarke's of the athletics world, but no, its still elder brother Dick - "It took a lot for him to get from 40 cigarettes a day to a 1:56.9 half mile in two years". Cliff has no coach but works to a well thoughtout schedule which includes a Lydiard type jog of 15-20 miles every Sunday. His best marks to date from 880 yds to 6 miles are 2:11, 4:52, 10:48, 16:30 and 33:16 - times he confidently expects to slash this year. The performance which has given him most pleasure so far was his winning of the Belgrave Junior Cross Country Championship this season, whilst still a youth. It seems fairly certain that he has far greater pleasures to come. Clifford Owen Calderwood CLIFF CALDERWOOD CLIFF CALDERWOOD Clifford Owen Calderwood Cliff Dick Calderwood Dick Jim Ryun Jim Ryun Kip Keino Kip Keino Ron Clarke Ron Clarke Belgrave Harriers Junior Cross Country Championship 1968 Isleworth, Middlesex

items.label: March 1968
items.sum: The editor's personal opinion piece arguing that the I.A.A.F. and I.O.C. amateur rules are outdated and that athletes should be free of the amateur/professional distinction.
items.s: REMOVE THE SHACKLES! The editor's personal opinion piece arguing that the I.A.A.F. and I.O.C. amateur rules are outdated and that athletes should be free of the amateur/professional distinction. In writing the following article your editor speaks only for himself and, in doing so, hopes to provoke sufficient feeling on your part to send in your views, for or against, on whether we have reached the time to REMOVE THE SHACKLES! Perhaps the greatest difficulty besetting mankind in this so-called space age is the inability to recognise and move with the times. Progress, however cynically one may view it, proceeds at an ever increasing rate and improvements that once took 2,000 years to achieve will soon be gained in a single generation. Civilization is in a state of flux and the codes of one year are often discarded by the next. Those that drag their feet for more than an instant will soon be left trailing in the wake. Already there are signs in the athletics world of this failure to move with the times. Those Victorian citadels of power that worship the divine right of amateurism, the I.A.A.F. and the I.O.C., each year bog themselves down a little more as they fight their losing battle to preserve amateur laws and definitions that were framed to suit conditions at the turn of the century. Slowly but surely they are working their way into a tortuous situation that could eventually lead to a major split in world athletics. With Avery Brundage floating gently in the clouds, reminiscing over his boyhood days, his Olympic committee have issued their latest amateur proclamation which, if enforced, would eliminate all athletes who have accepted prizes worth more that $50, have received athletic scholarships or have spent more than 4 weeks a year in a training camp - that covers virtually all the top athletes in the world! Imagine the I.O.C. trying to invoke this rule against the national heroes of some lands. We could well be on the way to two Olympic Games - the official one and the unofficial one. Meanwhile, the I.A.A.F. has not been standing still. Don Pain, their part-time secretary of this world-wide federation, is very cross at the practice of bringing into the arenas hold-all bags carrying trade names. "....we intend to stamp out this growing practice" he is reported as saying and, sure enough, an additional rule is hatched out. Not, of course, one that is in the interests of the athlete - only the rules first-ever devized did that. Part of the new I.A.A.F. rule says "when and where it is proved that the name or the picture of the athlete was used for the purpose of this paragraph without his knowledge the indemnity to be collected from the person or persons responsible for the injury, privately agreed or stipulated by the courts, will revert to the Federation to which the athlete belongs". How's that for a gem! Who takes who to court? Supposing the athlete is innocent but doesn't wish to take proceedings against the Advertiser? Is he guilty unless proved innocent? A few test cases would prove most interesting but would only serve to show up the pathetic state of today's outlook. Since the last world war the percentage of college-sponsored or state-sponsored athletes in the world's best performances lists has increased greatly. This trend will continue for as long as the Arthur Rowes and the Berwyn Jones's of this world are discriminated against by rules that only sort out the "private" offender. Despite the barriers, one day we shall all be called just "athletes" with no strings - similar to table-tennis players, cricketers and soon no doubt, tennis players - and the little man at the White City who spends his time sticking blank paper on hold-all bags will be out of a job. Unfortunately there are signs that the rule-book formulators intend to go on burying themselves in more paper. Their only hope of survival is to join the Hockey Federation whose President is against league and knock-out competitions and dislikes "highly organised competition in an amateur game" - so much for hockey! When are we going to realise that the best athletes are only interested in meeting the best opponents and beating them on equal physical terms. We are not interested in our opponent's colour, religion, country's policy, class or how he amasses his "wealth", but simply in crushing him competitively. This is part and parcel of dedication, whatever the ethics, and those that don't like it can stick to the inter-club scene which will go on as always. Although there have been political withdrawals from time to time I have yet to meet the athlete who would refuse to compete against a "professional" on the grounds of unfair advantage, potential corruption, or his wealth. Unwittingly, these international bodies are protecting the very elements they consider to be undesirable and are discriminating against the athlete who is unable to obtain "approved" sponsorship. It will not be long before ALL Olympic finalists will, by necessity, need to be students, civil servants or members of the armed forces. An indication of this trend is the world's No. 1 shot putter Randy Matson. For some undisclosed reason he did not take his examinations in his final year at college and it has now been announced that he will have a year's special extension to take them. He will not be eligible for any N.C.A.A. competition but, coincidentally, his extra time occupies Olympic year 1968. If Matson was an Eastern European he would also be able to rely on being looked after and would certainly undergo no hardship when he attended the lengthy training camps held by such nations. He would have no fear of being branded a professional,because communist countries simply do not recognise professionalism - what an admirable solution to the problem! It has already enabled the U.S.S.R. and other countries to field their World Cup squads in the soccer qualifying matches for the Olympic Games. (Cont'd on page 30) REMOVE THE SHACKLES (Cont'd from page 15) The professional-amateur distinction was drawn in most sports because of the unfair advantage of full-time training over part-time training. This still applies to a few sports but in athletics no such distinction exists. There are many many international athletes, swimmers and tennis players who would not spend any more time training than they do now, even if they did have all day, every day. My plea is not to stop the widespread breaches of these unnatural laws butto remove the shackles and discourage no one from taking part in sport. Give them all a chance by calling them just "athletes" and if they can earn pin-money in advertising or pro football good luck to them, because it won't be for long and when they lose their form they will bite the dust quicker than ever - athletically and financially. In conclusion, I quote Leonard Cawley, whose comments on the croquet-putter dispute in the golf world could be applied to many of our sports. "And if the Rules of Golf Committees start telling us how we should even grip our clubs they will soon become like governments who wake up one morning and find themselves with no one to govern". Can you hear us up there in the clouds, Avery? items.s: Foiled by injuries and MITCHAM Report of the Surrey cross-country championship at Farthing Downs on 6 January 1968, won individually by Gerry North for a hat-trick, with an injury-hit Belgrave losing the team title to Mitcham by 5 points. Farthing Downs, Coulsdon - 6th January. By a mere margin of 5 points Belgrave lost the privilege of taking the Surrey Co. Championship for the third consecutive year. It was ironical that our team, as entered, was stronger than ever. Yet a series of unfortunate circumstances forced us into a desperate fight - a fight that required all our starters to run at best;and one that nearly came off. Firstly, John Thresher (4th last year) had an injured ankle, then Charlie Dabbs (4th in our Club 7 four weeks earlier) went down with injury a few days before the race and, to crown it all, Bill Dance had spent most of the week in bed with 'flu . With reserves also incapacitated, we couldn't even start a full team. Because of the battle ahead Bill gallantly insisted on turning out, but was probably unwise to have done so. Mitcham got an excellent start and the rest of the race was spent in pulling them back. Inspiring our team out front was Gerry North, in great form, who took less than a lap to shake off Bob Holt, his main rival. Fairclough, Major & Bicourt gradually moved through the field and we soon had four in fifteen, so all depended on our last two scorers who were obviously better placed to gain points. Any two from three was the permutation we needed from Bill Dance, Derek Fernee and Chris Steer. The latter was the man expected to pull it out of the bag, after his forward running in the league match the previous week, but it was not Chris's day and certainly not his course and it was left to the other two to close in. Bill was obviously under the weather and it was apparent near the end that we would not see his usual final flourish. Our first four ran particularly well and Tony Fairclough was passed by training companion Biscoe only in the last 200 yards. There are so many "ifs" that space does not permit their enumeration, but it was comforting to see a full strength Mitcham team having to pull out all the stops before they could take advantage of our setbacks. Equally comforting, of course, to see Gerry North score his personal hat-trick. Pos Name Time 1. Gerry North (Bels) 36:49 2. R. Holt (Herc/Wim) 37:42 3. G. Biscoe (Mitcham) 38:02 4. A. items.sum: Report of the club Senior 10 miles and Junior 5 miles cross-country championships at Wimbledon on 20 January 1968, won by Dick Piotrowski and Cliff Calderwood.
items.s: DICK'S '10' ~ CLIFF'S '5' Report of the club Senior 10 miles and Junior 5 miles cross-country championships at Wimbledon on 20 January 1968, won by Dick Piotrowski and Cliff Calderwood. Senior & Junior Championships - Wimbledon, January 20th. The "Macher" &"Savage" shields are in new hands. Our bright young prospects, Dick Piotrowski and Cliff Calderwood pulled off the Club 10 miles and 5 miles championships respectively and impressed the onlookers with a brand of running that holds a bright future for both. There were ten starters in the Junior event and John Kelly, runner up to Adrian Major last year, must have been hoping to step up a place before he joins the Senior ranks. John, in fact, was the only competitor to have also run in last year's race - but Calderwood was in no mood for sentiment and set about the opposition in relentless fashion to win in a time 2:45 outside Adrian Major's winning effort of last year. A pretty fit Tony Brooks popped up to split the two favourites and Kelly had to be content with a bronze medal to partner his silver of last year. The Senior race produced over 30 starters, including the holder, Laurie O'Hara, out for his third consecutive win, Trevor Hart third last year and John Thresher, out to give his recently injured ankle a rigorous test. The first of the four laps saw Thresher forcing an exceptionally fast pace and at 2 miles he was 30 yds clear of O'Hara, Piotrowski, Hart and Whewell who were also well clear of the field. On the second lap John eased up and retired at the halfway mark feeling it unwise to press his injured ankle any further. Meanwhile O'Hara & Piotrowski had drawn away from Hart & Whewell who were at 15 yds intervals behind the leading pair. Apart from variations in the gaps it stayed this way to the end and was clearly a race between Laurie and Dick for the title. The pair were inseparable for the full distance and Laurie said afterwards how impressed he was with Dick's form. As the finishing straight was reached, everyone waited for the famous O'Hara finish but inseparable they had been throughout and inseparable they intended to remain. Only when informed they must be split did Laurie ease back inches from the line - an encouraging gesture that was appreciated by all. (Cont'd on page 20) (Cont'd from page 17) Trevor was third again and fast approaching his old form. Surprises in the middle of the field were Chris Fairfield, John Hilton and our veteran ex marathon champion Colin Collis. Battling together for much of the race these three didn't realise they were fighting for two of the handicap prizes! Just to underline Dick Piotrowski's improvement in form he also took first handicap award. Albert Macher very kindly appeared with his daughter to present the "Macher" shield to our new champion. items.sum: Humorous mock Hansard in which club members, cast as ministers and MPs, debate a proposed rise in club subscriptions, shower economies and charging for the Belgravian.
items.s: COMMON HOUSE OFFICIAL REPORT Humorous mock Hansard in which club members, cast as ministers and MPs, debate a proposed rise in club subscriptions, shower economies and charging for the Belgravian. COMMON HOUSE OFFICIAL REPORT THE HOUSE MET AT HALF PAST SIX O'CLOCK PRAYERS MK. SQUEAKER IN THE CHAIR ******* PUBLIC EXPENDITURE The Chancellor of the Exchequer (Mr. Dave Martin-Shepherd): I beg to move, that this house approves the raising of the Club Subscriptions to £83..9..2d. per capita per annum. Mr. John Martin (Clapham): Perhaps - Mr. D. Shepherd: Ignoring the flippant remark which the right Hon. Gentleman tosses in so lightly, I will explain the need for the proposed increase. My office has been aware for some time that Hon. Members are getting away with it insomuch as their current subscriptions are not covering the cost of their keep. You do not need a breakdown on your current subscriptions, that was ably given to you by my goodself at our A.G.M., but a word about the structure of the proposed increases. Firstly, as defined in our rules section four, object of the Club, etc., we consider it right that more teams should be sent to first class fixtures, Hilton-Pullmanwise. Mr. Reg. Hopkins (Bermondsey): I've had 18 youths in my banger, M.O.T. tested of course, which is two more than the Hon. Gentleman from Streatham, Mr. Tom Carter has. The Prime Minister, Mr. Alf. Harley (Ruislip): Very public spirited of you - it is probably fortunate that our Hon. Member the Minister of Transport is still under treatment at the Alcoholics Anonymous Centre. But we mustn't expect our key athletes to be moved around like the general public and so I ask you to earnestly consider your Chancellor's proposals. Mr. D. Martin-Shepherd: It has been pointed out by the Minister without Portfolio, Mr. William (known as Bill to all the Youths, Juniors and Field Events men who are placed in the Yacht 3) Lucas, the great benefit that trips abroad have for the individual - I beg your pardon - I mean the Club. Therefore, the money set aside for this will be doubled, hence the 2d. on the proposed increase. The nine shillings will cover the cost of reserving tracks, heat, light and water at the hall, whilst the eighty three pounds will provide much needed improvements for the Committee's comfort - this includes their beer naturally. Secretary of State for Middlesex, Mr. K. Stimpson: Frankly Hon. Chancellor, I think you are going a bit too far there, I mean can't we economise ourselves - (Cries of resign) let's face it we could cut down on the list of cheeses available for the Committee Room Traps. Mr. Ron Langheim (Sunbury) : Why don't we give it away. Mr. K. Stimpson: It's nice to welcome back the Hon. Member. His constituents in Sunbury must be very proud he raises his voice between long periods of lethargy to say the same thing. Mr. Ron Langheim: Zzzzzzzzzz. Mr. Pat Duncan (Economics Adivser to The Old Lady): I would strongly advise this House to act as a kind of unit trust, i.e. all the moneys that are received for so called Guilt Edged Government Stocks should be salted away very quickly into Equities - Victor Value even without the stamps are better than our best customer, B.S.A. - not - I repeat not, because we don't pay but my department sent 1,500 men, one section, all established, to do a market survey and even without the one and half million pound computor, I soon analysed the fact that for the general populace pineapple chunks have a greater turn around than 0.38 calibre revolvers. Mr. George Piddington (Hayling Island): Whilst I do not wish to agrieve the Hon.Gentleman from the Treasury or expose my own limited intelligence - Wot the 'ell does he mean? At this juncture the Chief Whip, Mr. Chris. (Kinky) Steer, moved an adjournment for lunch. For this, as with a division, he adjourns to a special small lobby with the recent elected Scottish Nationalist to multiply. The Debate continued ... Mr. A. Penstone (Minister of Housing): My department has made a thorough examination of the House and have come to the conclusion that great economies could be made by reducing the flow of water in the showers - Mr. W. Dance (Northumberland and Durham): Does the Right Honourable Gentleman propose any curtailment of services in this way? Surely he realises that this would cause great hardship to those very people he was elected to represent. Mr. A. Penstone: I hadn't finished. Mr. W. Dance: Nevertheless - Mr. Speaker (Mr. F. Jarvis): Will the Hon. member for Northumberland and Durhan please give the Minister the floor. Mr. A. Penstone: As I was saying - Mr. J. Goswell (Lewisham) When we were in power we never had any trouble with water shortage. It seems to me that everyone has to suffer for the extravagence and bungling of the party opposite. Mr. A. Penstone: The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Goswell) shows a complete lack of regard for the wider implications of the matter. As usual he and his party only concern themselves with their own section of society. Mr. R. Hall (City of London): We're as public spirited as you - (Cries of Rhubarb, Shut up, Rubbish, etc.) Mr. Speaker: Order, Order. There is no need to behave like children - Mr. G. Biscoe (Chiswick) Send them to the kids' party, we need a comedy turn. (Uproar) Mr. A. Penstone: We are simply trying to organise - Mr. T. Carter (Streatham): You couldn't organise a sex orgy in a broth- Mr. Speaker: Will the Hon. Member for Streatham withdraw - Mr. T. Carter: I always do. Safety first you know. (Laughter, cries of Dirty Old Man) Mr. A. Penstone: Anyway whatever you lot think I've already installed low pressure, economy size sprays on all the showers so there! (Loud booing, cries of resign, fascist, etc.) Mr. N. Dewberry (Under Secretary of State at the Treasury): If we must make economies why don't we alter the showers at the Hall. (Ironic cheers and slow handclaps) Mr. H. Shields (Outer Hebrides) Well I don't know. I mean Good Heavens, good gracious me, really well I mean to say Ho Ho, golly, I mean well it's - I mean to say well really - Mr. T. Carter: What are you on about Harry? Mr. H. Shields: What I'm trying to say is, well what I mean to say is (Cries of Get on with it) Mr. H. Shields: No well really - The Prime Minister: (Groan) Mr. H. Shields: When the Prime Minister and myself were on a five thousand mile walk to Istanbul across The Pyrenees we used to bathe in icy cold streams. I don't see why you young fellows can't have a dip in the Rushmere after a run. I think it would be a jolly good idea to dismantle the showers completely. I jolly well wouldn't mind a cold dip. Mr. A. Penney (Raynes Park): We're not all barmy like you. (Laughter, shouts of 'Want to bet') President of the Board of Trade (Right Hon. Mr. Ted Stimpson): Well the thing is, gentlemen shall we get back to the business in hand. The Home Secretary (Rt. Hon. C. Manning): In this present financial crisis, the fifteenth this year (or month or week, as the case may be) all I need hardly add thanks to the years (or months or weeks as the case may be) of misrule by our predecessors - I intend to take revolutionary measures - Mr. C. Steer (Notting Hill): Like burning down Buckingham Palace? Mr. Manning: I shall ignore that typically anti-patriotic remark. My proposal is to convert this noble house into a palatial casino where the elite can spend their evenings in luxury and comfort and thereby contributing considerably to the exchequer. Of course all other functions of the place would have to be suspended - Mr. Steer: There you go again. Not only do you deprive honest workers of the opportunity of healthy recreation, you throw the place open to capitalistic money-grabbing scum. Mr. Manning: The Hon. Member's views on honest to goodness private enterprise are well known. However, if he will listen to my other proposal which is to build an extension for the purpose of Bingo I think even his anxiety for the proletariat will be appeased. The new edifice will have many attractions not least of which will be a staff of fifty young ladies all of whom will be hand-picked. Mr. Carter: By whom? Mr. Manning: Me, of course. (Loud whistles from all sides of the House) The Post-Master General (Rt.Hon.Mr.F.Webb): The economies my department will make is to stop putting stamps on all official letters, thereby saving seventy million pounds a year. This will also benefit the economy generally because of money members will pay in excess postal charges. The Chancellor of the Exchequer: Highly commendable I must say. Mr. H. Shields: Well really I don't know - (Cries of 'Oh my God he's off again, get stuffed etc.) The Minister of Propaganda (Mr. C. Shippen): One sweeping change which has long been overdue will be brought in shortly. Hitherto members have received the official organ,I refer of course to the 'Belgravian', absolutely free of charge. Therefore, I propose to introduce a fee for this publication.The charge I have in mind is purely nominal - a mere twenty five shillings - a small price to pay for this unique service. Hon. Members: What ! ! ! ! Mr. Shippen: There will of course be a rebate for Old Age Pensioners and those who are chronically sick. Mr. Donald Maclean (Oxford and Cambridge): If you think I'm actually going to pay money for that libellous rag ... Mr. A. Penney: Your organ isn't worth the paper it's printed on let alone ... (General uproar, cries of resign, sounds of breaking glass, furniture, etc.) Mr. C. McLennan (John O'Groats):I've had enough of this. I'm for a wee beer. items.s: FROM 'THE BELGRAVIAN' 40 years ago and 25 years ago Column reprinting items from the Belgravian of March 1928 (third in the South of Thames championship) and May 1943 (Southern C.C.A. race at Epsom). 40 years ago MARCH 1928 - Congratulations !!! At long last ! Twenty four years ago (1904) we gained 3rd place in this Championship (South of Thames) at Redhill with a score of 158 points. Since then we have striven hard - very hard - but were never successful in gaining a place until this time (3rd again). May I (Editor Ben Knifton) prophesy a win next year to welcome another quarter of a century, and the dawn of a more successful period ? First team were Reading AC with 61 pts, second S.L.H. with 165 pts and third Belgrave H. with 177 points (Apart from S.L.H. being replaced by Mitcham, the result and points totals were remarkably similar to the 1968 event at Epsom - 40 years later). and 25 years ago MAY 1943 Having won the first two of the Southern C.C.A. races "the third race of the series was held at Epsom.- - - We welcomed the re-appearance of Len Herbert, Ted Stimpsom and Charlie Smart, all home on short leave, and also a newcomer Sam Beer - - - - - -,Jimmy Green (future founder - Editor of 'Athletics Weekly') also ran very well after his recent illness. - - - - Len Herbert & Tom Carter finished together in 3rd place and in true Belgrave spirit Tom waived any claim to the medal and it was handed to Len who had not previously won a Southern medal. The 'B' team were 8th. items.s: 3rd again in SOUTH of THAMES Report of the South of Thames cross-country championship on Epsom Downs, 27 January 1968, won by Reading with Belgrave third team, with a photo of Dick Piotrowski and Peter Whewell. Epsom Downs - January 27th Last year, on our own territory, we had to give best to Blackheath and Ranelagh. With the "Heathens" scorers barred from this year event we were widely tipped as likely winners but, not for the first time, it didn't work out that way. Despite being without the Stevens brothers, Merriman and MacAndrew, Reading proved easy winners and established themselves as a serious threat to our Southern & National teams. To rub it in the Mitcham boys ran to form and took the silver medals. What happened? Well, the whole team got a good start with Dick Piotrowski showing good form these days, well to the fore closely followed by John Bicourt and Peter Whewell, both surely destined for the first 10? At 2 miles Dick was 7th, John Bicourt 15th, Adrian Major 22nd and Peter 35th. The move through the field must begin; but as Bill Dance (48), John Dear (53) and Whewell made ground slowly so our leading two lost it and 5½ miles later our final points score was six greater at 186. Except for Adrian Major who improved 34 places on last yea r most of the others were half a dozen places or so worse off. Perhaps it blew the cobwebs out of their system in time for the Southern! 4.Westbury 209 pts, 5.Windsor 258 pts, 6.Herc/Wim 306 pts, 7.Camb.H. 362 pts. items.label: March 1968
items.sum: Report of the Southern cross-country championships at Parliament Hill Fields on 11 February 1968, where Gerry North was second and Belgrave second team behind Reading, with youths 18th and no complete junior team.
items.s: SOUTHERN SILVER AGAIN Report of the Southern cross-country championships at Parliament Hill Fields on 11 February 1968, where Gerry North was second and Belgrave second team behind Reading, with youths 18th and no complete junior team. Parliament Hill Fields - February 11th It has become normal practice to run these championships at Parliament Hill and the usual efficient arrangements of the G.L.C. made for a successful promotion. The course was made difficult by being soft under foot and in parts it was very treacherous resulting in a number of falls. The first race was for Youths in which we fielded a full team although none of our runners excelled themselves. Although we have a very keen crowd of youngsters it will be a year or two before we are really prominent in this class. Our team were 18th with 419 points. Next came the Seniors and now that Portsmouth, who have beaten us into 2nd place the last two years, are a waning force we had hoped for a win - although we knew that Reading AC were extremely confident. Their confidence proved to be well founded and with excellent packing and strong running on the last lap they took the championship for the first time since the controversial race of 1937,with 138 points. Although on paper we had a stronger team than in preceding years our score of 179 was some 30 points more than in either 1966 or 1967. All our runners appeared to lack spirit. They lacked the fire and snap needed to win races such as this. It is to be hoped that there will be an improvement before the National on March 2nd. We have been beaten before in the Southern and have been successful in the National - it could happen again. At the top of the first hill our team was well placed and the claret and gold was very prominent. At the end of the first lap we were well placed and scoring equal points with Reading. Peter Whewell whom we hoped to see near the front was well back but we learnt later that he had lost a shoe and was forced to stop to replace it. Laurie O'Hara was also badly placed due to a bad cold. However with Gerry lying 3rd and Geoff 8th and six in forty and three other runners handily placed we were not very worried. The next time round Gerry was in the lead but looking tired and the rest of our scoring six, except Adrian Major, had fallen back. A quick estimate of the scores found us ten points down on Reading. Soon after the start of the second lap Gerry had suffered a heavy fall and this later proved to have sapped his energy. On the last lap Reading, encouraged by possible success, moved up whereas our runners were suffering badly and were losing ground and the gap between the two teams widened to forty points. Gerry finished a tired second to Ashton of Reading who really ran a blinder. The Junior race provided no joy for our supporters. We are very weak in this age group and were unable to complete a team. items.sum: Belgrave's third successive North Surrey League seniors/juniors title in 1967-68, with Gerry North individual champion, the final table and reports and results of races 3 (Morden Park) and 4 (Richmond Park); the race 4 results are printed at the foot of page 22.
items.s: NORTH SURREY LEAGUE Seniors/Juniors Belgrave's third successive North Surrey League seniors/juniors title in 1967-68, with Gerry North individual champion, the final table and reports and results of races 3 (Morden Park) and 4 (Richmond Park); the race 4 results are printed at the foot of page 22. FINAL TABLE Belgrave scored a hat-trick of titles with perhaps their easiest win so far. The points score was the lowest yet recorded because Race No. 2, usually held over Walton's course at Esher, was abandoned due to frozen conditions and a blizzard. However, this in no way affected the first three team positions. Although in the three races we fielded 46,23 and 25 runners respectively our ten scorers on each occasion were drawn from only 13 names, which illustrates the excellent support our leading runners are giving these fixtures. Gerry North was a popular winner of the individual title with a low 9½ points and, with our Youths/Boys also winning their section, it was a clean sweep for Belgrave. The league is now very well established as the premier Surrey league and the Mid-Surrey league as the second division. A policy of promotion and relegation was introduced this season and, as a result, Surrey AC go down (runners-up last year) and Herne Hill Harriers earn promotion. It is interesting to see that South London Harriers are considering whether to bid for entry. They had an opportunity to be founder members, which they turned down. Now they would have to obtain entry through the Mid-Surrey league. Nevertheless, their prescence would be most welcome. The first race of the season was reported in the last issue of "The Belgravian"; the final two races were as follows:- RACE No.3. - MITCHAM (Morden Park), December 30th. With our first fixture lead of 90 points still under our belts, it was gratifying to see the good turn out at Morden Park for the penultimate race. Belgrave eyes were focussed on the men of unknown form, Dick Piotrowski and Trevor Hart. Both ran well above expectations (it was Trevor's first race since last winter) and were our fourth and fifth scorers - things looked good for 1968. They were not the only ones to please. Bicourt & Steer displayed their best form and Roger Donnison produced his best running since joining us earlier in the year. Young Blair-Fish (53rd) also looked good. The Mitcham vests were dangerously prominent in the early stages of the race but, as our men went from strength to strength, the blue & white's faded - eventually being pipped also by Hercules/Wimbledon. Once again Gerry North won the individual race, though this time having to share first place with the runner-up at Wimbledon, Bob Holt. Belgrave doubled their lead in the league table and go into the last race with a handy margin of 182 points - our highest ever. RACE NO.4-----(Ranelagh) Richmond Park, February 24th With the 'National' only 7 days away and a handy lead of points our runners did not intend to hurt themselves. John Thresher and Geoff North were a little short of racing and made the most of this sharpener---looking very impressive in the process. Once again we took the team result and, at the same time retained the league title. Gerry North won the individual title with no difficulty. Apart from our first two men, the runner to catch the eye was Roger Donnison whose steady improvement is most welcome. (Cont'd at foot of opposite page) Pos Club Points 1.
