items.h: 'I WAS THERE' No. 5: by Alf Harley
items.sum: Alf Harley recalls Belgrave's first English National cross-country team title in 1935 at Beaconsfield, with the team result and individual placings (the text gives the date both as March 9th and March 11th 1935).
items.s: 'I WAS THERE' No. 5: by Alf Harley Alf Harley recalls Belgrave's first English National cross-country team title in 1935 at Beaconsfield, with the team result and individual placings (the text gives the date both as March 9th and March 11th 1935). During over forty years of membership I have been privileged to be present at many of the Club's individual and team successes, all of which have given great pleasure and satisfaction - but the outstanding occasion, because it was the first time ever, was the winning of the English Cross-country team title in 1935. Even now I can recall the thrill,when acting as Disc-recorder, of accepting the numbered discs from our men, of rapidly totalling our score, of checking with the officials of other leading clubs, and the deep satisfaction of knowing that we really had won! Success was really ours. Not that there was anything fortuitous about our success. Our Cross-country captain BERT FOOTER had directed all his efforts towards this eventual success for many years before. Other victories on the way were welcome, but no substitute for the Championship title that was to be ours. Two years earlier, 1933, we had been placed second in the "Southern" at Chingford; and a fortnight later in the "National" at Alderley Edge, Cheshire we were placed for the first time. FOOTER and ARTHUR PENNY gave us a glorious start in finishing 4th and 5th and our team position was third with 233 points against Birchfield's 80, and the 101 of Salford H. The following season we scored our first Southern win at Taplow; and at the E.C.C.U. Championship held at Himley Park, with Penny 4th and Footer 9th, we were again placed third, but this time our score was 113 points, one point only behind the Northern Champions, SALFORD HARRIERS. Birchfield were again the winners, with 88 points. So came March 9th 1935 when the Championship was staged at Beaconsfield. In the "Southern" a fortnight earlier at HASSOCKS we had displeased some of our supporters by finishing only second, beaten a point - but nevertheless we were quietly confident. 295 runners thundered from the pens and within the first few yards two of our men, BERT SHAW and HARRY SHIELDS were prostrate on the ground. However, they picked themselves up and chased the field. At four miles JIM GINTY was leading our hopes in fourth position and we seemed well-placed, though accurate team scoring was impossible. We could see however that Surrey A.C. (who had beaten us in the "Southern") had their sixth man behind our eighth, that Salford had three men well up but the others were not prominent, that Birchfield Harriers, Champions on so many occasions, were far from happy with two men only in the earlier placings and CURRIE, Midland Champion, retired from the race. At seven miles our confidence knew no bounds! Excepts for accidents the Title was ours! JIM GINTY, BERT FOOTER and DAN PATIENCE were more or less together in the first twenty places or so. A few seconds behind them, a most encouraging sight - ALF TAYLOR, HARRY SHIELDS and TOM CARTER running together in good heart. Not so far away were BERT SHAW, ARTHUR ALLUM and JACK FLOWER; and we rejoiced that our nine men were all in front of Birchfield's sixth! On the last three mile lap many places were gained, the TAYLOR-SHIELDS-CARTER trio pegging back many positions. In the last mile our runners gave all they had and we finished with the remarkable scoring sequence of 11,14, 15,18,19,20 - six men in a range of ten placings. Our next three soon followed in and we had our nine finishers in 57 scoring positions. Truly a great day! I can assure you it is no joke acting as disc-recorder when the Club runners follow one another in so rapidly - but it gives great satisfaction! The congratulations poured in - the foundation had been laid on which many further victories in Championship events could be built, and on which we can still build. A really great day, a day of critical importance; for thereafter we competed as Champions. The minor successes of yester year no longer held importance - to take second place in the Championship was failure. Such was the significance of March 11th 1935 - things could never be the same again! For the record I give the relevant detail below and you will be struck by the handsome nature of our win. A word of sympathy, even at this late stage, for ARTHUR PENNY, who was nursing a broken bone in the foot at that time, and so missed running and scoring on this eventful day. items.s: TRACK AND FIELD Bill Couzens' report and results of the club's winter Sunday field events meetings at Battersea Park (26 November, 17 December 1967; 7 January, 28 January, 18 February 1968), including trial 440 yds hurdles, plus Jim Vivian's sprint wins at Redhill. RESULTS OF FIELD EVENTS MEETINGS HELD AT BATTERSEA PARK. With two of our nine Sunday morning Winter competitions to go, I can confidently say they have been a success with a good turnout at every competition no matter how inclement the weather. These competitions have included throws, jumps, hurdles and sprints with Arthur Penny as official starter. With the coming National league fixtures it was decided to tryout a 440 yds Hurdles race which suprisingly had 12 entries. Tony Brooks was the eventual winner in the fastest race with 62.0 secs. with Denzil Winsborrow, after falling, a close second. I am sure that three of the competitors for this event will break 60 seconds during the summer which will be very useful for our A & B strings in the National league. DONT FORGET our 12th Open Field Events Meeting at Tooting Bec on Saturday 23rd March - start 1.30 p.m. Bill Couzens. items.s: WALKING Walking section notes congratulating new walking secretary Pat Duncan on a Garnet Cup win and giving news of Dave King, Bob Picton, Brian Ward, Ray Hall and Bob Farley. A word of congratulation to our new Walking Hon Secretary PAT DUNCAN, who has already conjured together a team to win the Garnet Cup Race. May he be equally successful in the Championship events which will soon be breaking over us. Dave King, in his final year at Hull University, writes that exams will prevent him from competing until June but then he expects to be back fighting for his team place. In the Southern Counties Track '7' both Bob Picton and Brian Ward broke 60 Minutes to win their '7' in the hour badges. Ray Hall is on the trail back to fitness again, giving Carl Lawton a close shave in the SCAAA six at Battersea the other week. Bob Farley is another whose recent form suggests that he will be getting near the leaders over the longer ones this summer. "That old man" quite suprised some of our younger men. McLennan's photo montage of the race and presentation. February 3rd. Bexley - The Garnet Cup. Dave Mayo, Carl Lawton, Bernard Capener and Brian Ward gave Belgrave a magnificent start to 1968 by defeating strong opposition from Trowbridge and winning the Garnet Cup by just two points. John Kirk, a new find, moved straight into a lead which he increased by six minutes. Dave, Carl and Delaney of the Vidarians grouped further back and although walking together for much of the race Dave fought clear over the closing stages leaving Carl who although losing one place hung on grimly to his sixth position. Bernard, short of racing found the last few miles heavy work but with fourth Brian Ward walking really strongly the cup was ours. Team: 1. BELGRAVE 37 pts., 2. Trowbridge 39 pts., 3. Southend 72 pts. items.label: March 1968
items.sum: Club news column: births for Barry Sawyer and Rangit Bhatia, Frank Simmons out of hospital, Chris Steer's new job near the Wormwood Scrubs track, and a tribute to recovering past-president Tom Morrell.
items.s: HERE & THERE Club news column: births for Barry Sawyer and Rangit Bhatia, Frank Simmons out of hospital, Chris Steer's new job near the Wormwood Scrubs track, and a tribute to recovering past-president Tom Morrell. Congratulations to BARRY SAWYER on the birth of his Australian daughter. The joy of the occasion helped to temper the disappointment he suffered in December when gastro-enteritis broke his remarkable training sequence of 708 consecutive days. He didn't give up without a struggle though and timed his final run beautifully - just reaching the front door in time ! Congratulations also to RANGIT BHATIA on the birth of his Indian daughter. He hopes she will be India's answer to Mary Rand! Rangit recently finished 5th in the 5,000 m event at the National Inter-State Championships in Madras. It is good to see FRANK SIMMONS out and about again. He came out of hospital on November 29th for what he intends to be the last time and, apart from some pain in his legs, feels fighting fit! Is this to be Chris Steer's year? But of course it is. He has been biding his time waiting for the announcement to be made. He even took a job at the nearby B.B.C. in anticipation of it. And at last it came. "The Wormwood Scrubs running track will open shortly". Now he can swing into those lunch-time training schedules. It's especially convenient too when one's cell is on the ground floor anyway! Members will be relieved to hear that TOM MORRELL is making good progress after his heart attack in early December. Tom, our President of 13 years ago, has never ceased to serve the Club in a multitude of ways. His readiness to take on the unpopular backroom jobs has always been appreciated and this dates back to those early days when the tin baths had to be filled and the pennies collected. During the war years, as helpers came and went, he continued to keep our HQ in a good state of repair and, for a good 16 years or so, stocked and sold Club clothing et. This latter job led to that unenviable task of obtaining medals, arranging engraving and buying handicap prizes for what must have amounted to several hundred events - and it only needs a couple of these arrangements to go wrong to incur the wrath of the side-lines! As with most long-serving officials he carries this burden resolutely and still has enough enthusiasm left over to assist our Hon Treasurer and act as competitors steward and/or recorder at all our home fixtures, summer and winter. These are just a few of the thoughts that come to mind on hearing of our Past-President's misfortune. Get well soon TOM, we look forward to your return. Barry Sawyer BARRY SAWYER Rangit Bhatia RANGIT BHATIA RANGIT BHATIA Rangit Mary Rand Mary Rand Frank Simmons FRANK SIMMONS Chris Steer Chris Steer Tom Morrell TOM MORRELL TOM MORRELL Tom TOM Indian National Inter-State Championships 1968 Madras Wormwood Scrubs B.B.C.

items.label: March 1968
items.sum: Cross-country column reflecting on Belgrave's National at Sutton Coldfield, with a graph of the club's National placings since 1946, comments on 'local lads' and Mitcham, the new 9-month qualifying period and John Bicourt's London Colleges win.
items.s: A COUNTRYMAN'S JOTTINGS Cross-country column reflecting on Belgrave's National at Sutton Coldfield, with a graph of the club's National placings since 1946, comments on 'local lads' and Mitcham, the new 9-month qualifying period and John Bicourt's London Colleges win. How wrong can you get! In the December issue I wrote "Portsmouth-----they are a spent force. Nth Staffs, now reputed to have broken up-------". Yet both teams pushed us out of National medals on the last lap of that fateful Sutton Coldfield course! Not because they were especially good but because our runners failed to click yet again. Coventry were deserved winners on the day and proved that 6 in 60 is now necessary to win the 'National'----the 'retired' Basil Heatley closing-in in 63rd place. What went wrong? Well, Whewell and Fairclough at their best are both capable of finishing in the thirties or forties, and that alone would have given us a win. Poor Bill Dance, after 2½ laps of his best form to date, suffered calf muscle cramp and our supporters witnessed the unusual sight of Bill losing no less than 15 places on the run in. It was ironical that the team who beat us in the Southern, Reading AC, should finish only seventh and that Portsmouth (only 4th at Parliament Hill) should finish 2nd! Pompey deserve all the praise they can get. For the second successive year every runner rose to the occasion and fooled the forecasters; they would certainly have repeated their win of last year if Tim Johnston could have got home from Mexico. And so we have to wait for another year. Can we go on improving or is time running out? Are we doomed to hover on the fringe eternally or can runners like Major, Bicourt, Piotrowski, Williams etc give us a lift up into the medals next year?. Like all clubs we have our ups and downs. The ups can be frustratingly "almost up" and the downs depressingly "very down". The following graph shows our 'National' placings since World War II----you may interpret them how you will. [Graph: NATIONAL PLACINGS SINCE 1946. POSITIONS 1-25 against years 1946-1968] We have always enjoyed very friendly relations with our neighbouring athletic clubs, particularly Mitcham AC whose many successes in recent years have been largely due to the Mitchell brothers, who are former Belgravians. On more than one occasion recently though, I have heard the comments "of course, all our boys are local lads" and "no imports in our team" and "all Surrey runners at Mitcham". All said, we hope, in good humour, but one wonders whether the inference is that Belgrave rely on athletes "drafted in" from the rest of the country, whilst Mitcham raise their own. I wonder what Thresher, Fairclough, Major, Bicourt, O'Hara, Hart, Dabbs, Steer etc. think of that. Agreed that the North brothers, Dance, Whewell, Williams, Kerr and others have played parts of varying degrees in our success but they joined us on moving to London because they had to change their club. I wonder how necessary it was for Dunphy and Murray (Hercules), Kortenray(Wimbledon) Smallbone (Epsom and Ewell) and--almost--Collins (Surrey) to change their's. I would have thought that a "local lad" is one who LIVES within comfortable distance of his club's facilities---his place of birth or life history is quite irrelevant. Many view the recently introduced 9 months qualifying period (instead of 14 months) for athletes changing clubs within a 20 miles radius of their home, as a go-ahead for widespread movement. A runner can now resign immediately after the 'National', qualify for his new club by Christmas and wear his new colours thro' all the championships from the County onwards. For the cross-country enthusiast this is no penalty at all. JOHN BICOURT scored a fine win in the final race of the London Colleges Cross-Country league at Twickenham on March 8th. He beat Grice, Mouat, Stock and Buchanan in good time. JOHN is all set for an even better track season than 1967, when he recorded 8:57.6 for 3,000 metres steeplechase. He recently ran a time trial in 9:17--pretty sharp for this time of the year--and is now all set for the National Road Relay at Leicester and could well be one of our leading performers in that event. We say farewell to Peter Whewell who returned to South Africa the day after the 'National'. During his stay here he worked for a firm of auditors, and it was the frequent spells of late working and consequent lack of training that led to his loss of form between arrival and departure. Nevertheless, he always threw himself enthusiastically into all of our activities and we valued his membership highly. Thank you Peter for your support, and don't forget to keep in touch. Our team was unable to go to Hannut, Belgium, this year to defend "Le Soir" inter-club title they won in 1967 because the sponsors were unable to contribute towards the cost. If we had been informed early enough perhaps something could have been done but, as it was, we were unable to go. The cup we won last year, to keep, has been entitled the "Le Soir" Cup and will be awarded to the winning team each year in our "Southern" Invitation Road Relay. On April 27th we tackle the National road relay championship at Leicester. If ever a race should suit Belgrave it is this one. With twelve stages to run our depth is of great advantage---or should be. Once again we can expect to see our runners fighting desperately for inclusion in our team whilst many other clubs are having trouble finding that last man. But finding a strong twelve is no good if they don't hit form on the day and the test of our fortunes will almost certainly lie in the on-day form of the three runners who will join the North brothers and Thresher on the six long stages. On the short stages we match anyone; witness last year's one fastest and three second fastest stage runs. Of the opposition we face, Coventry (the holders) must be favourites. With Heatley and Kilby both in form again and Bartlett and Lancaster to join their winning 'National' team (9 in 117) they should be a stronger force than last year's winning dozen. Second last year were Derby and, although they only managed ninth at Sutton Coldfield (7 in 150) they have three outstanding Juniors to come in. Bronze medallists were Portsmouth---but I really will eat my hat if they match that this time! Manchester D.L.C. pretty well matched us man for man in the 'National'; they have no difficulty with depth either and should beat Nth. Staffs. My forecast is 1. Coventry. 2. Belgrave. 3. Derby. 4. Manchester. 5. Reading. 6. Nth. Staffs. 7. Portsmouth, but I am hoping I have one and two round the wrong way! Countryman NATIONAL PLACINGS SINCE 1946. items.label: March 1968
items.sum: Report and results of the 1968 National cross-country championships at Sutton Coldfield on 8 March, where Belgrave were fourth for the third year running with Gerry North 11th.
items.s: 4th AGAIN ! MEDALS ELUDE 'NATIONAL' TEAM Report and results of the 1968 National cross-country championships at Sutton Coldfield on 8 March, where Belgrave were fourth for the third year running with Gerry North 11th. SUTTON COLDFIELD ---March 8th This year's race proved without a shadow of doubt that nine miles is too far for most of the Belgrave team---the valuable points lost on the last lap when we should have been moving up were the difference between winning and 4th place. With one lap to go we were definitely second and still with a chance to overtake Coventry but at the end we were beaten back and missed the championship by 98 points and second place by only 23 points. This was a repetition of the Southern where Reading beat us in a similar manner. After half a mile our runners were most prominent---Geoff North was 3rd and Gerry North, Thresher, Dance, Hart and Fairclough were in close attendance. What a change at 3 miles when only Gerry North was anywhere near the leaders and was running with his usual flair for the big occasion. From then on it became a dreary procession-only Gerry stayed in touch, the others looking tired and beaten. Tony Fairclough was unfortunate to suffer two falls one of which involved an argument with an irremovable post and in consequence he finished well below his usual placings. Bill Dance also suffered a muscle sprain which impaired his performance. Adrian Major in his first year of Senior competition ran well up to expectations to take 78th place and to show some of his more experienced club mates how it should be done. There are no real excuses-the course was by no means difficult, being dry with fast going and this should have suited us admirably. Gerry was unfortunate in the end not to get his colours again, being selected only as a reserve for the International in Tunisia later in March. Many of our members will consider that 4th place (out of 84 teams to close in) for our Senior team is a good performance but to those of us who know the potential of our runners this was a most disappointing result. This is the third year in succession that we have occupied this position and although we move nearer to the leaders year by year there is no doubt whatsoever that our team this year could with the right preparation and right approach have won handsomely. Low winning scores are now a thing of the past--the days when a club could finish (as we did in 1946 and 1948) its six scorers in the first twenty places are gone. It would need almost a full international team to achieve this now that the standard generally has greatly improved and the size of the fields has gone up from 300 to almost a 1000 in twenty years. It is therefore only necessary to place the scoring six in the first sixty positions with the leading three in the first twenty five--by no means an impossible task for Belgrave with their present runners. Unfortunately the whole approach to a National Cross Country win is indifferent-no one likes to be left out of the team but with a few exceptions the will and spirit to become the top cross country club in Britain is missing. Our teams are made up mainly of individualists (they are proud to call themselves this who do not achieve the fame they envisage in other spheres of athletics and consequently fall between two stools. If they trained wholeheartedly over the country perhaps the best of both worlds could be gained. Think of the prestige to the Club and its members and the resultant invitations to the Continent which are lost by a half hearted approach. We fielded teams in the Youth and Junior races but as we are particularly weak in these classes at the present time there is little to be said except that Peter Blair-Fish who finished 108th in the Junior race ran reasonably well. 7. items.sum: Report and results of the Southampton-Bournemouth road relay on 10 March 1968, where the leading teams went off course and Belgrave finished second to Portsmouth.
items.s: SOUTHAMPTON-BOURNEMOUTH RELAY Report and results of the Southampton-Bournemouth road relay on 10 March 1968, where the leading teams went off course and Belgrave finished second to Portsmouth. SOUTHAMPTON-BOURNEMOUTH RELAY---Sunday, March 10th As if the disappointment of the National was not enough! All set to show our mettle on the road, we had John Thresher within an ace of taking the lead on the third stage when the first six teams went off course to the extent of 2 minutes. First became fifth and although we fought back to 2nd our old rivals Portsmouth scored a hollow victory. Adrian Major continued his good form with 4th place on stage 1, handing over to Gerry North, who, despite a troublesome knee, broke Trevor Hart's old stage record by 18 secs. Then came John's eventful run and it had to be Hyman of Portsmouth, seventh at the time and 70 seconds behind the leaders, who was the first to realise the race was going astray, took the right course and a lead his club held to the end. John ran the latter half of his stage with Francis of Westbury who was credited with the day's fastest of 28:34 against John's 30:42! Laurie O'Hara took us up to 3rd, Geoff North maintained it and Bill Dance passed the Reading man and held off Bob Holt to finish a worthy second and a moral 1st. Of the teams to go off course only Hercules/Wimbledon and ourselves got back into the first six. We also had the first 'B' team to finish. Pos Team Time 1. Portsmouth AC 2:26:07 2. items.label: March 1968
items.sum: Humorous piece in which a frustrated supporter hears Belgrave's Mr. Maclean ('Mac') end a radio discussion of the silver market with 'UP THE BELS!'.
items.s: SUPERMAC! Humorous piece in which a frustrated supporter hears Belgrave's Mr. Maclean ('Mac') end a radio discussion of the silver market with 'UP THE BELS!'. The winter of disappointments was well underway. Weren't Belgrave going to win anything? Seven days between fixtures is an eternity and my nerves were already badly strained. I mean, you can beat your wife after a couple of disappointments but you musn't let it show too much. I confess that my behaviour for 3 days after defeat is despicable, but for three days prior to defeat it is less despicable, I have my friends back and we speculate about next Saturday. Wednesday is a hiatus---I just brood. I had been having quite an enjoyable brood this particular hiatus and was almost tempted to unlock my wife from the cellar a day early. Weren't Belgrave ever going to hit the headlines this season, I thought, and idly twiddled the radio knobs. The rasping cacophony of sound was suddenly broken by the 10o'clock "News and Comment" man. Perhaps, I thought, I could devise some means of drugging the opposition next Saturday or-------"Mr. Maclean who is in the studio with us". I cocked one ear. "Mr. Maclean"--I was right, that was the name he'd said---"what are the reasons for this spate of buying in the silver market?". "Well-----"; the dulcet tones of Mac got no further. "It's him" I cried. My saviour had arrived. He had carried our colours over track, country and road; he had carried our written word to the local papers; he had put an inch on Belgrave chests when he dived into the freezing Thames for a rescue and now he was on the air. What a genius he is, why hadn't I thought of it before? But how could he plug Belgrave in a programme discussing the silver market? I sobered down, and Mac's closing remarks gradually became discernible "-----but of course there will soon be greater speculation in gold, particularly claret and gold, Goodnight,and UP THE BELS!". My hero! He'd done it! I'm sure that's what he said and no one will talk me out of it--- least of all my wife, who is eternally grateful. Mr. Maclean Mr. Maclean Mr. Maclean Mac Thames

items.label: June 1968
items.sum: Editorial congratulating Alf Harley on becoming the first Belgravian President of the Southern Counties A.A.A., and calling for a review of the club's track and field standards.
items.s: EDITORIAL Editorial congratulating Alf Harley on becoming the first Belgravian President of the Southern Counties A.A.A., and calling for a review of the club's track and field standards. The congratulations of all Belgravians go out to our General Honorary Secretary who,last month, was elected to the Presidency of the Southern Counties Amateur Athletic Association. A.A.Harley is the first Belgravian to hold this prestigious office and all will agree that "Mr Belgrave", as he is sometimes called, is the fitting person for such a "first". A prodigious worker for the club and the associations to which we are affilliated, he is a highly respected figure in the world of athletics and it is with a sense of real pride that we welcome his Presidency. The road he has travelled since his election to Belgrave membership in 1926 has been long, with many turnings. His record during that journey suggests that he has not yet reached it's end. In that 42 years he filled a multitude of offices including the Presidencies of the R.W.A., and the Middlesex County A.A.A. He is a member of the British Olympic Council, the A.A.A. General Committee and, for many years, Chairman and Treasurer of the Association of London Athletic Clubs. To list his achievements within our own club is too much. Suffice to say that he has held almost every office, including the Presidency (3 years); and as Honorary Editor, he produced no less than 59 editions of "The Belgravian". But 1968 is a landmark for Alf Harley and Belgrave Harriers in more than one respect. September marks the 30th anniversary of his election to the General Honorary Secretaryship of this club. Apart from a break during the war years and his Presidency, he has held the reins of our administration continuously. It is no coincidence that the late Jack Crump should refer to Belgrave as one of Britain's "largest, most successful and most affluent athletic organisations". Some have even applied this to Alf Harley himself! On his election to the Presidency of the S.C.A.A.A. we offer our congratulations; and as the 30th anniversary of his election to the Club Secretaryship approaches we tender our heartfelt thanks. On another page you will find the 1968 track and field standards (page 42) Alongside the three AAA marks for each event are shown our own club standards, where they exist. It does not require a careful study for two points to become immediately apparent. Firstly, our standards need reviewing again - particularly the field events - and secondly, standard medals are unobtainable in all Youth and most Junior events. This latter point exists because our standard awards are linked to Club Championships only. When the AAA changed to the graded meeting rule should we not have followed suit? Is it right that our runners can pick up standard medals in a variety of events yet our pole-vaulters not have an opportunity? Look again at the list. Is it a picture of encouragement to the Youth, Junior or cinderella-event athlete? It would not be amiss for the Club to study the possibility of establishing Club standards for every recognised AAA event and investigating the question of where and when such marks may be obtained. Furthermore, our standards should bear some regular relationship with those of the AAA which reflect National progress - a kind of grade IV standard. Such a relationship should produce a minimum standard. Where our strength warrants it there is no reason why the mark should not be made superior to the AAA grade III, as in the 20 miles mark at present. But never disproportionately inferior. The subject could do with careful study before 1969. Members views would be welcomed by the Club officers and your members of Committee. Alf Harley A.A.Harley A.A.Harley Alf Harley Mr Belgrave Jack Crump Jack Crump Southern Counties Amateur Athletic Association S.C.A.A.A. R.W.A. Middlesex County A.A.A. British Olympic Council A.A.A. items.sum: The Hon. Secretary's notes: Chris Steer's marriage and emigration, Tom Pritchard co-opted to committee, the A.G.M. date, G.L.C. matters at Battersea Park, the S.C.A.A.A. '200 Competition', the Frank Simmons Cup, an A.A.A. dance and the cancelled Wandsworth 7 miles.
items.s: HON SEC'S NOTES The Hon. Secretary's notes: Chris Steer's marriage and emigration, Tom Pritchard co-opted to committee, the A.G.M. date, G.L.C. matters at Battersea Park, the S.C.A.A.A. '200 Competition', the Frank Simmons Cup, an A.A.A. dance and the cancelled Wandsworth 7 miles. Our felicitations to Chris Steer and his wife on their recent marriage; and our very good wishes to them on their new life in Canada. Tom Pritchard, a member for over forty years, has been invited to fill the vacancy on Committee, as he headed the list of unsuccessful candidates at the Annual General Meeting last September. Incidentally this year's A.G.M. will be held on Wednesday September 18th at Belgrave Hall. Please note in your diaries. Our representations to the G.L.C. some months ago have borne fruit and the Pole Vault facilities at Battersea Park Track have been much improved. We are grateful for this attention. More recently we have asked the G.L.C. to consider removing the incinerator plant in the north east corner of the Park. There are occasions when the wind blows the noxious smoke and fumes across the track and tennis courts to the detriment of the health and pleasure of those using these facilities, and of the public generally. It seems absurd to develop the park over many years as a recreational centre, and as one of London's lungs, where people may enjoy reasonably fresh air and the many amenities provided; and then permit toxic choking smoke to poison and distress those who visit the park. Our desire for clean air is very real, and competitors in our events inhaling deeply for that extra oxygen to get them to the tape first, or to put that extra effort in the field events, need the purist air available, uncontaminated by smoke and fumes. Lets hope G.L.C. will ensure that they get it ! With our large number of Boy members attending the track regularly for their planned training; we are concerned at the increase in charges for the use of the Dressing Room to 1/-. There may possibly be justification for the increase in charges as applied to adult members; but our Boys with their three or four visits a week to the track plus other expenses involved, cannot be expected to pay a shilling at each visit. We are asking the G.L.C. whether they can extend a concession to those still attending school and now await an answer to our urgent enquiries. From the poorer to the richer club members! As the president of the Southern Counties AAA, I should like to call attention to the "200 Competition" promoted by that body. Membership involves a payment of 5/- per week (paid monthly by Bankers order) of which approximately 2/- goes to help athletics and 3/- goes back in substantial prizes to you and for your friends in the competition. You may be lucky enough to win a monthly prize (our Hon. Treasurer has just received £25) or one of the special six-monthly prizes of £500 which are payable when the competition is fully subscribed with 200 members. You have the satisfaction of knowing you are helping our sport in the South; and are one of only 200 with a chance of three cash prizes each month, and two super prizes at six monthly intervals. I shall be very glad to see that full details reach you if you would let me have your name - there are still a few vacancies to fill. We are greatly indebted to Dr. J. TADYAN who has recently presented us with a "FRANK SIMMONS" Cup, which has been allocated to a Boys High Jump Championship. The A.A.A. is organising an Athletics Dance at the Lyceum Ballroom on Friday Sept. 27th. Tickets to members of AAA Clubs are 12/6 each (normal price £1-1-0) which reduces to 10/- for orders of ten or more tickets. It is expected that HARRY SECOMBE will make the draw for the winning ticket in the competition which is being promoted by the A.A.A, with a Car as first prize and other generous prizes in plenty. items.s: Do you want something ---- for almost nothing? Boxed appeal listing what membership provides and reminding members that the £2 annual subscription is nine months overdue, payable to Dave Shepherd. Of course you do. And you joined BELGRAVE to get it. What do you get? Well, you get four editions of this gazette for a start, and if you don't think it's worth it how about contributing something yourself? Then there's BELGRAVE HALL with its endless hot water (almost) it's tea and cakes, the welcome smiles of Wynn Shepherd, Mrs Savage and the other numerous lady helpers. And, what's more, the building was bought with our own hard saved money. Then there's the 40 odd Club Championship events with their trophies and sets of medals that are fought for each year. One mustn't forget the numerous handicap events either, which produce attractive prizes for those capable of beating the Hon . Handicappers. Then there's the handbook, fixture cards and, of course, those that plan it all. There are our famous socials which are worth twice what you pay. And behind it all are those 30-odd members of General Committee beavering away on your behalf to provide the competition and facilities an athlete needs---to give Belgravians a service second to none. In the midst of all this activity stands the man with the heavily-worn purse strings,the Hon. Treasurer. He bears no small burden and he has ulcers to prove it. All for you. That's the "SOMETHING", now for the "ALMOST NOTHING"-----it's a 40/- subscription. Yes, believe it or not, a mere £2 PER YEAR---just 9d per week. Because it is such a ridiculously small sum, some of you have naturally forgotten to pay it. Don't let us have to send you an unpleasant reminder that you are 9 months overdue---just tie a knot in your tie this instant to remind you to send it to Dave Shepherd whose address is on the Editorial page. As compensation for the torture you have inflicted upon him, why not send him next year's sub as well. If you are truly repentant you could include a donation also. The supreme sacrifice, of course, would be to offer to take over his job--- but then you'd never stand it! SUBSCRIPTIONS ARE 9 MONTHS OVERDUE. Wynn Shepherd Wynn Shepherd Mrs Savage Mrs Savage Dave Shepherd Dave Shepherd Belgrave Hall

items.s: ROAD RELAY ROUND-UP Round-up of Belgrave's 1968 spring road relay season (two firsts, two seconds, two thirds) including third in the National at Leicester, with results from Cranford, Reading and Brighton and a photo of Chris Steer handing over to Jim Rimmer. TWO FIRSTS - TWO SECONDS - TWO THIRDS Our best for many many years. That must be the undisputed verdict on a Spring road relay season that saw our team do battle on six occasions and return home with awards every time. Agreed we chalked up three wins in 1966 and 1967, but our performances were erratic overall and don't really match those of 1968. The peak of this brief but high pressured season was undoubtedly the National Relay at Leicester.where Coventry Godiva, aided and abetted by our 'own' Mel Thorpe, ran out deserved winners. The arrival at Godiva of Colin Kirkham and the revival of Kilby and Heatley were too much for the opposition, and although our team ran well it was evident early on that it was all in an effort to get second place. That Derby should edge us out by a hair just 11 seconds broad may seem rough justice, but with international Dominic Keily on the side lines no one begrudged them their 'silver'. Watching this Derby team on the short legs made one realise just how old our fellows are by comparison. Including our reserve (Dabbs), five of our thirteen runners are over 30 years of age---headed by Bill Kerr, 36 next month. On June 1st the average age of the team was 28 years-4 months. Unfortunately, there is nothing on the horizon to suggest it will be under 30 in the 1970 event. It will be up to our three under-24's Bicourt, Major and Donnison to share an ever increasing degree of responsibility in our future teams, especially with the loss of Peter Whewell to South Africa, Gerry Williams to Venezuela, Chris Steer to Canada and Geoff North to retirement (again). Such thoughts were far from one's mind when the first relay of the season(Southampton to Bournemouth) arrived on Sunday March 10th---just 8 days after the National Cross-Country. With a long winter behind them, the smell of Spring in the air and the prospect of fast running on good surfaces, runners always seem to find a new lease of life when the road relays come round. Unfortunately they let their fervour carry them away in this opening event---to the extent of two minutes off course!! Only the wily Hyman, of the first seven, trod the correct route and, as described in the March 'BELGRAVIAN', Portsmouth were the official winners. The lads had nearly 3 weeks to forget their Southampton luck---or lack of it---before they descended upon Thames Valley Harriers at Cranford, determined to wrest this Trophy from Polytechnic. Rivalry for the National Relay team showed itself straight away when Bicourt (B) beat Major (A) on the first stage run in, to finish 4th----a grand start. Back in 27th place Dabbs (C) and Black (D) were having a similar tussle, the former scraping home by a one second margin. With 65 starters, and four Belgrave teams in 28, we looked pretty strong. Trevor Hart followed on with his usual reliable run to take us to the front; Bill Dance held this with a slower time and then Geoff North had the galling experience of recording 3rd fastest time of the day, only to see his 8 seconds lead turned into a 6 seconds deficit by Bob Holt of Hercules/Wimbledon. No change on the final stage meant another second place for the record. This was frustrating. But the team had no intention of spending a week licking their wounds. Within 24 hours they were gunning for action at Reading, where fresh sextets from Bristol, Mitcham and the home club were eagerly awaiting us. Their eagerness soon changed to disillusionment as our lads hit the front right from the start, set a course record and chalked up the three fastest times of the day. Only a dozen of the 150 runners broke 17 mins and five of those were Belgravians. Our tails were now really up and when we visited Brighton 6 days later for the Front Relay there was never any doubt that we would retain the trophy we won last year. Our 'A' team was made up of the six long-stage probables for the 'National' team and the 'B' team of contenders for the short stages. A below form run by Chris Steer brought the 'B' team home on the first stage in a lowly 30th place. The interesting feature of the race was how far they could recover. Jim Rimmer ( a man who could soon make our 'A' team if he works hard at it) picked up 4 places and the remaining four worked their way up to a praiseworthy 11th. With Donnison and Dance running they would almost certainly have finished 4th. The score now read two seconds, two firsts. We now, disappointingly, had to face our two thirds. The first of these was at Blackpool,where the event favoured Bolton no end. With only four stages to run, and Hill and Freary in terrific form, it soon became a race for second and North Staffs got us by 17 seconds. The two Bolton stars were each 39 seconds faster than the North brothers---truly fantastic. But we were not deterred, for the event served as no guide to the 12 man National event the following week. What happened the following week at Leicester is now well known to all and can be read in detail on another page. As a team, we ran well. One or two have run better, but no one ran badly and it is on this latter score that they deserved their 3rd place---after all, a very high position for what is a National final. Furthermore, it is 4 places higher than last year. Yes, the 1968 Spring season was definitely one of our best ever---will 1969 be even better?. SUMMARY: SOUTHAMPTON-BOURNEMOUTH--March 10th. items.s: WIMBLEDON CUP for O'HARA Report and results of the club 5¾ miles road championship on 16 March 1968, won by Laurie O'Hara for the Wimbledon Cup, with handicap prizes to Brian Gorman, Peter Blair-Fish and George Piddington. Club 5¾ Miles Road Championship - March 16th. With the North brothers out of the way for this title race, at least the engraver was going to get a bit of variety ! With Thresher also absent O'Hara was the favourite - just. Our President, Ted Stimpson, sent the 45 starters scurrying up Lauriston Road and as they swirled round the corner one caught brief glimpses of "flash"Dance, "T.K.", "I'm only doing 60 miles a week" Newell, "Carnaby" Steer, "Photos" Linstead, Brian Gorman - or was it Hamilton, "What do you think?" himself, the Bishop of Brighton, Supermac and the whole motley crowd were past, already eating up the first lap of the "top". On the second small lap a group of ten detached itself from the field and, with Hart forcing the pace they headed out for Copse Hill. Things were now hotting up and at the bottom of Copse, Hart, O'Hara, Bicourt and Major had broken away from Bill Dance with Bill Kerr and John Dear close up and the rest strung out in single file. On hitting the hills Laurie made his break. Adrian was the first to tail off and then the order settled down to O'Hara, Bicourt, Hart. For the last 1¼ miles no more than ten seconds covered the three but for all the striving their positions remained unchanged. John Dear had his best ever run in this event and Lionel Mann was only 2 seconds outside his best. A dramatic finish was enacted between Ron Linstead and Jim Rimmer with "no one shall pass me" Linstead getting the verdict by the thickness of his number card and being incommunicado for the next five minutes. Brian Gorman produced a most encouraging run and fooled the handicapper by a 45 seconds margin - he deserved his first prize; make the most of it Brian, our handicapper doesn't forget treatment of this sort ! Second and third prizes went to Peter Blair-Fish, who is showing steady improvement, and George Piddington - obviously the sea air agrees with him. Pos Name Handicap Time 1. L.O'Hara (0:45) 27:58 2. items.label: June 1968
items.h: Bronze in National Relay DERBY SNATCH SILVER
items.sum: Stage-by-stage report of the A.A.A. National 12-stage road relay at Leicester on 27 April 1968, where Belgrave took bronze 11 seconds behind Derby and two minutes behind Coventry Godiva, with results, fastest times and a photo of Adrian Major handing over to Gerry North.
items.s: Bronze in National Relay DERBY SNATCH SILVER Stage-by-stage report of the A.A.A. National 12-stage road relay at Leicester on 27 April 1968, where Belgrave took bronze 11 seconds behind Derby and two minutes behind Coventry Godiva, with results, fastest times and a photo of Adrian Major handing over to Gerry North. LEICESTER SPORTS CENTRE - April 27th If Coventry hadn't spoiled it all by being out in front almost all the way this would have been the most exciting relay for many years. As it was, the field were racing for the silver medals and for 4¼ hours Derby and Belgrave fought a see-saw battle that was in doubt to the very end, when the holders of the Northern title squeezed home by the narrow margin of 11 secs. Throughout that 4¼ hours the two teams were never further apart than 48 secs. With interest centred on this dual struggle, it came as a surprise after Stage 8 to find that Godiva were suddenly vulnerable - Derby having got to within 21 seconds of them. Any raising of additional hopes were soon put down by Dick Taylor on the next stage who for the second year stamped his authority on this contest. The venue was an improvement on last year, the weather a little kinder (it was at least warmer) and the Belgrave performances free of disaster. Yes, there were some disappointments, but one cannot expect 12 men to hit peak on the same day. Our all-round solid performance was worthy of praise, and praise it got, particularly from that vociferous bank of supporters who, loyally shuttling from long to short stages and replenishing their "flasks" en-route, cheered on our runners at those vital moments. The long lap was 5 miles - 1492 years in length and the short one 2 miles - 1502 yards. The change-overs were effected on the new running track. STAGE 1. John Bicourt (28:23 - 12th fastest) A late start, by five minutes, permitted Manchester D.L.C. to just make the line but Blackpool had to run a substitute while they awaited the bulk of their team - they remained in last place throughout. John dashed to the front, ostentatiously asked for guidance out of the grounds, and disappeared up Saffron Lane shoulder to shoulder with Mike Fuller - Fowler, Haslam, Francis and Kirkham in hot pursuit. At Wigston village (3 miles), with the fast run home ahead of them, the first dozen were closely grouped with John just maintaining contact. The fast pace gradually reduced the numbers until only 4 remained to fight it out round the track. John held his form well and, although 12th, was only 36 seconds behind the leader. Coventry ominously, were second, Derby 5th, Manchester 14th and Portsmouth (Meadows) a disastrous 21st. STAGE 2. Tony Fairclough (14:49 - 12th fastest) Dogged by injury for several weeks Tony was not yet back to full fitness. Neverthless, he ran his heart out as usual taking two places but losing three on the track when he had nothing left. We were now 13th, 64 secs down on Coventry and 44 secs. behind Derby. STAGE 3. Geoff North (27:33 - 2nd fastest) With the opposition nicely strung out ahead Geoff raced through the field, catching the Derby runner (Calladine) after only 3 miles and only just failing to beat Perry of Birchfield for second place. His invaluable effort left Derby trailing by 25 seconds, but Coventry's lead had been increased to 1:28 due to a scintillating run by Adcocks (27:09). Manchester were 11th, Tipton 15th and Portsmouth 21st and way out of the reckoning. STAGE 4. Roger Donnison (14:55 - 10th fastest) Roger will not need to be reminded of Birchfield's colours. After nearly 3 miles of desperate struggle he cut their lead from 8 seconds to 4 seconds! He was also faster than the Coventry runner (Godfrey) but had to give way to another of Derby's short-leg stars (Hinton) who took them back up to 2nd. 35 seconds behind Roger was ex-Belgravian Hugh Barrow (14:45) running for Sale. 12 seconds now covered Derby, Birchfield and Bels with Coventry 52 seconds ahead. STAGE 5. Laurie O'Hara (28:10 - 5th fastest) A ding-dong battle was now developing between Derby and Bels, and Laurie had tough opposition in Leeming. However, our man was still riding high after his excellent win in the Wycombe '5' road race and gradually he pulled back the Derby man's 90 yard lead, yard by yard, in a workmanlike manner. With the Birchfield man well dropped, it must have been a shock for Laurie at the 4 miles mark to see Mike Freary of Bolton surge past and go on to clock a fantastic 26:33;the only man to beat 27 minutes on the day. With the stadium close at hand Laurie caught Leeming and his finishing sprint took him 2 seconds clear. His effort of 28:10 was only 5 seconds away from being 3rd fastest, behind Freary and Tipton's Jim Wright, and was just one second better than Basil Heatley, out again up front for Coventry. STAGE 6. Bill Dance (14:29 - 2nd fastest) With the Derby/Belgrave dual now 3-2 to our rivals, Bill set out to hold our lead and make it 3-3 at the halfway mark. Eley of Derby soon took back the two seconds leeway and, to the horror of our supporters gradually went ahead. Bill, wearing his most determind look - complete with the closed eyes treatment - restricted the lead to 10 yards until, on entering the stadium, he cut loose like a quarter miler to hand over.six seconds ahead. What an entertainer ! "Just a flash runner" said Brenda Dance. Trevor Hart said nothing - he was going to need his breath. STAGE 7. Trevor Hart (28:19 - 7th fastest) Trevor found himself in hot company. Brian Kilby 52 seconds ahead, Simmons (the Derby No.1) on his heels and another three of the day's top runners, Rushmer, Holt and Jackson chasing hard. Simmons had no easy task in getting ahead of the bearded Hart and, when he did go past, Trevor fought every yard of the way to keep the margin down. To be sandwiched between the two fastest men of the stage was a real test of courage and he came through with flying colours - Simmons held to 27 seconds and Rushmer kept off by 13 seconds. 86 seconds now covered the first four teams. STAGE 8. John Dear (14:51 - 8th fastest) For several years John has been destined to serve as a regular reserve in our teams, so it was good to see him gaining his place this time as a first choice. His selection was justified and must have been all the sweeter to him when he took 4 seconds off our old friend Mel Thorpe who was busy maintaining Coventry's front position. While the Coventry/Belgrave gap remained at just over a minute, Derby (Peake) had moved up to within 21 secs of Godiva - closer than anyone had managed to get since Stage 2. STAGE 9. John Thresher (28:00 - 4th fastest) Although not as dramatic as his run of last year, Dick Taylor raced away to wrap it up for Coventry with a lead of 1:48. John's task was to catch Eccles of Derby and put us back in the race for second place. He did not disappoint and, with a final flourish on the track, gave our next man a two-second lead. Manchester (Gregory) and Hercules/Wimbledon (R.Holt) had closed up to within 30 seconds. At this point our supporters felt more confident of receiving second place than at anytime. Belgrave's strong finish of Major, Gerry North & Kerr looked certain to have the mastery of Derby's Domleo, Bullivant and Taylor. If only Gerry North could be given a lead. STAGE 10. Adrian Major (14:54 - 7th fastest) Adrian's recent form had been such to justify consideration for a long stage. Although a few days short of his 21st birthday he had already attained his athletic majority with 78th in the National cross-country championships and, as he set off hotly pursued by Domleo, there was an air of confidence in the Belgrave camp. Fourteen minutes later it had changed to shocked surprise when a red and white vest was the first to appear, and became dismay as the next 20 seconds seemed like hours before Adrian's appearance. Although "not my day" he was still able to chalk up 7th fastest time, which indicated that Derby had played quite a big part in the struggle. STAGE 11. Gerry North (27:54 - 3rd fastest) Not for some time had Gerry looked so nervous before a race. During his warm up he was thinking in terms of holding a lead over Bullivant, and North in full flight takes some catching. Faced with the task instead, of pulling back 150 yards he fairly streaked after his quarry and, within 2 miles, had caught the Derby international. Bullivant latched on to Gerry and, although the Belgrave man had edged away by 6 yards at Wigston, that early effort up hill and against wind took it's toll. When they turned into the fast second half a revived Bullivant, in his best track style and with the wind behind him, surged back to the front again going away to make up all but one second of his original lead. Gerry fought on as only Gerry can, but it was not his day either, for even if he had held Bullivant his time would still have been less than he had hoped for. STAGE 12. Bill Kerr (14:38 - 2nd fastest) Bill was his usual unruffled self at the takeover and, as he left the stadium in that misleadingly nonchalant style, many thought that Taylor of Derby would consolidate their lead. But their worries were not yet over. 36 year old Kerr, the oldest member of the team, was out to show everyone that the old zip was still there and the cause not yet lost. Only the shortness of the distance prevented him from becoming the day's hero for, after making little impression over the first 1½ miles, he hauled back 6 of the 17 seconds deficit in the last mile and the men from Derbyshire didn't relax until their man actually reached the track - just 80 yards ahead. So, after 4¼ hours of running, the two teams finished only 11 seconds apart. Coventry were 2 mins ahead and Manchester 2 minutes behind. And so Godiva scored a National double, taking both cross-country and relay titles, but no one else bettered our combined placings of 4th and 3rd respectively so until we renew our assault next season we give best only to Coventry Godiva - a great team. items.label: June 1968
items.sum: Profile of John Thresher, born 1939, tracing his running from joining Belgrave in 1957 to his 1967 Southern 3 miles title and Olympic 5,000m ambitions, with three photographs.
items.s: SPOTLIGHT ON ... JOHN THRESHER Profile of John Thresher, born 1939, tracing his running from joining Belgrave in 1957 to his 1967 Southern 3 miles title and Olympic 5,000m ambitions, with three photographs. The place is Motspur Park Track, the date 24th June 1967 and the race about to start is the S.C.A.A.A. three miles championship. As the runners stoop forward and peer at their reflections in the flooded track the starter raises his arm and sends them splattering round the first bend in a shower of liquified cinders. As the lap count down progresses so the leading group diminishes in size, until there is only the holder Gibson, the favourite Johnstone, the Holt twins and two Belgravians. "Two laps to go" is the cry and Johnstone breaks for home. Gibson goes with him followed by Bob Holt and a mud bespattered runner whose spectacles look more like sun-glasses. The crowd cheers, and the "blind" man surges forward as though suddenly equipped with an outboard motor, races past the surprised leaders in the straight and scores what looks to be a ridiculously easy win. Next day millions of sleepy citizens opened their Sunday papers to see the happy, muddy face of JOHN THRESHER smiling at them. Some thought, no doubt, that they had more to laugh at than him; but then they didn't know of the events that led up to his first major championship success. John Thresher was born at Merton on 16th December 1939. When at school, he disliked playing rugby; the only alternative was cross-country and he enjoyed it probably because he was fairly good at it. In the next road to John there lived a certain Raymond Braine of Belgrave Harriers who had no idea of the service he was rendering the Club each time he pounded his way up Erroll Gardens sporting his brightly lettered track-suit top. A few brief words of introduction and 17 year old John Thresher became a Belgravian in October 1957. No-one noticed. But they began to a few weeks later when, over Herne Hill Harriers course at Addington, he carried our colours for the first time. "Young Thresher showed delightful form in winning the Youths race" read THE BELGRAVIAN of that time, and John well remembers how encouraged he was at receiving such early recognition. His first track season produced a 4:29 mile and a 9:53 two miles, yet three years later his mile had dropped only 9 seconds and his 9:53 still stood as a personal best. There were many who thought that if progress was not forthcoming in the formative years 18 - 21 there was little prospect of much following. They hadn't reckoned with John Thresher. They were also not aware of the priority he gave to his studies and work as an articled accountant. His training continued to be remarkably light, but regular - "I owed a great deal to Arthur Penny during this period for his continual encouragement and the holding together of our Youths team". Came the track season of 1961 and studies for his Chartered Accountancy examinations. He reflects "While existing on one five miles training run every Wednesday and the occasional Saturday race, I distinctly remember running a 1:59 half in the Club Champs and realising I was wasting my time. I decided to train harder there and then". Before the season was out he ran 1:55 on three occasions. The writing was on the wall. Illness that Autumn (6 weeks) put him back a long way but only made him more determined than ever and he resolved to do a regular weekly mileage of 40. From December 1961 onwards John could be seen in the heart of all our training packs. Repetition climbs up the horse-rides in the darkness of Tuesday evenings chasing the unseen figures of Robinson, Miller, Shippen and Thompson; out on the dimly lit roads of Wimbledon on Thursdays, gasping behind Linstead, Dabbs, Gebbett & Co. as they did the "seven hills"; sometimes on the "Warren 9" with Bird, Walker, Baulch & Co. And gradually it came. The results were soon apparent when in the South of Thames Senior at Maidenhead in 1962 Thresher finished 26th helping our team to second place medals. The hard winter's work reaped dividends that track season and in one fell swoop he chopped his times to 4:09.4 and 9:04, and tasted his first Championship success by annexing the L.C.C. mile in 4:12. These rewards induced him to adopt a policy of increasing his training work-load each year. The times came down. 1963 - 1:53.0/4:07.5/8:48.4 (and a 2nd place in the London v Munich 1500 metres). 1964 - 1:52.4/4:02.1 (and runner up in the County mile). 1965 - 4:02.7/13:54.0 (and a great win in Milan over 1500 metrs for London, in 3:46.7). In 1966 John Thresher reached the final of the A.A.A. mile - "I finished 7th in 4:04.6, having run the last lap in 56 seconds and been left standing! I resolved to run 3 miles in 1967". Some had expected him to make this decision a season earlier but, nonetheless, all were agreed it was a right one. An 8:42.2 two miles soon endorsed this and before the season was through he had his first B.A.A.B. trip to Vienna where, with Dick Taylor of Coventry Godiva, he ran against Ron Clarke and Lazlo Mecser over 5,000 metres where he clocked a personal best 14:05. Shortly afterwards he finished second to the great Michel Jazy over 3,000 metres at La Baule. Our subject had not been idle during the intervening winters. "I have never been very fond of cross-country due to an old ankle injury - and especially over 9 miles" but he was still a regular member of our winter teams, and the 1966/7 winter would have to be his best ever if he was to become a successful 12 lap exponent. It was. Second in the Surrey Co., 16th in the Inter-Counties and 50th in the National ("I was disappointed not to have had a good one") and John had a good foundation for his season of three miling. He did not realise that it would bring him his finest victory and his most disappointing defeat. After a second place in the Surrey Co. (13:40.4) and a promising 4th in the Inter-Counties at the White City (13:40.8) the way was paved for that exciting battle in the muddied cinders of Motspur Park. ATHLETICS WEEKLY wrote "John Thresher, although handicapped by mud plastering his glasses ran the fastest race of his career - - - - - his time of 13:35.8 might have been 10 seconds faster on a dry track". And so he was Southern Champion - feeling on top of the world. "I felt very confident during my warm up and as I stood on the line I looked around and thought 'I can beat this lot'. The pace felt so slow, I had to keep holding in, checking all the while and jockeying for position. When Johnston burst away two laps from home I had to school myself to wait even then. I felt great on that last lap and could see just enough to keep my feet. Now for the AAA's". He was soon to find out that his rivals had not been standing still during his progress, and at the Championships on July 15th he finished 13th in a best ever 13:27.2. Despite the time his disappointment was greater than ever before. It was obvious then, as it is now, that the three hot favourites for representation in the 5,000 metres at Mexico were McCafferty, Taylor and Rushmer. John has resolved to harry this trio at every opportunity throughout 1968 and, should something go wrong for them, be right at hand as the logical replacement. It will require a lot of hard early-season racing to make his mark and the ability to hold his form - a challenge he is well fitted to meet. What of the future? Well, he hopes to go on competing until he can no longer make Belgrave road-relay teams, and there is always the possibility of turning to coaching or administration. For the present he prefers to be 'spoon-fed' and concentrate on his running - an attitude, he thinks, that many officials fail to understand. He admires Gerry North immensely for his wholehearted approach and has a high regard for Bill Kerr - "A beautifully relaxed performer whom I tried to copy". Of Belgrave? "Well it is the best club anyone could belong to, but it could be even better". Last year John Thresher had a taste of the rarefied atmosphere at Font Romeu in the Pyrenees - he is "hooked" on it. McCafferty, Taylor & Rushmer had better beware; he has an insatiable desire for the Mexico City flavour ! John fights it out with Alan Rushmer during the 1967 AAA championships at White City. M. items.sum: Gordon Biscoe's road running introduction noting improving fortunes and congratulating Bill Dance and Lionel Mann on AAA first-class standards in the Surrey 20.
items.s: ROAD RUNNING Gordon Biscoe's road running introduction noting improving fortunes and congratulating Bill Dance and Lionel Mann on AAA first-class standards in the Surrey 20. GORDON BISCOE WRITES :- This being the main season for distance races our fortunes do seem to be improving slowly but surely compared with recent years. A roundup of the main events since the last Belgravian would show the latest 'State of Parties' as, trophies won - one; lost - one; retained - one; several 'Independant' victories and various others where we have more than 'held our deposit'. It is also good to note that in certain events in the past where we have only been able to raise one team we are now fielding two or more. In the last Belgravian I commented on the excess of distance races nowadays; even this number does not appear to satisfy Lionel Mann's appetite for competition and its even rumoured that he is looking forward to the advent of organised Sunday sport in this country when he can maybe run two 20's on consecutive days - providing of course it does not interfere with his football and golf in the morning ! However, hard work has its rewards and we have to congratulate Bill Dance and Lionel for obtaining AAA 1st class standards and, hence, club honours badges, with times of 1:50:18 and 1:52:17 respectively in the recent Surrey 20. Gordon Biscoe GORDON BISCOE Lionel Mann Lionel Mann Lionel Mann Lionel Bill Dance Bill Dance Surrey 20 Miles 1968 AAA

items.s: AN EASTER DOUBLE Report and results of the Maidenhead 10 miles and Feltham 5 miles road races on Easter Monday, 15 April 1968, won by Gerry North and Laurie O'Hara respectively, with Belgrave taking the Maidenhead team trophy. VICTORY IN MAIDENHEAD 10M & FELTHAM 5M Run in sunshine, as opposed to last year's snow storm, the Maidenhead 10 turned out to be one of mixed fortunes for our runners, but one which gave Gerry,having led virtually from the start,a convincing win (54secs) over old rival on the road, Mick Price (Bristol). It also resulted in us taking the team trophy which eluded us last year. For Trevor Hart it was a 'battle royal' all the way with C. Wade (Ranelagh) who got the better of him only in the closing stages. Bill Kerr's decision to run at almost the eleventh hour meant he was not in our team entry and hence not able to score, thus making Lionel Mann with another good run our third scoring member. Bob Glover, straight from his speed work on the track, showed he still had'nt lost his ability on the road with a very good run---he did'nt even say "That was hard" at the end so he must have felt good! Pat O'Connor showed a slight improvement on his loss of form of late but Chris Keavey and Bernard Merry would prefer to write this off as just not being their day. Whilst Gerry was leading them home at Maidenhead Laurie O'Hara was repeating the act at Feltham in the annual 5 mile race where he scored a nicely judged victory over another evergreen, Mike Barrett (Ealing & Southall). Whilst Laurie did not have as strong a supporting cast as Gerry, we again had two teams out with Charlie Walker still keeping in trim, and Bill Laws making a welcome return to the road. Pete Sutton also took his first prize home for being the first vet to finish, and Glimpy Jones scored his first victory over Chas. Smart. We knew Charlie has been unfit, and probably stopped to buy some antiques on the way---sorry Glimpy you'll have to do it again to convince us!! TEAMS: 1. BELGRAVE 14 pts. 2. Ranelagh 23 pts. 3. items.s: LOST! ONE COUNTY TITLE Report and results of the Surrey 20 miles road championship on 4 May 1968 in heavy rain, where Belgrave lost the county team title to Ranelagh, with Gerry North third in the county championship. SURREY 20m - 4th MAY. With Chris Steer now missing from our team, our chances of retaining the title took rather a knock. However, with Gerry North and Bill Dance stepping up their normal distances to join the "Charlies" (Dabbs & Walker) in its defence, hopes rose. Trevor Hart, Lionel Mann and Pat O'Connor although in the race as guests do not qualify for Surrey. The course this year was over six laps of the Walton road relay circuit and all seemed set for a fine afternoon. However, hardly had the 37 starters got under way when the rains came and over the following two hours deteriorated into a miserable downpour. At the end of one lap the early leader was Chris Wade (Ranelagh) with a following group consisting of Gerry, Trevor, Lionel, Bill and Chas Dabbs only 5 secs behind, a further 20 secs back came "old faithful" Charlie Walker with Pat O'Connor in the second group; at this stage we had the first scoring three. Basically, these positions remained unchanged until just before the half distance when it was obvious Charlie Dabbs was far from his best and steadily dropping back, soon to be passed by Fowler (Ranelagh) who completed the Ranelagh scoring three. Although it was obvious the title had slipped from us, the race remained very much alive until the end, with the last lap providing the final break up of the leading group. With M. Fuller proving a surprise winner it was realised that Hercules-Wimb. also had their 3rd scoring man in before us, and so beat us for second place with an equal number of points. All credit though to Trevor, Gerry and Bill for producing the performances they did in such horrible conditions, especially as it was their first outing over this distance this year. Also to Chas Walker, over 9 mins faster than his time last year - what would he do if he started training again !! (Jack Brown please note !!!) Teams: 1. Ranelagh (2,5,6) 13pts 2. items.s: NO CHANGE - HAMPSTEAD '10' - 18th MAY. Charlie Dabbs reports the Hampstead 10 miles on 18 May 1968, where Gerry North retained the individual title in a record and Belgrave 'A' retained the team trophy. CHARLIE DABBS REPORTS :- On cup-final day 1967 a Belgrave team of Gerry North, Trevor Hart and Charlie Dabbs won the Hampstead '10' team trophy and Gerry won the individual event. On cup-final day one year later the same trio managed to retain the same trophy and Gerry similarly retained his individual title although forced by Martin Craven to a record breaking run. Since previous fast times on this course have been run by Kilby, Juan & Dick Taylor, Adcocks and Tim Johnston, this run of Gerry's is indicative of his present excellent form. Trevor Hart found that a combination of battered shoes and "micro laces" not entirely suitable to a race of this nature and his footwear disintegrated after one mile had been covered. However, after temporary repairs were made (not to mention a loss of 30-40 seconds in time) he pursued the leaders with his usual forcefulness. Charlie Dabbs has only recently emerged from his winter of semi-hibernation, but his position and time reflects his steady return to form. The rest of the lads all ran well on a reasonably tough course, but a club of our size should provide a stronger team than this. Since we have before now turned out between 20 and 30 athletes at road races like Bracknell and Wycombe there is no real reason why such support should not be extended to races like this one. items.label: June 1968
items.h: TRACK AND FIELD - THE TIMES-THEY ARE A-CHANGING.
items.sum: Tony Brooks (track) and Bill Couzens (field) preview Belgrave's prospects event by event for the first National League 'B' league season in 1968.
items.s: TRACK AND FIELD - THE TIMES-THEY ARE A-CHANGING. Tony Brooks (track) and Bill Couzens (field) preview Belgrave's prospects event by event for the first National League 'B' league season in 1968. TONY BROOKS WRITES ON TRACK: This year, Belgrave Harriers will be one of the twelve clubs who will help re-write British club-athletics history. On July 21st we compete in the first match of the 'B' league against Sale Harriers, T.V.H., Birchfield, Notts A.C. and L.C.A.T. A.C., all of which are clubs of no mean ability. How will Belgrave make out? Will we emerge victorious, or as an also ran? This question can be best answered by the athletes themselves, who they will be will depend largely upon the results of the coming trophy and club meetings, and those who prove themselves to be true Belgravians will be the ones who will be selected to compete in these meetings. Let us then look at the events and the people who will be fighting for the places in the teams. 100/200 mtrs. For the past couple of years, the Vivian/Mitchell/Martin combine has dominated these events, but now that John Mitchell has had an unlucky start to the season due to glandular fever Jim Vivian and Chris Martin had both better look out for the fast improving Steve White, who has recorded times over the longer sprint that Jim and Chris have yet to beat this year. 400 mtrs. In relation to the other clubs, this is the event where we are at our weakest. With Chris Martin being the only one to have recorded a respectable time, our outlook is gloomy. However, if Jim Vivian were to concentrate on quarter miling he could well find himself amongst the top in the country. 800 mtrs. Although having been weak in this event for the past few years, it looks as if in the foreseeable future this could be one of our stronger points. John Thresher is capable of holding his own against other club half milers, but as he specialises in longer events, it looks as if Tom Carter's school will produce Belgrave's future half milers. With Tony Brooks and Alan Mead both under two minutes after only a few outings, Pete Hillier and Lionell Mann close behind them and Bill Curtin (still a youth doing 2:03.0) the prospects look fair. 1500 mtrs. On paper it looks like John Thresher, but look out for Bill Kerr who has improved tremendously over the mile. Also Geoff North who if encouraged enough could give both of these a run for their money. Others to watch include Laurie O'Hara and Adrian Major. 3000 mtrs. Geoff North, Gerry North, Laurie O'Hara, Bill Kerr, Bill Dance, Tony Fairclough, Trevor Hart. Any one of these is capable of emerging as Belgrave's hope for a winner in this event. 5000 mtrs. Roughly the same field again with the added threat of Thresher who has said that he is good enough to take them all on over this distance. 3000 mtrs/stpchse. In this event we are lucky to be able to pick from any one of five men. John Bicourt looks favourite, but just how far behind him John Dear, Bill Dance and Dick Piotrowski are when it comes to selection remains to be seen. Alan Black could prove the suprise in this event once he has regained fitness, as his time last year placed him second behind Bicourt. This then, at the beginning of the season is how Belgrave shapes up. Who is selected remains to be seen, but whoever it is will certainly have to prove himself against strong competition. BILL COUZENS WRITES ON FIELD. With prospects for the National league looking pretty good on the track, let me outline our prospects in the field events. High Jump. We have never had it so good in this event with Arnold Bent (Junior) already clearing 6'1½" this season Barry Townsend 5'10", Denzil Winsborrow 5'8" and Shola Ipaye 5'8" we could well have both A and B strings over 6 feet. Pole Vault. Our two pole vaulters Denzil Winsborrow and Barry Townsend who have always scored high points in trophy meetings will be a great asset. Long Jump. Derek Wade and John Mitchell are our outstanding pair in this event with capabilities of 24 feet plus. Our first reserve in this event would be a difficult choice between Bob Couillault, Arnold Bent, Barry Townsend, George Borkowski and Denzil Winsborrow all with distances around 21 feet. Triple Jump. Derek Boosey is our tower of strength with Bob Couillault as first choice for the B string. (Dave Ansell forecasts Bob will clear 46' this year). Cliff Brooks not being far behind. 120yd Hurdles. Probably nobody outstanding at this event but Barry Townsend, Denzil Winsborrow, Bob Couillault, Derek Boosey and Cliff Brooks can score valuable points. 440yd Hurdles. No stars at this event but our beginners Bob Couillault and Denzil Winsborrow only need a couple of seconds off their best time to bring them to the fore. Javelin. Nick Head and field events captain Brian King make this one of our strong events and the right day could have both men over 200 ft. Shot. We depend on Nick Head to push the 16lb weight around 43 feet with improving John Martin getting close to 40ft. to make our presence felt in this event. Discus. Nick Head & Frank Glass with personal bests within inches of each other are the obvious choice. with new member Paul Emson as a very promising first reserve. Hammer. New member Malcolm Robertson is a fully fledged Hammer Thrower with a choice of B string from yours truly, Nick Head & Brian King. May 4th-- Despite an early start to the season, some very good performances were set up on a very dismal day. In the sprints, Steve White (17) pushed international Dave Dear all the way in the 'A' 100 and coasted to an easy victory in the 'B' 220. A fine run by John Dear in the steeplechase and a promising 440 by Jim Vivian on the last leg of the medly relay were also noteworthy, but the finest performance of the afternoon was undoubtedly the 6'-0" high jump of our junior, Arnold Bent. items.s: VANCOUVER TROPHY Report and results of the Vancouver Trophy meeting at Woodford Bridge on 12 May 1968, where Belgrave were seventh of twelve clubs and Steve White ran a British junior season's best 22.1 for 200m. May 12th---Woodford Bridge Arriving with great hopes of sucess, Belgrave had to be content with a seventh placing out of twelve clubs. Despite a windy and rain swept afternoon, some very good performances were set up; the most notable being Steve White's 200 metres run of 22.1 which is the fastest time this year by a British junior over the distance. John Thresher running his first track race over 1500 metres produced a time equivalent to a 4.08 mile and showed great promise for the coming season. Encouraging performances were also shown by Denzil Winsborrow and Bob Couillault who both did sub-60 seconds in the 440 hurdles. RESULTS Heats:- 100m: 3. S. White 11.3, 2. C. Martin 11.5, 200m: 1. S.
