items.s: 'THE MILE' HURLINGHAM DRAGSTERS Humorous motor-racing style commentary on the club championship mile at Hurlingham on 25 May 1968, won by John Thresher from Bill Kerr. SPORT 25TH MAY '68 Tension in the stands is building up to fever pitch as down on the track competitors are stripping off for the Championship Mile..the strident voice of Bill Lucas is crackling over the P.A. ... Harry Shields is allocating them their grid positions. Tony Brooks anxiously looking over his shoulder ... a lot of revving up and down ... I can see down there from our colony in the South Seas - George Piddington - and fresh from his long retirement - John Davies ... the whistle goes, they are under starters orders ... suddenly the sun comes out on to the rain sodden track ... Arthur Penny is ready ... down comes the flag and with a deafening roar they are away ... Howard Satchell in the pole position and John Bicourt quickly go into the lead followed up by Adrian Major and John Thresher ... in the back straight Bill Kerr quickly overtakes the early leaders ... Thresher trying to make up ground in 5th position ... down the home straight Kerr in the lead followed by Bicourt, Major and Thresher ... Lionel Mann trying desperately to improve his position and gets in front of Brian Hamilton, who knows how many grooves on a 78 ... Bernard Merry beautifully turned out thinking it was the Dressage instead of a race, was originally up with the group of leaders but has now dropped well back to join Davies and Piddington... coming up to the line it is Bill Kerr, Thresher and Major ... pulled out for a pit stop just after the line - yes, he's out for good - transmission has gone - John Dear ... on the line Davies has gone in front of Merry and Piddington who are hanging on grimly ... at the front the four leaders are drawing steadily away from the field led by Dance, Satchell and Donnison ... Thresher makes a striking effort to take over at the Bell - he is four yards up on Kerr - who is ten yards in front of Bicourt and Major ... the second group now headed by Satchell, Dance and Donnison and at the back Bob Glover has gone in front of Tony Brooks whose recent success in the half has gone to his head ... and who is striking down the home straight like a champion? ...it's Thresher. Major is fighting Bill Kerr for second place ... Kerr finishes second and steaming up at the back is Lionel Mann ... closing in at the rear John Davies followed by Bernard Merry and George Piddington ... the stands have erupted in a jubilation they normally reserve for Billy Graham or Chelsea ... Thresher removes his goggles and receives his trophy, a horse shoe of laurel leaves and a big kiss from Frank Jarvis then shakes hands solemnly with the President's Lady ... meanwhile John Davies prodding me with his finger says "No, they gave me 5/5 but I KNOW it's 5/4. I'm not going to say anything!" (Any errors in the above were beyond my control, p'raps because the stenographer was drunk.) items.s: WHAT ABOUT YOU! Humorous feature matching club members to motor cars, with photo-montages of members alongside vehicles (pictures acknowledged to Beaulieu). Is your personality reflected in your choice of vehicle? Consider Bill Lucas, 'Something in the City' and other interests! He would slide naturally into the class of a Humber, whilst good solid upright Clive Shippen would be at home in the thoroughly British Daimler. But how about Nigel 'Danish' Bacon. What kind of decorated hot-rod for Datona or Southend beach and what about MacLennon, Mead and Kelly, our redoubtable Keystone boys? Difficulty arises with Thresher who has a Morris Cowley for his home in Ewell but dreams of a 2.4 Jaguar Coupé for his pad in Chelsea. With acknowledgements to Beaulieu for reproduction of pictures. Mini Merry De-Luxe - a beautiful little model in elegant colours and always immaculate. Contrary to rumours about performance it lacks a bit of power under the bonnet. A real robust job - The Land Glover - delicate handling is required to bring up to scratch but once under way a true Champion. Fuel consumption is apt to be high but it will burn anything particularly good on nuts and chocolate. Read this with a Pernod in one hand and a Gauloises in the other, reflect on the Gallic Citroen d'Bicourt and life becomes easier - it would charm a bird from a tree and is deceptively light on the pocket. Normally £600, but to you 'cause you're my friend...£660. Bull-Nosed 'T' Carter sterling performer from the past. Aspirants still seek this model because of it's rich experience but despite the clean lines has a job making 18 holes. Trevor 'K' Fiat Coupé of Foreign origin, Rome or Ruislip, top speed just sufficient to make Grand Prix fixtures, instantly recognised by Hairy Trim, responds amazingly to mild abuse. Pontiac Steer, very fast company, requested to vacate these shores by the Home Office as Politically undesirable - now a missionary for Trotsky in the Americas. Agent in U.K. P. Duncan. items.label: June 1968
items.sum: Report and full results of the club track and field championships at Hurlingham Park on 25 May 1968, highlighting Steve White, Chris Martin and Nick Head's trebles and John Thresher's 880/mile double.
items.s: CLUB CHAMPIONSHIPS Report and full results of the club track and field championships at Hurlingham Park on 25 May 1968, highlighting Steve White, Chris Martin and Nick Head's trebles and John Thresher's 880/mile double. HURLINGHAM PARK - MAY 25th The outstanding performers at this year's championships were Steve White, Chris Martin and Nick Head. The first two chalked up sprint trebles in the Junior & Senior grades respectively, and the latter repeated his "pinta" treble of last year shot/discus/javelin. Once again performances were not outstanding, but in a very homely affair of this sort there is not the 'needle' of outside competition. This, coupled with the early date and an afternoon of almost continous drizzle was not conducive to the exceptional. Nevertheless, some exciting contests were seen and the boys played a major part in the entertainment. Their half mile was fascinating. Fifteen lads, their ages ranging from 9 - 14 yrs and with height differences up to 1'6", made the event seem a most unequal contest. This was not the case though when they got their legs moving, and many a good little'un beat a good big'un; best of all, they all enjoyed it - who notices the rain anyway? Richard Langley was a convincing winner and a boy worth watching. Nine-year-old Ian Gillings, not content with a stylish run in the 'half', went pot hunting in the interval and scooped a prize in the children's race; after a flyer too! The weather was a bit tough on the field events competitors. The greasy arena, wet implements and the low temperature didn't give them much good cheer and most were well below their season bests. Arnold Bent repeated his Sen/Jnr high jump double of last year and Bob Couillault clinched a useful triple/long jump double. Carl Lawton had a stylish win in the 2 miles walk after a fast start by Brian Ward that suggested an upset was due. Several of our leading walkers were unable to be present due to a clash of dates with the Leicester '20'. Date clashes also accounted for the absence of our Middlesex County six-milers, Trevor Hart and Laurie O'Hara; whereas illness kept out Geoff North and Jim Vivian who, between them, would have been leading contenders for five titles. One of the most exciting contests of the afternoon was between two runners who didn't even meet; Chris Martin and Steve White. Each time Steve chalked up a win in one of the junior sprints, Chris followed suit in the Senior - but he couldn't match the junior times and Steve won the three mythical contests by margins of about 4 yards (100), 5 yards (220) and 3 yards (440). John Thresher took the 880 and mile in a canter; waiting for the bell in both before making his move. Marathoner Lionel Mann shook up the two-lap merchants with the fastest finishing burst of the day and snatched the bronze medal. Bill Kerr towed the mile field through the first three laps and Thresher was the only one with him at the bell. Bill was in his most stylish form and looks well set for some good 3's this season. Last year's steeplechase result was reversed when John Dear just held off the Dance finish to score a popular win. (Our 8:52.0 chaser, John Bicourt, opted for the mile, as did our sub 9:20 man Alan Black.) Perhaps some of the massive mile field would surprise themselves if they tackled this event next year. Many moderate runners have shown a remarkable aptitude "over the sticks". While the boys high jump went on into the evening like an Olympic pole-vault contest, the President and his Lady, with the able assistance of Frank Webb, went about the task of disposing of the 21 trophies and the multitude of medals. The recorders were there to the bitter end as, indeed, was Bob Taylor who organised it all with such success. The only black-spot, perhaps, was the lack of times for the also-rans. The importance of times for these fellows cannot be overstressed and if it requires special arrangements in future then they should be considered for next year. items.s: INTER - COUNTIES Report and Belgrave results from the Inter-Counties championships at Crystal Palace and White City on 2-3 June 1968, with John Thresher second in the 3 miles and Alan Lerwill second in the long jump. June 2nd/3rd---Crystal Palace and White City Belgravians played no small part in this year's Championships, but the six that competed could have done with a little more luck. Unluckiest of all was Jim Vivian who, in a blanket finish semi-final of the 100 yards was adjudged 5th when many observers felt he had clinched the third place needed to reach the final. The nearest to glory was John Thresher who, after seeming to be well positioned for a win, was outkicked by Cheshire's Blinston---a surprise winner who ran nearly 20 seconds fastest than his previous best. We had two seventh places, each only one spot away from a scoring position (6th earns 2 points), Gerry North and John Bicourt. Gerry's performance was in the '20' at Battersea Park where a quarter of the 64 starters retired in the hot and humid conditions. His time of 1:45:42 was 2:24 behind winner Ron Grove. John Bicourt produced his second sub 8.55 'chase in the course of 10 days. Taking the lead twice in the early stages he kept his form well and was edged out of a scoring position by McAndrew, who finished stronger over the last 500 yards than most of a class field. John's time was a personal best and only 6.2 seconds away from an Olympic qualifying time. Len Duquemin, walking for Hampshire, turned in an excellent effort inthe '7'. His fifth place put him only 40 yards behind 2 miles holder Arthur Jones and was nearly a half minute faster than Ray Middleton's best of last year. Alan Lerwill helped Middlesex towards the retention of their Inter-County title by clinching second place in the long jump with a 24'-3¼" leap that pushed Lynn Davis's protegé Williams back into third position. items.s: FROM 'THE BELGRAVIAN' 25 years ago and 40 years ago Column reprinting items from the Belgravian of May 1943 (new Police walkers, Percy Wright's Overseas Cup) and June 1928 (W.H. Hare President of the S.T.C.C.A., the Griffin Cup, and the National R.W.A. team title); the 1928 individual placings (4, 7, 14, 16) differ from the team placings printed (2, 5, 12, 14). 25 years ago MAY 1943 - Since our last issue no fewer than 12 walkers have joined our ranks, eight of whom have been recruited from our old friends the Police, and for which our thanks are mainly due to Bob Readman. Such progress in these difficult times is sure proof of the popularity both of the Club and the sport. - - - - - the keenness which is being displayed by all concerned leaves no doubt whatever that when the regular championships are resumed, the Belgrave colours will be well to the fore. Percy Wright still continues to do good work with the Belgrave News Letter, and now has another new idea, namely, collecting airgraphs for which he has a market at 1/- a time. With the proceeds, which are getting quite considerable, he hopes to acquire a cup, to be called the "OVERSEAS CUP", for some sort of competition among club members. (Ed. This cup was eventually obtained and is awarded annually to the winner of the Belgrave 3 miles Youths Cross Country Championship). and 40 years ago JUNE 1928 - Our President (W.H. HARE) has been elected President of the South of the Thames C.C.A. Of course, we know that he is equal to any position of honour in the athletic world and we congratulate him on his appointment. Mr. Hare has remarked that he is glad to accept the position, as a mark of recognition of our Club's part in the activities of S.T.C.C.A. Mr. Griffin, our landlord at the "Rising Sun" and a keen Vice-President, has presented to the Club a new trophy, to be held by the winner of our newly-instituted three miles track championship. (Ed. The "Griffin Cup" is now one of our most keenly contested trophies). Five of our Club stalwarts, in three thrilling and exciting hours, won a title which gives distinction to the Club name wherever athletes are gathered - The NATIONAL R.W.A.CHAMPIONSHIP. Our chances of winning were not apparent until the latter part of the race - - - - At half distance Derby (20pts) and Birmingham (26pts) still led with Belgrave and Surrey A.C. thirty points behind ! items.sum: Report and Belgrave results from the Surrey championships at Motspur Park on 5, 6 and 8 June 1968, with Steve White's junior treble, Arnold Bent's 6'1" high jump and John Thresher second in the 3 miles to Bob Holt.
items.s: Surrey Championships Report and Belgrave results from the Surrey championships at Motspur Park on 5, 6 and 8 June 1968, with Steve White's junior treble, Arnold Bent's 6'1" high jump and John Thresher second in the 3 miles to Bob Holt. JUNE 5th,6th & 8th---Motspur Park Belgravians made quite a mark in the 1968 Champioships, held on the fast London University track. The weather threatened continously but never quite carried it out and conditions were generally good. Star of the Championships was undoubtedly Steve White who pulled off an excellent treble in the Junior 100, 220 and long jump events. His 22'-4" in the latter was only 1" inferior to that of the senior winner, international John Howell. Just to show that we were not a one man outfit Arnold Bent turned on the heat with a Junior high jump win of 6'-1" and, to keep Steve company, finished runner-up in the long-jump just 7" behind his club mate. Both Steve and Arnold are 1st year juniors, so what of next year! Our Junior sprint champion was absolutely untouchable in the 100 and although run closer in the furlong was always in control. In the Senior sprints Jim Vivian resumed his duels with Tymms (Surrey AC) and had Chris Martin to keep him company in both finals. Jim could not reproduce the excellent start he gained in his 100 heat and trailed Tymms throughout by a frustrating yard. Chris chased hard for fifth. The furlong saw almost a repeat performance with the Surrey AC man's margin stretched from a tenth to a fifth of a second. Photo by: R. Linstead Tymms wins the 100 from VIVIAN with MARTIN fifth The Hamilton twins reached the finals of the Junior 440 and 880, John doing a personal best 53.5 in the quarter and Bob 2:06.3 in the half, just ahead of T. Day (2:06.6). Another Junior to reach the finals was D.B. Rees who finished 5th in the short sprint. With Steve White and Arnold Bent having collected four golds and a silver between them our supporters were really cock-a-hoop, for young L.J. Sullivan had already scooped the Youths long jump on the Wednesday evening with an excellent 20'-6½". Sullivan is a promising athlete of whom we should hear a lot more. It was unfortunate to see that other outstanding Youth, Bill Curtin, standing on the side lines with a leg injury. We could have seen him add to our medal tally in the Youths 880. Alan Mead stood in for Tony Brooks in the final of the Senior 440 as fastest non-qualifier. Although last, he ran a personal best 51.9 and was given more publicity than the winner Cohen. Charles Elliott announced that Alan had been on duty at the Trooping the Colour all morning and had just made the final---such is fame! The star event of these Championships is the 3 miles. Surrey must have the greatest depth of any county at this distance. There were 39 entries and of the 16 that went through to the final the slowest qualifier did 14:13.2! Poor Tony Fairclough found himself in the wrong heat and his 14:12.8 was not good enough to qualify, yet it was not many years ago that this time was sufficient to win. After his second place in the inter-counties 3 on the previous Monday John Thresher was favourite to win and it was rumoured that Mick Gowan (HHH) would tow him through a fast '2' in an effort to gain the Olympic qualifying time of 13:23.0. It was apparent after one mile (4:29.6) that there was no such effort and with the Holts alternating the lead and John tucked in about 4th, the 2 miles came up in 9:05.4. With two laps to go, and Dave Holt leading into the first bend, the pace seemed to falter momentarily and in an instant brother Bob stepped smartly round the leader and hugging the kerb as he sped round the bend opened up 10 yards before John had stepped clear and gathered himself for pursuit. It was a brilliant piece of tactical running by the slower finisher and try as he did John could make no impression over those final two circuits which Holt covered in 2:09. Derek Fernee, our second claim member, was an excellent third, 20 seconds inside his previous best. Next claret and gold vest to hit the finish was that old faithful Gerry North who had still not run off the effects of his inter-counties '20' 5 days earlier yet was able to turn in a useful 13:45.4 for 6th place. John Bicourt found the going too hard after his recent heavy programme and dropped out. Adrian Major was also unable to re-charge his batteries after his qualifying run and had to be content with 12th---though 14:09.0 was not exactly hanging about for a 21 years old! As the 3-milers recuperated, it was announced that the first 10 had run faster than the winner of their rival County, Middlesex; the winner being none other than our own Bill Kerr. And so the 1968 Championships ended with much promise for the future. It is always an interesting well-organised occasion and there's always the annual reunion in the Pavilion bar afterwards to add a bit of spice. More of you ought to come next year. items.sum: Pat Duncan's walking section report on Belgrave's best short-distance season, including the first National 20 km team title, international selection for Ray Middleton and promising newcomers.
items.s: WALKING Pat Duncan's walking section report on Belgrave's best short-distance season, including the first National 20 km team title, international selection for Ray Middleton and promising newcomers. PAT DUNCAN REPORTS:- Belgrave have always been a good distance team but this year they have been setting the scene alight over the shorter ones as well. Since January we have finished second in the national '10', first in the Garnett, first in the Met 20 Kilos and now to crown it all first in the national 20 kilos Championship. The first time Bels have won this event and the more pleasing because Club President Ted Stimpson was there to cheer us on. Ray Middleton and Len Duquemin were subsequently selected for altitude training in France and Ray has once again been selected to represent Britain, this time over 35 kilos in western Germany. Pat Duncan and John Moullin have been assisting Dr Griffith Pugh with some very fast 25 Mile times down at Bracknelland recent results show that we now have a formidable 20 Mile team in the making. More important perhaps is the second line of walkers poised to thrash our established men at any opportunity which presents itself. Gerry Cameron and Dave Mayo are both going great guns at the moment and Bob Farley lacks none of his old fire. Ray Hall too seemed to have taken on a new lease of life although his recent exploits with the paint brush have set him back a bit. Meanwhile it is newcomer Bob Coates who is causing all the suprises. Bob, a cyclist, has taken to walking like the proverbial duck. He sports a beard and scots accent which puts Gerry somewhere in BBC Oxford country. items.label: June 1968
items.sum: Harry Shields reports Belgrave's first R.W.A. National 20 km team title at Coventry on 11 May 1968, led by Ray Middleton in sixth, the club's 32nd R.W.A. team championship win.
items.s: NATIONAL 20 kilos Champions Harry Shields reports Belgrave's first R.W.A. National 20 km team title at Coventry on 11 May 1968, led by Ray Middleton in sixth, the club's 32nd R.W.A. team championship win. R.W.A. 20 KM Championship, Woodlands School, Broad Lane, Coventry. May 11th. HARRY SHIELDS WRITES:- What walkers ! What a record ! Ignoring wins in Junior events London - Brighton and other recognised classic walking fixtures, which many clubs would be only too pleased to notch, from my records this was our 32nd R.W.A. team win in R.W.A. Championships. No wonder our President, whom we were very pleased to see, was struck silent and had a look of awe and respect mixing with these mighty men who win National Championships more or less as a matter of course. These are not glamour men seeking the tinsel praise of the crowd, but sound dedicated craftsmen hardened by weather and from many hours on the road and track, able to endure when others fail. It is no sport for the faint hearted, but the material on which the country has come to rely on occasions such as the Olympic Games & European Championships. In this Belgrave has a proud record to maintain. From the starter's gun it was evident our men were out for the kill, led by Ray Middleton in his quest for Olympic honours. How superb and exciting it was. 20 KM (12½ miles) is the shorter of the Olympic walking distances and hardly Ray's speciality. This did not deter him from thrashing many of the fancied sprint walkers to lead our team home, and to be named among the six probabilities for the Olympics. He will be included in those to receive specialised acclimatisation training for the more strenuous 50 KM which is his proven distance. I know our thoughts and best wishes are with him during the anxious months ahead. This was a comparatively new team and an indication of the enthusiasm engendered by Pat Duncan and Ray Hall as Captain and Secretary is seen by the number who travelled to Coventry, enabling 15 to start in the race and leaving a good number of supporters and the usual officials. The Championship was ours from the start, with Len Duquemin, Bob Barnes and John Moullin completing the team, closely supported by Gerry Cameron. The need for this support was seen at 15 KM when that bane of distant walkers, cramp, struck John Moullin and Gerry walking like the champion that he must eventually be,advanced from the forties to 28th team position and maintained our position. With everyone giving of his best it is difficult to single out individual performances but it says much for the future to see Carl Lawton and Brian Ward, both only 20, in such forward positions. A word of praise for Steve Black for his perseverance. I am sure this will bear fruit and encourage others. Team Championship Result: 1. BELGRAVE 'A' 60 pts. 2. Sheffield U.H. 69 pts. 3. items.label: June 1968
items.sum: Edmund P. Donovan, a pre-1914 Belgravian who emigrated to New York, recalls joining the club about 1911 and its early headquarters, courses, personalities and track meetings.
items.s: More Reminiscences Edmund P. Donovan, a pre-1914 Belgravian who emigrated to New York, recalls joining the club about 1911 and its early headquarters, courses, personalities and track meetings. EDMUND P. DONOVAN emigrated to the USA just after World War 1. He had been a Belgravian for some years and was also a member of Prices AC, at whose ground we held our first championship meeting in 1922. He is resident in New York and has for some time been President of the St. Georges Club---a well known club for New Yorkers of English nationality. He was responsible for many of the arrangements when Her Majesty the Queen visited New York in 1957, and was subsequently awarded the O.B.E. The following notes were penned during a brief visit to London last year; and with them go his best wishes to all Belgravians, "the present members, veterans like myself and all those who are continuing to carry forward the Claret and Gold to still greater success". I think it was the summer of 1911 that I first knew of the Belgrave Harriers. It came about more or less by accident, as such things often do, and was the result of some good natured kidding. As was the custom then, and perhaps still is, new and junior employees to a firm were fair game for practical jokes of all kinds. In my case, as a result of speaking out of turn regarding my powers as a runner at school, a match was cooked up between a fellow worker, also an easy mark, and myself for a half mile race to be held on Clapham Common which happened to also be used on occasions by a few of the Belgrave Harriers. A silver medal was donated by a former athlete. I would not mention the time of the race even if I remembered; neither do I remember what eventually happened to the medal which I won. I do remember the two brothers who introduced me to the Bels though, their name if memory serves was Blow. My first recollection was the opening of the Winter season at the Spencer Arms Lower Richmond Road, Putney, almost opposite the Cricketers Headquarters of our then traditional rivals Ashcombe Athletic Club. The Spencer Arms was being run at that time by the former British Professional Sculling champion Tom Sullivan, who left England for Germany about 1913 to coach the Berlin Rowing Club and was interned in Germany during the 1st World War. The cross country course in those days was across Putney Common, Barnes Common, up Sheen Lane and into Richmond Park. Another feature of the Bels of those days for a short time, was a Boxing Section in the Club and a working agreement with the Bellevue Cycling Club, this faded out after a time however. The cross country champion at that time was Sergeant Carroll of the Irish Guards, who informed me on noticing I had a blistered toe after a training spin that I should cut my toe nails, a fact I passed on many times later during Army Service. Lew Causer then celebrating his 20th season at cross country was leader and coach of the novice pack and a fine coach he was,ably assisted at times by George Tyrer. About this time George still ran with the club occasionally, although I think only as second claim, his original club being the Highgate Harriers. Later during the war he was engaged full time on war work in the City but kept fit by walking to and from business every day,about 10 to 15 miles round trip. The next winter quarters I remember were at the Boileau Arms at the Barnes end of Hammersmith Bridge this did not last long as there was more road work than cross country to the course. It was then that the Club moved to St. Saviours Parish Hall, Raynes Park. These quarters were used until the outbreak of the 1914 - 18 war. Among the members joining during the years just preceeding the war was Jimmy Belchamber who after a season or two became an outstanding member of the long distance walking team in the London to Brighton Walk. An amusing sidelight in connection with Raynes Park quarters was the special issue of railway tickets, from Clapham Junction to Raynes Park, by Battersea Borough Council for cemetery visitors. A surprising number of Belgrave Harriers seemed to have relatives interned from Battersea! While winter quarters at Raynes Park sufficed for Saturday training spins, inter club races and championships, it did not solve the problem of mid-week training. This was solved by using the Rising Sun in Tite Street Chelsea and running through Belgravia into Hyde Park and along Rotten Row; this still entailed considerable road work. The problem of finding adequate country headquarters was always a problem even over fifty years ago, and must be even more of a headache today. It was, I think, the season of 1913-14 that the club got placed in the South of Thames Junior C.C. Championships for the first time in many years. While visiting Battersea Park and Hurlingham recently my thoughts went back to pre 1st war days and the problems facing the committee of arrangements for club track meets. Once or twice a meeting was held at Stamford Bridge, but more often in the interest of economy Battersea Park was the venue, this meant several of us getting to the park an hour or two before the meet to mark the course and starts. Dressing facilities were provided by the use of the old cricket dressing room, showers or any other kind of baths were unheard of. A great number of people often talk of the good old days, perhaps they were for some but for most athletes they were ones of considerable inconvenience and sometimes financial hardship. However, what we lacked in ability was more than made up in the good fellowship on the part of all the members of the club. Edmund P. Donovan EDMUND P. items.label: June 1968
items.sum: Reg Hopkins introduces the youths and boys section, praising its progress and urging members to look smart as athletes.
items.s: YOUTHS & BOYS Reg Hopkins introduces the youths and boys section, praising its progress and urging members to look smart as athletes. REG HOPKINS WRITES :- Once again I have pleasure in reporting further progress in our section, with all Champions, almost Champions and Champions -to-be knocking time and distance off their events. I know we are the envy of other Clubs with our number of members and their enthusiasm. The wind of change is about to blow through Athletics, we all hope for the better, and it is on you younger members that the future of our sport depends; both on the track and in the committee room. As Belgravians you will play your full part and help to keep our Club to the forefront of British Athletics. It is also the duty of every Club member to look as smart as possible when competing and training. Members of the public are always watching and it is how we look that influences their opinion of our Club and sport. We not only pride ourselves as being the best and biggest Club but we also wish to look like Athletes - Fit, Healthy, Clean, Spartan, Colourful and Happy. Reg Hopkins REG HOPKINS

Gordon Doubleday tells us :- This race was held in conjunction with the Redhill Charity '10' and was won by Bill Curtin in the good time of 10:12. It was an out and back course with the out being uphill and the home run downhill. With only 300 yards to the finish Bill and two others were leading together. items.s: BARNET BOYS ROAD RELAY Report and leg times from the Barnet boys road relay, where Belgrave fielded three teams and Bill Curtin ran the fourth fastest time, with a photo of the start of the first leg. 14 Bels Boys made the trip up to Barnet, Herts for this relay and so we were able to field 3 complete teams and two reserves. Richard Langley ran the first leg for us and came in a creditable 10th, Richard was slightly disappointed with his run and thought that he should have done better, but it was obvious to those watching that he was doing his utmost in spite of losing against boys two years or so older than himself. Richard, like the majority of our boys when compared with other clubs, is much younger than the opposition but although this goes against us at the moment we know that if we stick together, in a year or two we will have winning teams. Bill Curtin ran a blinder on the second leg and put us into 3rd position with 4th fastest time of the day. Eddy McNally, although dropping us to 6th place, ran perhaps his best run to date; he improves with every race. Reg Hopkins dropped us to 9th position but like Richard was given a difficult task for his age. Other members of the B and C teams deserving special praise were Paul Jablonski, Martin Bloice and, comming back to the form we know he can show, Michael Kane. items.label: June 1968
items.h: The Easter Holiday - Halls Green, Training Camp.
items.sum: Reg Hopkins' account of the boys' Easter training camp at Halls Green, listing the fourteen who went.
items.s: The Easter Holiday - Halls Green, Training Camp. Reg Hopkins' account of the boys' Easter training camp at Halls Green, listing the fourteen who went. Reg Hopkins reports: This was the first of what I hope will become a regular feature for our younger members. Being the first, however, we naturally had teething troubles. A late start going was most disappointing and the cancellation of a proposed road relay on the homeward trip due to expected Bank holiday traffic conditions, that didn't materialise, was most unfortunate. And all, of course missed Mum's cooking ! Knowing now the possibilities of this place, and by planning our programme rather better, and making our own travelling arrangements we can eliminate those points that didn't favour us and spend an even better weekend next time. All 14 Boys certainly did enjoy themselves. The weather, although not warm, did stay dry and allow us to spend most of the day out and about in the country. We spent one whole day canoeing on the river Medway (very tough on the arms - good for the throwers) and this was great fun for all, only one boy(who shall remain nameless) fell in. Having been told that rock climbing could be dangerous we gave that a miss, but we did have an enjoyable afternoon hill climbing. Ascending a steep hill with loose soil and very few handholds took quite a lot of strength and determination and was pretty hard on the seat of one's pants coming down. Among other activities we enjoyed were high jump and javelin contests. We also had weight training sessions every day and these proved most popular. I think, however, that the most popular pastime was throwing Nigel Bacon in the swimming pool ! We played some good games of football too (we have quite a good team - how about a match you seniors?) The funniest occurance throughout the weekend, apart from Nigel being chased "Starkers" through the countryside, was being confronted by the bigest Great Dane we have ever seen, during a cross country run. All put on a brave front and tried to frighten it away but the look of terror on our faces was hilarious. As we had planned, we showed some movie films, including Belgrave's own classic; this the boys loved and it certainly increased their pride in being "Bels Boys". Tom Carter and Tony Brooks paid us a visit on the Saturday. It was a great pleasure to all when they arrived just in time to give lifts back to the camp; we had been on the return march of an 8 mile cross country ramble and still had some way to go. All in all it was a good weekend and I am already planning the next one. To conclude, I would very much like to pass on some comments from various people outside the club regarding the behaviour of our lads. For example, "what a friendly and cheerful crowd they all were" and "how willing to share the chores that had to be done". Well done lads, we are proud of you. Those who went. items.s: SOUTH LONDON SCHOOLS CHAMPIONSHIPS Report of the South London Schools championships at Crystal Palace on 21 May 1968 with records for Steve White, Arnold Bent and Bill Curtin, plus a stop-press on Arnold Bent's 6'3" high jump. May 21st--Crystal Palace We had 16 of our Club members taking part in this schools meeting, which was the first to be held on the already famous "Tartan" track. Most outstanding were Steve White in the 200 metres and Arnold Bent in the High Jump and Bill Curtin winning the 800 metres once again. Steve looked terrific, and who can say where this fellow will advance in the world of sprinting. Arnold injured himself on the last of his jumps otherwise he would have most certainly improved even more than the new personal and championship best that he gained. Bill, showing all the ability he has displayed so often, attacked in the finishing straight and broke his opponents completely. A word about young Reg Hopkins. Still only a second year boy, he won his place in his school team by proving beforehand that he is better than any 3rd or 4th year pupil at his school. He has, therefore, two more years in this same race and hopes that he will follow in the footsteps of his idol Bill Curtin and be a future winner. items.label: June 1968
items.h: Camberley and District Young Athletes Meeting Bracknell Berks.
items.sum: Reg Hopkins reports the Camberley and District young athletes meeting at Bracknell on 3 June 1968, where eight Belgrave boys won six medals and Richard Langley set a boys' half-mile record (continued on page 24).
items.s: Camberley and District Young Athletes Meeting Bracknell Berks. Reg Hopkins reports the Camberley and District young athletes meeting at Bracknell on 3 June 1968, where eight Belgrave boys won six medals and Richard Langley set a boys' half-mile record (continued on page 24). Monday---June 3rd REG HOPKINS WRITES:-- 8 Boys went along to this all day meeting and I am delighted to say we met with great success. This without doubt is a meeting of a very high standard, and so coming away with 6 medals, with so small a team,was a grand effort. But through some bad luck--Bill Curtin being injured (although he did come along and give the boys his support) and a thunderstorm just before the start of the 100 yds--we might well have had two more winners. Our principal victory was Richard Langley's winning of the boys half mile in a new record time (previously held by none other than our own Bill Curtin). He won in a most impressive way and looked every inch a champion--what a great prospect we have in this youngster---and his winning time of 2:09.9 will only be a personal best for a very short time I know. He took 2.3 off Bill's best of last year and we all know this must be a feat in itself. He also took the Cup. The next thing to please us was Barry Quirk's 2nd place in the 80 metres Hurdles where he shared the same time as the winner (12.0). How the judges managed to split them I don't know. He started without blocks, allowing the other boy a couple of yards on him up to the first Hurdle but from there on he was moving faster, and had the race been half a yard longer he must have won. The race that gave me greatest pleasure was the 4x110 yd Relay. In spite of our team having only the briefest baton changing practice (this is going to be rectified) the boys won themselves 3rd place medals. Martin Bloice was moving with tremendous speed on his leg, and indicated that had the weather not changed just before his heat of the 100 yds, which unsettled him a great deal, his entry into the final would have been almost certain; likewise his chance for a medal. Another of our boys who won fame for himself was Vic Butcher. Although only placing 4th in the 1000 metres steeplechase (his first ever) he gained for himself A.A.A. 2nd Class standard with a time of 3min:8secs--no mean feat. Mick Harvey also ran in this race and was only fractionally outside A.A.A. 3rd Class standard of 3min:25secs. What is important for him, however, is that he has at last proved to himself that he can do it--now watch out all you other blokes. David Wilkinson had his first outing for some time; having just returned from Germany where he has been living since last summer. Finishing fourth in the Javelin with a personal best throw of 139ft-5" delighted him and now he is looking for some expert coaching to improve still more. Another of our throwers, Jimmy Paraskeva, had personal bests of 100ft-7" (Javelin) and 85ft-1" (Discus) to his credit. (Cont'd on page 24) (Cont'd from page 40) Reg Hopkins had a successful day with a 2:28 half mile on a well churned up track and by helping the relay team to its 3rd place--not bad for a 13 years old ! A word of thanks to Nigel Bacon who was too old to run at this meeting; this did not stop him from breaking into his holiday and coming all the way from Brighton to cheer us on in his own inimitable way. This is the spirit that is going to make our boys the best in the country before long. Also,a word of thanks to the parents who made the trip to see our team perform. I wish more would follow their example. It is a terrific stimulus to us all.to see and hear them in the stands. items.sum: Golden Wonder crisps advertisement for an Olympic competition, donating money from returned crisp packets to British Olympic training.
items.s: Help get our Athletes fit for Mexico Golden Wonder crisps advertisement for an Olympic competition, donating money from returned crisp packets to British Olympic training. Help get our Athletes fit for Mexico DOWN the grimy streets of industrial Britain, a hopeful athlete slogs his way to a place on our Olympic team. He only finished work a few hours ago. Shortly he'll be working again. His chances in Mexico aren't very bright. We at Golden Wonder would like to change things. We'd like to see a British winner on that proud rostrum in Mexico. We'd like to see lots of them. To hear our National Anthem played time and time again. We'd like you to help us (and help yourself). And here's how. British athletes in the past have been unable to match the state-sponsored supermen from the Iron Curtain. Or from the States. And with Mexico's dizzy altitude things are going to be even tougher. We've already donated £3,000 for high altitude training in the Pyrenees. You can help us donate a lot more. And win yourself a trip to Mexico to see it all happening. How you can get to Mexico... Five prizes of two weeks for two people at the Olympic Games. That'll be our Golden Award to you for helping Britain's Olympic effort. Just look at the questions on the right and send your answers to us together with your empty Golden Wonder packs. We promise to donate 2d. to the British Amateur Athletic Board for every five empty Golden Wonder Crisp packets we receive; for every one Golden Wonder Nuts packet we receive, we'll donate 1d.* And remembering that over 40 million packets of crisps are sold in Britain every week, we could, between us, go a long way towards helping Britain strike gold. Golden Wonder Olympic Competition With every five empty Golden Wonder Crisp packets that you send to the address below or with each empty Golden Wonder Nuts packet, you are entitled to one entry in the competition. What to do: Re-arrange the letters below so as to form in each case the name of an event in the Olympic Games. 1. LETPEASCHEES 2. PHANTOLENT 3. HAMTRONA 4. SLUDREH Then 5. Which do you consider to be the most exciting event and why? (Answer in not more than 30 words) Enter the competition as many times as you like on plain paper. Don't forget The more Golden Wonder packets you send in—the more money we'll donate for training Britain's athletes, and the more chance you'll have of being one of the lucky winners. If you don't want to enter the competition, still send the packets in. They will all count. Send to: Answers, together with the empty packets and your name and address, should be sent to: Golden Wonder Olympic Competition, London, S.E.99. A full copy of the rules can be obtained from the above address on receipt of a stamped addressed envelope. (All requests must be marked "Rules"). *Closing date 17th August, 1968. items.label: June 1968
items.sum: Postbag column with news of walker John Knifton in New York, Harry Shields' letter criticising the Byers Report and the trade-name ruling, and Chris Steer's farewell before leaving for Canada.
items.s: POSTBAG Postbag column with news of walker John Knifton in New York, Harry Shields' letter criticising the Byers Report and the trade-name ruling, and Chris Steer's farewell before leaving for Canada. JOHN KNIFTON, one of our leading walkers a few years back, has been in the U.S.A now for three years--- and he is still in the heel and toe game. Not just, but to the tune of a 92:46 20 Kilos! The occasion was the annual Nat Osk Memorial 20 Kilos in New York's Central Park and, of the 52 competitors, John finished third behind two top American walkers, Dave Romansky (90:04) and Ray Somers (91:35). His 4 minutes allowance enabled him to take the handicap award. John, who works at the Texaco Oil Company's Research Centre, writes "I am presently training five times a week but have changed my schedule. I no longer bother with strolling, instead I've reverted to strip training spins of 15-20 miles twice a week. This type of training gives, I feel, increased strength without jeopardising speed". A foot injury in the week preceding the American National 25 Kilos race upset his preparation, but he still finished 10th in 2:05:32 over a measured course (Ron Laird, the U.S.A.'s No.1 was 3rd). By the birth of his son, Matthew, last December John made former Belgravian Editor BEN KNIFTON a proud grandfather. The article in the March BELGRAVIAN entitled "Remove the Shackles" has galvanised Past President HARRY SHIELDS into literary action. Harry has been right through the mill of club athletics and no one is ever likely to match his achievement of gaining a team-winners medal in the National Cross-Country Championship and the National Race Walking Championship. He knows what makes clubs tick and, like many others, is sceptical of the Byers Report. He writes"The Byers Report suggests the cure to the malaise to be lots of money and an omnipotent overlord. The Sunday Telegraph suggests that a strong candidate is John Disley and quote no less a sponsorship than the International Athletes"Club" and in particular Peter Hildreth, Chris Brasher and Derek Johnson. How on earth these qualify to give opinions I do not know------while the good they have done (in voluntary work) compared with our own officials is beyond me". Harry continues "The need for a centralised administration combining the work of the AAA, BAAB and WAAA etc. has long been appreciated but I have yet to read of any understanding of club organisation. In due time it appears to me that the chasm between the A.A.A.'s administration and clubs like our own will be so wide as not to require each other". Harry mentions that for many years he has been a "hanger-on" to that band of voluntary workers who organise our top athletic meetings, and he wonders "how the gaps will be bridged between the professional administration at the top, club organisation and the body of people at present prepared to turn out in all weathers, using their extensive knowledge without recompense". He adds a tail-piece on that hysterical ruling regarding trade names on hold-alls. "I have reached the exalted position of 'Chief Blanker Out'. What a lot of nonsense it is, particularly when you think of the Stadium being full of 'Pepsi-Cola', 'News of the World' and other adverts on which the television cameras are constantly trained. This does not seem to offend the aesthetic sense of Don Pain and the Marquess". Harry always was a bit of a rebel---The I.A.A.F. and Lord Byers should keep him going for some time!. CHRIS STEER wrote the day before he left for Canada and sends best wishes to all his 'mates' in the Club. Rivals of Steer cannot afford to ease up, for he says"I shall be taking my running kit with me to keep my hand---or should I say foot-in". He continues "I'll keep in touch with the Club of course (I've even paid my subs) and perhaps a 'letter from America' column à la Alistaire Cooke will be appropriate". It will be interesting to see by how much Chris swells our Postbag column in future editions. items.s: Stop Press! KINNAIRD TROPHY RESULT Stop-press result of the Kinnaird Trophy, where Belgrave were sixth of ten clubs in their first year back, with a John Thresher 1500m win. Belgrave can feel well pleased with this result. Polytechnic invite the ten clubs they consider to be the strongest in the land and this was our first year back in. Birchfield, Achilles and Poly were always reckoned to be out of reach but the points score shows that not much extra was needed to get in amongst these teams. After all, if Derek Boosey and Arnold Bent had been available our points score would very likely have been boosted to 36 or 37---by such margins are these trophies won or lost. Full strength teams are absolutely vital for the forthcoming National League matches. John Thresher had one of the easiest wins of the afternoon, taking the 1500 metres by a 3 seconds margin in 3:46.2---equivalent to a 4min-4sec mile. The heat was oppressive and Bill Kerr, running at the worst time of all, showed magnificent fighting qualities in the 5000 metres. He finished 4th in 14:36.2, 14.2 seconds behind P. Stewart (Birchfield). What team spirit by Laurie O'Hara! Having done his day's training, and all set for an afternoon's spectating, he was roped in for the 5,000 metres and finished 9th of the 17 runners. Nick Head did season's bests in Javelin and Shot, as did Tony Brooks in his heat of the 800 metres. Jim Vivian finished 5th in the 200 metres final and John Dear 4th in steeplechase (9:51.6). items.label: September 1968
items.sum: Editorial congratulating Derek Boosey on Olympic triple jump selection for Mexico, commiserating with John Thresher and Ray Middleton on missing out, and criticising the organisation of the pilot National League.
items.s: EDITORIAL Editorial congratulating Derek Boosey on Olympic triple jump selection for Mexico, commiserating with John Thresher and Ray Middleton on missing out, and criticising the organisation of the pilot National League. Our congratulations go to Derek Boosey who has been selected to represent Great Britain and Northern Ireland in the Triple Jump at the Mexico Olympic Games in October. He partners Fred Alsop of Havering A.C., who was 4th in Tokyo in 1964. All Belgravians will be with him in spirit when he takes his turn on that very lonely Tartan strip in Mexico City.Another to tread that important run-up will be our second claim member from Q.P.H. Alan Lerwill, who is coached by our own Dave Ansell. We wish him also every success. Whilst recording our pleasure at Derek Boosey's selection we also extend our sympathies to two club-mates who so very nearly joined our leading field events man - John Thresher and Ray Middleton. Until a week or so before the selectors met, John was one of only three Britons who had done the Olympic qualifying time for 5,000 metres (the others were Taylor and Rushmer). When it came to the final qualifying race our top track man couldn't make it. Until the National 50 Kilos Championship, few would have wagered against Ray Middleton representing his country again. Ray's wonderful record, which includes a Commonwealth Games 'silver', and his ability to 'come good' at the right time seemed sufficient to carry him through. Well, even the Greats cannot be great all the time, and our top walker had to give way to those fine prospects Eley and Lightman. Thresher and Middleton live to fight another day, and while they relax after their battle, our thoughts, hopes and good wishes go out to the whole Olympic team for whom the battle has barely begun. * * * * * In the excitement of the recent rush to attain Olympic qualifying standards, the pilot National League meetings have faded into obscurity, with the two Midland fixtures so far held not even reaching the pages of the National Press. However, from Belgrave's point of view, the publicity would have been received with mixed feelings as we could finish only 4th on each occasion. Whilst we at press the third and last meeting will be held at West London Stadium. We might do better: we might not. Either way, the National League will only be a success if it receives the full and unqualified support of every potential team member. However, no amount of support on the part of visiting teams will off-set poor organisation by the host club and at Perry Barr our athletes were far from impressed. To be a success this league needs publicity, a show of imagination and, yes, expense on the part of the organisers. Until the athletes are made to feel it is something different from an ordinary inter-club fixture then it stands little hope of arousing any wider interest. items.label: September 1968
items.sum: The Hon. Secretary's notes: club news, fixture changes, the A.G.M., the A.A.A. draw, league plans, a request for a Schools Relay trophy, a roll of the club's longest-serving members after the deaths of the Macher brothers, a lost 440 yards relay record and the Football Competition.
items.s: HON SEC'S NOTES The Hon. Secretary's notes: club news, fixture changes, the A.G.M., the A.A.A. draw, league plans, a request for a Schools Relay trophy, a roll of the club's longest-serving members after the deaths of the Macher brothers, a lost 440 yards relay record and the Football Competition. We congratulate our President, TED STIMPSON, and Evelyn on the 25th anniversary of their marriage which falls in the latter part of Ted's Presidential year, and wish them many more years of health and happiness to come! As suggested in our last issue, the Borough of Wandsworth now confirms that owing to financial stringency the Wandsworth Show and Seven miles road race, planned for September 7th, will not now take place. Also it should be noted that our twleve-aside Road Relay will not take place on Saturday, October 12th but will be promoted in conjunction with the Southern Counties A.A.A. from our Wimbledon Headquarters on Saturday, March 29th, 1969. This is at the request of the A.A.A. who are desirous that all Areas should hold their Road Relay events on the same day, and thus afford a sound basis for the acceptance or refusal of Clubs' entries in the National Road Relay which will follow in April. Our popular Youths Open Road Relay will take place at Wimbledon on October 19th when we hope for a first class entry. Incidentally, our hard working Race Hon. Secretary and Road Running and Social Hon. Secretary, Gordon Biscoe, has recently changed his address which is now:- 34 PAMS WAY, EWELL, SURREY (Telephone 01 393 4433) On another page will be found the official notification of the Annual General Meeting to be held on Wednesday, September 18th. No other notice will be circulated. It is hoped that all members will book the date immediately and do their utmost to attend this meeting which marks the birth of another Club year. By the time this is read, you will have received from that 'glutton for hard work on behalf of the Club', Past President FRANK WEBB, some A.A.A. Draw books. Please do your best to dispose of them all and return the counterfoils and cash in good time. And if you have been overlooked, or require further books, do not hesitate to get in touch with Frank at 50 Longford Avenue, Southall, Middlesex. The actual draw will be in the hands of Harry Secombe, engagements permitting, at the Athletes Dance at the Lyceum Ballroom on Friday, September 27th. Over £1,000 of prizes have been guaranteed and the first is a FORD Escort 1100 c.c. Super. One-third of all our Club sales will form a very welcome addition to our own Club funds and we ask your full support on behalf of the A.A.A., the sport, and ourselves. Our Social Hon. Secretary has details of the Athletes Dance if you should wish to be present and perhaps drive the first prize away! WANTED - a young member who would be prepared to assist with envelope addressing from time to time. Many of us have started on Club work in this way - who knows where it may lead? If you can help please let the Hon. Secretary know. Athletic leagues loom before us in 1969 and we expect to take part in the principal National League (three divisions each consisting of nine clubs) as of right. These competitions will make heavy demands on our all-round ability, however, and on our ability to get all the right people in the right place,in the right frame of mind,at the right time. However, our Club spirit is as strong as that to be found anywhere and we are reasonably sure that no-one will fail us except for the very best of reasons, and even then will give adequate notice so that a reserve can be substituted. Obviously, and we are far from being alone in this, we need strengthening in some events, particularly in the 'heavy' competitions - the Shot, the Hammer Throw, the Discus, etc. If you know any young giants who can be enthused into training and taking advantage of our Coaches' skill and attention, bring them along and we'll make something of them! Our annual Schools Track Relay Race would be made much more attractive if a suitable Challenge trophy could be provided. If any of our older members has a cup or trophy mouldering into blackness, tucked away under the bed or stowed away in the loft, and really doing no good at all and would like to present it to the Club, we for our part would be very glad of the opportunity of considering its acceptance! Keep in the queue, please! The recent deaths of the Brothers Macher, who were elected to membership in 1912, robs us of our longest serving members, and it is now necessary to leap over the 1914-1918 War (Cont'd on page 6) HON.SEC'S NOTES (Cont'd from page 4) period (when the Club ceased to exist except as a name), to December 1919 when CHARLIE SPEECHLEY was elected to membership, and it must have been about this time that Past President HARRY HARE came into the Club. 1920 members still showing themselves frequently are BERT EAST and GEORGE POWELL. The Brothers McKAY,FRED STONE, JIMMY FLATT and MICK PYER came into the fold in 1921,and 1922 gave us WALLY BAYLISS (Hon. Secretary for eleven years and President for three), the incomparable BERT FOOTER, and champion walker HAROLD KING. KEN O'KELL first showed himself in 1923 and 1924* followed with that great walker FRED RICKARDS, TOM PRITCHARD and a very loyal member of earlier days, SYD KING. JOE SCAMELL and BEN KNIFTON joined Belgrave in 1925, and the following year TOM MORELL, CHARLIE JONES, ALF HARLEY and LEN ROLLINS were accepted into membership. 1927 was a bumper year indeed with TOMMY SCRIMSHAW (three times an International at 880 yards before he was 21), JOE COLEMAN, ERNIE DUFFETT, who guided the destinies of our runners for 25 years, and Olympic champion TOMMY GREEN all signing Belgrave forms. International and Empire Games Champion ARTHUR PENNY was elected in 1928 as was also NORMAN DEWBERRY and FRANK WEBB. JACK BIDGOOD, LEN COLEMAN and TOM COTTON donned Belgrave vests in 1929 and that great character, International and Champion runner, and Past President TOM CARTER was persuaded into the claret and gold in August 1930. So much for our old-timers and most of them still playing their parts in the Club's activities, and setting an example of service to the Club over a long period for the younger members to follow. There may be some omissions from the above list - if so, apologies, and let's hear from you! The recent A.A.A. Championships programme proudly showed under the heading 'Junior 440 yards Relay' A.A.A. Club Record (under 19) and Best Championship performance, 42.8 secs. Belgrave H., at Hurlingham, August 28th, 1965. In the second heat, however, Wolverhampton and Bilston A.C. trimmed a tenth of a second off our record and in the final brought the time down to 42.5 secs. So our winning team of 1965 (J. MITCHELL, D. GLEESON, C. MARTIN, J. VIVIAN) have lost a record, but they may well come back and create a senior best performance . Meantime, further junior runners are maturing and Belgrave should regain their record in the not too far distant future. Our Football Competition will be starting again soon and we ask for your support. It means so much to us, and helps considerably to keep your Club at the top. Full details may be had from the Hon. Treasurer. * 1924 was also the year that ERNEST NEVILLE joined our Vice-Presidents list and ALBERT WATTAM (who made his annual pilgrimage from Wainfleet Lines to compete in the Brighton Walk for many years) was elected to membership. items.sum: Outgoing President Ted Stimpson's farewell letter thanking members, congratulating the walkers and track and field men, and urging attendance at the A.G.M.
items.s: A PRESIDENT'S Adieu Outgoing President Ted Stimpson's farewell letter thanking members, congratulating the walkers and track and field men, and urging attendance at the A.G.M. Dear Belgravians, By the time you read this letter my term of office will almost be completed and so I would like to take this opportunity to tell you how much I have enjoyed this last year. I have tried to spend as much time as possible with each section and in doing so have come to know many more members. We have had quite a successful year and my congratulations go to the walkers for winning two National Championships. My thanks also go to the track and field men for winning two trophy meetings and for retaining the Brockman Trophy. Being a country man I was a little disappointed that we were unable to make the grade in any major cross country championship, but I am hoping that our new President will have this honour. I am sure the juniors, youths and boys sections will continue to progress with as much enthusiasm as they have done in the past. I would like to thank the Committee for all their help and support during the past year; also my thanks go to all the ladies who have kindly given their time to assist in various activities for the Club. (Cont'd opposite) ( Cont'd from opposite page) In closing may I remind you that your attendance would be greatly appreciated at the A.G.M. to welcome your new President and to help select the officers for the following year. May I wish all members success in their different fields of sport during the coming year. Yours sincerely, Ted Stimpson Ted Stimpson Ted Stimpson Brockman Trophy 1968 Belgrave Harriers Annual General Meeting 1968

items.label: September 1968
items.sum: Obituary of brothers Albert and Gus Macher, Vice-Presidents and members since 1912, recalling their part in finding Belgrave Hall and in the club's cross-country rise between the wars.
items.s: A.E. & J.W. MACHER Obituary of brothers Albert and Gus Macher, Vice-Presidents and members since 1912, recalling their part in finding Belgrave Hall and in the club's cross-country rise between the wars. It is with sorrow that we record the deaths of Albert and Gus Macher, Vice Presidents of the Club for many years, and members since 1912. Albert was also a Life Member, an honour accorded him for his many services to the Club and in appreciation of his work as Hon. Treasurer and Social Hon. Secretary. Neither Albert nor Gus had any pretensions of being good athletes. They ran because they enjoyed it and the last twenty placings in the'Southern', if and when the Club competed, were bound to embrace the MACHERS. Their happy outlook was communicated to others, however, and they found great pleasure in their service to the Club, in which their father - PAST PRESIDENT A.F.W. MACHER also shared. They were at their happiest taking out the beginners' pack, acting as pointsmen, and in assisting the Club to progress in a hundred different ways. Their integrity, their work for the Club, their desire to see it move from the ranks of the Junior clubs to Senior status (which it did in 1929) created enthusiasm in others and this was the spirit which carried the Club upwards through the 1930's to the highest honours. After the World War of 1914-18 the Club resumed its Cross-country activities in the Wimbledon area, and our Headquarters were at 'The Swan', Ridgway, the skittle alley being used as the dressing accommodation. A jump through the low window, a trot up Lauriston Road and the Belgrave Harriers of those days were on ground very familiar to us. The day came, however, when the skittle alley was to be converted into a Lounge Bar and the Club was compelled to look for new quarters. Bob Ricketts, our dynamic President of those days, asked various Committee men to keep their eyes open for alternative accommodation and Albert Macher did just this and discovered St. John's Hall, Denmark Road, as it was then known. Enquiries of the caretaker, however,revealed that another caller had been interested in the premises and had the first refusal. This saddened Albert and he reported back to the President in a miserable mood which quickly turned to joy and pleasure when it was found that the other caller with the option was Harry HARE, the Club Hon Secretary. It's history now that we rented the Hall for years and later acquired the leasehold, and still later the freehold of what is now known as Belgrave Hall The Machers early realised that the Club would never make its mark in the Cross country world if we conducted ourselves as all the other clubs of our size did and virtually looked upon seven miles as the limit of distance to be run, except on the occasional entry into Southern and English Championships when our runners were not distance-fit. At that time the 'peak' of the season was the 7 miles Championship which took place well after Christmas. The three Machers presented a Shield to the Club (carrying their name) for a 10 miles Cross country Championship and this had the effect of changing the approach and the emphasis of the Cross Country season within the Club. The seven miles championship was brought forward before Christmas and the runners trained on for the longer distance and the Club 10 miles Championship in the New Year. A new mental approach now became obvious and with the emergence of Bert Footer, whose main interest from his early running days was always in the E.C.C.U. Championships, we were all set to win the major Cross country Championships. This found its ultimate expression in the winning of medals in ten successive E.C.C.U. Championships! We certainly owed the Machers a lot. They generously dipped deeply into their pockets when the first Club Track Championships were introduced in 1922 and on many other occasions. It was a great pleasure to us that ALBERT was fit enough to attend our Track Championships just over a year ago and meet an old club friend in Edmund Donovan from New York; and that in January last he was present at Wimbledon to present the MACHER Shield to the winner. We honour the memory of two great Club men and offer sincere condolences to their families. R.I.P. Albert Macher Albert Albert Albert Macher ALBERT Gus Macher Gus Macher Gus Macher Gus A.F.W. Macher A.F.W. items.s: ROAD RUNNING: CONSOLATION 'WIN' AT PAIGNTON Report of four Belgrave runners at the Paignton '15' road race on 22 June 1968, where John Hall was 14th and the trio later won a 'Knobbly Knees' competition, with a photograph of the winning team. June 22nd--PAIGNTON '15' Those four stalwarts G. Piddington, J. Hall, D. Bonsor and W. Matthews made the 200 miles trip to 'sunny' Paignton in June for some sun, relaxation and a race. Well, they got the latter alright but little of the first two. The '15' was held in torrential rain and George Piddington was brought to a walk at 12 miles (his last five took 45 mins!) but John Hall battled on to finish 14th with Bonsor 8 places behind. George's misfortune pushed our lads out of the 3rd place medals. Bill Matthews dropped out after being mis-directed by a policeman (so he says). This story took a knock that evening though when chauffeur Matthews lost our fun-seeking trio in the town---his navigation is definitely suspect! As the evening wore on spirits became high again and the rigours of the afternoon's race were forgotten. Our lads were determined to take back a prize of some sort and, with great confidence, entered a "Knobbly Knees " competition---you can guess who won. July 20th--Wimbledon Belgrave's 17th Open 20 miles was won by Ian MacIntosh (Ranelagh) in the good time of 1:47:30: a good time indeed, for in the oppressive heat 24 of the 84 starters were forced to retire, including our own Brian Gorman who spent the night in hospital suffering from heat exhaustion. MacIntosh went to the front right from the start and had dropped the field after only half a mile. He raced thro' five in 25:18, ten in 52:19 and fifteen in 79:32---an excellent performance in such conditions. Lionel Mann was first Belgravian to finish in a creditable fifth place, but he paid for a fast start and would probably have done better if he had stayed back with the trio that eventually passed him. Pat O'Connor maintained his recent good form for 10th and Bob Glover's 18th place was a particularly good effort. items.s: BRACKNELL '5' Report and result of the Bracknell 5 road race, where Belgrave A retained the team title by two points from Portsmouth with Gerry North second to Martin Hyman. Once again we had a very encouraging turn out for this popular event fielding no less than four teams. The team title we won last year was retained inspite of strong opposition from Portsmouth A.C., by the narrow margin of two points. No doubt a plan of campaign worked out by our A team to beat Pompey had a lot to do with it. From the start Gerry North,out to give himself a hard run,took an early lead and as the field completed a lap of the track before going out into the wood, all our 'A' team was inside the first eight positions. Gerry's efforts however took their toll over this pleasant but undulating course, and approximately half a mile from home Martin Hyman who till then had been 'sitting in ' opened up a lead which Gerry was unable to close as they came back onto the track. Laurie O'Hara and Trevor Hart put in another of their reliable runs apiece, to edge out Portsmouth men, with Lionel Mann following very closely behind---no doubt regarding it as a mere sprint!With Pat O'Connor now recording some of his best form,another good performance came from John Hall who improves with every outing irrespective of distance---Messrs. items.s: WHAT IS A ROAD RUNNER? Humorous piece quoting Collier's Encyclopaedia on the road runner bird with club in-jokes, illustrated by two cartoons of 'The Greater Road Runner' and 'The Lesser Road Runner'. According to Collier's Encyclepaedia a ROAD RUNNER is "A terrestrial New World cuckoo! One road runner, G. Californianus (which Club is he from?) ranges from the southwestern United States to central Mexico, while G. Affinis, a smaller bird (and better medal bet?), occurs genrally throughout Mexico and northern Central America." 'They have erectile feathers on the crown, a rather long bill, a very long tail, and powerful legs for running. Their plumage is brown above, glossed with green, and everywhere streaked with white and buff, and buffywhite beneath, streaked on the breast with black." THE GREATER ROAD RUNNER (G. CALIFORNIANUS) THE LESSER ROAD RUNNER (G. AFFINIS) 'ROAD RUNNERS feed on small rodents (preferably from Coventry Godiva!) reptiles, mollusks, centipedes and insects of all kinds. The western road runner is known for it's ability to kill rattlesnakes." 'Their nests are compact structures of sticks, lined with grass, feathers, bark, snake skin and roots, built in cacti, bushes or low trees" (or if really desperate, at Belgrave Hall). 'They rarely take to their wings, though they are good fliers. They can outrun a horse or horse drawn vehicle (such as George Piddington's car!) and are famous for their former(?) habit of racing travellers along a highway.." And What of the bearded variety, Lionel Mannicus? THE GREATER ROAD RUNNER (G. CALIFORNIANUS) / THE LESSER ROAD RUNNER (G. AFFINIS) George Piddington George Piddington Lionel Mann Lionel Mannicus Bert Footer BERT FOOTER Belgrave Hall Coventry Godiva

items.h: TRACK AND FIELD: BILL COUZEN REVIEWS FIELD EVENTS
items.sum: Bill Couzen reviews the 1968 field events season, noting the Ryder and Brockman trophy wins, weakness in the throws, and plans for winter pole vault and hurdles sessions at Battersea Park.
items.s: TRACK AND FIELD: BILL COUZEN REVIEWS FIELD EVENTS Bill Couzen reviews the 1968 field events season, noting the Ryder and Brockman trophy wins, weakness in the throws, and plans for winter pole vault and hurdles sessions at Battersea Park. With the Summer Season all too quickly coming to an end and only two major meetings left (the Boughey trophy and the 3rd and last National League meeting at Twickenham) this is probably the best time to re-cap on the season so far. We can be pleased with winning the Ryder trophy and the Brockman trophy but disappointed with our 4th place in the two National League meetings. With Nick Head out of the Country and Frank Glass unable to attend the first two meetings this exposed our shallowness in the Shot and Discus with our men only picking-up a consolation point in each event. Without a doubt we must find a couple of heavy men who would take these two events seriously. The new Pole Vault pit is near completion at Battersea Park and we intend to take full advantage of this extra facility by holding Pole Vaulting sessions on Sunday Mornings every two weeks throughout the Winter under the guidance of Frank Simmons. Anyone interested is welcome: Seniors, Juniors, Youths and Boys, just let me know. We will be holding our Sunday Morning Winter meetings at Battersea Park again this coming winter with special emphasis on the Hurdles events. Dates for these fixtures will be in the New Handbook. * * * * * In our next issue Tony Brooks will review Track. Only a first year junior and showing all the class of an international, Steve White hit the straight yards up on Dave Williams of Notts A.C. and only in the last few yards did Williams pull past to win; leaving Steve second with a Club Junior Record. items.sum: Tony Brooks reports how Belgrave, first announced as second, were found on recount to have won the Ryder Trophy at Southampton on 6 July 1968 for the first time, with full results.
items.s: RYDER 'STOLEN' BUT REGAINED Tony Brooks reports how Belgrave, first announced as second, were found on recount to have won the Ryder Trophy at Southampton on 6 July 1968 for the first time, with full results. With the Mayor of Southampton in a hurry to leave and two rather excitable women scorers fiddling with the points Bels. were adjudged second in this major trophy meeting. On a recount, made after the presentation was over, it was agreed that we had in fact won by 3 points and not lost by 9 as was announced and later published by the Press. Thus our moment of glory was snatched from us on the day it really counted. John Mitchell, as strong as ever, won the 'A' hundred, was second in the long jump and ran in both the relays. Chris Martin did both sprints and both of the relays. Adrian Major ran the mile and 3 miles, Tony Brooks the half mile,triple jump and both relays, Denzil Winsborrow 3 events and Bob Couillault 3 events. In other words, all who went along did more than their share of work and the reward was the Ryder Trophy for the first time and victory against Pilot league 'A' leaders, Southampton and 'Poly'.
