items.sum: Report of the club's Annual General Meeting at Belgrave Hall on 18 September 1968: tributes, the Secretary's and Treasurer's reports, Life Membership for Ray Middleton and Tom Pritchard, election of Frank Simmons as President, and presentation of the youths and boys medal-competition cups.
items.s: The A.G.M. Report of the club's Annual General Meeting at Belgrave Hall on 18 September 1968: tributes, the Secretary's and Treasurer's reports, Life Membership for Ray Middleton and Tom Pritchard, election of Frank Simmons as President, and presentation of the youths and boys medal-competition cups. Approximately 70 Belgravians were in attendance at Belgrave Hall on September 18th to say goodbye to the Club's 81st year and to welcome in the 82nd. The proceedings began on a sad note when the meeting stood in memory of those who had passed on during the last year. ALBERT MACHER, JACK MACHER and JACK FLOWER were collectively in our thoughts during that minute of remembrance; and sharing that moment too was JACK HARTLEY of Coventry Godiva, guest at our last dinner in his capacity as ECCU President, and whose loss is mourned by the Midland club and its neighbours. On opening the official proceedings our Honorary Secretary said he would not be presenting a formal detailed report as "the regular appearance of our excellent gazette THE BELGRAVIAN relieves me of the necessity to read a report of facts and figures". Our Secretary then summarised the year in general terms but made special mention of Derek Boosey, our Olympic representative and new holder of the "Tommy Green" Cup for the year's most meritorious performance, and Ray Middleton who was so unlucky to miss selection, "We are, indeed, very sympathetic towards him" said Mr. Harley Turning to our team efforts our Secretary acknowledged the excellent 4 wins and 2 seconds chalked up by our walkers in the six premier events, and the second and fourth placings by our runners in the Southern and National Championships - "fourth may seem to lose the glitter of success but bearing in mind the class and colossal size of today's fields it is really a very excellent achievement" he said. So too was our winning of the Brockman and Ryder tropies during the track season. "Our consistency of performance overall, for nearly 60 years, has established us as one of the leading clubs in the country. Despite the fact that many of our old recruiting grounds now come within the spheres of newer clubs our success is undiminished: our younger members have indeed inherited a splendid heritage". Tributes were then made to A.A. Harley by W.E. Lucas and our outgoing President who reminded the meeting that our Secretary was the first Belgravian to become President of the Southern Counties A.A.A. Our Hon. Treasurer, D.M. Shepherd explained the shortage of balance sheets as being "my means of effecting an economy!" The recent increase in subscriptions did not have a marked effect on the year's income,and excess of expenditure over income was £163. In answer to a question, the Treasurer said he did not agree with laying down formal hire charges for the Hall but preferred to rely on donations from the users. The high cost (£129) of medals, prizes, engraving etc. was pointed out. After a thorough explanation of the accounts the meeting voted their approval. A.A. Harley spoke in appreciation of Dave Shepherd's work and reminded the meeting that handling the financial affairs of a club of our size was a major task. The names of Ray Middleton and Tom Pritchard were then put up for Life Membership. Frank Jarvis spoke on behalf of Ray Middleton "not just as your Assistant Honorary Secretary, but also as Honorary Secretary of the Southern R.W.A." Ray had served his Club and country exceptionally well for many years now and the Club now wished to show its appreciation. Frank referred to Middleton as "the original boy from West Side Story" and spoke of his trips overseas, mentioning his preference for training rather than sightseeing. In proposing Tom Pritchard, Frank Simmons told the meeting how Tom had been an ever present loyal member since 1924. Although he would not be remembered for his athletic achievements, this was not the criterion. He had instead always been ready to help the Club by carrying out many of the smaller thankless tasks and was regularly seen patrolling our cross-country courses or acting as pointsman in road races. Belgrave needed men such as he and Frank was proud to propose him. Both candidates were elected with acclamation. Elections were next on the agenda and the outgoing President (Ted Stimpson) and the President-elect (Frank Simmons) both got in a little practice for their Club Dinner speeches on November 16th. In proposing his successor Ted spoke of Frank's sprinting days, how he really shone when he turned to coaching and of his immense courage which enabled him to walk again after a spinal operation. A.A. Harley said "Frank's love for the Club goes very deep and a fitting testimonial to his coaching skill was the team which won the A.A.A. 4 x 110 yds relay in 1954. We are pleased to honour him in this way." In adding his tribute, Tom Carter recalled that Frank was at one time a blood donor. "Whenever he sprinted his face went sheet white and he looked as though he had come straight from the van!" Our new President then thanked the meeting for their kind words. "You have given me a hard task, but I shall strive to follow the high standards of my predecessors. My athletic career was during our glory as Cross-Country Champions. I hope that my year of office as your President will see our cross-country runners take the National again." M. Pyer and B. Eglington were then elected unanimously as Vice-Presidents. If anything, Mick Pyer's election was overdue. A club stalwart back in the twenties he has given nearly 50 years of service. For many years his coaching was a by-word in club athletics and he was the "father" of our boys coaching scheme. Bernard Eglington, shortly to retire from the R.A.F. joined us as a runner but turned to walking and did very well. His service took him throughout the world and his Belgrave colours went with him. He brought us many new members. In proposing that Alf Harley continue as Hon. Sec., Frank Jarvis and Frank Simmons said how lucky Belgrave were to have such a Secretary. "We are the luckiest club in athletics to have such a man at the helm of our affairs" said F.J. In thanking the meeting our Hon. Sec. appealed for young men to take on senior admin tasks. Young blood was needed. When he joined the Club, W.H. Hare was the greatly admired and respected Secretary at the age of 33 - "and I thought he had one foot in the grave!" Alf Harley thanked his assistants but felt that a successor would enable him to be better employed acting as a roving ambassador. Dave Shepherd was re-elected as Hon. Treasurer unanimously but Frank Jarvis pointed out that "You can only retire if you find a successor. Others may have been unlucky but I found a candidate for Assistant Hon. Sec. 3 or 4 months ago! - I propose Bill Ashford!" Bill was duly elected, and is ideal "cabinet" material. The long list of sectional appointments were then dealt with and the result of these can be found in the Club Handbook. Bill Lucas changed his mind at the eleventh hour and the Club is blessed after all with his 17th year in this post - they will have to win the National now! Tribute was paid to Ernie Kemp "One of the hardest worked timekeepers in the country". Presentation of awards for the Youths and Boys medal competitions were then made by the President. The "Mrs. L. Ryan" Cup was awarded to Richard Langley for his maximum points win in the Boys competition and the "H.W. Shields" Cup to Vic Butcher for the Youths competition. With the official proceedings at an end, the meeting was declared closed and unofficially resumed in "The Swan" ten minutes later - with far less order of course! items.sum: Extract from the December 1928 Belgravian in which 'Observer' blames foreigners' seriousness, broken-time payments and dancing for British athletic decline.
items.s: FROM 'THE BELGRAVIAN' 40 years ago Extract from the December 1928 Belgravian in which 'Observer' blames foreigners' seriousness, broken-time payments and dancing for British athletic decline. DECEMBER 1928 - "Observer" writes '..... of the alleged decline in athletics. Many reasons are being advanced but, so far as international races are concerned, I think the same applies here as in other branches of the sport. No matter what the game is, there is no denying the fact that slowly and surely foreigners triumph over Britishers. Why? Firstly, because they take their sport so much more seriously than the average Englishman. Whereas the majority of our athletes treat running as an enjoyable hobby and a means of keeping fit, the foreigner goes right out and practically lives only for his running. Then, secondly, it is well known "broken-time" payments are given abroad, whilst our men have to train and race in their spare time and, given some occupations, they get precious little of that. I see that one whose opinion is to be respected mentions dancing, as indulged in at present, as a curse to running; I agree. To remain for many hours in an atmosphere such as you experience in modern dance halls IS injurious' Observer "Observer"

items.label: December 1968
items.sum: Report of the club dinner at the Wimbledon Hill Hotel on 16 November 1968, with toasts by Ted Sutters, Alf Harley and Ron Goodman and a raffle for the Children's Christmas Party.
items.s: THE CLUB DINNER Report of the club dinner at the Wimbledon Hill Hotel on 16 November 1968, with toasts by Ted Sutters, Alf Harley and Ron Goodman and a raffle for the Children's Christmas Party. Wimbledon Hill Hotel, November 16th Wimbledon can now rest at peace for another year - the great social event of the season is over again. The Club Dinner was, as usual, a roaring success, a good time being had by old and young alike. It is always pleasing to see both familiar and unfamiliar faces, the regular attenders and those who can only make it to see us on such occasions. Judging by the way Club members polished their plates one can only assume that the food was good, that they had been starved for a week beforehand in anticipation of a good 'nosh' or perhaps that they had been out in the afternoon training or racing to work up a good appetite! The turkey and its accompaniments went down very well but the 'Peach Melba' caused some comment. Was it Melba, Flan or Gateaux? The final decision rests with the individual. The meal over we settled back to listen to the pearls of wisdom from the speakers. The toast to the Club was very ably proposed by Ted Sutters, President of the E.C.C.U., who after admitting to doing some Belgrave homework, coloured his remarks with some background knowledge of his own. He also made observations regarding the Registration Scheme pointing out that Belgravians should have no difficulty in affording to pay up if judgement could be made by counting the number of bottles on the dinner tables. Is he right!? Pat Duncan's reply to Mr. Sutters proposal was very amusing and provided a welcome 'light interlude' to the more serious side of the proceedings. We can always rely on Alf Harley to keep the interest of his listeners and he didn't fail us on this occasion. Who better to propose the toast to the guests than our distinguished Club Secretary, and the response by Ron Goodman, President of the Surrey County A.A.A. was a good follow up. Our guests are usually drawn from the official front ranks and this year proved to be no exception. Our new President had the right idea in keeping his speech brief and we all joined whole-heartedly with Ted Stimpson in wishing Frank a very successful and happy year in office and an improvement in mobility to complete the picture. If determination has anything to do with it I am sure he will win through. The formalities over the 'knees up' began. Everyone joined in with the usual waltz, fox-trot and quickstep (knowledge of these gained from 'Come Dancing') and some were dragged, not altogether without resistance, into doing the twist and the march of the mods. It certainly sorts out the fit from the rest!!! During the evening we had a raffle for the Children's Christmas Party (needless to say in true Belgrave style the lucky winners were heckled and booed - such sportsmanship we all show!) and the funds collected from this were augmented by the auction of a beautiful white Teddy Bear which was generously given by that grand gentleman, Ernest Neville. Our grateful thanks must be extended to him. It is always a shame that this part of the evening goes so quickly and has to close just when we are all in full swing, but it is heartening to see our Club and guests enjoying themselves. Many thanks to all who organise this function and long may this Belgrave tradition continue. S.L. FIRST CLAIM MEMBERS ONLY 'm' denotes conversion from metric, and figures in brackets alongside, e.g. (m-28.4) indicate 'metric time minus 28.4 secs'. C.R. denotes Club record. Figures in brackets beneath event title indicate best performances 1966-7. TONY BROOKS WRITES: Although only two trophies will adorn the mantlepieces of Belgrave Harriers this year, we can proudly say that they are two of the most coveted trophies in the South of England. Ryder Trophy A great team effort helped Belgrave to win this trophy from National League 'A' winners Southampton. Brockman Trophy Retaining this trophy for another year, by beating Blackheath by one point, Belgrave proved that on the day they can more than hold their own against the best. Photos: Ron Linstead John Mitchell, top of the long jump rankings, in action during the London Championships where he also finished 2nd in the 100 yds. The only member to have bettered John's long jump is second claim Olympian Alan Lerwill. Through the season certain names have been prominent amongst the results. Such names as Adrian Major, Bill Kerr, Chris Martin, 'Snowy' Brooks and Phillip Gee. These fellows were always prepared to turn up to any meeting in any conditions and without them Bels would certainly not have fared as well as they did. It is noticeable that the performances of these members improved vastly during the season and one wonders whether or not the performances of some of the better runners who think they can produce better times at invitation meetings might not have improved as well. Looking ahead, however, Belgrave can expect great things in the not too distant future. The majority of our track runners are only just out of their teens and with a little effort it could soon be that instead of just the odd county and area representation 'Bels' could be fielding a full county team. Breaking down the various events, this was the structure of 'Bels' 1968 track team. 100 yds/100 mtrs. John Mitchell and Jim Vivian share equal honours in this event. Both were credited with a 9.8. John, however, has recorded 10.6 for 100 metres which converts to 9.7 for 100 yards. 200 yds/200 mtrs. Jim Vivian with a 21.8 yards remains top dog, but close behind is first year junior, Steve White, 22.1. Chris Martin with 22.2 fills third place. 440 yds/400 mtrs. Tony Brooks with a 50.2 metres fills first place while Steve White 50.5 metres in second. 'Snowy' Brooks 50.8 metres third gives him the edge over Alan Mead and Chris Martin 51.6 yards. 880 yds/800 mtrs. A vast improvement from Adrian Major to 1:55.7 metres. John Thresher on one of his rare runs recorded 1:57.1 yards. Alan Mead and Pete Hilliar both recorded 1:57.4 metres and Tony Brooks 1:58.2 yards. Lionel Mann, a distance runner of repute, also encroached on this event with a 1:58.1 metres. 1500 metres Although never extended John Thresher again has the fastest time for the distance of 3:44.6 and one feels that this, and not the 3 miles, is John's event. Close behind him are John Bicourt and Adrian Major, the real prospects for the near future. 1 mile More of a token run than a race gave John Thresher a time of 4:14.3. Close behind was evergreen Bill Kerr with 4:14.6. A very good season for Adrian Major, finishing with a best of 4:15.0. 2 miles Yet again John Thresher heads the lists with a very good time of 8:44.6. items.s: Boxing Day History of the club's Boxing Day 120 yards sprint handicap since 1887, promoting the 1968 meeting at Battersea Park, with photographs of the 1899 race on the Embankment and part of the 1896 tenth annual programme. At 11 a.m. on 26th December 1968, Belgrave Harriers will once again be staging their Boxing Day track and field handicap meeting at Battersea Park track. "So what!", you may say, "it's just another meeting; and who wants to run on turkey and Christmas pudding anyway". Well, that may be the view of the unitiated, but for 81 years there has been sufficient support from our other members to keep the meeting firmly established on our fixtures list and, through doing so, the occasion is steeped in more tradition than the rest of our events put together. It was in 1887, only a few months after the Club's formation, that our founder members voted to hold a 120 yards sprint handicap along the Embankment on the morning of Boxing Day. The details of that race are not known. Would there have been two heats, or three? (heat composition was small in number in those days). Was there more than one judge? A timekeeper? Was the course the same as that used in subsequent years? To all of these we can only hazard guesses but as to whether it was a success or not we have more evidence. THE 1899 FINAL In 1896, only nine years after the inaugural race, the event justified a printed programme, eight heats, semi-finals and final. Part of the programme is reproduced opposite. It is fair to assume that for some years the occasion had attracted some public interest; for only three years later (1899) a photographer was in attendance and the pictures shown above and opposite were taken from beneath his black shroud. Eventually the meeting moved to the track and, over the years, further events were introduced until we reached the present programme of handicaps: 2 miles run, 3 miles walk, putting the shot and, of course, the premier event celebrating its 82nd birthday, the 120 yards sprint handicap. Times have changed a lot since 1887, the venue is different, the dress is different - but the Christmas spirit is still there and so is that inextinguishable spirit that launched the meeting long ago in 1887. Why not come along and rub shoulders with tradition at 11 a.m. on 26th December 1968? BELGRAVE HARRIERS. AFFILIATED TO A.A.A. President--H. MORTON CARR, ESQ. items.label: December 1968
items.sum: Chris Steer, who emigrated to Canada in April 1968, describes training under coach Paul Poce at the Toronto Olympic Club and compares the Canadian coach-led system with British club athletics.
items.s: COACH! Chris Steer, who emigrated to Canada in April 1968, describes training under coach Paul Poce at the Toronto Olympic Club and compares the Canadian coach-led system with British club athletics. It was only last April that CHRIS STEER entered the marriage stakes, ran his last race in England and upped all to go to Canada. Needless to say he took his running kit with him and, in the hope of carrying on where he left off---with a club like Belgrave---soon contacted the Toronto Olympic Club. He soon discovered that methods are different 3,000 miles away. The occasion was a cool October evening with a cool breeze blowing off Lake Ontario. As I walked from the subway station across High Park, Toronto, running gear over shoulder, my mind was occupied with what little training I could reasonably get away with that evening. Pushing past a crowd of padded and helmeted football players and sitting thoughtfully on the dressing room bench, inhaling the fragrant odour of orange peel and embrocation, remnants of same football players, I came to the conclusion that a steady half-dozen would suffice for that evening. No sooner had I made this difficult decision when other members of Toronto Olympic Club came drifting in, followed by the imposing figure of one Paul Poce, or 'Coach' as he is known to one and all. 'Okay you guys. Let's get moving. Repetition miles tonight.' I was just about to suggest that I was not exactly in the mood for repetition miles and that I thought I would do six miles steady on the country when I was forestalled. 'Steer you hairy hippy. I'm not sure which team to put you in on Saturday. You better work out with Nick and Rudi. You should manage to keep up with them.' My pride feeling slightly dented (Nick and Rudi were 'C' team runners) I conceded that an easy run was out for that evening. After four one mile laps on the road at eyeballs-out pace, coach called me over. 'Okay Chris, you've made your point. I'll put you in the 'B' team.' I relate this incident, not in self-congratulation, but to illustrate some of the differences I have encountered between training in England and 'working out' in Canada. Whereas in England the run-of-the-mill athlete is only required to show up for races and the question of what training he does is left up to him, in Canada great emphasis is placed on collective training and club work outs take place every night under the close supervision of the club coach. When attending a club session, the athlete is told exactly how far and how fast to run and is expected to carry out these instructions to the letter. It may be instructive to pause at this point to explain that the institution of 'coach' on this continent has somewhat different connotations than that in England. Broadly speaking, in most sports the coach's position is comparable to that of the manager of an English soccer team. Although not completely omnipotent, Baseball, Football and Hockey coaches and to only a slightly lesser extent athletics, coaches are solely responsible for the training, selection and overall performance of their charges. Because of this responsibility, most professional coaches rule their teams with a rod of iron and their word is law. This is not so evident in Track and Field, being an amateur sport, but the theory remains the same. 'Coach' selects teams, enters teams, treats injuries and just about runs the club single handed. This invites the inevitable comparison with the British method with its sectional secretaries, selection committees and generally disorganised, or unorganized, training methods. From the point of view of tangible success the Canadian method could be held to be better. Most runners are undoubtedly good and extremely dedicated (in my club anyway). Out of a membership of about 100, Toronto Olympic provided eight members of the thirty strong Canadian Olympic squad. There are few, if any 'scrubbers' - they couldn't stand the pace. On the debit side several runners seem to place an undue reliance on coach. One of our stars whilst running in the Canadian 10,000 metres championship was heard to ask where he should start his final sprint - this was during the race. He received his instructions and finished a creditable second, but to my mind a runner of this class should have the brains to work out his own tactics. The encouragement and incentive is certainly greater this side of the Atlantic. Athletes are not regarded as eccentric freaks by members of the general public and facilities are far better - four all-weather tracks within a mile of my apartment. In spite of all this I look forward to the time when I shall once again be splashing round Richmond Park on a Summer day with the exciting prospect of Wyn Shepherd's tea and buns before me. items.sum: Review of Belgrave's weak autumn 1968 road relay season (Surrey, Blackheath, Johnston, Walton and the new Dudley-Bridgnorth relay) with full results of the Surrey, Blackheath and Walton relays.
items.s: ROAD RELAY ROUND-UP Review of Belgrave's weak autumn 1968 road relay season (Surrey, Blackheath, Johnston, Walton and the new Dudley-Bridgnorth relay) with full results of the Surrey, Blackheath and Walton relays. The Autumn road relay results for 1968 were the worst for several years. Contributory factors were undoubtedly the transfer of the Belgrave 'Southern' Relay to the Spring and the cancellation of the Bristol-Weston event. These were the two premier events in the Autumn season and their loss seemed to take away our enthusiasm as well. Missing, was the fight for places. Missing, was the rivalry for times. Missing, was the endless gossip and speculation over team selections for our own relay and the Bristol-Weston. And not once did we get our best men together in anything like their usual form. The short season's events went as follows: September 14th Surrey County Road Relay 12th September 21st Blackheath Road Relay 5th September 29th 'Johnston' Road Relay 4th October 5th Walton Road Relay 3rd October 19th Dudley - Bridgenorth Road Relay 2nd At least the results showed week by week improvement. Once again we performed badly in the opening event at Woking and our 'A' team contained not one of our best ten runners. Piotrowski and Hart were obliged to run in the 'B' team, being non-Surrey men, which didn't help a situation that was aggravated still further by Shippen running faster than four of the 'A' team. So after 3 stages the 'B' team headed the 'A' by 1:51. It was not until the closing stages of the final leg that Donnison put the teams the right way round. The following week our '5¾' road race clashed with the Blackheath relay, so only one team was sent to the relay. The team was by no means our best and their 5th placing was all that was expected of them. Thresher was overweight and running for almost the first time in two months and it was no surprise to find him a minute below his best. It was only on the last stage that Gerry North put S.L.H. behind us and take 5th position - but we were still a minute behind Mitcham and 2½ minutes behind Hercules/Wimbledon who won every relay in which they competed this Autumn. The 'Johnston' was held the following week and this is reported on another page. Once again we were not at full strength and 4th was no surprise - it was no disgrace either, for only Hercules/Wimbledon, Coventry Godiva and Manchester DLC were ahead of us. Even the Walton relay reflected our below-par form. Two years ago we were easy winners and last year we were pipped by Bristol. This time we put Bristol behind us and broke the course record, only for H/W and Pompey to steal our thunder. Lionel Mann ran a great first stage to come in 2nd but, as good as it was, Major, Fairclough, Thresher and O'Hara should never have permitted him to finish up second fastest Belgravian of the day to Gerry North. Our turnout for this race was excellent, with six teams being fielded and the 'B', 'C' and 'D' being the first home in their categories. For four consecutive weeks H/W had beaten us on the road and there is no doubt that this amalgamation is already a threat to us. They have shown fine form and fully justified their wins, but the real test will be in the 'Southern' and 'National' relays next Spring. To help retain at least one major relay event in the Autumn, Tipton Harriers did a rapid piece of promotional work when the cancellation of the famous Bristol-Weston was announced, and organised a new relay called the "Dudley to Bridgenorth and Back" on October 19th. This effort on the part of Tipton is greatly appreciated by the 'Bristol' regulars. The report is covered elsewhere in this gazette and, considering the short notice, the event was a success. Derby were comfortable winners but our second place was praiseworthy for putting Tipton and Coventry behind us. So, just as the season ended we seemed to be clicking into gear; and the early cross-country races seem to be reaping the benefit. There is no doubt that the nine-week long Spring season is now the premier one, and following on from the National cross-country championships, makes February/March/April the toughest 3 months of the year. items.sum: Report of the club 5¾ mile road race at Wimbledon on 21 September 1968, won by Pat O'Connor from Dick Piotrowski and Roger Donnison, with 15-year-old Bill Curtin eighth.
items.s: O CONNOR BREAKS THROUGH Report of the club 5¾ mile road race at Wimbledon on 21 September 1968, won by Pat O'Connor from Dick Piotrowski and Roger Donnison, with 15-year-old Bill Curtin eighth. 5¾ Mile Road Race - Wimbledon, September 21st, 1968 This is not our road championship, the Wimbledon Cup Race being held in March each year, but it was pleasing to see over forty runners facing the starter although most of our leading runners were absent for reasons best known to themselves. A small but select pack detached themselves from the main field round the first lap of the common with Pat O'Connor, Dick Piotrowski, Trevor Hart, Alan Black and a new member from New Zealand, Kelly Diprose, prominent. The latter at one time looked as if he intended to race away from the field but lack of training soon made itself felt and common sense dictated a more suitable pace. Down Copse Hill the race resolved itself into a battle between O'Connor, Piotrowski and Donnison and it was to the surprise of most spectators that Patrick came up Cambridge Road like a champion and round the final lap of the common left the field spreadeagled behind. Never had O'Connor run like this but it was soon rumoured that this little man from Ireland had been putting in the miles and his hard work was obviously paying dividends. The change from a virtual scrubber to potential champion was miraculous and he is to be congratulated on his achievement. Not only did he win but he won in good time. Dick Piotrowski never gave up chasing Pat over the last mile and Roger Donnison in taking third place again produced a steady and consistent performance. Alan Black again failed to make use of his considerable talents - when is this man going to learn that he could be our leading runner if he trained the right way? - perhaps a chat with Pat O'Connor or Lionel Mann might help. The only training for running is to run and to keep on running - no-one can hope to do really well these days on less than 75 miles per week. Mention must be made of Bill Curtin who, although only fifteen and against the advice of the pundits decided to run in this race, finished eighth in a time that many of our more seasoned runners would have been delighted to have achieved. Keep at it Bill!!! - Munich in 1972 may be too early but 1976 should be just right. Kelly Diprose made a good start to his service with Belgrave - this boy is going to be a tower of strength - he also has a good sense of humour which he will need to combat our cross country courses after Christmas. Pat O'Connor easily won the handicap-it is doubtful whether anyone with a start of 3½ minutes has ever won the scratch race before. W.E.L. items.sum: Stage-by-stage report of the Johnstone Relay on 29 September 1968, in which Belgrave finished fifth on the road but were placed officially fourth after Polytechnic's disqualification, 3 min 34 sec behind winners Hercules/Wimbledon.
items.s: 4th AGAIN IN 'Johnstone' Stage-by-stage report of the Johnstone Relay on 29 September 1968, in which Belgrave finished fifth on the road but were placed officially fourth after Polytechnic's disqualification, 3 min 34 sec behind winners Hercules/Wimbledon. Johnstone Relay, September 29th, 1968 There seems to be some reluctance on the part of some of our top runners to either take part or be sufficiently fit to run well in this race and as a result we have yet to show our true form over this course. This year was no exception and in finishing actually fifth but officially fourth our performance was definitely sub-standard. The winners Hercules/Wimbledon finished 3 minutes and 34 seconds ahead and this is the largest thrashing we have received to date from this comparatively small but up and coming club - our reputation was well and truly dented and our local rivals will not cease to remind us of this performance for a long time to come. The story of the race can be summed up by saying that we were never in the hunt and were trailing with little or no prospects of pulling back early deficits at any time. Pat O'Connor after winning our 5¾ miles road race in grand style one week earlier, took the first stage and brought us in sixth but we were 35 seconds behind Manchester and District Lads Club who were to be prominent throughout the race. Pat should become a great asset to our teams in the next year or two but at present lacks experience and the necessary fire in his running for this type of event. We looked to Laurie O'Hara to bring us up to the leaders on Stage 2 but we were to be disappointed for although he had the usual fast finish Laurie seemed unable to consolidate in the middle part of the leg and lost much ground on the leaders and was forced to give way to Fuller of Hercules/Wimbledon who came up from 9th to 3rd. Next came Adrian Major who had been suffering from achilles tendon trouble and was short of training. Adrian held on to 5th but had to give a lot away to Mike Beevor who took Hercules/Wimbledon into the lead - we were at this point 55 seconds behind. Roger Donnison who is now becoming one of our regular team members was on the first of the short stages and ran most of the way with Geoff Biscoe (Mitcham) who left him on the run in and forced us back to 6th. Hercules were still in the lead and pulled away a little to leave us exactly one minute adrift. When Gerry North takes over everthing usually looks more rosy and our hopes rise. Today wasn't any exception for he soon set about Dave Smallbone (Mitcham) and pursued the clubs ahead. He managed to catch and pass Poly and Coventry but Bob Holt (Hercules/Wimbledon) and Wilde (Manchester and District) were in great form and both widened the gap considerably. Wilde in fact lowered the stage record held by Mike Turner of Liverpool by no less than 24 sec. and Bob Holt was 35 secs. faster than Gerry. Although we were 3rd we were 95 secs. behind the leaders. Tony Fairclough came next and was soon caught and passed by Joslin of Poly who recorded the fastest time of the day on this leg and equalled the stage record. Later Tony had to give way to Hammond of Coventry who was only 3 seconds slower than Joslin. Although back to 5th our overall position behind the leaders was virtually unchanged. Manchester had at this point taken a short lead over Hercules. Dick Piotrowski was on Stage 7 and although staying in 5th place dropped away from the leaders. Ernie Earl that old battler for Hercules was in great form and took his club into the lead once more and following him was a fight between Coventry, Poly and Manchester which resulted in Poly taking 2nd place through an excellent run by Campbell. Our deficit at this point - 2 minutes and 7 seconds. John Thresher had been laying off after his summer activities and was obviously well over weight so we gave him one of the 'boys' legs. He was able to gain 21 seconds on the leaders (still Hercules) but could not improve on our fifth position. Stage 9 is a long leg and Lionel Mann had run well in our track 6 miles championship so we expected great things from him but sheer inexperience of this type of running plus the fact that he raced on the preceeding day (quite unknown to the team manager) lost us much ground and although still fifth the position was impossible as with only one leg to go go we were almost four minutes behind the leaders. Bill Dance who had only a few days previously moved house to Huddersfield came back specially for this race and ran in his usual indomitable style to preserve our fifth place and in fact to gain a little on Hercules/Wimbledon with the third fastest time of the day. items.s: A DUKE'S SPRINGER Report and full result of the club's Yacht '3' handicap at Wimbledon on 12 October 1968, won by over-40 novice Longshaw off a 5-minute start, entered by the 'Duke of York's' Sunday group. LONGSHAW WINS YACHT '3' - Wimbledon, October 12th For weeks the Duke of York's mob had been up to something. You couldn't quite put your finger on it, but it was there. A certain air of expectation. Ace handicap man Arthur Bruce had been bringing in his Sunday morning pack a little sweatier than usual of late - and why was 'Glimpy' carrying his watch about so frequently these days? Yes, the 'Dukes' were up to something and even Gordon Biscoe was caught smirking up his sleeve, mumbling something about 'doing' Bill Lucas. Well, nothing is likely to stop a combination as formidable as that, so our Hon. Handicapper can be excused for responding to Arthur Bruce's smooth "... and this is Longshaw, Bill, he's going to have a go but he's over 40 and has never raced before" by giving the fellow a cool 5 minutes start! John Baker was first off with a start of 6:30, followed by Ted Stimpson (6:00). On 5:00 was McNally, McMillan and Longshaw. Almost immediately the 'springer' had the two macs trailing in his wake and bore down on our President and the front marker as though his life, as well as the shirts of the 'Dukes' themselves, depended on it. He was in front long before the village and broke the tape a mammoth 32 seconds clear of the field. Even a Keino or Clarke wouldn't have stopped him and Gerry North had to settle for 24th place 77 seconds down. There is no doubt of course that Longshaw ran well. He is a novice and 17 of the field were unable to match his 'actual' time. Our 'team' still had to show some restraint at the presentation but it is rumoured that the pubs in Chelsea were extra merry that night! The most notable performances amongst the remainder were by Bill Curtin and Jim Rimmer. The latter gave Bill a ten-seconds start, caught him after a half mile, towed him through the field for a further 1½ miles only to see the 15 years old Curtin run away from him in the closing stages. Both were unlucky to be out of the prizes, but credit must be given to those two youths Breslin and Stow who also surprised the handicapper, with second and third. Pos Name Handicap Time 1. O. items.sum: Stage-by-stage report of Tipton Harriers' new Dudley to Bridgnorth and back road relay on 19 October 1968, in which Belgrave were second to Derby & County, with Geoff North and Gerry North both in the team.
items.s: A Good Second Stage-by-stage report of Tipton Harriers' new Dudley to Bridgnorth and back road relay on 19 October 1968, in which Belgrave were second to Derby & County, with Geoff North and Gerry North both in the team. Dudley to Bridgenorth and back Road Relay, October 19th, 1968 This race was promoted at very short notice by Tipton Harriers to take the place of the Bristol to Weston Super Mare and back relay which has been discontinued because of the traffic difficulties. We agreed to send a team and the first impressions are that this could become a well supported annual event. The course is largely on country lanes and comprises ten stages varying in distance between 2.5 miles and 6.2 miles. Some of the legs are very hilly and are suitable only for fit runners. On the whole a sporty course and a race which can be well enjoyed by both competitors and spectators. The first promotion was not well supported numerically probably because of the short notice but teams from Birchfield, Bristol, Coventry, Derby, Notts. A.C. and Tipton in addition to ourselves provided good competition and we can be pleased with our second place behind a very strong Derby team. It should be remembered that Derby finished second in the 1968 National Road Relay only a few seconds ahead of ourselves. Adrian Major took the first lap and was 6th at the finish, twenty seven seconds down on the leaders, City of Stoke; a small club who did very well throughout the whole race to finish 5th. Tony Fairclough brought us up to fourth and on this leg through a good run by Eccles, Derby went into the lead which they were to maintain to the end. Trevor Hart convinced the team manager that he was suffering from a cold and talked himself into the short 2½ miles leg. He took us up to third and gained an invaluable thirteen seconds on the leaders. Tipton at this point were second about fifty yards ahead. Next came Roger Donnison and although achieving third best time of the day had to be content with remaining in third place. He caught and passed Tipton but in turn was displaced by Hammond of Coventry who put up the fastest time on this stage. We were at this point 58 seconds behind Derby and 27 seconds behind Coventry. Geoff North returning to the team for the first time after his wedding fought hard to get with the leaders but Rhodes of Derby and Kilby of Coventry proved to be better and we dropped back to a deficit of 1 min. 44 secs although staying in third place. John Thresher took the first of the stages on the return journey from Bridgenorth which was by a different route. His leg of 5.4 miles proved to be a very tough one and John was forced to fight hard to keep us in the race. He lost ground on Derby who were well out in front but gained steadily on Coventry. Shelley running now for City of Stoke was working hard behind John and with the fastest time of the day caught our runner near the end of the stage. We were then back to fourth. By a lucky piece of team selection we found that Bill Dance was set to chase Mel Thorpe who left us to go to Coventry last year. This was the ideal situation for Bill revelled in the position he found himself and after quickly passing the Stoke runner set off after Mel like a man possessed. Over his 4 miles stage he picked up the 27 seconds deficit and brought us in second with a further 13 seconds advantage over Coventry. John Dear on Stage 8 had to contend with Grant of Coventry and at one stage it looked as if the Coventry runner would gain a large lead but John recovered well from a bad patch and in the end was only 8 seconds behind. Gerry North again ran a captain's stage and with the best time of the day on the longest leg of 6.2 miles devastated Phil Lancaster running for Coventry and brought us back to a secure 2nd place. Derby at this point were well over 2 minutes ahead. The last leg had been allocated to our new member from New Zealand, Kelly Diprose, and there is little doubt that he will remember his first serious outing for Belgrave for a long time to come. Although the stage was only four miles the majority was almost continuous uphill work and it required all of Kelly's considerable determination to tackle the ever upward grind. Tipton who had reserved one of their best runners for this leg having the advantage of knowing the course were confident that they would catch us but they had not bargained for Kelly's pluck and we were able to hold our second place. This new member is going to be a considerable asset to us - he has natural speed and no lacking in confidence and when really fit will trouble our best runners. Lack of knowledge of the course produced some incorrect team allocations but we shall be wiser next year and will be keen to add our name to the winners list. We must make this race one of our targets - it would be useless to take a partially fit team. cont'd opposite Cont'd from opposite page Team: Major(6th),22.46, Fairclough (4th) 21.28, Hart (3rd) 11.49, Donnison (3rd) 22.1, Geoff North (3rd) 21.45, Thresher (4th), 28.48, Dance (2nd) 19.28, Dear (3rd) 18.30, Gerry North (2nd) 29.39, Diprose (2nd) 21.48 Pos Team Time 1. items.sum: Letters column with news from members abroad and away: Chris Steer in Canada, George Isaac, Dave Mitchell, walker Eric Froude in Melbourne, Ranjit Bhatia in India and Barry Sawyer's Victoria marathon wins.
items.s: Postbag: Letters column with news from members abroad and away: Chris Steer in Canada, George Isaac, Dave Mitchell, walker Eric Froude in Melbourne, Ranjit Bhatia in India and Barry Sawyer's Victoria marathon wins. CHRIS STEER writes from Canada where he has done a little racing. He recently finished second in a road race, beating Mick Hamlin and Chris Henty in the process. There are other expatriates on the athletics scene out there "so it is not exactly lonely". He hopes to be back for the next cross-country season and conveys his best wishes to all Belgravians hoping "to read of their long overdue success in the Southern and National". GEORGE ISAAC, one of our esteemed old members and an AAA coach, writes from Bournemouth. He is expecting to sail to South Africa in the New Year and we are sure that all Belgravians will wish him well. George must have been clearing out his attic, for he sent a bumper parcel of old athletics literature, magazines, programmes etc. to the Editor---helping to boost the reference 'library'. Are there any other attics requiring a spring-clean?. All matter on athletics, including cuttings are welcomed. Former co-editor DAVE MITCHELL writes from Tonbridge, which is sufficiently far away to keep him safe from the 'Harriers'! He is seriously thinking of getting involved in athletics again, but possibly as a coach. Any comment, Dave Ansell?. Walker ERIC FROUDE writes from Melbourne, Australia where the track season has just started. His club is short of walkers, which is just as well he thinks, in view of his 9 minute miles. He should have no difficulty getting in speed work, as the programme includes walking races over a distance of 880 yards! RANJIT BHATIA sends his regular letter and his regards to all at Belgrave Hall. Unfortunately, Ranjit sustained a leg injury in a recent car accident and was hospitalised for a time. He will miss the start of the Indian track season. Ranjit seems to be a lone voice in Indian athletics and is most upset at the way other sports there get preferential treatment. He cites Derek Boosey as an example of a man who, after receiving no encouragement, made good only after leaving India. The National Federation would only selct four athletes for Mexico and the Government cut this to two. No wonder he is disillusioned. No one can cover an airmail letter-form so adeptly as BARRY SAWYER. It would take a whole gazette to reproduce the wealth of information he squeezes into a letter, but it is worth noting that Barry won all three Victoria State marathons this year---the 'Country' marathon championship in 2:26:53 and the State title in 2:24:16. At the former event he was pronounced unfit to run at the pre-race medical! Whatever the reasons were, Barry ignored them with typical stubbornness and led from start to finish to win by 11 minutes---"quite a training run" he quips. He missed the State '15 through a septic blister and blood poisoning, but shook this off just in time to resume twice a day training and clock up 122 miles in the week preceding the State Championship. "Having read through the programme I was reconciled to finishing 15th, but determined to stay with the leaders as long as possible. This I did to such good effect that I was alone in front at 11 miles-----when I coasted along until a few miles from the finish---applied a little pressure---to come in a winner by 4 minutes 12 seconds". Barry's form prompted the Japanese to invite him to Fukuoka in December, but he cannot afford to leave. However, he hopes to run the Master's Marathon in Las Vegas on January 29th. If he does, our thoughts will be with him. items.sum: Reg Hopkins on the club's ideal of valuing members of every ability, the boys' athletics display at the National Boys Club Week festival at Crystal Palace, a track round-up of junior honours, and the new boys' club room and gymnasium in Southwark (continued on page 28 after the rankings page).
items.s: YOUTHS & BOYS Reg Hopkins on the club's ideal of valuing members of every ability, the boys' athletics display at the National Boys Club Week festival at Crystal Palace, a track round-up of junior honours, and the new boys' club room and gymnasium in Southwark (continued on page 28 after the rankings page). "IF you can meet with triumph and disaster And treat these two imposters just the same" Kipling Reg. Hopkins reports The object of the Belgrave Harriers shall be the encouragement of amateur athletics with membership open to all regardless of race, creed or ability. This is the charter of our Club. It is upon the last word in this sentence that I would comment now. Ability. We have in Belgrave many fine athletes. We have had many in the past, and I am sure we will have many more in the future; but is is also true we have less gifted members, who not for the want of trying have not as yet met with success. I wish to make it quite clear that I regard these members as being equal in importance to the award-winning Belgravians. And if, at the moment, a member finds himself in a winning streak, it is bad sportsmanship and bad manners to knock less fortunate team members, and is certainly no way to bring the best out of them. It is a marked distinction of the true Champion that he is always willing to help other competitors from his Club, knowing that if he could raise their standard he would benefit accordingly. By leading and encouraging; by example and understanding; by team backing, through trying their hardest at all times in races and by helping build a team spirit, not allowing pettiness to govern words and actions. This is the only way to success. We know this at Belgrave because we have had many many successes. * * * * * On 23rd October at Crystal Palace indoor arena a festival of sport was presented to an invited audience as part of the National Boys Club Week. Cricket, Table Tennis, Football, Swimming, Diving, Canoeing, Boxing, Gymnastics, Basket Ball, were some of the sports exhibited. It fell to the Belgrave Boys to demonstrate Athletics and Cross-Country which they did in a most impressive way, I was assured by members of the audience (fresh with the memory of the Olympics in mind) that we stole the limelight with our ability, enthusiasm and smart appearance. Many famous sporting personalities were present so a lot of good will was gained for our Club and sport. * * * * * TRACK ROUND UP Congratulations to Arnold Bent, picked as 1st reserve in junior international match England v Germany at Crystal Palace on 7th September. Bill Curtin won a fine 1500 metre race against a classy field in order to gain selection for the "London v Vienna v Israel" Schools match. Bill's time of 4:16 placed him in front of C. Jones (V.P.H.) 4.25 C. Taylor (Woodford Green) G. Walsh (H.H.H.) A. Bull (Hercules Wim.) and our own Richard Langley In the international match at Crystal Palace, Bill (4:07) placed 2nd to the German boy (4:05) who must have had to go some to beat Bill on this track. Also now sporting a German vest (exchanged at this meeting) is Lee Sullivan who represented London in the long jump. Well done both! Hurlingham - G.L.C. Champiomships Youths 880 yds: 3. Bill Curtin 2:4.7 100 yds: 2. Steve White 10.4 We have been fortunate in being allowed the use of a large room at a local boys Club in Southwark and during the past weeks the boys have been busy cleaning and painting it to our own requirements putting up pictures of favorite athletes (excellent photographs kindly given to us by Ed Lacy). We also have use of a Gymnasium. This should prove most useful to us in the winter months when we are unable to use the track. We are planning weight training, circuit training, and indoor jumping sessions. And, if we can get them to come along, visits and lectures from prominent athletes and coaches. We are also rigged up for film shows and Dave Ansell has promised to show pictures of the Mexico Olympics. So it does look like we shall have a sports centre of our own in S.E. London! One other thing I would like the junior section to have is its own reference library. I appeal to any Club member who has any books on Athletics, weight training or similar subjects to donate them to the cause so that our younger members can learn from their pages. items.sum: Report of the Coventry Godiva Harriers boys' and youths' road relays on 28 September 1968, where the young Belgrave boys' team was sixth and the youths fourteenth.
items.s: COVENTRY RELAY Report of the Coventry Godiva Harriers boys' and youths' road relays on 28 September 1968, where the young Belgrave boys' team was sixth and the youths fourteenth. September 28th - Coventry Godiva Harriers Boys Road Relay (4 x 1.9 miles) A good first leg run from Barry Quirk, making his debut in the Boys team, brought us home in 6th position (time 10.19) 64 secs behind the leaders Small Heath. Richard Langley, not quite his usual self and possibly upset by the long journey, did nevertheless gain us two places (time 9.46) and close us up to the leaders. Reg Hopkins, still only a Colt, ran very well to hold his position (time 10.42) and Martin Bloice closed in our team with a good last effort. Martin is better at the shorter distances on the track but is such a good Club man that he delights in running for the Club at any distance. Sixth position was a very good effort from our young team (three aged 14 and one aged 13) against ages up to 16 years. We felt we were putting our heads in the lion's mouth in going up to the Midlands, but we found that it was us that were treated with respect - Belgrave being a name held in the highest regard - we hope we helped to keep it that way. The gear worn by our boys, particularly the shorts (recently bought in Spain), were looked at with envy by our adversaries - as was our Belgrave flag flying over the van! In the Youths race over 2¾ miles we were less successful, only managing to get 14th spot. None of the boys were at their best and we were never in the hunt for medals. items.s: NORTH SURREY LEAGUE Youths/Boys Race No. 1 Report and result of North Surrey League youths/boys race No. 1 at Wimbledon on 26 October 1968, won by Bill Curtin, with Belgrave third team behind Mitcham and Walton. Race No. 1 Wimbledon - October 26th Bill Curtin scored an excellent win in beating Martin of Walton in exactly the same time as last year's winner (Hayes of Mitcham). Showing great form, he improved by 40 seconds on his sixth place of last year and led our team to a useful third place - the same as 12 months ago. Once again, M. Day was the first to provide support, having improved four places to 7th, but Crockford our third lad was unable to keep with Day as he did last year and had to be content with 17th place. It was good to see Richard Langley scoring in his first league outing and if he can repeat Bill's 40 seconds time reduction each season he will win the season after next! Mitcham finished 18 points ahead of us, but last year we got 5 back at Esher, 22 back at Morden Park and a draw at Richmond Park to take the title. We must strive to repeat this performance. Everybody out!! items.h: October 5th - Brighton & Hove A.C. Road Relays
items.sum: Report of the Brighton & Hove boys' and youths' road relays on 5 October 1968, where the boys broke the course record but finished fourth and Bill Curtin ran second fastest time and an individual record.
items.s: October 5th - Brighton & Hove A.C. Road Relays Report of the Brighton & Hove boys' and youths' road relays on 5 October 1968, where the boys broke the course record but finished fourth and Bill Curtin ran second fastest time and an individual record. We broke the course record by 4 secs and yet only got 4th position. Such is the speed with which Boys standards are improving year by year. John Stow ran a fine opening leg for us coming in 9th (11.21), not too far behind the leaders. We felt that we might now get into the medals with Bill Curtin going on the next leg. Bill justified our hopes by running a stormer to bring us up to third (time 10.17). Richard Langley took the 3rd leg and ready to take on the challenge put in a great effort moving us into second place with a time of 11.08. If only Paddy Breslin could hold on to what we already had. He tried really hard to the very end, but Paddy has not yet got the experience (being new to our sport) and he must have put too much in early on - leaving little to hold them off towards the end and conceding two places. We were a bit disappointed to have been so near and yet not to have pulled it off but were cheered up a lot when we heard Bill had got a medal for second fastest time of the day (First fastest: Davis, Cranford School). He also broke the individual record previously held by P. Banning (Andover and District). This means he has been second fastest two years running. A special word of praise to Martin. Although in great pain with stomach cramp he forced himself to finish to that his team mate, Reg, would get a run - even though he knew there was no 4th member to run and complete the team. items.s: Youth section notes: Richard Langley's Milocarian Schools award, Barry Quirk's English Schools basketball selection, the members' new basketball team, and Dave Ansell's Mexico Olympics film show at the Canterbury Club, Bermondsey. Richard Langley was recently presented with the Best Individual Winner award in the under-15 section of the Milocarian Schools Competition, for his 2.05.0 880 yds in the English Schools Championships. He also placed equal 2nd for his 4.47 mile. His school, Raines Foundation Grammar, won the Team award---Richard and another Belgrave boy, Barry Quirk, contributing a great deal towards this victory. These were most outstanding performances as some of the best schools in the country support the Competition----including public schools. * * * * * Incidentally, Barry Quirk has been picked for the English Schools Basketball team. * * * * * Talking of Basketball, we recently formed a team amongst our members, played our first League match, and won by 41 points to 38.in a very close and exciting game! Our object in this is to use Basketball as a means of training together in the winter, particularly for our high and long jumpers who will gain enormously from exercise. * * * * * On Wednesday 27th Nov. at the Canterbury Club Bermondsey, Dave Ansell gave a showing of film he took of the Mexico Games to a large group of our junior members--and very good it was too. He had managed to capture all the outstanding moments and we all thrilled to see again, Hemery, Board, Beamon, Fosbury and all the other Olympic stars. A particularly large cheer greeted the sight of our own Alan Lerwill and Derek Boosey. Frank Simmons honoured us with his presence. Tom Carter did likewise, and also showed film of Belgrave stars from the past which was enjoyed by all---particularly Tom! THe evening closed with Pepsi Cola and Sandwiches and everyone agreed that it had been such a success that others similar gatherings would be arranged for later in the year. items.sum: Reprint of Alf Harley's October 1943 fantasy 'extract' from a 1960 newspaper imagining Belgrave Harriers' grand future and members' unlikely careers, with an editorial postscript inviting predictions for 1993.
items.s: A FLIGHT OF FANCY Reprint of Alf Harley's October 1943 fantasy 'extract' from a 1960 newspaper imagining Belgrave Harriers' grand future and members' unlikely careers, with an editorial postscript inviting predictions for 1993. 25 years ago, in THE BELGRAVIAN of October 1943, ALF HARLEY took a flight of fancy 17 years into the future with a mythical extract from "The Daily Press" of April 1960. His predictions were not wholly serious, of course, but it is always interesting to see just how fanciful they were, or were not, 25 years later. The following is an abridged version of the "extract". 'As I look down on the swirl of traffic which flows eastwards through Hyde Park towards the new double cross-over traffic bridge at Piccadilly Circus, my thoughts turn on this Spring morning through the years,and I ponder on the position the Belgrave Harriers have now attained when contrasted with their humble origins of nearly seventy-five years ago. I am sitting in one of the offices devoted to the production of THE BELGRAVIAN (lavishly illustrated these days and published weekly and recognised as the leading authority on all matters concerning athletics). These offices form part of the magnificient building in Knightsbridge which houses the Club's Town Headquarters and preserves its associations with the City of Westminster and from which training takes place most evenings over Rotten Row. At Wimbledon the Belgrave Harriers still have their weekend headquarters, now situated on Common Side, and every Saturday throughout the winter hundreds of athletes in the familiar claret and gold enjoy their favourite sport in the neighbouring roads and common land. The Committee many years ago realised in its wisdom that the facilities the Club can offer, which are unrivalled anywhere in the world, might well attract a type of member who was merely interested in its restaurant, its billiard room, its luxurious lounges, with no interests in running, walking or field events, and so all members are called upon during their first ten years of membership to make at least 20 appearances in athletic races or competitions each year The subscription remains at the humble few shillings which ruled at the commencement of the Second World War and the frequent social evenings are still a great feature of the Club life. It must be admitted that the Club hardly expected to be owners of such magnificent quarters at Wimbledon and Westminster in such a comparatively short time, but the new outlook towards amateur sport which followed the War, plus a munificent grant from the Anglo-American Philanthropic Association for the finest example of 'self help' in the first half of the Twentieth Century, together with the funds accumulated by decades of enthusiastic Club members, made all things possible. Many of the Club's members have gained positions of considerable importance in our present day world. A notable example if bluff Sir Harry Shields, Bart., whose contributions to the solution of post war traffic problems are well known, and whose baronetcy derives mainly from the original and brilliant idea of bringing all London's Underground train services to the surface and of directing all surface routes underground. Lord Parker, of New Malden, to whom much of the credit for the Belgrave Harriers' progress goes, was awarded his peerage in the Peace Honours List 'for distinguished services to Amateur Athletics and the public'. Tom Cotton, M.P. for the Battersea Park Division, is universally known for his fighting speeches in the House and his consummate command of language, and is ably supported from the back benches by A.W. Penny, whose rallying call of "Up Surrey!" has often been heard in the House. The erstwhile cross-country champion, Bert Footer, now leads a quiet life in the bosom of his family as "Mine Host" at "The Spiked Shoe", Putney Heath. It will be remembered that on leaving the Royal Marines, Footer secretly married Miss 'Fluffy' Blonde from the Windmill Theatre, and later became Minister for Cross-Country Running. Gordon Doubleday is now Managing Director of "Nutty Foods Limited" and Tommy Green is Mayor of Eastleigh permanently. Charlie Churcher can still be seen dancing with his former grace, to which is allied these days an Egyption mysticism. Percy Wright is leader of the Welsh Nationalist Party; Frank Webb remains a bachelor and pursues his sinuous course; and so on ... To all who have contributed to the amazing success of the Belgrave Harriers in the past and to those who help to guide and maintain its traditions in our time a great deal of gratitude is due from the World; for these amateur sportsmen have shown that ideals worth pursuing and fighting for can come to realisation. There is a message in this achievement for all of us' So ends a flight of fancy taken 25 years ago. What is 1993 likely to show? Well, apart from 106 years old Avery Brundage defending the International Prolympic Committee's decision to hold the 1996 Games on the moon, most things will be surprising. For instance ............. well, how about some suggestions from our members? Alf Harley ALF HARLEY Harry Shields Sir Harry Shields, Bart. Parker Lord Parker, of New Malden Tom Cotton Tom Cotton A.W. Olympics The Sunday Times team is on the starting blocks THREE WEEKS TO MEXICO . . . and today the Sunday Times launches its full coverage of the 1968 Olympics. On page 22 . . . a Prediction Chart, forecasting the winners in all the 19 sports. On the same page . . . Roger Bannister, writing the first of two special previews, analyses with his unique combination of medical and [illegible] and scientific aspects [illegible], and comment on the [illegible] long-distance running [illegible] Brooks-Ward, the correspondent of the [illegible] since the 1964 [illegible] will report the show jumping and the Three-day event. Ed Lacey, who has been photographing athletics and other sports for eighteen years. He will be at his third Olympics. His dramatic and illuminating pictures will appear exclusively in the Sunday Times. Three weeks before the 1968 Olympic Games THE SUNDAY TIMES announced it's "team" for Mexico. It was no surprise to the Athletics world in general, and Belgrave in particular, that Eddie Lacey should be chosen to stand alongside Lovesey, Glanville, Bannister and Brooks-Ward. A staunch Belgravian for 20 years, his generosity with photographs for the Club is legion---whether they be of racing, training, the Club Dinner, the New Year's Dance or the Children's Party. The greatest beneficiary is undoubtedly your Honorary Editor who has no hesitation in devoting these two pages to a small part of Eddie's Mexico work. It is worth noting that over half of the 60 odd photographs in America's 'Track and Field News' Olympic edition are by Ed Lacey. His shot of Bob Beamon soaring 29'-2½" across the long jump pit warranted a whole page and is the photograph by which posterity will remember Mexico 1968--and by which Belgravians will be reminded that winning races is not the only way of bringing fame to Belgrave. items.label: December 1968
items.sum: Olympian Derek Boosey describes life in the Mexico Olympic village, his narrow failure to qualify for the triple jump final (placed sixteenth) and his observations on the record-breaking final, with a photograph of him jumping.
items.s: MEXICO 68 Olympian Derek Boosey describes life in the Mexico Olympic village, his narrow failure to qualify for the triple jump final (placed sixteenth) and his observations on the record-breaking final, with a photograph of him jumping. What was Mexico like for the competitors? What did they know about their rivals before the big day and what did they think of them afterwards? Views must have changed very quickly, many times. Our own DEREK BOOSEY never expected the record breaking triple-jump final to be quite so fantastic---a final he missed so narrowly. But as he writes of his experience he remarks"---I must now work very hard". On arrival in the Olympic village, I decided to get into a daily routine. As the qualifying rounds were scheduled for 10 a.m. I decided to have breakfast at 6.30 a.m. and commence my training at 9 a.m. This was essential for me, as I find it very difficult to jump well in the morning. Before the Games opened I never saw the village track deserted; there was always somebody training and the 'rush' hours were between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. Naturally, I spent my time observing the triple jumpers when I was not doing anything specific myself. Gentile, who was to surprise most people with a world record in the qualifying rounds, did not impress me in his training. He had his thigh heavily strapped up, but I think it was only psychological, as he did not appear to be injured. According to Starmynski, Joseph Schmidtz's coach, Gentile had spent a considerable time in Poland last winter 'working out' with the Polish squad. In the qualifying rounds the conditions could have been called ideal, except for a slight head wind. It was a warm, sunny morning and considering the time of the day there were a considerable number of enthusiastic spectators. I had no trouble with my run up but ruined my first round by hopping and stepping too far which resulted in a very poor last phase, giving me only 49'5". In the second round I moved up to 52'5", but still felt that I was not 'getting up' for the last phase. Then just before I took my last round Gentile caused quite a stir by jumping 56'1¼" for a new world record. His run up was not impressive and neither was his hop - but then he bounced into a big step and his last phase was really huge - surely it must have been close to 21'? Next round I took my last jump but as usual my last phase let me down. The figure '16' went up on the score board, and so did my hopes, only to be dashed in the next moment when the figure one centimetre was lit up - nine centimetres (3¾") short of the qualifying distance of 52'10". Then came a tense twenty minutes wait as no one was sure how many had qualified and whether there was a chance that the best 'failures' would make the last twelve. Unfortunately for me, thirteen qualified and I was placed sixteenth. At that time I was very disappointed but on reflection I don't feel so bad, just the thought that I must now work very hard. The triple jump final was just fantastic. It is described very well in Athletics Weekly, so I will just mention one or two observations I made. Saneyev the Russian looked very strong and was very consistent. Even on his 57'0¾" he still had about six inches to spare. Prudencio the Brazilian is a very fast, bouncy jumper. He did not look like a weight-trained athlete, and if this is the case, there is definitely room for improvement. Gentile was very unlucky; first a world record in the qualifying rounds followed by another world record in the first round of the final; he surely must have thought it was 'in the bag'. In my opinion Art Walker (U.S.) was the best jumper, but not once did he hit the board, and his final effort of 56'2" was really worth about 57'10" from take-off to landing. Dudkin was the typical Russian technician with bags of strength. Phil May, the Australian, jumped exceptionally well. His last phase let him down, so it seems he also has lots of room for improvement. He is tall and (continued opposite) lean with a 10.4 second 100 metres to his credit. Schmidt the 'old man' came through with an excellent 55'5" - he is the perfect technician. Mansour Dia, the 6' 8" negro from Senegal, can be relied on to jump 54' any time. He is slow but has fairly good rhythm: his 54'10¾" would have given him a silver medal in 1964, but was only good enough for 8th place. The conditions were superb; brilliant warm sunshine and a strong wind in favour. items.label: December 1968
items.sum: Former co-editor Dave Mitchell argues after Mexico that British athletics' cross-country-based club system cannot produce speed, and calls on Belgrave to set track targets and a professional attitude for Munich 1972.
items.s: MEXICO 68 Former co-editor Dave Mitchell argues after Mexico that British athletics' cross-country-based club system cannot produce speed, and calls on Belgrave to set track targets and a professional attitude for Munich 1972. For some time former co-Editor DAVE MITCHELL has been threatening to go into print, but it never seemed to happen---until the Mexico Olympics that is. The Games has prompted his call for change, but is it the right one?. Our cross-country and road runners will probably not like it but, as Charlie Walker would say,"What do you think?". Now the Mexico Olympics are over. Now the post mortems will begin. Apart from that glorious 400m hurdles final and possibly Whetton's determined running in the 1500m, Britain made little or no impression in any of the finals. The tragedy is that nobody ever really expected Britons to do well. Of course we expected the explosive events to be dominated by the big powerful Americans. We all knew that the altitude problem would inhibit and handicap the unacclimatised athletes. Performances from Hines, Carlos, Evans and company confirmed the former and our fears over the altitude question were supported not only by abysmal British performances but also by below par efforts by 'greats' such as Ryun, Roelants and Haase. Are we convinced, however, that if the Olympiad had taken place on the shores of the Dead Sea we would have improved our gold reserves? Did our sprinters even look world class? Where was the Brightwell strength and the Metcalfe flair in the one lap event? Then, even allowing the criminal handicap of altitude running, can we in any way equate Messrs Herriot, Taylor and Blinston with the Ibbotsons, Piries and Norrises of little more than a decade ago. The simple answer, of course, is that relatively we have improved our times less rapidly than almost all other nations. Strangely enough the U.S.S.R. seems to be in very much the same boat at the moment. Also of course, ignoring Mexico, many of the new stars are from the newly emerging African and Central American states with their great natural speed and strength. But why is it that Australia can produce Ralph Doubell almost out of the blue (certainly out of season) and our representatives in the same event (shades of Derek Johnson) run like novices? Although Dave Hemery acknowledged his debt to Harrow's Fred Housden and although he may have been home grown he was certainly ripened in the American collegiate hot house. Not that that lessened the thrill of seeing the Union Jack at the masthead for a change. So we come down to the system. The old professional versus amateur argument. One T.V. commentator (I.T.V. not Auntie) accused our athletes of lacking dedication. My comments at this were unprintable (but I am fortunately speaking to my wife again). Anybody who turns out in our climate for cross-country runs, practices pole-vaulting at Tooting Bec or runs the roads because he hasn't a local track must be dedicated. It's not the athletes, neither let me hasten to add is it the officials, who are to blame. It's the system. What is the system? Basically it's a set up consisting of about 4,000 clubs of all sizes producing the best cross-country and road runners in depth in the world. Perhaps we ought to reinstate cross-country as an Olympic event! Certainly our system, our approach and our facilities are not geared to track and field events. Personally I've always felt that most athletes in this country regard the track season as that pleasant lull between the National and next season,or to Belgravians of any age at all,between the Brightons. Cross-country is organised - of course it's easier. You all go out,in any weather, and run. In the summer the edge seems to go - very little is organised by way of specialist training. Where do most of the coaches go in summer anyway? At last I think I know what I'm trying to say. Let's throw cross-country and road running out of the window. They're fine in their own way - excellent training, marvellous for producing stamina, determination etc. But none of these qualities will ever compensate for speed. At Mexico we were represented in the 1500m by two steady plodders and one nippy finisher (providing it's a slow first 1400m). If we want to be revolutionary how about changing our name from Belgrave Harriers to Belgrave Comets or Belgrave Bombers. Munich 1972 will be tough, times will be fast and they won't be won on Wimbledon Common but on the tracks of Hurlingham and Battersea. Let's set targets. Not to win'n' trophies but to have 10 men inside 51 secs for the quarter or 4:10 for the mile. Coaches must be in the van of this revolution. Not necessarily coaches brought up in the old world of repetition 70 second laps but motivators prepared to handle a small group of athletes who can work as a group and develop the competitive instinct. Cross-country breeds sufferance and patience, we want temperament and aggression. We don't need professional athletes but we do need athletes with a professional attitude. Otherwise in 1972 we won't have anybody in the Olympic finals. items.s: ROAD RUNNING Road running review of the 1968 season with tributes to the club's road stalwarts and results from ten-mile, 20, 25 km, 30-mile, track 25 and marathon races, August-October 1968. Once again the time of the year has arrived when we enter the quiet period for road running. This time we can look back on a fairly successful season over distances up to 10 miles but have yet to make that major break through in the 20's and marathons. However, our placings in this year's Poly Marathon suggested this could be around the corner, and if Pat O'Connor can retain the tremendous improvement he has shown this autumn he may well join Trevor Hart and Lionel Mann to form our strongest and most well balanced team for some time. We must not, of course, forget Charlie Dabbs who, if he can free himself of injury, may well come back to show them all a thing or two. Whilst 'name dropping' for hopes of future successes we must not forget those such as Messrs. Hall, Bonser, Mathews, Baker, etc. - a band of stalwarts who with Lionel have travelled many expensive miles this season to take part in some gruelling events and have made sure that Belgrave has been represented far and near. Also, congratulations to Geoff Pearson who this year 'became of age' by running his 21st Poly Marathon - surely a record which will take some beating. Having raced over 300 miles on the road this season, Lionel Mann received his just reward for such enthusiasm by being elected Vice Captain at the A.G.M. Having just received an addition to his family around this time (and with Charlie Dabbs and Gordon Biscoe old bachelors) he was probably considered just the person to keep a fatherly eye on some of our runners. items.s: TANSWELL '10' Lionel Mann reports the inaugural Harry Tanswell memorial ten-mile road race at Basildon on 15 September 1968, run on a flooded course and won by Gerry North, with Belgrave taking the team trophy. Lionel Mann reports: The inaugural ten mile road race for the "Harry Tanswell memorial trophy' was held from Gloucester Park, Basildon, Essex on Sunday, 15th September, 1968. The weather was a trifle wet and the conditions in which the race was to be run were so poor due to the rainfall being so heavy that a new course had to be mapped out by the organisers, who showed great resilience and determination in enabling the race to commence at all. Eventually nearly fifty athletes (aqua-lungs, snorkles and flippers were ruled out!) came under starter's orders to splash their way through ten very wet miles of Essex roadways; the course was nearly always ankle deep, often knee deep and at one unforgetable pool - waist high. To coin a phrase, it made Wimbledon Common seem like an arid desert. Nevertheless the Belgrave Aqua-Harriers remained damply undeterred. Gerry North surfaced in first place with Lionel Mann and Bill Dance in seventh or ninth places claiming the 'Tanswell Trophy' for Belgrave. P.S. Bill Dance won an umbrella, so at least arrived home in the dry. Pos Name Club Time 1. G. North Belgrave 51.05 2. I. Mackintosh Ranalagh 51.26 3. F. Gannwell Ilford 52.00 7. L. Mann Belgrave 53.50 9.
