items.h: FROM THE BELGRAVIAN 25 years ago ... and 40 years ago
items.sum: Extracts from The Belgravian of October 1944 (the 'Flying Bomb Number') and September 1929 (AGM report on membership, the walkers' successes, George Dunckley and Tommy Green).
items.s: FROM THE BELGRAVIAN 25 years ago ... and 40 years ago Extracts from The Belgravian of October 1944 (the 'Flying Bomb Number') and September 1929 (AGM report on membership, the walkers' successes, George Dunckley and Tommy Green). 25 years ago OCTOBER 1944----"This edition might well be called the "Flying Bomb Number", as much of what is recorded took place whilst Southern England, and particularly London, was under attack by these missiles. In conjunction with Polytechnic Harriers, a full and ambitious programme had been arranged. A number of fixtures had to be cancelled, whilst the remainder were contested by scratch teams from either side. This was not surprising as Police and Civil Defence were fully occupied. A number of members were able to find or make the time to turn out for the Club and we are all grateful to those who helped to keep Belgrave to the fore during most trying times". "A glance at the Club address book shows that we have manny members living in some of the most heavily damaged areas. No serious injuries to members have been reported, but many of our members' homes have been damaged, some completely destroyed. To all who have suffered, the Club offers their deepest sympathy, and we hope that lost and damaged homes will be quickly restored. We also extend condolences to those who have lost relations and friends". and 40 years ago SEPTEMBER 1929----"This year the Annual General Meeting was held at St. Gabriel's Hall, Lupus Street (near the foot of Vauxhall Bridge) and was fairly well attended". "The Honorary Secretary commenced his report by giving some details of the Club membership. He announced that 138 new members had joined during the past year, against 23 resignations, and said that the Club membership now stood at 508. In the matter of performances, the Club had just completed it's best season yet, forty two years after the formation of the Club. The walkers had opened the year by winning the R.W.A. scratch team cup and had finished by annexing the Brighton Walk Team Shield. In between these two races, the National Championship had again been won (for the fourth time in five years) and second place gained in the Junior Championship held at Birmingham. The runners also had their share of wins. Both the Junior and Senior Championships of the South of the Thames Association had been won and also the Surrey Championship, by a very large margin. The Club's showing in the Southern and National Championships was disappointing after the early season wins, but amends were made in the London to Brighton Relay. In this race the Bels finished seventh, gaining the special medals and completing the course in time which a few years ago would have beaten the record". "There had been two outstanding individuals during the past year, G. R. Dunckley and T.W. Green. George Dunckley had represented England v Germany in two races and had shown some remarkably running. He had been timed to do his stage of the 4x440 yards relay in 48.3 seconds---a wonderful performance". "Tommy Green had shown notably consistent distance walking and the Club were justified in regarding him as the fastest man at the longer distances in the Country, and possibly the World. His last performance, that of winning the Brighton walk in the second fastest time ever recorded, came as a fine finish to the year's efforts". George Dunckley G. R. Dunckley G. R. JUNIOR ~ STEVE SECOND Report and Belgrave results from the AAA Junior and Youth Championships at Crystal Palace, where Steve White was second in the 200m and Paul Duckett sixth in the 3,000m walk. Crystal Palace--August 8th/9th Producing his usual blazing burst round the turn, Steve White led the finalists into the straight and looked set to win his first AAA Championship, but he faded badly down the straight and Griffith swept past to take the title by a tenth in 21.7. Our only other finalist was Paul Duckett who finished 6th in the 3,000 metres walk with a time of 14:52.2, but there were no qualifying races for this event. Of the remainder, Peter Carton and John Stow set or equalled personal bests but Martin Bloice and Bill Curtin were below their bests, particularly Bill who was last in his heat and seemed very jaded. Mick Marshall produced a very useful long jump but found that another 5" was necessary to make the first six in the Youth event. JUNIORS 200m (Final): 2. S White 21.8 3,000mW (Final): 6. P. items.s: EDITORIAL Christmas editorial greeting members worldwide, appealing for material for an official club history, and introducing the magazine's first advertisement (W. & G. Hales). A MERRY CHRISTMAS and a PROSPEROUS NEW YEAR to all Belgravians, wherever you may be. A special greeting goes out to those members in distant parts, whether they be in far off Australia, India and U.S.A. or in the nearby British provinces. We are pleased to enjoy your continued support and the good work you do as ambassadors of Belgrave. Special greetings also to those regular contributors who have assisted your Honorary Editor over the past year; and to our principal photographer, Ron Linstead,whose work plays such an important part in the Gazette's production. As we leave another decade behind us this is an appropriate moment to remind our readers that the Club is still gathering together all material relevant to the history of Belgrave Harriers. If you have any photos, cuttings or other literature even remotely concerning Belgrave then we would appreciate the loan of such material. Eventually , an official Belgrave History will be produced---your contribution, however small, might well play a part. How about giving that old loft a 1970 springclean?. On another page can be found our first advertisement. Each copy of the Belgravian you receive costs the Club about 1/9d, and costs rise annually. Advertisers help to keep those costs down so its in our interests to support our advertisers when we can. W. & G. HALES are not unknown to some of our members, but there are many who are unaware of the wide range of athletic gear available at this shop, one of whose suppliers is our own Gerry North. Open on Saturday afternoons, it is conveniently placed for buying shoes etc. on your way to or from Belgrave Hall. And don't forget to mention Belgrave when you make a purchase. With a circulation approaching 600 and a readership probably nearer the thousand mark there must be many readers in a position to sell advertising space. Please contact the Editor if you have a recommendation to make. And if anyone is interested in becoming Advertising Manager. let him please step forward---quickly!. Ron Linstead Ron Linstead Gerry North Gerry North Australia India U.S.A. Belgrave Hall W. & G. HALES

items.label: December 1969
items.sum: The Hon. Secretary's notes on old member Edmund Donovan, loyal supporter Mick Pyer, changes to the 1970 fixtures, the coming centenary of the Wimbledon and Putney Commons Act, honours for Harry Shields and Doug Fotheringham, and visits from Tommy Green and Fred Stone.
items.s: HON. SECRETARY'S NOTES The Hon. Secretary's notes on old member Edmund Donovan, loyal supporter Mick Pyer, changes to the 1970 fixtures, the coming centenary of the Wimbledon and Putney Commons Act, honours for Harry Shields and Doug Fotheringham, and visits from Tommy Green and Fred Stone. A letter of good wishes and a cheque for $ 25 has been received from Edmund P. Donovan, O.B.E., now of New York; and a member of the Club way back in 1911. He recalls with pleasure his visit to our Club Track Championships a couple of years ago, and hopes probably to renew acquaintance at our Boxing Day Meeting as he aims to be in England at that time. If there was an award for our most loyal supporter it would go assuredly to MICK PYER, who must now be within months of fifty years of membership. Wherever our teams go MICK is to be found and we trust it will long be so. The Committee have invited him to serve as a co-opted member so that we may benefit from his experience and enthusiasm. It will be remembered by the few that it was one of Mick's proposals many years ago on our Committee that led to the inauguration of Youth's Track and Field Championships in the South. Following the International Fixture Conference held at Bucharest recently there have been changes in the Summer fixtures. The A.A.A. Championships will be held on August 7th and 8th instead of July 10th and 11th as previously announced and as shown in our current Handbook. This change will accommodate the East German team who will visit this country on the dates previously announced for the AAA Championships, which will now be held after the Edinburgh Commonwealth Games on July 16th-25th. There may yet be other changes in the domestic programme, but no doubt these will be settled within the next few weeks. August 16th 1971 will be the centenary of the Wimbledon and Putney Commons Act which dedicated the Commons to the use of the public. Much of this land was previously in the ownership of Earl Spencer, by whose permission Thames Hare and Hounds held the first cross country races ever, celebrating their centenary last year, it will be recalled. We have made good use of the Commons since before the first World War; and have been grateful indeed to have had country and road courses with so much natural beauty and so very convenient of access,on hand for pleasure and our sport. Undoubtedly, as a Club we have benefited considerably in having the Commons at our disposal, with no pen of the speculative builder driving us outward. So many cross country clubs have fought losing battles with the so-called "developers"---especially is this true in Middlesex---that we must count ourselves very fortunate indeed to have conducted our sport for well over fifty years under relatively stable conditions. The Ranger, Mr. F.G.P. QUIXLEY, has invited representatives of the various clubs and societies with interests in the Commons to meet soon and possibly arrange to play some part in the making of the centenary in 1971. We congratulate most heartily Past President Harry Shields on being honoured with Life Membership of the English Cross Country Union. Fortunately Harry's health is now much improved and he is to be seen at many of our fixtures once again. We also congratulate DOUG FOTHERINGHAM on being elected Chairman of the Race Walking Association, Southern Area Committee. How very pleased to see TOMMY GREEN with his wife at Wimbledon recently, when he started our 50th Annual Open Walk. Tommy has his own particular niche in Belgrave history with his Olympic Games win, his London to Brighton and Manchester to Blackpool Walk wins, and dozens of other victories from two miles up to 100 Kilometres. Tommy looks remarkably well and capable of repeating some of his wins of years ago! His age? Well he was 39 when he won his Olympic title at Los Angeles in 1932, so work it out for yourself!. Seen in Town recently, Vice President Fred M. STONE. He was in London to lecture on Youth Movements, which seems just the thing for a 72 year old who has tackled almost everything in the world of sport. He will be remembered as one of the bravest Metropolitan Policemen ever, and the recipient of many awards for gallantry and devotion td duty, the last one from the hands of Her Majesty The Queen. He was featured in the television series "This is your life" some years ago, in which the late Harry Evans also appeared. Fred sends his best wishes to all. Also seen. items.sum: New President Gordon Doubleday thanks members for electing him, recalls joining in 1934 and praises the club's boys and youths.
items.s: THE PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE New President Gordon Doubleday thanks members for electing him, recalls joining in 1934 and praises the club's boys and youths. Dear Belgravians, I would like to thank all of the members who elected me President at the A.G.M. I regret that I was not at the meeting as I was in hospital at the time. I am stepping into the shoes of our Past Presidents, who have over the years given stirling service to the Club; I hope to be worthy of their example. I have had to miss some of our early fixtures and I am grateful to Past Presidents who have kindly stood in for me. When I joined the Club in 1934 I was attracted by the good sport, the good sportsmanship and the good friendship which the Belgrave Harriers offered. These qualities are as strong as ever and, over the years, I have enjoyed them with countless others. I am now no longer active in the athletic sense and have transferred my interest to the official side, and it has been brought home to me how much our sport owes to its officials. Fortunately in Belgrave we have many who are willing to help in this direction and I am proud that I have recently joined their number as an Hon. Timekeeper. Belgrave have always been renowned for their team performances and over the whole range of athletics we can claim to be second to none.Readers of the "Belgravian" are well aware of our present strength, but to me one of the brightest signs is the prowess and enthusiasm of our Boys and Youths and I hope that they will mature to be the team-men, the champions, and indeed the Internationals of tomorrow. I wish the Club and all its members a very happy and successful year. Gordon S. Doubleday. Gordon S. Doubleday Gordon S. Doubleday Belgrave Harriers Annual General Meeting 1969

items.label: December 1969
items.sum: Profile of new President Gordon S. Doubleday, from his 1934 novice race win through his walking, editorship, treasurership and officiating, with two photographs.
items.s: Our President Profile of new President Gordon S. Doubleday, from his 1934 novice race win through his walking, editorship, treasurership and officiating, with two photographs. In September 1934, Gordon S. Doubleday ran in a Novice race from our Wimbledon Headquarters. He duly won and was elected to membership the following month. So began 35 years of loyalty and conscientious hard work for the Club which have culminated in his election and installation as President. He is in every way worthy of this honour and we are sure that the Club will enjoy continuing success under his leadership. Following his novice success "Doub" turned out regularly in our cross country events without any conspicuous success; but thoroughly enjoying his running and the companionship it brought him---and this is of course, the prime reason for our existence. In 1935 he climbed to higher positions in our races, and began to contribute regularly to the pages of "The Belgravian". He also joined our Sunday strolling parties and made his contribution to the flights of worldly and athletic wisdom that enlivened our weekly jaunts. Even at a distance of over thirty years there is recollection of frost-laden clear air, brilliant star-lit evenings and a good road under our feet---and Gordon's rendering of "David in the Lion's Den" and Ravel's Bolero"!. Gordon Doubleday (left) and Alf Harley (right) try their hand at putting snow balls during one of their climbing holidays in the "Thirties". Alf Taylor is in the centre. The action photo shows our President after the war racing at Tooting Bec track, Christmas 1948. In 1937 our President was persuaded to essay his first walk to Brighton and this he accomplished successfully, and repeated on later occasions. Now he applied himself to Walking at the shorter distance and accomplished an excellent Croydon to Godstone and back in his first season. In the Junior 10 miles Championship at Hampstead in 1938 when, let us remember, we had a record winning score with Len and Joe Coleman dead-heating for first place, Colin Sutton 6th and Reg Elson 7th, Doub finished 24th of the 127 finishers. In September 1938 he accomplished an outstanding "double" in getting married and becoming Hon. Editor of the Belgravian!. His walking continued to improve and in the Surrey County 10 miles Championship he finished ninth--but was the sixth Belgrave man!. However, reward came in the 10 miles Championship at Manchester when he was in our winning team---and on later occasions he scored in our winning Surrey County teams. The coming of War translated Doub to Exeter, where he became a Vice-Captain of Exeter Harriers, and he did his best to keep in touch during those trying years. Eventually, in happier days, the call of Belgravian duty persuaded Doub to be our Hon. Treasurer which he carried through for two years; and on his retirement from office he was made a Life Member--a proposition the writer was able to make on behalf of the committee at the AGM with great personal satisfaction and pleasure. Doub's work for our sport did not end here. He has walked his hundred miles inside 24 hours to become a Centurion, and is now Hon. Treasurer of that exclusive body. He is also President of the Road Runners Club, and well on his way to becoming a first class timekeeper. Gordon Doubleday has won a Club Honours Badge for Marathon running; has strengthened our Walking teams; enlivened our strolling and our holidays; worked hard in two important offices (and now a third) within the Club; contributed time and time again to the Belgravian; served us conscientiously as a timekeeper; and made his services and abilities to other sporting associations. All this, plus his pleasing personality, his ability to enthuse, and his great loyalty to Belgrave make us fortunate indeed in our selection of President. May he enjoy good health to enjoy his year of office, and to give us the full benefit of his talents and enthusiasms!. A.A.H. items.sum: Report of the annual dinner and dance at the Wimbledon Hill Hotel on 15 November 1969, with Sydney Wooderson as guest of honour.
items.s: Dinner & Dance Report of the annual dinner and dance at the Wimbledon Hill Hotel on 15 November 1969, with Sydney Wooderson as guest of honour. The annual dinner and dance held at the Wimbledon Hill Hotel on the 15th November followed the successful pattern of recent years. Certainly the large attendance consisting of members of all ages accompanied by their nearest and dearest bore witness to the slogan "Nothing breeds success like success". It was fitting that Sydney Wooderson, as President of Blackheath Harriers in this their Centenary Year, should be our guest of honour. In reply to his short but well received address Reg Hopkins displayed none of the nervousness generally encountered in maiden speeches, and achieved a fine blend of wit and invective. The overall brevity of speeches appeared to the connoisseurs to have resulted from an attempt to "keep 'em clean". Certainly there was a distinct lack of blue jokes and not even a single reference to Gerry North's support. Tributes were paid to both the retiring President and to the new incumbent. The dancing that followed was enthusiastically enjoyed by all concerned and for those whose education in this art stopped at the twist the band's repertoire was sufficient. As a result of Ted Stimpson's persuasive pen numerous local firms and well wishers had contributed a vast array of prizes for the raffle. No wonder the dark mutterings from certain tables as prize after prize fell to Charlie Manning. All in all a most successful 'do' appreciated by athletes, officials and guests. One final suggestion, couldn't next year's menu be NORFOLK TURKEY AU VIN PECHE BONNE SURPRISE Only the names need be changed to protect the innocent............. 'CORDON BLEU'. items.s: THE A.G.M. Carl Lawton's report of the 1969 Annual General Meeting at Belgrave Hall: the Hon. Secretary's review, the Treasurer's report, life memberships for Ray Hall and Clive Shippen, and the election of officers (continued on page 12; a line appears to be missing before 'entertaining.'). CARL LAWTON WRITES With the attendance figure at around the 60 mark the A.G.M. of the Belgrave Harriers was convened at Belgrave Hall on the evening of Thursday, 18th September at 6-45pm. The retiring President Mr. Simmons was in the chair. Apologies were received from various members of the club for non attendance, including those of the President elect, Mr. Doubleday who was suffering from a touch of the other in hospital, and Mr. Middleton who although performing magnificently in Athens at the time of the meeting regretted that he could not make it as he had walked enough *!?*! kilos for one day. Mr. Harley proceeded to give a run down on the previos year's events in and around the club. He mentioned with regret the loss to the club of two outstanding and devoted men Mr. Rollins and Mr. Harley Senior. Their devotion to the club was exceptional and they would be missed. Mr. Harley made it known that he had been a member since 1926 and had watched its growth since that time. "The success over the years", he said "had been due to the supreme effort of the athletes and officials,and the past year had been no exception". The club was estimated to enter more individual events than any other club in the country but this gave no excuse for the disappointment of the club being relegated instead of promoted in the National League. The reason for this was the failure of a few, and only a few, to turn out when requested. the many successes of the club during the year would not be described as an excellent coverage had been provided in the Belgravian. The General Hon. Sec. closed with a word of praise for our internationals during the year, Middleton, Thresher, Bicourt, Geoff North, Boosey and Lerwill as well as the promising juniors without whom the club would have no future. He then requested a vote of thanks to the retiring President, the retiring Hon. Treasurer, and the retiring Cross Country Secretary. They step down in the knowledge that the club is where it is due to their work over the years. The Hon. Treasurer, Mr. Shepherd, in his report on the world monetary situation gave a detailed account of the income and expenditure, ably assisted by Balance sheets carefully distributed around the hall. After much deliberation we were informed that the club had made a loss of £3 in the last financial year. "This was a bit near the mark" he said. It was pointed out that much of the income was spent in sending teams to national championships and this cost was increasing annually. However it was concluded that so long as nobody removed the hall we were still in good financial standing!. The meeting moved on to the election to life membership of Mr. R. Hall and Mr. C. Shippen. A brief review of Mr. Hall's stirling support of athletics both as participant and official was given by Mr. Harley and Mr. Maclennon. Perhaps his main achievement being one of a few who have beaten 8 hours for the Brighton. Mr. Wesch, showing his knowledge of English, wished it to be known that it was one of 6. Mr. Shippen was proposed by Mr. Lucas who described the efforts of the Hon. Editor of the Belgravian. He had worked hard for our benefit and his own athletics always took second place in the club. Mr. Manning seconded Mr. Shippen, but stated he was not going to say anything. Five minutes later he sat down. (Cont'd on page 12) A.G.M.----Cont'd from page 7 The election of Officers was begun with the position of the president being filled by Mr. G. Doubleday. A letter was read from him regretting his non appearance but he hoped to be back in circulation very shortly. Mr. Harley was re-elected as General Secretary but stressed his desire to find a successor by next elections. Senior posts in the club were filled by Mr. Baker as treasurer and Mr. Biscoe as Cross Country Secretary, election of the commitee then followed. Mr. Pollock moved that he had not read rule 6 of the club and also that he preferred to have the annual dinner on an alternative day to a Saturday. Due to a misunderstanding of his queries, owing to the convening of certain unofficial sub-committees and Mr. Duncan who wished to see his Doctor, the replies given were not relevant to the question. The percolating Mr. Pollock threatened under his press card to depart and write an article on the misfortune of being a misunderstood reporter. The mention of the annual dinner brought a response from the floor as to the length of speeches and made the initiator of the subject wish he had not brought it up. The election of certain officers brought to notice that several members not wishing re-election had not informed the General Secretary and furthermore were not there to do so. As a result of the changing of the name of the Junior Section Captain to Junior Team Manager a motion from the floor suggested that the Social Secretary's title should be changed to Social Discotequery, or words to that effect. The stunned listeners were then informed it was only a joke.which brought a weak round of laughter from one or two but this was probably due to their not having heard the original remark anyway. entertaining. Those who had not enjoyed themselves sorrowfully filed into the "Duke and the "Swan"--The bars were soon filled!. Carl Lawton CARL LAWTON Mr. Simmons Mr. Simmons G. items.label: December 1969
items.h: TRACK AND FIELD — PETER HILLIAR (Track Captain) WRITES
items.sum: Track captain Peter Hilliar reviews a disappointing 1969 track season that ended in relegation from the National League, event by event.
items.s: TRACK AND FIELD — PETER HILLIAR (Track Captain) WRITES Track captain Peter Hilliar reviews a disappointing 1969 track season that ended in relegation from the National League, event by event. The 1969 track season was extremely disappointing and was climaxed by our relegation from a weak division of the National League to the first division of the Southern League. We only managed to annexe one trophy, The Jim Peters Trophy, which we only won with the considerable assistance of a strong contingent of juniors and youths. What went wrong then, following our earlier anticipation of an outstanding season? It is difficult to put one's finger accurately on the pulse of the trouble, but I am tempted to hazard a guess that the modern athlete is so well provided with competition at all levels by his club, his area and national organisers, universities and various other bodies such as the BMC, that he can no longer raise any particular enthusiasm for competitions such as the National League. This naturally affects athletes belonging to other clubs, so it could be a case of loyalties and / or priorities, which I feel are not taken seriously by some members of our club. To get down off the metaphorical high horse, I now propose to summarise events. 100/200 metres. Probably our strongest events on paper with Steve White, Jim Vivian, John Mitchell and Chris Martin and able assistance from Aris Sapountzoglou, Tony and Cliff Brooks. However, through injury and other commitments, we have usually been weak in top-class competition. 400 metres. The most exciting occasion was the emergence of Mel Ford with 49.3 in the Brockman. Otherwise, we had sound and loyal contributions from Tony Brooks, Philip Gee, Philip Smith and Dave Rees (a startling improvement to sub-55 by Dave). 800 metres. I think we could at last have some strength in depth in the future in what has been our "Cinderella" event since the retirement of Dave Cocks; through such competitors as Mel Ford (around 1-56 relay), John Boardman, John Kelly and Doug Jardine. Nevertheless, 1969 wasn't their year, unfortunately. 1500 metres. Our best performers in this event were all basically under-distance in John Thresher, Geoff North, Adrian Major and Bill Kerr, well though they performed. 5000/10,000 metres. Geoff North's brilliant Southern run was the obvious highlight, but at National League and Trphy level, we were generally under-represented. It was encouraging, however, to welcome Gerry North and Bob Smith back to fitness by the end of the season. 3000metre Steeplechase. John Bicourt continued his steady improvement and it was encouraging to see Peter Morris and Dick Piotrowski (despite a nasty mid-season injury) not far behind. Also, the season witnessed the resurgence of Alan Black. To wind up, I should like to praise the enthusiasm of such members as Tony Brooks, Philip Gee, Dave Rees and Philip Smith, always willing to have a go at anything. Without them the season might have been disastrous. Finally, I feel a tribute should be paid to an immensely hard-working track secretary, Bob Taylor; a pillar of a great club. items.label: December 1969
items.sum: Bill Couzens on field events and the athletes lost to postings and injury that cost Belgrave its National League place in 1969.
items.s: BILL COUZENS writes on FIELD Bill Couzens on field events and the athletes lost to postings and injury that cost Belgrave its National League place in 1969. I am sure that everybody knows Belgrave are relegated from the National League. This time last year we were considering which club would be promoted with us into the second division of the National League, but when it came to it we fizzed out like a damp firework. Was it all bad luck? We were without the following athletes, in most cases in all three National League meetings, for reasons beyond their control. Glyn Ratcliffe (Shot, Discus) posted to Ireland with the Grenadier Guards. Mel Ford (400m Hurdles, 4X400m Relay) also posted to Ireland. Steve Inman (Pole Vault) also posted to Ireland. Charlie Gillett (400m Hurdles, 4 X 440 Relay) Injured. John Mitchell (Long Jump, Sprints) Injured. Nick Head (Javelin, Shot) In Germany during 2 meetings. With these men in the team we would certainly have avoided relegation, but what of our cert promotion prospects into the Second division? These could not be achieved without our top runners turning out at each League Meeting, so where were our sprinters? After all, this is where we should be strongest. Luckily we have a nucleus of men in Belgrave who will do two, three or even four events; their names can be seen quite easily in the results. I, like others, left the last National League Meeting with a great lump in my throat. I hope next year we will be celebrating our return. items.s: SAD NEWS! Note that javelin thrower and Field Events Captain Brian King is leaving for Huntingdon, with a photograph of a javelin throw. We will be losing our javelin thrower Brian King in the near future as he will be moving to Huntingdon. This will be a great loss to the Club as Brian is one of our most stalwart members, he will always turn out to represent the Club and has not missed more than two meetings in five years, he has been Field Events Captain and has served on Committee. I know Brian will be continuing his athletics and wish him every success. Brian King Brian King Huntingdon

items.label: December 1969
items.sum: Coaching secretary Dave Ansell profiles sprinter and long jumper John Mitchell's 1969 season and lists the S.C.A.A.A. winter lecture series at Crystal Palace.
items.s: The COACHING HON. SEC. speaks Coaching secretary Dave Ansell profiles sprinter and long jumper John Mitchell's 1969 season and lists the S.C.A.A.A. winter lecture series at Crystal Palace. Dave Ansell writes:- Few men could have been so near to gaining a full international vest as the athlete who heads our 100 metres and long jump rankings for 1968---JOHN MITCHELL. He must have been a marginal omission from the Great Britain team in the Finland and France matches. John takes his final exams in medicine next year, but between now and then fall the Commonwealth Games in Edinburgh. He has both English and Scottish qualifications so must stand a good chance of appearing at the Games, should studies permit. Our leading long jumper started his season in PARIS on May 10th, competing for London University, and recorded 10.8 (second) and 23'-7" (first). Four days later he chalked up 10.7/21.9/23'-2"; the 200m time being a personal best. John was running into form nicely and in June won the B.U.S.F. long jump title, beating K. Snelgrove, with 23'-11". However, Snelgrove got his revenge in the Southern, 23'-7¾"/23'-6½" squeezing John into 4th place. The height of John Mitchell's season was the A.A.A. Championships on August 2nd at the White City. Watching that claret and gold figure flashing down the Tartan strip it was obvious that only Lynn Davies was running faster. He qualified for the final : Hudson, among other good performers, failing. In a tremendous tussle for third place with Williams and Scott he was beaten by a mere ½" (24'-1", 24'-1", 24'-½") yet he had the best second jump and two hair-line fouls at 24'-5". By such margins are vests won and lost. However, John has tremendous determination and this should see him through to that International vest and help him to overcome the injuries which restricted his gallant efforts to help our National League team. His new Club record (24'-5¾") was set at Portsmouth on August 20th when jumping for the B.U.S.F. against Combined Services and S.C.A.A.A. It placed him second, only 6¼" behind Olympian Alan Lerwill. But for wind assistance, the jump would place him 4th in the U.K. rankings---and all but John of the top eight are Internationals!. John Mitchell has suggested retirement, but surely he is just about to reap the fruits of all his hard work. If he can maintain fitness through his studies then he has a great chance of competing in Edinburgh, and even Munich. The S.C.A.A.A. have arranged a series of lectures at Crystal Palace, in room G55, at 7.00p.m. to 9.00.p.m. as follows:- Dec 2nd Triple Jumping T. McNab. 9th The treatment of Athletic Injuries. Dr. P. Sperryn. 16th Sprinting. J. Le Masurier. Jan 6th The Mechanics of Athletic Performance. B. Hopper. 13th Hurdling. J. Le Masurier. 20th Long Jumping and High Jumping. D. Ansell & K.Hipwell 27th Shot Putting and Discus Throwing. To be announced. Feb 3rd Steeplechase and Pole Vaulting. W. Coyne & M. Evans. 10th Modern Strength Training. T. McNab. 17th Javelin and Hammer. C.Smith & R.Bowden. 24th International Forum J. Le Masurier. The cost is 5/- per lecture and all details are available from Dave Ansell, Coaching Sec., who points out that although these lectures will prove of help to all active athletes they will be of particular advantage to Coaches and Potential Coaches, and strongly advises those members who would like to improve their knowledge with a view to taking the HON. COACHES and SENIOR HON. COACHES EXAMS, to attend. If there are still any club members who require advice and/or coaching then contact the Hon. Coaching Sec. who will be pleased to put you in touch with a Specialist Coach for your event. Dave Ansell Dave Ansell Dave Ansell D. items.label: December 1969
items.sum: Review of Belgrave's autumn 1969 road relay season (Surrey, Johnston, Walton, Dudley-Bridgnorth and the first National six-stage relay), with Ron Linstead's photo of Geoff North handing over to Gerry North.
items.s: ROAD RELAY ROUND-UP Review of Belgrave's autumn 1969 road relay season (Surrey, Johnston, Walton, Dudley-Bridgnorth and the first National six-stage relay), with Ron Linstead's photo of Geoff North handing over to Gerry North. Last year's Autumn road relay season was disappointing for Belgrave, but the 1969 season was most encouraging. There was more spirit this year, and whilst we only chalked up one win we did at least gain medals in the four premier events. The season went as follows:- Once again, our worst turn-out of the year was at the Surrey race. With barring clauses, holidays, injuries and general apathy taking their toll it was a dismal occasion with Belgrave never in the hunt. Each year, with the Surrey relay behind them our runners become transformed as though they've got something nasty out of their system and this was how it went with the Johnston relay. Coventry and Manchester were missing this year but the holders (Hercules-Wimbledon) who thrashed us last year were done down by our lads in a close fought struggle. This was our first victory in this relay. The following week at Walton we faced our local rivals again, with Portsmouth thrown in for good measure. Lionel Mann was an impressive winner of the first stage, but by the third leg Dave Holt had taken Hercules-Wimbledon into their winning lead: they are a difficult club to beat over six stages. Our old enemies Portsmouth were never in the hunt really and finished 1¼ minutes behind in third place. Our strength in this well supported relay was indicated by our 'B' team which finished 6th. (Photo:Ron Linstead) GEOFF NORTH hands over to brother GERRY for the last stage of the Walton Relay. Such strength in depth augured well for Tipton's Dudley to Bridgenorth and back relay of ten stages, where we finished second to Derby. Our optimism was justified for, as in the Johnston , we beat the holders; but instead of taking the winning awards we were destined to be second again through the emergence of a strengthened North Staffs and Stone team now called City of Stoke AC. We were to hear more from them the following week and they are certain to provide very serious opposition in the coming months. Our second place should not detract from the fine running of our lads who finished inside the previous record and 3:48 faster than last year. In addition, new stage records were set by Bill Kerr, Gerry North and Peter Morris. The short season was rounded off with what should have been it's major event---the inaugural 6-stage National Relay at the Crystal Palace. Not only was it the poorest supported event of all but it also produced the least enthusiasm. Six 2½ miles stages was far too brief for us to hold out much hope of winning and not only did the Stoke outfit score another win but Blackheath pipped us for second. Although we were not exactly elated at our relay record this Autumn, many clubs would have been delighted to scoop one gold, two silvers and a bronze from five outings. items.sum: Stage-by-stage report and results of the Johnston(e) Road Relay on 28 September 1969, Belgrave's first win in the event in a course record, with David Hart's team photograph (the name is printed both Johnston and Johnstone); a stray word 'Olympian' is printed in display type beside the result.
items.s: BELGRAVE WIN 'Johnstone' Stage-by-stage report and results of the Johnston(e) Road Relay on 28 September 1969, Belgrave's first win in the event in a course record, with David Hart's team photograph (the name is printed both Johnston and Johnstone); a stray word 'Olympian' is printed in display type beside the result. Sunday September 28th Owing to a proposed Southern Counties six man relay, which did not materialise, the entry for the Johnston was somewhat depleted with only nineteen teams starting. Coventry and Tipton have in the past contested this relay but were amongst the absentees. Nevertheless it was to be a hard fought battle between ourselves and our local rivals Hercules/Wimbledon who had won in 1968 in record time. Pat O'Connor took the first stage and did well to bring us in third only eight seconds behind the leaders (Woodford Green and Ealing - Southall). Hercules/Wimbledon were at this stage back in 9th place. Lionel Mann held 3rd place on Stage two by displacing Woodford but had to give way to an evergreen Ken Harland who took Cambridge H. from 5th to 2nd. Bivens of Ealing was the leader and Mike Fuller brought Hercules up to 4th. John Thresher on Stage three took us up to 2nd and gained a few seconds on Ealing who were still out in front. John Sullivan of Hercules brought his club into 3rd place with a time one second faster than John. Stage 4 saw us in the lead for the first time with a very good run by Trevor Hart who turned a 21 second deficit into a six second advantage. Gerry North on the first of the long stages was well chased by Mike Barratt of Ealing but kept us in first place with a lead of 14 secs. Dave Holt gained a little ground for Hercules who were still third. Stage 6 saw Hercules make a strong bid for the lead with a record breaking run by Mike Beevor who started 58 secs behind Bill Dance and brought his team up to a mere 9 secs behind us. We must again thank Bill for his ardent devotion to the Club by making the long journey from Huddersfield for this race. Dick Piotrowski on Stage 7 was not in the least deterred by the closeness of Hercules and proceeded to open up a gap of 63 secs which later in the race proved invaluable. Bas. Collins on Stage 8 gained two seconds on Laurie O'Hara, these two being by far the fastest runners on this stage. Ealing were now having trouble keeping in touch and were over two minutes adrift. Although we all know the potential of Bob Holt on the road we also knew Geoff North to be running well as witnessed by his comfortable win in our own road race only one week earlier We were not therefore prepared for Bob to catch up the 61secs deficit and turn this into a lead of 11 secs. It was not that Geoff ran badly, for he was credited with the second fastest time of the day, but that Holt was in his most devastating form. Peter Morris was not in the least concerned about giving a start to Mullholland of Hercules and it was not long before he was running at the opposition's shoulder. Entreaties from our supporters to pull away were accepted and Pete came into the Stadium with fifteen seconds to spare. Asking afterwards why everyone was panicking he was told that we did not wish to see him beaten in a desperate finish with Mullholland. His effort gained for him a stage record. items.s: Another Second Report and results of the Dudley to Bridgnorth and back road relay on 18 October 1969, where Belgrave were second to the newly formed City of Stoke AC. Dudley to Bridgenorth and back Road Relay October 18th With a team only slightly changed from that which won the Johnstone Relay some three weeks before we made our second trip to this Midland race (the only southern club to do so) hoping that with the experience gained last year of the various stages we would be able to turn last year's second place into a first. However, although beating last year's winner (Derby County) we reckoned without the 'unknown quantity' City of Stoke A.C. who went into the lead in the first stage and, with the exception of one stage, held it to the finish. City of Stoke are a recent amalgamation of three clubs in the Midlands and with some of the talent they now possess re definitely a force to be reckoned with in the future, particularly in relays of 6 to 10 legs As the results show our effort was a steady progression through the field with Gerry putting us in the medals with a fine run over a tough sixth stage. Some great running by Trevor Hart and Peter Morris took us to within a few seconds of the leaders at the end of stage 8 but some of the opposition was just too strong for Lionel Mann and he finally handed over to Bill Dance with a 45 sec dificit. Bill fought hard all the way but could hardly be expected to take that off Roy Fowler (C. of Stoke) on a tough up hill last leg. Thanks were due to Bill Lucas who was one who bothered to make the journey to cheer the lads on and help deliver some to their various stages; and to Doug Brew who willingly undertook the glamour-less, but important role,of travelling first reserve. Rumour has it that the whole team was almost put in jeopardy when, in the early hours of the morning before leaving London, Pat O'Connor and Bill Kerr went searching for Lionel Mann inside the grounds of Buckingham Palace---sounds like another of these "An Englishman, an Irishman and a Scotsman tales"!!. items.label: December 1969
items.sum: Report and results of the inaugural AAA National Six Stage Road Relay at Crystal Palace on 25 October 1969, where Belgrave were third behind City of Stoke and Manchester & District L.C.
items.s: NATIONAL SIX STAGE RELAY Report and results of the inaugural AAA National Six Stage Road Relay at Crystal Palace on 25 October 1969, where Belgrave were third behind City of Stoke and Manchester & District L.C. CRYSTAL PALACE---October 25th A'Damp Squib'---such is one headline already given to this race born in a rather wet Crystal Palace Sports Centre. Certainly it will go down as one of the non events of the year, with the title 'National' being a complete misnomer. Prior to the above date much controversy had centred around the introduction of this race, having been campaigned for by some of the smaller clubs for quite some time, but considered by others as completely unwarranted, in view of the existing 12 stage relay held at Leicester. However, with little or no consultation with clubs the date was fixed, in an already over-loaded calendar, only to clash with several important cross country fixtures including our own N.S. League event. The actual course of 6X2 laps (ie 2½m per leg) of the Crystal Palace motor racing circuit was also rather unimaginative. In view of all these factors several clubs decided to boycott the event as a form of protest. Although many of our members had varying views on the subject, it was considered we should support the venture rather than condemn it 'out of hand', although we would probably not have our strongest of teams out on the day. Of the 19 clubs entered only 9 finally came under starters orders and from the start it was obvious that the main challenge was coming from City of Stoke AC, (our victors of the previous week in the Dudley to Bridgenorth Relay), and Manchester and District L.C, with Blackheath H. and Ealing and Southall AC providing further danger. Stage 1.- An early lead, which they were never to lose, for City of Stoke (S.Hope 12:52) with Ealing and Southall second (P.Fagin 13:01) and our own Dick Piotrowski (13:03) doing our second fastest time of the day for third place. Stage 2.- In spite of Bill Kerr promising to close the gap it was not to be one of his good runs and although we retained our third position Stoke had increased their lead from 9 to 22s with MDLC second and Blackheath close on our heels some 3secs behind. Stage 3.- With Gerry North taking over for Bels and Bob Richardson for Blackheath a battle royal seemed inevitable. After one lap of the stage Bob had closed the three second deficit and was seen to be opening a gap of his own. Gerry,however, is not easily beaten, and as they swept into view again for the last 400 yards he proceeded to close the gap again; but with Gerry getting the worse of a large puddle in the final straight it was Richardson who just got home first by a whisker. It was now Stoke(1) Blackheath (2) and Belgrave (3) with Ealing and Manchester having been relegated to 4th and 5th respectively. Stage 4.- On this leg Laurie O'Hara, like Bill Kerr, did not get into top gear but none the less produced one of his characteristically steady runs to maintain 3rd position. Stage 5.- Exitement rose here when Tony Fairclough, although only doing our 5th fastest time, took us through to 2nd place. With Stoke now some 49 secs in the lead it was obvious, barring accidents, we would have to forget gold medals but the silver seemed in our grasp for the first time, although M and D were in third place just 17 secs behind us. Stage 6.- Our hopes were not to be realised. John Thresher, we knew, was not at his best and with an in-form Ravald (12:42) anchoring Manchester John was passed with half a lap to go and in spite of a great fight was forced to bring us home in our final 3rd place. A fit John would have seen a different result; so for that matter would a second or so off everyone else's time!. RESULT---At foot of page opposite G.I.B. items.s: THAT OLD ONE-TWO AGAIN Report and full result of the club 5¾ mile road race (handicap) at Wimbledon on 20 September 1969, won by Geoff North from his brother Gerry, with youth John Stowe winning on handicap, and Ron Linstead's photo (on page 18). 5¾ mile road race---Wimbledon, September 20th With Geoff and Gerry North on the start line one can always expect fireworks. No one has ever got within 20 seconds of their best times so the fireworks are usually confined to the family when they appear together. And so it was on this occasion, though Geoff ran out a clearer winner than Gerry would have liked. Geoff set a brisk pace right from the start and looked as though he was after his record of 27:14. On the first circuit of the common a pack of nine detached itself from the remaining thirty five runners; the Norths, Morris, O'Connor, Mann, Thresher, Hart, Kerr and Piotrowski steadily moving clear of the ruck. On leaving the Common,Geoff was five seconds clear with Dick Piotrowski showing up well, just ahead of the following bunch. At the bottom of Copse Hill the leader had stretched the gap to 15 seconds ahead of brother Gerry and Dick who were in turn 15 seconds clear of the next six. The rest of the field were now a further 50 seconds in arrears. As usual the Cambridge Road drag and the "Kiss of Death" climb sorted every one out. Kerr was the first to tail off, then Hart, then Thresher. Dick did well to hold Gerry to the top of the hills but he faded badly. At the oak tree, with a lap of the Common to go, Geoff's lead remained the same but a strong finish increased his margin by 27 seconds. Meanwhile, Mann, O'Connor and Morris were chasing hard and simply scorched round "the top" leaving the rest of their companions trailing. Lionel fired his booster rocket on the run in and nearly caught a surprised Gerry North; it's a pity the seven seconds gap wasn't six for then Lionel would have become only the ninth man to have broken the magical 28 minutes. The shape of things to come was shown by Bill Curtin and John Stowe (both Youths) placing 11th and 12th---John scooping the handicap to boot!. Ray Beaumont was a deserved second and that popular "vet" Joe McDonald third. Joe was delighted at being amongst the prizes and also at beating his training companion, the evergreen Charlie Smart; though he would probably agree that their handicap allowances should have been reversed on pre-race form. items.s: YACHT '3' Report and full result of the club's 3 miles Yacht handicap on 11 October 1969, won by Dave McMillan, with Tony Fairclough and Adrian Major fastest. October 11th Regularly at this time of the year we have that old Belgrave custom of 'Beat the Handicapper'. This year many thought that Bill Lucas when giving up his job of Cross Country Secretary had also given up his job as handicapper and thus their old 'enemy' had gone. There were many surprised faces therefore when they learnt the horrible truth, that this was not so and that Bill was still at large, casting his beady eye over current form,completely immune to any smooth talk or enquiries over his good health. In spite of Bill's vigilance someone nearly always manages to pull a fast one and this year was no exception with Dave McMillan first in view at Wimbledon Village well clear of the large field. David Davies ran a well deserved 2nd place whilst another face to reappear after a long absence from the athletic scene was Bob James in 3rd spot---some shady training in the Coulsdon area indicated here; no doubt catching the habit from near neighbour Clive Shippen!!. With the field significantly lacking many of our 'star performers' it was Tony Fairclough and Adrian Major who had the lonely 'last-men-to-go'spot, but undaunted they set about chasing the field to record the fastest times of the day. It is also worth noting that the next three fastest times were recorded by juniors!. G.I.B. Pos Name Handicap Time 1. D. McMillan (6:00) 12:24 2. D. Davies (4:20) 13:11 3. R. James (3:00) 13:33 4. W. items.label: December 1969
items.sum: Postbag column of news and letters from Eric Hall (on Tommy Green), Barry Sawyer in Melbourne (with news of Percy Cerutty), 'Minnie Bannister', Peter Whewell in Johannesburg, John Baker, Mal Robinson in Iowa and George Piddington on Hayling Island (continued on page 23).
items.s: POSTBAG Postbag column of news and letters from Eric Hall (on Tommy Green), Barry Sawyer in Melbourne (with news of Percy Cerutty), 'Minnie Bannister', Peter Whewell in Johannesburg, John Baker, Mal Robinson in Iowa and George Piddington on Hayling Island (continued on page 23). ERIC HALL recently sent us a cutting from the Portsmouth Evening News which featured an article on our famous Olympian, Tommy Green. Eric writes, "It has often struck me as strange that most of what I know of Tommy Green is of the nature of legend; even how he came to be a Bel. has at least two stories to it, and the only concrete things available are the bare statistics of races won and records set up. Is it possible that a contemporary account of Tommy and his deeds is in the Editorial files and if so do you think it worth re-publishing? That photograph of him finishing the Brighton which used to hang in the Hall and is now upstairs I think speaks for itself and when I spoke to Tommy about it in 1956 he said that he and his helpers were convinced that he broke the 8 hours that day but he was never credited with it. To me he is a legend and I take encouragement from the fact that his walking was done at the age of 39 and over--me, I'm only 37 now so there is hope yet!. (Ed: A "Spotlight" on Tommy Green is in the course of preparation). Yet another immaculate letter has been received from BARRY SAWYER in distant Australia (South Yarra, Melbourne). Barry, who is the Victorian State marathon champion has fought his way to personal bests from 1500 metres to the marathon, despite worsening achilles tendon trouble. Only when he was no longer able to hobble to the start line did this obstinate character give in and begin serving a medical "sentence" of twelve weeks off running. Daily swimming was recommended as an alternative and it will be no surprise to those that knew Barry to hear that he had soon reached 50 lengths a night!. "It's amazing what one can do with a little obstinacy and determination" he says. It is fitting that he and that well-known Aussie iron-man Percy Cerutty should continue to see a lot of each other. Barry writes:"Percy is now living with his son Neil just around the corner. He recently returned from a month in Mount Isa in outback Queensland with a few lectures at Sydney University on the way back. He is quite fit but definitely not eating enough as both he and Neil lead a very bachelor life. "I'm sure the only decent meals Perce has are when we fill him up around here. At the moment he intends leaving for the States in April to promote a series of books he is writing. Bert Nelson of Track and Field News is very keen for him to go,as is Fred Wilt who leaves the F.B.I next year and plans to open an Athletic Clinic. I hope something eventuates as Percy is very unhappy here right now. Besides,there might be some opening for me too--it's about time I made another move!". After reading our version of the Radio Times on the centre pages of the September Gazette, "MINNIE BANNISTER" took time off from the Goon Show rehearsals to deliver her retort to the Woman Hour comment which said"All girls should learn how to do housework, some of them may never have a husband". Disguising herself as a bottle of ink she smuggled herself into the Editorial offices during the night, and as the Editor's quill approached the ink-well next morning, leapt on to the manuscript, complete with clenched fist and wet black socks, and screamed "SOME WOMEN WHO HAVE HUSBANDS NEVER SEE THEM!!!". PETER WHEWELL sends best wishes to the Club from Johannesburg and writes, "I have been receiving The Belgravian each quarter and it is good to see that most of the fellows I ran with are still competing. My congratulations go out to those who were in the team that were placed second in the National Relay. I would have liked to have been in that team---it was a really great effort". Peter continued to train seriously when he first returned to South Africa and finished fourth in his National Cross Country Championships, but since then he has been studying hard and doing little competitive running. He resumes serious training this month and says, "I am hoping to be over in England within the next couple of years for a short holiday, and to renew old acquaintances". It would be Belgrave's good fortune if they were renewed down the funnel of the National Championships!. Well, we always thought our members would have some difficulty in appreciating our centre page spreads. After all, who but a few could understand all those subtle satirical gems we produce each quarter? But we've been caught at our own game. JOHN BAKER sent us three cartoons that required the formation of an investigating committee to unravel the meaning. The frustrated committee are now begging for an explanation from John. Watch this column for further news!. Another colourful letter has arrived from former Co-Editor MAL ROBINSON. Mal now lives in Des Moines, Iowa, U.S.A. but finds it difficult to fit in a regular training schedule these days. Of Iowa he says "Here, track is a Cinderella-gone-sour. True we have the Drake Relays where are gathered many of the finest schools in the Nation, but this is a once a year happening. While it is on,everybody in town is a track and field fan, but as soon as the Sunday paper is out everybody is a baseball fan and we track people belong to a minority sport. Officials are non-existent. We put on our own meets, run in them,and then write about them ourselves. Thirty people to run, jump,skip,and dance in many events at the State Championships is a good turn-out. Dotted about the Nation are several fine meets of course, but who can afford to travel 1,000 miles for a race? So most of us slip into a weekly routine of running for fun, and try to steer promising kids on to the big meets". Mal is at present running a publishing-house division and is comfortably placed, but he still yearns for England at times and would like to know if any members have contacts in the British Publishing world so that he can at least start making some enquiries. Any offers?. Cont'd on page 23 POSTBAG---Cont'd from page 19 GEORGE PIDDINGTON writes from Hayling Island to tell us that he is now a qualified County Youth Leader and has his club members taking part in judo, fencing and trampoline, besides athletics. He assures us that "any possible stars will become members of Belgrave". George's training took an exciting turn last September. As he left the factory for his lunch-time spin he passed a mini-skirted typist seated on the factory wall. "Bring your gear on Monday and I'll take you for a quick one in the field" chirped George, showing the bravado of all runners when on the move. "O.K." came the swift reply "I'll take you up on that". This worried George first of all because he wasn't clear whether she realised he meant for a training session, and then he worried even more when he thought she did!. Came Monday, and there she was, exactly as on Friday. George sighed with relief. But the relief was short lived as the mini-skirted doll bounded from the wall and running alongside him said "I'm coming training with you". As they entered the field George began shedding his track-suit, still a little perplexed. As he turned to stride away in his best Belgrave style he was staggered to see his immodest companion disrobing in broad daylight. Noticing the speechless Piddington standing there with knees trembling she said "Oh!. I hope you don't mind my taking a few things off first". George stuttered that he certainly did not mind and was all for the encouragement of athletics. And so began the first training session of the week. The next few were very similar, though the local boys school had got wise (they included some of George's youth club members) and the sessions were accompanied by unrepeatable ribald comments. Unfortunately this beautiful friendship was not allowed to flourish---she was a temporary typist who did not re-appear again. But George will always remember the happiest training week of his life. By the way, if anyone comes accross a half clad typist in their travels would they please contact George at 1, St. Hermans Road, Hayling Island---she's got the wrong shorts.. items.sum: Gordon Biscoe reviews Belgrave's best road season for years and sets the 1970 target of the combined Poly and AAA Marathon.
items.s: ROAD RUNNING Gordon Biscoe reviews Belgrave's best road season for years and sets the 1970 target of the combined Poly and AAA Marathon. GORDON BISCOE WRITES: Having written in earlier editions of our hopes and aspirations for the road season which has just closed (or should we say nowadays---eased off!), we can in a sense report a mission accomplished; for there is no doubt that this has been our best season for quite a few years. The fact that we have been placed in every event for which we have made a serious team entry is surely proof enough. However, the operative word here is 'placed', for although we have had our share of 'golds' there is still plenty of room for improvement. Some of our success this year has been due to following up an earlier request to concentrate our efforts on certain events as opposed to tackling the lot; let's continue in the same vein. Every one by now is probably fully aware of the overloaded calendar we have, and it's good to hear that the R.R.C. are sharing a load (not for the first time) in attempting to resolve the problem; at least from the point of longer races. For many years now our 'goal' in the cross country world has been to win the 'National', for 1970 I think we should add a further target--the Poly & AAA Marathon. Next year these two are to be combined over the now classic course and it would be a fine tribute to our President Gordon Doubleday, in his year of office, to present him with this one, as well as all the others!! Gordon Biscoe GORDON BISCOE Gordon Doubleday Gordon Doubleday National Cross Country Championships 1970 Polytechnic Marathon 1970 AAA Marathon Championship 1970 R.R.C.

Hercules--Wimbledon '10'---October 11th This "Ten" had the support of some extra top line athletes this year--yet all our boys excelled themselves to finish a close second to the Hercules-Wimbledon trio. Gerry North threw caution to the winds early on and was almost a hundred yards clear of the two Holts, Tagg and Richardson at four miles. However our Gerry was soon to be caught by the bunch, although shortly afterwards Richardson was dropped. Gerry eventually fell away leaving the Holt twins and Tagg to sort out the medals. Of course, Tagg's finishing speed proved decisive. Gerry finished in an excellent 48:54 still keeping Richardson at bay. Lionel and Dick gave him the sort of backing he deserves and finished strongly with 50:10 and 50:13 respectively. Pat ran steadily through the field for a well deserved 11th place in 50:54. Teams: 1. items.sum: Christmas humour centre spread: jokes, a play-title quiz, a club parody of A Christmas Carol starring 'Ebenezer Baker', and a photo-collage cartoon of Belgrave Hall.
items.s: Unashamed! Unexpurgated! Unreadable! The Belgravian "U" and Non "U" Christmas humour centre spread: jokes, a play-title quiz, a club parody of A Christmas Carol starring 'Ebenezer Baker', and a photo-collage cartoon of Belgrave Hall. I have a terrible conscience - it doesn't keep me from doing things; it just keeps me from enjoying them. Unashamed! Unexpurgated! Unreadable! The Belgravian "U" and Non "U" Personell Director: "You're asking big pay for a beginner". Applicant: "Well, the work is harder when you don't know anything about it." Prosecutor: "Now tell the jury the truth, please, why did you shoot your husband with a bow and arrow?" Defendant: "I didn't want to wake the children." QUIZ TIME FOR THE WELL-READ 2" | 6" | 12" | DRY | WET | OO & OOO These represent titles from plays - five from the Bard 'isself (William Shakespeare) and one from the Irish playwright, Bernard Shaw. The answers will not be given because it could be said they are rude ... if you are not rude ... read on. 'twas the night before christmas With continually saying, "Bah!" and "Humbug", Ebenezer Baker had a relapsed throat, and that was only part of the trouble. He was engaged with the annual visitation of the Ghost of Christmas Past, who looked remarkably like Tom Carter. "I'm telling you, Ebenezer," he said, "try to look back and see the gay cavorting youngster you used to be when money was no object. Remember the Folkestone Fiasco. They were the days and ...." His time up, he was wafted away to make room for the Ghost of Christmas Present. "Ah! You gave me quite a start", said Ebenezer to the latest apparition which was regaled in a tassellated leather jacket embroidered with butterflies, a lacy shawl, pink trews and boots, one hand carrying flowers, the other twiddling with rows of beads, a dolly clung possessively to each arm and a copy of the Thoughts of Mao stuck out from his back pocket. "Still," continued Ebenezer, "it's nice to see you back, Chris". Master Steer gazed tolerantly at the wizened figure before him. "You gotta come across babe, I mean, it ain't no use fight'n it - a few lousey bucks an' you'd have a team that'd clean up in the Boston. Take that guy Hart, when he'd finished he could learn 'em natives English and Mann could show 'em how to jelly eels, and young North could gab on about thrift whilst Dabbs could instruct the injuns how to dress and yer kantankerous Team Manager, Biscoe ..." But the witching hour disposed of the rest. In a few minutes the diaphanous form of Tony Brooks gelled as the Ghost of Christmas to Come. "Tut, Tut! So they've sent you again have they?" sighed the Old Man, "Bell Graves answer to Jack Dash as the red hot radical and the poor girls' Steve McQueen. What now Anthony?" "I can point to a very restricted future", said The Ghost of Christmas to Come. "With the old order - your stone - from the rubble of the crumbled edifice that you abortively tried to keep together is already marked 'John Ebenezer Baker, mourned by the Golden Guinea', and the top heavy administering establishment has choked on ..." but his time was up and just a whisp of haze was all that remained. Ebenezer finished off his concentrated lime cordial (you'll observe he never offered his visitors drinks - it's because he didn't believe in serving spirits) then in the time honoured way, he went to the window, threw it open and addressed a young street arab kicking his heels in the snow. "Hey, boy, what's your name?" "Wesch, Sir, Willie Wesch". "Well, cut along to the poulterer, Wiener Schnitzel's and procure the largest bird he has, and if you're back within five minutes there's a florin in it for you." Willie returned in four minutes for a journey of less than a quarter of a mile which was prodigiously long and Ebenezer would have done better to send the other ragamuffin playing with Willie, namely, Robert Coates. However, Willie pulled up short in front of Ebenezer. "How about this, sir?" "Oh Lord!" exclaimed Ebenezer as he gazed at the plump frauline on Willie's arm. "Not Wiener Schnitzel's daughter, Helga". Willie dismissed, Ebenezer wound eight yards of woollen scarf around his scrawny neck and set off. With difficulty he fixed on a wooden smile and bid all a "Merry Christmas". After obtaining the largest turkey he could find he headed for his clerk's residence, R. Hopkins Crackett, "I've come to give you the bird", said his uncle. "Ha, Ha; You are a teeze,uncle, but don't stand out on the step, Come in, come in". What a festive board they had and after the plum pudding, Tiny Bernard merrily leapt to his feet, striving to preserve his balance on rickety legs and declared in a high voice " 'an God Bless every one of us!" Whereupon, the ladies with kerchieves to their eyes and hearts overflowing with compassion responded as one."Such a dear!" "How sweet" "Touching" and such like phrases fell from their lips. His atonement made, Ebenezer Baker reverted to his "Bah!" and "Humbug" for another 364 days. A precis of this cautionary tale can be obtained in a booklet entitled "A Christmas Carol". items.sum: Pat Duncan's review of Belgrave's 'fantastic' 1969 walking season and prospects for 1970, including the Commonwealth Games and Lugano Cup.
items.s: WALKING Pat Duncan's review of Belgrave's 'fantastic' 1969 walking season and prospects for 1970, including the Commonwealth Games and Lugano Cup. Pat Duncan writes: There was a time, not very long passed, when it used to be a hard job getting together material for the Belgravian and pretty easy to get a mention - partly because I wrote it but mainly because there was not much competition. Its still a hard job getting the stuff together but this is because of the difficulty of deciding what to leave out. Week after week superb performances come rolling in and now I never get a mention. I thought things would go better in the long ones but no, could'nt make the national team the others walked so well. Brighton I thought,but Claret and Gold in my eyes all the way,John Moullin turning in another great one so soon after the Hastings. Ray Middleton, fantastic as ever in his British vest, shakes off a bad season with a superlative display in Athens comes back and Wilf Wesch beats him. Wilf turns in another great one in Lugano, comes home and Carl Lawton beats him one week and then Bob Coates does it the next. Barry Ingarfield and Doug Fotheringham, now there's two I can thrash - or can I ? After the One Hour I thought Len Duquemin's age had at last caught up on him but where is he now?right up there again far out of my failing sight. Ray Hall; now I had written him off, two children and pressure of work he'll never make it now I thought - not without some satisfaction. But who was that just slipped inside the Hour at Enfield ? Brian Ward, Gerry Cameron and Bob Picton all looked to be on the trail again and up north Dave King and Paul Duckett are sure to be slipping in some crafty sessions. It only needs Bob Barnes to comeback and thats my lot! On a more serious note 1970 is an important year for Bob Coates, Ray Middleton, Len Duquemin and John Moullin who all have a chance in the Commonwealth Games for Scotland, England, and the Channel Islands respectively. Gerry Cameron must also make his effort now. For the Long Distance men it is rumoured that the 100 Kilometres at Lugano will include an international four a side, no doubt Ray will be putting in his usual appearance for Britain in the Lugano Cup 50 Kilos. On the other side for Germany it must be Wilf Wesch. On the home front ALL the Nationals and the Garnett Cup is what the President ought to be able to expect,with the Brighton chucked in for good measure. To all the walkers of Belgrave at the close of one of our greatest years I can only say that it has been a fantastic year. We have never been out of the first three and over the year the team has so developed that no one can be sure of a place. I think too that the spirit of Belgrave whether it be that of the first or last man is something we can be really proud of - we must also live up to it and that is our task for the next decade,win or lose we'll have our laughs. Now back to that training ! items.s: LONDON - BRIGHTON HAT-TRICK Report and result of the London to Brighton walk, in which Belgrave won the team title for the third year running and John Moullin won the Belgrave Cup. Pat Duncan, Dave King, Bob Farley and John Keown must be among the most reliable distance walkers in the country. Add to them John Moullin, Belgrave's latest distance champion and you have a formidable team who once again took the team title to make it three in a row. A great performance by our guest from America Klopfer and John Moullin close behind. John suffered some at Crawley but one sighting of the holder Pat Duncan sent him away to a really strong finish and victory in the Belgrave Cup. Dave King had his usual Mackeson inspired blinder, a word to for Bob & John who were there as always to anchor our leading men - Bob to score in the team and John, crafty to the end, to be the last man to beat the 10 hours second class standard. Full Marks to Ray Hall for getting a Youths team to the start but confusion with the disciplins led to Belgrave losing men and therefore not finishing a team. Andy Hinchcliff walked well to record 26:45 finishing 11th while McAnally can reckon he's in the top thirty with a plucky 31.01. In the Junior Five Mile Race our only starter Paul Duckett banged in a useful 41.08. Paul is now at Manchester University and has already made his mark with our friends in Lancashire Walking Club. We hope he does not give too much away as our training methods might be turned against us! items.s: THE GERMAN TRIP Report and result of the Frankfurt Inter Club 30 kilometres walk on 13 October 1969, won by Wilf Wesch with Belgrave taking the first five places. October 13th- Frankfurt Inter Club 30 Kilos After a very rough journey to Frankfurt, thick fog all the way, we were glad to relax in the splendid hospitality laid on by our German hosts who had arranged for us to stay at the local sports centre. Obviously terrified by Wilf Wesch's rising reputation Frankfurt's two leading men thought better of even starting the race which was held over a very fast 15 lap course closed to all traffic except prams ( and to our cost,Kite strings!) The lead was taken by the young East German Schuster who piled on the pace over the first 20 Kilos which he covered in 94.00 minutes with Wilf 1½ minutes down and Ray not far behind. Wilf closed the gap and then Schuster retired leaving Wilf a clear lead. Ray nearly closed this towards the finish but rising to his own crowd Wilf held him off to win. Bob Coates and Len Duquemin walked together for most of the race both producing very fast times. Carl Lawton in what amounts to his first 20 Mile race started with Pat Duncan but after halfway closed on Bob and Len overtaking them before tiring and being re-caught. His time was really nothing short of fantastic for a first attempt. The first german finished next leaving our two Brighton stars to settle their differences not far behind. Pat caught an exhausted John with a lap to go but did'nt wait in case the hot water ran out. In the presentation which followed the German National Coach paid tribute to the determination, style and sportsmanship of the Belgrave team. From our visit it is quite clear that no country can compare with Britain for the high standard of domestic competition and as for Frankfurt they have a lot of training to do before the return match !
