items.label: December 1969
items.sum: John Keown's review of Belgrave's 1968/69 walking season, in which the club won three of the four National senior road walking titles and the London to Brighton.
items.s: A YEAR TO REMEMBER John Keown's review of Belgrave's 1968/69 walking season, in which the club won three of the four National senior road walking titles and the London to Brighton. Belgrave's walking teams are becoming almost invincible, going from strength to strength with no limits yet in sight. Last year was highly successful with Belgrave winning three of the four National titles. JOHN KEOWN reviews that 1968/9 season and regards it as---- A YEAR TO REMEMBER During the R.W.A. year 1968-69 (September '68 to August '69) Belgrave Harriers' Walking Section equalled, if not surpassed, the achievements of the great club teams of 1957 and 1960 The year ended with the club having won many races including the classic London to Brighton and three of the four National Senior Road Walking Championships. The walkers also secured second place in the remaining Senior event and a fourth place in the National Junior 5 Miles. In 1957 and 1960 when Belgrave teams won all three National Senior titles (a fourth, the National 20 Kilos, was added in 1965), the club had the advantage of being able to call upon the sevices of such internationals as Stan Vickers, Eric Hall and George Williams. Today, with only one international, Ray Middleton, among the active club walkers, success depends more on the efforts of the ordinary clubman and the drive and initiative of the Hon. Walking Secretary and the section captain. Much of the credit for the success of Belgrave walkers during the year must go to Pat Duncan, the Hon. Walking Secretary. Pat is not only a hard working secretary but a capable leader and a very gifted long distance walker. Nothing is too much trouble for this tall Sussex man, for in addition to his other duties, he drives fellow Belgravians and others in his own mini-bus many miles, to races all over the country. Unfortunately his tremendous efforts on behalf of the club, during the period under review, meant a slight falling off in the standard of his own performances in such races as the Manchester to Blackpool and the London to Brighton. In June the previous year, Pat established a new course record of 7:57:01 for the 51¾ miles manchester to Blackpool race. Ray Hall, the road walking captain, also contributed much to Belgrave's success. Ray, no longer as active a competitor as in the past, lightened considerably the burden of the Hon. Secretary with his help in the clubhouse, on the road and with transport. Alf Harley, Jack Goswell and Frank Jarvis, although required to devote a large proportion of their time to R.W.A. activities, played a not insignificant part in the Belgrave success story. Others who played their part were all those club members and friends who looked after the needs of the walkers during the middle and long distance races. The story began on Saturday, September 7th, 1968 when the Belgrave team of Pat Duncan, Dave King, Bob Farley and George Beecham snatched victory from Bristol Walking Club in the London to Brighton by the narrow margin of 3 points (24 to 27). Pat finished third in the race, 23 minutes behind Bristol's Brian Eley, with a time of 8:23:24. This was the club's 17th victory in this race. Their first was back in 1921. Since 1958, when Belgrave recorded their only win in the National Junior 5 Miles Championship, the club have had great difficulty fielding a team in this event. However on October 19th, at Manchester, Carl Lawton, Brian Ward and Paul Duckett filled fourth team position. The winter season began well for Belgrave with Len Duquemin and the club taking top honours in the Highgate Open Seven. During the weeks that followed the team won the Enfield Open Seven and filled second place in both the Belgrave and Metro. Police Open Sevens. In November, whilst others struggled for top honours at home, Pat Duncan competed against the top long distance men of seven nations at Lugano in an International 100 Kms. race. He took second place behind S. Lindberg (Sweden) in 10:20:56. Our ever cheerful West German, Will Wesch, set the race walking world alight in the early months of 1969, when he won the Southern 'Garnet' 10 Miles Championship, the Surrey Co. 10 Miles Championship, the Ipswich H. Open 10 and finished third in the Basingstoke A.C. Open 10. By winning the 'Garnet' he followed in the footsteps of Belgrave internationals, Stan Vickers and Ray Middleton who both began their rise to fame by winning this championship. The club secured third place in the 'Garnet' team race, a very creditable performance in view of the fact that Belgrave had filled first place the previous year. Barring clauses in this Junior status championship prevent previous winners from competing again. Will Wesch led the team to victory in both the Ipswich and Basingstoke races. Unfortunately his mode of progression did not satisfy the judges in the R.W.A. National 10 Miles Championship at Morden on March 15th, so Belgrave had to be content with second place behind Leicester W.C. Three weeks later in the Metropolitan W.C. 20 Kilos. at Battersea Park the club tied with Coventry Godiva H. on points, each scoring 32. Under the A.A.A. rules first place went to Coventry as their fourth scoring man finished nearest the winner. May was a great month for the walkers who wear the claret and gold. On the 3rd at Bexley in a two race, four a side international match between West Germany and Great Britain, Ray Middleton finished second in the 35 Kms. in 3:3:15 and thus helped his country to a team victory. A week later Ray led Belgrave to their second successive National 20 Kilos. victory. Other members were Len Duquemin, John Moullin and Will Wesch. At the end of the month the same team, this time lead by Will Wesch, who finished in 4th individual position, won the Leicester Mercury Open 20 Miles. In June the club scored its 12th win in the National 20 Miles Championship. This was indeed a welcomed success for the walkers as they had not fared too well in this Championship since 1965 when they found themselves outside the medals for the first time since 1932. The scoring four were the same as those who took top honours in the National 20 Kilos. The forward walking of the other four members of the eight man team; Bob Coates, Pat Duncan, Bob Farley and Dave DeBondi enabled Belgrave to win the Nijmegen Shield awarded to the first team to finish its declared eight. During the month Bob Coates, an ex-Scottish Junior racing cyclist, covered 3,000 metres on the track at Brighton in the fast time of 13:16:4. At the beginning of July Belgrave took first place in their own invitation Inter-Club Track Walks at Battersea Park. In the Birmingham Outer Circle 25 Miles Walk on July 5th, Ray Middleton finished second and lead the club to a very easy team victory. Later in the month the club were again in action in the Midlands, this time in the National 50 Kms. Championship at Redditch. Belgrave started 11 walkers including new recruit, G. Klopfer from the U.S.A. Klopfer walked as a guest and finished third just in front of Ray Middleton who was placed third in the championship thus making sure of selection for the European Games 50 Kilos Walk. Ray with the support of John Moullin, Len Duquemin and Dave King took the team title. This was Belgrave's 15th team victory in this race. In fact the club have only been outside the first three on 4 occasions since a team-championship was added to this event in 1932. Once again the reliability of our walkers was clearly demonstrated when they were the first team to finish their declared eight, thus winning the Milan Trophy. The year ended with Belgrave recording a good victory in the Annual Hastings to Brighton 38 Miles Walk. The club finished 4 walkers in the first six and with only three to score easily retained their team title, with the very low score of 9 points. Ray Middleton took third individual prize whilst Pat Duncan in 5th position got the prize for being the first Sussex man to finish. The year 1968-69 was certainly a great year for Belgrave walkers, perhaps they will make the present year an even more memorable one. Can they win all four National Senior titles? Their easy win in the recent London to Brighton certainly shows that it will take some very high class performances by their opponents to stop them. items.label: December 1969
items.sum: Ray Middleton's first-hand account of finishing fifth in the 50 km walk at the 1969 European Championships in Athens, with the result.
items.s: Four Minutes From Bronze Ray Middleton's first-hand account of finishing fifth in the 50 km walk at the 1969 European Championships in Athens, with the result. Three months have elapsed since the European Athletics Championships were held in Athens but the thrills of British successes are still fresh in our minds. Paul Nihill's great win in the 20 Kilos Walk tended to overshadow Britain's performance in the 50 Kilos event when two of our trio were unable to finish. But who better was there to carry the burden alone than our own RAY MIDDLETON. One of the Country's most reliable performers, and a seasoned international with a Commonwealth "silver" and two European "fifths" to his credit, Ray tells of that hot September day in Athens and how, after nearly 4½ hours of walking, he was just---- Four Minutes From Bronze With so many good performances by British Athletes in Athens my 5th place seems a bit low in the order of merit. However, I was quite pleased with my performance. Having gone well in training since my arrival in Athens I thought that given a hot day I might have a good one; and sure enough the day of the race was hot. I had been stocking up with salt over the previous week as I no longer take salt on race days; only a small drop in drinks. I find that this cuts out sickness during the race. The course was along the coast road with very little shade, and that blue sea to keep your mind off walking!. Hohne of East Germany went right from the gun with the Russians in the next three places, then two groups some way behind the leaders. I think the first 10 Kilos was the hardest bit as the sun was at it's hottest. I started out with sun glasses but could not see half the time so I had to whip them off. The first drink I had was a life saver, from that point on I could not wait to get to the next drinking point;in all I drank 14 bottles of Coke each one going down better than the last! It's true what they say about Coke("things do go better")--for me anyway!. At 20 Kilos I had got with the main bunch. Up to this point the course had been flat but to the surprise of many we found we were now walking up what seemed like the side of a mountain, and I do believe this was the turning point for many of the more fancied boys. At the turn I still felt quite good and I think I must have been about ninth at this point. I was walking with the two East Germans but I felt that once we were back on the flat I might have a job to match their speed. I soon passed one of the Russians who looked far from happy and this bucked me up quite a bit but at 30 Kilos the Germans put the speed work in and I found myself walking on my own once again . I passed our Hotel with 20 Kilos to go and this was just like walking past one's house but not stopping to have a quick chat to the wife and a quick drink, as I do at home. Once past this point I felt strong again and realised I had gained another place as I passed one of the Germans sitting in the road---disqualified. Despite the heat of competition I felt sorry for him as it had happened to me in Belgrade 7 years ago. But now I had the second Russian in my sights with 10 Kilos left. Pushed on by supporting John Webb I did all I could to nail him but with the sight of home ahead he just held me off. At first I felt disgusted at not catching him but he had walked well and that's all that counts in Walking. It was a wonderful trip with great performances from British Athletes but I also remember the sadness of Dick Taylor and Bill Adcocks who, with so many good runs behind them, had to have a bad one on the big day. This also went for my own walking team who failed to finish the '50'---for them let's hope that they get another chance to prove their worth. Pos Name Club Performance 1. C. items.sum: Report and result of the 50th Belgrave Open 7 miles walk at Wimbledon on 22 November 1969, started by Tommy Green and won by Mexico's P. Colin, with Belgrave winning the team race; two Ron Linstead photos.
items.s: 50th BELGRAVE OPEN '7' Report and result of the 50th Belgrave Open 7 miles walk at Wimbledon on 22 November 1969, started by Tommy Green and won by Mexico's P. Colin, with Belgrave winning the team race; two Ron Linstead photos. November 22nd 1969 50 open 7's is quite some record for a promoting club so that it was only right that the 50th should be started by Tommy Green who took the Gold Medal for the 50 Kilometres Walk in the 1932 Olympics . Tommy looked far too fit to be standing on the side of the road but it gave great pleasure to his many friends and admirers to see him back at Wimbledon. For the younger members it also provided the opportunity, not the only one we hope, for them to take a close look at an Olympic Gold, both the man and the medal! Anyway,Tommy sent the 150 or so walkers on their way and immediately the visiting Mexicans took the front with Suan Lightman also prominent. Our leading four were also well up to put us comfortably ahead in the team race. Some doubts were expressed as to the quality of the Mexican's walking for although they passed the judges their frequent spurts must inevitably stretch the rules of fair walking to the limit (Photo:Ron Linstead) CARL LAWTON leads JOHN MOULLIN. By the end of the first lap the field had stretched right out with Colin and Lightman locked together closely followed by Oliveros, Ramirez Wil Wesch and Bob Coates who were both walking superbly. Len Duquemin was also walking very smoothly,Carl Lawton too was well up although clearly such pace must make even the strongest suffer. Ray Middleton was clearly feeling the effects of losing his father in law but did not let his team place go without a battle. Wife Jean was also much in evidence helping as always and pushing the boys along with vocal support. Further back things were going well for Fotheringham, Ward and Ingarfield who were grouped closely together while newcomer to walking, but not running, John Bromley was giving a good account of himself at the heel and toe game. Over the Second lap Colin broke clear of Shuan who tired a bit and had to give second best to Oliveros and Ramirez. For Belgrave Bob pulled away from Wilf over the last half mile and was involved in a thrilling finish,with Campos just edging him out. Once again the Belgrave scoring four really showed the others,beating Surrey by a fantastic 84 Points! The boys also picked up the handicap team prizes for the second race in a row and Bob Coates certainly deserved better than third in the handicap on the tremendous form he showed. Bob must certainly be regarded as a great prospect for the Commonwealth Games; not only for selection. For the many senior Belgravians present it was a great pleasure to see such a strong team performance, there can be few occasions when the white stick for the first unplaced Belgravian is won by the same man who a few weeks earlier finished fifth in the whole of Europe. For the many walkers present we must express our profound thanks to all the many Belgravians who over the years have put so much into the club;to mention names is always difficult but Alf Harley, Jack Goswell, Frank Jarvis, Ernie Kemp, Dave Shepherd Gordon Doubleday and Harry Hathway must surely be thanked;Ray Hall too for his behind the scenes work and finally Mrs Savage who was present at the first open 7 and despite making tea for the walkers ever since was there large as life for the 50th. items.sum: Boxed anecdote about the walking secretary marking the 7 mile course with flour on Cambridge Road.
items.s: Scene: The Middle of Cambridge Road. Boxed anecdote about the walking secretary marking the 7 mile course with flour on Cambridge Road. Scene: The Middle of Cambridge Road. Action: Walking Secretary marking 7 Mile course with bag of white flour. Car draws up and window is lowered - Passenger to Driver " Do you think he's alright ?" Driver to figure in road " I say, are you alright, what are you doing"?" Now if nothing else our walking secretary is never stuck for words - quick as a flash he replies " Making drop scones, can't you see ?" " Should'nt we do something?" asks Passenger at which moment 150 men in various stages of undress come belting round the corner. That did it ! Belgrave Harriers Open 7 Miles Walk 1969 Cambridge Road

items.h: FROM 'THE BELGRAVIAN' 25 years ago ... and 40 years ago
items.sum: Extracts from The Belgravian of October 1944 (wartime deaths, prisoners and bomb damage among members) and December 1929 (J.E. Flower's South of Thames Junior win and the club's best year).
items.s: FROM 'THE BELGRAVIAN' 25 years ago ... and 40 years ago Extracts from The Belgravian of October 1944 (wartime deaths, prisoners and bomb damage among members) and December 1929 (J.E. Flower's South of Thames Junior win and the club's best year). 25 years ago OCTOBER 1944------Since the last issue we have learned, with great sorrow, of the following deaths:- K.N. WOODS died from wounds in Normandy. He was a former Surrey Junior Cross-Country Champion and was placed in the South of Thames Junior race. KEN SHEAIL was killed in action with the Hampshire Regiment in Italy, having previously been wounded there. His favourite distance with us was the 880 yards. FRANK HANDLEY was killed in action with the Irish Guards. LIONEL PENNY was killed in action with the Recce Corps. He was one of our most promising cross-country runners. Prisoner of War news is scant. LES BENNETT is still in Japanese hands. ARTHUR BEALES seems to have settled down to life in a prison camp and has "made himself at home"---if such a phrase applies!. FRANK HALLS was wounded in the legs before capture and it is feared that he will not beable to race walk again. DAN & ALEC PATIENCE were taken prisoners during the fighting around the Anzio beachhead and sent to Germany.(Dan had earlier been wounded in N. Africa and was home for a while). Their older brother GEORGE, with whom they were inseparable since the outbreak of war and have fought together during the whole of the North African and Sicilian Campaigns, was killed in the same engagement. PAT DRISCOLL has been posted as missing with his fighter ten days after D-day-and REG SHEPHERD is still amongst the missing. BERT FOOTER has been right up in the front at Normandy and would welcome a rest in the rear. JOHN FLOWER is back in England after sixteen months sojourn in the "White man's grave", and now has one ring on his sleeve. LEN ROLLINS is on board H.M.S. Lochaibort. ALF MILLER was slightly wounded in Italy and was pleased to have a clubmate as a visitor---ALF HARLEY!. We have recently learned with regret that he has been reported missing, probably a prisoner of war. LAURIE JACKSON was wounded in Normandy by shrapnel from a mortar bomb and spent a time in hospital at Bradford. His last copy of the "Belgravian" has a large hole in it---it was in his pocket when he stopped his "packet". We'll try and get the next copy on bullet-proof paper!. ERNIE DUFFETT lost his home through a direct hit from a flying bomb. Mrs Duffett and some of their children were buried in the debris and were rescued, fortunately without injury. Ernie (a War Reserve Policeman) was on duty at the time. Prospective "pot-hunters" are warned that Ernie has recovered his handicap sheets!. CHARLIE COOK also had his home demolished by a flying bomb and sustained minor injuries necessitating a short stay in hospital. JOHN BROWN lost his mother and a sister when their home was destroyed, and we extend to him our deepest sympathies. John himself was taken to hospital for a short while as he sustained minor injuries. and 40 years ago DECEMBER 1929----This month we must congratulate J.E. Flower upon winning the South of Thames Junior race. He is the first winner of this event we have ever had---and a worthy one at that. We are expecting big things of Jack in the future and are not likely to suffer disappointment. Very shortly we shall be bidding goodbye to 1929, and a retrospective glance shows that we have had our most successful year in the Club's history. The South of the Thames Championship has been won for the first time, the National Road Walking Championship retained and many minor successes of varying importance recorded. In addition, the membership has increased considerably and the Club attained a higher position than ever before in the athletic world. Our great hope is that 1930 will surpass even 1929, wonderful though it has been, and that a year hence we may beable to look back with even greater pride and satisfaction than we do this year. items.s: YOUTHS & BOYS — Reg. Hopkins reports Reg Hopkins on the youths' and boys' strong start to the 1969-70 season, with results of the Maidenhead Youth and Boy races on 27 September, won by Belgrave's youth team. Of the six races in which we have competed so far this season we have been placed in all except one (Redhill & Reigate) and in that we were without the services of John Stow and Peter Carton. This is an excellent start to the season when one remembers that all except one of our Youths will still be eligible for this grade of competition next year. Our potential is better than it has ever been, and our depth so strong that with 8 or 10 to score we would be almost unbeatable. This is due not only to the hard work of our front runners but by the keen backing of the remainder. Our packs from Belgrave Hall are showing great enthusiasm and on a recent perishing cold Tuesday evening I counted 20 youths and boys setting out together. We have some fine runners in the making. items.sum: Notes on Belgrave's youngsters: sons of members racing, the Junior Inter-County match, schools races, Reg Hopkins's chauffeuring mishaps and newcomer Tony Binda.
items.s: HERE & THERE Notes on Belgrave's youngsters: sons of members racing, the Junior Inter-County match, schools races, Reg Hopkins's chauffeuring mishaps and newcomer Tony Binda. Nice to see two sons of Club members, Ivan Beaumont (son of Ray) and Stephen Walker (son of Chas.) running for the Club in the K.L.G. 3000 metres Cross-Country races for colts recently. Ivan finished 30th in 22:31 and Stephen 55th in 25:32--a promising start, by both. Ian Gillings was leading the field with only a quarter of a mile to go but was forced to drop out with stitch. Never mind Ian, it happens to the best of them. Another son in regular training is John Baker (son of Jack). With over 300 senior members in the Club we should have a lot more!. In the Junior Inter-County track and field match at Erith on August 16th, Peter Carton (4:29.2) and John Stow (4:36.0) finished 2nd and 5th respectively in the mile for Surrey. Steve White scored a sprint double (10.5 y/22.5y) while Arnold Bentt leapt a season's best 22'-1¼" to finish 2nd in the long jump and followed up with a below par high jump (5'-7") for 6th. Other Belgravians in the Surrey team were John Hamilton (54.2y) and Paul Duckett (7:35.8 mile walk). John Stow had the fastest lap of the day while representing his school in the annual Walton A.C. schools road relay on Oct. 25th. John's time--11:33. Paddy Breslin, also a member of the Richard Challoner team, helped bring them into 3rd team place with 12:28. John Cambridge was 4th in a schools Cross-Country race over 2½ miles at Ewell recently. He goes to the same school as Martin Bloice (Spencer Park) and looks as if he is going to be useful.He is still only a colt. With Reg chauffeuring our youngsters to their many fixtures some odd things have happened. Once, he even managed to get lost in Hyde Park and on another occasion found himself in an Atomic Power Station. But by far the most interesting occurence was when he found himself caught up in the Lord Mayor's Show---but for the Police , half the Show would have ended up at Luton!. In a S.C.A.A.A. v London Junior match at Crystal Palace on August 24th the Carton/Stow combination were out again, this time in the 1500 metres where they were 3rd (4:08.1) and 7th (4:14.1) respectively. Steve White got his revenge over his A.A.A. conqueror, Griffiths, by scoring another sprint double (11.1/22.1), a yard clear each time. Arnold Bentt was second in the high jump (5'-8") and Paul Duckett 5th in the 3,000 metres walk (15:15.8). Two great wins for Peter Carton---1st in the H.H.H. schools Cross-Country race breaking the previous record by over a minute and 1st in the South London schools Senior Cross-Country Championships at Morden winning by over 1½ minutes. Les Harris was an excellent 4th in this race. Lee Sullivan shared the same time (11.5) as the first and second when being placed third in the Junior 100 metres in a S.C.A.A.A. open meeting at Crystal Palace on Oct 15th. How well Tony Binda has fitted into the Youths team, he has only been with us a few weeks but has already won the hearts of his team mates by some really gritty running, both in training and races. He has all the hall-marks of a true Belgravian---a sense of humour, a friendly manner, and a desire to succeed. We welcome him into our ranks. It is reported that at the moment Vic Butcher is unattached; but between girl friends! items.s: Surrey County Road Relay Youths 4 X 2 miles---Woking Lido, September 6th Report and result of the Surrey County youths 4x2 miles road relay at Woking Lido on 6 September 1969, Belgrave's best-ever second place. Our second place was the highest we have notched in this event, and with three of the same team still eligible next year we can hardly wait!. Les Harris had one of his best runs to date to finish second on the opening stage, just eight seconds in arrears, but Vic Butcher was not at his best and had the misfortune to face Adams of West Surrey who raced away to record second fastest time of the day. Although over a minute down we still held second place. John Stow produced his usual gutty run to cut our deficit to 39 seconds but Peter Carton was left to chase an invincible Ford (W.Surrey) who disappeared to set a new lap record (9:17). Nevertheless, Peter clocked fourth fastest time of the day and consolidated our second position. Pos Team Time 1. West Surrey H. 39:58 2. BELGRAVE H. 41:26 3. Walton A.C. 41:56 Runner Time L. Wimbledon---October 25th Race No.1 Bill Curtin looked all set to repeat his win of last year when Fromant of Mitcham put in a finishing kick to squeeze ahead by inches. The Mitcham lad's effort was a supreme one and he knew he had been in a race when he finished! Bill was philosophical "I should never have let him beat me, it'll be different later on". Hot on his heels was Peter Carton, who becomes a greater force each time he runs; and, not all that far behind, T. Bindar our third scorer who produced an excellent effort to finish 10th. Last year we were third in this opener, 18 points behind Mitcham. This year the margin was a mere 3 points and we look to have a great chance of regaining the title we lost last season. items.s: BELGRAVE OPEN YOUTHS ROAD RELAY Report and results of the Belgrave Open Youths Road Relay on 18 October 1969, won by Shaftesbury with Belgrave A third. BELGRAVE OPEN RELAY---October 18th As far as the winners, Shaftesbury, were concerned this year's race was a procession. Bober clocked 11:16 on the first stage to give them a mammoth lead of 40 seconds, which was stretched still further by Jones on stage two. With Goater (11:04) doing fastest time of the day on the fourth and final stage they were invincible. Although three of the Shaftesbury quartet were faster than any of our runners, Belgrave were by no means out of the medals hunt. Vic Butcher did not produce one of his best runs in finishing 10th on the first stage but Bill Curtin, Peter Carton and John Stow all put in useful sub-12 efforts to gain us deserved third place medals. In the 'B' team, Yianni and Binda also showed their paces with useful times. The first school to finish and collect the special set of medals awarded by former International Arthur Penny were Whitgift in 8th place. items.label: December 1969
items.h: THE MEN BEHIND THE TROPHIES — R.W. RICKETTS
items.sum: Profile of Bob Ricketts, pre-1927 club President who built up Belgrave and gave the R.W. Ricketts Cup and Shield, the Belgrave Cup and the Doris Shield, with his portrait.
items.s: THE MEN BEHIND THE TROPHIES — R.W. RICKETTS Profile of Bob Ricketts, pre-1927 club President who built up Belgrave and gave the R.W. Ricketts Cup and Shield, the Belgrave Cup and the Doris Shield, with his portrait. R.W. RICKETTS Much has been written at various times of that great personality BOB RICKETTS, who probably wielded more influence on the Club than has any other man, alive or dead,in our 82 years of history. Bob had run in our events in the 1890's but it was immediately after the first World War that his sense of leadership caused him to work incessantly for Belgrave, and to lay the foundations for the greater things to come. As President of the Club he naturally seemed to be the dominant personality --in the pleasantest possible way. He had that great asset of being able to get others to share and work for his enthusiasms; and he was able to impress his personality on everyone he met. He had run at most distances, was a boxer of no small repute; and on the persuasion of Jimmy Belchamber, had become a distance walker of outstanding merit. However his greatest work for the Club lay in the planning and building of the Club for which he had so much affection. His powerful personality attracted other members, he fought the London County Council over and over again for a cinder track in Battersea Park, and when it was eventually installed fought again for adequate dressing accomodation to allow it to be used with advantage. He had a welcome for every newcomer; and had a keen eye to discover, and to use everyone's talents to the best advantage. And he worked and worked for Belgrave in the days when money was scarce indeed; and he himself was an example of intense enthusiasm for all the Club to see. His outstanding personality, fortunately, was such that the Club was never in the position of becoming a one-man band. His qualities rather melded with the keeness and abilities of many other workers for the Club contemporary with him; and Belgrave gradually grew from an unimportant and relatively unknown group to a Club with a personality and a future. Unfortunately Bob never lived to see the really great days for he died at the early age of 47, in 1927. The torch was passed to other hands. During his lifetime Bob made many presentations to the Club which still endure. He gave us the "R.W. RICKETTS" Cup for our Junior 220 yards Championship; and the "R.W. RICKETTS" Shield for our 20 miles Walking Championship. The "Belgrave" Cup for the Long distance Walking Championship also came from him; as did also the "DORIS" Shield (named after his daughter) for inter-club competition. He gave of himself in ample measure in his years with the Club; and we still have the permanent records of his generosity in the form of trophies as detailed above to remind us, and to encourage us, and to enthuse us. A.A.H. R.W. Ricketts BOB RICKETTS BOB RICKETTS R.W. RICKETTS Bob Jimmy Belchamber Jimmy Belchamber A.A.H. A.A.H. R.W. Ricketts Cup R.W. items.label: December 1969
items.h: CROSS COUNTRY — Our new Honorary Cross Country Secretary GORDON BISCOE writes
items.sum: New Cross Country Secretary Gordon Biscoe thanks Bill Lucas for 17 years in the post (page 44 says 14) and calls for team effort in the 1969-70 season.
items.s: CROSS COUNTRY — Our new Honorary Cross Country Secretary GORDON BISCOE writes New Cross Country Secretary Gordon Biscoe thanks Bill Lucas for 17 years in the post (page 44 says 14) and calls for team effort in the 1969-70 season. Has Bill Lucas finally gone? Has been the question asked in recent weeks; although I don't think anything was implied by the word "gone". However after 17 years as cross country secretary one cannot just leave the matter there without first expressing our grateful thanks to him for all the efforts, frustrations and pitfalls--endured in that time, as well as the successes and triumphs. (For records please see 17 years of Belgravian! ). He hands over a legacy of hard work which I know will be hard to follow. Since taking on the job, opinions have been expressed to me about a new approach and fresh ideas being a good thing---this might well be true, but whatever fresh approach there might be one fact still remains,---that anything we achieve will only be done with a maximum effort from all concerned. With training schedules now common place at around 80-100 miles (or more!) per week no one will appreciate just being told to train harder---(although if the cap fits-wear it!). But we must expect everyone to be fit at the right time for the right occasion and then having got there to give of his best. We have, for example, already suffered two defeats this season at the hands of City of Stoke A.C., another 'new' club resulting from an amalgamation. This is the modern trend we have to face as well as the 'old enemies!. It is no use saying we have'strength in depth' and leaving it to someone else, for it is obvious there is no room for complacency or passengers. In short we must think and run like a team. Once again in the new year we shall start the string of championship races leading up to the National. If every one does his best (we can ask no more) I'm sure success will be ours again. Gordon Biscoe GORDON BISCOE Bill Lucas Bill Lucas National Cross Country Championships 1970 City of Stoke A.C.

REIGATE PRIORY RELAY----(6 X 2¼M)---November 1st Although we won this event last year this is not one of the most popular races and was consequently given a miss by several of our 'A' team members this year. As a result we had to take 2nd place behind a very in-form Medway team. The almost spring like conditions, very firm going, (most unusual on this course), and the possible shortening of the course explained why no less than seven runners broke Gerry North's record (12:40 in 1968) as well as being equalled by Lionel Mann and Dick Piotrowski. The late arrival of Alan Black and Charlie Walker prevented their getting more favourable runs in the B team, whilst Bob James showed a fine return to fitness after being inactive for so long. In the annual CYCLISTS v HARRIERS cross-country race, held over a tough 5 miles course at Coulsdon on November 8th, Alan Black was the fifth harrier to finish and D. Jardine the eighteenth. Fifty-one harriers and thirty-three cyclists started, and for the first time in several years the cyclists won. VERNE BLOWFIELD, Belgrave's most forward placed runner ever in the National (he was passed by Sydney Wooderson in the closing stages of the 1948 Championship when victory seemed in his grasp) was placed second in a Veterans AC cross-country handicap on October 18th from a mark of 5:30. Wimbledon---October 25th Race No.1. Last year was one of our best ever starts in the opening match, when we finished 10 in 23. This year's event clashed with the new National 6-stage road relay at Crystal Palace and although our best seven men were absent from Wimbledon we expected our rivals to suffer more as a result of the clash. As it happened the National event was a flop and only S.L.H. of our six rivals had a team at the Palace. Strong support was needed to overcome our disadvantage---and strong support we got. Forty-two Belgravians toed the line and ten finished in the first 34 of the 140 finishers to clinch a win that certainly shook our opponents. items.label: December 1969
items.sum: 'Countryman' cross-country column on Charlie Smart's 60th birthday, Bill Lucas stepping down after 14 years (page 42 says 17), new secretary Gordon Biscoe, departures of Peter Morris and Kelly Diprose, the youth talent of Peter Carton and Richard Langley, prospects for the season and criticism of the first National six-stage relay; two Ron Linstead photos.
items.s: A COUNTRYMAN'S JOTTINGS 'Countryman' cross-country column on Charlie Smart's 60th birthday, Bill Lucas stepping down after 14 years (page 42 says 17), new secretary Gordon Biscoe, departures of Peter Morris and Kelly Diprose, the youth talent of Peter Carton and Richard Langley, prospects for the season and criticism of the first National six-stage relay; two Ron Linstead photos. Many happy returns of the day CHARLIE SMART. On December 9th the inimitable Charlie reaches the magnificent age of 60. Nothing special in that alone, perhaps, but couple it with a 5:17 mile and it makes him the Nation's top athlete in his age group. Charlie's long standing training routine of three mid-week visits to the Duke of York's track and Sunday mornings at Arthur Whitehead's has been a feature of the athletics scene for many years. Of late he can be seen regularly in the company of that other "character" and veteran, Joe McDonald. Thanks to each other they are both running better than for some time and Mac will be the first to vouch for the remarkable ability of his 60 years old companion. In his famous eloquent manner Mac described Charlie as "bloody great!". And few would disagree. After 14 years at the helm of Belgrave's cross-country affairs BILL LUCAS has finally decided to call it a day. He had dearly hoped to see the Club win the National during his term of office but three consecutive fourth places was the nearest our teams could get. In this day and age this is frustratingly close so his optimism to the bitter end was fully justified. Bill must have written several thousand cards during those years and spent hundreds of hours of telephone time encouraging, advising, persuading and cajoling runners so that Belgrave could produce a truly representative team on the Saturday. His prescence at virtually every fixture made him a familar figure to athletes from all clubs. Although Bill has relinquished the reins of the cross-country section he still remains one of it's most ardent supporters and already this season he has been seen fervently scribbling down race positions and times. He is still the Club's Hon. Handicapper, of course, so it will be some time before our runners are able to pull a fast one!. With Charlie Smart having preceded Bill Lucas as our cross-country secretary this is an appropriate spot to say something of "new man" Gordon Biscoe. Gordon is already a familar personality to active Belgravians through his former office of Social Hon. Sec. and his present position as Road Running Hon. Sec. If the cross-country men get the attention and service enjoyed by their road running colleagues then they will have much for which to be grateful. Gordon produced several useful runs himself in the "fifties" and has by no means thrown in the towel yet, but the emphasis of his devotion to Belgrave has gradually switched to administration where, if he takes on anything else, he will become a Les Cohen Mark II!. My picture was specially taken by Ron Linstead who had difficulty in getting Gordon's hand just right. Apparently the fingers have been trained to hold only pint beer mugs!. It is with many regrets that we say au revoir to PETER MORRIS who, after 6 months with us, has returned to his native Blackpool. If running was the only thing in life then Peter tells me he would have no hesitation in remaining down South, but personal and business committments oblige him to make the move. During his six months with Belgrave he has given stirling service and has been a popular personality with our runners. We will follow his career with great interest, wishing him the best possible success and should he ever return South again he can be sure of a warm welcome from Belgravians. The prize for the biggest anti-climax of the year goes to the A.A.A., inaugural six-stage National relay at Crystal Palace. Whether there was a strong demand for such a race in the first place is doubtful. Given that there was, then the consultation, planning, publicity and organisation in general was abysmal to say the least. Portsmouth were reputed to be one of the initiators of the six-stage idea, but they had pressed for 3 long and 3 short stages on a point to point course. The decisions on date, distance and venue were taken so arbitrarily that it was no surprise to those in the know to find a meagre NINE TEAMS on the start line. We were in two minds ourselves whether to appear. The presentation "ceremony" was even worse than the debâclé at Leicester earlier this year. Although there were medals this time, there was nowhere suitable to present them. For National championships to be handled in such a way is bad for the sport. They should be very special highly efficent affairs oozing with National "atmosphere". Unless this is done they are in danger of becoming just another race with no one caring very much who wins. Once again we say farewell to New Zealander Kelly Diprose, who is off globe-trotting once again. This popular Kiwi would have been a strong force in our teams if he had been able to stay here long enough to settle down. There are no such things as plans with Kelly so no-one will be surprised if he suddenly turns up at the start of some future race. His main rival over here, though they rarely clashed, was Bob Smith. It is Belgrave's good fortune that Aussie Bob has decided to settle in England---and to prove the point he recently got married and bought a house in Purley!. However, we shall not be reaping any dividends from his move until the Spring as Bob returned to Australia this month to wind up his affairs there (we presume he means business ones!). My picture of Peter Carton (Youth) and Richard Langley (Boy) was taken in Belgrave Hall. One day the backcloth might well be changed to that of a T.V. studio. Peter's progress this last year has been quite exceptional. Training with Bill Curtin induced him to haul himself up to Bill's standard in a matter of months, which was well illustrated by their first and second places in the Surrey County Youths 1500 metres this summer. Peter's efforts have induced others to follow suit and climb to the standards set by Bill Curtin, so instead of having a solitary spearhead and a group of supporting runners down the field we now have Curtin, Carton and John Stow with little separating them and Tony Binda and Les Harris determined to close that gap. If they can stick together for a few years and overcome the inevitable set backs then Belgrave has little to fear from the future. Peter CARTON (left) and Richard LANGLEY (Photo:Ron Linstead) Richard Langley is in an age-group behind Peter and is probably at his best on the track, where he looks a fine prospect. Nevertheless he is no slouch over the country and in 12 months time he should be repeating the present times of our top trio. Our wealth of Youth and Boy talent must eventually throw up a Junior team capable of winning the National. Prospects for the coming major cross-country events are far from clear. There are always ifs and buts of course but will the loss of Diprose, the absence of Smith, the increased business pressure on Thresher and the moving house to Rochester of Geoff North have any serious effect?. It is difficult to say. Geoff's move makes him a near neighbour of Tony Fairclough so a training partnership could be beneficial to both. Mann, O'COnnor and Piotrowski are all going better than ever while Bicourt has been showing excellent early form. Bill Dance is keeping in fine trim up in Huddersfield, and Major and O'Hara are also running into form again. Last, but by no means least, we have that ever-present spearhead Gerry North and the reliable Trevor Hart. There should be enough combinations from that lot to produce a powerful team, but much depends on non-athletic influences---we can only hope that such factors will be kind to us. items.s: G.L.C. - FOUR IN A ROW! Report and result of the G.L.C. cross-country championship at Parliament Hill on 22 November 1969, where Gerry North lost his title to Bob Richardson but Belgrave won the team title for the fourth year running. G.L.C. Cross-Country Championship--November 22nd A few days of steady rain coupled with the venue of Parliament Hill and one immediately thinks of that familar sea of mud and heavy going. This was what Gerry North had in mind too when he set out to defend his individual title for the fourth successive year. However fate was against him this day for on arrival he found Spring-like weather and very firm going. An hour or so later his title had gone to a fit Bob Richardson of Blackheath Harriers. Richardson had opened a gap of about 10 secs on Gerry at the half way stage which he maintained to the end. Lionel Mann showed Pat O'Connor (and everyone else!!) that he means business on the country as well as the road by being our next man home, whilst Trevor Hart was having a few shocks---being pressed in the latter stages by Laurie O'Hara and with Adrian Major, now returning to something like his proper fitness, breathing down his neck.For O'Connor, Fairclough and Kerr it was not their day. Worth noting was Jim Rimmer's good run in his first main outing of the season and Bob Glover's triumph over arch rival Brian Gorman. Although Gerry lost his title he nevertheless led Belgrave to victory again for the fourth successive year. Pos Name Club Time 1. R. Richardson (Blackheath H.) 28:56 2. items.s: Short notes: Ray Middleton's record Postmen's Walk win, Dick Piotrowski seventh in the Wolverton 5 and Lionel Mann eighth in the Rye 10. items.sum: Report and handicap result of the club 7 miles cross-country at Wimbledon on 6 December 1969, won by Lionel Mann for the Blackstaffe shield, with D. Trow winning on handicap; the 19th-placed name (C. Keavey) is overtyped in print and the winning handicap time is printed as 37:66.
items.s: MANN TO MANNING Report and handicap result of the club 7 miles cross-country at Wimbledon on 6 December 1969, won by Lionel Mann for the Blackstaffe shield, with D. Trow winning on handicap; the 19th-placed name (C. Keavey) is overtyped in print and the winning handicap time is printed as 37:66. Club '7'---Wimbledon, December 6th Lionel Mann means business. Up to now he has been regarded as a road man providing useful support over the country, but this year he intends to wear a cross-country label, as of right, and show his heels to those who reckon they make our scoring six. In annexing the "Blackstaffe" shield on a cold and wet December afternoon he showed a useful bunch of runners where to get off and stretched the field to such an extent that it was a quarter of an hour before near-namesake Manning closed them in. (It is rumoured that Charlie is to grow a beard and visit Somerset House!.). Thirty two runners started, getting away this year before the inter-Varsity race crossed their path. Forty eight seconds later a breathless Laurie O'Hara appeared at the start with the unenviable task of chasing the field. After the first lap (14:21) Adrian Major was towing Piotrowski, Mann, Dear and Fairclough round in a tight bunch. A hundred yards back were Black, Rimmer and Smith, and 150 yards further behind was John Kelly---with Laurie O'Hara hard on his heels. Laurie must have covered that first lap a good 8 to 10 seconds faster than the leaders!. With two laps complete it was Mann (28:37) setting the pace from Major, both 10 yards clear of Fairclough with John Dear running the race of his life another 50 yards back. Although still making places, O'Hara paid the penalty for his fast start and dropped about 40 seconds on the leaders. Adrian hung on doggedly during the final circuit but was outrun in the closing stages by the narrow margin of 5 seconds. Tony Fairclough was a none too cheerful third followed closely by an exuberant John Dear who looks set for his best ever Winter. The handicap went to D. Trow, who ran some five minutes faster than anyone thought him capable and who was fast closing on Charlie Walker in the finishing straight. Jim Rimmer ran better than his fourth handicap place suggested so perhaps we will be seeing more of him than usual this season. Handicap: 1. D. Trow 37:66 2. J. Kelly 39:57 3. J. Dear 40:50 4. J. items.sum: Notes on John Bicourt third in the London Colleges League and Tony Fairclough sixth for the Southern Counties at Isleworth.
items.s: Notes on John Bicourt third in the London Colleges League and Tony Fairclough sixth for the Southern Counties at Isleworth. JOHN BICOURT showed fine early season form at Parliament Hill on October 18th when he finished third behind Morrison and Gunstone in the London Colleges League. He also led his team (st. Mary's College) to victory. TONY FAIRCLOUGH produced a fine run for the Southern Counties in this match versus Borough Road College and the R.A.F. at Isleworth on November 5th. He finished sixth in a good class field 51 seconds behind winner M. Absolem and 4 seconds behind M. Barratt.
